Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Visuddhimaggo

The Path of Purification

(Dutiyo bhāgo)

(Second Part)

12. Iddhividhaniddeso

12. Exposition on the Kinds of Psychic Power

Abhiññākathā

Exposition of Direct Knowledge

365. Idāni [M 2.0001][V 2.0001] yāsaṃ lokikābhiññānaṃ vasena ayaṃ samādhibhāvanā abhiññānisaṃsāti vuttā, tā abhiññā sampādetuṃ yasmā pathavīkasiṇādīsu adhigatacatutthajjhānena yoginā yogo kātabbo. Evañhissa sā samādhibhāvanā adhigatānisaṃsā ceva bhavissati thiratarā ca, so adhigatānisaṃsāya thiratarāya samādhibhāvanāya samannāgato sukheneva paññābhāvanaṃ sampādessati. Tasmā abhiññākathaṃ tāva ārabhissāma.

365. Now, this development of concentration was said to have the benefit of direct knowledge by means of those worldly direct knowledges. To bring those direct knowledges to perfection, a yogin who has attained the fourth jhāna in the earth kasiṇa and so on should make an effort. For in doing so, that development of concentration of his will both have its benefit realized and become more stable. And he, endowed with a development of concentration that has its benefit realized and is more stable, will easily bring the development of wisdom to perfection. Therefore, we shall first begin the discourse on direct knowledge.

Bhagavatā hi adhigatacatutthajjhānasamādhīnaṃ kulaputtānaṃ samādhibhāvanānisaṃsadassanatthañceva uttaruttari paṇītapaṇītadhammadesanatthañca [V 2.0002] “so evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte anaṅgaṇe vigatūpakkilese mudubhūte kammaniye ṭhite āneñjappatte iddhividhāya cittaṃ abhinīharati abhininnāmeti. So anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhoti ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.238) nayena iddhividhaṃ, dibbasotadhātuñāṇaṃ, cetopariyañāṇaṃ, pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ, sattānaṃ cutūpapāte ñāṇanti pañca lokikābhiññā vuttā.

For the Blessed One, in order to show the benefits of the development of concentration to sons of good family who have attained the concentration of the fourth jhāna, and to teach progressively more sublime states, declared the five worldly direct knowledges by the method beginning: "When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, workable, steady, and imperturbable, he directs and inclines his mind to the kinds of psychic power. He experiences various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many..." (Dī. Ni. i, 77); namely, the kinds of psychic power, the divine-ear element knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.

Tattha [M 2.0002] ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotītiādikaṃ iddhivikubbanaṃ kātukāmena ādikammikena yoginā odātakasiṇapariyantesu aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu aṭṭha aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā –

Therein, a beginner yogin who wishes to perform the psychic transformation beginning with “having been one, he becomes many,” having produced eight attainments in each of the eight kasiṇas ending with the white kasiṇa—

Kasiṇānulomato, kasiṇapaṭilomato, kasiṇānulomapaṭilomato, jhānānulomato, jhānapaṭilomato, jhānānulomapaṭilomato, jhānukkantikato, kasiṇukkantikato, jhānakasiṇukkantikato, aṅgasaṅkantito, ārammaṇasaṅkantito, aṅgārammaṇasaṅkantito, aṅgavavatthāpanato, ārammaṇavavatthāpanatoti.

By forward order of the kasiṇas, by reverse order of the kasiṇas, by forward and reverse order of the kasiṇas; by forward order of the jhānas, by reverse order of the jhānas, by forward and reverse order of the jhānas; by skipping the jhānas, by skipping the kasiṇas, by skipping the jhānas and kasiṇas; by transition of the factors, by transition of the object, by transition of the factors and object; by defining the factors, and by defining the object.

Imehi cuddasahi ākārehi cittaṃ paridametabbaṃ.

The mind should be tamed by means of these fourteen modes.

366. Katamaṃ panettha kasiṇānulomaṃ…pe… katamaṃ ārammaṇavavatthāpananti. Idha bhikkhu pathavīkasiṇe jhānaṃ samāpajjati, tato āpokasiṇeti evaṃ paṭipāṭiyā aṭṭhasu kasiṇesu satakkhattumpi sahassakkhattumpi samāpajjati, idaṃ kasiṇānulomaṃ nāma.

366. Herein, what is the forward order of the kasiṇas? … and what is the defining of the object? Here, a bhikkhu attains jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, then in the water kasiṇa; thus in sequence he attains jhāna in the eight kasiṇas a hundred times, or even a thousand times. This is called the forward order of the kasiṇas.

Odātakasiṇato pana paṭṭhāya tatheva paṭilomakkamena samāpajjanaṃ kasiṇapaṭilomaṃ nāma.

Furthermore, attaining in the same way in reverse order, starting from the white kasiṇa, is called the reverse order of the kasiṇas.

Pathavīkasiṇato paṭṭhāya yāva odātakasiṇaṃ, odātakasiṇatopi paṭṭhāya yāva pathavīkasiṇanti evaṃ anulomapaṭilomavasena punappunaṃ samāpajjanaṃ kasiṇānulomapaṭilomaṃ nāma.

Repeatedly attaining by way of forward and reverse order—starting from the earth kasiṇa up to the white kasiṇa, and starting from the white kasiṇa up to the earth kasiṇa—is called the forward and reverse order of the kasiṇas.

Paṭhamajjhānato pana paṭṭhāya paṭipāṭiyā yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ, tāva punappunaṃ samāpajjanaṃ jhānānulomaṃ nāma.

Furthermore, repeatedly attaining in sequence, starting from the first jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is called the forward order of the jhānas.

Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanato [V 2.0003] paṭṭhāya yāva paṭhamajjhānaṃ, tāva punappunaṃ samāpajjanaṃ jhānapaṭilomaṃ nāma.

Repeatedly attaining, starting from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception up to the first jhāna, is called the reverse order of the jhānas.

Paṭhamajjhānato paṭṭhāya yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanato paṭṭhāya yāva paṭhamajjhānanti evaṃ anulomapaṭilomavasena punappunaṃ samāpajjanaṃ jhānānulomapaṭilomaṃ nāma.

Repeatedly attaining by way of forward and reverse order—starting from the first jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and starting from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception up to the first jhāna—is called the forward and reverse order of the jhānas.

Pathavīkasiṇe pana paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tattheva tatiyaṃ samāpajjati, tato tadeva ugghāṭetvā ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, tato ākiñcaññāyatananti [M 2.0003] evaṃ kasiṇaṃ anukkamitvā jhānasseva ekantarikabhāvena ukkamanaṃ jhānukkantikaṃ nāma. Evaṃ āpokasiṇādimūlikāpi yojanā kātabbā.

Furthermore, having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, one attains the third jhāna in that same kasiṇa. Then, having removed that very kasiṇa sign, one attains the base of infinite space, and then the base of nothingness. Thus, without skipping the kasiṇa, the skipping of the jhānas alone, leaving one in between, is called jhāna-skipping. In this way, the application should be made with the water kasiṇa, etc., as the basis.

Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā puna tadeva tejokasiṇe, tato nīlakasiṇe, tato lohitakasiṇeti iminā nayena jhānaṃ anukkamitvā kasiṇasseva ekantarikabhāvena ukkamanaṃ kasiṇukkantikaṃ nāma.

Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, one again attains that same jhāna in the fire kasiṇa, then in the blue kasiṇa, then in the red kasiṇa. In this way, without skipping the jhāna, the skipping of the kasiṇas alone, leaving one in between, is called kasiṇa-skipping.

Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tato tejokasiṇe tatiyaṃ, nīlakasiṇaṃ ugghāṭetvā ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, lohitakasiṇato ākiñcaññāyatananti iminā nayena jhānassa ceva kasiṇassa ca ukkamanaṃ jhānakasiṇukkantikaṃ nāma.

Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, then the third jhāna in the fire kasiṇa; having removed the blue kasiṇa sign, the base of infinite space; from the red kasiṇa, the base of nothingness. In this way, the skipping of both jhāna and kasiṇa is called jhāna-and-kasiṇa-skipping.

Pathavīkasiṇe pana paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tattheva itaresampi samāpajjanaṃ aṅgasaṅkantikaṃ nāma.

Furthermore, having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, attaining the other jhānas in that same kasiṇa is called factor-transition.

Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tadeva āpokasiṇe…pe… tadeva odātakasiṇeti evaṃ sabbakasiṇesu ekasseva jhānassa samāpajjanaṃ ārammaṇasaṅkantikaṃ nāma.

Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, and then that same jhāna in the water kasiṇa… and that same jhāna in the white kasiṇa—thus, attaining one and the same jhāna in all the kasiṇas is called object-transition.

Pathavīkasiṇe paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā āpokasiṇe dutiyaṃ, tejokasiṇe tatiyaṃ, vāyokasiṇe catutthaṃ, nīlakasiṇaṃ ugghāṭetvā ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, pītakasiṇato viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ[V 2.0004], lohitakasiṇato ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ, odātakasiṇato nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti evaṃ ekantarikavasena aṅgānañca ārammaṇānañca saṅkamanaṃ aṅgārammaṇasaṅkantikaṃ nāma.

Having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, one attains the second in the water kasiṇa, the third in the fire kasiṇa, the fourth in the air kasiṇa; having removed the blue kasiṇa sign, the base of infinite space; from the yellow kasiṇa, the base of infinite consciousness; from the red kasiṇa, the base of nothingness; from the white kasiṇa, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Thus, the transition of both factors and objects is called factor-and-object-transition.

Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ pana pañcaṅgikanti vavatthapetvā dutiyaṃ tivaṅgikaṃ, tatiyaṃ duvaṅgikaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti evaṃ jhānaṅgamattasseva vavatthāpanaṃ aṅgavavatthāpanaṃ nāma.

Furthermore, having defined the first jhāna as five-factored, the second as three-factored, the third as two-factored, and likewise the fourth, the base of infinite space… up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as two-factored—thus, the defining of the jhāna factors alone is called factor-defining.

Tathā idaṃ pathavīkasiṇanti vavatthapetvā idaṃ āpokasiṇaṃ…pe… idaṃ odātakasiṇanti evaṃ ārammaṇamattasseva vavatthāpanaṃ ārammaṇavavatthāpanaṃ nāma[M 2.0004]. Aṅgārammaṇavavatthāpanampi eke icchanti. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana anāgatattā addhā taṃ bhāvanāmukhaṃ na hoti.

Similarly, having established, 'This is the earth kasiṇa,' 'This is the water kasiṇa,'... up to... 'This is the white kasiṇa'—thus, the establishing of the object alone is called 'establishing the object' (ārammaṇavavatthāpana). Some also desire the establishing of factors and objects (aṅgārammaṇavavatthāpana). However, since this is not found in the Commentaries, it is certainly not an entrance to the development of meditation.

367. Imehi pana cuddasahi ākārehi cittaṃ aparidametvā pubbe abhāvitabhāvano ādikammiko yogāvacaro iddhivikubbanaṃ sampādessatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ādikammikassa hi kasiṇaparikammampi bhāro, satesu sahassesu vā ekova sakkoti. Katakasiṇaparikammassa nimittuppādanaṃ bhāro, satesu sahassesu vā ekova sakkoti. Uppanne nimitte taṃ vaḍḍhetvā appanādhigamo bhāro, satesu sahassesu vā ekova sakkoti. Adhigatappanassa cuddasahākārehi cittaparidamanaṃ bhāro, satesu sahassesu vā ekova sakkoti. Cuddasahākārehi paridamitacittassāpi iddhivikubbanaṃ nāma bhāro, satesu sahassesu vā ekova sakkoti. Vikubbanappattassāpi khippanisantibhāvo nāma bhāro, satesu sahassesu vā ekova khippanisantī hoti. Therambatthale mahārohaṇaguttattherassa gilānupaṭṭhānaṃ āgatesu tiṃsamattesu iddhimantasahassesu upasampadāya aṭṭhavassiko rakkhitatthero viya. Tassānubhāvo pathavīkasiṇaniddese (visuddhi. 1.78 ādayo) vuttoyeva. Taṃ panassānubhāvaṃ disvā thero āha “āvuso, sace rakkhito nābhavissa sabbe garahappattā assāma ‘nāgarājānaṃ rakkhituṃ nāsakkhiṃsū’ti. Tasmā attanā gahetvā vicaritabbaṃ āvudhaṃ nāma malaṃ sodhetvāva gahetvā vicarituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Te therassa ovāde ṭhatvā tiṃsasahassāpi bhikkhū khippanisantino ahesuṃ.

367. Furthermore, for a beginner yogin who has not tamed the mind in these fourteen ways and has not previously developed meditation, that he should accomplish psychic transformation—such a case does not exist. For a beginner, even the preliminary work on the kasiṇa is a burden; only one in hundreds or thousands is able. For one who has completed the preliminary work on the kasiṇa, producing the sign is a burden; only one in hundreds or thousands is able. When the sign has arisen, developing it to attain absorption is a burden; only one in hundreds or thousands is able. For one who has attained absorption, taming the mind in these fourteen ways is a burden; only one in hundreds or thousands is able. Even for one whose mind has been tamed in these fourteen ways, what is called psychic transformation is a burden; only one in hundreds or thousands is able. Even for one who has attained psychic transformation, what is called the state of quick proficiency is a burden; only one in hundreds or thousands becomes quickly proficient. It is like the Elder Rakkhiṭa, who was of eight years' standing since higher ordination, among some thirty thousand bhikkhus with psychic power who had come to attend to the ailing Elder Mahārohaṇagutta at Therambatthala. His power has been told in the exposition on the earth kasiṇa. Seeing his power, the Elder said: 'Venerable sirs, if Rakkhiṭa had not been here, we would all have incurred blame, it being said, "They were not able to protect the nāga king." Therefore, a weapon that is to be carried about should be taken up and carried about only after cleaning off the rust.' Having stood in the Elder's instruction, all thirty thousand bhikkhus became quickly proficient.

Khippanisantiyāpi [V 2.0005] ca sati parassa patiṭṭhābhāvo bhāro, satesu sahassesu vā ekova hoti, giribhaṇḍavāhanapūjāya mārena aṅgāravasse pavattite ākāse pathaviṃ māpetvā aṅgāravassaparittārako thero viya.

And even when there is quick proficiency, being a refuge for others is a burden; only one in hundreds or thousands becomes so, like the elder who, at the Giribhaṇḍavāhana festival, when Māra caused a rain of embers, created earth in the sky and became a protector from that rain of embers.

Balavapubbayogānaṃ pana buddhapaccekabuddhaaggasāvakādīnaṃ vināpi iminā vuttappakārena bhāvanānukkamena arahattapaṭilābheneva idañca iddhivikubbanaṃ aññe [M 2.0005] ca paṭisambhidādibhedā guṇā ijjhanti. Tasmā yathā piḷandhanavikatiṃ kattukāmo suvaṇṇakāro aggidhamanādīhi suvaṇṇaṃ muduṃ kammaññaṃ katvāva karoti, yathā ca bhājanavikatiṃ kattukāmo kumbhakāro mattikaṃ suparimadditaṃ muduṃ katvā karoti, evameva ādikammikena imehi cuddasahākārehi cittaṃ paridametvā chandasīsacittasīsavīriyasīsavīmaṃsāsīsasamāpajjanavasena ceva āvajjanādivasībhāvavasena ca muduṃ kammaññaṃ katvā iddhividhāya yogo karaṇīyo. Pubbahetusampannena pana kasiṇesu catutthajjhānamatte ciṇṇavasināpi kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Yathā panettha yogo kātabbo, taṃ vidhiṃ dassento bhagavā “so evaṃ samāhite citte”tiādimāha.

However, for those of powerful prior practice, such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, and others, this psychic transformation and other qualities, such as the various kinds of analytical knowledge, are accomplished simply by the attainment of Arahantship, even without this aforesaid sequence of development. Therefore, just as a goldsmith who wishes to make a special kind of ornament does so only after making the gold soft and workable by smelting with fire and so on; and just as a potter who wishes to make a special kind of vessel does so only after making the clay well-kneaded and soft; so too, a beginner should make the exertion for the kinds of psychic power after having tamed the mind in these fourteen ways and made it soft and workable, both by means of entering absorption with zeal, mind, effort, or investigation as foremost, and by means of the state of mastery beginning with adverting. But for one endowed with a previous cause, who has practiced mastery in only the fourth jhāna in the kasiṇas, it is also fitting to do so. In order to show how the exertion should be made in this matter, the Blessed One said, 'He, with a mind thus concentrated...' and so on.

368. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷinayānusāreneva vinicchayakathā. Tattha soti so adhigatacatutthajjhāno yogī. Evanti catutthajjhānakkamanidassanametaṃ. Iminā paṭhamajjhānādhigamādinā kamena catutthajjhānaṃ paṭilabhitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Samāhiteti iminā catutthajjhānasamādhinā samāhite. Citteti rūpāvacaracitte. Parisuddhetiādīsu pana upekkhāsatipārisuddhibhāvena parisuddhe. Parisuddhattāyeva pariyodāte, pabhassareti vuttaṃ hoti. Sukhādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ ghātena vihatarāgādiaṅgaṇattā anaṅgaṇe. Anaṅgaṇattāyeva vigatūpakkilese. Aṅgaṇena hi taṃ cittaṃ upakkilissati. Subhāvitattā mudubhūte, vasībhāvappatteti vuttaṃ hoti. Vase vattamānaṃ hi cittaṃ mudunti vuccati. Muduttāyeva ca kammaniye, kammakkhame kammayoggeti vuttaṃ hoti. Muduṃ hi cittaṃ kammaniyaṃ hoti sudantamiva suvaṇṇaṃ, tañca ubhayampi subhāvitattāyevāti. Yathāha “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ bhāvitaṃ bahulīkataṃ muduñca hoti kammaniyañca, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, citta”nti (a. ni. 1.22).

368. Herein, this is the definitive explanation according to the method of the Pāli text. Therein, 'he' (so) is that yogin who has attained the fourth jhāna. 'Thus' (evaṃ) is an indication of the sequence for the fourth jhāna; that is to say, 'having attained the fourth jhāna by this sequence beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna.' 'Concentrated' (samāhite) means concentrated by this concentration of the fourth jhāna. 'Mind' (citte) means the fine-material sphere mind. As for 'purified' (parisuddhe) and so on, it is purified by the state of purity of mindfulness through equanimity. Because it is purified, it is said to be 'bright' (pariyodāte) and 'luminous' (pabhassare). Because of the destruction of the conditions for pleasure and so on, it is 'stainless' (anaṅgaṇe), due to having its stains of lust and so on removed. Because it is stainless, it is 'without imperfections' (vigatūpakkilese); for that mind is corrupted by a stain. Because it is well-developed, it has 'become soft' (mudubhūte), meaning it has attained mastery. For a mind that functions under one's control is called 'soft' (mudu). And because it is soft, it is 'workable' (kammaniye), that is, 'capable of work' (kammakkhame), 'fit for work' (kammayogge). For a soft mind is workable like well-refined gold, and both are so because they are well-developed. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, I do not see a single other thing that, when developed and cultivated, is as soft and workable as this, bhikkhus: the mind' (A I 9).

Etesu parisuddhabhāvādīsu ṭhitattā ṭhite. Ṭhitattāyeva āneñjappatte, acale niriñjaneti vuttaṃ hoti. Mudukammaññabhāvena vā attano vase ṭhitattā ṭhite. Saddhādīhi pariggahitattā āneñjappatte[V 2.0006]. Saddhāpariggahitaṃ hi cittaṃ assaddhiyena na iñjati. Vīriyapariggahitaṃ kosajjena na iñjati. Satipariggahitaṃ pamādena na iñjati. Samādhipariggahitaṃ uddhaccena na iñjati[M 2.0006]. Paññāpariggahitaṃ avijjāya na iñjati. Obhāsagataṃ kilesandhakārena na iñjati. Imehi chahi dhammehi pariggahitaṃ āneñjappattaṃ hoti. Evaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ cittaṃ abhinīhārakkhamaṃ hoti abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhiññāsacchikiriyāya.

Because it is established in these states of purity and so on, it is 'established' (ṭhite). Because it is established, it has 'attained the imperturbable' (āneñjappatte), meaning it is 'unshakeable' (acale), 'unwavering' (niriñjane). Or, because it is established under its own control due to its softness and workability, it is 'established' (ṭhite). Because it is supported by faith and so on, it has 'attained the imperturbable' (āneñjappatte). For a mind supported by faith is not shaken by lack of faith. A mind supported by energy is not shaken by laziness. A mind supported by mindfulness is not shaken by heedlessness. A mind supported by concentration is not shaken by restlessness. A mind supported by wisdom is not shaken by ignorance. A mind that has attained light is not shaken by the darkness of the defilements. Supported by these six things, it attains the imperturbable. Thus, a mind endowed with eight factors is capable of being directed to the realization by direct knowledge of things to be realized by direct knowledge.

Aparo nayo, catutthajjhānasamādhinā samāhite. Nīvaraṇadūrabhāvena parisuddhe. Vitakkādisamatikkamena pariyodāte. Jhānapaṭilābhapaccayānaṃ icchāvacarānaṃ abhāvena anaṅgaṇe. Abhijjhādīnaṃ cittassa upakkilesānaṃ vigamena vigatūpakkilese. Ubhayampi cetaṃ anaṅgaṇasuttavatthasuttānusārena (ma. ni. 1.57 ādayo) veditabbaṃ. Vasippattiyā mudubhūte. Iddhipādabhāvūpagamena kammaniye. Bhāvanāpāripūriyā paṇītabhāvūpagamena ṭhite āneñjappatte. Yathā āneñjappattaṃ hoti, evaṃ ṭhiteti attho. Evampi aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ cittaṃ abhinīhārakkhamaṃ hoti abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhiññāsacchikiriyāya pādakaṃ padaṭṭhānabhūtanti.

Another method: When the mind is composed with the concentration of the fourth jhāna, it is purified by being remote from the hindrances; cleansed by transcending thought-conception and so on; unblemished due to the absence of base desires that are a condition for the attainment of jhāna; and free from corruptions due to the removal of the mind's corruptions, such as covetousness. Both of these should be understood in accordance with the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta and the Vatthasutta. When it has become pliable through the attainment of mastery; workable through having reached the state of a basis of psychic power; steady and having attained the imperturbable through the perfection of development and the attainment of the sublime state. The meaning is: as it attains the imperturbable, so it is steady. Thus, a mind endowed with these eight factors is fit to be directed, being a foundation and a basis for the realization by direct knowledge of those things that are to be realized by direct knowledge.

Dasaiddhikathā

An Exposition on the Ten Powers

369. Iddhividhāya cittaṃ abhinīharati abhininnāmetīti ettha ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi, nipphattiatthena paṭilābhaṭṭhena cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yañhi nipphajjati paṭilabbhati ca, taṃ ijjhatīti vuccati. Yathāha “kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa, tassa cetaṃ samijjhatī”ti (su. ni. 772). Tathā “nekkhammaṃ ijjhatīti iddhi, paṭiharatīti pāṭihāriyaṃ. Arahattamaggo ijjhatīti iddhi, paṭiharatīti pāṭihāriya”nti (paṭi. ma. 3.32).

369. In the phrase 'one directs and inclines the mind towards the various kinds of psychic power,' iddhi is so called in the sense of succeeding; that is, it is said to be in the sense of accomplishment and attainment. For whatever is accomplished and attained, that is said to 'succeed' (ijjhati). As it is said: 'For one desiring a sensual pleasure, if that succeeds for him' (Su.ni. 772). Likewise: 'Renunciation succeeds—this is iddhi; it removes the opposite—this is a marvel (pāṭihāriya). The path to Arahantship succeeds—this is iddhi; it removes the opposite—this is a marvel (pāṭihāriya)' (Paṭi. Ma. 3.32).

Aparo nayo, ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi. Upāyasampadāyetamadhivacanaṃ. Upāyasampadā hi ijjhati adhippetaphalappasavanato. Yathāha – “ayaṃ kho citto gahapati sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo, sace paṇidahissati ‘anāgatamaddhānaṃ rājā assaṃ cakkavattī’ti, tassa kho ayaṃ ijjhissati sīlavato cetopaṇidhi visuddhattā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.352).

Another method: Iddhi is so called in the sense of causing to succeed. This is a designation for the accomplishment of the means. For the accomplishment of the means 'succeeds' in that it produces the desired result. As it is said: 'This householder Citta is virtuous, of good character. If he should make an aspiration, "May I in the future be a wheel-turning monarch," this mental aspiration of his, being virtuous, will succeed on account of its purity' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.352).

Aparo nayo, etāya sattā ijjhantīti iddhi. Ijjhantīti iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti [V 2.0007] vuttaṃ hoti. Sā dasavidhā. Yathāha “kati iddhiyoti dasa iddhiyo”. Puna caparaṃ āha “katamā dasa iddhiyo[M 2.0007]? Adhiṭṭhānā iddhi, vikubbanā iddhi, manomayā iddhi, ñāṇavipphārā iddhi, samādhivipphārā iddhi, ariyā iddhi, kammavipākajā iddhi, puññavato iddhi, vijjāmayā iddhi, tattha tattha sammāpayogapaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.9).

Another method: It is called iddhi because 'by means of it, beings succeed' (ijjanti). 'They succeed' means they become prosperous, developed, and have reached excellence. It is tenfold. As it is said: 'How many powers (iddhi) are there? There are ten powers.' And further: 'What are the ten powers? The power of determination, the power of transformation, the mind-made power, the power of the pervasion of knowledge, the power of the pervasion of concentration, the noble power, the power born from the result of kamma, the power of a meritorious one, the power consisting of lore, and the power of succeeding in various instances due to right application' (Paṭi. Ma. 3.9).

370. Tattha “pakatiyā eko bahukaṃ āvajjati. Sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā satasahassaṃ vā āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti ‘bahuko homī’”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.10) evaṃ vibhajitvā dassitā iddhi adhiṭṭhānavasena nipphannattā adhiṭṭhānā iddhi nāma.

370. Therein: 'Being one by nature, one adverts to many. Having adverted to a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand, one determines with knowledge, "I shall become many"' (Paṭi. Ma. 3.10). The power shown and analyzed in this way, being accomplished by means of determination, is called the power of determination (adhiṭṭhānā-iddhi).

371. “So pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā kumārakavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti nāgavaṇṇaṃ vā…pe… vividhampi senābyūhaṃ dassetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.13) evaṃ āgatā iddhi pakativaṇṇavijahanavikāravasena pavattattā vikubbanā iddhi nāma.

371. 'Having abandoned one’s natural appearance, one displays the appearance of a youth, or the appearance of a nāga… or even displays a diverse military formation' (Paṭi. Ma. 3.13). The power that is presented in this way, because it proceeds by means of abandoning the natural appearance and by way of alteration, is called the power of transformation (vikubbanā-iddhi).

372. “Idha bhikkhu imamhā kāyā aññaṃ kāyaṃ abhinimmināti rūpiṃ manomaya”nti (paṭi. ma. 3.14) iminā nayena āgatā iddhi sarīrabbhantare aññasseva manomayassa sarīrassa nipphattivasena pavattattā manomayā iddhi nāma.

372. 'Here, a bhikkhu creates from this body another body, having material form, mind-made' (Paṭi. Ma. 3.14). The power that is presented in this way, because it proceeds by means of the accomplishment of another, separate mind-made body within the physical body, is called the mind-made power (manomayā-iddhi).

373. Ñāṇuppattito pana pubbe vā pacchā vā taṃkhaṇe vā ñāṇānubhāvanibbatto viseso ñāṇavipphārā iddhi nāma. Vuttañhetaṃ – “aniccānupassanāya niccasaññāya pahānaṭṭho ijjhatīti ñāṇavipphārā iddhi…pe… arahattamaggena sabbakilesānaṃ pahānaṭṭho ijjhatīti ñāṇavipphārā iddhi. Āyasmato bākkulassa ñāṇavipphārā iddhi. Āyasmato saṃkiccassa ñāṇavipphārā iddhi. Āyasmato bhūtapālassa ñāṇavipphārā iddhī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.15).

373. Now, the special quality produced by the power of knowledge—whether before, after, or at the very moment of the arising of knowledge—is called the power of the pervasion of knowledge (ñāṇavipphārā-iddhi). For this has been said: 'Through the contemplation of impermanence, the abandoning of the perception of permanence is accomplished; this is the power of the pervasion of knowledge… Through the path to Arahantship, the abandoning of all defilements is accomplished; this is the power of the pervasion of knowledge. The power of the pervasion of knowledge of the Venerable Bākkula. The power of the pervasion of knowledge of the Venerable Saṃkicca. The power of the pervasion of knowledge of the Venerable Bhūtapāla' (Paṭi. Ma. 3.15).

Tattha āyasmā bākkulo daharova maṅgaladivase nadiyā nhāpiyamāno dhātiyā pamādena sote patito. Tamenaṃ maccho gilitvā bārāṇasītitthaṃ agamāsi. Tatra taṃ macchabandho gahetvā seṭṭhibhariyāya vikkiṇi. Sā macche sinehaṃ uppādetvā ahameva naṃ pacissāmīti phālentī macchakucchiyaṃ suvaṇṇabimbaṃ viya dārakaṃ disvā putto me laddhoti somanassajātā ahosi. Iti macchakucchiyaṃ arogabhāvo āyasmato bākkulassa [M 2.0008] pacchimabhavikassa tena attabhāvena paṭilabhitabbaarahattamaggañāṇānubhāvena [V 2.0008] nibbattattā ñāṇavipphārā iddhi nāma. Vatthu pana vitthārena kathetabbaṃ.

Therein, the Venerable Bākkula, while still a young boy, was being bathed in the river on an auspicious day when, due to his nurse’s negligence, he fell into the current. A fish swallowed him and went to the landing place at Bārāṇasī. There, a fisherman caught that fish and sold it to a treasurer's wife. She, developing affection for the fish and thinking, 'I myself will cook it,' was cutting it open when she saw in the fish’s belly a child like a golden image. Overjoyed, she thought, 'I have gained a son!' Thus, the state of being without illness in the fish’s belly, on the part of the Venerable Bākkula, who was in his final existence, is called the power of the pervasion of knowledge, because it was produced by the power of the Arahant path-knowledge that was to be attained in that very existence. The story, however, should be told in detail.

Saṃkiccattherassa pana gabbhagatasseva mātā kālamakāsi. Tassā citakaṃ āropetvā sūlehi vijjhitvā jhāpiyamānāya dārako sūlakoṭiyā akkhikūṭe pahāraṃ labhitvā saddaṃ akāsi. Tato dārako jīvatīti otāretvā kucchiṃ phāletvā dārakaṃ ayyikāya adaṃsu. So tāya paṭijaggito vuddhimanvāya pabbajitvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Iti vuttanayeneva dārucitakāya arogabhāvo āyasmato saṃkiccassa ñāṇavipphārā iddhi nāma.

Furthermore, in the case of the Elder Saṃkicca, his mother passed away while he was still in the womb. As her body was being cremated, having been placed on a pyre and pierced with stakes, the child was struck on the corner of the eye by the tip of a stake and made a sound. Then, thinking, 'The child is alive,' they took her down, cut open her belly, and gave the child to his grandmother. Cared for by her, he grew up, went forth, and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Thus, in the manner already described, the state of being without illness on the wooden pyre is called the power of the pervasion of knowledge of the Venerable Saṃkicca.

Bhūtapāladārakassa pana pitā rājagahe daliddamanusso. So dārūnaṃ atthāya sakaṭena aṭaviṃ gantvā dārubhāraṃ katvā sāyaṃ nagaradvārasamīpaṃ patto. Athassa goṇā yugaṃ ossajjitvā nagaraṃ pavisiṃsu. So sakaṭamūle puttakaṃ nisīdāpetvā goṇānaṃ anupadaṃ gacchanto nagarameva pāvisi. Tassa anikkhantasseva dvāraṃ pihitaṃ. Dārakassa vāḷayakkhānucaritepi bahinagare tiyāmarattiṃ arogabhāvo vuttanayeneva ñāṇavipphārā iddhi nāma. Vatthu pana vitthāretabbaṃ.

Furthermore, the father of the boy Bhūtapāla was a poor man in Rājagaha. He went to the forest with a cart for the sake of wood, and having made a load of wood, he arrived near the city gate in the evening. Then his oxen, having cast off their yoke, entered the city. He, having made his young son sit at the base of the cart, followed the tracks of the oxen and entered the city himself. Before he could exit, the gate was closed. The boy's state of being unharmed for the three watches of the night outside the city, in a place frequented by fierce yakkhas, is called the iddhi of knowledge-pervasion, in the manner already described. The story, however, should be elaborated.

374. Samādhito pubbe vā pacchā vā taṃkhaṇe vā samathānubhāvanibbatto viseso samādhivipphārā iddhi. Vuttañhetaṃ “paṭhamajjhānena nīvaraṇānaṃ pahānaṭṭho ijjhatīti samādhivipphārā iddhi…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyā ākiñcaññāyatanasaññāya pahānaṭṭho ijjhatīti samādhivipphārā iddhi. Āyasmato sāriputtassa samādhivipphārā iddhi, āyasmato sañjīvassa, āyasmato khāṇukoṇḍaññassa, uttarāya upāsikāya, sāmāvatiyā upāsikāya samādhivipphārā iddhī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.16).

374. The distinction that arises from the power of serenity—whether before, after, or at the very moment of concentration—is the supernormal power of concentration-pervasion. For it is said: “Through the first jhāna, the state of abandoning the hindrances is accomplished—this is the supernormal power of concentration-pervasion… up to… through the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the state of abandoning the perception of the base of nothingness is accomplished—this is the supernormal power of concentration-pervasion. The Venerable Sāriputta’s supernormal power of concentration-pervasion, the Venerable Sañjīva’s, the Venerable Khāṇukoṇḍañña’s, the laywoman Uttarā’s, and the laywoman Sāmāvatī’s supernormal power of concentration-pervasion” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.16).

Tattha yadā āyasmato sāriputtassa mahāmoggallānattherena saddhiṃ kapotakandarāyaṃ viharato juṇhāya rattiyā navoropitehi kesehi ajjhokāse nisinnassa eko duṭṭhayakkho sahāyakena yakkhena vāriyamānopi sīse pahāramadāsi. Yassa meghassa viya gajjato [M 2.0009] saddo ahosi. Tadā thero tassa paharaṇasamaye samāpattiṃ appesi. Athassa tena pahārena na koci ābādho ahosi[V 2.0009]. Ayaṃ tassāyasmato samādhivipphārā iddhi. Vatthu pana udāne (udā. 34) āgatameva.

Therein, when the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling in Kapotakandara with the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, on a moonlit night, while he was sitting in the open with his hair freshly shaven, a wicked yakkha, though being restrained by his companion yakkha, gave him a blow on the head. The sound of it was like that of a thundering cloud. At that moment, at the time of the blow, the Elder entered into an attainment. Then, from that blow, no affliction whatsoever arose for him. This was that Venerable One’s supernormal power of concentration-pervasion. The story, however, is found in the Udāna (Udāna 34).

Sañjīvattheraṃ pana nirodhasamāpannaṃ kālakatoti sallakkhetvā gopālakādayo tiṇakaṭṭhagomayāni saṅkaḍḍhetvā aggiṃ adaṃsu. Therassa cīvare aṃsumattampi najjhāyittha. Ayamassa anupubbasamāpattivasena pavattasamathānubhāvanibbattattā samādhivipphārā iddhi. Vatthu pana sutte (ma. ni. 1.507) āgatameva.

Furthermore, cowherds and others, thinking that the Elder Sañjīva, who was absorbed in the attainment of cessation, had passed away, gathered grass, sticks, and cow dung and set it on fire. Not even a thread of the Elder’s robe was burned. This was his supernormal power of concentration-pervasion, which arose from the power of serenity that occurred by means of the successive attainments. The story, however, is found in the Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 1.507).

Khāṇukoṇḍaññatthero pana pakatiyāva samāpattibahulo. So aññatarasmiṃ araññe rattiṃ samāpattiṃ appetvā nisīdi. Pañcasatā corā bhaṇḍakaṃ thenetvā gacchantā “idāni amhākaṃ anupathaṃ āgacchantā natthī”ti vissamitukāmā bhaṇḍakaṃ oropayamānā “khāṇuko aya”nti maññamānā therasseva upari sabbabhaṇḍakāni ṭhapesuṃ. Tesaṃ vissamitvā gacchantānaṃ paṭhamaṃ ṭhapitabhaṇḍakassa gahaṇakāle kālaparicchedavasena thero vuṭṭhāsi. Te therassa calanākāraṃ disvā bhītā viraviṃsu. Thero “mā bhāyittha upāsakā, bhikkhu aha”nti āha. Te āgantvā vanditvā theragatena pasādena pabbajitvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.1). Ayamettha pañcahi bhaṇḍakasatehi ajjhotthaṭassa therassa ābādhābhāvo samādhivipphārā iddhi.

The Elder Khāṇukoṇḍañña, furthermore, was by nature one who frequently entered meditative attainments. In a certain forest, he entered an attainment at night and sat down. Five hundred thieves, having stolen goods and departed, thinking, “Now there are no others following our path,” and wishing to rest, began to unload their goods. Thinking, “This is a tree stump,” they placed all the goods on top of the Elder himself. When they had rested and were about to depart, at the time of taking up the bundle that had been placed first, the Elder emerged from his attainment in accordance with his pre-determination of time. Seeing the Elder’s movement, they were terrified and cried out. The Elder said, “Do not be afraid, lay followers, I am a monk.” They approached, paid homage, and with faith in the Elder, they went forth and attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (Dhammapada Aṭṭhakathā 1.1). Herein, the Elder’s freedom from affliction, though covered by five hundred bundles of goods, was the supernormal power of concentration-pervasion.

Uttarā pana upāsikā puṇṇaseṭṭhissa dhītā. Tassā sirimā nāma gaṇikā issāpakatā tattatelakaṭāhaṃ sīse āsiñci. Uttarā taṃkhaṇaññeva mettaṃ samāpajji. Telaṃ pokkharapattato udakabindu viya vivaṭṭamānaṃ agamāsi. Ayamassā samādhivipphārā iddhi. Vatthu pana vitthāretabbaṃ.

Furthermore, the laywoman Uttarā was the daughter of the merchant Puṇṇa. A courtesan named Sirimā, overcome by jealousy, poured a pan of boiling oil on her head. At that very moment, Uttarā entered into an attainment of loving-kindness. The oil rolled off like a drop of water from a lotus leaf. This was her supernormal power of concentration-pervasion. The story, however, should be elaborated.

Sāmāvatī nāma udenassa rañño aggamahesī. Māgaṇḍiyabrāhmaṇo attano dhītāya aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ patthayamāno tassā vīṇāya āsīvisaṃ [M 2.0010] pakkhipāpetvā rājānaṃ āha “mahārāja, sāmāvatī taṃ māretukāmā vīṇāya āsīvisaṃ gahetvā pariharatī”ti. Rājā taṃ disvā kupito sāmāvatiṃ vadhissāmīti dhanuṃ āropetvā visapītaṃ khurappaṃ sannayhi. Sāmāvatī saparivārā rājānaṃ mettāya phari. Rājā neva saraṃ khipituṃ na oropetuṃ sakkonto vedhamāno aṭṭhāsi. Tato naṃ devī āha “kiṃ, mahārāja, kilamasī”ti? “Āma kilamāmī”ti. “Tena [V 2.0010] hi dhanuṃ oropehī”ti. Saro rañño pādamūleyeva pati. Tato naṃ devī “mahārāja, appaduṭṭhassa nappadussitabba”nti ovadi. Iti rañño saraṃ muñcituṃ avisahanabhāvo sāmāvatiyā upāsikāya samādhivipphārā iddhīti.

Sāmāvatī was the chief queen of King Udena. The brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, desiring the position of chief queen for his own daughter, had a venomous snake placed in Sāmāvatī's lute and told the king, “Great King, Sāmāvatī wishes to kill you; she carries a venomous snake in her lute.” The king, seeing it, became enraged and, resolving to kill Sāmāvatī, strung his bow and fitted it with a poison-smeared, razor-tipped arrow. Sāmāvatī and her retinue suffused the king with loving-kindness. The king, unable to either shoot the arrow or to lower it, stood trembling. Then the queen asked him, “Great King, are you weary?” “Yes, I am weary.” “In that case, lower the bow.” The arrow fell right at the king’s feet. Then the queen advised him, “Great King, one should not harm one who is without fault.” Thus, the king’s inability to release the arrow was the supernormal power of concentration-pervasion of the laywoman Sāmāvatī.

375. Paṭikkūlādīsu appaṭikkūlasaññivihārādikā pana ariyā iddhi nāma. Yathāha – “katamā ariyā iddhi? Idha – bhikkhu sace ākaṅkhati ‘paṭikkūle appaṭikkūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, appaṭikkūlasaññī tattha viharati…pe… upekkhako tattha viharati sato sampajāno”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.17). Ayañhi cetovasippattānaṃ ariyānaṃyeva sambhavato ariyā iddhīti vuccati.

375. Furthermore, the practice of dwelling with the perception of the unrepulsive in the repulsive, and so forth, is called the noble supernormal power. As it is said: “What is the noble supernormal power? Here, if a monk wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive… he dwells there equanimous, mindful, and fully aware” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.17). This is called the noble supernormal power because it is possible only for noble ones who have attained mastery over the mind.

Etāya hi samannāgato khīṇāsavo bhikkhu paṭikkūle aniṭṭhe vatthusmiṃ mettāpharaṇaṃ vā dhātumanasikāraṃ vā karonto appaṭikkūlasaññī viharati. Appaṭikkūle iṭṭhe vatthusmiṃ asubhapharaṇaṃ vā aniccanti manasikāraṃ vā karonto paṭikkūlasaññī viharati. Tathā paṭikkūlāpaṭikkūlesu tadeva mettāpharaṇaṃ vā dhātumanasikāraṃ vā karonto appaṭikkūlasaññī viharati. Appaṭikkūlapaṭikkūlesu ca tadeva asubhapharaṇaṃ vā aniccanti manasikāraṃ vā karonto paṭikkūlasaññī viharati. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hotītiādinā nayena vuttaṃ pana chaḷaṅgupekkhaṃ pavattayamāno paṭikkūle ca appaṭikkūle ca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjitvā upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Paṭisambhidāyañhi “kathaṃ paṭikkūle appaṭikkūlasaññī viharati? Aniṭṭhasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ mettāya vā pharati dhātuso vā upasaṃharatī”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 3.17) nayena ayameva attho vibhatto. Ayaṃ cetovasippattānaṃ ariyānaṃyeva sambhavato ariyā iddhīti vuccati.

For a bhikkhu endowed with this, whose taints are destroyed, while suffusing with loving-kindness or attending to the elements in a repulsive, undesirable object, he dwells perceiving it as unrepulsive. While suffusing with the perception of foulness or attending to impermanence in an unrepulsive, desirable object, he dwells perceiving it as repulsive. Likewise, in objects that are both repulsive and unrepulsive, by applying the same suffusion with loving-kindness or attention to the elements, he dwells perceiving them as unrepulsive. And in objects that are both unrepulsive and repulsive, by applying the same suffusion with the perception of foulness or attention to impermanence, he dwells perceiving them as repulsive. Furthermore, by exercising the six-factored equanimity as stated in the method beginning, “Having seen a form with the eye, one is neither pleased…,” and having set aside both these states, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and fully aware. For in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, this very meaning is analyzed in the method beginning: “How does one dwell perceiving the repulsive as unrepulsive? One suffuses an undesirable object with loving-kindness or attends to it element-wise,” and so on. This is called noble power because it arises only for noble ones who have attained mastery over the mind.

376. Pakkhīādīnaṃ pana [M 2.0011] vehāsagamanādikā kammavipākajā iddhi nāma. Yathāha – “katamā kammavipākajā iddhi? Sabbesaṃ pakkhīnaṃ sabbesaṃ devānaṃ ekaccānaṃ manussānaṃ ekaccānañca vinipātikānaṃ ayaṃ kammavipākajā iddhī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.18). Ettha hi sabbesaṃ pakkhīnaṃ jhānaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā vināyeva ākāsena gamanaṃ. Tathā sabbesaṃ devānaṃ paṭhamakappikānañca ekaccānaṃ manussānaṃ. Tathā piyaṅkaramātā (saṃ. ni. 1.240) yakkhinī [V 2.0011] uttaramātā phussamittā dhammaguttāti evamādīnaṃ ekaccānaṃ vinipātikānaṃ ākāsena gamanaṃ kammavipākajā iddhīti.

376. Furthermore, for birds and others, the power of traveling through the sky and so forth is called power born of kamma-result. As it is said: “What is power born of kamma-result? For all birds, all devas, some humans, and some beings in the woeful states—this is power born of kamma-result.” Here, indeed, all birds travel through the sky even without jhāna or insight. Likewise for all devas, and for some humans of the first aeon. Similarly, for some beings in the woeful states—such as the yakkhinī Piyaṅkaramātā, Uttaramātā, Phussamittā, and Dhammaguttā—their traveling through the sky is power born of kamma-result.

377. Cakkavattiādīnaṃ vehāsagamanādikā pana puññavato iddhi nāma. Yathāha “katamā puññavato iddhi? Rājā cakkavattī vehāsaṃ gacchati saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya antamaso assabandhagobandhapurise upādāya. Jotikassa gahapatissa puññavato iddhi. Jaṭilakassa gahapatissa puññavato iddhi. Ghositassa gahapatissa puññavato iddhi. Meṇḍakassa gahapatissa puññavato iddhi. Pañcannaṃ mahāpuññānaṃ puññavato iddhī”ti. Saṅkhepato pana paripākaṃ gate puññasambhāre ijjhanakaviseso puññavato iddhi.

377. Furthermore, for wheel-turning monarchs and others, the power of traveling through the sky and so forth is called the power of the meritorious. As it is said: “What is the power of the meritorious? A wheel-turning monarch travels through the sky along with his fourfold army, down to the very horse-grooms and cowherds. The power of the meritorious belongs to the householder Jotika. The power of the meritorious belongs to the householder Jaṭilaka. The power of the meritorious belongs to the householder Ghosita. The power of the meritorious belongs to the householder Meṇḍaka. The power of the meritorious belongs to the five greatly meritorious ones.” In brief, however, the power of the meritorious is a special kind of success that arises when the accumulation of merit has ripened.

Ettha ca jotikassa gahapatissa pathaviṃ bhinditvā maṇipāsādo uṭṭhahi. Catusaṭṭhi ca kapparukkhāti ayamassa puññavato iddhi. Jaṭilakassa asītihattho suvaṇṇapabbato nibbatti. Ghositassa sattasu ṭhānesu māraṇatthāya upakkame katepi arogabhāvo puññavato iddhi. Meṇḍakassa ekakarīsamatte padese sattaratanamayānaṃ meṇḍakānaṃ pātubhāvo puññavato iddhi. Pañca mahāpuññā nāma meṇḍakaseṭṭhi, tassa bhariyā candapadumasirī, putto dhanañcayaseṭṭhi, suṇisā sumanadevī, dāso puṇṇo nāmāti. Tesu seṭṭhissa sīsaṃ nhātassa ākāsaṃ ullokanakāle aḍḍhateḷasakoṭṭhasahassāni ākāsato rattasālīnaṃ pūrenti. Bhariyāya nāḷikodanamattampi gahetvā sakalajambudīpavāsike parivisamānāya bhattaṃ na khīyati. Puttassa sahassatthavikaṃ gahetvā sakalajambudīpavāsikānampi dentassa kahāpaṇā na khīyanti. Suṇisāya ekaṃ [M 2.0012] vīhitumbaṃ gahetvā sakalajambudīpavāsikānampi bhājayamānāya dhaññaṃ na khīyati. Dāsassa ekena naṅgalena kasato ito satta ito sattāti cuddasa maggā honti. Ayaṃ nesaṃ puññavato iddhi.

Herein, for the householder Jotika, a jeweled palace arose, splitting the earth. And sixty-four wish-fulfilling trees arose—this was his power of the meritorious. For Jaṭilaka, a golden mountain eighty cubits high came into being. For Ghosita, his remaining unharmed even when attempts were made to kill him in seven places was the power of the meritorious. For Meṇḍaka, the appearance of rams made of the seven jewels in an area of one karīsa was the power of the meritorious. The five greatly meritorious ones were: Meṇḍaka the merchant, his wife Candapadumasirī, his son Dhanañcaya the merchant, his daughter-in-law Sumanadevī, and his slave named Puṇṇa. Among them, when the merchant had washed his head and looked up at the sky, twelve thousand five hundred granaries were filled with red rice from the sky. For his wife, when she took just a nāḷi-measure of cooked rice and served it to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, the food was not exhausted. For his son, when he took a purse of a thousand and gave to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, the coins were not exhausted. For his daughter-in-law, when she took a single basket of paddy and distributed it to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, the grain was not exhausted. For the slave, when he plowed with a single plow, fourteen furrows would appear: seven on this side and seven on that. This was their power of the meritorious.

378. Vijjādharādīnaṃ vehāsagamanādikā pana vijjāmayā iddhi. Yathāha “katamā vijjāmayā iddhi? Vijjādharā vijjaṃ parijapitvā vehāsaṃ gacchanti. Ākāse antalikkhe hatthimpi dassenti…pe… vividhampi senābyūhaṃ dassentī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.18).

378. Furthermore, for knowledge-holders and others, the power of traveling through the sky and so forth is power created by knowledge. As it is said: “What is power created by knowledge? Knowledge-holders, having recited their incantations, travel through the sky. In the air, in space, they display elephant troops… and even various military formations.”

379. Tena tena pana sammāpayogena tassa tassa kammassa ijjhanaṃ tattha tattha sammāpayogapaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi. Yathāha – “nekkhammena kāmacchandassa pahānaṭṭho ijjhatīti tattha [V 2.0012] tattha sammāpayogapaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi…pe… arahattamaggena sabbakilesānaṃ pahānaṭṭho ijjhatīti tattha tattha sammāpayogapaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.18). Ettha ca paṭipattisaṅkhātasseva sammāpayogassa dīpanavasena purimapāḷisadisāva pāḷi āgatā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana sakaṭabyūhādikaraṇavasena yaṃkiñci sippakammaṃ yaṃkiñci vejjakammaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bedānaṃ uggahaṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ piṭakānaṃ uggahaṇaṃ antamaso kasanavapanādīni upādāya taṃ taṃ kammaṃ katvā nibbattaviseso tattha tattha sammāpayogapaccayā ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhīti āgatā. (10)

379. Furthermore, the success of a particular task through a particular right endeavor is ‘power’ in the sense of succeeding because of right endeavor in that particular case. As it is said: “Through renunciation, the goal of abandoning sensual desire is achieved; this is ‘power’ in the sense of succeeding because of right endeavor in that particular case… Through the path of arahantship, the goal of abandoning all defilements is achieved; this is ‘power’ in the sense of succeeding because of right endeavor in that particular case.” And here, a passage similar to the preceding ones is given, showing that right endeavor is a matter of practice. In the commentary, however, it is stated that any special result produced by performing some task—by means of arranging a cart-flank formation and so on; any craft; any medical work; the learning of the three Vedas; the learning of the three Piṭakas; down to and including plowing, sowing, and so on—is ‘power’ in the sense of succeeding because of right endeavor in that particular case. (10)

Iti imāsu dasasu iddhīsu iddhividhāyāti imasmiṃ pade adhiṭṭhānā iddhiyeva āgatā. Imasmiṃ panatthe vikubbanāmanomayāiddhiyopi icchitabbā eva.

Thus, among these ten powers, in the term `iddhividhā`, only the power of determination is meant. However, in this context, the power of transformation and the mind-made power should also be included.

380. Iddhividhāyāti iddhikoṭṭhāsāya, iddhivikappāya vā. Cittaṃ abhinīharati abhininnāmetīti so bhikkhu vuttappakāravasena tasmiṃ citte abhiññāpādake jāte iddhividhādhigamatthāya parikammacittaṃ abhinīharati kasiṇārammaṇato apanetvā iddhividhābhimukhaṃ peseti. Abhininnāmetīti adhigantabbaiddhipoṇaṃ iddhipabbhāraṃ karoti. Soti so evaṃ katacittābhinīhāro bhikkhu. Anekavihitanti anekavidhaṃ nānappakārakaṃ. Iddhividhanti iddhikoṭṭhāsaṃ. Paccanubhotīti paccanubhavati, phusati [M 2.0013] sacchikaroti pāpuṇātīti attho. Idānissa anekavihitabhāvaṃ dassento “ekopi hutvā”tiādimāha. Tattha ekopi hutvāti iddhikaraṇato pubbe pakatiyā ekopi hutvā. Bahudhā hotīti bahūnaṃ santike caṅkamitukāmo vā sajjhāyaṃ vā kattukāmo pañhaṃ vā pucchitukāmo hutvā satampi sahassampi hoti. Kathaṃ panāyamevaṃ hoti? Iddhiyā catasso bhūmiyo cattāro pādā aṭṭha padāni soḷasa ca mūlāni sampādetvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhahanto.

380. The term `iddhividhāya` means 'for the category of psychic power' or 'for the variety of psychic power.' The phrase "He directs and inclines his mind" means that the monk, in the manner described, when that mind which is the basis for higher knowledge has arisen, directs his preparatory mind for the purpose of attaining the kinds of psychic power; he withdraws it from the kasiṇa object and sends it towards the kinds of psychic power. The term `abhininnāmeti` means he makes the mind inclined towards and prone to the psychic power to be attained. The term `so` refers to that monk who has thus directed his mind. The term `anekavihita` means 'manifold, of various kinds.' The term `iddhividha` means 'a category of psychic power.' The term `paccanubhoti` means 'he experiences, contacts, realizes, attains'—this is the meaning. Now, to show its manifold nature, it is said, "Having been one, he becomes many," and so on. Herein, "having been one" means that before performing the psychic feat, he was by nature one. "He becomes many" means that, desiring to walk, to recite, or to ask a question in the presence of many, he becomes a hundred or even a thousand. But how does he become so? By accomplishing the four planes, the four bases of psychic power, the eight factors, and the sixteen roots, and by determining this with knowledge.

381. Tattha catasso bhūmiyoti cattāri jhānāni veditabbāni. Vuttañhetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā “iddhiyā katamā catasso bhūmiyo? Vivekajabhūmi paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, pītisukhabhūmi dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ, upekkhāsukhabhūmi tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ, adukkhamasukhabhūmi catutthaṃ jhānaṃ. Iddhiyā imā catasso bhūmiyo iddhilābhāya iddhipaṭilābhāya iddhivikubbanatāya iddhivisavitāya iddhivasitāya iddhivesārajjāya saṃvattantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.9). Ettha ca purimāni tīṇi jhānāni yasmā pītipharaṇena ca sukhapharaṇena ca sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamitvā [V 2.0013] lahumudukammaññakāyo iddhiṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmā iminā pariyāyena iddhilābhāya saṃvattanato sambhārabhūmiyoti veditabbāni. Catutthajjhānaṃ pana iddhilābhāya pakatibhūmiyeva.

381. Herein, "the four planes" should be understood as the four jhānas. For this was said by the General of the Dhamma: "What are the four planes for psychic power? The plane born of seclusion is the first jhāna; the plane of joy and pleasure is the second jhāna; the plane of equanimity and pleasure is the third jhāna; the plane of neither-pain-nor-pleasure is the fourth jhāna. These are the four planes for psychic power. These planes conduce to the obtaining of psychic power, the re-obtaining of psychic power, the transformations of psychic power, the pervasion of psychic power, the mastery of psychic power, and the confidence in psychic power." Herein, the first three jhānas should be understood as preparatory planes because it is by means of the pervasion of joy and the pervasion of pleasure, and by entering upon the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness, that one, having become light, malleable, and wieldy of body, attains psychic power. Therefore, in this way, because they conduce to the attainment of psychic power, they are to be known as preparatory planes. The fourth jhāna, however, is the natural plane for the attainment of psychic power.

382. Cattāro pādāti cattāro iddhipādā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ “iddhiyā katame cattāro pādā? Idha bhikkhu chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Vīriya… citta… vīmaṃsāsamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Iddhiyā ime cattāro pādā iddhilābhāya…pe… iddhivesārajjāya saṃvattantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.9). Ettha ca chandahetuko chandādhiko vā samādhi chandasamādhi. Kattukamyatāchandaṃ adhipatiṃ karitvā paṭiladdhasamādhissetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Padhānabhūtā saṅkhārā padhānasaṅkhārā. Catukiccasādhakassa sammappadhānavīriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Samannāgatanti chandasamādhinā ca padhānasaṅkhārehi ca upetaṃ. Iddhipādanti nipphattipariyāyena vā ijjhanaṭṭhena, ijjhanti etāya sattā iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti iminā vā pariyāyena iddhīti saṅkhaṃ gatānaṃ abhiññācittasampayuttānaṃ chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārānaṃ [M 2.0014] adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena pādabhūtaṃ sesacittacetasikarāsinti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ “iddhipādoti tathābhūtassa vedanākkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho”ti (vibha. 434).

382. By "the four bases" are to be understood the four bases of psychic power. For it is said: "What are the four bases for psychic power? Here, a bhikkhu develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and formations of exertion. He develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy... with concentration due to consciousness... with concentration due to investigation and formations of exertion. These are the four bases for psychic power. These bases conduce to the obtaining of psychic power... to the confidence in psychic power." Herein, concentration that has desire as its cause or has desire as its dominant factor is 'concentration due to desire.' This is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the desire to act the dominant factor. Formations that are foremost are 'formations of exertion.' This is a designation for the energy of right exertion that accomplishes the fourfold task. 'Endowed' means possessed of concentration due to desire and formations of exertion. The term `iddhipāda` has this meaning: it is the remaining aggregate of consciousness and mental factors that serves as a basis (`pāda`), in the sense of a foundation, for concentration due to desire and formations of exertion. These latter are associated with the consciousness of direct knowledge and are called `iddhi` (power) either by way of accomplishment, in the sense of 'succeeding' (`ijjhana`), or by way of the saying: 'By this, beings succeed (`ijjanti`), become prosperous, grow, and attain excellence.' For it is said: "The basis of psychic power is, for one who has become thus, the aggregate of feeling... the aggregate of consciousness."

Atha vā pajjate anenāti pādo. Pāpuṇīyatīti attho. Iddhiyā pādo iddhipādo. Chandādīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yathāha – “chandañce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu nissāya labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassekaggataṃ, ayaṃ vuccati chandasamādhi. So anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ…pe… padahati, ime vuccanti padhānasaṅkhārā. Iti ayañca chando ayañca chandasamādhi ime ca padhānasaṅkhārā, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgato iddhipādo”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.825). Evaṃ sesiddhipādesupi attho veditabbo.

Alternatively, `pāda` means 'that by which one proceeds' (`pajjate anena`), in the sense of 'attaining' (`pāpuṇīyati`). The basis (`pāda`) of psychic power (`iddhi`) is `iddhipāda`. This is a designation for desire and the others. As it is said: "Monks, if a monk, relying on desire, attains concentration, attains unification of mind, this is called concentration due to desire. He generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil... he strives. These are called the formations of exertion. Thus, this desire, this concentration due to desire, and these formations of exertion—this, monks, is called the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and formations of exertion." The meaning should be understood similarly for the other bases of psychic power.

383. Aṭṭha padānīti chandādīni aṭṭha veditabbāni. Vuttañhetaṃ “iddhiyā katamāni aṭṭha padāni? Chandañce bhikkhu nissāya labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassekaggataṃ. Chando na samādhi, samādhi na chando. Añño chando, añño samādhi. Vīriyañce bhikkhu… cittañce bhikkhu… vīmaṃsañce bhikkhu nissāya labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassekaggataṃ. Vīmaṃsā na samādhi, samādhi na vīmaṃsā. Aññā vīmaṃsā, añño samādhi. Iddhiyā imāni aṭṭha padāni iddhilābhāya…pe… iddhivesārajjāya saṃvattantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.9). Ettha hi iddhimuppādetukāmatāchando [V 2.0014] samādhinā ekato niyuttova iddhilābhāya saṃvattati; tathā vīriyādayo. Tasmā imāni aṭṭha padāni vuttānīti veditabbāni.

383. By "the eight factors" (`aṭṭha padāni`) are to be understood the eight items beginning with desire. For it is said: "What are the eight factors for psychic power? If a monk, relying on desire, attains concentration, attains unification of mind—desire is not concentration, concentration is not desire; desire is one thing, concentration is another. If a monk, relying on energy... if a monk, relying on consciousness... if a monk, relying on investigation, attains concentration, attains unification of mind—investigation is not concentration, concentration is not investigation; investigation is one thing, concentration is another. These are the eight factors for psychic power. These factors conduce to the obtaining of psychic power... to the confidence in psychic power." For here, the desire which is the wish to produce psychic power, only when yoked together with concentration, conduces to the attainment of psychic power; likewise for energy and the others. Therefore, it should be understood that these eight factors are mentioned.

384. Soḷasa mūlānīti soḷasahi ākārehi āneñjatā cittassa veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ – “iddhiyā kati mūlāni? Soḷasa mūlāni – anonataṃ cittaṃ kosajje na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, anunnataṃ cittaṃ uddhacce na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, anabhinataṃ cittaṃ rāge na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, anapanataṃ cittaṃ byāpāde na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, anissitaṃ cittaṃ diṭṭhiyā na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, appaṭibaddhaṃ cittaṃ chandarāge na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, vippamuttaṃ cittaṃ kāmarāge na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, visaṃyuttaṃ cittaṃ kilese na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, vimariyādikataṃ cittaṃ kilesamariyāde na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, ekattagataṃ cittaṃ nānattakilese na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, saddhāya pariggahitaṃ [M 2.0015] cittaṃ assaddhiye na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, vīriyena pariggahitaṃ cittaṃ kosajje na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, satiyā pariggahitaṃ cittaṃ pamāde na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, samādhinā pariggahitaṃ cittaṃ uddhacce na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, paññāya pariggahitaṃ cittaṃ avijjāya na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ, obhāsagataṃ cittaṃ avijjandhakāre na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Iddhiyā imāni soḷasa mūlāni iddhilābhāya…pe… iddhivesārajjāya saṃvattantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.9).

384. By ‘the sixteen roots’ is meant that the imperturbability of the mind is to be understood through sixteen aspects. For it is said: "How many roots are there for spiritual power? There are sixteen roots: 1. A mind not bent down (anonataṃ) by laziness does not waver—this is imperturbability. 2. A mind not raised up (anunnataṃ) by restlessness does not waver—this is imperturbability. 3. A mind not inclined towards (anabhinataṃ) lust does not waver—this is imperturbability. 4. A mind not turned away from (anapanataṃ) ill will does not waver—this is imperturbability. 5. A mind not dependent (anissitaṃ) on views does not waver—this is imperturbability. 6. A mind not bound (appaṭibaddhaṃ) by sensual desire does not waver—this is imperturbability. 7. A mind liberated (vippamuttaṃ) from sensual lust does not waver—this is imperturbability. 8. A mind detached (visaṃyuttaṃ) from defilements does not waver—this is imperturbability. 9. A mind made boundless (vimariyādikataṃ) does not waver with respect to the limits of defilements—this is imperturbability. 10. A mind that has attained unification (ekattagataṃ) does not waver due to the diversity of defilements—this is imperturbability. 11. A mind upheld (pariggahitaṃ) by faith does not waver due to lack of faith—this is imperturbability. 12. A mind upheld (pariggahitaṃ) by energy does not waver due to laziness—this is imperturbability. 13. A mind upheld (pariggahitaṃ) by mindfulness does not waver due to heedlessness—this is imperturbability. 14. A mind upheld (pariggahitaṃ) by concentration does not waver due to restlessness—this is imperturbability. 15. A mind upheld (pariggahitaṃ) by wisdom does not waver due to ignorance—this is imperturbability. 16. A mind that has attained luminosity (obhāsagataṃ) does not waver in the darkness of ignorance—this is imperturbability. These are the sixteen roots of spiritual power that lead to the attainment of spiritual power... to mastery in spiritual power." (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.9)

Kāmañca esa attho evaṃ samāhite cittetiādināpi siddhoyeva, paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ pana iddhiyā bhūmipādapadamūlabhāvadassanatthaṃ puna vutto. Purimo ca suttesu āgatanayo. Ayaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ. Iti ubhayattha asammohatthampi puna vutto.

Although it is true that this meaning is established by the phrase "with the mind thus concentrated," and so on, it is stated again to show that the first jhāna and so on are the ground, the foundation, the basis, and the root of spiritual power. The former method is the one that comes in the Suttas. This one is in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. Thus, it is stated again also for the purpose of avoiding confusion in both places.

385. Ñāṇena adhiṭṭhahantoti svāyamete iddhiyā bhūmipādapadabhūte dhamme sampādetvā abhiññāpādakaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya sace sataṃ icchati “sataṃ homi sataṃ homī”ti parikammaṃ katvā puna abhiññāpādakaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya adhiṭṭhāti, adhiṭṭhānacittena saheva sataṃ hoti. Sahassādīsupi eseva nayo. Sace evaṃ na ijjhati puna parikammaṃ katvā dutiyampi samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ hi ekavāraṃ dvevāraṃ samāpajjituṃ vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Tattha pādakajjhānacittaṃ nimittārammaṇaṃ. Parikammacittāni satārammaṇāni vā sahassārammaṇāni vā, tāni ca kho vaṇṇavasena, no paṇṇattivasena. Adhiṭṭhānacittampi tatheva satārammaṇaṃ [V 2.0015] vā sahassārammaṇaṃ vā. Taṃ pubbe vuttaṃ appanācittamiva gotrabhuanantaraṃ ekameva uppajjati rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānikaṃ.

385. ‘One who resolves through knowledge’: This bhikkhu, having accomplished these states that are the ground, foundation, and basis of spiritual power, and having attained the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, emerges from it. If he wishes for a hundred, he performs the preliminary work, thinking, “May I become a hundred, may I become a hundred.” He then again attains the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, emerges from it, and resolves. Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, he becomes a hundred. This is the same method for a thousand and so on. If it does not succeed in this way, one should again perform the preliminary work, attain the jhāna a second time, emerge, and resolve. For in the Commentary to the Saṃyutta Nikāya it is said that it is permissible to attain it once or twice. Therein, the mind of the foundational jhāna has the sign as its object. The minds of the preliminary work have a hundred or a thousand as their object, and they do so by way of appearance, not by way of concept. The mind of resolution similarly has a hundred or a thousand as its object. Like the absorption-consciousness mentioned before, it is a single mind belonging to the fourth jhāna of the form realm that arises immediately after the change-of-lineage consciousness.

386. Yampi paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttaṃ “pakatiyā eko bahukaṃ āvajjati sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā satasahassaṃ vā, āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti ‘bahuko homī’ti, bahuko hoti, yathā āyasmā cūḷapanthako”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.10). Tatrāpi āvajjatīti parikammavaseneva vuttaṃ. Āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhātīti abhiññāñāṇavasena vuttaṃ. Tasmā bahukaṃ āvajjati, tato tesampi parikammacittānaṃ avasāne samāpajjati, samāpattito vuṭṭhahitvā puna bahuko homīti āvajjitvā tato paraṃ pavattānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ catunnaṃ vā pubbabhāgacittānaṃ anantarā uppannena sanniṭṭhāpanavasena adhiṭṭhānanti [M 2.0016] laddhanāmena ekeneva abhiññāñāṇena adhiṭṭhātīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

386. And that which is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: ‘By nature, one adverts to many—a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand. Having adverted, one resolves with knowledge, “May I become many,” and one becomes many, like the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka’ (Paṭi. ma. 3.10). Therein, ‘adverts’ is stated by way of the preliminary work. ‘Having adverted, one resolves with knowledge’ is stated by way of the knowledge of direct knowledge. Therefore, one adverts to many; then, at the conclusion of those very minds of preliminary work, one attains the absorption. Having emerged from the attainment, one again adverts, thinking, ‘May I become many.’ Then, with the single knowledge of direct knowledge—which has obtained the name ‘resolution’ by way of its function of establishing, and which arises immediately after the three or four preceding minds of the preliminary stage—one resolves. Thus the meaning here should be understood.

Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “yathā āyasmā cūḷapanthako”ti, taṃ bahudhābhāvassa kāyasakkhidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana vatthunā dīpetabbaṃ. Te kira dvebhātaro panthe jātattā panthakāti nāmaṃ labhiṃsu. Tesaṃ jeṭṭho mahāpanthako, so pabbajitvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Arahā hutvā cūḷapanthakaṃ pabbājetvā –

As for the statement, ‘like the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka,’ this was said to show a personal witness to the state of being manifold. This should be illustrated with the story. It is said that the two brothers were born on a path and thus received the name Panthaka. The elder of them was Mahāpanthaka. He went forth and attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Having become an arahant, he gave Cūḷapanthaka the going forth and taught him:

Padumaṃ yathā kokanadaṃ sugandhaṃ, pāto siyā phullamavītagandhaṃ;

Aṅgīrasaṃ passa virocamānaṃ, tapantamādiccamivantalikkheti. (a. ni. 5.195) –

“Like a fragrant red lotus, blooming at dawn, its scent unfaded; see Aṅgīrasa shining, blazing like the sun in the sky.”

Imaṃ gāthaṃ adāsi. So taṃ catūhi māsehi paguṇaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ thero abhabbo tvaṃ sāsaneti vihārato nīhari. Tasmiñca kāle thero bhattuddesako hoti. Jīvako theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “sve, bhante, bhagavatā saddhiṃ pañcabhikkhusatāni gahetvā amhākaṃ gehe bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. Theropi ṭhapetvā cūḷapanthakaṃ sesānaṃ adhivāsemīti adhivāsesi.

He gave him this verse. He was unable to master it in four months. Then the elder expelled him from the monastery, saying, “You are incapable in this Dispensation.” At that time, the elder was the distributor of meals. Jīvaka approached the elder and said, “Venerable sir, tomorrow, please accept a meal at our house, bringing with you five hundred bhikkhus including the Blessed One.” The elder consented for the rest, excluding Cūḷapanthaka.

Cūḷapanthako dvārakoṭṭhake ṭhatvā rodati. Bhagavā dibbacakkhunā disvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā kasmā rodasīti āha. So taṃ pavattimācikkhi. Bhagavā na sajjhāyaṃ kātuṃ asakkonto mama [V 2.0016] sāsane abhabbo nāma hoti, mā soci bhikkhūti taṃ bāhāyaṃ gahetvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā iddhiyā pilotikakhaṇḍaṃ abhinimminitvā adāsi, handa bhikkhu imaṃ parimajjanto rajoharaṇaṃ rajoharaṇanti punappunaṃ sajjhāyaṃ karohīti. Tassa tathā karoto taṃ kāḷavaṇṇaṃ ahosi. So parisuddhaṃ vatthaṃ, natthettha doso, attabhāvassa panāyaṃ dosoti saññaṃ paṭilabhitvā pañcasu khandhesu ñāṇaṃ otāretvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā anulomato gotrabhusamīpaṃ pāpesi. Athassa bhagavā obhāsagāthā abhāsi –

Cūḷapanthaka stood at the gatehouse, weeping. The Blessed One, seeing him with the divine eye, approached and asked, "Why do you weep?" He explained what had happened. The Blessed One said, "One who is unable to recite is not, on that account, incapable in my dispensation. Do not grieve, bhikkhu." Taking him by the arm, the Blessed One led him into the monastery, created a piece of cloth by psychic power, and gave it to him, saying, "Here, bhikkhu, while rubbing this, repeatedly recite, 'dust-remover, dust-remover.'" As he did so, the cloth became dark-colored. He gained the perception: "The cloth is pure; there is no fault in it. This fault, however, is of one's own being." Having directed knowledge onto the five aggregates, he developed insight and brought it to the proximity of conformity and change-of-lineage knowledge. Then the Blessed One spoke to him the verses of illumination:

“Rāgo rajo na ca pana reṇu vuccati,

Rāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ rajoti;

Etaṃ rajaṃ vippajahitvā paṇḍitā,

Viharanti te vigatarajassa sāsane.

Lust is defilement, not what is called dust; 'Defilement' is a designation for lust. Having abandoned that defilement, the wise dwell in the dispensation of the one free from defilement.

“Doso [M 2.0017]…pe….

Hatred is defilement, not what is called dust; 'Defilement' is a designation for hatred. Having abandoned that defilement, the wise dwell in the dispensation of the one free from defilement.

“Moho rajo na ca pana reṇu vuccati,

Mohassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ rajoti;

Etaṃ rajaṃ vippajahitvā paṇḍitā,

Viharanti te vigatarajassa sāsane”ti. (mahāni. 209);

Delusion is defilement, not what is called dust; 'Defilement' is a designation for delusion. Having abandoned that defilement, the wise dwell in the dispensation of the one free from defilement.

Tassa gāthāpariyosāne catupaṭisambhidāchaḷabhiññāparivārā nava lokuttaradhammā hatthagatāva ahesuṃ.

At the end of the verses, the nine supramundane states, accompanied by the four analytical knowledges and the six direct knowledges, were as if they had come into his hand.

Satthā dutiyadivase jīvakassa gehaṃ agamāsi saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena. Atha dakkhiṇodakāvasāne yāguyā diyyamānāya hatthena pattaṃ pidahi. Jīvako kiṃ bhanteti pucchi. Vihāre eko bhikkhu atthīti. So purisaṃ pesesi “gaccha, ayyaṃ gahetvā sīghaṃ ehī”ti. Vihārato nikkhante pana bhagavati,

On the second day, the Teacher went to Jīvaka’s house together with the community of monks. Then, at the conclusion of the water dedication, when rice gruel was being offered, he covered his bowl with his hand. Jīvaka asked, "Why is this, Venerable Sir?" The Teacher replied, "There is a monk in the monastery." So Jīvaka sent a man, saying, "Go, fetch the venerable one and come back quickly." But after the Blessed One had departed from the monastery,

Sahassakkhattumattānaṃ[V 2.0017], nimminitvāna panthako;

Nisīdambavane ramme, yāva kālappavedanāti. (theragā. 563);

Having created a thousand likenesses of himself, Panthaka sat in the delightful mango grove until the time for the meal was announced.

Atha so puriso gantvā kāsāvehi ekapajjotaṃ ārāmaṃ disvā āgantvā bhikkhūhi bharito bhante ārāmo, nāhaṃ jānāmi katamo so ayyoti āha. Tato naṃ bhagavā āha “gaccha yaṃ paṭhamaṃ passasi, taṃ cīvarakaṇṇe gahetvā ‘satthā taṃ āmantetī’ti vatvā ānehī”ti. So taṃ gantvā therasseva cīvarakaṇṇe aggahesi. Tāvadeva sabbepi nimmitā antaradhāyiṃsu. Thero “gaccha tva”nti taṃ uyyojetvā mukhadhovanādisarīrakiccaṃ niṭṭhapetvā paṭhamataraṃ gantvā pattāsane nisīdi. Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “yathā āyasmā cūḷapanthako”ti.

Then that man went and, seeing the monastery shining as one blaze with saffron robes, returned and said, 'Venerable sir, the monastery is full of bhikkhus; I do not know which one is the venerable one.' Then the Blessed One said to him, 'Go, grasp the first one you see by the corner of his robe and, saying, “The Teacher summons you,” bring him here.' He went and grasped the elder’s robe-corner. At that very moment, all the created forms disappeared. The elder dismissed him, saying, 'You may go,' and after completing his morning ablutions and other bodily duties, he went ahead and sat in the prepared seat. This was said with reference to: 'Just as the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka.'

Tatra ye te bahū nimmitā te aniyametvā nimmitattā iddhimatā sadisāva honti. Ṭhānanisajjādīsu vā bhāsitatuṇhībhāvādīsu vā yaṃ yaṃ iddhimā karoti, taṃ tadeva karonti. Sace pana nānāvaṇṇe kātukāmo hoti, keci paṭhamavaye, keci majjhimavaye, keci pacchimavaye, tathā [M 2.0018] dīghakese, upaḍḍhamuṇḍe, muṇḍe, missakese, upaḍḍharattacīvare, paṇḍukacīvare, padabhāṇadhammakathāsarabhaññapañhapucchanapañhavissajjanarajanapacanacīvarasibbanadhovanādīni karonte aparepi vā nānappakārake kātukāmo hoti, tena pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya ettakā bhikkhū paṭhamavayā hontūtiādinā nayena parikammaṃ katvā puna samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Adhiṭṭhānacittena saddhiṃ icchiticchitappakārāyeva hontīti. Esa nayo bahudhāpi hutvā eko hotītiādīsu.

Therein, those many created forms, being created without being specified, are just like the one with psychic power. Whatever the one with psychic power does—whether in standing, sitting, and so on, or in speaking, being silent, and so on—they do that very thing. But if one wishes to make them of various kinds—some in their early years, some in their middle years, some in their later years; likewise with long hair, partially shaven heads, shaven heads, or mixed-colored hair; some with partially red robes, some with pale yellow robes; some engaged in reciting texts, delivering Dhamma talks, chanting, asking questions, answering questions, dyeing, cooking, sewing robes, washing robes, and so on—or if one wishes to make them of various other kinds, one should emerge from the base jhāna, perform the preliminary work by way of ‘Let so many bhikkhus be in their early years,’ and so on, then re-enter absorption, emerge, and resolve. Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, they become of the very kind that was wished for. This is the method in cases such as 'having become many, he becomes one,' and so forth.

Ayaṃ pana viseso, iminā bhikkhunā evaṃ bahubhāvaṃ nimminitvā puna “ekova hutvā caṅkamissāmi, sajjhāyaṃ karissāmi, pañhaṃ pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā vā, “ayaṃ vihāro appabhikkhuko, sace keci āgamissanti ‘kuto ime ettakā ekasadisā bhikkhū, addhā therassa esa ānubhāvo’ti maṃ jānissantī”ti appicchatāya vā antarāva “eko homī”ti icchantena pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya “eko homī”ti parikammaṃ katvā puna samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya “eko homī”ti adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Adhiṭṭhānacittena saddhiṃyeva eko hoti. Evaṃ akaronto pana yathā paricchinnakālavasena sayameva eko hoti.

But here is a distinction. Having thus created multiplicity, this bhikkhu may wish to become one again within the appointed time for one of two reasons. He may think, 'Having become one, I will walk, recite, or ask questions.' Or, out of modesty, he may think, 'This monastery has few bhikkhus; if some arrive, they will think, “Where did so many identical bhikkhus come from? Surely this is the elder’s power,” and they will recognize me as one with psychic power.' In that case, he should enter the base jhāna, emerge, perform the preparatory undertaking, 'Let me be one,' then again enter absorption, emerge, and resolve, 'Let me be one.' Simultaneously with the thought of resolution, he becomes one. But if he does not do so, he becomes one by himself according to the delimited period of time.

387. Āvibhāvaṃ tirobhāvanti ettha āvibhāvaṃ karoti tirobhāvaṃ karotīti ayamattho[V 2.0018]. Idameva hi sandhāya paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttaṃ “āvibhāvanti kenaci anāvaṭaṃ hoti appaṭicchannaṃ vivaṭaṃ pākaṭaṃ. Tirobhāvanti kenaci āvaṭaṃ hoti paṭicchannaṃ pihitaṃ paṭikujjita”nti (paṭi. ma. 3.11). Tatrāyaṃ iddhimā āvibhāvaṃ kātukāmo andhakāraṃ vā ālokaṃ karoti, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivaṭaṃ, anāpāthaṃ vā āpāthaṃ karoti. Kathaṃ? Ayañhi yathā paṭicchannopi dūre ṭhitopi vā dissati, evaṃ attānaṃ vā paraṃ vā kātukāmo pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya idaṃ andhakāraṭṭhānaṃ ālokajātaṃ hotūti vā, idaṃ paṭicchannaṃ vivaṭaṃ hotūti vā, idaṃ anāpāthaṃ āpāthaṃ hotūti vā āvajjitvā parikammaṃ katvā vuttanayeneva adhiṭṭhāti, saha adhiṭṭhānacittena yathādhiṭṭhitameva hoti. Pare dūre ṭhitāpi passanti. Sayampi passitukāmo passati.

387. Herein, ‘making manifest and making disappear’ means ‘one makes manifest and one makes disappear.’ With reference to this, it is indeed stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: “To make manifest means to be unobstructed by anything, uncovered, open, and apparent. To make disappear means to be obstructed by something, covered, closed, and concealed” (Paṭis. Ma. 3.11). Here, a person endowed with psychic power, wishing to make manifest, turns darkness into light, the concealed into the open, or the unseen into the seen. How? Just as one who is concealed or standing afar becomes visible, so too, one who wishes to make oneself or another visible emerges from the base jhāna, adverts the mind: ‘Let this dark place become filled with light,’ or ‘Let this concealed place become open,’ or ‘Let this unseen place become visible,’ performs the preliminary work, and resolves as described. Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, it becomes precisely as resolved. Others see them even when standing afar. One oneself sees if one wishes to see.

388. Etaṃ [M 2.0019] pana pāṭihāriyaṃ kena katapubbanti? Bhagavatā. Bhagavā hi cūḷasubhaddāya nimantito vissakammunā nimmitehi pañcahi kūṭāgārasatehi sāvatthito sattayojanabbhantaraṃ sāketaṃ gacchanto yathā sāketanagaravāsino sāvatthivāsike, sāvatthivāsino ca sāketavāsike passanti, evaṃ adhiṭṭhāsi. Nagaramajjhe ca otaritvā pathaviṃ dvidhā bhinditvā yāva avīciṃ ākāsañca dvidhā viyūhitvā yāva brahmalokaṃ dassesi.

388. Now, who has performed this miracle before? The Blessed One. For the Blessed One, having been invited by Cūḷasubhaddā, was proceeding from Sāvatthī to Sāketa—a distance of seven yojanas—with five hundred peaked mansions created by Vissakamma, and he resolved that the residents of Sāketa would see the residents of Sāvatthī, and the residents of Sāvatthī would see the residents of Sāketa. And having descended into the middle of the city, he split the earth in two, revealing it down to the Avīci hell, and parted the sky in two, revealing it up to the Brahmā world.

Devorohaṇenapi ca ayamattho vibhāvetabbo. Bhagavā kira yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ katvā caturāsītipāṇasahassāni bandhanā pamocetvā atītā buddhā yamakapāṭihāriyāvasāne kuhiṃ gatāti āvajjitvā tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ gatāti addasa. Athekena pādena pathavītalaṃ akkamitvā dutiyaṃ yugandharapabbate patiṭṭhapetvā puna purimapādaṃ uddharitvā sinerumatthakaṃ akkamitvā tattha paṇḍukambalasilātale vassaṃ upagantvā sannipatitānaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatānaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya abhidhammakathaṃ ārabhi. Bhikkhācāravelāya nimmitabuddhaṃ māpesi. So dhammaṃ deseti. Bhagavā nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā anotattadahe mukhaṃ dhovitvā uttarakurūsu piṇḍapātaṃ gahetvā anotattadahatīre paribhuñjati. Sāriputtatthero tattha gantvā bhagavantaṃ vandati. Bhagavā ajja ettakaṃ dhammaṃ desesinti therassa nayaṃ deti. Evaṃ tayo māse abbocchinnaṃ abhidhammakathaṃ kathesi. Taṃ sutvā asītikoṭidevatānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi.
