This meaning should also be clarified in relation to the descent from the deva world. It is said that after performing the Twin Miracle and liberating eighty-four thousand beings from bondage, the Blessed One considered, ‘Where did the past Buddhas go at the conclusion of the Twin Miracle?’ and saw that they had gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Then, having placed one foot on the ground and the other on Mount Yugandhara, he lifted the first foot and planted it on the summit of Mount Sineru. There, on the Pāṇḍukambala stone slab, he entered the rains retreat and began the Abhidhamma discourse for the assembled ten thousand world-sphere devas from the beginning. During his alms-gathering time, he created a Created Buddha, who taught the Dhamma. The Blessed One chewed a nāgalatā toothstick, rinsed his mouth in Lake Anotatta, took almsfood in Uttarakuru, and partook of it on the bank of Lake Anotatta. The Venerable Sāriputta went there and paid homage to the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave the elder the method, saying, ‘Today I have taught this much of the Dhamma.’ Thus, he delivered the Abhidhamma discourse uninterruptedly for three months. Hearing this, eighty koṭi of devas attained comprehension of the Dhamma.

Yamakapāṭihāriye sannipatitāpi dvādasayojanā parisā bhagavantaṃ passitvāva gamissāmāti [V 2.0019] khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ cūḷaanāthapiṇḍikaseṭṭhiyeva sabbapaccayehi upaṭṭhāsi. Manussā kuhiṃ bhagavāti jānanatthāya anuruddhattheraṃ yāciṃsu. Thero ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā addasa dibbena cakkhunā tattha vassūpagataṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā ārocesi.

The assembly of twelve yojanas, having gathered for the Twin Miracle, pitched camp and remained, thinking, “We will depart only after seeing the Blessed One.” Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika the millionaire himself provided all their needs. People, wishing to know where the Blessed One was, requested the Venerable Anuruddha. The Elder increased the light and, with the divine eye, saw the Blessed One who had entered the rains retreat there, and informed them.

Te bhagavato vandanatthāya mahāmoggallānattheraṃ yāciṃsu. Thero parisamajjheyeva mahāpathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā sinerupabbataṃ nibbijjhitvā tathāgatapādamūle [M 2.0020] bhagavato pāde vandamānova ummujjitvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca “jambudīpavāsino, bhante, bhagavato pāde vanditvā passitvāva gamissāmāti vadantī”ti. Bhagavā āha “kuhiṃ pana te, moggallāna, etarahi jeṭṭhabhātā dhammasenāpatī”ti? “Saṅkassanagare bhante”ti. “Moggallāna, maṃ daṭṭhukāmā sve saṅkassanagaraṃ āgacchantu, ahaṃ sve mahāpavāraṇapuṇṇamāsīuposathadivase saṅkassanagare otarissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti thero dasabalaṃ vanditvā āgatamaggeneva oruyha manussānaṃ santikaṃ sampāpuṇi. Gamanāgamanakāle ca yathā naṃ manussā passanti, evaṃ adhiṭṭhāsi. Idaṃ tāvettha mahāmoggallānatthero āvibhāvapāṭihāriyaṃ akāsi.

They requested the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna to pay homage to the Blessed One. The elder, in the very midst of the assembly, plunged into the great earth, pierced through Mount Sineru, and, paying homage at the feet of the Blessed One, emerged and said: “Venerable sir, the inhabitants of Jambudīpa say they wish to pay homage at your feet and see you before they depart.” The Blessed One asked, “But where, Moggallāna, is your elder brother, the General of the Dhamma, now?” “At Saṅkassa, Venerable sir.” “Moggallāna, let those who wish to see me come to Saṅkassa tomorrow. I will descend to Saṅkassa tomorrow on the great Pavāraṇā full-moon Uposatha day.” “Very well, Venerable sir,” said the elder. Having paid homage to the Ten-Powered One, he descended by the path he came and arrived among the people. And he resolved that people would see him going and coming. This was the miracle of manifestation performed here by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.

So evaṃ āgato taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “dūranti saññaṃ akatvā katapātarāsāva nikkhamathā”ti āha. Bhagavā sakkassa devarañño ārocesi “mahārāja, sve manussalokaṃ gacchāmī”ti. Devarājā vissakammaṃ āṇāpesi “tāta, sve bhagavā manussalokaṃ gantukāmo, tisso sopānapantiyo māpehi ekaṃ kanakamayaṃ, ekaṃ rajatamayaṃ, ekaṃ maṇimaya”nti. So tathā akāsi. Bhagavā dutiyadivase sinerumuddhani ṭhatvā puratthimalokadhātuṃ olokesi, anekāni cakkavāḷasahassāni vivaṭāni hutvā ekaṅgaṇaṃ viya pakāsiṃsu. Yathā ca puratthimena, evaṃ pacchimenapi uttarenapi dakkhiṇenapi sabbaṃ vivaṭamaddasa. Heṭṭhāpi yāva avīci, upari yāva akaniṭṭhabhavanaṃ, tāva addasa.

Having thus arrived, he reported the matter and said, “Do not consider it far; set out after having eaten breakfast.” The Blessed One informed Sakka, the king of devas: “Great king, tomorrow I will go to the human world.” The king of devas instructed Vissakamma: “My dear, the Blessed One wishes to go to the human world tomorrow. Prepare three flights of stairs: one of gold, one of silver, and one of jewels.” He did so. The next day, the Blessed One stood atop Mount Sineru and surveyed the eastern world-system. Thousands upon thousands of world-systems became open, appearing like a single courtyard. Just as in the east, so too in the west, north, and south—everything appeared open. Below, as far as Avīci, and above, as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm, all was seen.

Taṃ divasaṃ kira lokavivaraṇaṃ nāma ahosi. Manussāpi deve passanti, devāpi manusse. Tattha neva manussā uddhaṃ ullokenti, na devā adho olokenti, sabbe sammukhāva aññamaññaṃ passanti. Bhagavā majjhe maṇimayena sopānena otarati, chakāmāvacaradevā vāmapasse kanakamayena, suddhāvāsā ca mahābrahmā ca dakkhiṇapasse rajatamayena. Devarājā pattacīvaraṃ aggahesi, mahābrahmā tiyojanikaṃ setacchattaṃ, suyāmo vāḷabījaniṃ, pañcasikho gandhabbaputto [V 2.0020] tigāvutamattaṃ beḷuvapaṇḍuvīṇaṃ gahetvā tathāgatassa pūjaṃ karonto otarati. Taṃdivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā buddhabhāvāya pihaṃ anuppādetvā ṭhitasatto nāma natthi. Idamettha bhagavā āvibhāvapāṭihāriyaṃ akāsi.

On that day, it is said, the miracle called the 'Opening of the World' occurred. Humans saw the devas, and the devas saw humans. There, humans did not look upwards, nor did the devas look downwards—all saw each other face to face. The Blessed One descended by the central jeweled staircase; the devas of the six sense-sphere realms descended on the left by the golden staircase, while the Suddhāvāsa devas and Mahā Brahmā descended on the right by the silver staircase. The king of devas took the bowl and robe, Mahā Brahmā held a white parasol three yojanas in extent, Suyāma held a yak-tail fan, and Pañcasikha, the gandhabba’s son, holding a beluva lute three gāvutas in length, descended while paying homage to the Tathāgata. On that day, there was no being who, having seen the Blessed One, did not generate an aspiration for Buddhahood. Herein, the Blessed One performed this miracle of manifestation.

Apica [M 2.0021] tambapaṇṇidīpe talaṅgaravāsī dhammadinnattheropi tissamahāvihāre cetiyaṅgaṇasmiṃ nisīditvā “tīhi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu apaṇṇakapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno hotī”ti apaṇṇakasuttaṃ (a. ni. 3.16) kathento heṭṭhāmukhaṃ bījaniṃ akāsi, yāva avīcito ekaṅgaṇaṃ ahosi. Tato uparimukhaṃ akāsi, yāva brahmalokā ekaṅgaṇaṃ ahosi. Thero nirayabhayena tajjetvā saggasukhena ca palobhetvā dhammaṃ desesi. Keci sotāpannā ahesuṃ, keci sakadāgāmī anāgāmī arahantoti.

Furthermore, on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, the elder Dhammadinna, a resident of Talaṅgara, while sitting in the courtyard of the Tissa Mahāvihāra and preaching the Apaṇṇaka Sutta, saying, “Monks, a bhikkhu endowed with three qualities is one who has entered upon the infallible practice,” pointed his fan downwards, and it became a single expanse as far as Avīci. Then he pointed it upwards, and it became a single expanse as far as the Brahmā world. The elder taught the Dhamma, threatening with the fear of hell and enticing with the bliss of heaven. Some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, non-returners, and arahants.

389. Tirobhāvaṃ kātukāmo pana ālokaṃ vā andhakāraṃ karoti, appaṭicchannaṃ vā paṭicchannaṃ, āpāthaṃ vā anāpāthaṃ karoti. Kathaṃ? Ayañhi yathā appaṭicchannopi samīpe ṭhitopi vā na dissati, evaṃ attānaṃ vā paraṃ vā kātukāmo pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya “idaṃ ālokaṭṭhānaṃ andhakāraṃ hotū”ti vā, “idaṃ appaṭicchannaṃ paṭicchannaṃ hotū”ti vā, “idaṃ āpāthaṃ anāpāthaṃ hotū”ti vā āvajjitvā parikammaṃ katvā vuttanayeneva adhiṭṭhāti. Saha adhiṭṭhānacittena yathādhiṭṭhitameva hoti. Pare samīpe ṭhitāpi na passanti. Sayampi apassitukāmo na passati.

389. One who wishes to perform an act of concealment, however, can make light into darkness, the unconcealed into the concealed, or the apparent into the non-apparent. How? This person with psychic power, wishing to make themself or another to be unseen even when unconcealed or standing nearby, arises from the base jhāna and, having adverted and performed the preliminary work, resolves in the manner already described, thinking: ‘Let this illuminated place become dark,’ or ‘Let this unconcealed thing become concealed,’ or ‘Let this apparent thing become non-apparent.’ Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, it becomes just as resolved. Others do not see them, even though standing nearby. If they themselves wish not to see, they do not see.

390. Etaṃ pana pāṭihāriyaṃ kena katapubbanti? Bhagavatā. Bhagavā hi yasaṃ kulaputtaṃ samīpe nisinnaṃyeva yathā naṃ pitā na passati, evamakāsi. Tathā vīsayojanasataṃ mahākappinassa paccuggamanaṃ katvā taṃ anāgāmiphale, amaccasahassañcassa sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpetvā, tassa anumaggaṃ āgatā sahassitthiparivārā anojādevī āgantvā samīpe nisinnāpi yathā saparisaṃ rājānaṃ na passati, tathā katvā “api, bhante, rājānaṃ passathā”ti vutte “kiṃ pana te rājānaṃ gavesituṃ varaṃ, udāhu attāna”nti? “Attānaṃ, bhante”ti vatvā nisinnāya tassā tathā dhammaṃ desesi, yathā sā saddhiṃ itthisahassena sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi, amaccā anāgāmiphale, rājā arahatteti. Apica tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ [M 2.0022][V 2.0021] āgatadivase yathā attanā saddhiṃ āgate avasese rājā na passati, evaṃ karontena mahindattherenāpi idaṃ katameva (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.tatiyasaṅgītikathā).

390. Now, by whom was this miracle previously performed? By the Blessed One. For the Blessed One made it so that Yasa the clansman, though seated right nearby, was not seen by his father. Similarly, after going one hundred and twenty yojanas to meet Mahākappina, the Blessed One established him in the fruit of non-returning and his thousand ministers in the fruit of stream-entry. Then Queen Anojā, who had come following his path with a retinue of a thousand women, arrived. The Blessed One made it so that, though she was seated nearby, she did not see the king with his retinue. When she asked, “Venerable sir, do you see the king?” he replied, “What is better for you—to seek the king or to seek yourself?” When she said, “To seek myself, venerable sir,” and sat down, the Blessed One taught her the Dhamma in such a way that she, along with the thousand women, was established in the fruit of stream-entry, the ministers in the fruit of non-returning, and the king in arahantship. Moreover, on the day of his arrival on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, the Elder Mahinda also performed this, making it so that the king did not see the others who had come with him.

391. Apica sabbampi pākaṭaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ āvibhāvaṃ nāma. Apākaṭapāṭihāriyaṃ tirobhāvaṃ nāma. Tattha pākaṭapāṭihāriye iddhipi paññāyati iddhimāpi. Taṃ yamakapāṭihāriyena dīpetabbaṃ. Tatra hi “idha tathāgato yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ karoti asādhāraṇaṃ sāvakehi. Uparimakāyato aggikkhandho pavattati, heṭṭhimakāyato udakadhārā pavattatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.116) evaṃ ubhayaṃ paññāyittha. Apākaṭapāṭihāriye iddhiyeva paññāyati, na iddhimā. Taṃ mahakasuttena (saṃ. ni. 4.346) ca brahmanimantanikasuttena (ma. ni. 1.501 ādayo) ca dīpetabbaṃ. Tatra hi āyasmato ca mahakassa, bhagavato ca iddhiyeva paññāyittha, na iddhimā.

391. Furthermore, any manifest miracle is known as a 'manifestation'; an unmanifest miracle is known as a 'concealment.' In a manifest miracle, both the psychic power and the one possessing it are perceived. This is to be illustrated by the Twin Miracle. For in that case it is said: “Here the Tathāgata performs the Twin Miracle, which is not shared by his disciples. From the upper part of his body a mass of fire proceeds; from the lower part of his body a stream of water proceeds.” Thus both were perceived. In an unmanifest miracle, only the psychic power is perceived, not the one possessing it. This is to be illustrated by the Mahaka Sutta and the Brahmanimantanika Sutta. For in those cases, only the psychic power of the Venerable Mahaka and of the Blessed One was perceived, not the ones possessing the power.

Yathāha –

As it is said:

“Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho citto gahapati āyasmantaṃ mahakaṃ etadavoca ‘sādhu me, bhante, ayyo mahako uttarimanussadhammā iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ dassetū’ti. Tena hi tvaṃ gahapati āḷinde uttarāsaṅgaṃ paññāpetvā tiṇakalāpaṃ okāsehīti. ‘Evaṃ, bhante’ti kho citto gahapati āyasmato mahakassa paṭissutvā āḷinde uttarāsaṅgaṃ paññāpetvā tiṇakalāpaṃ okāsesi. Atha kho āyasmā mahako vihāraṃ pavisitvā tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsi, yathā tālacchiggaḷena ca aggaḷantarikāya ca acci nikkhamitvā tiṇāni jhāpesi, uttarāsaṅgaṃ na jhāpesī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.346).

Citta the householder, seated to one side, said to the Venerable Mahaka: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the noble Mahaka would show me a superhuman feat of psychic power.” “Then, householder, spread your upper robe on the terrace and place a bundle of grass on it.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Citta the householder replied, and he spread his upper robe on the terrace and placed a bundle of grass on it. Then the Venerable Mahaka entered his dwelling and performed such a feat of psychic power that a flame shot out through the keyhole and the bolt-aperture, burned up the grass, but did not burn the upper robe.

Yathā cāha –

And as it is said:

“Atha khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsiṃ ‘ettāvatā brahmā ca brahmaparisā ca brahmapārisajjā ca saddañca me sossanti, na ca maṃ dakkhissantī’ti antarahito imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsiṃ –

“Then, bhikkhus, I performed such a feat of psychic power that Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmā, and the retinue of Brahmā would hear my voice but would not see me. Having become invisible, I recited this verse:

‘Bhave [M 2.0023][V 2.0022] vāhaṃ bhayaṃ disvā, bhavañca vibhavesinaṃ;

Bhavaṃ nābhivadiṃ kiñci, nandiñca na upādiyi’”nti. (ma. ni. 1.504);

‘Having seen fear in existence, and in the becoming of those who seek non-existence, I did not praise any kind of existence, nor did I cling to delight.’”

392. Tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati seyyathāpi ākāseti ettha tirokuṭṭanti parakuṭṭaṃ, kuṭṭassa parabhāganti vuttaṃ hoti. Esa nayo itaresu. Kuṭṭoti ca gehabhittiyā etamadhivacanaṃ. Pākāroti gehavihāragāmādīnaṃ parikkhepapākāro. Pabbatoti paṃsupabbato vā pāsāṇapabbato vā. Asajjamānoti alaggamāno. Seyyathāpi ākāseti ākāse viya. Evaṃ gantukāmena pana ākāsakasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya kuṭṭaṃ vā pākāraṃ vā sinerucakkavāḷesupi aññataraṃ pabbataṃ vā āvajjitvā kataparikammena ākāso hotūti adhiṭṭhātabbo. Ākāsoyeva hoti. Adho otaritukāmassa, uddhaṃ vā ārohitukāmassa susiro hoti, vinivijjhitvā gantukāmassa chiddo. So tattha asajjamāno gacchati.

392. “He goes unimpeded through a wall, through an enclosure, through a mountain, as if in open space.” Here, “through a wall” means to the other side of the wall, that is to say, the part beyond the wall. This same method applies to the others. “Wall” (kuṭṭa) is a term for the wall of a house. “Enclosure” (pākāra) refers to the surrounding wall of a house, monastery, village, and so on. “Mountain” means an earth mountain or a rock mountain. “Unimpeded” (asajjamāna) means not getting stuck. “As if in open space” means like in space. One wishing to go thus should enter and emerge from the space kasiṇa. Then, having adverted to a wall, an enclosure, or a mountain—even Sineru or the Cakkavāḷa range—and having done the preliminary work, one should resolve, “Let it be space!” It becomes space indeed. For one who wishes to descend below or ascend above, it becomes hollow; for one who wishes to pass right through, it becomes perforated. He then goes there unimpeded.

Tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero panetthāha – “ākāsakasiṇasamāpajjanaṃ, āvuso, kimatthiyaṃ, kiṃ hatthiassādīni abhinimminitukāmo hatthiassādi kasiṇāni samāpajjati, nanu yattha katthaci kasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā aṭṭhasamāpattivasībhāvoyeva pamāṇaṃ. Yaṃ yaṃ icchati, taṃ tadeva hotī”ti. Bhikkhū āhaṃsu – “pāḷiyā, bhante, ākāsakasiṇaṃyeva āgataṃ, tasmā avassametaṃ vattabba”nti. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

The Elder Tipiṭakacūḷābhaya then said: “Friend, what is the purpose of entering the space kasiṇa attainment? Does one who wishes to create elephants, horses, and so on, enter the kasiṇas of elephants, horses, and so on? Surely, having done the preliminary work on any kasiṇa whatsoever, mastery of the eight attainments is the standard. Whatever one wishes, that very thing comes to be.” The bhikkhus replied: “Venerable sir, in the Pāḷi only the space kasiṇa is mentioned; therefore, this must necessarily be stated.” Here is the Pāḷi text:

“Pakatiyā ākāsakasiṇasamāpattiyā lābhī hoti. Tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ āvajjati. Āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti – ‘ākāso hotū’ti. Ākāso hoti. Tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati. Yathā manussā pakatiyā aniddhimanto kenaci anāvaṭe aparikkhitte asajjamānā gacchanti, evameva so iddhimā cetovasippatto tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati, seyyathāpi ākāse”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.11).

“He is by nature an obtainer of the attainment of the space kasiṇa. He adverts to the other side of a wall, the other side of an enclosure, the other side of a mountain. Having adverted, he resolves with knowledge: ‘Let it be space.’ It becomes space. He goes unimpeded through a wall, through an enclosure, through a mountain. Just as ordinary people without psychic power go unimpeded through some unenclosed, unobstructed space, so too one with psychic power who has attained mastery of mind goes unimpeded through a wall, through an enclosure, through a mountain, as if in open space.” (Paṭis. M. iii, 11)

Sace [M 2.0024] panassa bhikkhuno adhiṭṭhahitvā gacchantassa antarā pabbato vā rukkho vā uṭṭheti, kiṃ puna samāpajjitvā adhiṭṭhātabbanti? Doso natthi. Puna samāpajjitvā adhiṭṭhānaṃ hi [V 2.0023] upajjhāyassa santike nissayaggahaṇasadisaṃ hoti. Iminā ca pana bhikkhunā ākāso hotūti adhiṭṭhitattā ākāso hotiyeva. Purimādhiṭṭhānabaleneva cassa antarā añño pabbato vā rukkho vā utumayo uṭṭhahissatīti aṭṭhānamevetaṃ. Aññena iddhimatā nimmite pana paṭhamanimmānaṃ balavaṃ hoti. Itarena tassa uddhaṃ vā adho vā gantabbaṃ.

But if, while this bhikkhu is proceeding after having made his resolution, a mountain or a tree arises in his path, must he enter absorption again and make a new resolution? There is no fault in doing so. For resolving again after re-entering absorption is like taking dependence anew on one's preceptor. And since this bhikkhu has resolved, “Let it be space,” it does indeed become space. It is impossible that another natural mountain or tree should arise in his path, given the power of his previous resolution. But when something is created by another person with psychic power, the first creation is more powerful. The other person must go above or below it.

393. Pathaviyāpi ummujjanimujjanti ettha ummujjanti uṭṭhānaṃ vuccati. Nimujjanti saṃsīdanaṃ. Ummujjañca nimujjañca ummujjanimujjaṃ. Evaṃ kātukāmena āpokasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā uṭṭhāya ettake ṭhāne pathavī udakaṃ hotūti paricchinditvā parikammaṃ katvā vuttanayeneva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Saha adhiṭṭhānena yathā paricchinne ṭhāne pathavī udakameva hoti. So tattha ummujjanimujjaṃ karoti. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

393. Regarding “emerging from and diving into the earth”: here “emerging” (ummujjana) means rising up; “diving” (nimujjana) means sinking down. Emerging and diving is “emerging-and-diving.” One who wishes to do this should enter and emerge from the water kasiṇa, and after demarcating a certain area of earth and doing the preliminary work, he should resolve in the way described, “Let this earth be water!” Simultaneously with his resolution, the earth in the demarcated area becomes water indeed. He then performs emerging and diving in it. Here is the Pāḷi:

“Pakatiyā āpokasiṇasamāpattiyā lābhī hoti. Pathaviṃ āvajjati. Āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti – ‘udakaṃ hotū’ti. Udakaṃ hoti. So pathaviyā ummujjanimujjaṃ karoti. Yathā manussā pakatiyā aniddhimanto udake ummujjanimujjaṃ karonti, evameva so iddhimā cetovasippatto pathaviyā ummujjanimujjaṃ karoti, seyyathāpi udake”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.11).

“He is by nature an obtainer of the attainment of the water kasiṇa. He adverts to the earth. Having adverted, he resolves with knowledge: ‘Let it be water.’ It becomes water. He performs emerging and submerging in the earth. Just as ordinary people without psychic power emerge and submerge in water, so too one with psychic power who has attained mastery of mind emerges and submerges in the earth, as if in water.” (Paṭis. M. iii, 11)

Na kevalañca ummujjanimujjameva, nhānapānamukhadhovanabhaṇḍakadhovanādīsu yaṃ yaṃ icchati, taṃ taṃ karoti. Na kevalañca udakameva, sappitelamadhuphāṇitādīsupi yaṃ yaṃ icchati, taṃ taṃ idañcidañca ettakaṃ hotūti āvajjitvā parikammaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhahantassa yathādhiṭṭhitameva hoti. Uddharitvā bhājanagataṃ karontassa sappi sappimeva hoti. Telādīni telādīniyeva. Udakaṃ udakameva. So tattha temitukāmova temeti, na temitukāmo na temeti. Tasseva ca sā pathavī udakaṃ hoti sesajanassa pathavīyeva. Tattha manussā pattikāpi gacchanti, yānādīhipi gacchanti, kasikammādīnipi karontiyeva. Sace panāyaṃ tesampi udakaṃ hotūti [M 2.0025] icchati, hotiyeva. Paricchinnakālaṃ pana atikkamitvā yaṃ pakatiyā ghaṭataḷākādīsu udakaṃ, taṃ ṭhapetvā avasesaṃ paricchinnaṭṭhānaṃ pathavīyeva hoti.

Not only emerging and submerging, but he does whatever else he wishes: bathing, drinking, washing his face, washing vessels, and so on. And not only water, but also ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so on—whatever he desires, he adverts, ‘Let this and that be so much,’ performs the preliminary work, and makes a determination, and it becomes just as he has determined. When he lifts it and places it in a vessel, ghee is just ghee, oils are just oils, and water is just water. There, he gets wet if he wishes to, but does not get wet if he does not wish to. For him alone that earth becomes water, but for other people it remains earth. People there walk on foot, travel by vehicles, and carry on with farming and other activities. If, however, he wishes it to become water for them too, it does so. But once the delimited time has passed, apart from the water that is naturally in pots, ponds, and so on, the remaining delimited area reverts to being earth.

394. Udakepi abhijjamāneti ettha yaṃ udakaṃ akkamitvā saṃsīdati, taṃ bhijjamānanti [V 2.0024] vuccati. Viparītaṃ abhijjamānaṃ. Evaṃ gantukāmena pana pathavīkasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya ettake ṭhāne udakaṃ pathavī hotūti paricchinditvā parikammaṃ katvā vuttanayeneva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Saha adhiṭṭhānena yathā paricchinnaṭṭhāne udakaṃ pathavīyeva hoti. So tattha gacchati, tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

394. On water without breaking up: Here, water on which one sinks when treading on it is called 'breaking up.' The opposite is 'not breaking up.' One who wishes to walk thus should enter and emerge from the earth-kasiṇa, delimit a certain area with the thought, ‘Let the water in this place become earth,’ perform the preliminary work, and make a determination in the way described. Simultaneously with his determination, the water in the delimited area becomes just earth. He walks there. On this there is the canonical text:

“Pakatiyā pathavīkasiṇasamāpattiyā lābhī hoti. Udakaṃ āvajjati. Āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti – ‘pathavī hotū’ti. Pathavī hoti. So abhijjamāne udake gacchati. Yathā manussā pakatiyā aniddhimanto abhijjamānāya pathaviyā gacchanti, evameva so iddhimā cetovasippatto abhijjamāne udake gacchati, seyyathāpi pathaviya”nti (paṭi. ma. 3.11).

‘He is by nature an obtainer of the attainment of the earth-kasiṇa. He adverts to water. Having adverted, he determines with knowledge: “Let it be earth.” It becomes earth. He walks on the water without it breaking up. Just as ordinary people without psychic power walk on the earth without it breaking up, so does that one with psychic power, who has attained mastery of mind, walk on the water without it breaking up, as if on earth.’

Na kevalañca gacchati, yaṃ yaṃ iriyāpathaṃ icchati, taṃ taṃ karoti. Na kevalañca pathavimeva karoti, maṇisuvaṇṇapabbatarukkhādīsupi yaṃ yaṃ icchati, taṃ taṃ vuttanayeneva āvajjitvā adhiṭṭhāti, yathādhiṭṭhitameva hoti. Tasseva ca taṃ udakaṃ pathavī hoti, sesajanassa udakameva, macchakacchapā ca udakakākādayo ca yathāruci vicaranti. Sace panāyaṃ aññesampi manussānaṃ taṃ pathaviṃ kātuṃ icchati, karotiyeva. Paricchinnakālātikkamena pana udakameva hoti.

Not only does he walk, but he can adopt any posture he wishes. Not only does he make it earth, but also gems, gold, mountains, trees, and so on—whatever he wishes, he adverts to it and determines it in the way described, and it becomes just as he has determined. For him alone that water becomes earth; for other people it is just water, and fish, turtles, water-crows, and so on move about in it as they please. If he wishes to make it earth for other people too, he can do so. But with the passing of the delimited time, it becomes water again.

395. Pallaṅkena kamatīti pallaṅkena gacchati. Pakkhī sakuṇoti pakkhehi yuttasakuṇo. Evaṃ kātukāmena pana pathavīkasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya sace nisinno gantumicchati, pallaṅkappamāṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ paricchinditvā parikammaṃ katvā vuttanayeneva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Sace nipanno gantukāmo hoti mañcappamāṇaṃ, sace padasā gantukāmo hoti maggappamāṇanti evaṃ yathānurūpaṃ ṭhānaṃ paricchinditvā vuttanayeneva pathavī hotūti adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ, saha adhiṭṭhānena pathavīyeva hoti. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

395. ‘He travels cross-legged’ means he goes while seated in the cross-legged posture. ‘A bird with wings’ means a bird endowed with wings. One who wishes to do this should enter and emerge from the earth-kasiṇa. If he wishes to go while seated, he should delimit a space the size of his cross-legged posture, perform the preliminary work, and determine in the way described. If he wishes to go while lying down, he should delimit a space the size of a couch; if he wishes to go on foot, a space the size of a path. Thus he should delimit a suitable space and determine in the way described, ‘Let it be earth.’ Simultaneously with the determination, it becomes just earth. On this there is the canonical text:

“Ākāsepi [M 2.0026] pallaṅkena kamati, seyyathāpi pakkhī sakuṇoti. Pakatiyā pathavīkasiṇasamāpattiyā lābhī hoti, ākāsaṃ āvajjati. Āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti – ‘pathavī hotū’ti. Pathavī hoti. So ākāse antalikkhe caṅkamatipi tiṭṭhatipi [V 2.0025] nisīdatipi seyyampi kappeti. Yathā manussā pakatiyā aniddhimanto pathaviyaṃ caṅkamantipi…pe… seyyampi kappenti, evameva so iddhimā cetovasippatto ākāse antalikkhe caṅkamatipi…pe… seyyampi kappetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.11).

“In the sky, he travels cross-legged, just as a bird with wings. He is by nature an obtainer of the attainment of the earth-kasiṇa; he adverts to the sky. Having adverted, he determines with knowledge: ‘Let it be earth.’ It becomes earth. He walks, stands, sits, and lies down in the sky, in the air. Just as ordinary people, without psychic power, walk, stand, sit, and lie down on the earth, so too does this one with psychic power, who has attained mastery of mind, walk, stand, sit, and lie down in the sky, in the air.”

Ākāse gantukāmena ca bhikkhunā dibbacakkhulābhināpi bhavitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Antare utusamuṭṭhānā vā pabbatarukkhādayo honti, nāgasupaṇṇādayo vā usūyantā māpenti, nesaṃ dassanatthaṃ. Te pana disvā kiṃ kātabbanti? Pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya ākāso hotūti parikammaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Thero panāha “samāpattisamāpajjanaṃ, āvuso, kimatthiyaṃ, nanu samāhitamevassa cittaṃ, tena yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ ākāso hotūti adhiṭṭhāti, ākāsoyeva hotī”ti. Kiñcāpi evamāha, atha kho tirokuṭṭapārihāriye vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ.

A bhikkhu who wishes to travel in the sky should also be one who has attained the divine eye. Why? Because in between there might be mountains, trees, etc., arisen from the seasons, or nāgas, supaṇṇas, etc., who, being jealous, might create them; this is for the purpose of seeing them. Seeing them, what should be done? He should attain the basis-jhāna, emerge, and having made the preliminary work, determine: ‘Let it be sky.’ But an elder said: “Friend, what is the purpose of re-entering absorption? Is not his mind already concentrated? By that, whatever place he determines: ‘Let it be sky,’ that place becomes sky.” Although he said so, one should proceed in the manner stated in the case of the wonder of passing through walls.

Apica okāse orohaṇatthampi iminā dibbacakkhulābhinā bhavitabbaṃ, ayañhi sace anokāse nhānatitthe vā gāmadvāre vā orohati. Mahājanassa pākaṭo hoti. Tasmā dibbacakkhunā passitvā anokāsaṃ vajjetvā okāse otaratīti.

Moreover, for the purpose of descending in a suitable place, this bhikkhu should also be one who has attained the divine eye. For if he descends in an unsuitable place, such as a bathing place or a village gate, he becomes conspicuous to the public. Therefore, having seen with the divine eye, he avoids an unsuitable place and descends in a suitable one.

396. Imepi candimasūriye evaṃmahiddhike evaṃmahānubhāve pāṇinā parāmasati parimajjatīti ettha candimasūriyānaṃ dvācattālīsayojanasahassassa upari caraṇena mahiddhikatā, tīsu dīpesu ekakkhaṇe ālokakaraṇena mahānubhāvatā veditabbā. Evaṃ upari caraṇaālokakaraṇehi vā mahiddhike teneva mahānubhāve. Parāmasatīti pariggaṇhati ekadese vā chupati. Parimajjatīti samantato ādāsatalaṃ viya parimajjati. Ayaṃ panassa iddhi abhiññāpādakajjhānavaseneva ijjhati, natthettha kasiṇasamāpattiniyamo. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ –

396. ‘Even these moon and sun, so powerful and mighty, he touches and strokes with his hand.’ Here, the great power of the moon and sun should be understood from their course above forty-two thousand yojanas, and their great might from illuminating the three continents in a single moment. Alternatively, by their course above and their illumination they are endowed with great power, and by that very fact, with great might. ‘He touches’ (parāmasati) means he grasps or touches a part. ‘He strokes’ (parimajjati) means he rubs all around like a mirror surface. This psychic power of his is accomplished solely by means of the jhāna that is the basis for the direct knowledges; there is no restriction here by way of kasiṇa attainment. For it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

“Imepi [M 2.0027] candimasūriye…pe… parimajjatīti idha so iddhimā cetovasippatto candimasūriye āvajjati, āvajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti – ‘hatthapāse hotū’ti. Hatthapāse hoti. So nisinnako vā nipannako vā candimasūriye pāṇinā āmasati parāmasati parimajjati. Yathā manussā pakatiyā aniddhimanto kiñcideva rūpagataṃ hatthapāse [V 2.0026] āmasanti parāmasanti parimajjanti, evameva so iddhimā…pe… parimajjatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.12).

“‘Even these moon and sun… he strokes.’ Here, one endowed with psychic power, having attained mastery of mind, adverts to the moon and sun. Having adverted, he determines with knowledge: ‘Let them be within arm’s reach.’ They are within arm’s reach. Whether seated or lying down, he touches, grasps, and strokes the moon and sun with his hand. Just as ordinary people, without psychic power, touch, grasp, or stroke some material thing within arm’s reach, so too does one endowed with psychic power… stroke them.”

Svāyaṃ yadi icchati gantvā parāmasituṃ, gantvā parāmasati, yadi pana idheva nisinnako vā nipannako vā parāmasitukāmo hoti, hatthapāse hotūti adhiṭṭhāti, adhiṭṭhānabalena vaṇṭā muttatālaphalaṃ viya āgantvā hatthapāse ṭhite vā parāmasati, hatthaṃ vā vaḍḍhetvā. Vaḍḍhentassa pana kiṃ upādiṇṇakaṃ vaḍḍhati, anupādiṇṇakanti? Upādiṇṇakaṃ nissāya anupādiṇṇakaṃ vaḍḍhati.

If this one wishes to go and touch them, he goes and touches them. But if, while seated or lying right there, he wishes to touch them, he determines: ‘Let them be within arm’s reach.’ By the power of his determination, like a palm fruit released from its stalk, they come and stand within arm’s reach, and he touches them; or he extends his hand and touches them. Now, when he extends it, does what is clung to extend, or what is not clung to? What is not clung to extends, dependent on what is clung to.

Tattha tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero āha “kiṃ panāvuso, upādiṇṇakaṃ khuddakampi mahantampi na hoti, nanu yadā bhikkhu tālacchiddādīhi nikkhamati, tadā upādiṇṇakaṃ khuddakaṃ hoti. Yadā mahantaṃ attabhāvaṃ karoti, tadā mahantaṃ hoti mahāmoggallānattherassa viyā”ti.

There, the elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga said: “But, friend, is it not the case that what is clung to is sometimes small and sometimes large? Indeed, when a bhikkhu passes through a keyhole or the like, then what is clung to is small. When he makes a large body, then it is large, like the elder Mahāmoggallāna’s was.”

Nandopanandanāgadamanakathā

The Story of the Taming of the Nāga Nandopananda

Ekasmiṃ kira samaye anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā “sve, bhante, pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ amhākaṃ gehe bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti nimantetvā pakkami. Bhagavā adhivāsetvā taṃdivasāvasesaṃ rattibhāgañca vītināmetvā paccūsasamaye dasasahassilokadhātuṃ olokesi. Athassa nandopanando nāma nāgarājā ñāṇamukhe āpāthamāgacchi. Bhagavā “ayaṃ nāgarājā mayhaṃ ñāṇamukhe āpāthamāgacchi, atthi nu kho assa upanissayo”ti āvajjento “ayaṃ micchādiṭṭhiko tīsu ratanesu appasannoti disvā ko nu kho imaṃ micchādiṭṭhito viveceyyā”ti āvajjento mahāmoggallānattheraṃ addasa.

On one occasion, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, invited him, saying, “Venerable sir, tomorrow, please accept alms in our home together with five hundred bhikkhus,” and then departed. The Blessed One, having accepted, spent the remainder of that day and the night, and at dawn surveyed the ten-thousandfold world-system. Then the Nāga king named Nandopananda came into the range of his knowledge. The Blessed One reflected, “This Nāga king has come into the range of my knowledge. Does he have a supporting condition?” Seeing that “He holds wrong views and has no faith in the Three Jewels,” he then reflected, “Who could separate him from this wrong view?” and he saw the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.

Tato [M 2.0028] pabhātāya rattiyā sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi – “ānanda, pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ ārocehi tathāgato devacārikaṃ gacchatī”ti. Taṃ divasañca nandopanandassa āpānabhūmiṃ sajjayiṃsu. So dibbaratanapallaṅke dibbena setacchattena dhāriyamānena tividhanāṭakehi ceva nāgaparisāya ca parivuto dibbabhājanesu upaṭṭhāpitaṃ annapānavidhiṃ olokayamāno nisinno hoti. Atha bhagavā yathā nāgarājā passati, tathā katvā tassa vitānamatthakeneva pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ tāvatiṃsadevalokābhimukho pāyāsi.

Then, when the night had dawned, having attended to his bodily needs, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda, “Ānanda, announce to the five hundred bhikkhus that the Tathāgata is going on a journey to the deva world.” On that day, they had prepared Nandopananda’s feasting ground. He was seated on a divine jeweled couch, with a divine white parasol held over him, surrounded by three kinds of dancers and a retinue of nāgas, surveying the arrangements of food and drink set out in divine vessels. Then the Blessed One, having made himself visible to the Nāga king, set out with the five hundred bhikkhus towards the Tāvatiṃsa deva world, passing right over the top of his canopy.

Tena [V 2.0027] kho pana samayena nandopanandassa nāgarājassa evarūpaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ uppannaṃ hoti – “ime hi nāma muṇḍakā samaṇakā amhākaṃ uparūparibhavanena devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ bhavanaṃ pavisantipi nikkhamantipi, na dāni ito paṭṭhāya imesaṃ amhākaṃ matthake pādapaṃsuṃ okirantānaṃ gantuṃ dassāmī”ti uṭṭhāya sinerupādaṃ gantvā taṃ attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā sineruṃ sattakkhattuṃ bhogehi parikkhipitvā upari phaṇaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ avakujjena phaṇena gahetvā adassanaṃ gamesi.

Now at that time, this evil wrong view had arisen in the Nāga king Nandopananda: “Indeed, these shaveling ascetics enter and leave the Tāvatiṃsa abode of the devas by passing right over our own abode! From now on, I will not allow them to pass, scattering the dust from their feet upon our heads.” Rising up, he went to the foot of Mount Sineru, abandoned his normal form, encircled Sineru seven times with his coils, spread his hood above, and then, covering the Tāvatiṃsa abode with his downturned hood, he made it invisible.

Atha kho āyasmā raṭṭhapālo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca “pubbe, bhante, imasmiṃ padese ṭhito sineruṃ passāmi, sineruparibhaṇḍaṃ passāmi, tāvatiṃsaṃ passāmi, vejayantaṃ passāmi, vejayantassa pāsādassa upari dhajaṃ passāmi. Ko nu kho, bhante, hetu ko paccayo, yaṃ etarahi neva sineruṃ passāmi…pe… na vejayantassa pāsādassa upari dhajaṃ passāmī”ti. “Ayaṃ, raṭṭhapāla, nandopanando nāma nāgarājā tumhākaṃ kupito sineruṃ sattakkhattuṃ bhogehi parikkhipitvā upari phaṇena paṭicchādetvā andhakāraṃ katvā ṭhito”ti. “Damemi naṃ, bhante”ti. Na bhagavā anujāni. Atha kho āyasmā bhaddiyo āyasmā rāhuloti anukkamena sabbepi bhikkhū uṭṭhahiṃsu. Na bhagavā anujāni.

Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, previously, while standing in this place, I could see Sineru, I could see the girdle of Sineru, I could see Tāvatiṃsa, I could see the Vejayanta palace, and I could see the banner atop the Vejayanta palace. What, venerable sir, is the reason, what is the cause, that I now see neither Sineru… nor the banner atop the Vejayanta palace?” “Raṭṭhapāla, the Nāga king named Nandopananda is angry with you all. He has encircled Sineru seven times with his coils, covered it with his hood, created darkness, and remains there.” “I will tame him, venerable sir,” he said. The Blessed One did not give permission. Then the Venerable Bhaddiya, the Venerable Rāhula, and so, in succession, all the bhikkhus rose up. The Blessed One did not give permission.

Avasāne mahāmoggallānatthero “ahaṃ, bhante, damemi na”nti āha. “Damehi moggallānā”ti bhagavā anujāni. Thero attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā mahantaṃ nāgarājavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā nandopanandaṃ cuddasakkhattuṃ bhogehi parikkhipitvā tassa phaṇamatthake attano phaṇaṃ ṭhapetvā sinerunā [M 2.0029] saddhiṃ abhinippīḷesi. Nāgarājā padhūmāyi. Theropi na tuyhaṃyeva sarīre dhūmo atthi, mayhampi atthīti padhūmāyi. Nāgarājassa dhūmo theraṃ na bādhati. Therassa pana dhūmo nāgarājānaṃ bādhati. Tato nāgarājā pajjali. Theropi na tuyhaṃyeva sarīre aggi atthi, mayhampi atthīti pajjali. Nāgarājassa tejo theraṃ na bādhati. Therassa pana tejo nāgarājānaṃ bādhati. Nāgarājā ayaṃ maṃ sinerunā abhinippīḷetvā dhūmāyati ceva pajjalati cāti cintetvā “bho tvaṃ kosī”ti paṭipucchi. “Ahaṃ kho, nanda, moggallāno”ti. “Bhante, attano bhikkhubhāvena tiṭṭhāhī”ti.

Finally, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna said, “Venerable sir, I will tame him.” “Tame him, Moggallāna,” the Blessed One gave permission. The Elder abandoned his own form, created the appearance of a great Nāga king, encircled Nandopananda fourteen times with his coils, placed his own hood on top of Nandopananda’s hood, and pressed down on him together with Sineru. The Nāga king emitted smoke. The Elder also emitted smoke, as if to say, “Smoke is not only in your body; it is in mine too.” The Nāga king’s smoke did not afflict the Elder, but the Elder’s smoke afflicted the Nāga king. Then the Nāga king burst into flames. The Elder also burst into flames, as if to say, “Fire is not only in your body; it is in mine too.” The Nāga king’s fire did not afflict the Elder, but the Elder’s fire afflicted the Nāga king. The Nāga king, thinking, “This one presses down on me with Sineru, emits smoke, and bursts into flames,” asked, “Sir, who are you?” “I, Nanda, am Moggallāna.” “Venerable sir, please remain in your form as a bhikkhu.”

Thero taṃ attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā tassa dakkhiṇakaṇṇasotena pavisitvā vāmakaṇṇasotena nikkhami[V 2.0028], vāmakaṇṇasotena pavisitvā dakkhiṇakaṇṇasotena nikkhami, tathā dakkhiṇanāsasotena pavisitvā vāmanāsasotena nikkhami, vāmanāsasotena pavisitvā dakkhiṇanāsasotena nikkhami. Tato nāgarājā mukhaṃ vivari. Thero mukhena pavisitvā antokucchiyaṃ pācīnena ca pacchimena ca caṅkamati. Bhagavā “moggallāna, manasikarohi mahiddhiko esa nāgo”ti āha. Thero “mayhaṃ kho, bhante, cattāro iddhipādā bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā, tiṭṭhatu, bhante, nandopanando, ahaṃ nandopanandasadisānaṃ nāgarājānaṃ satampi sahassampi satasahassampi dameyya”nti āha.

The Elder, abandoning that form, entered through the Nāga's right ear-passage and exited through the left; he entered through the left ear-passage and exited through the right. Likewise, he entered through the right nostril-passage and exited through the left; he entered through the left nostril-passage and exited through the right. Then the Nāga king opened his mouth. The Elder entered through his mouth and paced back and forth inside his belly, from east to west. The Blessed One said, “Moggallāna, be mindful! That Nāga has great psychic power.” The Elder replied: “Venerable sir, for me the four bases of psychic power have been developed, cultivated, made into a vehicle, made into a foundation, established, mastered, and well undertaken. Let Nandopananda be, venerable sir. I could tame a hundred or even a thousand Nāga kings like Nandopananda.”

Nāgarājā cintesi “pavisanto tāva me na diṭṭho, nikkhamanakāle dāni naṃ dāṭhantare pakkhipitvā saṅkhādissāmī”ti cintetvā nikkhama bhante, mā maṃ antokucchiyaṃ aparāparaṃ caṅkamanto bādhayitthāti āha. Thero nikkhamitvā bahi aṭṭhāsi. Nāgarājā ayaṃ soti disvā nāsavātaṃ vissajji. Thero catutthaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji. Lomakūpampissa vāto cāletuṃ nāsakkhi. Avasesā bhikkhū kira ādito paṭṭhāya sabbapāṭihāriyāni kātuṃ sakkuṇeyyuṃ, imaṃ pana ṭhānaṃ patvā evaṃ khippanisantino hutvā samāpajjituṃ na sakkhissantīti tesaṃ bhagavā nāgarājadamanaṃ nānujāni.

The Nāga king thought: “He was not seen by me when entering, but now at the time of his exit, I shall place him between my fangs and chew him to powder.” Having thought this, he said: “Come out, venerable sir. Do not trouble me by walking back and forth inside my belly.” The Elder came out and stood outside. The Nāga king, seeing him and thinking, "This is he," released a blast of wind from his nostrils. The Elder entered the fourth jhāna. The wind was unable to stir even a single hair follicle of his. It is said that while the other bhikkhus could perform all manner of miracles from the beginning, upon reaching this point, however, they would not be able to attain absorption by becoming so quick in perception. Therefore, the Blessed One did not permit them to tame the Nāga king.

Nāgarājā [M 2.0030] “ahaṃ imassa samaṇassa nāsavātena lomakūpampi cāletuṃ nāsakkhiṃ, mahiddhiko samaṇo”ti cintesi. Thero attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā supaṇṇarūpaṃ abhinimminitvā supaṇṇavātaṃ dassento nāgarājānaṃ anubandhi. Nāgarājā taṃ attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā māṇavakavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā “bhante, tumhākaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti vadanto therassa pāde vandi. Thero “satthā, nanda, āgato, ehi gamissāmā”ti nāgarājānaṃ damayitvā nibbisaṃ katvā gahetvā bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi. Nāgarājā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā “bhante, tumhākaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti āha. Bhagavā “sukhī hohi, nāgarājā”ti vatvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto anāthapiṇḍikassa nivesanaṃ agamāsi.

The Nāga king thought: “With the wind from my nostrils, I was unable to stir even a hair follicle of this ascetic; this ascetic is of great psychic power.” The Elder, abandoning his own form, created the form of a Garuḍa and, displaying the Garuḍa-wind, pursued the Nāga king. The Nāga king, abandoning that form, created the form of a young man and, saying, “Venerable sir, I go to you for refuge,” bowed at the Elder’s feet. The Elder said: “Nanda, the Teacher has come. Come, let us go.” Having thus subdued the Nāga king, making him free of venom, he took him and went to the presence of the Blessed One. The Nāga king bowed to the Blessed One and said: “Venerable sir, I go to you for refuge.” The Blessed One said: “May you be well, Nāga king,” and, surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, he went to Anāthapiṇḍika’s residence.

Anāthapiṇḍiko “kiṃ, bhante, atidivā āgatatthā”ti āha. Moggallānassa ca nandopanandassa ca saṅgāmo ahosīti. Kassa, bhante, jayo, kassa parājayoti. Moggallānassa jayo, nandassa parājayoti. Anāthapiṇḍiko “adhivāsetu me, bhante, bhagavā sattāhaṃ [V 2.0029] ekapaṭipāṭiyā bhattaṃ, sattāhaṃ therassa sakkāraṃ karissāmī”ti vatvā sattāhaṃ buddhapamukhānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ akāsi. Iti imaṃ imasmiṃ nandopanandadamane kataṃ mahantaṃ attabhāvaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “yadā mahantaṃ attabhāvaṃ karoti, tadā mahantaṃ hoti mahāmoggallānattherassa viyā”ti. Evaṃ vuttepi bhikkhū upādiṇṇakaṃ nissāya anupādiṇṇakameva vaḍḍhatīti āhaṃsu. Ayameva cettha yutti.

Anāthapiṇḍika asked: “Why, venerable sir, have you come so late in the day?” “There was a battle between Moggallāna and Nandopananda.” “Whose, venerable sir, was the victory, and whose the defeat?” “Moggallāna’s was the victory, Nanda’s the defeat.” Anāthapiṇḍika then said: “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One consent to my offering of a meal for seven days in continuous succession. For seven days, I will pay homage to the Elder.” Having said this, for seven days he made a great offering to the five hundred bhikkhus with the Buddha at their head. Thus, with reference to this great form created in the taming of Nandopananda, it was said: “When he creates a great form, it is great like that of the great Elder Mahāmoggallāna.” Even when this was said, the bhikkhus stated: “It is only the unappropriated matter that increases, based on the appropriated matter.” This, indeed, is the correct reasoning here.

So evaṃ katvā na kevalaṃ candimasūriye parāmasati. Sace icchati pādakathalikaṃ katvā pāde ṭhapeti, pīṭhaṃ katvā nisīdati, mañcaṃ katvā nipajjati, apassenaphalakaṃ katvā apassayati. Yathā ca eko, evaṃ aparopi. Anekesupi hi bhikkhusatasahassesu evaṃ karontesu tesañca ekamekassa tatheva ijjhati. Candimasūriyānañca gamanampi ālokakaraṇampi tatheva hoti. Yathā hi pātisahassesu udakapūresu sabbapātīsu ca candamaṇḍalāni dissanti. Pākatikameva ca candassa gamanaṃ ālokakaraṇañca hoti. Tathūpamametaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ.

Having done so, he not only touches and strokes the moon and sun. If he wishes, he can create a foot-scraper and place his feet on it, create a chair and sit on it, create a couch and lie on it, or create a backrest and lean against it. And as one can do this, so can another. Indeed, even if hundreds of thousands of bhikkhus were doing this, it would succeed in the same way for each and every one of them. And the movement of the moon and sun and their giving of light would continue just as before. It is like how, in thousands of bowls filled with water, the orb of the moon is seen in every bowl, while the natural movement of the moon and its giving of light continue. This miracle is of such a nature.

397. Yāva brahmalokāpīti brahmalokampi paricchedaṃ katvā. Kāyena vasaṃ vattetīti tattha brahmaloke kāyena attano vasaṃ vatteti. Tassattho pāḷiṃ anugantvā veditabbo. Ayañhettha pāḷi –

397. ‘Even up to the Brahmā world’ means: having made the Brahmā world the limit. ‘He wields mastery with the body’ means: there, in the Brahmā world, he wields mastery with his body according to his will. Its meaning is to be understood by referring to the Pāḷi. This, here, is the Pāḷi:

“Yāva [M 2.0031] brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vattetīti. Sace so iddhimā cetovasippatto brahmalokaṃ gantukāmo hoti, dūrepi santike adhiṭṭhāti santike hotūti, santike hoti. Santikepi dūre adhiṭṭhāti dūre hotūti, dūre hoti. Bahukampi thokanti adhiṭṭhāti thokaṃ hotūti, thokaṃ hoti. Thokampi bahukanti adhiṭṭhāti bahukaṃ hotūti, bahukaṃ hoti. Dibbena cakkhunā tassa brahmuno rūpaṃ passati. Dibbāya sotadhātuyā tassa brahmuno saddaṃ suṇāti. Cetopariyañāṇena tassa brahmuno cittaṃ pajānāti. Sace so iddhimā cetovasippatto dissamānena kāyena brahmalokaṃ gantukāmo hoti, kāyavasena cittaṃ pariṇāmeti, kāyavasena cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, kāyavasena cittaṃ pariṇāmetvā kāyavasena cittaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamitvā dissamānena kāyena brahmalokaṃ gacchati. Sace so iddhimā cetovasippatto adissamānena kāyena brahmalokaṃ gantukāmo hoti, cittavasena kāyaṃ pariṇāmeti, cittavasena [V 2.0030] kāyaṃ adhiṭṭhāti. Cittavasena kāyaṃ pariṇāmetvā cittavasena kāyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamitvā adissamānena kāyena brahmalokaṃ gacchati. So tassa brahmuno purato rūpaṃ abhinimmināti manomayaṃ sabbaṅgapañcaṅgiṃ ahīnindriyaṃ. Sace so iddhimā caṅkamati, nimmitopi tattha caṅkamati. Sace so iddhimā tiṭṭhati, nisīdati, seyyaṃ kappeti, nimmitopi tattha seyyaṃ kappeti. Sace so iddhimā dhūmāyati, pajjalati, dhammaṃ bhāsati, pañhaṃ pucchati, pañhaṃ puṭṭho vissajjeti, nimmitopi tattha pañhaṃ puṭṭho vissajjeti. Sace so iddhimā tena brahmunā saddhiṃ santiṭṭhati, sallapati, sākacchaṃ samāpajjati, nimmitopi tattha tena brahmunā saddhiṃ santiṭṭhati, sallapati, sākacchaṃ samāpajjati. Yaṃ yadeva hi so iddhimā karoti, taṃ tadeva nimmito karotī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.12).

“As for the saying, ‘He wields mastery with the body even up to the Brahma world’: If that one with psychic powers, having attained mastery of the mind, wishes to go to the Brahma world, he resolves regarding what is far, ‘Let it be near!’ and it becomes near. He resolves regarding what is near, ‘Let it be far!’ and it becomes far. He resolves regarding what is much, ‘Let it be little!’ and it becomes little. He resolves regarding what is little, ‘Let it be much!’ and it becomes much. With the divine eye, he sees the form of that Brahma. With the divine ear element, he hears the sound of that Brahma. With the knowledge of others’ minds, he knows the mind of that Brahma. If that one with psychic powers, having attained mastery of the mind, wishes to go to the Brahma world with a visible body, he directs the mind by means of the body and resolves the mind by means of the body. Having directed the mind by means of the body and resolved the mind by means of the body, and having entered into the perception of ease and the perception of lightness, he goes to the Brahma world with a visible body. If that one with psychic powers, having attained mastery of the mind, wishes to go to the Brahma world with an invisible body, he directs the body by means of the mind and resolves the body by means of the mind. Having directed the body by means of the mind and resolved the body by means of the mind, and having entered into the perception of ease and the perception of lightness, he goes to the Brahma world with an invisible body. He creates in front of that Brahma a mind-made form, complete in all its major and minor parts, with unimpaired faculties. If that one with psychic powers walks, the created one also walks there. If that one with psychic powers stands, sits, or lies down, the created one also lies down there. If that one with psychic powers emits smoke, blazes, speaks the Dhamma, asks a question, or answers a question when asked, the created one also answers the question there when asked. If that one with psychic powers stands together with that Brahma, converses, or engages in discussion, the created one also stands together with that Brahma, converses, and engages in discussion there. For whatever that one with psychic powers does, that very same thing the created one does.”

Tattha [M 2.0032] dūrepi santike adhiṭṭhātīti pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya dūre devalokaṃ vā brahmalokaṃ vā āvajjati santike hotūti. Āvajjitvā parikammaṃ katvā puna samāpajjitvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti santike hotūti, santike hoti. Esa nayo sesapadesupi.

Herein, ‘he resolves regarding what is far as near’ means this: emerging from the foundational jhāna, he adverts to a distant deva-world or Brahma-world, thinking, ‘Let it be near!’ Having adverted and performed the preliminary work, he enters the attainment again and resolves with knowledge, ‘Let it be near!’—and it becomes near. This same method should be understood in the remaining phrases as well.

Tattha ko dūraṃ gahetvā santikaṃ akāsīti? Bhagavā. Bhagavā hi yamakapāṭihāriyāvasāne devalokaṃ gacchanto yugandharañca sineruñca santike katvā pathavītalato ekapādaṃ yugandhare patiṭṭhapetvā dutiyaṃ sinerumatthake ṭhapesi. Añño ko akāsi? Mahāmoggallānatthero. Thero hi sāvatthito bhattakiccaṃ katvā nikkhantaṃ dvādasayojanikaṃ parisaṃ tiṃsayojanaṃ saṅkassanagaramaggaṃ saṅkhipitvā taṅkhaṇaññeva sampāpesi.

In this context, who took what was far and made it near? The Blessed One did. For at the conclusion of the Twin Miracle, the Blessed One, while going to the deva world, made Mount Yugandhara and Mount Sineru near. From the earth's surface, he placed one foot on the peak of Yugandhara and the second on the summit of Sineru. Who else did so? The Elder Mahāmoggallāna did. For the elder, having finished his meal and departed from Sāvatthī, shortened the thirty-yojana road to the city of Saṅkassa for the twelve-yojana-long assembly that had departed, and made them arrive in that very moment.

Apica tambapaṇṇidīpe cūḷasamuddattheropi akāsi. Dubbhikkhasamaye kira therassa santikaṃ pātova satta bhikkhusatāni āgamaṃsu. Thero “mahā bhikkhusaṅgho kuhiṃ bhikkhācāro bhavissatī”ti cintento sakalatambapaṇṇidīpe adisvā “paratīre pāṭaliputte bhavissatī”ti disvā bhikkhū pattacīvaraṃ gāhāpetvā “ethāvuso, bhikkhācāraṃ gamissāmā”ti pathaviṃ saṅkhipitvā pāṭaliputtaṃ gato. Bhikkhū “kataraṃ, bhante, imaṃ nagara”nti pucchiṃsu. Pāṭaliputtaṃ, āvusoti. Pāṭaliputtaṃ nāma dūre bhanteti. Āvuso, mahallakattherā nāma dūrepi gahetvā santike karontīti. Mahāsamuddo kuhiṃ, bhanteti? Nanu, āvuso, antarā ekaṃ nīlamātikaṃ atikkamitvā [V 2.0031] āgatatthāti? Āma, bhante. Mahāsamuddo pana mahantoti. Āvuso, mahallakattherā nāma mahantampi khuddakaṃ karontīti.

Moreover, on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, the Elder Cūḷasamudda also did this. It is said that during a time of famine, seven hundred monks came to the Elder's presence early in the morning. The Elder, thinking, ‘The community of monks is large. Where will there be an alms-round?’ and seeing no place in the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi, he perceived, ‘There will be one on the far shore in Pāṭaliputta.’ Having had the monks take their bowls and robes, he said, ‘Come, friends, we shall go for an alms-round.’ Then, by contracting the earth, he went to Pāṭaliputta. The monks asked, ‘Venerable sir, what city is this?’ ‘It is Pāṭaliputta, friends.’ ‘But, venerable sir, is not Pāṭaliputta far away?’ ‘Friends, great elders are able to take what is far and make it near.’ ‘Venerable sir, where is the great ocean?’ ‘Friends, did you not come here having crossed a dark watercourse along the way?’ ‘Yes, venerable sir.’ ‘But the great ocean is vast.’ ‘Friends, great elders are able to make even what is vast small.’”

Yathā cāyaṃ, evaṃ tissadattattheropi sāyanhasamaye nhāyitvā katuttarāsaṅgo mahābodhiṃ vandissāmīti citte uppanne santike akāsi.

Just as this elder did, so too the Elder Tissadatta, in the evening after bathing and putting on his upper robe, when the thought, ‘I will pay homage to the Great Bodhi Tree,’ arose, he made it near.

Santikaṃ pana gahetvā ko dūramakāsīti? Bhagavā. Bhagavā hi attano ca aṅgulimālassa (ma. ni. 2.348) ca antaraṃ santikampi dūramakāsīti.

But who, taking what was near, made it far? The Blessed One did. For the Blessed One made even the short distance between himself and Aṅgulimāla far.

Atha ko bahukaṃ thokaṃ akāsīti? Mahākassapatthero. Rājagahe kira nakkhattadivase pañcasatā kumāriyo candapūve gahetvā nakkhattakīḷanatthāya gacchantiyo bhagavantaṃ disvā kiñci nādaṃsu. Pacchato āgacchantaṃ pana theraṃ disvā amhākaṃ thero eti pūvaṃ dassāmāti sabbā pūve [M 2.0033] gahetvā theraṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu. Thero pattaṃ nīharitvā sabbaṃ ekapattapūramattamakāsi. Bhagavā theraṃ āgamayamāno purato nisīdi. Thero āharitvā bhagavato adāsi.

Then, who made what was much into what was little? The Elder Mahākassapa did. It is said that in Rājagaha, on a festival day, five hundred maidens, taking moon-cakes, were going to enjoy the festival. Seeing the Blessed One, they gave nothing. But seeing the Elder coming behind them, they thought, ‘Our elder is coming; let us give him a cake.’ All of them, taking their cakes, approached the elder. The elder took out his bowl and made all of them into a single bowlful. The Blessed One, waiting for the elder, was seated ahead. The elder brought the bowl and gave it to the Blessed One.

Illisaseṭṭhivatthusmiṃ pana mahāmoggallānatthero thokaṃ bahukamakāsi, kākavaliyavatthusmiñca bhagavā. Mahākassapatthero kira sattāhaṃ samāpattiyā vītināmetvā daliddasaṅgahaṃ karonto kākavaliyassa nāma duggatamanussassa gharadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Tassa jāyā theraṃ disvā patino pakkaṃ aloṇambilayāguṃ patte ākiri. Thero taṃ gahetvā bhagavato hatthe ṭhapesi. Bhagavā mahābhikkhusaṅghassa pahonakaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Ekapattena ābhatā sabbesaṃ pahosi. Kākavaliyopi sattame divase seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ alatthāti.

Furthermore, in the story of Illisaseṭṭhi, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna made a little into much, and in the story of Kākavaliya, the Blessed One did likewise. It is said that the Elder Mahākassapa, having spent seven days in attainment, while undertaking to assist the poor, stood at the door of a destitute man named Kākavaliya. The man’s wife, seeing the elder, poured the cooked, saltless sour gruel prepared for her husband into the bowl. The elder took it and placed it in the Blessed One’s hand. The Blessed One, having made it sufficient for the great community of monks, made a determination. What was brought in a single bowl sufficed for all. Kākavaliya, too, attained the position of a wealthy man on the seventh day.

Na kevalañca thokassa bahukaraṇaṃ, madhuraṃ amadhuraṃ, amadhuraṃ madhurantiādīsupi yaṃ yaṃ icchati, sabbaṃ iddhimato ijjhati. Tathā hi mahāanuḷatthero nāma sambahule bhikkhū piṇḍāya caritvā sukkhabhattameva labhitvā gaṅgātīre nisīditvā paribhuñjamāne disvā gaṅgāya udakaṃ sappimaṇḍanti adhiṭṭhahitvā sāmaṇerānaṃ saññaṃ adāsi. Te thālakehi āharitvā bhikkhusaṅghassa adaṃsu. Sabbe madhurena sappimaṇḍena bhuñjiṃsūti.

And it is not only the making of a little into much; in matters such as making the sweet unsweet and the unsweet sweet, whatever one with psychic power wishes, all is accomplished. For instance, when the Elder named Mahāanuḷa saw many monks who, having gone for alms, had received only dry food and were sitting and eating on the bank of the Ganges, he determined, 'Let the water of the Ganges become ghee,' and gave a sign to the novices. They brought it in small bowls and gave it to the community of monks. All ate with the sweet ghee.

Dibbena [V 2.0032] cakkhunāti idheva ṭhito ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā tassa brahmuno rūpaṃ passati. Idheva ca ṭhito sabbaṃ tassa bhāsato saddaṃ suṇāti. Cittaṃ pajānāti. Kāyavasena cittaṃ pariṇāmetīti karajakāyassa vasena cittaṃ pariṇāmeti. Pādakajjhānacittaṃ gahetvā kāye āropeti. Kāyānugatikaṃ karoti dandhagamanaṃ. Kāyagamanaṃ hi dandhaṃ hoti. Sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamatīti pādakajjhānārammaṇena iddhicittena sahajātaṃ sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamati pavisati phasseti sampāpuṇāti. Sukhasaññā nāma upekkhāsampayuttasaññā. Upekkhā hi santaṃ sukhanti vuttā. Sāyeva ca saññā nīvaraṇehi ceva vitakkādīhi paccanīkehi ca vimuttattā lahusaññātipi veditabbā. Taṃ okkantassa panassa karajakāyopi tūlapicu viya sallahuko hoti. So evaṃ vāyukkhittatūlapicunā [M 2.0034] viya sallahukena dissamānena kāyena brahmalokaṃ gacchati. Evaṃ gacchanto ca sace icchati pathavīkasiṇavasena ākāse maggaṃ nimminitvā padasā gacchati. Sace icchati vāyokasiṇavasena vāyuṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā tūlapicu viya vāyunā gacchati. Apica gantukāmatā eva ettha pamāṇaṃ. “Sati hi gantukāmatāya” evaṃ katacittādhiṭṭhāno adhiṭṭhānavegukkhittova so issāsakhittasaro viya dissamāno gacchati.

With the divine eye: standing right here, he extends the light and sees the form of that brahmā. And standing right here, he hears all the sounds of his speech. He knows his mind. 'He makes the mind conform to the body' means he makes the mind conform by means of the physical body. He takes the mind of the basic jhāna and imposes it on the body. He makes the going slow, in conformity with the body. For the body’s movement is slow. 'He enters upon the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness' means he enters upon, penetrates, contacts, and attains the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness that have arisen together with the mind of psychic power, which has the basic jhāna as its object. The perception of pleasure is the name for perception associated with equanimity. For equanimity, being peaceful, is called 'pleasure.' And that same perception, because it is liberated from the hindrances and from opposing states such as initial thought, should also be understood as the perception of lightness. When he has entered upon that, his physical body becomes very light, like a tuft of cotton wool. Thus, with a visible body as light as a tuft of cotton wool tossed by the wind, he goes to the brahmā world. And when going thus, if he wishes, by means of the earth-kasiṇa he creates a path in the air and goes on foot. If he wishes, by means of the air-kasiṇa he determines the air and goes by the air like a tuft of cotton wool. Moreover, the desire to go is the measure here. For when there is the desire to go, having thus made the mind-determination, launched by the impetus of his determination, he goes visibly, like an arrow shot by an archer.

Cittavasena kāyaṃ pariṇāmetīti kāyaṃ gahetvā citte āropeti. Cittānugatikaṃ karoti sīghagamanaṃ. Cittagamanaṃ hi sīghaṃ hoti. Sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamatīti rūpakāyārammaṇena iddhicittena sahajātaṃ sukhasaññañca lahusaññañca okkamatīti. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ pana cittagamanameva hoti. Evaṃ adissamānena kāyena gacchanto panāyaṃ kiṃ tassa adhiṭṭhānacittassa uppādakkhaṇe gacchati, udāhu ṭhitikkhaṇe bhaṅgakkhaṇe vāti vutte tīsupi khaṇesu gacchatīti thero āha. Kiṃ pana so sayaṃ gacchati nimmitaṃ pesetīti. Yathāruci karoti. Idha panassa sayaṃ gamanameva āgataṃ.

'He makes the body conform to the mind' means he takes the body and imposes it on the mind. He makes the going swift, in conformity with the mind. For the movement of the mind is swift. 'He enters upon the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness' means he enters upon the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness that have arisen together with the mind of psychic power, which has the physical body as its object. The rest should be understood in the way already described. This, however, is just like the movement of the mind. When he is going thus with an invisible body, does he go at the arising moment of that mind of determination, or at its presence moment, or at its dissolution moment? When this was said, an elder replied that he goes in all three moments. But does he go himself or does he send a created form? He does as he wishes. Here, however, his own going is what is presented.

Manomayanti adhiṭṭhānamanena nimmitattā manomayaṃ. Ahīnindriyanti idaṃ cakkhusotādīnaṃ saṇṭhānavasena vuttaṃ. Nimmitarūpe pana pasādo nāma natthi. Sace iddhimā caṅkamati nimmitopi tattha caṅkamatītiādi sabbaṃ sāvakanimmitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Buddhanimmito pana yaṃ yaṃ bhagavā karoti, taṃ tampi karoti. Bhagavato rucivasena aññampi karotīti. Ettha ca yaṃ so iddhimā idheva ṭhito dibbena cakkhunā rūpaṃ passati, dibbāya sotadhātuyā saddaṃ suṇāti, cetopariyañāṇena [V 2.0033] cittaṃ pajānāti, na ettāvatā kāyena vasaṃ vatteti. Yampi so idheva ṭhito tena brahmunā saddhiṃ santiṭṭhati sallapati sākacchaṃ samāpajjati, ettāvatāpi na kāyena vasaṃ vatteti. Yampissa dūrepi santike adhiṭṭhātītiādikaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ, ettāvatāpi na kāyena vasaṃ vatteti. Yampi so dissamānena vā adissamānena vā kāyena brahmalokaṃ gacchati, ettāvatāpi na kāyena vasaṃ vatteti. Yañca kho so tassa brahmuno purato rūpaṃ abhinimminātītiādinā nayena [M 2.0035] vuttavidhānaṃ āpajjati, ettāvatā kāyena vasaṃ vatteti nāmaṃ. Sesaṃ panettha kāyena vasaṃ vattanāya pubbabhāgadassanatthaṃ vuttanti ayaṃ tāva adhiṭṭhānā iddhi.

'Mind-made': because it is created by the mind of determination, it is called mind-made. 'With faculties undiminished': this is said with reference to the configuration of the eye, ear, and so on. But in a created form, there is no such thing as sensitive matter. The entire passage beginning, 'If the one with psychic power walks, the created form also walks there,' is said in reference to a creation by a disciple. A creation of a Buddha, however, does whatever the Blessed One does; and by the Blessed One’s wish, it can also do other things. And herein, when that one with psychic power, standing right here, sees a form with the divine eye, hears a sound with the divine ear-element, or knows a mind with the knowledge of others’ minds, he does not yet, by that much, exercise mastery with the body. When, standing right here, he stands with that brahmā, converses with him, or engages in discussion, even by that much he does not exercise mastery with the body. And whatever determination he makes, such as 'he determines what is far to be near,' even by that much he does not exercise mastery with the body. And when he goes to the brahmā world with a visible or invisible body, even by that much he does not exercise mastery with the body. But when he accomplishes the procedure described in the passage beginning, 'He creates a form in front of that brahmā,' it is by this much that he is called one who exercises mastery with the body. The rest here has been said to show the preliminary part of exercising mastery with the body. This, for now, is the psychic power of determination.

398. Vikubbanāya pana manomayāya ca idaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ. Vikubbanaṃ tāva karontena “so pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā kumārakavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, nāgavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, supaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, asuravaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, indavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, devavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, brahmavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, samuddavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, pabbatavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, sīhavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, byagghavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, dīpivaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, hatthimpi dasseti, assampi dasseti, rathampi dasseti, pattimpi dasseti, vividhampi senābyūhaṃ dassetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.13) evaṃ vuttesu kumārakavaṇṇādīsu yaṃ yaṃ ākaṅkhati, taṃ taṃ adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Adhiṭṭhahantena ca pathavīkasiṇādīsu aññatarārammaṇato abhiññāpādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya attano kumārakavaṇṇo āvajjitabbo. Āvajjitvā parikammāvasāne puna samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya evarūpo nāma kumārako homīti adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Saha adhiṭṭhānacittena kumārako hoti devadatto viya (cūḷava. 333). Esa nayo sabbattha.

398. Furthermore, this is the distinction between the power of transformation and the mind-made power. First, regarding transformation: when one performs a transformation, 'having abandoned one's natural appearance, one displays the appearance of a boy, or displays the appearance of a nāga, or displays the appearance of a garuḍa, or displays the appearance of an asura, or displays the appearance of Indra, or displays the appearance of a deva, or displays the appearance of Brahmā, or displays the appearance of the ocean, or displays the appearance of a mountain, or displays the appearance of a lion, or displays the appearance of a tiger, or displays the appearance of a leopard; one displays an elephant, one displays a horse, one displays a chariot, one displays infantry, one displays various military arrays' (Paṭi. Ma. 3.13). Among these appearances mentioned, such as that of a boy, whatever one desires should be determined. When determining, one should emerge from the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, which has one of the kasiṇas as its object, and advert to the appearance of a boy for oneself. Having adverted and completed the preliminary work, one should re-enter the jhāna, emerge, and determine: 'May I become a boy of such a kind.' Simultaneously with the mind-moment of determination, one becomes a boy, like Devadatta (Cūḷavagga 333). This is the method in all cases.

Hatthimpi dassetītiādi panettha bahiddhāpi hatthiādidassanavasena vuttaṃ. Tattha hatthī homīti anadhiṭṭhahitvā hatthī hotūti adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ, assādīsupi eseva nayoti. Ayaṃ vikubbanā iddhi.

The phrase 'one displays an elephant,' etc., is said here also with reference to displaying external things such as elephants. There, instead of determining, 'I shall be an elephant,' one should determine, 'Let there be an elephant.' This is the method for horses and so on too. This is the psychic power of transformation.

399. Manomayaṃ kātukāmo pana pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya kāyaṃ tāva āvajjitvā vuttanayeneva susiro hotūti adhiṭṭhāti, susiro hoti. Athassa abbhantare aññaṃ kāyaṃ āvajjitvā parikammaṃ katvā vuttanayeneva adhiṭṭhāti, tassa abbhantare añño kāyo hotūti. So taṃ muñjamhā īsikaṃ viya kosiyā asiṃ viya karaṇḍāya ahiṃ viya ca abbāhati[V 2.0034]. Tena vuttaṃ “idha bhikkhu imamhā kāyā aññaṃ kāyaṃ abhinimmināti rūpiṃ manomayaṃ sabbaṅgapaccaṅgiṃ ahīnindriyaṃ. Seyyathāpi puriso muñjamhā īsikaṃ pavāheyya, tassa evamassa ayaṃ muñjo ayaṃ īsikā[M 2.0036], añño muñjo aññā īsikā, muñjamhātveva īsikā pavāḷhā”tiādi (paṭi. ma. 3.14). Ettha ca yathā īsikādayo muñjādīhi sadisā honti, evaṃ manomayarūpaṃ iddhimatāsadisameva hotīti dassanatthaṃ etā upamā vuttāti. Ayaṃ manomayā iddhi.

399. One who wishes to create a mind-made body, however, should emerge from the basic jhāna and first advert to his own body. Then, in the way already described, he determines, 'Let it be hollow,' and it becomes hollow. Next, having adverted to another body inside it and done the preliminary work, he determines in the way already described, 'Let another body be inside it,' and another body comes to be inside it. He draws it out like a reed from its sheath, a sword from its scabbard, or a snake from its basket. Hence it is said: 'Here, a bhikkhu creates from this body another body—material, mind-made, complete with all its limbs and parts, not deficient in any faculty. It is just as if a man were to draw a reed from its sheath. He would know: "This is the reed, this is the sheath. The reed is one thing, the sheath another. It is from the sheath that the reed has been drawn."' and so on (Paṭi. Ma. 3.14). And here, these similes are given to show that just as the reed and so on are similar to the sheath and so on, so the mind-made form is similar to the one possessing psychic power. This is the psychic power of the mind-made body.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in The Path of Purification, composed for the delight of good people,

Iddhividhaniddeso nāma

The Exposition of Psychic Powers

Dvādasamo paricchedo.

The Twelfth Chapter.

13. Abhiññāniddeso

THE EXPOSITION OF THE DIRECT KNOWLEDGES

Dibbasotadhātukathā

The Account of the Divine Ear Element

400. Idāni [M 2.0037][V 2.0035] dibbasotadhātuyā niddesakkamo anuppatto. Tattha tato parāsu ca tīsu abhiññāsu so evaṃ samāhite cittetiādīnaṃ (dī. ni. 1.240 ādayo) attho vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Sabbattha pana visesamattameva vaṇṇayissāma. Tatra dibbāya sotadhātuyāti ettha dibbasadisattā dibbā. Devānaṃ hi sucaritakammanibbattā pittasemharuhirādīhi apalibuddhā upakkilesavimuttatāya dūrepi ārammaṇaṃ sampaṭicchanasamatthā dibbapasādasotadhātu hoti. Ayañcāpi imassa bhikkhuno vīriyabhāvanābalanibbattā ñāṇasotadhātu tādisāyevāti dibbasadisattā dibbā. Apica dibbavihāravasena paṭiladdhattā attanā ca dibbavihārasannissitattāpi dibbā. Savanaṭṭhena nijjīvaṭṭhena ca sotadhātu. Sotadhātukiccakaraṇena ca sotadhātu viyātipi sotadhātu. Tāya dibbāya sotadhātuyā.

13. Now the turn for the exposition of the divine ear element has come. In this and in the three direct knowledges that follow, the meaning of the passage beginning 'With his mind thus concentrated...' (Dī. Ni. 1.240, etc.) should be understood in the way already stated. We shall, however, comment only on the specific points in each case. Herein, in the phrase 'with the divine ear element': it is 'divine' (dibba) because it is like the divine. For the devas have a sensitive ear element produced by wholesome kamma, which is unimpeded by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., and is capable of receiving even distant objects because it is free from defilements. And this bhikkhu’s knowledge-ear-element, produced by the power of the development of energy, is also of the same kind; hence it is called 'divine' because it is like the divine. Furthermore, it is 'divine' because it is obtained by means of the divine abiding and because it is itself dependent on the divine abiding. It is an 'ear element' (sotadhātu) in the sense of hearing and in the sense of being non-sentient. And because it performs the function of the ear element, it is like an ear element, thus it is an 'ear element.' With that divine ear element...

Visuddhāyāti parisuddhāya nirupakkilesāya. Atikkantamānusikāyāti manussūpacāraṃ atikkamitvā saddasavanena mānusikaṃ maṃsasotadhātuṃ atikkantāya vītivattitvā ṭhitāya. Ubho sadde suṇātīti dve sadde suṇāti. Katame dve? Dibbe ca mānuse ca, devānañca manussānañca saddeti vuttaṃ hoti. Etena padesapariyādānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ye dūre santike cāti ye saddā dūre paracakkavāḷepi ye ca santike antamaso sadehasannissitapāṇakasaddāpi, te suṇātīti vuttaṃ hoti. Etena nippadesapariyādānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

‘Purified’ means perfectly pure, free from defilements. ‘Surpassing the human’ means that, by hearing sounds beyond the human range, it has surpassed the human fleshly ear element and stands having gone beyond it. ‘He hears both sounds’ means he hears two sounds. Which two? Divine and human, that is, the sounds of gods and humans. By this, a partial comprehension should be understood. ‘Those that are distant and those that are near’ means he hears sounds that are far away, even in other world-systems, as well as those nearby, even down to the sounds of creatures dependent on his own body. By this, a complete comprehension should be understood.

Kathaṃ panāyaṃ uppādetabbāti? Tena bhikkhunā abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya parikammasamādhicittena paṭhamataraṃ pakatisotapathe dūre oḷāriko araññe sīhādīnaṃ saddo āvajjitabbo. Vihāre ghaṇḍisaddo, bherisaddo, saṅkhasaddo, sāmaṇeradaharabhikkhūnaṃ sabbathāmena sajjhāyantānaṃ [V 2.0036] sajjhāyanasaddo, pakatikathaṃ kathentānaṃ “kiṃ bhante, kimāvuso”tiādisaddo, sakuṇasaddo, vātasaddo, padasaddo, pakkuthitaudakassa [M 2.0038] cicciṭāyanasaddo, ātape sussamānatālapaṇṇasaddo, kunthakipillikādisaddoti evaṃ sabboḷārikato pabhuti yathākkamena sukhumasaddā āvajjitabbā. Tena puratthimāya disāya saddānaṃ saddanimittaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Pacchimāya, uttarāya, dakkhiṇāya, heṭṭhimāya, uparimāya disāya, puratthimāya anudisāya, pacchimāya, uttarāya, dakkhiṇāya anudisāya saddānaṃ saddanimittaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Oḷārikānampi sukhumānampi saddānaṃ saddanimittaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Tassa te saddā pākatikacittassāpi pākaṭā honti. Parikammasamādhicittassa pana ativiya pākaṭā.

But how is this to be produced? That bhikkhu, having attained the absorption that is the basis for direct knowledge, should emerge and, with a mind in preparatory concentration, first advert to a coarse sound in the normal range of hearing in a remote forest—such as the sound of lions, etc. In a monastery, he should advert to the sound of a gong, the sound of a drum, the sound of a conch shell, the sound of recitation by young novices and junior bhikkhus reciting with all their might, the sound of ordinary conversation like 'What, venerable sir? What, friend?' and so on, the sound of birds, the sound of wind, the sound of footsteps, the sizzling sound of boiling water, the sound of palm leaves drying in the sun, the sound of ants and other insects—thus, from the coarsest onwards, he should gradually advert to subtle sounds in due order. He should attend to the sign of sound in the eastern direction, then in the western, northern, southern, lower, and upper directions, and in the southeastern, southwestern, northwestern, and northeastern intermediate directions. He should attend to the sign of both coarse and subtle sounds. For him, those sounds are manifest even to a normal mind, but they are exceedingly manifest to a mind in preparatory concentration.

Tassevaṃ saddanimittaṃ manasikaroto idāni dibbasotadhātu uppajjissatīti tesu saddesu aññataraṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā manodvārāvajjanaṃ uppajjati. Tasmiṃ niruddhe cattāri pañca vā javanāni javanti, yesaṃ purimāni tīṇi cattāri vā parikammaupacārānulomagotrabhunāmakāni kāmāvacarāni, catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ vā appanācittaṃ rūpāvacaraṃ catutthajjhānikaṃ. Tattha yaṃ tena appanācittena saddhiṃ uppannaṃ ñāṇaṃ, ayaṃ dibbasotadhātūti veditabbā. Tato paraṃ tasmiṃ sote patito hoti. Taṃ thāmajātaṃ karontena “etthantare saddaṃ suṇāmī”ti ekaṅgulamattaṃ paricchinditvā vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Tato dvaṅgulacaturaṅgulaaṭṭhaṅgulavidatthiratanaantogabbhapamukhapāsādapariveṇasaṅghārāmagocaragāmajanapadādivasena yāva cakkavāḷaṃ tato vā bhiyyopi paricchinditvā paricchinditvā vaḍḍhetabbaṃ.

When he thus attends to the sound sign, at the point when the divine ear element is about to arise, mind-door adverting arises, taking one of those sounds as its object. When that ceases, four or five impulsions occur. Among them, the first three or four are sense-sphere mind-states known as preparatory, access, conformity, and change-of-lineage. The fourth or fifth is an absorption mind-state, belonging to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere. Here, the knowledge that arises together with that absorption mind-state should be understood as the divine ear element. Thereafter, he is established in that ear. To strengthen it, he should define a boundary—such as, “Within this space, I hear sounds”—about the size of a finger’s breadth, and then expand it. Next, he should repeatedly define and expand the boundary—progressing to two fingers’ breadth, four fingers’ breadth, eight fingers’ breadth, a span, a cubit, the interior of a room, a mansion, a monastic compound, a monastery, an alms-resort village, a district, and so on—up to the world-sphere or even beyond.

Evaṃ adhigatābhiñño esa pādakajjhānārammaṇena phuṭṭhokāsabbhantaragatepi sadde puna pādakajjhānaṃ asamāpajjitvāpi abhiññāñāṇena suṇātiyeva. Evaṃ suṇanto ca sacepi yāva brahmalokā saṅkhabheripaṇavādisaddehi ekakolāhalaṃ hoti, pāṭiyekkaṃ vavatthapetukāmatāya sati ayaṃ saṅkhasaddo ayaṃ bherisaddoti vavatthapetuṃ sakkotiyevāti.

Thus, one who has attained this direct knowledge hears with the knowledge of direct knowledge even sounds occurring within the space pervaded by the object of the basic jhāna, without having to re-enter that jhāna. And while hearing thus, even if there is a single uproar with the sounds of conches, drums, and tambourines, etc., extending as far as the Brahmā world, if he wishes to distinguish them individually, he is able to determine, 'This is the sound of a conch, this is the sound of a drum,' and so on.

Dibbasotadhātukathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of the Divine Ear Element is concluded.

Cetopariyañāṇakathā

Account of the Knowledge of Encompassing Mind

401. Cetopariyañāṇakathāya [M 2.0039][V 2.0037] cetopariyañāṇāyāti ettha pariyātīti pariyaṃ, paricchindatīti attho. Cetaso pariyaṃ cetopariyaṃ. Cetopariyañca taṃ ñāṇañcāti cetopariyañāṇaṃ. Tadatthāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Parasattānanti attānaṃ ṭhapetvā sesasattānaṃ. Parapuggalānanti idampi iminā ekatthameva. Veneyyavasena pana desanāvilāsena ca byañjananānattaṃ kataṃ. Cetasā cetoti attano cittena tesaṃ cittaṃ. Paricca pajānātīti paricchinditvā sarāgādivasena nānappakārato jānāti.

401. In the account of the knowledge of encompassing mind (cetopariyañāṇa), in the phrase 'for the knowledge of encompassing mind' (cetopariyañāṇāya), 'pariya' is from 'pariyāti' (he encompasses), and means 'he delimits.'
