'Cetaso pariyaṃ' is 'cetopariyaṃ' (the encompassing of mind). And that which is both an encompassing of mind and a knowledge is 'knowledge of encompassing mind' (cetopariyañāṇaṃ). 'For that purpose' is the meaning. By 'other beings' (parasattānaṃ) is meant beings other than oneself. By 'other individuals' (parapuggalānaṃ) is meant the same thing. However, the difference in expression is made according to the suitability for the audience and the elegance of the teaching. By 'mind with mind' (cetasā ceto) is meant 'their mind with one's own mind'. By 'he discerns by encompassing' (paricca pajānāti) is meant 'he knows by delimiting it in various ways, such as with or without passion'.

Kathaṃ panetaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppādetabbanti? Etañhi dibbacakkhuvasena ijjhati, taṃ etassa parikammaṃ. Tasmā tena bhikkhunā ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbena cakkhunā parassa hadayarūpaṃ nissāya vattamānassa lohitassa vaṇṇaṃ passitvā cittaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Yadā hi somanassacittaṃ vattati, tadā rattaṃ nigrodhapakkasadisaṃ hoti. Yadā domanassacittaṃ vattati, tadā kāḷakaṃ jambupakkasadisaṃ. Yadā upekkhācittaṃ vattati, tadā pasannatilatelasadisaṃ. Tasmā tena “idaṃ rūpaṃ somanassindriyasamuṭṭhānaṃ, idaṃ domanassindriyasamuṭṭhānaṃ, idaṃ upekkhindriyasamuṭṭhāna”nti parassa hadayalohitavaṇṇaṃ passitvā cittaṃ pariyesantena cetopariyañāṇaṃ thāmagataṃ kātabbaṃ. Evaṃ thāmagate hi tasmiṃ anukkamena sabbampi kāmāvacaracittaṃ rūpāvacarārūpāvacaracittañca pajānāti cittā cittameva saṅkamanto vināpi hadayarūpadassanena. Vuttampi cetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “āruppe parassa cittaṃ jānitukāmo kassa hadayarūpaṃ passati, kassindriyavikāraṃ oloketīti? Na kassaci. Iddhimato visayo esa yadidaṃ yattha katthaci cittaṃ āvajjanto soḷasappabhedaṃ cittaṃ jānāti. Akatābhinivesassa pana vasena ayaṃ kathā”ti.

But how is this knowledge to be produced? Indeed, this is achieved through the divine eye, which serves as its preparatory practice. Therefore, that bhikkhu, having increased the light and having seen with the divine eye the color of the blood flowing in dependence on another's physical heart, should seek out the mind. For when a mind accompanied by joy is present, the blood is red, like a ripe banyan fruit. When a mind accompanied by displeasure is present, it is dark, like a ripe jambu fruit. When a mind accompanied by equanimity is present, it is clear, like sesame oil. Thus, by seeing the color of another's heart-blood and seeking out the mind, thinking, 'This form arises from the faculty of joy, this from the faculty of displeasure, this from the faculty of equanimity,' one should make the knowledge of encompassing mind firm. Indeed, when it is thus made firm, one gradually understands all sense-sphere consciousness, form-sphere consciousness, and formless-sphere consciousness, passing from mind to mind, even without seeing the physical heart. This is also stated in the commentary: 'If one wishes to know the mind of another in the formless sphere, whose physical heart does one see? Whose changes in faculties does one observe?' 'No one's. This is the domain of one with psychic power—wherever one directs attention, one knows the sixteen types of mind. But this explanation is for one who has not yet attained mastery.'

Sarāgaṃ vā cittantiādīsu pana aṭṭhavidhaṃ lobhasahagataṃ cittaṃ sarāgaṃ cittanti veditabbaṃ. Avasesaṃ catubhūmakaṃ kusalābyākataṃ cittaṃ vītarāgaṃ. Dve domanassacittāni dve vicikicchuddhaccacittānīti imāni pana cattāri cittāni imasmiṃ duke saṅgahaṃ na gacchanti. Keci pana therā tānipi saṅgaṇhanti. Duvidhaṃ pana domanassacittaṃ sadosaṃ cittaṃ nāma. Sabbampi catubhūmakaṃ [V 2.0038] kusalābyākataṃ vītadosaṃ. Sesāni dasākusalacittāni imasmiṃ duke saṅgahaṃ na gacchanti. Keci pana therā tānipi saṅgaṇhanti.

Furthermore, in such passages as 'consciousness with lust' (sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ), the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed should be understood as 'consciousness with lust'. The remaining wholesome and indeterminate consciousness of the four planes is 'consciousness free from lust'. However, the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure and the two consciousnesses accompanied by doubt and restlessness—these four consciousnesses are not included in this pair. Some elders, however, do include them. Furthermore, the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure are called 'consciousness with aversion'. All wholesome and indeterminate consciousness of the four planes is 'consciousness free from aversion'. The remaining ten unwholesome consciousnesses are not included in this pair. Some elders, however, do include them as well.

Samohaṃ [M 2.0040] vītamohanti ettha pana pāṭipuggalikanayena vicikicchuddhaccasahagatadvayameva samohaṃ, mohassa pana sabbākusalesu sambhavato dvādasavidhampi akusalacittaṃ samohaṃ cittanti veditabbaṃ. Avasesaṃ vītamohaṃ. Thinamiddhānugataṃ pana saṃkhittaṃ. Uddhaccānugataṃ vikkhittaṃ. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaraṃ mahaggataṃ. Avasesaṃ amahaggataṃ. Sabbampi tebhūmakaṃ sauttaraṃ. Lokuttaraṃ anuttaraṃ. Upacārappattaṃ appanāppattañca samāhitaṃ. Ubhayamappattaṃ asamāhitaṃ. Tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedapaṭipassaddhinissaraṇavimuttippattaṃ vimuttaṃ. Pañcavidhampi etaṃ vimuttimappattaṃ avimuttanti veditabbaṃ. Iti cetopariyañāṇalābhī bhikkhu sabbappakārampi idaṃ sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ…pe… avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ avimuttaṃ cittanti pajānātīti.

Furthermore, in the pair 'with delusion' (samohaṃ) and 'free from delusion' (vītamohaṃ), according to the specific individual method, only the pair of consciousnesses accompanied by doubt and restlessness is 'with delusion'. However, since delusion is present in all unwholesome states, all twelve types of unwholesome consciousness should be understood as 'consciousness with delusion'. The remainder is 'free from delusion'. Furthermore, consciousness accompanied by sloth and torpor is 'contracted'. Consciousness accompanied by restlessness is 'distracted'. Form-sphere and formless-sphere consciousness is 'exalted'. The remainder is 'unexalted'. All consciousness belonging to the three planes is 'that which has a superior'. The supramundane is 'that which has no superior'. That which has attained access and absorption concentration is 'concentrated'. That which has not attained either is 'unconcentrated'. That which has attained liberation by substitution, by suppression, by eradication, by tranquilization, and by escape is 'liberated'. That which has not attained this fivefold liberation is to be understood as 'unliberated'. Thus, a bhikkhu who has obtained the knowledge of others' minds understands in all these various ways: 'consciousness with lust...' and so on... 'or consciousness that is unliberated,' he knows as 'unliberated consciousness'.

Cetopariyañāṇakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Knowledge of Others' Minds is concluded.

Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇakathā

The Discourse on the Knowledge of Recollection of Past Lives

402. Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇakathāyaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāyāti (dī. ni. 1.244) pubbenivāsānussatimhi yaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tadatthāya. Pubbenivāsoti pubbe atītajātīsu nivutthakkhandhā. Nivutthāti ajjhāvutthā anubhūtā attano santāne uppajjitvā niruddhā. Nivutthadhammā vā. Nivutthāti gocaranivāsena nivutthā attano viññāṇena viññātā paricchinnā, paraviññāṇaviññātāpi vā chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇādīsu, te buddhānaṃyeva labbhanti. Pubbenivāsānussatīti yāya satiyā pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, sā pubbenivāsānussati. Ñāṇanti tāya satiyā sampayuttañāṇaṃ. Evamimassa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa atthāya pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya etassa ñāṇassa adhigamāya pattiyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

402. In the discourse on the knowledge of recollecting past abodes, the phrase 'for the knowledge of recollecting past abodes' (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇāya) means 'for the sake of that knowledge which is in the recollection of past abodes'. 'Past abodes' (pubbenivāsa) refers to the aggregates that were dwelt in during previous, past existences. 'Dwelt in' (nivutthā) means inhabited, experienced, having arisen and ceased within one's own continuum. Alternatively, it refers to phenomena that were dwelt in. 'Dwelt in' also means dwelt in by way of a resort, known and defined by one's own consciousness. Or, as in such cases as the recollection of those whose round of rebirth has been severed, it can refer to that which was known by another's consciousness; these are attainable only by the Buddhas. 'Recollection of past abodes' (pubbenivāsānussati) is the mindfulness by which one recollects past abodes. 'Knowledge' (ñāṇa) is the knowledge associated with that mindfulness. Thus, it is said that 'for the knowledge of recollecting past abodes' means 'for the purpose of this knowledge of recollecting past abodes, for its attainment, for its achievement'.

Anekavihitanti anekavidhaṃ, anekehi vā pakārehi pavattitaṃ, saṃvaṇṇitanti attho. Pubbenivāsanti samanantarātītabhavaṃ ādiṃ katvā tattha tattha nivutthasantānaṃ. Anussaratīti khandhapaṭipāṭivasena [V 2.0039] cutipaṭisandhivasena vā anugantvā anugantvā sarati. Imañhi pubbenivāsaṃ cha janā anussaranti – titthiyā, pakatisāvakā, mahāsāvakā, aggasāvakā, paccekabuddhā, buddhāti.

The phrase 'of many kinds' (anekavihitaṃ) means 'of many varieties', or 'set forth in many ways', that is, 'well-expounded'. 'Past abodes' (pubbenivāsaṃ) refers to the continuum dwelt in here and there, beginning with the immediately preceding existence. 'He recollects' (anussarati) means that he remembers by repeatedly tracing back, either by way of the sequence of aggregates or by way of death and rebirth. Indeed, six types of persons recollect past abodes: sectarians, ordinary disciples, great disciples, foremost disciples, Paccekabuddhas, and Buddhas.

Tattha [M 2.0041] titthiyā cattālīsaṃyeva kappe anussaranti, na tato paraṃ. Kasmā, dubbalapaññattā. Tesañhi nāmarūpaparicchedavirahitattā dubbalā paññā hoti. Pakatisāvakā kappasatampi kappasahassampi anussarantiyeva, balavapaññattā. Asītimahāsāvakā satasahassakappe anussaranti. Dve aggasāvakā ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ satasahassañca. Paccekabuddhā dve asaṅkhyeyyāni satasahassañca. Ettako hi etesaṃ abhinīhāro. Buddhānaṃ pana paricchedo nāma natthi.

Among these, sectarians recollect only forty eons, and not beyond that. Why? Because their wisdom is weak. Indeed, their wisdom is weak because they are devoid of the comprehension of name-and-form. Ordinary disciples, because their wisdom is strong, recollect even a hundred eons or a thousand eons. The eighty great disciples recollect a hundred thousand eons. The two foremost disciples recollect one incalculable and a hundred thousand eons. The Paccekabuddhas recollect two incalculables and a hundred thousand eons. For this is the extent of their aspiration. For the Buddhas, however, there is no limit.

Titthiyā ca khandhapaṭipāṭimeva saranti, paṭipāṭiṃ muñcitvā cutipaṭisandhivasena sarituṃ na sakkonti. Tesañhi andhānaṃ viya icchitapadesokkamanaṃ natthi. Yathā pana andhā yaṭṭhiṃ amuñcitvāva gacchanti, evaṃ te khandhānaṃ paṭipāṭiṃ amuñcitvāva saranti. Pakatisāvakā khandhapaṭipāṭiyāpi anussaranti cutipaṭisandhivasenapi saṅkamanti. Tathā asītimahāsāvakā. Dvinnaṃ pana aggasāvakānaṃ khandhapaṭipāṭikiccaṃ natthi. Ekassa attabhāvassa cutiṃ disvā paṭisandhiṃ passanti, puna aparassa cutiṃ disvā paṭisandhinti evaṃ cutipaṭisandhivaseneva saṅkamantā gacchanti. Tathā paccekabuddhā.

Furthermore, sectarians recollect only the sequence of aggregates; they are unable to let go of that sequence and recollect by way of death and rebirth. Indeed, for them, there is no leaping to a desired point, just as for the blind. For just as the blind proceed without letting go of their staff, so too do they recollect without letting go of the sequence of aggregates. Ordinary disciples recollect by way of the sequence of aggregates and also transition by way of death and rebirth. So too do the eighty great disciples. For the two foremost disciples, however, there is no need for the sequence of aggregates. Seeing the death of one existence, they see the rebirth; again, seeing the death of another, they see the rebirth. In this way, they proceed by transitioning solely by way of death and rebirth. So too do the Paccekabuddhas.

Buddhānaṃ pana neva khandhapaṭipāṭikiccaṃ, na cutipaṭisandhivasena saṅkamanakiccaṃ atthi. Tesañhi anekāsu kappakoṭīsu heṭṭhā vā upari vā yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ icchanti, taṃ taṃ pākaṭameva hoti. Tasmā anekāpi kappakoṭiyo peyyālapāḷiṃ viya saṃkhipitvā yaṃ yaṃ icchanti, tatra tatreva okkamantā sīhokkantavasena gacchanti. Evaṃ gacchantānañca nesaṃ ñāṇaṃ yathā nāma katavālavedhaparicayassa sarabhaṅgasadisassa dhanuggahassa khitto saro antarā rukkhalatādīsu asajjamāno lakkheyeva patati, na sajjati, na virajjhati, evaṃ antarantarāsu jātīsu na sajjati, na virajjhati, asajjamānaṃ avirajjhamānaṃ icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃyeva gaṇhāti.

For the Buddhas, however, there is no need for the sequence of aggregates, nor is there a need to transition by way of death and rebirth. Indeed, for them, across countless crores of eons, whatever place they wish for, whether below or above, becomes manifest. Therefore, compressing even many crores of eons as if they were an abbreviated text passage, they proceed by way of a lion's leap, descending upon whatever place they wish. And as they proceed in this way, their knowledge is like an arrow shot by an archer, like Sarabhaṅga, who has practiced hitting a horsehair target: just as the released arrow does not get stuck on trees or vines in between but falls right on the target, not sticking, not straying, so too their knowledge does not get stuck or stray among the intervening births. Unsticking and unstraying, it seizes the very place that is wished for.

Imesu ca pana pubbenivāsaṃ anussaraṇasattesu titthiyānaṃ pubbenivāsadassanaṃ khajjupanakapabhāsadisaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Pakatisāvakānaṃ dīpappabhāsadisaṃ. Mahāsāvakānaṃ ukkāpabhāsadisaṃ[V 2.0040]. Aggasāvakānaṃ osadhitārakappabhāsadisaṃ. Paccekabuddhānaṃ candappabhāsadisaṃ. Buddhānaṃ rasmisahassapaṭimaṇḍitasaradasūriyamaṇḍalasadisaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti.

Furthermore, among these beings who recollect past lives, the vision of past lives appears to heretics like the light of a firefly. For ordinary disciples, it is like the light of a lamp. For great disciples, it is like the light of a torch. For chief disciples, it is like the light of the morning star. For Paccekabuddhas, it is like the light of the moon. For Buddhas, it appears like the disk of the autumn sun, adorned with a thousand rays.

Titthiyānañca [M 2.0042] pubbenivāsānussaraṇaṃ andhānaṃ yaṭṭhikoṭigamanaṃ viya hoti. Pakatisāvakānaṃ daṇḍakasetugamanaṃ viya. Mahāsāvakānaṃ jaṅghasetugamanaṃ viya. Aggasāvakānaṃ sakaṭasetugamanaṃ viya. Paccekabuddhānaṃ mahājaṅghamaggagamanaṃ viya. Buddhānaṃ mahāsakaṭamaggagamanaṃ viya.

Furthermore, for heretics, the recollection of past lives is like a blind person's going by the tip of a staff. For ordinary disciples, it is like crossing a log bridge. For great disciples, it is like crossing a footbridge. For chief disciples, it is like crossing a cart bridge. For Paccekabuddhas, it is like traveling on a great footpath. For Buddhas, it is like traveling on a great cart road.

Imasmiṃ pana adhikāre sāvakānaṃ pubbenivāsānussaraṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “anussaratīti khandhapaṭipāṭivasena cutipaṭisandhivasena vā anugantvā anugantvā saratī”ti.

However, in this context, the recollection of past lives by disciples is intended. Therefore it was said: ‘He recollects’ means that he remembers by tracing back again and again, either by way of the sequence of aggregates or by way of death and rebirth-linking.

403. Tasmā evamanussaritukāmena ādikammikena bhikkhunā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantena rahogatena paṭisallinena paṭipāṭiyā cattāri jhānāni samāpajjitvā abhiññāpādakacatutthajjhānato vuṭṭhāya sabbapacchimā nisajjā āvajjitabbā. Tato āsanapaññāpanaṃ, senāsanappavesanaṃ, pattacīvarapaṭisāmanaṃ, bhojanakālo, gāmato āgamanakālo, gāme piṇḍāya caritakālo, gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhakālo, vihārato nikkhamanakālo, cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇavandanakālo, pattadhovanakālo, pattapaṭiggahaṇakālo, pattapaṭiggahaṇato yāva mukhadhovanā katakiccaṃ, paccūsakāle katakiccaṃ, majjhimayāme katakiccaṃ, paṭhamayāme katakiccanti evaṃ paṭilomakkamena sakalaṃ rattindivaṃ katakiccaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ. Ettakaṃ pana pakaticittassapi pākaṭaṃ hoti. Parikammasamādhicittassa pana atipākaṭameva.

403. Therefore, a bhikkhu who is a beginner and wishes to recollect in this way, after his meal, having returned from his alms round, should go into solitude and be secluded. Having attained the four jhānas in succession, he should emerge from the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for the direct knowledges, and advert to his very last sitting. From there, he should advert to: the preparing of the seat, entering his dwelling, putting away his bowl and robes, the time of eating, the time of returning from the village, the time of walking for alms in the village, the time of entering the village for alms, the time of leaving the monastery, the time of venerating at the cetiya-precinct and the Bodhi-tree precinct, the time of washing the bowl, the time of receiving the bowl, the duties performed from receiving the bowl up to washing his face, the duties performed in the early morning, the duties performed in the middle watch of the night, and the duties performed in the first watch of the night. In this way, he should advert in reverse order to all the duties he has performed during the entire day and night. This much is manifest even to an ordinary mind, but to a mind in preparatory concentration, it is exceedingly manifest.

Sace panettha kiñci na pākaṭaṃ hoti, puna pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya āvajjitabbaṃ. Ettakena dīpe jalite viya pākaṭaṃ hoti. Evaṃ paṭilomakkameneva dutiyadivasepi tatiyacatutthapañcamadivasepi dasāhepi aḍḍhamāsepi māsepi yāva saṃvaccharāpi katakiccaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ. Eteneva upāyena dasavassāni vīsativassānīti yāva imasmiṃ bhave attano paṭisandhi, tāva āvajjantena purimabhave cutikkhaṇe pavattitanāmarūpaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ. Pahoti hi paṇḍito bhikkhu paṭhamavāreneva paṭisandhiṃ ugghāṭetvā cutikkhaṇe nāmarūpamārammaṇaṃ kātuṃ.

If anything here does not become manifest, he should again attain the base jhāna, emerge from it, and advert to it. By doing so, it becomes manifest as if a lamp were lit. In this way, proceeding in reverse order, he should advert to what was done on the second day, on the third, fourth, and fifth days, for ten days, for a fortnight, for a month, and up to a year. By this same method, for ten years, twenty years, and so on, up to his own rebirth-linking in this present existence, he should advert. Having done so, he should advert to the mentality-materiality that occurred at the moment of death in the previous existence. For a wise bhikkhu is capable, on the very first attempt, of breaking through the rebirth-linking and making the mentality-materiality at the moment of death his object.

Yasmā [V 2.0041] pana purimabhave nāmarūpaṃ asesaṃ niruddhaṃ aññaṃ uppannaṃ, tasmā taṃ ṭhānaṃ āhundarikaṃ andhatamamiva hoti duddasaṃ duppaññena. Tenāpi “na sakkomahaṃ [M 2.0043] paṭisandhiṃ ugghāṭetvā cutikkhaṇe pavattitanāmarūpamārammaṇaṃ kātu”nti dhuranikkhepo na kātabbo. Tadeva pana pādakajjhānaṃ punappunaṃ samāpajjitabbaṃ. Tato ca vuṭṭhāya vuṭṭhāya taṃ ṭhānaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ.

However, since in the previous existence the mentality-materiality has ceased without remainder and another has arisen, that state is obscure and like utter darkness, difficult to see for one with weak wisdom. Even so, one should not give up the task, thinking: 'I am unable to break through the rebirth-linking and make the mentality-materiality that occurred at the moment of death my object.' Rather, that same base jhāna should be attained again and again. And emerging from it repeatedly, one should advert to that state.

Evaṃ karonto hi seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso kūṭāgārakaṇṇikatthāya mahārukkhaṃ chindanto sākhāpalāsacchedanamatteneva pharasudhārāya vipannāya mahārukkhaṃ chindituṃ asakkontopi dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvāva kammārasālaṃ gantvā tikhiṇaṃ pharasuṃ kārāpetvā puna āgantvā chindeyya, puna vipannāya ca punapi tatheva kāretvā chindeyya. So evaṃ chindanto chinnassa chinnassa puna chetabbābhāvato acchinnassa ca chedanato nacirasseva mahārukkhaṃ pāteyya, evamevaṃ pādakajjhānā vuṭṭhāya pubbe āvajjitaṃ anāvajjitvā paṭisandhimeva āvajjanto nacirasseva paṭisandhiṃ ugghāṭetvā cutikkhaṇe pavattitanāmarūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ kareyyāti. Kaṭṭhaphālakakesohārakādīhipi ayamattho dīpetabbo.

For it is just as a strong man, felling a great tree for the pinnacle of a gabled house, might find the blade of his axe blunted after cutting only the branches and leaves. Though unable to fell the great tree, he does not give up the task but goes to a smithy, has a sharp axe made, comes back, and cuts again. If the blade gets blunted again, he has it remade in the same way and cuts again. As he cuts in this way, since what has been cut does not need to be cut again and what is uncut is being cut, he will before long fell the great tree. In the very same way, emerging from the base jhāna and not adverting to what was previously adverted to, but adverting only to the rebirth-linking, one will before long break through the rebirth-linking and make the mentality-materiality occurring at the moment of death the object. This meaning should also be illustrated by such examples as the wood-splitter and the one who removes hair.

Tattha pacchimanisajjato pabhuti yāva paṭisandhito ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ nāma na hoti. Taṃ pana parikammasamādhiñāṇaṃ nāma hoti. Atītaṃsañāṇantipi eke vadanti. Taṃ rūpāvacaraṃ sandhāya na yujjati. Yadā panassa bhikkhuno paṭisandhiṃ atikkamma cutikkhaṇe pavattitanāmarūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā manodvārāvajjanaṃ uppajjati, tasmiñca niruddhe tadevārammaṇaṃ katvā cattāri pañca vā javanāni javanti. Sesaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva purimāni parikammādināmakāni kāmāvacarāni honti. Pacchimaṃ rūpāvacaraṃ catutthajjhānikaṃ appanācittaṃ. Tadāssa yaṃ tena cittena saha ñāṇaṃ uppajjati, idaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ nāma. Tena ñāṇena sampayuttāya satiyā anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Seyyathidaṃ, ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussaratīti (dī. ni. 1.244).

Herein, the knowledge that proceeds by taking as its object the sequence from the last sitting up to the rebirth-linking is not called the knowledge of past lives. It is, however, called the knowledge associated with preparatory concentration. Some also call it knowledge of past portions. This is not tenable with reference to the fine-material sphere. But when, for that bhikkhu, after he has transcended the rebirth-linking, mind-door adverting arises taking as its object the mentality-materiality that occurred at the moment of death, and when that has ceased, four or five impulsions run on that same object. The preceding impulsions are of the sense-sphere, designated as preparation, and so on. The last is an attainment consciousness of the fourth jhāna belonging to the fine-material sphere. The knowledge that arises together with that consciousness is called the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. With the mindfulness associated with that knowledge, he recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: ‘One birth, two births… and so on… Thus with their aspects and details he recollects his manifold past lives.’

404. Tattha ekampi jātinti ekampi paṭisandhimūlaṃ cutipariyosānaṃ ekabhavapariyāpannaṃ khandhasantānaṃ. Esa nayo dvepi jātiyotiādīsupi. Anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappetiādīsu pana parihāyamāno kappo saṃvaṭṭakappo, vaḍḍhamāno vivaṭṭakappoti veditabbo. Tattha saṃvaṭṭena saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī [M 2.0044] gahito [V 2.0042] hoti, taṃmūlakattā. Vivaṭṭena ca vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī, evañhi sati yāni tāni “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, kappassa asaṅkhyeyyāni. Katamāni cattāri? Saṃvaṭṭo, saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī, vivaṭṭo, vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyīti (a. ni. 4.156 thokaṃ visadisaṃ) vuttāni, tāni pariggahitāni honti.

404. Herein, 'even one birth' means a single stream of aggregates, having rebirth-linking as its root and death as its end, comprised within one existence. This same method applies to 'even two births' and so on. In phrases such as 'even many aeons of contraction,' however, it should be understood that a devolving aeon is an aeon of contraction, and an evolving aeon is an aeon of expansion. Herein, by 'contraction' the aeon of remaining contracted is included, because it is rooted in the former. And by 'expansion,' the aeon of remaining expanded is included. For when this is so, those things spoken of—'Bhikkhus, there are these four incalculables of an aeon. What four? The aeon of contraction, the aeon of remaining contracted, the aeon of expansion, and the aeon of remaining expanded'—are thereby comprehended.

Tattha tayo saṃvaṭṭā – āposaṃvaṭṭo, tejosaṃvaṭṭo, vāyosaṃvaṭṭoti. Tisso saṃvaṭṭasīmā – ābhassarā, subhakiṇhā, vehapphalāti.

Herein, there are three kinds of contraction: by water, by fire, and by wind. There are three limits of contraction: the Ābhassara realm, the Subhakiṇha realm, and the Vehapphala realm.

Yadā kappo tejena saṃvaṭṭati, ābhassarato heṭṭhā agginā ḍayhati. Yadā āpena saṃvaṭṭati, subhakiṇhato heṭṭhā udakena vilīyati. Yadā vāyunā saṃvaṭṭati, vehapphalato heṭṭhā vātena viddhaṃsati. Vitthārato pana sadāpi ekaṃ buddhakhettaṃ vinassati.

When an aeon contracts by fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm is burnt up by fire. When it contracts by water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by water. When it contracts by wind, everything below the Vehapphala realm is scattered by wind. In extent, however, one Buddha-field is always destroyed.

Buddhakhettaṃ nāma tividhaṃ hoti – jātikhettaṃ, āṇākhettaṃ, visayakhettañca. Tattha jātikhettaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷapariyantaṃ hoti. Yaṃ tathāgatassa paṭisandhigahaṇādīsu kampati. Āṇākhettaṃ koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷapariyantaṃ, yattha ratanasuttaṃ (khu. pā. 6.1 ādayo) khandhaparittaṃ (cūḷava. 251; a. ni. 4.67) dhajaggaparittaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.249) āṭānāṭiyaparittaṃ (dī. ni. 3.275 ādayo) moraparittanti (jā. 1.2.17-18) imesaṃ parittānaṃ ānubhāvo vattati. Visayakhettaṃ anantamaparimāṇaṃ. Yaṃ “yāvatā vā pana ākaṅkheyyā”ti (a. ni. 3.81) vuttaṃ, yattha yaṃ yaṃ tathāgato ākaṅkhati, taṃ taṃ jānāti. Evametesu tīsu buddhakhettesu ekaṃ āṇākhettaṃ vinassati. Tasmiṃ pana vinassante jātikhettampi vinaṭṭhameva hoti. Vinassantañca ekatova vinassati, saṇṭhahantampi ekato saṇṭhahati. Tassevaṃ vināso ca saṇṭhahanañca veditabbaṃ.

A Buddha's field is threefold: the birth-field, the authority-field, and the range-field. Of these, the birth-field extends for ten thousand world-systems; it is this that trembles at the Tathāgata's conception and other such events. The authority-field extends for a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems; it is here that the protective power of chants such as the Ratana Sutta, Khandha Paritta, Dhajagga Paritta, Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, and Mora Paritta is effective. The range-field is infinite, immeasurable; it is of this that it is said, 'as far as he might wish,' for within it the Tathāgata knows whatever he wishes to know. Among these three Buddha-fields, it is the authority-field that is destroyed. But when it is destroyed, the birth-field is destroyed along with it. And when it is destroyed, it is destroyed all at once; when it is reconstituted, it is reconstituted all at once. This is how its destruction and reconstitution should be understood.

405. Yasmiṃ hi samaye kappo agginā nassati, āditova kappavināsakamahāmegho vuṭṭhahitvā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷe ekaṃ mahāvassaṃ vassati. Manussā tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā sabbabījāni nīharitvā vapanti. Sassesu pana gokhāyitakamattesu jātesu gadrabharavaṃ ravanto ekabindumpi na vassati, tadā pacchinnaṃ pacchinnameva vassaṃ hoti. Idaṃ sandhāya hi bhagavatā “hoti kho so, bhikkhave, samayo yaṃ bahūni vassāni bahūni vassasatāni [M 2.0045] bahūni vassasahassāni bahūni [V 2.0043] vassasatasahassāni devo na vassatī”ti (a. ni. 7.66) vuttaṃ. Vassūpajīvino sattā kālaṅkatvā brahmaloke nibbattanti, pupphaphalūpajīviniyo ca devatā. Evaṃ dīghe addhāne vītivatte tattha tattha udakaṃ parikkhayaṃ gacchati, athānupubbena macchakacchapāpi kālaṅkatvā brahmaloke nibbattanti, nerayikasattāpi. Tattha nerayikā sattamasūriyapātubhāve vinassantīti eke.

405. For at the time when the aeon is destroyed by fire, first a great aeon-destroying cloud arises and rains a great rain upon a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems. People, delighted and joyful, bring out all their seeds and sow them. But when the crops have grown only to a height a cow can eat, it thunders with the bray of a donkey but does not rain even a single drop; then the rain is cut off for good. It is in reference to this that the Blessed One said: 'There comes a time, bhikkhus, when for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, the deva does not rain.' Beings who subsist on rain die and are reborn in the Brahma-world, as do the devatās who subsist on flowers and fruits. Thus, as a long period passes, the water here and there dries up. Then, successively, the fish and turtles also die and are reborn in the Brahma-world, and so too the beings in hell. Some say that the beings in hell perish at the appearance of the seventh sun.

Jhānaṃ vinā natthi brahmaloke nibbatti, etesañca keci dubbhikkhapīḷitā keci abhabbā jhānādhigamāya, te kathaṃ tattha nibbattantīti. Devaloke paṭiladdhajjhānavasena. Tadā hi “vassasatasahassassaccayena kappuṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti lokabyūhā nāma kāmāvacaradevā muttasirā vikiṇṇakesā rudamukhā assūni hatthehi puñchamānā rattavatthanivatthā ativiya virūpavesadhārino hutvā manussapathe vicarantā evaṃ ārocenti “mārisā ito vassasatasahassassaccayena kappavuṭṭhānaṃ bhavissati, ayaṃ loko vinassissati, mahāsamuddopi ussussissati, ayañca mahāpathavī sineru ca pabbatarājā uddayhissanti vinassissanti. Yāva brahmalokā lokavināso bhavissati. Mettaṃ mārisā bhāvetha, karuṇaṃ, muditaṃ, upekkhaṃ mārisā bhāvetha, mātaraṃ upaṭṭhahatha, pitaraṃ upaṭṭhahatha, kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino hothā”ti.

Without jhāna, there is no rebirth in the Brahma-world. But some of these beings are afflicted by famine and some are incapable of attaining jhāna, so how are they reborn there? By means of jhāna attained in the deva world. For at that time, kāmāvacara devas named Lokabyūha, with their hair unbound and disheveled, with weeping faces, wiping their tears with their hands, wearing red garments, and having assumed a very ugly appearance, roam the paths of humans and make this announcement: 'Sirs, in a hundred thousand years the dissolution of the aeon will take place. This world will be destroyed. The great ocean will dry up. This great earth and Sineru, king of mountains, will be burnt up and destroyed. The destruction of the world will extend as far as the Brahma-world. Sirs, develop loving-kindness! Develop compassion, altruistic joy, and equanimity! Attend to your mother, attend to your father! Be respectful to the elders in the family!'

Tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā yebhuyyena manussā ca bhummadevatā ca saṃvegajātā aññamaññaṃ muducittā hutvā mettādīni puññāni karitvā devaloke nibbattanti. Tattha dibbasudhābhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā vāyokasiṇe parikammaṃ katvā jhānaṃ paṭilabhanti. Tadaññe pana aparāpariyavedanīyena kammena devaloke nibbattanti. Aparāpariyavedanīyakammarahito hi saṃsāre saṃsaramāno satto nāma natthi. Tepi tattha tatheva jhānaṃ paṭilabhanti. Evaṃ devaloke paṭiladdhajjhānavasena sabbepi brahmaloke nibbattantīti.

Hearing their words, for the most part humans and earth-deities become spiritually agitated. Having become soft-hearted toward one another, they perform meritorious deeds such as the development of loving-kindness and are reborn in the deva world. There, having eaten divine ambrosia, they do the preliminary work on the wind kasiṇa and attain jhāna. Still others are reborn in the deva world by means of kamma that is experienceable in a subsequent existence. For there is no being wandering in saṃsāra who is devoid of kamma that is experienceable in a subsequent existence. They too attain jhāna there in the very same way. Thus, by means of jhāna attained in the deva world, all are reborn in the Brahma-world.

Vassūpacchedato pana uddhaṃ dīghassa addhuno accayena dutiyo sūriyo pātubhavati. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā “hoti kho so, bhikkhave, samayo”ti sattasūriyaṃ (a. ni. 7.66) vitthāretabbaṃ. Pātubhūte ca pana tasmiṃ neva [M 2.0046] rattiparicchedo, na divāparicchedo paññāyati. Eko sūriyo uṭṭheti, eko atthaṃ gacchati. Avicchinnasūriyasantāpova loko hoti. Yathā ca pakatisūriye sūriyadevaputto hoti, evaṃ kappavināsakasūriye natthi. Tattha pakatisūriye [V 2.0044] vattamāne ākāse valāhakāpi dhūmasikhāpi caranti. Kappavināsakasūriye vattamāne vigatadhūmavalāhakaṃ ādāsamaṇḍalaṃ viya nimmalaṃ nabhaṃ hoti. Ṭhapetvā pañca mahānadiyo sesakunnadīādīsu udakaṃ sussati.

Then, after the cessation of the rains, with the passing of a long period, a second sun appears. This has been stated by the Blessed One: 'There comes a time, bhikkhus...' The discourse on the seven suns (AN 7.66) should be elaborated in full. When that sun has appeared, no division of night and day is discerned. One sun rises and one sun sets. The world is subject to the uninterrupted heat of the sun. And just as there is a sun-deva in the normal sun, there is none in the eon-destroying sun. When the normal sun is present, clouds and wisps of smoke move in the sky. When the eon-destroying sun is present, the sky is clear and spotless like a mirror disk, devoid of smoke and clouds. Except for the five great rivers, the water in the remaining small rivers and streams dries up.

Tatopi dīghassa addhuno accayena tatiyo sūriyo pātubhavati. Yassa pātubhāvā mahānadiyopi sussanti.

Thereafter, with the passing of a long period, a third sun appears. With its appearance, even the great rivers dry up.

Tatopi dīghassa addhuno accayena catuttho sūriyo pātubhavati. Yassa pātubhāvā himavati mahānadīnaṃ pabhavā “sīhapapāto haṃsapātano kaṇṇamuṇḍako rathakāradaho anotattadaho chaddantadaho kuṇāladaho”ti ime satta mahāsarā sussanti.

Thereafter, with the passing of a long period, a fourth sun appears. With its appearance, these seven great lakes from which the great rivers of the Himālayas originate—Sīhapapāta, Haṃsapātana, Kaṇṇamuṇḍaka, Rathakāradaha, Anotattadaha, Chaddantadaha, and Kuṇāladaha—dry up.

Tatopi dīghassa addhuno accayena pañcamo sūriyo pātubhavati. Yassa pātubhāvā anupubbena mahāsamudde aṅgulipabbatemanamattampi udakaṃ na saṇṭhāti.

Thereafter, with the passing of a long period, a fifth sun appears. With its appearance, the water in the great ocean successively diminishes until not even enough to wet a finger joint remains.

Tatopi dīghassa addhuno accayena chaṭṭho sūriyo pātubhavati. Yassa pātubhāvā sakalacakkavāḷaṃ ekadhūmaṃ hoti. Pariyādiṇṇasinehaṃ dhūmena. Yathā cidaṃ, evaṃ koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷānipi.

Thereafter, with the passing of a long period, a sixth sun appears. With its appearance, the entire world-system becomes a single mass of smoke, its moisture consumed by the smoke. Just as this one, so too the hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems.

Tatopi dīghassa addhuno accayena sattamo sūriyo pātubhavati. Yassa pātubhāvā sakalacakkavāḷaṃ ekajālaṃ hoti saddhiṃ koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷehi. Yojanasatikādibhedāni sinerukūṭānipi palujjitvā ākāseyeva antaradhāyanti. Sā aggijālā uṭṭhahitvā cātumahārājike gaṇhāti. Tattha kanakavimānaratanavimānamaṇivimānāni jhāpetvā tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ gaṇhāti. Eteneva upāyena yāva paṭhamajjhānabhūmiṃ gaṇhāti. Tattha tayopi brahmaloke jhāpetvā ābhassare āhacca tiṭṭhati. Sā yāva aṇumattampi saṅkhāragataṃ atthi, tāva na nibbāyati. Sabbasaṅkhāraparikkhayā pana sappitelajhāpanaggisikhā viya chārikampi [M 2.0047] anavasesetvā nibbāyati. Heṭṭhāākāsena saha upariākāso eko hoti mahandhakāro.

Thereafter, with the passing of a long period, a seventh sun appears. With its appearance, the entire world-system becomes a single mass of flame, together with the hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems. The peaks of Sineru, hundreds of yojanas high, crumble and disappear in the sky. That mass of flame, having arisen, seizes the realm of the Four Great Kings. Having burnt up the golden mansions, jewel mansions, and gem mansions there, it seizes the Tāvatiṃsa realm. In the same way, it seizes up to the plane of the first jhāna. Having burnt up the three Brahma-worlds there, it stops, having reached the Ābhassara realm. As long as there is even a minute particle of a formation, it is not extinguished. But with the utter exhaustion of all formations, it is extinguished without leaving any ash, like the flame of a lamp burning on ghee and oil. The space below becomes one with the space above, a great darkness.

406. Atha dīghassa addhuno accayena mahāmegho uṭṭhahitvā paṭhamaṃ sukhumaṃ sukhumaṃ vassati[V 2.0045]. Anupubbena kumudanāḷayaṭṭhimusalatālakkhandhādippamāṇāhi dhārāhi vassanto koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷesu sabbaṃ daḍḍhaṭṭhānaṃ pūretvā antaradhāyati. Taṃ udakaṃ heṭṭhā ca tiriyañca vāto samuṭṭhahitvā ghanaṃ karoti parivaṭumaṃ paduminipatte udakabindusadisaṃ. Kathaṃ tāva mahantaṃ udakarāsiṃ ghanaṃ karotīti ce? Vivarasampadānato. Tañhissa tamhi tamhi vivaraṃ deti. Taṃ evaṃ vātena sampiṇḍiyamānaṃ ghanaṃ kariyamānaṃ parikkhayamānaṃ anupubbena heṭṭhā otarati. Otiṇṇe otiṇṇe udake brahmalokaṭṭhāne brahmalokā, upari catukāmāvacaradevalokaṭṭhāne ca devalokā pātubhavanti.

406. Then, with the passing of a long period, a great cloud arises and at first rains very fine drops. Successively, it rains with streams the size of lotus stalks, staffs, pestles, and palm trunks, and after filling all the burnt places in the hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems, it disappears. A wind arises below and around that water and makes it solid and round, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. If it is asked how it makes such a great mass of water solid, it is by the provision of openings. For that water yields an opening to the wind here and there. Thus, being compressed, solidified, and reduced by the wind, it successively descends. As the water descends, the Brahma-worlds appear in the place of the Brahma-worlds, and above, in the place of the four kāmāvacara deva worlds, the deva worlds appear.

Purimapathaviṭṭhānaṃ otiṇṇe pana balavavātā uppajjanti. Te taṃ pihitadvāre dhamakaraṇe ṭhitaudakamiva nirassāsaṃ katvā rundhanti. Madhurodakaṃ parikkhayaṃ gacchamānaṃ upari rasapathaviṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Sā vaṇṇasampannā ceva hoti gandharasasampannā ca nirudakapāyāsassa upari paṭalaṃ viya.

Then, when the water has descended to the place of the former earth, strong winds arise. They contain it, making it unable to escape, like water held in a water-strainer with its openings covered. As the sweet water is being consumed, it gives rise to the savory earth on its surface. This was endowed with color, scent, and taste, like the skin that forms on top of boiled milk-rice as it cools.

Tadā ca ābhassarabrahmaloke paṭhamatarābhinibbattā sattā āyukkhayā vā puññakkhayā vā tato cavitvā idhūpapajjanti. Te honti sayaṃpabhā antalikkhacarā. Te aggaññasutte (dī. ni. 3.119) vuttanayena taṃ rasapathaviṃ sāyitvā taṇhābhibhūtā āluppakārakaṃ paribhuñjituṃ upakkamanti. Atha nesaṃ sayaṃpabhā antaradhāyati, andhakāro hoti. Te andhakāraṃ disvā bhāyanti.

At that time, beings who were first reborn in the Ābhassara Brahma-world, with the exhaustion of their lifespan or the exhaustion of their merit, pass away from there and are reborn here. They are self-luminous and travel through the air. In the way stated in the Aggañña Sutta (DN 27), they taste that savory earth and, being overcome by craving, they start to eat it in lumps. Then their self-luminosity disappears and it becomes dark. Seeing the darkness, they become afraid.

Tato nesaṃ bhayaṃ nāsetvā sūrabhāvaṃ janayantaṃ paripuṇṇapaṇṇāsayojanaṃ sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ pātubhavati, te taṃ disvā “ālokaṃ paṭilabhimhā”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭhā hutvā “amhākaṃ bhītānaṃ bhayaṃ nāsetvā sūrabhāvaṃ janayanto uṭṭhito, tasmā “sūriyo hotū”ti sūriyotvevassa nāmaṃ karonti.

Then, dispelling their fear and generating courage, the sun's disk, a full fifty yojanas in size, appears. Seeing it, they become happy and joyful and say, 'We have obtained light!' Since it arose dispelling the fear of the frightened and generating courage, they give it the name 'Suriya,' saying, 'Therefore, let it be Suriya!'

Atha [M 2.0048] sūriye divasaṃ ālokaṃ katvā atthaṅgate yampi ālokaṃ labhimhā, sopi no naṭṭhoti puna bhītā honti. Tesaṃ evaṃ hoti “sādhu vatassa sace aññaṃ ālokaṃ labheyyāmā”ti. Tesaṃ cittaṃ ñatvā viya ekūnapaṇṇāsayojanaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ pātubhavati. Te taṃ disvā bhiyyoso mattāya haṭṭhatuṭṭhā hutvā “amhākaṃ chandaṃ ñatvā viya uṭṭhito, tasmā cando hotū”ti [V 2.0046] candotvevassa nāmaṃ karonti. Evaṃ candimasūriyesu pātubhūtesu nakkhattāni tārakarūpāni pātubhavanti.

Then, when the sun, having made daylight, had set, the light they had obtained also vanished, and they became frightened again. They thought, “It would be good if we could obtain another light.” As if knowing their thought, the moon’s disk, forty-nine yojanas in size, appeared. Seeing it, they rejoiced even more and declared, “Since it has arisen as if knowing our desire, let it be called ‘Canda.’” When the moon and the sun appeared, constellations and stars also appeared.

Tato pabhuti rattindivā paññāyanti, anukkamena ca māsaddhamāsautusaṃvaccharā. Candimasūriyānaṃ pana pātubhūtadivaseyeva sinerucakkavāḷahimavantapabbatā pātubhavanti. Te ca kho apubbaṃ acarimaṃ phagguṇapuṇṇamadivaseyeva pātubhavanti. Kathaṃ? Yathā nāma kaṅgubhatte paccamāne ekappahāreneva pupphuḷakāni uṭṭhahanti. Eke padesā thūpathūpā honti, eke ninnaninnā, eke samasamā. Evamevaṃ thūpathūpaṭṭhāne pabbatā honti, ninnaninnaṭṭhāne samuddā, samasamaṭṭhāne dīpāti.

From then on, nights and days were distinguished, and in due course, half-months, months, seasons, and years. On the very day the moon and sun appeared, Mount Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, and the Himavanta mountains also manifested. And these appeared simultaneously, not one after another, on the full moon day of Phagguṇa. How so? Just as when millet rice is being cooked, bubbles arise all at once. Some places became raised and elevated, some low and sunken, and some perfectly level. In the same way, mountains arose in the raised and elevated places, oceans in the low and sunken places, and islands in the perfectly level places.

Atha tesaṃ sattānaṃ rasapathaviṃ paribhuñjantānaṃ kamena ekacce vaṇṇavanto, ekacce dubbaṇṇā honti. Tattha vaṇṇavanto dubbaṇṇe atimaññanti. Tesaṃ atimānapaccayā sāpi rasapathavī antaradhāyati. Bhūmipappaṭako pātubhavati. Atha nesaṃ teneva nayena sopi antaradhāyati. Padālatā pātubhavati. Teneva nayena sāpi antaradhāyati. Akaṭṭhapāko sāli pātubhavati akaṇo athuso suddho sugandho taṇḍulapphalo.

Then, as those beings were partaking of the earth-essence, in due course some became beautiful in complexion, while others became ugly. There, the beautiful ones looked down upon the ugly ones. Due to their conceit, that earth-essence also disappeared. An earth-crust appeared. Then, in the same way, that too disappeared. A creeper called Padālatā appeared. In the same way, that too disappeared. Rice that ripens without cultivation appeared, without broken grains or husk, pure, fragrant, and yielding only rice grains.

Tato nesaṃ bhājanāni uppajjanti. Te sāliṃ bhājane ṭhapetvā pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyā ṭhapenti, sayameva jālasikhā uṭṭhahitvā taṃ pacati. So hoti odano sumanajātipupphasadiso, na tassa sūpena vā byañjanena vā karaṇīyaṃ atthi. Yaṃ yaṃ rasaṃ bhuñjitukāmā honti, taṃ taṃ rasova hoti. Tesaṃ taṃ oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āharayataṃ tato pabhuti muttakarīsaṃ sañjāyati. Atha nesaṃ tassa nikkhamanatthāya vaṇamukhāni pabhijjanti, purisassa purisabhāvo, itthiyāpi itthibhāvo pātubhavati.

Then vessels arose for them. They placed the rice in a vessel and set it on a stone slab, and a tongue of flame arose of its own accord and cooked it. That cooked rice was like a jasmine flower; it required neither soup nor curry. Whatever flavor they wished to eat, that very flavor it became. As they consumed that coarse food, from then on urine and feces were produced in them. Then, for their expulsion, orifices broke open on their bodies; the male characteristic appeared in the male, and the female characteristic in the female.

Tatra [M 2.0049] sudaṃ itthī purisaṃ, puriso ca itthiṃ ativelaṃ upanijjhāyati. Tesaṃ ativelaṃ upanijjhāyanapaccayā kāmapariḷāho uppajjati. Tato methunadhammaṃ paṭisevanti. Te asaddhammapaṭisevanapaccayā viññūhi garahiyamānā viheṭhiyamānā tassa asaddhammassa paṭicchādanahetu agārāni karonti. Te agāraṃ ajjhāvasamānā anukkamena aññatarassa alasajātikassa sattassa diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjantā sannidhiṃ karonti. Tato pabhuti kaṇopi thusopi taṇḍulaṃ pariyonandhati, lāyitaṭṭhānampi na paṭivirūhati.

Thereupon, a woman would gaze excessively at a man, and a man at a woman. Due to their excessive gazing, the fever of sensual passion arose. Then they engaged in sexual intercourse. Because of indulging in this unrighteous practice, being censured and harassed by the wise, they built houses for the purpose of concealing this unrighteous practice. Dwelling in houses, they gradually followed the example of a certain lazy being and began to accumulate stores. From then on, both fine and coarse husk enveloped the rice grain, and where it was reaped, it did not grow back.

Te [V 2.0047] sannipatitvā anutthunanti “pāpakā vata bho dhammā sattesu pātubhūtā, mayaṃ hi pubbe manomayā ahumhā”ti aggaññasutte (dī. ni. 3.128) vuttanayena vitthāretabbaṃ. Tato mariyādaṃ ṭhapenti. Atha aññataro satto aññassa bhāgaṃ adinnaṃ ādiyati. Taṃ dvikkhattuṃ paribhāsetvā tatiyavāre pāṇileṭṭudaṇḍehi paharanti. Te evaṃ adinnādānagarahamusāvādadaṇḍādānesu uppannesu sannipatitvā cintayanti “yaṃnūna mayaṃ ekaṃ sattaṃ sammanneyyāma, yo no sammā khīyitabbaṃ khīyeyya, garahitabbaṃ garaheyya, pabbājetabbaṃ pabbājeyya, mayaṃ panassa sālīnaṃ bhāgaṃ anuppadassāmā”ti.

Gathering together, they lamented: “Alas, evil things have appeared among beings! For we were once mind-made…”—this should be elaborated in the manner spoken in the Aggañña Sutta. Then they established boundaries. Then a certain being took another’s portion, which was not given. After reviling him twice, on the third occasion, they struck him with their hands, with clods, and with sticks. When taking what was not given, censure, false speech, and the taking up of sticks had thus arisen, they gathered and reflected: “What if we were to appoint one being who would rightly reproach the one who should be reproached, censure the one who should be censured, and banish the one who should be banished? We, in turn, would give him a portion of our rice.”

Evaṃ katasanniṭṭhānesu pana sattesu imasmiṃ tāva kappe ayameva bhagavā bodhisattabhūto tena samayena tesu sattesu abhirūpataro ca dassanīyataro ca mahesakkhataro ca buddhisampanno paṭibalo niggahapaggahaṃ kātuṃ. Te taṃ upasaṅkamitvā yācitvā sammanniṃsu. So tena mahājanena sammatoti mahāsammato, khettānaṃ adhipatīti khattiyo, dhammena samena pare rañjetīti rājāti tīhi nāmehi paññāyittha. Yañhi loke acchariyaṭṭhānaṃ, bodhisattova tattha ādipurisoti evaṃ bodhisattaṃ ādiṃ katvā khattiyamaṇḍale saṇṭhite anupubbena brāhmaṇādayopi vaṇṇā saṇṭhahiṃsu.

Among those beings who had thus made their resolution, in this very eon, this Blessed One himself, then a Bodhisatta, was at that time the most handsome, the most pleasing to see, the most powerful, and, being endowed with wisdom, was capable of suppression and encouragement. They approached him, requested him, and appointed him. Because he was agreed upon by the great multitude, he was called Mahāsammata. Because he was the lord of the fields, he was called Khattiya. Because he delights others with righteousness and impartiality, he was called Rājā. Thus, he became known by these three names. Indeed, whatever is a wonder in the world, the Bodhisatta is the first person there. Thus, with the Bodhisatta as the first, the circle of nobles was established, and in due course, the castes of brahmins and others were also established.

Tattha kappavināsakamahāmeghato yāva jālupacchedo, idamekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ saṃvaṭṭoti vuccati.

Therein, from the great world-destroying cloud until the cessation of the flame, this one incalculable eon is called the eon of contraction.

Kappavināsakajālupacchedato [M 2.0050] yāva koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷaparipūrako sampattimahāmegho, idaṃ dutiyaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyīti vuccati.

From the cessation of the world-destroying flame until the great cloud of accomplishment that fills a hundred thousand koṭi of world-systems, this second incalculable eon is called the eon of the duration of contraction.

Sampattimahāmeghato yāva candimasūriyapātubhāvo, idaṃ tatiyaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ vivaṭṭoti vuccati.

From the great cloud of accomplishment until the appearance of the moon and sun, this third incalculable eon is called the eon of expansion.

Candimasūriyapātubhāvato yāva puna kappavināsakamahāmegho, idaṃ catutthaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyīti vuccati. Imāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni eko mahākappo hoti. Evaṃ tāva agginā vināso ca saṇṭhahanañca veditabbaṃ.

From the appearance of the moon and sun until the great world-destroying cloud comes again, this fourth incalculable eon is called the eon of the duration of expansion. These four incalculable eons make one great eon. Thus, the destruction by fire and the re-establishment should be understood.

407. Yasmiṃ pana samaye kappo udakena nassati, āditova kappavināsakamahāmegho uṭṭhahitvāti [V 2.0048] pubbe vuttanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso, yathā tattha dutiyasūriyo, evamidha kappavināsako khārudakamahāmegho vuṭṭhāti. So ādito sukhumaṃ sukhumaṃ vassanto anukkamena mahādhārāhi koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷānaṃ pūrento vassati. Khārudakena phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhā pathavīpabbatādayo vilīyanti, udakaṃ samantato vātehi dhāriyati. Pathavito yāva dutiyajjhānabhūmiṃ udakaṃ gaṇhāti. Tattha tayopi brahmaloke vilīyāpetvā subhakiṇhe āhacca tiṭṭhati. Taṃ yāva aṇumattampi saṅkhāragataṃ atthi, tāva na vūpasammati. Udakānugataṃ pana sabbasaṅkhāragataṃ abhibhavitvā sahasā vūpasammati antaradhānaṃ gacchati. Heṭṭhāākāsena saha upariākāso eko hoti mahandhakāroti sabbaṃ vuttasadisaṃ. Kevalaṃ panidha ābhassarabrahmalokaṃ ādiṃ katvā loko pātubhavati. Subhakiṇhato ca cavitvā ābhassaraṭṭhānādīsu sattā nibbattanti.

407. Now, at a time when the aeon is destroyed by water, it should be explained in detail as before, beginning with 'the great world-destroying cloud arose…' This, however, is the difference: just as there a second sun appeared, so here a great, world-destroying cloud of salty water pours forth. At first, it rains very finely, then by stages with great torrents, it rains, filling a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems. Touched by the salty water, the earth, mountains, and so on, dissolve. The water is held up on all sides by winds. The water seizes everything from the earth up to the plane of the second jhāna. There, having caused the three Brahma worlds to dissolve, it stops, having reached the Subhakiṇha realm. As long as even a minute amount of conditioned phenomena exists, it does not subside. But having overwhelmed all conditioned phenomena touched by the water, it suddenly subsides and vanishes. The space below and the space above become one, and there is great darkness—all this is as was said before. Here, however, the world reappears beginning with the Ābhassara Brahma world. And beings, having passed away from the Subhakiṇha realm, are reborn in the Ābhassara realm and other such places.

Tattha kappavināsakamahāmeghato yāva kappavināsakudakūpacchedo, idamekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ. Udakūpacchedato yāva sampattimahāmegho, idaṃ dutiyaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ. Sampattimahāmeghato…pe… imāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni eko mahākappo hoti. Evaṃ udakena vināso ca saṇṭhahanañca veditabbaṃ.

Therein, from the great world-destroying cloud up to the cessation of the world-destroying water, this is one incalculable period. From the cessation of the water up to the great world-forming cloud, this is the second incalculable period. From the great world-forming cloud… and so on… these four incalculable periods are one great aeon. Thus should the destruction by water and the re-establishment be understood.

408. Yasmiṃ [M 2.0051] samaye kappo vātena vinassati, āditova kappavināsakamahāmegho uṭṭhahitvāti pubbe vuttanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso, yathā tattha dutiyasūriyo, evamidha kappavināsanatthaṃ vāto samuṭṭhāti. So paṭhamaṃ thūlarajaṃ uṭṭhāpeti. Tato saṇharajaṃ sukhumavālikaṃ thūlavālikaṃ sakkharapāsāṇādayoti yāva kūṭāgāramatte pāsāṇe visamaṭṭhāne ṭhitamahārukkhe ca uṭṭhāpeti. Te pathavito nabhamuggatā na ca puna patanti. Tattheva cuṇṇavicuṇṇā hutvā abhāvaṃ gacchanti.

408. At a time when the aeon is destroyed by wind, it should be explained in detail as before, beginning with 'the great world-destroying cloud arose…' This, however, is the difference: just as there a second sun appeared, so here a wind arises for the purpose of destroying the aeon. First, it lifts up coarse dust. Then, it lifts up fine dust, fine sand, coarse sand, gravel, stones, and so on, up to rocks the size of a gabled house and great trees standing on uneven ground. Having risen from the earth into the sky, they do not fall again. There, in that very place, they are pulverized and vanish.

Athānukkamena heṭṭhā mahāpathaviyā vāto samuṭṭhahitvā pathaviṃ parivattetvā uddhaṃmūlaṃ katvā ākāse khipati. Yojanasatappamāṇāpi pathavippadesā dviyojanatiyojanacatuyojanapañcayojanasatappamāṇāpi bhijjitvā vātavegena khittā ākāseyeva cuṇṇavicuṇṇā hutvā abhāvaṃ gacchanti. Cakkavāḷapabbatampi sinerupabbatampi vāto ukkhipitvā ākāse khipati. Te aññamaññaṃ abhihantvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇā hutvā vinassanti. Eteneva upāyena bhummaṭṭhakavimānāni ca ākāsaṭṭhakavimānāni ca vināsento chakāmāvacaradevaloke vināsetvā koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷāni [V 2.0049] vināseti. Tattha cakkavāḷā cakkavāḷehi himavantā himavantehi sinerū sinerūhi aññamaññaṃ samāgantvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇā hutvā vinassanti. Pathavito yāva tatiyajjhānabhūmiṃ vāto gaṇhāti. Tattha tayopi brahmaloke vināsetvā vehapphalaṃ āhacca tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ sabbasaṅkhāragataṃ vināsetvā sayampi vinassati. Heṭṭhāākāsena saha upariākāso eko hoti mahandhakāroti sabbaṃ vuttasadisaṃ. Idha pana subhakiṇhabrahmalokaṃ ādiṃ katvā loko pātubhavati. Vehapphalato ca cavitvā subhakiṇhaṭṭhānādīsu sattā nibbattanti.

Then, by stages, a wind arises from beneath the great earth, turns the earth over, makes it bottom-up, and hurls it into the sky. Regions of the earth measuring a hundred yojanas, and those measuring two, three, four, and five hundred yojanas, are shattered and, being hurled by the force of the wind, are pulverized in the sky itself and vanish. The wind lifts up the Cakkavāḷa mountain range and Mount Sineru and hurls them into the sky. They strike one another, are pulverized, and are destroyed. By this same method, destroying the terrestrial and celestial mansions, and having destroyed the six heavens of the sense-sphere, it destroys a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems. Therein, the Cakkavāḷa ranges collide with other Cakkavāḷa ranges, the Himavanta mountains with other Himavanta mountains, and Sineru mountains with other Sineru mountains; coming together, they are pulverized and are destroyed. The wind seizes everything from the earth up to the plane of the third jhāna. There, having destroyed the three Brahma worlds, it stops, having reached the Vehapphala realm. In this way, having destroyed all conditioned phenomena, it perishes itself. The space below and the space above become one, and there is great darkness—all this is as was said before. Here, however, the world reappears beginning with the Subhakiṇha Brahma world. And beings, having passed away from the Vehapphala realm, are reborn in the Subhakiṇha realm and other such places.

Tattha kappavināsakamahāmeghato yāva kappavināsakavātūpacchedo, idamekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ. Vātūpacchedato yāva sampattimahāmegho, idaṃ dutiyaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ…pe… imāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni eko mahākappo hoti. Evaṃ vātena vināso ca saṇṭhahanañca veditabbaṃ.

Therein, from the great world-destroying cloud up to the cessation of the world-destroying wind, this is one incalculable period. From the cessation of the wind up to the great world-forming cloud, this is the second incalculable period… and so on… these four incalculable periods are one great aeon. Thus should the destruction and re-establishment by wind be understood.

409. Kiṃkāraṇā [M 2.0052] evaṃ loko vinassati? Akusalamūlakāraṇā. Akusalamūlesu hi ussannesu evaṃ loko vinassati. So ca kho rāge ussannatare agginā vinassati. Dose ussannatare udakena vinassati. Keci pana dose ussannatare agginā. Rāge ussannatare udakenāti vadanti. Mohe ussannatare vātena vinassati. Evaṃ vinassantopi ca nirantarameva sattavāre agginā vinassati. Aṭṭhame vāre udakena. Puna sattavāre agginā. Aṭṭhame vāre udakenāti evaṃ aṭṭhame aṭṭhame vāre vinassanto sattakkhattuṃ udakena vinassitvā puna sattavāre agginā nassati. Ettāvatā tesaṭṭhi kappā atītā honti. Etthantare udakena nassanavāraṃ sampattampi paṭibāhitvā laddhokāso vāto paripuṇṇacatusaṭṭhikappāyuke subhakiṇhe viddhaṃsento lokaṃ vināseti.

409. For what reason does the world perish in this way? For the reason of the unwholesome roots. For when the unwholesome roots are excessive, the world perishes thus. And when greed is more excessive, it perishes by fire. When hatred is more excessive, it perishes by water. Some, however, say that when hatred is more excessive, it perishes by fire, and when greed is more excessive, by water. When delusion is more excessive, it perishes by wind. And even while perishing thus, it is destroyed by fire seven times consecutively. On the eighth occasion, it is destroyed by water. Again, seven times by fire. On the eighth occasion, by water. In this way, perishing on the eighth and eighth occasion, having been destroyed seven times by water, it is again destroyed seven times by fire. By this much, sixty-three aeons have passed. In the interim, although the turn for destruction by water has arrived, the wind, having gained its opportunity, wards it off and destroys the world, demolishing the Subhakiṇha beings, whose lifespan is a full sixty-four aeons.

410. Pubbenivāsaṃ anussarantopi ca kappānussaraṇako bhikkhu etesu kappesu anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe anekepi vivaṭṭakappe anekepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe anussarati. Kathaṃ? “Amutrāsi”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 1.244) nayena.

410. Furthermore, a bhikkhu who recollects past lives, one who recollects the aeons, remembers among these aeons many aeons of contraction, many aeons of expansion, and many aeons of contraction and expansion. How so? By the method beginning, 'There I was…' (Dī. Ni. 1.244).

Tattha amutrāsinti amumhi saṃvaṭṭakappe ahaṃ amumhi bhave vā yoniyā vā gatiyā vā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyā vā sattāvāse vā sattanikāye vā āsiṃ. Evaṃnāmoti tisso vā phusso vā. Evaṃgottoti kaccāno vā kassapo vā. Idamassa atītabhave attano nāmagottānussaraṇavasena [V 2.0050] vuttaṃ. Sace pana tasmiṃ kāle attano vaṇṇasampattiṃ vā lūkhapaṇītajīvikabhāvaṃ vā sukhadukkhabahulataṃ vā appāyukadīghāyukabhāvaṃ vā anussaritukāmo hoti, tampi anussaratiyeva. Tenāha “evaṃvaṇṇo…pe… evamāyupariyanto”ti.

Therein, 'there I was' means: in that aeon of contraction I was in such-and-such an existence, or womb, or destination, or station of consciousness, or abode of beings, or company of beings. 'With such a name' means Tissa or Phussa. 'Of such a clan' means Kaccāna or Kassapa. This is said by way of recollecting one's own name and clan in a past existence. But if at that time one wishes to recollect one's own perfection of complexion, or one's coarse or refined livelihood, or one's abundance of pleasure and pain, or one's short or long lifespan, one recollects that too. Hence it is said: 'of such an appearance … with such a life span.'

Tattha evaṃvaṇṇoti odāto vā sāmo vā. Evamāhāroti sālimaṃsodanāhāro vā pavattaphalabhojano vā. Evaṃ sukhadukkhapaṭisaṃvedīti anekappakārena kāyikacetasikānaṃ sāmisanirāmisādippabhedānaṃ vā sukhadukkhānaṃ paṭisaṃvedī. Evamāyupariyantoti evaṃ vassasataparimāṇāyupariyanto vā caturāsītikappasatasahassāyupariyanto vā. So tato cuto amutra udapādinti sohaṃ tato [M 2.0053] bhavato yonito gatito viññāṇaṭṭhitito sattāvāsato sattanikāyato vā cuto puna amukasmiṃ nāma bhave yoniyā gatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyā sattāvāse sattanikāye vā udapādiṃ. Tatrāpāsinti atha tatrāpi bhave yoniyā gatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyā sattāvāse sattanikāye vā puna ahosiṃ. Evaṃnāmotiādi vuttanayameva.

Therein, 'of such an appearance' means fair or golden. 'Having such food' means one whose food was fine rice and meat, or one who ate fallen fruit. 'Experiencing such pleasure and pain' means experiencing in various ways bodily and mental pleasures and pains, of such kinds as the worldly and the spiritual. 'With such a life span' means with a life span limited to a hundred years, or with a life span of eighty-four hundred thousand aeons. 'Passing away from there, I arose there' means: I, having passed away from that existence, womb, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or company of beings, arose again in such-and-such an existence, womb, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or company of beings. 'There too I was' means: then there too, in that existence, womb, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or company of beings, I was again. 'With such a name,' and so on, is in the way already stated.

Apica yasmā amutrāsinti idaṃ anupubbena ārohantassa yāvadicchakaṃ anussaraṇaṃ. So tato cutoti paṭinivattantassa paccavekkhaṇaṃ, tasmā “idhūpapanno”ti imissā idhūpapattiyā anantaramevassa upapattiṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya “amutra udapādi”nti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tatrāpāsinti evamādi panassa tatra imissā upapattiyā anantare upapattiṭṭhāne nāmagottādīnaṃ anussaraṇadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. So tato cuto idhūpapannoti svāhaṃ tato anantarūpapattiṭṭhānato cuto idha asukasmiṃ nāma khattiyakule vā brāhmaṇakule vā nibbattoti. Itīti evaṃ. Sākāraṃ sauddesanti nāmagottavasena sauddesaṃ, vaṇṇādivasena sākāraṃ. Nāmagottena hi satto tisso kassapoti uddisīyati. Vaṇṇādīhi sāmo odātoti nānattato paññāyati. Tasmā nāmagottaṃ uddeso, itare ākārā. Anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsamanussaratīti idaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

Furthermore, since 'there I was' is the recollection, as much as one wishes, while ascending in sequence, and 'passing away from there' is the reviewing while descending, it should therefore be understood that the words 'I arose there' are said with reference to the place of rebirth immediately preceding this present rebirth as 'one reborn here.' The words 'There too I was,' and so on, are said for the purpose of showing the recollection of name, clan, etc., in that place of rebirth immediately preceding this one. 'Passing away from there, I was reborn here' means: 'I, having passed away from that immediately preceding place of rebirth, have been born here in such-and-such a khattiya or brahmin family.' 'Thus' means in this way. 'With its aspects and particulars' means: with particulars by way of name and clan, and with aspects by way of appearance, etc. For by name and clan a being is designated as Tissa or Kassapa, while by appearance, etc., one is discerned in one's diversity as golden or fair. Therefore, name and clan are the particulars, the others are the aspects. 'He recollects his manifold past lives'—the meaning of this is plain.

Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇakathā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the knowledge of the recollection of past lives is concluded.

Cutūpapātañāṇakathā

The Explanation of the Knowledge of Passing Away and Reappearance

411. Sattānaṃ [V 2.0051] cutūpapātañāṇakathāya cutūpapātañāṇāyāti (dī. ni. 1.247) cutiyā ca upapāte ca ñāṇāya. Yena ñāṇena sattānaṃ cuti ca upapāto ca ñāyati, tadatthaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Cittaṃ abhinīharati abhininnāmetīti parikammacittaṃ abhinīharati ceva abhininnāmeti ca. Soti so katacittābhinīhāro bhikkhu. Dibbenātiādīsu pana dibbasadisattā dibbaṃ. Devatānañhi sucaritakammanibbattaṃ pittasemharuhirādīhi apalibuddhaṃ upakkilesavimuttatāya dūrepi ārammaṇaṃ sampaṭicchanasamatthaṃ dibbaṃ pasādacakkhu hoti. Idañcāpi vīriyabhāvanābalanibbattaṃ ñāṇacakkhu [M 2.0054] tādisamevāti dibbasadisattā dibbaṃ. Dibbavihāravasena paṭiladdhattā attanā ca dibbavihārasannissitattāpi dibbaṃ. Ālokapariggahena mahājutikattāpi dibbaṃ. Tirokuṭṭādigatarūpadassanena mahāgatikattāpi dibbaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ saddasatthānusāreneva veditabbaṃ.

411. In the explanation of the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings, 'for the knowledge of passing away and reappearance' means for the knowledge concerning passing away (cuti) and reappearance (upapāta). The knowledge by which the passing away and reappearance of beings are known is said to be for the purpose of the divine eye-knowledge. 'He directs and inclines his mind' means he directs and inclines the preparatory mind (parikammacitta). 'So' refers to that bhikkhu who has directed his mind. In phrases like 'with the divine,' it is called 'divine' because it is similar to the divine. For the divine eye of deities, produced by good kamma, is unimpeded by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., and being free from imperfections, is capable of receiving objects even from a distance. This knowledge-eye, too, produced by the power of developing energy, is just like that; hence, because of its similarity to the divine, it is called 'divine.' It is also 'divine' because it is attained through a divine abiding and because it is itself dependent on a divine abiding. It is also 'divine' because of its great radiance, achieved through the grasping of light. It is also 'divine' because of its great range, being able to see forms beyond walls, etc. All this should be understood in accordance with the exegesis of the terms.

Dassanaṭṭhena cakkhu. Cakkhukiccakaraṇena cakkhumivātipi cakkhu. Cutūpapātadassanena diṭṭhivisuddhihetuttā visuddhaṃ. Yo hi cutimattameva passati, na upapātaṃ. So ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Yo upapātamattameva passati, na cutiṃ, so navasattapātubhāvadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāti. Yo pana tadubhayaṃ passati, so yasmā duvidhampi taṃ diṭṭhigataṃ ativattati. Tasmāssa taṃdassanaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhihetu hoti. Ubhayampi cetaṃ buddhaputtā passanti. Tena vuttaṃ “cutūpapātadassanena diṭṭhivisuddhihetuttā visuddha”nti.

It is an 'eye' in the sense of seeing. It is also an 'eye' because it performs the function of an eye. It is 'purified' because, through the seeing of passing away and reappearance, it is a cause for the purification of view. For one who sees only passing away and not reappearance adopts the annihilationist view. One who sees only reappearance and not passing away adopts the view of the manifestation of a new being. But one who sees both transcends both kinds of wrong view. Therefore that seeing of his becomes a cause for the purification of view. The sons of the Buddha see both. Hence it is said: 'It is purified because, through the seeing of passing away and reappearance, it is a cause for the purification of view.'

Manussūpacāraṃ atikkamitvā rūpadassanena atikkantamānusakaṃ, mānusakaṃ vā maṃsacakkhuṃ atikkantattā atikkantamānusakanti veditabbaṃ. Tena dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena. Satte passatīti manussānaṃ maṃsacakkhunā viya satte oloketi.

'Surpassing the human': it is so called because it sees forms by transcending the human range; or it should be understood as 'surpassing the human' because it has transcended the human flesh-eye. 'With that divine eye, purified, surpassing the human, he sees beings' means that he observes beings just as humans do with the flesh-eye.

Cavamāne upapajjamāneti ettha cutikkhaṇe upapattikkhaṇe vā dibbacakkhunā daṭṭhuṃ na sakkā. Ye pana āsannacutikā idāni cavissanti, te cavamānā. Ye ca gahitapaṭisandhikā sampatinibbattāva, te upapajjamānāti adhippetā. Te evarūpe cavamāne ca upapajjamāne ca passatīti dasseti.

Here, regarding the phrase 'passing away, reappearing': it is not possible to see with the divine eye at the very moment of death or at the moment of rebirth. Rather, those who are near death and about to pass away are meant by 'passing away.' And those who have taken rebirth-linking and have just been reborn are meant by 'reappearing.' This is what is intended. It shows that one sees such beings passing away and reappearing.

Hīneti [V 2.0052] mohanissandayuttattā hīnānaṃ jātikulabhogādīnaṃ vasena hīḷite ohīḷite oññāte avaññāte. Paṇīteti amohanissandayuttattā tabbiparīte. Suvaṇṇeti adosanissandayuttattā iṭṭhakantamanāpavaṇṇayutte. Dubbaṇṇeti dosanissandayuttattā aniṭṭhākantaamanāpavaṇṇayutte. Anabhirūpe virūpetipi attho. Sugateti sugatigate. Alobhanissandayuttattā vā aḍḍhe mahaddhane. Duggateti duggatigate. Lobhanissandayuttattā vā dalidde appannapāne.

‘Inferior’: because they are connected with the result of delusion, they are despised, scorned, looked down upon, and disdained on account of inferior birth, family, wealth, and so on. ‘Superior’: because they are connected with the result of non-delusion, the opposite of that. ‘Of good complexion’: because they are connected with the result of non-hatred, they possess a desirable, pleasing, and agreeable complexion. ‘Of bad complexion’: because they are connected with the result of hatred, they possess an undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable complexion. The meaning is also ‘unattractive’ or ‘deformed.’ ‘In a good destination’: gone to a good destination; or, because they are connected with the result of non-greed, they are affluent and very wealthy. ‘In a bad destination’: gone to a bad destination; or, because they are connected with the result of greed, they are poor, with little food and drink.

Yathākammupageti yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ upacitaṃ, tena tena upagate. Tattha purimehi cavamānetiādīhi dibbacakkhukiccaṃ vuttaṃ. Iminā pana padena yathākammupagañāṇakiccaṃ. Tassa ca ñāṇassa ayamuppattikkamo, idha bhikkhu heṭṭhā nirayābhimukhaṃ [M 2.0055] ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nerayike satte passati mahādukkhamanubhavamāne. Taṃ dassanaṃ dibbacakkhukiccameva. So evaṃ manasikaroti “kiṃ nu kho kammaṃ katvā ime sattā etaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavantī”ti. Athassa idaṃ nāma katvāti taṃkammārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Tathā uparidevalokābhimukhaṃ ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nandanavanamissakavanaphārusakavanādīsu satte passati mahāsampattiṃ anubhavamāne. Tampi dassanaṃ dibbacakkhukiccameva. So evaṃ manasikaroti “kiṃ nu kho kammaṃ katvā ime sattā etaṃ sampattiṃ anubhavantī”ti. Athassa idaṃ nāma katvāti taṃkammārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Idaṃ yathākammupagañāṇaṃ nāma. Imassa visuṃ parikammaṃ nāma natthi, yathā cimassa, evaṃ anāgataṃsañāṇassāpi. Dibbacakkhupādakāneva hi imāni dibbacakkhunā saheva ijjhanti.

‘Faring according to their kamma’: this means faring in accordance with whatever kamma they have accumulated. In the preceding phrases, ‘passing away,’ etc., the function of the divine eye was stated. By this phrase, however, the function of the knowledge of how beings fare according to their kamma is stated. The process of arising for this knowledge is as follows: Here, a bhikkhu extends light downwards towards hell and sees beings in hell experiencing great suffering. That seeing is just the function of the divine eye. He gives attention thus: ‘Having done what kamma, I wonder, do these beings experience this suffering?’ Then knowledge arises in him with that kamma as its object, to the effect that ‘they have done this particular kamma.’ Similarly, extending light upwards towards the deva world, he sees beings in the Nandana Grove, the Missaka Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, etc., experiencing great prosperity. That seeing, too, is just the function of the divine eye. He gives attention thus: ‘Having done what kamma, I wonder, do these beings experience this prosperity?’ Then knowledge arises in him with that kamma as its object, to the effect that ‘they have done this particular kamma.’ This is called the knowledge of how beings fare according to their kamma. There is no separate preliminary work for this, nor for the knowledge of the future. For these have the divine eye as their basis and are accomplished together with it.

Kāyaduccaritenātiādīsu duṭṭhu caritaṃ, duṭṭhaṃ vā caritaṃ kilesapūtikattāti duccaritaṃ. Kāyena duccaritaṃ, kāyato vā uppannaṃ duccaritanti kāyaduccaritaṃ, itaresupi eseva nayo. Samannāgatāti samaṅgībhūtā. Ariyānaṃ upavādakāti buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakānaṃ ariyānaṃ antamaso gihisotāpannānampi anatthakāmā hutvā antimavatthunā vā guṇaparidhaṃsanena vā upavādakā akkosakā garahakāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha natthi imesaṃ samaṇadhammo, assamaṇā eteti vadanto antimavatthunā upavadati. Natthi imesaṃ jhānaṃ vā vimokkho vā maggo vā phalaṃ vātiādīni vadanto guṇaparidhaṃsanavasena upavadatīti veditabbo. So ca jānaṃ vā upavadeyya ajānaṃ vā, ubhayathāpi ariyūpavādova hoti. Bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ ānantariyasadisaṃ saggāvaraṇañca maggāvaraṇañca, satekicchaṃ pana hoti. Tassa āvibhāvatthaṃ idaṃ vatthu veditabbaṃ.

In such phrases as ‘with bodily misconduct’: ‘misconduct’ (duccarita) is badly conducted, or it is corrupt conduct because it is putrid with defilements. Misconduct by means of the body, or misconduct arisen from the body, is ‘bodily misconduct.’ The same method applies to the others. ‘Endowed with’ means possessed of. ‘Revilers of noble ones’: this means those who, wishing them ill, revile, abuse, and censure noble ones—Buddhas, paccekabuddhas, and disciples, down to lay stream-enterers—either by the ultimate charge or by denigrating their good qualities. Here, one who says, ‘These have no quality of a recluse, they are not recluses,’ reviles by the ultimate charge. It should be understood that one who says, ‘These have no jhāna, liberation, path, or fruition,’ etc., reviles by denigrating their good qualities. And whether one reviles knowingly or unknowingly, in both cases it is reviling a noble one. It is weighty kamma, similar to an immediately resultant action, an obstruction to heaven and to the path, but it is remediable. To illustrate this, the following story should be known.

Aññatarasmiṃ [V 2.0053] kira gāme eko thero ca daharabhikkhu ca piṇḍāya caranti. Te paṭhamaghareyeva uḷuṅkamattaṃ uṇhayāguṃ labhiṃsu. Therassa ca kucchivāto rujjhati. So cintesi “ayaṃ yāgu mayhaṃ sappāyā, yāva na sītalā hoti, tāva naṃ pivāmī”ti. So manussehi ummāratthāya āhaṭe dārukhaṇḍe nisīditvā pivi. Itaro taṃ jigucchanto “atikhuddābhibhūto mahallako, amhākaṃ lajjitabbakaṃ akāsī”ti āha. Thero [M 2.0056] gāme caritvā vihāraṃ gantvā daharabhikkhuṃ āha “atthi te, āvuso, imasmiṃ sāsane patiṭṭhā”ti? Āma, bhante, sotāpanno ahanti. Tena hāvuso, uparimaggatthāya vāyāmaṃ mā akāsi. Khīṇāsavo tayā upavaditoti. So taṃ khamāpesi. Tenassa taṃ kammaṃ pākatikaṃ ahosi.

It is said that in a certain village an elder bhikkhu and a young bhikkhu were walking for alms. At the very first house they received a ladleful of hot gruel. The elder was suffering from a stomach wind. He thought: ‘This gruel is suitable for me. I shall drink it before it gets cold.’ So he sat on a piece of wood that people had brought for a door-post and drank it. The other, feeling disgusted at him, said: ‘This old man is overcome by great hunger; he has done something to make us ashamed.’ After walking through the village, the elder went to the monastery and said to the young bhikkhu: ‘Friend, have you any footing in this Dispensation?’ ‘Yes, venerable sir, I am a stream-enterer.’ ‘In that case, friend, do not strive for the higher paths. You have reviled one whose taints are destroyed.’ The young bhikkhu asked him for forgiveness, and so that kamma of his was restored to its original state.

Tasmā yo aññopi ariyaṃ upavadati, tena gantvā sace attanā vuḍḍhataro hoti, ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā “ahaṃ āyasmantaṃ idañcidañca avacaṃ, taṃ me khamāhī”ti khamāpetabbo. Sace navakataro hoti, vanditvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā “ahaṃ, bhante, tumhe idañcidañca avacaṃ, taṃ me khamathā”ti khamāpetabbo. Sace disāpakkanto hoti, sayaṃ vā gantvā saddhivihārikādike vā pesetvā khamāpetabbo.

Therefore, if anyone else reviles a noble one, he should go to him and ask for forgiveness. If he himself is the senior, he should squat down and say: ‘I said such and such to the venerable one; please forgive me for that.’ If he himself is the junior, he should pay homage, squat down, raise his hands in añjali, and say: ‘Venerable sir, I said such and such to you; please forgive me for that.’ If the other has departed to another region, he should ask for forgiveness either by going himself or by sending a co-resident or someone else.

Sace ca nāpi gantuṃ, na pesetuṃ sakkā hoti, ye tasmiṃ vihāre bhikkhū vasanti, tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā sace navakatarā honti, ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā, sace vuḍḍhatarā, vuḍḍhe vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitvā “ahaṃ, bhante, asukaṃ nāma āyasmantaṃ idañcidañca avacaṃ, khamatu me so āyasmā”ti vatvā khamāpetabbaṃ. Sammukhā akhamantepi etadeva kattabbaṃ.

If it is not possible either to go or to send someone, one should go to the bhikkhus living in that monastery. If they are his juniors, he should squat down; if they are his seniors, he should act in the way described for seniors, and then ask for forgiveness, saying: ‘Venerable sirs, I said such and such to the venerable one named so-and-so; may that venerable one forgive me.’ This same thing should be done even if the other does not grant forgiveness when face to face.

Sace ekacārikabhikkhu hoti, nevassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ, na gataṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati, ekassa paṇḍitassa bhikkhuno santikaṃ gantvā “ahaṃ, bhante, asukaṃ nāma āyasmantaṃ idañcidañca avacaṃ, taṃ me anussarato vippaṭisāro hoti, kiṃ karomī”ti vattabbaṃ. So vakkhati “tumhe mā cintayittha, thero tumhākaṃ khamati, cittaṃ vūpasamethā”ti. Tenāpi ariyassa gatadisābhimukhena añjaliṃ paggahetvā khamatūti vattabbaṃ. Sace so parinibbuto hoti, parinibbutamañcaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā yāvasivathikaṃ gantvāpi khamāpetabbaṃ. Evaṃ kate neva saggāvaraṇaṃ, na maggāvaraṇaṃ hoti, pākatikameva hotīti.

If he is a bhikkhu who practices solitude, and neither his dwelling place nor his destination is known, one should go to a wise bhikkhu and say: 'Venerable sir, I said such and such to the venerable one named so-and-so, and I feel remorse when I recollect it. What should I do?' He will say: 'Do not worry, the elder forgives you; calm your mind.' Then, facing the direction in which the noble one went, one should raise one's hands in añjali and say, 'May he forgive me.' If that noble one has attained Parinibbāna, one should go to the place of his deathbed, or even to the charnel ground, and ask for forgiveness. When this is done, it is no longer an obstruction to heaven or to the path; it is restored to its original state.

Micchādiṭṭhikāti [V 2.0054] viparītadassanā. Micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānāti micchādiṭṭhivasena samādinnanānāvidhakammā, ye ca micchādiṭṭhimūlakesu kāyakammādīsu aññepi samādapenti. Ettha ca vacīduccaritaggahaṇeneva ariyūpavāde manoduccaritaggahaṇena ca micchādiṭṭhiyā saṅgahitāyapi imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puna vacanaṃ [M 2.0057] mahāsāvajjabhāvadassanatthanti veditabbaṃ. Mahāsāvajjo hi ariyūpavādo, ānantariyasadisattā. Vuttampi cetaṃ “seyyathāpi, sāriputta, bhikkhu sīlasampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno diṭṭheva dhamme aññaṃ ārādheyya, evaṃsampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto, evaṃ niraye”ti (ma. ni. 1.149). Micchādiṭṭhito ca mahāsāvajjataraṃ nāma aññaṃ natthi. Yathāha “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, micchādiṭṭhi. Micchādiṭṭhiparamāni, bhikkhave, vajjānī”ti (a. ni. 1.310).

'Those with wrong view' means those with perverted seeing. 'Those who undertake actions based on wrong view' refers to those who have undertaken various actions due to wrong view, and also to those who encourage others in bodily actions and so on that are rooted in wrong view.
