Here, although reviling the noble ones is included by the mention of verbal misconduct, and wrong view by the mention of mental misconduct, the repetition of these two should be understood as for the purpose of showing their gravely faulty nature. For reviling the noble ones is gravely faulty, being similar to an immediately resultant kamma. And this was said: 'Sāriputta, just as a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue, concentration, and wisdom might attain final knowledge in this very life—so too, Sāriputta, I say of that speech: without abandoning it, without abandoning that mind, without relinquishing that view, one is deposited in hell as if brought there.' And there is nothing more gravely faulty than wrong view. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, I do not see even one other thing that is so gravely faulty as this: wrong view. Bhikkhus, faults have wrong view as their foremost.'

Kāyassa bhedāti upādiṇṇakkhandhapariccāgā. Parammaraṇāti tadanantaraṃ abhinibbattikkhandhaggahaṇe. Atha vā kāyassa bhedāti jīvitindriyassa upacchedā. Parammaraṇāti cuticittato uddhaṃ. Apāyanti evamādi sabbaṃ nirayavevacanameva.

“With the breakup of the body” means from the abandonment of the clung-to aggregates. “After death” refers to the grasping of newly arisen aggregates immediately thereafter. Alternatively, “with the breakup of the body” means from the cutting off of the life faculty. “After death” means subsequent to the death-consciousness. “The plane of misery” and so on are all merely synonyms for hell.

Nirayo hi saggamokkhahetubhūtā puññasammatā ayā apetattā, sukhānaṃ vā āyassa abhāvā apāyo. Dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti duggati, dosabahulatāya vā duṭṭhena kammunā nibbattā gatīti duggati. Vivasā nipatanti ettha dukkaṭakārinoti vinipāto. Vinassantā vā ettha patanti saṃbhijjamānaṅgapaccaṅgātipi vinipāto. Natthi ettha assādasaññito ayoti nirayo.

Indeed, it is a 'plane of misery' (apāya) because it is devoid of the good fortune (aya) which is merit, the cause for heaven and liberation, or because it lacks an influx (āya) of happiness. It is a 'woeful destination' (duggati) because it is a destination and resort of suffering, or it is a destination produced by corrupt kamma due to an abundance of hatred. It is a 'place of ruin' (vinipāta) because evildoers fall there helplessly, or because beings fall there while perishing, their limbs and members shattering. It is 'hell' (niraya) because there is no good fortune (aya) in it, which is known as gratification.

Atha vā apāyaggahaṇena tiracchānayoniṃ dīpeti. Tiracchānayoni hi apāyo sugatito apetattā, na duggati mahesakkhānaṃ nāgarājādīnaṃ sambhavato. Duggatiggahaṇena pettivisayaṃ. So hi apāyo ceva duggati ca, sugatito apetattā dukkhassa ca gatibhūtattā. Na tu vinipāto asurasadisaṃ avinipatitattā. Vinipātaggahaṇena asurakāyaṃ. So hi yathāvuttena atthena apāyo ceva duggati ca sabbasamussayehi ca vinipatitattā vinipātoti vuccati. Nirayaggahaṇena [V 2.0055] avīciādianekappakāraṃ nirayamevāti. Upapannāti upagatā, tattha abhinibbattāti adhippāyo. Vuttavipariyāyena sukkapakkho veditabbo.

Alternatively, by the term ‘plane of misery’ the animal womb is indicated. Indeed, the animal womb is a plane of misery because it is devoid of a good destination, but it is not a woeful destination because of the existence of powerful nāga kings and so on. By the term ‘woeful destination’ the sphere of the petas is indicated. Indeed, this is both a plane of misery and a woeful destination, because it is devoid of a good destination and is a destination of suffering. But it is not a place of ruin, for there is no falling into ruin as there is for the asuras. By the term ‘place of ruin’ the host of asuras is indicated. Indeed, this, in the sense stated, is a plane of misery and a woeful destination, and it is called a ‘place of ruin’ because it has fallen from all prosperity. By the term ‘hell’ the many kinds of hells, such as Avīci, are indicated. ‘Are reborn’ means have gone to; the intention is having arisen there. The bright side should be understood as the reverse of what has been said.

Ayaṃ [M 2.0058] pana viseso, tattha sugatiggahaṇena manussagatipi saṅgayhati. Saggaggahaṇena devagatiyeva. Tattha sundarā gatīti sugati. Rūpādīhi visayehi suṭṭhu aggoti saggo. So sabbopi lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti ayaṃ vacanattho.

This, however, is the distinction: by the term ‘good destination’ the human destination is also included, while by ‘heaven’ only the celestial destination is meant. Therein, because it is an excellent (sundarā) destination (gati), it is a ‘good destination’ (sugati). Because it is thoroughly excellent (suṭṭhu aggo) in regard to sense objects such as forms, it is ‘heaven’ (sagga). All of this, in the sense of breaking up and dissolving, is ‘world’ (loka)—this is the meaning of the word.

“Iti dibbena cakkhunā”tiādi sabbaṃ nigamanavacanaṃ. Evaṃ dibbena cakkhunā…pe… passatīti ayamettha saṅkhepattho.

The passage beginning “Thus, with the divine eye…” is all a concluding statement. “In this way, with the divine eye…pe… one sees”—this is the summary meaning here.

412. Evaṃ passitukāmena pana ādikammikena kulaputtena kasiṇārammaṇaṃ abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ sabbākārena abhinīhārakkhamaṃ katvā “tejokasiṇaṃ, odātakasiṇaṃ, ālokakasiṇa”nti imesu tīsu kasiṇesu aññataraṃ āsannaṃ kātabbaṃ. Upacārajjhānagocaraṃ katvā vaḍḍhetvā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Na tattha appanā uppādetabbāti adhippāyo. Sace hi uppādeti, pādakajjhānanissayaṃ hoti, na parikammanissayaṃ. Imesu ca pana tīsu ālokakasiṇaṃyeva seṭṭhataraṃ. Tasmā taṃ vā itaresaṃ vā aññataraṃ kasiṇaniddese vuttanayena uppādetvā upacārabhūmiyaṃyeva ṭhatvā vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Vaḍḍhanānayopi cassa tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

412. However, a clansman who is a beginner and wishes to see in this way should make the jhāna that is the basis for the direct knowledges, with a kasiṇa as its object, capable of being directed in every way. Then he should take up one of these three kasiṇas: the fire kasiṇa, the white kasiṇa, or the light kasiṇa. Having made it the object of access concentration, he should develop and establish it. The intention is that absorption should not be produced there. For if he produces it, the object becomes the support for the basic jhāna, not the support for the preliminary work. Among these three, the light kasiṇa is the most excellent. Therefore, having produced that one or one of the others in the way stated in the Exposition on the Kasiṇas, he should develop it while remaining right in the plane of access. The method for its development should also be understood in the way stated there.

Vaḍḍhitaṭṭhānassa antoyeva rūpagataṃ passitabbaṃ. Rūpagataṃ passato panassa parikammassa vāro atikkamati. Tato āloko antaradhāyati. Tasmiṃ antarahite rūpagatampi na dissati. Athānena punappunaṃ pādakajjhānameva pavisitvā tato vuṭṭhāya āloko pharitabbo. Evaṃ anukkamena āloko thāmagato hotīti ettha āloko hotūti yattakaṃ ṭhānaṃ paricchindati, tattha āloko tiṭṭhatiyeva. Divasampi nisīditvā passato rūpadassanaṃ hoti. Rattiṃ tiṇukkāya maggapaṭipanno cettha puriso opammaṃ.

A material form should be seen only within the extended area. But if one sees a material form outside this area, the turn for preliminary work is passed. Then the light disappears. When it has disappeared, the material form is also not seen. Then he should repeatedly enter the basic jhāna, and after emerging from it, he should pervade the area with light. Thus, gradually, the light becomes powerful. Herein, whatever area he defines with the thought, ‘Let there be light,’ the light remains just there. Even when sitting all day, the seeing of forms occurs. Herein, a man who has set out on a path at night with a grass torch is the simile.

Eko kira rattiṃ tiṇukkāya maggaṃ paṭipajji. Tassa sā tiṇukkā vijjhāyi. Athassa samavisamāni na paññāyiṃsu. So taṃ tiṇukkaṃ bhūmiyaṃ ghaṃsitvā tiṇukkā puna ujjālesi. Sā pajjalitvā purimālokato mahantataraṃ ālokaṃ akāsi. Evaṃ punappunaṃ vijjhātaṃ [V 2.0056] ujjālayato kamena sūriyo uṭṭhāsi. Sūriye uṭṭhite ukkāya kammaṃ natthīti taṃ chaḍḍetvā divasampi agamāsi. Tattha ukkāloko viya parikammakāle kasiṇāloko. Ukkāya [M 2.0059] vijjhātāya samavisamānaṃ adassanaṃ viya rūpagataṃ passato parikammassa vārātikkamena āloke antarahite rūpagatānaṃ adassanaṃ. Ukkāya ghaṃsanaṃ viya punappunaṃ pavesanaṃ. Ukkāya purimālokato mahantatarālokakaraṇaṃ viya puna parikammaṃ karoto balavatarālokapharaṇaṃ. Sūriyuṭṭhānaṃ viya thāmagatālokassa yathāparicchedena ṭhānaṃ. Tiṇukkaṃ chaḍḍetvā divasampi gamanaṃ viya parittālokaṃ chaḍḍetvā thāmagatenālokena divasampi rūpadassanaṃ.

It is said that a certain man set out on a path at night with a grass torch. His grass torch went out. Then the even and uneven places were not apparent to him. He rubbed the grass torch on the ground and lit it again. It blazed up and made a light greater than before. As he repeatedly lit it when it went out, the sun gradually rose. When the sun had risen, there was no more work for the torch, so he discarded it and went on his way by day. Herein, the light of the torch is like the kasiṇa light at the time of the preliminary work. The non-seeing of the even and uneven places when the torch has gone out is like the non-seeing of material forms when the light has disappeared because the turn of the preliminary work has been passed. The rubbing of the torch is like the repeated entering into the basic jhāna. The torch making a greater light than before is like the pervading with a stronger light when one does the preliminary work again. The rising of the sun is like the establishment of the powerful light in the defined area. Discarding the grass torch and going on by day is like discarding the limited light and seeing material forms all day with the powerful light.

Tattha yadā tassa bhikkhuno maṃsacakkhussa anāpāthagataṃ antokucchigataṃ hadayavatthunissitaṃ heṭṭhāpathavītalanissitaṃ tirokuṭṭapabbatapākāragataṃ paracakkavāḷagatanti idaṃ rūpaṃ ñāṇacakkhussa āpāthaṃ āgacchati, maṃsacakkhunā dissamānaṃ viya hoti, tadā dibbacakkhu uppannaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Tadeva cettha rūpadassanasamatthaṃ, na pubbabhāgacittāni.

Therein, when a material form that is beyond the range of the bhikkhu’s fleshly eye—located inside the belly, based on the heart-basis, based on the ground below, located behind a wall, mountain, or rampart, or located in another world-system—comes into the range of the knowledge-eye and appears as if seen by the fleshly eye, then it should be understood that the divine eye has arisen. And only that is capable of seeing forms here, not the preliminary-part consciousnesses.

Taṃ panetaṃ puthujjanassa paribandho hoti. Kasmā? So hi yasmā yattha yattha āloko hotūti adhiṭṭhāti, taṃ taṃ pathavīsamuddapabbate vinivijjhitvāpi ekālokaṃ hoti, athassa tattha bhayānakāni yakkharakkhasādirūpāni passato bhayaṃ uppajjati. Yena cittavikkhepaṃ patvā jhānavibbhantako hoti, tasmā rūpadassane appamattena bhavitabbaṃ.

But this is an obstruction for a worldling. Why? Because wherever he resolves, “Let there be light,” even after piercing through earth, ocean, and mountains, it becomes a single light. Then, when he sees there fearful forms of yakkhas, rakkhasas, and the like, fear arises in him. By this he reaches distraction of mind and becomes deranged in respect to jhāna. Therefore, one must be heedful regarding the seeing of forms.

Tatrāyaṃ dibbacakkhuno uppattikkamo. Vuttappakārametaṃ rūpamārammaṇaṃ katvā manodvārāvajjane uppajjitvā niruddhe tadeva rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā cattāri pañca vā javanāni uppajjantīti sabbaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Idhāpi pubbabhāgacittāni savitakkasavicārāni kāmāvacarāni. Pariyosāne atthasādhakacittaṃ catutthajjhānikaṃ rūpāvacaraṃ. Tena sahajātaṃ ñāṇaṃ sattānaṃ cutūpapāte ñāṇantipi dibbacakkhuñāṇantipi vuccatīti.

Herein, this is the process of arising for the divine eye. Having made a material form of the kind described the object, when mind-door adverting has arisen and ceased, then, taking that same material form as object, four or five impulsions arise—all this should be understood in the same way as before. Here too, the preliminary-part consciousnesses are accompanied by initial and sustained application and are of the sense sphere. At the end, the consciousness that accomplishes the purpose is of the fourth jhāna and belongs to the fine-material sphere. The knowledge that is co-nascent with it is called both the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings and the knowledge of the divine eye.

Cutūpapātañāṇakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Passing Away and Reappearance of Beings is concluded.

Pakiṇṇakakathā

Miscellaneous Discourse

413.

413.

Iti [V 2.0057] pañcakkhandhavidū, pañca abhiññā avoca yā nātho;

Tā ñatvā tāsu ayaṃ, pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyā.

Thus the Protector, knower of the five aggregates, declared the five direct knowledges. Having known them, in regard to them this miscellaneous discourse should also be understood.

Etāsu [M 2.0060] hi yadetaṃ cutūpapātañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ dibbacakkhu, tassa anāgataṃsañāṇañca yathākammupagañāṇañcāti dvepi paribhaṇḍañāṇāni honti. Iti imāni ca dve iddhividhādīni ca pañcāti satta abhiññāñāṇāni idhāgatāni. Idāni tesaṃ ārammaṇavibhāge asammohatthaṃ –

For among these, that which is the divine eye, known as the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings, has two subsidiary knowledges: the knowledge of the future and the knowledge of the destination of beings according to their kamma. Thus these two, and the five beginning with the kinds of supernormal power, make seven kinds of direct knowledge that are treated here. Now, to avoid confusion in the analysis of their objects—

Ārammaṇattikā vuttā, ye cattāro mahesinā;

Sattannamapi ñāṇānaṃ, pavattiṃ tesu dīpaye.

Four triads of objects have been stated by the Great Sage; I shall now explain the occurrence of the seven knowledges in terms of them.

Tatrāyaṃ dīpanā. Cattāro hi ārammaṇattikā mahesinā vuttā. Katame cattāro? Parittārammaṇattiko, maggārammaṇattiko, atītārammaṇattiko, ajjhattārammaṇattikoti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 13, 16, 19, 21).

Here is the explanation. Four triads of objects have been stated by the Great Sage. Which four? The triad of limited objects, the triad of path objects, the triad of past objects, and the triad of internal objects.

414. Tattha iddhividhañāṇaṃ parittamahaggataatītānāgatapaccuppannaajjhattabahiddhārammaṇavasena sattasu ārammaṇesu pavattati. Kathaṃ? Tañhi yadā kāyaṃ cittasannissitaṃ katvā adissamānena kāyena gantukāmo cittavasena kāyaṃ pariṇāmeti, mahaggatacitte samodahati samāropeti, tadā upayogaladdhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hotīti katvā rūpakāyārammaṇato parittārammaṇaṃ hoti. Yadā cittaṃ kāyasannissitaṃ katvā dissamānena kāyena gantukāmo kāyavasena cittaṃ pariṇāmeti, pādakajjhānacittaṃ rūpakāye samodahati samāropeti, tadā upayogaladdhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hotīti katvā mahaggatacittārammaṇato mahaggatārammaṇaṃ hoti.

414. Herein, the knowledge of the kinds of supernormal power operates with seven kinds of objects: limited, exalted, past, future, present, internal, and external. How? For when one, wishing to travel with an invisible body, makes the body dependent on the mind and transforms the body by the mind’s power, placing it upon and merging it with an exalted mind, then because its object is the material body, it has a limited object. When one, wishing to travel with a visible body, makes the mind dependent on the body and transforms the mind by the body’s power, placing upon and merging with the material body the mind of the basic jhāna, then because its object is the exalted mind, it has an exalted object.

Yasmā pana tadeva cittaṃ atītaṃ niruddhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, tasmā atītārammaṇaṃ hoti. Mahādhātunidhāne mahākassapattherādīnaṃ viya anāgataṃ adhiṭṭhahantānaṃ anāgatārammaṇaṃ hoti. Mahākassapatthero kira mahādhātunidhānaṃ karonto “anāgate aṭṭhārasavassādhikāni dvevassasatāni ime gandhā mā sussiṃsu, pupphāni mā milāyiṃsu, dīpā mā nibbāyiṃsū”ti [V 2.0058] (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1434) adhiṭṭhahi. Sabbaṃ tatheva ahosi. Assaguttatthero vattaniyasenāsane bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sukkhabhattaṃ bhuñjamānaṃ disvā udakasoṇḍiṃ divase divase purebhatte dadhirasaṃ hotūti adhiṭṭhāsi. Purebhatte gahitaṃ dadhirasaṃ hoti. Pacchābhatte pākatikaudakameva (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1434). Kāyaṃ pana cittasannissitaṃ [M 2.0061] katvā adissamānena kāyena gamanakāle paccuppannārammaṇaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, since that same mind takes as its object what is past and has ceased, it has a past object. For those who make a determination about the future, like the Elder Mahākassapa and others at the Great Relic Chamber, it has a future object. It is said that the Elder Mahākassapa, while establishing the Great Relic Chamber, made a determination: 'In the future, for two hundred and eighteen years, may these perfumes not dry up, may these flowers not wither, may these lamps not be extinguished!' And everything happened just so. The Elder Assagutta, seeing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus eating dry food at the Vattaniya monastery, made a determination: 'May the water pot yield curd every day before the meal.' When taken before the meal, it is curd; after the meal, it is just ordinary water. And when one travels with an invisible body, having made the body dependent on the mind, it has a present object.

Kāyavasena cittaṃ, cittavasena vā kāyaṃ pariṇāmanakāle attano kumārakavaṇṇādinimmānakāle ca sakāyacittānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇato ajjhattārammaṇaṃ hoti. Bahiddhā hatthiassādidassanakāle pana bahiddhārammaṇanti evaṃ tāva iddhividhañāṇassa sattasu ārammaṇesu pavatti veditabbā.

When one transforms the mind by means of the body or the body by means of the mind, and when one creates a form for oneself such as that of a boy, it has an internal object because it takes one’s own body and mind as its object. But at the time of displaying external forms such as those of elephants and horses, it has an external object. Thus the occurrence of the knowledge of the kinds of supernormal power in these seven objects should be understood.

415. Dibbasotadhātuñāṇaṃ parittapaccuppannaajjhattabahiddhārammaṇavasena catūsu ārammaṇesu pavattati. Kathaṃ? Tañhi yasmā saddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, saddo ca paritto, tasmā parittārammaṇaṃ hoti. Vijjamānaṃyeva pana saddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattanato paccuppannārammaṇaṃ hoti. Taṃ attano kucchisaddasavanakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ. Paresaṃ saddasavanakāle bahiddhārammaṇanti evaṃ dibbasotadhātuñāṇassa catūsu ārammaṇesu pavatti veditabbā.

415. The knowledge of the divine ear element operates with four kinds of objects: limited, present, internal, and external. How? Since it takes sound as its object, and sound is limited, it has a limited object. Since it operates by taking an actually existing sound as its object, it has a present object. When one hears the sound in one’s own stomach, it has an internal object. When one hears the sounds of others, it has an external object. Thus the operation of the knowledge of the divine ear element in these four objects should be understood.

416. Cetopariyañāṇaṃ parittamahaggataappamāṇamaggaatītānāgatapaccuppannabahiddhārammaṇavasena aṭṭhasu ārammaṇesu pavattati. Kathaṃ? Tañhi paresaṃ kāmāvacaracittajānanakāle parittārammaṇaṃ hoti. Rūpāvacaraarūpāvacaracittajānanakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ hoti. Maggaphalajānanakāle appamāṇārammaṇaṃ hoti.

416. The knowledge of encompassing the minds of others operates with eight kinds of objects: limited, exalted, immeasurable, path, past, future, present, and external. How? When knowing the sense-sphere consciousness of others, it has a limited object. When knowing form-sphere or formless-sphere consciousness, it has an exalted object. When knowing path and fruition consciousness, it has an immeasurable object.

Ettha ca puthujjano sotāpannassa cittaṃ na jānāti. Sotāpanno vā sakadāgāmissāti evaṃ yāva arahato netabbaṃ. Arahā pana sabbesaṃ cittaṃ jānāti. Aññopi ca uparimo heṭṭhimassāti ayaṃ viseso veditabbo. Maggacittārammaṇakāle maggārammaṇaṃ hoti. Yadā pana atīte sattadivasabbhantare ca anāgate sattadivasabbhantare ca paresaṃ cittaṃ jānāti, tadā atītārammaṇaṃ anāgatārammaṇañca hoti.

Here, a worldling does not know the mind of a stream-enterer. A stream-enterer, in turn, does not know the mind of a once-returner, and so on up to the level below the arahant. But an arahant knows the minds of all. This distinction, too, should be understood: a higher one knows the mind of a lower one. When it takes path consciousness as its object, it has a path object. But when one knows the minds of others within seven days in the past and within seven days in the future, it has a past object and a future object, respectively.

Kathaṃ [V 2.0059] paccuppannārammaṇaṃ hoti. Paccuppannaṃ nāma tividhaṃ – khaṇapaccuppannaṃ, santatipaccuppannaṃ, addhāpaccuppannañca. Tattha uppādaṭṭhitibhaṅgappattaṃ khaṇapaccuppannaṃ. Ekadvesantativārapariyāpannaṃ santatipaccuppannaṃ. Tattha andhakāre nisīditvā ālokaṭṭhānaṃ gatassa na tāva ārammaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, yāva pana taṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti[M 2.0062], etthantare ekadvesantativārā veditabbā. Ālokaṭṭhāne vicaritvā ovarakaṃ paviṭṭhassāpi na tāva sahasā rūpaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, yāva pana taṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, etthantare ekadvesantativārā veditabbā. Dūre ṭhatvā pana rajakānaṃ hatthavikāraṃ, ghaṇḍibherīākoṭanavikārañca disvāpi na tāva saddaṃ suṇāti, yāva pana taṃ suṇāti, etasmimpi antare ekadvesantativārā veditabbā. Evaṃ tāva majjhimabhāṇakā.

How does it have a present object? The present is of three kinds: the momentary present, the continuity-present, and the duration-present. Therein, the momentary present is what has reached arising, presence, and dissolution. The continuity-present is what is comprised in one or two continuity-processes. For one who has been sitting in darkness and goes to a lighted place, the object is not yet apparent; in the interval until it becomes apparent, one or two continuity-processes should be understood. For one who has been walking about in a lighted place and enters a chamber, a form is not immediately apparent; in the interval until it becomes apparent, one or two continuity-processes should be understood. And for one standing at a distance, even after seeing the hand movements of washermen and the motion of striking a bell or drum, one does not yet hear the sound; in the interval until one hears it, one or two continuity-processes should be understood. So say the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya.

Saṃyuttabhāṇakā pana rūpasantati arūpasantatīti dve santatiyo vatvā udakaṃ akkamitvā gatassa yāva tīre akkantaudakalekhā na vippasīdati, addhānato āgatassa yāva kāye usumabhāvo na vūpasammati, ātapā āgantvā gabbhaṃ paviṭṭhassa yāva andhakārabhāvo na vigacchati, antogabbhe kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karitvā divā vātapānaṃ vivaritvā olokentassa yāva akkhīnaṃ phandanabhāvo na vūpasammati, ayaṃ rūpasantati nāma. Dve tayo javanavārā arūpasantati nāmāti vatvā tadubhayampi santatipaccuppannaṃ nāmāti vadanti.

The reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, however, speak of two continuities, material continuity and immaterial continuity. They say: 'When one has walked after stepping into water, the line of disturbed water on the bank does not clear for some time; when one has arrived from a journey, the heat in the body does not subside for some time; when one has come from the sun and entered a chamber, the impression of darkness does not depart for some time; when one, while attending to a meditation subject inside a chamber, opens a window by day and looks out, the flickering of the eyes does not subside for some time—this is called material continuity.' And saying that two or three javana-processes are called immaterial continuity, they state that both of these are called the continuity-present.

Ekabhavaparicchinnaṃ pana addhāpaccuppannaṃ nāma. Yaṃ sandhāya bhaddekarattasutte “yo cāvuso, mano ye ca dhammā ubhayametaṃ paccuppannaṃ, tasmiṃ ce paccuppanne chandarāgappaṭibaddhaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ, chandarāgappaṭibaddhattā viññāṇassa tadabhinandati, tadabhinandanto paccuppannesu dhammesu saṃhīratī”ti (ma. ni. 3.284) vuttaṃ. Santatipaccuppannañcettha aṭṭhakathāsu āgataṃ. Addhāpaccuppannaṃ sutte.

The duration-present, however, is what is limited to a single existence. It is in reference to this that it is said in the Bhaddekaratta Sutta: 'Friend, the mind and mental objects—both these are the present. If consciousness is bound by desire and lust for what is present, then because of that bondage to desire and lust, one delights in it. Delighting in it, one is ensnared by present phenomena.' Here, the continuity-present is found in the commentaries, the duration-present in the Sutta.

Tattha keci khaṇapaccuppannaṃ cittaṃ cetopariyañāṇassa ārammaṇaṃ hotīti vadanti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Yasmā iddhimato ca parassa ca ekakkhaṇe cittaṃ uppajjatīti. Idañca nesaṃ opammaṃ, yathā ākāse khitte pupphamuṭṭhimhi avassaṃ ekaṃ pupphaṃ ekassa vaṇṭena vaṇṭaṃ paṭivijjhati, evaṃ parassa cittaṃ jānissāmīti rāsivasena mahājanassa citte āvajjite avassaṃ ekassa cittaṃ ekena cittena uppādakkhaṇe vā ṭhitikkhaṇe vā bhaṅgakkhaṇe vā paṭivijjhatīti. Taṃ pana vassasatampi vassasahassampi āvajjanto yena ca cittena āvajjati[V 2.0060], yena ca jānāti. Tesaṃ dvinnaṃ sahaṭhānābhāvato āvajjanajavanānañca aniṭṭhaṭṭhāne nānārammaṇabhāvappattidosato ayuttanti aṭṭhakathāsu paṭikkhittaṃ.

Some say that a mind in the momentary present is the object of the knowledge of penetrating others’ minds. For what reason? Because, they say, the mind of one with psychic power and the mind of another person arise in the same moment. And this is their simile: just as when a handful of flowers is thrown into the air, one flower will inevitably pierce another, stem to stem, so too, when one adverts to the minds of a great crowd by way of the mass with the thought, 'I will know another's mind,' one's own mind will inevitably penetrate another's at the moment of arising, the static moment, or the moment of dissolution. But this is rejected in the commentaries as incorrect, for the mind with which one adverts and the mind with which one knows cannot exist together—even if one were to advert for a hundred or a thousand years—and because of the fault that, in an undesirable situation, the adverting consciousness and the impulsion consciousnesses would come to have different objects.

Santatipaccuppannaṃ [M 2.0063] pana addhāpaccuppannañca ārammaṇaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Tattha yaṃ vattamānajavanavīthito atītānāgatavasena dvittijavanavīthiparimāṇe kāle parassa cittaṃ, taṃ sabbampi santatipaccuppannaṃ nāma. “Addhāpaccuppannaṃ pana javanavārena dīpetabba”nti saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ suṭṭhu vuttaṃ.

However, it should be understood that the continuity-present and the duration-present are its objects. Therein, another’s mind that occurs within a period of two or three javana-processes, past or future in relation to the present javana-process—all this is called the continuity-present. It is said in the Commentary to the Saṃyutta Nikāya: 'But the duration-present should be explained by way of the javana-round.' That is well said.

Tatrāyaṃ dīpanā, iddhimā parassa cittaṃ jānitukāmo āvajjati, āvajjanaṃ khaṇapaccuppannaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā teneva saha nirujjhati. Tato cattāri pañca vā javanāni. Yesaṃ pacchimaṃ iddhicittaṃ, sesāni kāmāvacarāni, tesaṃ sabbesampi tadeva niruddhaṃ cittamārammaṇaṃ hoti, na ca tāni nānārammaṇāni honti, addhāvasena paccuppannārammaṇattā. Ekārammaṇattepi ca iddhicittameva parassa cittaṃ jānāti, na itarāni. Yathā cakkhudvāre cakkhuviññāṇameva rūpaṃ passati, na itarānīti. Iti idaṃ santatipaccuppannassa ceva addhāpaccuppannassa ca vasena paccuppannārammaṇaṃ hoti. Yasmā vā santatipaccuppannampi addhāpaccuppanneyeva patati, tasmā addhāpaccuppannavasenevetaṃ paccuppannārammaṇanti veditabbaṃ. Parassa cittārammaṇattāyeva pana bahiddhārammaṇaṃ hotīti evaṃ cetopariyañāṇassa aṭṭhasu ārammaṇesu pavatti veditabbā.

Here is the explanation: One with psychic power who wishes to know another’s mind adverts to it. The adverting, taking the momentarily present mind as its object, ceases together with it. Then, four or five impulsions arise. The last of these is the consciousness of psychic power, while the rest are of the sense sphere. For all of them, that same ceased mind is the object, and they do not have different objects, because they have an object that is present by way of duration. Even though they have a single object, only the consciousness of psychic power knows another’s mind, not the others—just as, at the eye-door, only eye-consciousness sees a form, not the other consciousnesses. Thus, this has a present object by way of both the continuity-present and the duration-present. Or, since what is present by way of continuity also falls within what is present by way of duration, it should be understood as having a present object by way of duration alone. Moreover, precisely because it takes another’s mind as its object, it has an external object. In this way, the operation of the knowledge of penetrating minds should be understood in regard to the eight kinds of objects.

417. Pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ parittamahaggataappamāṇamaggaatītaajjhattabahiddhānavattabbārammaṇavasena aṭṭhasu ārammaṇesu pavattati. Kathaṃ? Tañhi kāmāvacarakkhandhānussaraṇakāle parittārammaṇaṃ hoti. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakkhandhānussaraṇakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ. Atīte attanā parehi vā bhāvitamaggaṃ sacchikataphalañca anussaraṇakāle appamāṇārammaṇaṃ. Bhāvitamaggameva anussaraṇakāle maggārammaṇaṃ. Niyamato panetaṃ atītārammaṇameva.

417. The knowledge of recollecting past lives operates in regard to eight kinds of objects: limited, exalted, immeasurable, the path, past, internal, external, and inexpressible. How so? When it recollects the aggregates of the sense sphere, it has a limited object. When it recollects the aggregates of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere, it has an exalted object. When it recollects a path developed or a fruit realized by oneself or by others in the past, it has an immeasurable object. When it recollects only a developed path, it has the path as its object. As a rule, however, it has only a past object.

Tattha kiñcāpi cetopariyañāṇayathākammupagañāṇānipi atītārammaṇāni honti, atha kho tesaṃ cetopariyañāṇassa sattadivasabbhantarātītaṃ cittameva ārammaṇaṃ. Tañhi aññaṃ khandhaṃ vā khandhapaṭibaddhaṃ vā na jānāti. Maggasampayuttacittārammaṇattā pana pariyāyato maggārammaṇanti [V 2.0061] vuttaṃ. Yathākammupagañāṇassa ca atītaṃ cetanāmattameva ārammaṇaṃ. Pubbenivāsañāṇassa pana atītā khandhā khandhapaṭibaddhañca kiñci anārammaṇaṃ nāma natthi[M 2.0064]. Tañhi atītakkhandhakhandhapaṭibaddhesu dhammesu sabbaññutaññāṇagatikaṃ hotīti ayaṃ viseso veditabbo. Ayamettha aṭṭhakathānayo. Yasmā pana “kusalā khandhā iddhividhañāṇassa cetopariyañāṇassa pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇassa yathākammupagañāṇassa anāgataṃsañāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.404) paṭṭhāne vuttaṃ. Tasmā cattāropi khandhā cetopariyañāṇayathākammupagañāṇānaṃ ārammaṇā honti. Tatrāpi yathākammupagañāṇassa kusalākusalā evāti.

Here, although the knowledge of penetrating minds and the knowledge of beings' faring according to their kamma also have past objects, for the knowledge of penetrating minds, only a mind within the past seven days is its object. For it does not know any other aggregate or what is connected with the aggregates. However, because it has as its object a mind associated with the path, it is said figuratively to have the path as its object. And for the knowledge of beings' faring according to their kamma, only past volition is the object. But for the knowledge of recollecting past lives, there is nothing among past aggregates or what is connected with the aggregates that is not an object. For in regard to past aggregates and what is connected with them, its range is like that of the knowledge of omniscience—this distinction should be understood. This is the method of the commentary here. However, because it is said in the Paṭṭhāna: 'Wholesome aggregates are a condition by way of object condition for the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power, the knowledge of penetrating minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of beings' faring according to their kamma, and the knowledge of the future,' therefore, the four aggregates are also objects for the knowledge of penetrating minds and the knowledge of beings' faring according to their kamma. And even in that case, for the knowledge of beings' faring according to their kamma, only wholesome and unwholesome aggregates are its objects.

Attano khandhānussaraṇakāle panetaṃ ajjhattārammaṇaṃ. Parassa khandhānussaraṇakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ. “Atīte vipassī bhagavā ahosi. Tassa mātā bandhumatī, pitā bandhumā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.12) nayena nāmagottapathavīnimittādianussaraṇakāle navattabbārammaṇaṃ hoti. Nāmagottanti cettha khandhūpanibandho sammutisiddho byañjanattho daṭṭhabbo, na byañjanaṃ. Byañjanañhi saddāyatanasaṅgahitattā parittaṃ hoti. Yathāha “niruttipaṭisambhidā parittārammaṇā”ti (vibha. 749). Ayamettha amhākaṃ khanti. Evaṃ pubbenivāsañāṇassa aṭṭhasu ārammaṇesu pavatti veditabbā.

When it recollects one's own aggregates, it has an internal object. When it recollects another's aggregates, it has an external object. When it recollects names, clans, the earth-kasina sign, etc., in the manner of, 'In the past there was the Blessed One Vipassī. His mother was Bandhumatī, his father Bandhumā,' it has an inexpressible object. Here, by 'name and clan' should be understood the meaning of the expression, which is established by convention and connected with the aggregates, not the expression itself. For the expression, being included in the sound base, is limited. As it is said: 'The discrimination of language has a limited object.' This is our accepted position here. Thus, the operation of the knowledge of recollecting past lives should be understood in regard to the eight kinds of objects.

418. Dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ parittapaccuppannaajjhattabahiddhārammaṇavasena catūsu ārammaṇesu pavattati. Kathaṃ? Tañhi yasmā rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, rūpañca parittaṃ, tasmā parittārammaṇaṃ hoti. Vijjamāneyeva ca rūpe pavattattā paccuppannārammaṇaṃ. Attano kucchigatādirūpadassanakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ. Parassa rūpadassanakāle bahiddhārammaṇanti evaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇassa catūsu ārammaṇesu pavatti veditabbā.

418. The knowledge of the divine eye operates in regard to four kinds of objects, by way of the limited, the present, the internal, and the external. How so? For since it takes material form as its object, and material form is limited, it therefore has a limited object. And since it operates only in regard to actually existing material form, it has a present object. When it sees material form located in one's own belly, etc., it has an internal object. When it sees the material form of another, it has an external object. In this way, the operation of the knowledge of the divine eye in regard to four kinds of objects is to be understood.

419. Anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ parittamahaggataappamāṇamaggaanāgataajjhattabahiddhānavattabbārammaṇavasena aṭṭhasu ārammaṇesu pavattati. Kathaṃ? Tañhi “ayaṃ anāgate kāmāvacare nibbattissatī”ti jānanakāle parittārammaṇaṃ hoti. “Rūpāvacare arūpāvacare vā nibbattissatī”ti jānanakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ. “Maggaṃ bhāvessati, phalaṃ sacchikarissatī”ti jānanakāle [V 2.0062] appamāṇārammaṇaṃ. “Maggaṃ bhāvessati”cceva jānanakāle maggārammaṇaṃ. Niyamato pana taṃ anāgatārammaṇameva.

419. The knowledge of the future operates in regard to eight kinds of objects, by way of the limited, the exalted, the immeasurable, the path, the future, the internal, the external, and the inexpressible. How so? For when it knows, ‘This one will be reborn in the sense-sphere in the future,’ it has a limited object. When it knows, ‘This one will be reborn in the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere,’ it has an exalted object. When it knows, ‘This one will develop the path and realize the fruit,’ it has an immeasurable object. When it knows just, ‘This one will develop the path,’ it has the path as its object. As a rule, however, it has only a future object.

Tattha [M 2.0065] kiñcāpi cetopariyañāṇampi anāgatārammaṇaṃ hoti, atha kho tassa sattadivasabbhantarānāgataṃ cittameva ārammaṇaṃ. Tañhi aññaṃ khandhaṃ vā khandhapaṭibaddhaṃ vā na jānāti. Anāgataṃsañāṇassa pubbenivāsañāṇe vuttanayena anāgate anārammaṇaṃ nāma natthi. “Ahaṃ amutra nibbattissāmī”ti jānanakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ. “Asuko amutra nibbattissatī”ti jānanakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ. “Anāgate metteyyo bhagavā uppajjissati (dī. ni. 3.107). Subrahmā nāmassa brāhmaṇo pitā bhavissati. Brahmavatī nāma brāhmaṇī mātā”tiādinā pana nayena nāmagottajānanakāle pubbenivāsañāṇe vuttanayeneva na vattabbārammaṇaṃ hotīti evaṃ anāgataṃsañāṇassa aṭṭhasu ārammaṇesu pavatti veditabbā.

Herein, although the knowledge of penetrating minds also has a future object, its object is only a mind that is future within the next seven days. For it does not know any other aggregate or what is connected with the aggregates. For the knowledge of the future, in the way stated for the knowledge of recollecting past lives, there is nothing in the future that is not its object. When it knows, ‘I will be reborn there,’ it has an internal object. When it knows, ‘So-and-so will be reborn there,’ it has an external object. And when it knows names and clans in the way beginning, ‘In the future, the Blessed One Metteyya will arise. A brahmin named Subrahmā will be his father, and a brahmin woman named Brahmavatī will be his mother,’ and so on, it has an inexpressible object, in the same way as stated for the knowledge of recollecting past lives. Thus, the operation of the knowledge of the future in regard to the eight kinds of objects should be understood.

420. Yathākammupagañāṇaṃ parittamahaggataatītaajjhattabahiddhārammaṇavasena pañcasu ārammaṇesu pavattati. Kathaṃ? Tañhi kāmāvacarakammajānanakāle parittārammaṇaṃ hoti. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakammajānanakāle mahaggatārammaṇaṃ. Atītameva jānātīti atītārammaṇaṃ. Attano kammaṃ jānanakāle ajjhattārammaṇaṃ. Parassa kammaṃ jānanakāle bahiddhārammaṇaṃ hoti. Evaṃ yathākammupagañāṇassa pañcasu ārammaṇesu pavatti veditabbā. Yañcettha ajjhattārammaṇañceva bahiddhārammaṇañcāti vuttaṃ, taṃ kālena ajjhattaṃ kālena bahiddhā jānanakāle ajjhattabahiddhārammaṇampi hotiyevāti.

420. The knowledge of beings’ faring according to their kamma operates in regard to five kinds of objects, by way of the limited, the exalted, the past, the internal, and the external. How so? For when it knows kamma of the sense-sphere, it has a limited object. When it knows kamma of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, it has an exalted object. Since it knows only the past, it has a past object. When it knows its own kamma, it has an internal object. When it knows another’s kamma, it has an external object. Thus, the operation of the knowledge of beings’ faring according to their kamma in regard to these five kinds of objects should be understood. And as for what is stated herein as ‘both an internal object and an external object,’ this is said because when it knows the internal at one time and the external at another, it can indeed also have an internal-and-external object.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus, in the Path of Purification, composed for the delight of good people,

Abhiññāniddeso nāma

the Exposition of the Direct Knowledges, so named,

Terasamo paricchedo.

is the thirteenth chapter.

14. Khandhaniddeso

14. The Exposition of the Aggregates

Paññākathā

The Discourse on Wisdom

421. Idāni [M 2.0066][V 2.0063] yasmā evaṃ abhiññāvasena adhigatānisaṃsāya thiratarāya samādhibhāvanāya samannāgatena bhikkhunā sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayanti ettha cittasīsena niddiṭṭho samādhi sabbākārena bhāvito hoti.

421. Now, a bhikkhu endowed with the development of concentration that is very firm, the benefits of which have been realized in this way by means of the direct knowledges, has thereby developed in all respects the concentration indicated by the head-term ‘mind’ in the passage, ‘A wise person established in virtue develops mind and wisdom.’

Tadanantarā pana paññā bhāvetabbā. Sā ca atisaṅkhepadesitattā viññātumpi tāva na sukarā, pageva bhāvetuṃ. Tasmā tassā vitthāraṃ bhāvanānayañca dassetuṃ idaṃ pañhākammaṃ hoti.

Next, however, wisdom is to be developed. But since it is taught very concisely, it is not easy even to understand, let alone to develop it. Therefore, to show its detailed explanation and the method for its development, this series of questions is posed.

Kā paññā, kenaṭṭhena paññā, kānassā lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni, katividhā paññā, kathaṃ bhāvetabbā, paññābhāvanāya ko ānisaṃsoti?

What is wisdom? In what sense is it wisdom? What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? How many kinds of wisdom are there? How is it to be developed? What is the benefit of developing wisdom?

422. Tatridaṃ vissajjanaṃ, kā paññāti paññā bahuvidhā nānappakārā. Taṃ sabbaṃ vibhāvayituṃ ārabbhamānaṃ vissajjanaṃ adhippetañceva atthaṃ na sādheyya, uttari ca vikkhepāya saṃvatteyya, tasmā idha adhippetameva sandhāya vadāma. Kusalacittasampayuttaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ paññā.

422. Herein is the answer. As to the question, ‘What is wisdom?’: wisdom is of many kinds and various types. An explanation undertaken to clarify all of that would not accomplish the intended meaning and would, moreover, lead to distraction. Therefore we speak here only with reference to what is intended in this context. Wisdom is the insight knowledge associated with wholesome consciousness.

423. Kenaṭṭhena paññāti pajānanaṭṭhena paññā. Kimidaṃ pajānanaṃ nāma? Sañjānanavijānanākāravisiṭṭhaṃ nānappakārato jānanaṃ. Saññāviññāṇapaññānaṃ hi samānepi jānanabhāve, saññā “nīlaṃ pītaka”nti ārammaṇasañjānanamattameva hoti. “Aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkoti. Viññāṇaṃ “nīlaṃ pītaka”nti ārammaṇañca jānāti, lakkhaṇapaṭivedhañca pāpeti. Ussakkitvā pana maggapātubhāvaṃ pāpetuṃ na [V 2.0064] sakkoti. Paññā vuttanayavasena ārammaṇañca jānāti, lakkhaṇapaṭivedhañca pāpeti, ussakkitvā maggapātubhāvañca pāpeti.

423. In what sense is it wisdom? It is wisdom in the sense of discerning. What, now, is this discerning? It is a knowing in various ways, a knowing distinguished from the modes of perceiving and cognizing. For though perception (saññā), consciousness (viññāṇa), and wisdom (paññā) have knowing in common, perception is merely the perceiving of an object as ‘blue’ or ‘yellow’; it cannot bring about the penetration of the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Consciousness both knows the object as ‘blue’ or ‘yellow’ and brings about the penetration of the characteristics; but by striving further, it cannot bring about the manifestation of the path. Wisdom, in the way described, both knows the object and brings about the penetration of the characteristics, and by striving further, it also brings about the manifestation of the path.

Yathā hi heraññikaphalake ṭhapitaṃ kahāpaṇarāsiṃ eko ajātabuddhidārako, eko gāmikapuriso, eko heraññikoti tīsu janesu passamānesu [M 2.0067] ajātabuddhidārako kahāpaṇānaṃ cittavicittadīghacaturassaparimaṇḍalabhāvamattameva jānāti, “idaṃ manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogaṃ ratanasammata”nti na jānāti. Gāmikapuriso cittavicittādibhāvaṃ jānāti, “idaṃ manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogaṃ ratanasammata”nti ca. “Ayaṃ cheko, ayaṃ kūṭo, ayaṃ addhasāro”ti imaṃ pana vibhāgaṃ na jānāti. Heraññiko sabbepi te pakāre jānāti, jānanto ca kahāpaṇaṃ oloketvāpi jānāti, ākoṭitassa saddaṃ sutvāpi, gandhaṃ ghāyitvāpi, rasaṃ sāyitvāpi, hatthena dhārayitvāpi, asukasmiṃ nāma gāme vā nigame vā nagare vā pabbate vā nadītīre vā katotipi, asukācariyena katotipi jānāti, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Suppose a heap of coins is placed on a money-changer's board, and three people are looking at it: a child of undeveloped intelligence, a villager, and a money-changer. The child of undeveloped intelligence knows only that the coins are colorful and variegated, long, square, or round; he does not know: 'This is considered a treasure for people’s use and enjoyment.' The villager knows that they are colorful and variegated, etc., and he also knows: 'This is considered a treasure for people’s use and enjoyment.' But he does not know this distinction: 'This one is genuine, this is counterfeit, this is of half-value.' The money-changer knows all these aspects. Knowing them, he recognizes a coin by looking at it, by hearing its sound when struck, by smelling it, by tasting it, and by weighing it in his hand. He even knows: 'This was made in such and such a village, market town, or city, or on such and such a mountain or riverbank,' and 'It was made by such and such a master.' This is how the matter should be understood.

Saññā hi ajātabuddhino dārakassa kahāpaṇadassanaṃ viya hoti, nīlādivasena ārammaṇassa upaṭṭhānākāramattagahaṇato. Viññāṇaṃ gāmikassa purisassa kahāpaṇadassanamiva hoti, nīlādivasena ārammaṇākāragahaṇato, uddhaṃpi ca lakkhaṇapaṭivedhasampāpanato. Paññā heraññikassa kahāpaṇadassanamiva hoti, nīlādivasena ārammaṇākāraṃ gahetvā, lakkhaṇapaṭivedhañca pāpetvā, tato uddhampi maggapātubhāvapāpanato. Tasmā yadetaṃ sañjānanavijānanākāravisiṭṭhaṃ nānappakārato jānanaṃ. Idaṃ pajānananti veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ sandhāya hi etaṃ vuttaṃ “pajānanaṭṭhena paññā”ti.

For perception is like the seeing of the coins by the child of undeveloped intelligence, since it grasps only the mode of the object's presentation by way of 'blue,' etc. Consciousness is like the seeing of the coins by the villager, since it grasps the mode of the object by way of 'blue,' etc., and also brings about the penetration of the characteristics. Wisdom is like the seeing of the coins by the money-changer, since after grasping the mode of the object by way of 'blue,' etc., and leading to the penetration of the characteristics, it leads still further to the manifestation of the path. Therefore, that knowing in various ways which is distinguished from the modes of perceiving and cognizing should be understood as 'discerning.' It is with reference to this that it was said: 'Wisdom is in the sense of discerning.'

Sā panesā yattha saññāviññāṇāni, na tattha ekaṃsena hoti. Yadā pana hoti, tadā avinibbhuttā tehi dhammehi “ayaṃ saññā, idaṃ viññāṇaṃ, ayaṃ paññā”ti vinibbhujjitvā alabbhaneyyanānattā sukhumā duddasā. Tenāha āyasmā nāgaseno “dukkaraṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā kata”nti. Kiṃ, bhante, nāgasena bhagavatā dukkaraṃ katanti? ‘Dukkaraṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā kataṃ yaṃ arūpīnaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekārammaṇe pavattamānānaṃ vavatthānaṃ akkhātaṃ ayaṃ phasso, ayaṃ vedanā, ayaṃ saññā, ayaṃ cetanā, idaṃ citta’”nti (mi. pa. 2.7.16).

But this wisdom is not invariably present where there are perception and consciousness. When it is present, however, it is inseparable from those states. They are subtle and hard to see, and their diversity cannot be grasped by distinguishing them thus: 'This is perception, this is consciousness, this is wisdom.' Thus the Venerable Nāgasena said: 'Great king, what the Blessed One has done is difficult to do.' 'Venerable Nāgasena, what has the Blessed One done that is difficult to do?' 'Great king, it is a difficult thing that the Blessed One has done, to have declared the distinction among immaterial mental states occurring with a single object, thus: "This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness."'

424. Kānassā [M 2.0068][V 2.0065] lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānānīti ettha pana dhammasabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇā paññā, dhammānaṃ sabhāvapaṭicchādakamohandhakāraviddhaṃsanarasā, asammohapaccupaṭṭhānā. “Samāhito yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passatī”ti (a. ni. 10.2) vacanato pana samādhi tassā padaṭṭhānaṃ.

424. As to the question, 'What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?': Here, wisdom has the penetration of the true nature of phenomena as its characteristic. Its function is to dispel the darkness of delusion that conceals the true nature of phenomena. Its manifestation is non-delusion. And since it is said, 'One who is concentrated knows and sees things as they really are,' concentration is its proximate cause.

Paññāpabhedakathā

Exposition on the Divisions of Wisdom

425. Katividhā paññāti dhammasabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇena tāva ekavidhā. Lokiyalokuttaravasena duvidhā. Tathā sāsavānāsavādivasena, nāmarūpavavatthāpanavasena, somanassupekkhāsahagatavasena, dassanabhāvanābhūmivasena ca. Tividhā cintāsutabhāvanāmayavasena. Tathā parittamahaggataappamāṇārammaṇavasena, āyāpāyaupāyakosallavasena, ajjhattābhinivesādivasena ca. Catubbidhā catūsu saccesu ñāṇavasena catupaṭisambhidāvasena cāti.

425. How many divisions of wisdom are there? In the first place, it is of one kind by the characteristic of penetrating the intrinsic nature of phenomena. It is twofold by way of the mundane and the supramundane. Similarly, it is twofold by way of being with and without taints, by way of the determination of mentality-materiality, by way of being accompanied by gladness or equanimity, and by way of the planes of seeing and development. It is threefold by way of being comprised of reflection, learning, and mental development. Likewise, it is threefold by way of having limited, exalted, or immeasurable objects; by way of skill in progress, decline, and means; and by way of application to the internal, etc. And it is fourfold by way of knowledge in the four truths and by way of the four analytical knowledges.

426. Tattha ekavidhakoṭṭhāso uttānatthoyeva. Duvidhakoṭṭhāse lokiyamaggasampayuttā lokiyā. Lokuttaramaggasampayuttā lokuttarāti evaṃ lokiyalokuttaravasena duvidhā.

426. Herein, the section on the onefold division is of obvious meaning. In the section on the twofold division, wisdom associated with the mundane path is mundane; wisdom associated with the supramundane path is supramundane. Thus it is twofold by way of the mundane and the supramundane.

Dutiyaduke āsavānaṃ ārammaṇabhūtā sāsavā. Tesaṃ anārammaṇā anāsavā. Atthato panesā lokiyalokuttarāva hoti. Āsavasampayuttā sāsavā. Āsavavippayuttā anāsavātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ sāsavānāsavādivasena duvidhā.

In the second pair, wisdom that has become an object for the taints is 'with taints.' Wisdom that is not their object is 'taintless.' But in meaning, this is just the mundane and the supramundane. Wisdom associated with the taints is 'with taints'; wisdom dissociated from the taints is 'taintless'—this same method applies in other such cases. Thus it is twofold by way of being with and without taints, etc.

Tatiyaduke yā vipassanaṃ ārabhitukāmassa catunnaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ vavatthāpane paññā, ayaṃ nāmavavatthāpanapaññā. Yā rūpakkhandhassa vavatthāpane paññā, ayaṃ rūpavavatthāpanapaññāti evaṃ nāmarūpavavatthāpanavasena duvidhā.

In the third pair, for one who wishes to begin insight meditation, the wisdom in the determination of the four formless aggregates is the 'wisdom in the determination of mentality.' The wisdom in the determination of the aggregate of materiality is the 'wisdom in the determination of materiality.' Thus it is twofold by way of the determination of mentality and materiality.

Catutthaduke dvīsu kāmāvacarakusalacittesu soḷasasu ca pañcakanayena catukkajjhānikesu maggacittesu paññā somanassasahagatā. Dvīsu kāmāvacarakusalacittesu catūsu ca pañcamajjhānikesu maggacittesu paññā upekkhāsahagatāti evaṃ somanassupekkhāsahagatavasena duvidhā.

In the fourth pair, wisdom is accompanied by gladness in two wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses and in the sixteen path consciousnesses of the first four jhānas (in the fivefold classification). Wisdom is accompanied by equanimity in the other two wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses and in the four path consciousnesses of the fifth jhāna. Thus it is twofold by way of being accompanied by gladness or equanimity.

Pañcamaduke [V 2.0066] paṭhamamaggapaññā [M 2.0069] dassanabhūmi. Avasesamaggattayapaññā bhāvanābhūmīti evaṃ dassanabhāvanābhūmivasena duvidhā.

In the fifth pair, the wisdom of the first path is the plane of seeing. The wisdom of the remaining three paths is the plane of development. Thus it is twofold by way of the planes of seeing and development.

427. Tikesu paṭhamattike parato assutvā paṭiladdhapaññā attano cintāvasena nipphannattā cintāmayā. Parato sutvā paṭiladdhapaññā sutavasena nipphannattā sutamayā. Yathā tathā vā bhāvanāvasena nipphannā appanāppattā paññā bhāvanāmayā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

427. In the triads, in the first triad: wisdom acquired without hearing from another, being accomplished by way of one's own reflection, is wisdom comprised of reflection. Wisdom acquired by hearing from another, being accomplished by way of learning, is wisdom comprised of learning. Wisdom that has reached absorption, being accomplished in one way or another by way of mental development, is wisdom comprised of mental development. For it has been said:

“Tattha katamā cintāmayā paññā? Yogavihitesu vā kammāyatanesu yogavihitesu vā sippāyatanesu yogavihitesu vā vijjāṭṭhānesu kammassakataṃ vā saccānulomikaṃ vā rūpaṃ aniccanti vā vedanā…pe… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ aniccanti vā, yaṃ evarūpiṃ anulomikaṃ khantiṃ diṭṭhiṃ ruciṃ mutiṃ pekkhaṃ dhammanijjhānakhantiṃ parato assutvā paṭilabhati, ayaṃ vuccati cintāmayā paññā…pe… sutvā paṭilabhati, ayaṃ vuccati sutamayā paññā. Sabbāpi samāpannassa paññā bhāvanāmayā paññā”ti (vibha. 768).

“Herein, what is wisdom comprised of reflection? When, without hearing it from another, one acquires such adaptive acceptance, view, inclination, approval, consideration, and reflective acceptance of a doctrine regarding fields of work, crafts, or branches of science undertaken with effort, or regarding ownership of kamma, or conformity with the truth, or that ‘form is impermanent,’ ‘feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness is impermanent’—this is called wisdom comprised of reflection…. When one acquires this after hearing it from another, it is called wisdom comprised of learning. All the wisdom of one who has attained a meditative state is wisdom comprised of mental development.”

Evaṃ cintāsutabhāvanāmayavasena tividhā.

Thus it is threefold by way of being comprised of reflection, learning, and mental development.

Dutiyattike kāmāvacaradhamme ārabbha pavattā paññā parittārammaṇā. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacare ārabbha pavattā mahaggatārammaṇā. Sā lokiyavipassanā. Nibbānaṃ ārabbha pavattā appamāṇārammaṇā. Sā lokuttaravipassanāti evaṃ parittamahaggatāppamāṇārammaṇavasena tividhā.

In the second triad, wisdom that proceeds by taking as its object sense-sphere phenomena has a limited object. Wisdom that proceeds by taking as its object form-sphere and formless-sphere phenomena has an exalted object; this is mundane insight. Wisdom that proceeds by taking Nibbāna as its object has an immeasurable object; this is supramundane insight. Thus it is threefold by way of having a limited, exalted, and immeasurable object.

Tatiyattike āyo nāma vuddhi, sā duvidhā anatthahānito atthuppattito ca. Tattha kosallaṃ āyakosallaṃ. Yathāha –

In the third triad, ‘progress’ (āya) means growth (vuddhi). This is twofold: through the decline of the unbeneficial and through the arising of the beneficial. Skill therein is skill in progress. As it is said:

“Tattha katamaṃ āyakosallaṃ? Ime me dhamme manasikaroto anuppannā ceva akusalā dhammā na uppajjanti, uppannā ca akusalā dhammā pahīyanti, ime vā panime dhamme manasikaroto anuppannā ceva kusalā dhammā uppajjanti. Uppannā ca kusalā dhammā bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattantīti, yā tattha paññā [V 2.0067] pajānanā…pe… amoho dhammavicayo sammādiṭṭhi, idaṃ vuccati āyakosalla”nti (vibha. 771).

“Herein, what is skill in progress? ‘When I attend to these states, unarisen unwholesome states do not arise, and arisen unwholesome states are abandoned; or when I attend to these states, unarisen wholesome states arise, and arisen wholesome states conduce to increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment’—the wisdom, understanding… non-delusion, investigation of states, right view that is there, this is called skill in progress.”

Apāyoti [M 2.0070] pana avuddhi, sāpi duvidhā atthahānito ca anatthuppattito ca. Tattha kosallaṃ apāyakosallaṃ. Yathāha “tattha katamaṃ apāyakosallaṃ? Ime dhamme manasikaroto anuppannā ceva kusalā dhammā na uppajjantī”tiādi (vibha. 771).

‘Decline’ (apāya), however, means non-growth. It too is twofold: through the loss of the beneficial and through the arising of the unbeneficial. Skill therein is skill in decline. As it is said: “Herein, what is skill in decline? ‘When one attends to these states, unarisen wholesome states do not arise,’” etc.

Sabbattha pana tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ upāyesu nibbattikāraṇesu taṃkhaṇappavattaṃ ṭhānuppattikaṃ kosallaṃ upāyakosallaṃ nāma. Yathāha – “sabbāpi tatrupāyā paññā upāyakosalla”nti (vibha. 771). Evaṃ āyāpāyaupāyakosallavasena tividhā.

But in all cases, the ready-witted skill that occurs at that moment regarding the means and the productive causes of those various phenomena is called skill in means. As it is said: “All wisdom regarding the means thereto is skill in means.” Thus it is threefold by way of skill in progress, decline, and means.

Catutthattike attano khandhe gahetvā āraddhā vipassanā paññā ajjhattābhinivesā. Parassa khandhe bāhiraṃ vā anindriyabaddharūpaṃ gahetvā āraddhā bahiddhābhinivesā. Ubhayaṃ gahetvā āraddhā ajjhattabahiddhābhinivesāti evaṃ ajjhattābhinivesādivasena tividhā.

In the fourth triad, insight wisdom that is begun by taking one's own aggregates is ‘application to the internal.’ That which is begun by taking another's aggregates or external materiality not bound up with the faculties is ‘application to the external.’ That which is begun by taking both is ‘application to the internal and external.’ Thus it is threefold by way of application to the internal, etc.

428. Catukkesu paṭhamacatukke dukkhasaccaṃ ārabbha pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ dukkhe ñāṇaṃ. Dukkhasamudayaṃ ārabbha pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ dukkhasamudaye ñāṇaṃ. Dukkhanirodhaṃ ārabbha pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ dukkhanirodhe ñāṇaṃ. Dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ārabbha pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇanti evaṃ catūsu saccesu ñāṇavasena catubbidhā.

428. In the tetrads, in the first tetrad: knowledge that proceeds by taking as its object the truth of suffering is knowledge in suffering; knowledge that proceeds by taking as its object the origin of suffering is knowledge in the origin of suffering; knowledge that proceeds by taking as its object the cessation of suffering is knowledge in the cessation of suffering; knowledge that proceeds by taking as its object the path leading to the cessation of suffering is knowledge in the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Thus it is fourfold by way of knowledge in the four truths.

Dutiyacatukke catasso paṭisambhidā nāma atthādīsu pabhedagatāni cattāri ñāṇāni. Vuttañhetaṃ – “atthe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā. Dhamme ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Tatradhammaniruttābhilāpe ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā. Ñāṇesu ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 718).

In the second tetrad, the so-called four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are four kinds of knowledge distinguished in regard to meaning, etc. For it has been said: “Knowledge in meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning. Knowledge in the Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. Knowledge in the language used to express that Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of language. Knowledge in the foregoing kinds of knowledge is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity.”

Tattha atthoti saṅkhepato hetuphalassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Hetuphalaṃ hi yasmā hetuanusārena ariyati adhigamiyati sampāpuṇiyati, tasmā atthoti vuccati. Pabhedato pana yaṃ kiñci paccayasambhūtaṃ, nibbānaṃ, bhāsitattho, vipāko, kiriyāti ime pañca dhammā atthoti veditabbā[V 2.0068]. Taṃ atthaṃ paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ atthe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā. Dhammotipi saṅkhepato paccayassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paccayo hi yasmā taṃ taṃ dahati pavatteti vā sampāpuṇituṃ vā deti, tasmā dhammoti vuccati. Pabhedato [M 2.0071] pana yo koci phalanibbattako hetu, ariyamaggo, bhāsitaṃ, kusalaṃ, akusalanti ime pañca dhammā dhammoti veditabbā. Taṃ dhammaṃ paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ dhamme pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā.

Herein, in brief, ‘meaning’ (attha) is a designation for the effect of a cause. For since the effect of a cause is arrived at, attained, and reached in accordance with the cause, it is called ‘meaning.’ In detail, however, these five things are to be understood as ‘meaning’: anything produced from a condition, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, the resultant, and the functional. For one who reviews that meaning, the knowledge that has become distinguished in that meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning. In brief, ‘Dhamma’ is a designation for a condition. For since a condition supports, sets going, or allows one to reach this or that, it is called ‘Dhamma.’ In detail, however, these five things are to be understood as ‘Dhamma’: any cause that produces a result, the noble path, what is spoken, the wholesome, and the unwholesome. For one who reviews that Dhamma, the knowledge that has become distinguished in that Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma.

Ayameva hi attho abhidhamme –

For this is the very meaning in the Abhidhamma:

“Dukkhe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā. Dukkhasamudaye ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Hetuphale ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā. Ye dhammā jātā bhūtā sañjātā nibbattā abhinibbattā pātubhūtā. Imesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā. Yamhā dhammā te dhammā jātā bhūtā sañjātā nibbattā abhinibbattā pātubhūtā, tesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Jarāmaraṇe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā. Jarāmaraṇasamudaye ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā…pe… saṅkhāranirodhe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā. Saṅkhāranirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Idha bhikkhu dhammaṃ jānāti suttaṃ geyyaṃ…pe… vedallaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati dhammapaṭisambhidā. So tassa tasseva bhāsitassa atthaṃ jānāti ‘ayaṃ imassa bhāsitassa attho, ayaṃ imassa bhāsitassa attho’ti. Ayaṃ vuccati atthapaṭisambhidā. Katame dhammā kusalā? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti…pe… ime dhammā kusalā. Imesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”tiādinā (vibha. 719 ādayo) nayena vibhajitvā dassito.

“Knowledge in suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning. Knowledge in the origin of suffering is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. Knowledge in the cause is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. Knowledge in the effect of the cause is the analytical knowledge of meaning. Knowledge in those phenomena that are born, have come to be, have arisen, are produced, brought forth, and manifested—this is the analytical knowledge of meaning. Knowledge in those phenomena from which these phenomena are born, have come to be, have arisen, are produced, brought forth, and manifested—this is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. Knowledge in aging-and-death is the analytical knowledge of meaning. Knowledge in the origin of aging-and-death is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma…. Knowledge in the cessation of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of meaning. Knowledge in the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. Here, a bhikkhu knows the Dhamma—prose discourses, mixed prose and verse… question-and-answer texts. This is called the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. He knows the meaning of each particular statement: ‘This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of this statement.’ This is called the analytical knowledge of meaning. What are wholesome states? At a time when a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen… these are wholesome states. Knowledge in these states is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. Knowledge in their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning.” It is shown analyzed by the method beginning thus (in Vibhaṅga 719ff).

Tatradhammaniruttābhilāpe ñāṇanti tasmiṃ atthe ca dhamme ca yā sabhāvanirutti abyabhicārī vohāro. Tadabhilāpe tassa bhāsane udīraṇe taṃ bhāsitaṃ lapitaṃ udīritaṃ sutvāva ayaṃ sabhāvanirutti, ayaṃ na sabhāvaniruttīti evaṃ tassā dhammaniruttisaññitāya sabhāvaniruttiyā māgadhikāya sabbasattānaṃ mūlabhāsāya pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā. Niruttipaṭisambhidāppatto hi phasso vedanāti evamādivacanaṃ sutvāva ayaṃ sabhāvaniruttīti jānāti. Phassā vedanoti evamādikaṃ pana ayaṃ na sabhāvaniruttīti.

Herein, 'knowledge in the expression of the language of the Dhamma' is as follows: Concerning that meaning and that Dhamma, there is a natural expression, an unerring conventional usage. In its expression, its speech, its utterance, upon hearing what is spoken, talked, and uttered, one immediately knows: 'This is the natural expression; this is not the natural expression.' Thus, the knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions of that natural expression called the language of the Dhamma—which is Māgadhī, the root language of all beings—is the analytical knowledge of language. For one who has attained the analytical knowledge of language, on hearing such a statement as 'phasso, vedanā,' immediately knows: 'This is the natural expression.' But on hearing such a statement as 'phassā, vedano,' he knows: 'This is not the natural expression.'

Ñāṇesu [M 2.0072][V 2.0069] ñāṇanti sabbattha ñāṇamārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa ñāṇārammaṇaṃ ñāṇaṃ, yathāvuttesu vā tesu ñāṇesu sagocarakiccādivasena vitthārato ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāti attho.

Knowledge in knowledges: For one who reviews by taking all knowledge as the object, it is the knowledge that has knowledge as its object. Or, it is the knowledge in detail of those aforesaid knowledges in terms of their respective domains, functions, and so on. This is the meaning of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity.

429. Catassopi cetā paṭisambhidā dvīsu ṭhānesu pabhedaṃ gacchanti sekkhabhūmiyañca asekkhabhūmiyañca.

429. These four analytical knowledges are differentiated in two planes: the plane of the trainee and the plane of the adept.

Tattha aggasāvakānaṃ mahāsāvakānañca asekkhabhūmiyaṃ pabhedagatā. Ānandattheracittagahapatidhammikaupāsakaupāligahapatikhujjuttarāupāsikādīnaṃ sekkhabhūmiyaṃ. Evaṃ dvīsu bhūmīsu pabhedaṃ gacchantiyopi cetā adhigamena pariyattiyā savanena paripucchāya pubbayogena cāti imehi pañcahākārehi visadā honti.

Among them, for the chief disciples and the great disciples, they are differentiated in the plane of the adept. For the Venerable Ānanda, the householder Citta, the lay follower Dhammika, the householder Upāli, the laywoman Khujjuttarā, and others, they are differentiated in the plane of the trainee. Thus, although they are differentiated in these two planes, they become clear in five ways: through attainment, through study of the scriptures, through hearing, through inquiry, and through previous practice.

Tattha adhigamo nāma arahattappatti. Pariyatti nāma buddhavacanassa pariyāpuṇanaṃ. Savanaṃ nāma sakkaccaṃ atthiṃ katvā dhammassavanaṃ. Paripucchā nāma pāḷiaṭṭhakathādīsu gaṇṭhipadaatthapadavinicchayakathā, pubbayogo nāma pubbabuddhānaṃ sāsane gatapaccāgatikabhāvena yāva anulomaṃ gotrabhusamīpaṃ, tāva vipassanānuyogo.

Herein, attainment means the attainment of arahantship. Study of the scriptures means mastering the Buddha's word. Hearing means listening to the Dhamma respectfully and attentively. Inquiry means discussion for resolving knotty points and the meaning of words in the Pāli, the commentaries, and so on. Previous practice means the practice of insight meditation up to conformity knowledge near the change-of-lineage, by one who has come and gone in the dispensation of past Buddhas.

Apare āhu –

Others say:

“Pubbayogo bāhusaccaṃ, desabhāsā ca āgamo;

Paripucchā adhigamo, garusannissayo tathā;

Mittasampatti cevāti, paṭisambhidapaccayā”ti.

“Previous practice, great learning, local language, and the scriptures; inquiry, attainment, and reliance on a teacher; and accomplishment in friendship—these are the conditions for the analytical knowledges.”

Tattha pubbayogo vuttanayova. Bāhusaccaṃ nāma tesu tesu satthesu ca sippāyatanesu ca kusalatā. Desabhāsā nāma ekasatavohārakusalatā. Visesena pana māgadhike kosallaṃ. Āgamo nāma antamaso opammavaggamattassapi buddhavacanassa pariyāpuṇanaṃ. Paripucchā nāma ekagāthāyapi atthavinicchayapucchanaṃ. Adhigamo nāma sotāpannatā vā…pe… arahattaṃ vā. Garusannissayo [V 2.0070] nāma sutapaṭibhānabahulānaṃ garūnaṃ santike vāso. Mittasampatti nāma tathārūpānaṃyeva mittānaṃ paṭilābhoti.

Herein, previous practice is as already stated. Great learning means skill in the various sciences and arts. Local language means skill in the speech of a hundred and one regions, but especially skill in Māgadhī. The scriptures means mastering the Buddha's word, at least to the extent of the Chapter of Similes. Inquiry means asking to determine the meaning of even a single verse. Attainment means stream-entry… or… arahantship. Reliance on a teacher means dwelling near teachers who are rich in learning and perspicuity. Accomplishment in friendship means the acquisition of friends of such a kind.

Tattha buddhā ca paccekabuddhā ca pubbayogañceva adhigamañca nissāya paṭisambhidā pāpuṇanti. Sāvakā sabbānipi etāni kāraṇāni. Paṭisambhidāppattiyā ca pāṭiyekko [M 2.0073] kammaṭṭhānabhāvanānuyogo nāma natthi. Sekkhānaṃ pana sekkhaphalavimokkhantikā. Asekkhānaṃ asekkhaphalavimokkhantikāva paṭisambhidāppatti hoti. Tathāgatānaṃ hi dasabalāni viya ariyānaṃ ariyaphaleneva paṭisambhidā ijjhantīti imā paṭisambhidā sandhāya vuttaṃ catupaṭisambhidāvasena catubbidhāti.

Herein, Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas attain the analytical knowledges by relying on previous practice and attainment. Disciples attain them through all these causes. For the attainment of the analytical knowledges, there is no specific practice of developing a meditation subject. For trainees, however, the attainment of the analytical knowledges culminates in the liberation of the trainee's fruition. For adepts, it culminates in the liberation of the adept's fruition. For just as the ten powers of the Tathāgatas are accomplished with the noble fruition, so for the noble ones the analytical knowledges are accomplished with their respective noble fruitions. It is with reference to these analytical knowledges that it is said to be 'fourfold by way of the four analytical knowledges.'

Paññābhūmi-mūla-sarīravavatthānaṃ

The Determination of the Ground, Root, and Body of Wisdom

430. Kathaṃ bhāvetabbāti ettha pana yasmā imāya paññāya khandhāyatanadhātuindriyasaccapaṭiccasamuppādādibhedā dhammā bhūmi. Sīlavisuddhi ceva cittavisuddhi cāti imā dve visuddhiyo mūlaṃ. Diṭṭhivisuddhi, kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi, maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi, paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi, ñāṇadassanavisuddhīti imā pañca visuddhiyo sarīraṃ. Tasmā tesu bhūmibhūtesu dhammesu uggahaparipucchāvasena ñāṇaparicayaṃ katvā mūlabhūtā dve visuddhiyo sampādetvā sarīrabhūtā pañca visuddhiyo sampādentena bhāvetabbā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo.

430. How should it be developed? Herein, since for this wisdom the phenomena distinguished as aggregates, sense bases, elements, faculties, truths, dependent origination, and so forth, are the ground; and since the two purifications—purification of virtue and purification of mind—are the root; and since the five purifications—purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is path and not-path, purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision—are the body; therefore, having gained familiarity with knowledge concerning those phenomena that are the ground through study and inquiry, one should develop it by first accomplishing the two purifications that are the root, and then accomplishing the five purifications that are the body. This is the summary here.

431. Ayaṃ pana vitthāro, yaṃ tāva vuttaṃ “khandhāyatanadhātuindriyasaccapaṭiccasamuppādādibhedā dhammā bhūmī”ti, ettha khandhāti pañca khandhā rūpakkhandho vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho viññāṇakkhandhoti.

431. But this is the detailed explanation. As to what was said, “The phenomena distinguished as aggregates, sense bases, elements, faculties, truths, dependent origination, etc., are the ground”: herein, “aggregates” means the five aggregates, namely, the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.

Rūpakkhandhakathā

Exposition on the Aggregate of Form

432. Tattha yaṃ kiñci sītādīhi ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ dhammajātaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekato katvā rūpakkhandhoti veditabbaṃ.

432. Herein, whatever kind of phenomenon has the characteristic of being afflicted by cold and so on, all of that, taken together, should be understood as the aggregate of form.

Tadetaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇena ekavidhampi bhūtopādāyabhedato duvidhaṃ.

This form, though onefold by its characteristic of being afflicted, is twofold when divided into primary matter and derived matter.

Tattha [V 2.0071] bhūtarūpaṃ catubbidhaṃ – pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātūti. Tāsaṃ lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānāni catudhātuvavatthāne vuttāni. Padaṭṭhānato pana tā sabbāpi avasesadhātuttayapadaṭṭhānā.

Herein, primary matter is fourfold: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element. Their characteristics, functions, and manifestations have been stated in the “Analysis of the Four Elements.” As to proximate cause, however, all of them have the remaining three elements as their proximate cause.

Upādārūpaṃ catuvīsatividhaṃ – cakkhu, sotaṃ, ghānaṃ, jivhā, kāyo, rūpaṃ, saddo, gandho, raso, itthindriyaṃ, purisindriyaṃ, jīvitindriyaṃ, hadayavatthu, kāyaviññatti, vacīviññatti, ākāsadhātu, rūpassa lahutā, rūpassa mudutā[M 2.0074], rūpassa kammaññatā, rūpassa upacayo, rūpassa santati, rūpassa jaratā, rūpassa aniccatā, kabaḷīkāro āhāroti.

Derived form is twenty-fourfold: the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, visible form, sound, odor, taste, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, the heart-base, bodily intimation, verbal intimation, the space element, lightness of matter, malleability of matter, wieldiness of matter, production of matter, continuity of matter, aging of matter, impermanence of matter, and physical nutriment.

433. Tattha rūpābhighātārahatappasādalakkhaṇaṃ daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ vā cakkhu, rūpesu āviñchanarasaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

433. Herein, the eye has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements suitable for the impact of visible form, or the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma that has the desire to see as its source. Its function is to draw in visible forms. It is manifested as the basis for eye-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma that has the desire to see as its source.

Saddābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ, sotukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ vā sotaṃ, saddesu āviñchanarasaṃ, sotaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, sotukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

The ear has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements suitable for the impact of sound, or the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma that has the desire to hear as its source. Its function is to draw in sounds. It is manifested as the basis for ear-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma that has the desire to hear as its source.

Gandhābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ, ghāyitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇaṃ vā ghānaṃ, gandhesu āviñchanarasaṃ, ghānaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ghāyitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

The nose has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements suitable for the impact of odor, or the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma that has the desire to smell as its source. Its function is to draw in odors. It is manifested as the basis for nose-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma that has the desire to smell as its source.

Rasābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇā, sāyitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇā vā jivhā, rasesu āviñchanarasā, jivhāviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, sāyitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhānā.

The tongue has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements suitable for the impact of taste, or the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma that has the desire to taste as its source. Its function is to draw in tastes. It is manifested as the basis for tongue-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma that has the desire to taste as its source.

Phoṭṭhabbābhighātārahabhūtappasādalakkhaṇo, phusitukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhānabhūtappasādalakkhaṇo vā kāyo, phoṭṭhabbesu āviñchanaraso, kāyaviññāṇassa ādhārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno, phusitukāmatānidānakammajabhūtapadaṭṭhāno.

The body has the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements suitable for the impact of tangibles, or the characteristic of being a sensitivity of the primary elements originated by kamma that has the desire to touch as its source. Its function is to draw in tangibles. It is manifested as the basis for body-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the primary elements born of kamma that has the desire to touch as its source.

434. Keci [V 2.0072] pana “tejādhikānaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasādo cakkhu, vāyupathavīāpādhikānaṃ bhūtānaṃ pasādā sotaghānajivhā, kāyo sabbesampī”ti vadanti. Apare “tejādhikānaṃ pasādo cakkhu, vivaravāyuāpapathavādhikānaṃ sotaghānajivhākāyā”ti vadanti. Te vattabbā “suttaṃ āharathā”ti. Addhā suttameva na dakkhissanti. Keci panettha “tejādīnaṃ guṇehi rūpādīhi anugayhabhāvato”ti kāraṇaṃ dassenti. Te vattabbā “ko panevamāharūpādayo tejādīnaṃ guṇā’ti. Avinibbhogavuttīsu hi bhūtesu ayaṃ imassa guṇo ayaṃ imassa guṇoti na labbhā vattu”nti. Athāpi vadeyyuṃ “yathā tesu tesu sambhāresu tassa tassa [M 2.0075] bhūtassa adhikatāya pathavīādīnaṃ sandhāraṇādīni kiccāni icchatha, evaṃ tejādiadhikesu sambhāresu rūpādīnaṃ adhikabhāvadassanato icchitabbametaṃ rūpādayo tesaṃ guṇā”ti. Te vattabbā “iccheyyāma, yadi āpādhikassa āsavassa gandhato pathavīadhike kappāse gandho adhikataro siyā, tejādhikassa ca uṇhodakassa vaṇṇato sītudakassa vaṇṇo parihāyetha”. Yasmā panetaṃ ubhayampi natthi, tasmā pahāyetaṃ etesaṃ nissayabhūtānaṃ visesakappanaṃ, “yathā avisesepi ekakalāpe bhūtānaṃ rūparasādayo aññamaññaṃ visadisā honti, evaṃ cakkhupasādādayo avijjamānepi aññasmiṃ visesakāraṇe”ti gahetabbametaṃ.

434. Some, however, say: “The eye is the sensitivity of the primary elements with a predominance of fire; the ear, nose, and tongue are the sensitivities of those with a predominance of wind, earth, and water; the body is the sensitivity of all of them.” Others say: “The eye is the sensitivity of those with a predominance of fire; the ear, nose, tongue, and body are the sensitivities of those with a predominance of space, wind, water, and earth.” They should be told: “Produce a sutta.” Surely, they will not find a sutta. Some here offer the reason: “Because they are assisted by the qualities—form, etc.—of the elements fire, etc.” They should be told: “But who maintains that form, etc., are qualities of fire, etc.?
