For in the primary elements, which are inseparable, it is impossible to say, ‘This is a quality of this, and that is a quality of that.’” And if they should say: “Just as you maintain that in various compositions the functions of the primary elements, such as supporting, etc., are due to the predominance of this or that element, so too, since in compositions where fire, etc., are predominant one sees a predominance of form, etc., it should be maintained that form, etc., are their qualities,” they should be told: “We would maintain this, if the smell of cotton, where earth is predominant, were stronger than the smell of fermented liquor, where water is predominant, and if the color of cold water were inferior to the color of hot water, where fire is predominant.” But since neither is the case, this fabrication of a distinction among their supporting elements should be abandoned. It should be understood thus: “Just as, even when the primary elements in a single material group are undifferentiated, form, taste, etc., are dissimilar to one another, so too, the eye sensitivity and the others are dissimilar even in the absence of any other distinguishing cause.”

Kiṃ pana taṃ yaṃ aññamaññassa asādhāraṇaṃ? Kammameva nesaṃ visesakāraṇaṃ. Tasmā kammavisesato etesaṃ viseso, na bhūtavisesato. Bhūtavisese hi sati pasādova na uppajjati. Samānānañhi pasādo, na visamānānanti porāṇā.

But what then is that which is unique to each? Kamma itself is their distinguishing cause. Therefore, the distinction among them is due to the diversity of kamma, not from any difference in the primary elements. For if there were a difference in the primary elements, sensitivity itself would not arise. Indeed, the ancients say: “Sensitivity is of the balanced, not of the unbalanced.”

435. Evaṃ kammavisesato visesavantesu ca etesu cakkhusotāni asampattavisayagāhakāni, attano nissayaṃ anallīnanissaye eva visaye viññāṇahetuttā. Ghānajivhākāyā sampattavisayagāhakā, nissayavasena ceva, sayañca, attano nissayaṃ allīneyeva visaye viññāṇahetuttā.

435. Thus, as these faculties are distinct due to the distinction of kamma, the eye and ear apprehend objects that have not arrived in contact, because they are a cause for consciousness in relation to an object whose own base has not adhered to their physical base. The nose, tongue, and body apprehend objects that have arrived in contact, because they are a cause for consciousness in relation to an object that has adhered to their physical base, this being so both by means of the object's base and by the object itself.

436. Cakkhu cettha yadetaṃ loke nīlapakhumasamākiṇṇakaṇhasukkamaṇḍalavicittaṃ nīluppaladalasannibhaṃ cakkhūti vuccati. Tassa sasambhāracakkhuno setamaṇḍalaparikkhittassa kaṇhamaṇḍalassa majjhe abhimukhe ṭhitānaṃ sarīrasaṇṭhānuppattipadese sattasu picupaṭalesu āsittatelaṃ picupaṭalāni viya satta akkhipaṭalānibyāpetvā dhāraṇanhāpanamaṇḍanabījanakiccāhi [V 2.0073] catūhi dhātīhi khattiyakumāro viya sandhāraṇabandhanaparipācanasamudīraṇakiccāhi catūhi dhātūhi katūpakāraṃ utucittāhārehi upatthambhiyamānaṃ āyunā anupāliyamānaṃ [M 2.0076] vaṇṇagandharasādīhi parivutaṃ pamāṇato ūkāsiramattaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati. Vuttampi cetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā –

436. Herein, the eye is that which in the world is called the ‘eye,’ variegated with black and white circles, strewn with blue eyelashes, and resembling a blue lotus petal. Within that eye with its components, surrounded by the white circle, in the middle of the black circle, in the place where the reflection of the bodily form of those standing in front appears, pervading the seven membranes of the eye like oil poured on seven cotton wicks; helped by the four great elements with their respective functions of supporting, binding, maturing, and impelling, just as a royal prince is helped by four nurses with their duties of carrying, bathing, adorning, and fanning; supported by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment; maintained by the life faculty; surrounded by color, odor, taste, and so on; in size like a louse’s head; it stands, accomplishing as appropriate its function as base and door for eye-consciousness and the rest. This was also stated by the General of the Dhamma:

“Yena cakkhupasādena, rūpāni manupassati;

Parittaṃ sukhumaṃ etaṃ, ūkāsirasamūpama”nti.

“With that sensitivity of the eye by which a person sees forms; it is minute, subtle, and comparable to the head of a louse.”

Sasambhārasotabilassa anto tanutambalomācite aṅgulivedhakasaṇṭhāne padese sotaṃ vuttappakārāhi dhātūhi katūpakāraṃ utucittāhārehi upatthambhiyamānaṃ āyunā anupāliyamānaṃ vaṇṇādīhi parivutaṃ sotaviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati.

Inside the ear canal with its components, in a place shaped like a finger-ring and fringed with fine, coppery hairs, the ear sensitivity stands. It is helped by the primary elements in the way described, supported by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, maintained by the life faculty, and surrounded by color, etc. It stands, accomplishing as appropriate its function as base and door for ear-consciousness and the rest.

Sasambhāraghānabilassa anto ajapadasaṇṭhāne padese ghānaṃ yathāvuttappakārupakārupatthambhanānupālanaparivāraṃ ghānaviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati.

Inside the nostril with its components, in a place shaped like a goat's hoof, the nose sensitivity stands. Having help, support, maintenance, and surroundings of the kind already described, it stands, accomplishing as appropriate its function as base and door for nose-consciousness and the rest.

Sasambhārajivhāmajjhassa upari uppaladalaggasaṇṭhāne padese jivhā yathāvuttappakārupakārupatthambhanānupālanaparivārā jivhāviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamānā tiṭṭhati.

On the surface of the middle of the tongue with its components, in a place shaped like the tip of a lotus petal, the tongue sensitivity stands. Having help, support, maintenance, and surroundings of the kind already described, it stands, accomplishing as appropriate its function as base and door for tongue-consciousness and the rest.

Yāvatā pana imasmiṃ kāye upādiṇṇarūpaṃ nāma atthi. Sabbattha kāyo kappāsapaṭale sneho viya vuttappakārupakārupatthambhanānupālanaparivārova hutvā kāyaviññāṇādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ vatthudvārabhāvaṃ sādhayamāno tiṭṭhati.

However, throughout all the appropriated form that exists in this body, the body sensitivity is found everywhere, like oil pervading a cotton cloth. Having help, support, maintenance, and surroundings of the kind already described, it stands, accomplishing as appropriate its function as base and door for body-consciousness and the rest.

Vammikaudakākāsagāmasivathikasaṅkhātasagocaraninnā viya ca ahisusumārapakkhīkukkurasiṅgālārūpādisagocaraninnāva ete cakkhādayoti daṭṭhabbā.

And it should be understood that these faculties—the eye and so on—are inclined to their respective domains of visible form and so on, just as snakes, crocodiles, birds, dogs, and jackals are inclined to their respective domains, namely, an anthill, water, the sky, a village, and a charnel ground.

437. Tato paresu pana rūpādīsu cakkhupaṭihananalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇassa visayabhāvarasaṃ[V 2.0074], tasseva gocarapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, catumahābhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Yathā cetaṃ tathā sabbānipi upādārūpāni. Yattha pana viseso atthi, tattha vakkhāma. Tayidaṃ nīlaṃ pītakantiādivasena anekavidhaṃ.

437. Among the remaining phenomena, visible form has the characteristic of impinging on the eye. Its function is to be the object of eye-consciousness. Its manifestation is to be the domain for that same consciousness. Its proximate cause is the four great elements. As this is, so are all derived material forms. But where there is a difference, we shall explain. This form is of many kinds, such as blue, yellow, and so on.

Sotapaṭihananalakkhaṇo [M 2.0077] saddo, sotaviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarapaccupaṭṭhāno. Bherisaddo mudiṅgasaddotiādinā nayena anekavidho.

Sound has the characteristic of impinging on the ear. Its function is to be the object of ear-consciousness. Its manifestation is as the domain of that same consciousness. It is of many kinds, such as the sound of a kettledrum, the sound of a small drum, and so on.

Ghānapaṭihananalakkhaṇo gandho, ghānaviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarapaccupaṭṭhāno. Mūlagandho sāragandhotiādinā nayena anekavidho.

Odor has the characteristic of impinging on the nose. Its function is to be the object of nose-consciousness. Its manifestation is as the domain of that same consciousness. It is of many kinds, such as root-odor, heartwood-odor, and so on.

Jivhāpaṭihananalakkhaṇo raso, jivhāviññāṇassa visayabhāvaraso, tasseva gocarapaccupaṭṭhāno. Mūlaraso khandharasotiādinā nayena anekavidho.

Taste has the characteristic of impinging on the tongue. Its function is to be the object of tongue-consciousness. Its manifestation is as the domain of that same consciousness. It is of many kinds, such as root-taste, stem-taste, and so on.

438. Itthibhāvalakkhaṇaṃ itthindriyaṃ, itthīti pakāsanarasaṃ, itthiliṅganimittakuttākappānaṃ kāraṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Purisabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ purisindriyaṃ, purisoti pakāsanarasaṃ, purisaliṅganimittakuttākappānaṃ kāraṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Tadubhayampi kāyappasādo viya sakalasarīraṃ byāpakameva, na ca kāyapasādena ṭhitokāse ṭhitanti vā aṭṭhitokāse ṭhitanti vāti vattabbataṃ āpajjati, rūparasādayo viya aññamaññaṃ saṅkaro natthi.

438. The female faculty has the state of femininity as its characteristic, its function is to indicate “this is a woman,” and its manifestation is being the cause for the female gender, signs, deportment, and appearance. The male faculty has the state of masculinity as its characteristic, its function is to indicate “this is a man,” and its manifestation is being the cause for the male gender, signs, deportment, and appearance. Both of these pervade the entire body just like bodily sensitivity. And it cannot be said that they are located where bodily sensitivity is, nor where it is not; and like visible form, taste, and so on, they do not intermingle with each other.

439. Sahajarūpānupālanalakkhaṇaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ, tesaṃ pavattanarasaṃ, tesaññeva ṭhapanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, yāpayitabbabhūtapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Santepi ca anupālanalakkhaṇādimhi vidhāne atthikkhaṇeyeva taṃ sahajarūpāni anupāleti udakaṃ viya uppalādīni. Yathāsakaṃ paccayuppannepi ca dhamme pāleti dhāti viya kumāraṃ. Sayaṃ pavattitadhammasambandheneva ca pavattati niyāmako viya. Na bhaṅgato uddhaṃ pavattati, attano ca pavattayitabbānañca abhāvā. Na bhaṅgakkhaṇe ṭhapeti, sayaṃ bhijjamānattā. Khīyamāno viya vaṭṭisneho dīpasikhaṃ. Na ca anupālanapavattanaṭṭhapanānubhāvavirahitaṃ, yathāvuttakkhaṇe tassa tassa sādhanatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

439. The life faculty has the characteristic of maintaining co-nascent material phenomena; its function is to cause them to continue; its manifestation is to establish them; its proximate cause is the primary elements that are to be maintained. And although it has this function of maintaining, etc., it maintains the co-nascent material phenomena only at their moment of presence, like water sustaining lotuses. It also protects phenomena that have arisen from their respective conditions, like a nurse protecting a child. It continues only in connection with the phenomena it causes to continue, like a pilot. It does not continue beyond the moment of dissolution, owing to the absence of both itself and the phenomena to be made to continue. It does not establish them at the moment of dissolution, because it is itself disintegrating, just as a diminishing wick and oil cannot sustain a lamp flame. Yet it should be understood that it is not devoid of the power to maintain, cause to continue, and establish, because at the aforementioned moments it serves to accomplish each of these.

440. Manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ nissayalakkhaṇaṃ hadayavatthu, tāsaññeva dhātūnaṃ ādhāraṇarasaṃ[V 2.0075], ubbahanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Hadayassa anto kāyagatāsatikathāyaṃ [M 2.0078] vuttappakāraṃ lohitaṃ nissāya sandhāraṇādikiccehi bhūtehi katūpakāraṃ utucittāhārehi upatthambhiyamānaṃ āyunā anupāliyamānaṃ manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnañceva taṃsampayuttadhammānañca vatthubhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati.

440. The heart-base has the characteristic of being the support for the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element; its function is to uphold them; its manifestation is to carry them. Depending on the blood of the kind described in the discourse on mindfulness directed to the body, which is located inside the heart, this heart-base—assisted by the primary elements with their functions of supporting, etc., upheld by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, and maintained by life—stands, accomplishing its function as the physical basis for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and their associated mental states.

441. Abhikkamādipavattakacittasamuṭṭhānavāyodhātuyā sahajarūpakāyathambhanasandhāraṇacalanassa paccayo ākāravikāro kāyaviññatti, adhippāyapakāsanarasā, kāyavipphandanahetubhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, cittasamuṭṭhānavāyodhātupadaṭṭhānā. Sā panesā kāyavipphandanena adhippāyaviññāpanahetuttā, sayañca tena kāyavipphandanasaṅkhātena kāyena viññeyyattā “kāyaviññattī”ti vuccati. Tāya ca pana calitehi cittajarūpehi abhisambandhānaṃ utujādīnampi calanato abhikkamādayo pavattantīti veditabbā.

441. Bodily intimation is an alteration of mode which is a condition for the stiffening, supporting, and moving of the co-nascent material body, this alteration being of the air element originated from consciousness that brings about forward movement, etc.; its function is to reveal intention; its manifestation is being the cause of bodily agitation; its proximate cause is the air element originated from consciousness. It is called “bodily intimation” because it is a cause for intimating intention by means of bodily agitation, and because it is itself cognizable by means of the body, which is designated as that bodily agitation. And it should be understood that forward movement and so on occur because, when the mind-born material phenomena are moved by it, the connected phenomena born of temperature and so on also move.

Vacībhedapavattakacittasamuṭṭhānapathavīdhātuyā upādiṇṇaghaṭṭanassa paccayo ākāravikāro vacīviññatti, adhippāyappakāsanarasā, vacīghosahetubhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, cittasamuṭṭhānapathavīdhātupadaṭṭhānā. Sā panesā vacīghosena adhippāyaviññāpanahetuttā, sayañca tāya vacīghosasaṅkhātāya vācāya viññeyyattā “vacīviññattī”ti vuccati. Yathā hi araññe ussāpetvā bandhagosīsādiudakanimittaṃ disvā udakamettha atthīti viññāyati, evaṃ kāyavipphandanañceva vacīghosañca gahetvā kāyavacīviññattiyopi viññāyanti.

Vocal intimation is an alteration of mode that is a condition for the striking of appropriated matter, this alteration being of the earth element originated from consciousness that brings about the production of speech; its function is to reveal intention; its manifestation is being the cause of vocal sound; its proximate cause is the earth element originated from consciousness. It is called “vocal intimation” because it is a cause for intimating intention by means of vocal sound, and because it is itself cognizable by means of the speech designated as that vocal sound. Just as, on seeing in a forest a sign for water such as a cow's skull set up and tied, one knows, “There is water here,” so too, by grasping bodily agitation and vocal sound, bodily and vocal intimations are also known.

442. Rūpaparicchedalakkhaṇā ākāsadhātu, rūpapariyantappakāsanarasā, rūpamariyādāpaccupaṭṭhānā, asamphuṭṭhabhāvacchiddavivarabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, paricchinnarūpapadaṭṭhānā. Yāya paricchinnesu rūpesu idamito uddhamadho tiriyanti ca hoti.

442. The space element has the characteristic of delimiting material form; its function is to reveal the boundary of material form; its manifestation is the confines of form, or its manifestation is the state of being untouched and the state of holes and apertures; its proximate cause is the material form that is delimited. It is by this that, with respect to delimited material forms, there are the distinctions of “above,” “below,” and “across.”

443. Adandhatālakkhaṇā rūpassa lahutā, rūpānaṃ garubhāvavinodanarasā, lahuparivattitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, lahurūpapadaṭṭhānā. Athaddhatālakkhaṇā rūpassa mudutā, rūpānaṃ thaddhabhāvavinodanarasā, sabbakiriyāsu avirodhitāpaccupaṭṭhānā, mudurūpapadaṭṭhānā. Sarīrakiriyānukūlakammaññabhāvalakkhaṇā rūpassa [M 2.0079] kammaññatā, akammaññatāvinodanarasā, adubbalabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, kammaññarūpapadaṭṭhānā.

443. Lightness of matter has the characteristic of non-sluggishness; its function is to eliminate the heaviness of material phenomena; it manifests as quick transformation; its proximate cause is light material phenomena. Softness of matter has the characteristic of non-rigidity; its function is to eliminate the rigidity of material phenomena; it manifests as non-opposition to all actions; its proximate cause is soft material phenomena. Wieldiness of matter has the characteristic of a state of wieldiness favorable to bodily actions; its function is to eliminate unwieldiness; it manifests as a state of non-incapacity; its proximate cause is wieldy material phenomena.

Etā [V 2.0076] pana tisso na aññamaññaṃ vijahanti, evaṃ santepi yo arogino viya rūpānaṃ lahubhāvo adandhatā lahuparivattippakāro rūpadandhattakaradhātukkhobhapaṭipakkhapaccayasamuṭṭhāno, so rūpavikāro rūpassa lahutā. Yo pana suparimadditacammasseva rūpānaṃ mudubhāvo sabbakiriyāvisesesu vasavattanabhāvamaddavappakāro rūpatthaddhattakaradhātukkhobhapaṭipakkhapaccayasamuṭṭhāno, so rūpavikāro rūpassa mudutā. Yo pana sudantasuvaṇṇasseva rūpānaṃ kammaññabhāvo sarīrakiriyānukūlabhāvappakāro sarīrakiriyānaṃ ananukūlakaradhātukkhobhapaṭipakkhapaccayasamuṭṭhāno, so rūpavikāro rūpassa kammaññatāti evametāsaṃ viseso veditabbo.

These three, however, do not abandon each other. Even so, lightness of matter is that modification of matter which is the lightness of material phenomena, like that of a healthy person, has the mode of non-sluggishness and quick transformation, and arises from conditions that are the opposite of the disturbance of elements that causes sluggishness in matter. Softness of matter is that modification of matter which is the softness of material phenomena, like well-tanned leather, has the mode of amenability and pliancy in all kinds of actions, and arises from conditions that are the opposite of the disturbance of elements that causes rigidity in matter. Wieldiness of matter is that modification of matter which is the wieldiness of material phenomena, like well-refined gold, has the mode of being favorable to bodily action, and arises from conditions that are the opposite of the disturbance of elements that makes it unfavorable to bodily action. Thus the distinction between them should be understood.

444. Ācayalakkhaṇo rūpassa upacayo, pubbantato rūpānaṃ ummujjāpanaraso, niyyātanapaccupaṭṭhāno, paripuṇṇabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno vā, upacitarūpapadaṭṭhāno. Pavattilakkhaṇā rūpassa santati, anuppabandhanarasā, anupacchedapaccupaṭṭhānā, anuppabandhakarūpapadaṭṭhānā. Ubhayampetaṃ jātirūpassevādhivacanaṃ, ākāranānattato pana veneyyavasena ca “upacayo santatī”ti uddesadesanā katā. Yasmā panettha atthato nānattaṃ natthi, tasmā imesaṃ padānaṃ niddese “yo āyatanānaṃ ācayo, so rūpassa upacayo. Yo rūpassa upacayo, sā rūpassa santatī”ti (dha. sa. 641-642) vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyampi “ācayo nāma nibbatti, upacayo nāma vaḍḍhi, santati nāma pavattī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 641) vatvā “nadītīre khatakūpakamhi udakuggamanakālo viya ācayo nibbatti, paripuṇṇakālo viya upacayo vaḍḍhi, ajjhottharitvā gamanakālo viya santati pavattī”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 641) upamā katā.

444. Accumulation of matter has gathering as its characteristic; its function is to make material phenomena emerge from a past beginning; its manifestation is delivering or as a state of fullness; its proximate cause is accumulated material phenomena. Continuity of matter has continuance as its characteristic; its function is to connect them in a sequence; its manifestation is uninterruptedness; its proximate cause is material phenomena that connect in a sequence. Both these are synonyms for born material phenomena, but the teaching is given under the heading “accumulation and continuity” because of the difference in mode and out of regard for the trainees. Since there is no difference here in meaning, it is said in the explanation of these terms: “That which is the gathering of the bases is the accumulation of matter. That which is the accumulation of matter is the continuity of matter.” In the Commentary, too, it is said: “Gathering means generation, accumulation means growth, and continuity means continuance.” An analogy is given: “Like the time when water rises in a pit dug on a riverbank—that is generation (gathering); when it is full—that is growth (accumulation); when it flows over and spreads—that is continuance (continuity).”

Upamāvasāne ca “evaṃ kiṃ kathitaṃ hoti? Āyatanena ācayo kathito, ācayena āyatanaṃ kathita”nti vuttaṃ. Tasmā yā rūpānaṃ paṭhamābhinibbatti, sā ācayo. Yā tesaṃ upari aññesampi nibbattamānānaṃ nibbatti, sā vaḍḍhiākārena upaṭṭhānato upacayo. Yā tesampi upari punappunaṃ [M 2.0080] aññesaṃ nibbattamānānaṃ nibbatti, sā anupabandhākārena upaṭṭhānato santatīti ca pavuccatīti veditabbā.

At the end of the analogy, it is said: “What is stated by this? By the base, gathering is stated; by gathering, the base is stated.” Therefore, it should be understood that the initial production of material phenomena is gathering. The production of other phenomena arising on top of them is accumulation, because it manifests in the mode of growth. And the production of still other phenomena arising again and again on top of those is called continuity, because it manifests in the mode of an uninterrupted sequence.

Rūpaparipākalakkhaṇā jaratā, upanayanarasā, sabhāvānapagamepi navabhāvāpagamapaccupaṭṭhānā vīhipurāṇabhāvo viya, paripaccamānarūpapadaṭṭhānā. Khaṇḍiccādibhāvena dantādīsu vikāradassanato [V 2.0077] idaṃ pākaṭajaraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Arūpadhammānaṃ pana paṭicchannajarā nāma hoti, tassā esa vikāro natthi, yā ca pathavī udakapabbatacandimasūriyādīsu avīcijarā nāma.

Aging has the ripening of material form as its characteristic; its function is to lead on to death; its manifestation is the disappearance of newness even while its intrinsic nature has not disappeared, like the oldness of rice; its proximate cause is material form that is ripening. This is stated with reference to evident aging, since alteration is seen in teeth and so on through their becoming broken, etc. For immaterial phenomena, however, there is what is called concealed aging, which has no such alteration. And that of the earth, water, mountains, moon, sun, and so on, is called continuous aging.

Paribhedalakkhaṇā rūpassa aniccatā, saṃsīdanarasā, khayavayapaccupaṭṭhānā, paribhijjamānarūpapadaṭṭhānā.

Impermanence of matter has destruction as its characteristic; its function is to cause subsidence; its manifestation is destruction and passing away; its proximate cause is matter that is being destroyed.

445. Ojālakkhaṇo kabaḷīkāro āhāro, rūpāharaṇaraso, upatthambhanapaccupaṭṭhāno, kabaḷaṃ katvā āharitabbavatthupadaṭṭhāno. Yāya ojāya sattā yāpenti, tassā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

445. Nutriment in morsels has nutritive essence as its characteristic; its function is to produce material form; its manifestation is supporting; its proximate cause is the physical thing to be made into a morsel and consumed. This is a designation for that nutritive essence by which beings are maintained.

446. Imāni tāva pāḷiyaṃ āgatarūpāneva. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana balarūpaṃ sambhavarūpaṃ jātirūpaṃ rogarūpaṃ ekaccānaṃ matena middharūpanti evaṃ aññānipi rūpāni āharitvā “addhā munīsi sambuddho, natthi nīvaraṇā tavā”tiādīni (su. ni. 546) vatvā middharūpaṃ tāva natthiyevāti paṭikkhittaṃ. Itaresu rogarūpaṃ jaratāaniccatāggahaṇena gahitameva, jātirūpaṃ upacayasantatiggahaṇena, sambhavarūpaṃ āpodhātuggahaṇena, balarūpaṃ vāyodhātuggahaṇena gahitameva. Tasmā tesu ekampi visuṃ natthīti sanniṭṭhānaṃ kataṃ.

446. So far these are the material forms that have come down in the Pāli Canon. But in the commentaries other material forms are brought in, thus: strength-form, origin-form, birth-form, sickness-form, and, in the opinion of some, torpor-form. Having cited such texts as “Surely you are the enlightened sage, you have no hindrances,” torpor-form is rejected as non-existent. Among the others, sickness-form is included by the inclusion of aging and impermanence; birth-form by the inclusion of accumulation and continuity; origin-form by the inclusion of the water element; and strength-form by the inclusion of the air element. Therefore, the conclusion is reached that not one of these exists separately.

Iti idaṃ catuvīsatividhaṃ upādārūpaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ catubbidhaṃ bhūtarūpañcāti aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ rūpaṃ hoti anūnamanadhikaṃ.

Thus, this twenty-fourfold derived matter, along with the previously mentioned fourfold primary matter, makes twenty-eight kinds of matter—no less, no more.

447. Taṃ sabbampi na hetu ahetukaṃ hetuvippayuttaṃ sappaccayaṃ lokiyaṃ sāsavamevātiādinā nayena ekavidhaṃ.

447. All of this matter is not a root, is rootless, dissociated from roots, conditioned, mundane, and subject to taints—in this way, etc., it is of one kind.

Ajjhattikaṃ bāhiraṃ, oḷārikaṃ sukhumaṃ, dūre santike, nipphannaṃ anipphannaṃ, pasādarūpaṃ napasādarūpaṃ, indriyaṃ anindriyaṃ, upādiṇṇaṃ anupādiṇṇantiādivasena duvidhaṃ.

It is internal or external; gross or subtle; far or near; concrete or abstract; sensitive matter or non-sensitive matter; a faculty or a non-faculty; grasped by kamma or not grasped by kamma—in these ways, etc., it is of two kinds.

Tattha [M 2.0081] cakkhādipañcavidhaṃ attabhāvaṃ adhikicca pavattattā ajjhattikaṃ, sesaṃ tato bāhirattā bāhiraṃ. Cakkhādīni nava āpodhātuvajjitā tisso dhātuyo cāti dvādasavidhaṃ ghaṭṭanavasena gahetabbato oḷārikaṃ, sesaṃ tato viparītattā sukhumaṃ. Yaṃ sukhumaṃ tadeva duppaṭivijjhasabhāvattā [V 2.0078] dūre, itaraṃ suppaṭivijjhasabhāvattā santike. Catasso dhātuyo, cakkhādīni terasa, kabaḷīkārāhāro cāti aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ paricchedavikāralakkhaṇabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā sabhāveneva pariggahetabbato nipphannaṃ, sesaṃ tabbiparītatāya anipphannaṃ. Cakkhādipañcavidhaṃ rūpādīnaṃ gahaṇapaccayabhāvena ādāsatalaṃ viya vippasannattā pasādarūpaṃ, itaraṃ tato viparītattā napasādarūpaṃ. Pasādarūpameva itthindriyādittayena saddhiṃ adhipatiyaṭṭhena indriyaṃ, sesaṃ tato viparītattā anindriyaṃ. Yaṃ kammajanti parato vakkhāma, taṃ kammena upādiṇṇattā upādiṇṇaṃ, sesaṃ tato viparītattā anupādiṇṇaṃ.

Herein, the fivefold matter, the eye faculty, etc., is internal because it occurs in connection with one's own being; the rest, being external to that, is external. The twelve kinds of matter—the nine beginning with the eye faculty and the three primary elements excluding the water element—are gross because they are to be apprehended by way of impingement; the rest, being the opposite, are subtle. That which is subtle is far because its nature is difficult to penetrate; the other is near because its nature is easy to penetrate. The eighteen kinds of matter—the four primary elements, the thirteen beginning with the eye faculty, and nutritive essence—are concrete because they are to be apprehended by their own intrinsic nature, having transcended the state of being a limitation, alteration, or characteristic; the rest, being the opposite, are abstract. The fivefold matter, the eye faculty, etc., is sensitive matter because it is clear like the surface of a mirror, serving as the condition for apprehending visible forms, etc.; the rest, being the opposite, is non-sensitive matter. Sensitive matter itself, along with the triad of femininity, masculinity, and life faculty, is a faculty due to its governing role; the rest, being the opposite, is a non-faculty. That which we will later call kamma-born is called 'grasped' because it is grasped by kamma; the rest, being the opposite, is 'not grasped'.

448. Puna sabbameva rūpaṃ sanidassanakammajādīnaṃ tikānaṃ vasena tividhaṃ hoti. Tattha oḷārike rūpaṃ sanidassanasappaṭighaṃ, sesaṃ anidassanasappaṭighaṃ. Sabbampi sukhumaṃ anidassanaappaṭighaṃ. Evaṃ tāva sanidassanattikavasena tividhaṃ. Kammajādittikavasena pana kammato jātaṃ kammajaṃ, tadaññapaccayajātaṃ akammajaṃ, nakutocijātaṃ neva kammajaṃ nākammajaṃ. Cittato jātaṃ cittajaṃ, tadaññapaccayajātaṃ acittajaṃ, nakutocijātaṃ neva cittajaṃ nācittajaṃ, āhārato jātaṃ āhārajaṃ, tadaññapaccayajātaṃ anāhārajaṃ, nakutocijātaṃ neva āhārajaṃ naanāhārajaṃ. Ututo jātaṃ utujaṃ, tadaññapaccayajātaṃ anutujaṃ, nakutocijātaṃ neva utujaṃ naanutujanti evaṃ kammajādittikavasena tividhaṃ.

448. Again, all matter is threefold by way of triads such as that of the visible. Herein, of gross matter, one part is visible and resistant, while the rest is invisible and resistant. All subtle matter is invisible and non-resistant. Thus it is threefold by way of the triad of the visible. Further, by way of the triad of the kamma-born, etc.: what is born from kamma is kamma-born; what is born from other conditions is not kamma-born; what is born from no cause is neither kamma-born nor not kamma-born. What is born from mind is mind-born; what is born from other conditions is not mind-born; what is born from no cause is neither mind-born nor not mind-born. What is born from nutriment is nutriment-born; what is born from other conditions is not nutriment-born; what is born from no cause is neither nutriment-born nor not nutriment-born. What is born from temperature is temperature-born; what is born from other conditions is not temperature-born; what is born from no cause is neither temperature-born nor not temperature-born. Thus it is threefold by way of the triad of the kamma-born, etc.

449. Puna diṭṭhādirūparūpādivatthādicatukkavasena catubbidhaṃ. Tattha rūpāyatanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ nāma dassanavisayattā, saddāyatanaṃ sutaṃ nāma savanavisayattā, gandharasaphoṭṭhabbattayaṃ mutaṃ nāma sampattagāhakaindriyavisayattā, sesaṃ viññātaṃ nāma viññāṇasseva visayattāti evaṃ tāva diṭṭhādicatukkavasena catubbidhaṃ.

449. Again, it is fourfold by way of tetrads such as that of the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. Herein, the visible-form base is called 'seen' because it is the object of seeing; the sound base is called 'heard' because it is the object of hearing; the triad of odor, taste, and tangible bases is called 'sensed' because they are objects of faculties that grasp upon contact; and the remainder is called 'cognized' because it is the object of mind-consciousness alone. Thus it is fourfold by way of the tetrad of the seen, etc.

Nipphannarūpaṃ panettha rūparūpaṃ nāma, ākāsadhātu paricchedarūpaṃ nāma, kāyaviññattiādi kammaññatāpariyantaṃ vikārarūpaṃ nāma, jātijarābhaṅgaṃ lakkhaṇarūpaṃ nāmāti evaṃ rūparūpādicatukkavasena catubbidhaṃ.

Herein, concrete matter is called 'matter-as-matter'; the space element is called 'limiting matter'; bodily intimation, etc., up to adaptability, is called 'matter of alteration'; arising, aging, and dissolution is called 'characteristic matter'. Thus it is fourfold by way of the tetrad of matter-as-matter, etc.

Yaṃ [M 2.0082] panettha hadayarūpaṃ nāma, taṃ vatthu na dvāraṃ. Viññattidvayaṃ dvāraṃ na vatthu. Pasādarūpaṃ vatthu ceva dvārañca. Sesaṃ neva vatthu na dvāranti evaṃ vatthādicatukkavasena catubbidhaṃ.

Herein, what is called the heart-matter is a base but not a door. The two intimations are a door but not a base. Sensitive matter is both a base and a door. The rest is neither a base nor a door. Thus it is fourfold by way of the tetrad of base, etc.

450. Puna [V 2.0079] ekajaṃ, dvijaṃ, tijaṃ, catujaṃ, nakutocijātanti imesaṃ vasena pañcavidhaṃ. Tattha kammajameva cittajameva ca ekajaṃ nāma. Tesu saddhiṃ hadayavatthunā indriyarūpaṃ kammajameva. Viññattidvayaṃ cittajameva. Yaṃ pana cittato ca ututo ca jātaṃ, taṃ dvijaṃ nāma, taṃ saddāyatanameva. Yaṃ utucittāhārehi jātaṃ, taṃ tijaṃ nāma, taṃ pana lahutādittayameva. Yaṃ catūhipi kammādīhi jātaṃ, taṃ catujaṃ nāma, taṃ lakkhaṇarūpavajjaṃ avasesaṃ hoti. Lakkhaṇarūpaṃ pana nakutocijātaṃ. Kasmā? Na hi uppādassa uppādo atthi, uppannassa ca paripākabhedamattaṃ itaradvayaṃ. Yampi “rūpāyatanaṃ saddāyatanaṃ gandhāyatanaṃ rasāyatanaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ ākāsadhātu āpodhātu rūpassa lahutā, rūpassa mudutā, rūpassa kammaññatā, rūpassa upacayo, rūpassa santati, kabaḷīkāro āhāro, ime dhammā cittasamuṭṭhānā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1201) jātiyā kutocijātattaṃ anuññātaṃ, taṃ pana rūpajanakapaccayānaṃ kiccānubhāvakkhaṇe diṭṭhattāti veditabbaṃ.

450. Again, it is fivefold by way of these divisions: of single origin, of double origin, of triple origin, of quadruple origin, and of no origin. Herein, that which is born solely from kamma and that which is born solely from mind is called 'of single origin.' Among these, faculty matter, together with the heart-base, is born solely from kamma. The two intimations are born solely from mind. That which is born from both mind and temperature is called 'of double origin,' and this is only the sound base. That which is born from temperature, mind, and nutriment is called 'of triple origin,' and this is only the triad of lightness, etc. That which is born from all four—kamma, etc.—is called 'of quadruple origin,' and this is the remainder, excluding characteristic matter. Characteristic matter, however, is of no origin. Why? For there is no arising of arising, and for what has arisen, the other two are merely its maturation and dissolution. And where it is said, 'The visible object base, sound base, odor base, taste base, tangible object base, space element, water element, lightness of matter, softness of matter, adaptability of matter, accumulation of matter, continuity of matter, and edible food—these phenomena are mind-originated,' etc. (Dhs §1201), the fact that for arising its being born from some cause is conceded should be understood as being on account of its being seen at the moment of the function and power of the matter-generating conditions.

Idaṃ tāva rūpakkhandhe vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This, for now, is the introduction to the detailed exposition on the aggregate of matter.

Viññāṇakkhandhakathā

The Exposition on the Consciousness Aggregate

451. Itaresu pana yaṃkiñci vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekato katvā vedanākkhandho; yaṃkiñci sañjānanalakkhaṇaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekato katvā saññākkhandho; yaṃkiñci abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekato katvā saṅkhārakkhandho; yaṃkiñci vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekato katvā viññāṇakkhandho veditabbo. Tattha yasmā viññāṇakkhandhe viññāte itare suviññeyyā honti, tasmā viññāṇakkhandhaṃ ādiṃ katvā vaṇṇanaṃ karissāma.

451. As for the remaining aggregates, whatever has the characteristic of feeling, all that taken together is the feeling aggregate; whatever has the characteristic of perceiving, all that taken together is the perception aggregate; whatever has the characteristic of forming, all that taken together is the formations aggregate; whatever has the characteristic of cognizing, all that taken together is the consciousness aggregate, it should be understood. Among these, since the others are easily understood when the consciousness aggregate is understood, we shall begin our exposition with the consciousness aggregate.

Yaṃkiñci vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekato katvā viññāṇakkhandho veditabboti hi vuttaṃ. Kiñca vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ viññāṇaṃ? Yathāha “vijānāti vijānātīti kho, āvuso, tasmā viññāṇanti vuccatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.449). Viññāṇaṃ cittaṃ manoti atthato ekaṃ. Tadetaṃ vijānanalakkhaṇena sabhāvato [M 2.0083] ekavidhampi jātivasena tividhaṃ kusalaṃ, akusalaṃ, abyākatañca.

For it has been said: 'Whatever has the characteristic of cognizing, all that taken together is to be understood as the consciousness aggregate.' And what is the consciousness that has the characteristic of cognizing? As it is said: 'It cognizes, it cognizes, friend; therefore it is called consciousness.' Consciousness (viññāṇa), mind (citta), and mentality (mano) are one in meaning. Although this is single in its intrinsic nature, having the characteristic of cognizing, by way of class it is threefold: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

452. Tattha [V 2.0080] kusalaṃ bhūmibhedato catubbidhaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ lokuttarañca. Tattha kāmāvacaraṃ somanassupekkhāñāṇasaṅkhārabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhārañca, tathā ñāṇavippayuttaṃ. Upekkhāsahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhārañca, tathā ñāṇavippayuttaṃ.

452. Herein, wholesome consciousness is fourfold by division of plane: sense-sphere, form-sphere, formless-sphere, and supramundane. Among these, sense-sphere wholesome consciousness is eightfold by way of its distinctions regarding joy, equanimity, knowledge, and prompting. They are as follows: (1) accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, unprompted; (2) the same, but prompted; (3) accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge, unprompted; (4) the same, but prompted; (5) accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, unprompted; (6) the same, but prompted; (7) accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, unprompted; (8) the same, but prompted.

Yadā hi deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakādisampattiṃ aññaṃ vā somanassahetuṃ āgamma haṭṭhapahaṭṭho “atthi dinna”ntiādinayappavattaṃ (ma. ni. 1.441) sammādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā asaṃsīdanto anussāhito parehi dānādīni puññāni karoti, tadāssa somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ cittaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ hoti. Yadā pana vuttanayena haṭṭhatuṭṭho sammādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā amuttacāgatādivasena saṃsīdamāno vā parehi vā ussāhito karoti, tadāssa tadeva cittaṃ sasaṅkhāraṃ hoti. Imasmiñhi atthe saṅkhāroti etaṃ attano vā paresaṃ vā vasena pavattassa pubbapayogassādhivacanaṃ. Yadā pana ñātijanassa paṭipattidassanena jātaparicayā bāladārakā bhikkhū disvā somanassajātā sahasā kiñcideva hatthagataṃ dadanti vā vandanti vā, tadā tatiyaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati. Yadā pana “detha vandathāti” ñātīhi ussāhitā evaṃ paṭipajjanti, tadā catutthaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati. Yadā pana deyyadhammapaṭiggāhakādīnaṃ asampattiṃ aññesaṃ vā somanassahetūnaṃ abhāvaṃ āgamma catūsupi vikappesu somanassarahitā honti, tadā sesāni cattāri upekkhāsahagatāni uppajjantīti. Evaṃ somanassupekkhāñāṇasaṅkhārabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ kāmāvacarakusalaṃ veditabbaṃ.

For when someone, delighted and joyful on account of the excellence of the gift, the recipient, and so on, or some other cause for joy, performs meritorious deeds such as giving with right view at the forefront—a view that proceeds in the manner of 'There is what is given...'—acting without hesitation and unprompted by others, then their consciousness is one accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted. But when, joyful and happy in the same way, one performs such deeds with right view at the forefront but hesitating due to a lack of generous spirit, or prompted by others, then that same consciousness is prompted. In this context, 'prompting' is a term for the prior exertion that occurs on one's own initiative or on that of others. When young children, who have become familiar with such conduct by observing their relatives, see bhikkhus and, becoming joyful, spontaneously give whatever is in their hands or pay homage, then the third type of consciousness arises. But when, prompted by their relatives with 'Give! Pay homage!', they act accordingly, then the fourth type of consciousness arises. When, however, due to a lack of excellence in the gift, the recipient, and so on, or the absence of other causes for joy, they are without joy in all four of these cases, then the remaining four types of consciousness accompanied by equanimity arise. Thus, sense-sphere wholesome consciousness is to be understood as eightfold by way of its distinctions regarding joy, equanimity, knowledge, and prompting.

Rūpāvacaraṃ pana jhānaṅgayogabhedato pañcavidhaṃ hoti. Seyyathidaṃ, vitakkavicārapītisukhasamādhiyuttaṃ paṭhamaṃ, atikkantavitakkaṃ dutiyaṃ, tato atikkantavicāraṃ tatiyaṃ, tato virattapītikaṃ catutthaṃ, atthaṅgatasukhaṃ upekkhāsamādhiyuttaṃ pañcamanti.

Form-sphere consciousness, however, is fivefold according to the combination of jhāna factors. They are as follows: the first is accompanied by applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and concentration; the second has transcended applied thought; from that, the third has transcended sustained thought; from that, the fourth is with rapture faded away; the fifth has happiness subsided and is accompanied by equanimity and concentration.

Arūpāvacaraṃ catunnaṃ āruppānaṃ yogavasena catubbidhaṃ. Vuttappakārena hi ākāsānañcāyatanajjhānena sampayuttaṃ paṭhamaṃ, viññāṇañcāyatanādīhi dutiyatatiyacatutthāni[M 2.0084]. Lokuttaraṃ catumaggasampayogato catubbidhanti evaṃ tāva kusalaviññāṇameva ekavīsatividhaṃ hoti.

Formless-sphere consciousness is fourfold by way of its connection with the four formless attainments. For, in the manner already stated, the first is associated with the jhāna of the base of the infinity of space; the second, third, and fourth are associated with the base of the infinity of consciousness, and so on. Supramundane consciousness is fourfold due to its association with the four paths. Thus, for now, wholesome consciousness alone comes to be of twenty-one kinds.

453. Akusalaṃ [V 2.0081] pana bhūmito ekavidhaṃ kāmāvacarameva, mūlato tividhaṃ lobhamūlaṃ dosamūlaṃ mohamūlañca.

453. Unwholesome consciousness, however, is of one kind by plane—only sense-sphere—and threefold by root: rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, and rooted in delusion.

Tattha lobhamūlaṃ somanassupekkhādiṭṭhigatasaṅkhārabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, somanassasahagataṃ diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhārañca, tathā diṭṭhigatavippayuttaṃ. Upekkhāsahagataṃ diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhārañca, tathā diṭṭhigatavippayuttaṃ.

Herein, consciousness rooted in greed is eightfold by distinction of joy, equanimity, view, and prompting. They are as follows: (1) accompanied by joy, associated with wrong view, unprompted; (2) the same, but prompted; (3) accompanied by joy, dissociated from wrong view, unprompted; (4) the same, but prompted; (5) accompanied by equanimity, associated with wrong view, unprompted; (6) the same, but prompted; (7) accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from wrong view, unprompted; (8) the same, but prompted.

Yadā hi “natthi kāmesu ādīnavo”ti (ma. ni. 1.469) ādinā nayena micchādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā haṭṭhatuṭṭho kāme vā paribhuñjati, diṭṭhamaṅgalādīni vā sārato pacceti sabhāvatikkheneva anussāhitena cittena, tadā paṭhamaṃ akusalacittaṃ uppajjati. Yadā mandena samussāhitena cittena, tadā dutiyaṃ. Yadā micchādiṭṭhiṃ apurakkhatvā kevalaṃ haṭṭhatuṭṭho methunaṃ vā sevati, parasampattiṃ vā abhijjhāyati, parabhaṇḍaṃ vā harati sabhāvatikkheneva anussāhitena cittena, tadā tatiyaṃ. Yadā mandena samussāhitena cittena, tadā catutthaṃ. Yadā pana kāmānaṃ vā asampattiṃ āgamma aññesaṃ vā somanassahetūnaṃ abhāvena catūsupi vikappesu somanassarahitā honti, tadā sesāni cattāri upekkhāsahagatāni uppajjantīti evaṃ somanassupekkhādiṭṭhigatasaṅkhārabhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ lobhamūlaṃ veditabbaṃ.

For when one, with wrong view at the forefront—a view that proceeds in the manner of 'There is no danger in sensual pleasures,' and so on—joyfully and happily enjoys sensual pleasures or regards seen omens and the like as essential, with a mind that is naturally sharp and unprompted, then the first unwholesome consciousness arises. When this is done with a sluggish and prompted mind, the second arises. When, without wrong view at the forefront, one is simply joyful and happy and engages in sexual intercourse, covets another's property, or steals another's belongings, with a mind that is naturally sharp and unprompted, then the third arises. When this is done with a sluggish and prompted mind, then the fourth arises. But when, on account of not attaining sensual pleasures or due to the absence of other causes for joy, one is without joy in all four of these cases, then the remaining four types of consciousness accompanied by equanimity arise. Thus, consciousness rooted in greed is to be understood as eightfold by distinction of joy, equanimity, view, and prompting.

Dosamūlaṃ pana domanassasahagataṃ paṭighasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāranti duvidhameva hoti, tassa pāṇātipātādīsu tikkhamandappavattikāle pavatti veditabbā.

Consciousness rooted in hatred, however, is only twofold: accompanied by displeasure, associated with aversion, unprompted, and also prompted. Its occurrence should be understood in relation to its proceeding sharply or sluggishly at the time of such acts as killing living beings.

Mohamūlaṃ upekkhāsahagataṃ vicikicchāsampayuttaṃ uddhaccasampayuttañcāti duvidhaṃ. Tassa sanniṭṭhānavikkhepakāle pavatti veditabbāti evaṃ akusalaviññāṇaṃ dvādasavidhaṃ hoti.

Consciousness rooted in delusion is twofold: accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt, and also associated with restlessness. Its occurrence is to be understood at the time of indecision and distraction. Thus unwholesome consciousness is of twelve kinds.

454. Abyākataṃ jātibhedato duvidhaṃ vipākaṃ kiriyañca. Tattha vipākaṃ bhūmito catubbidhaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ lokuttarañca. Tattha [M 2.0085] kāmāvacaraṃ duvidhaṃ kusalavipākaṃ akusalavipākañca. Kusalavipākampi duvidhaṃ ahetukaṃ sahetukañca.

454. Indeterminate consciousness is twofold by distinction of class: resultant and functional. Herein, resultant consciousness is fourfold by plane: sense-sphere, form-sphere, formless-sphere, and supramundane. Of these, sense-sphere resultant consciousness is twofold: wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant. Wholesome-resultant consciousness is also twofold: rootless and with roots.

Tattha alobhādivipākahetuvirahitaṃ ahetukaṃ, taṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇaṃ[V 2.0082], sampaṭicchanakiccā manodhātu, santīraṇādikiccā dve manoviññāṇadhātuyo cāti aṭṭhavidhaṃ.

Herein, that which is devoid of resultant roots such as non-greed is rootless. It is eightfold: eye-consciousness; ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness; the mind-element with the function of receiving; and the two mind-consciousness-elements with the functions of investigating and so on.

Tattha cakkhusannissitarūpavijānanalakkhaṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, rūpamattārammaṇarasaṃ, rūpābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, rūpārammaṇāya kiriyamanodhātuyā apagamapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Sotādisannissitasaddādivijānanalakkhaṇāni sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇāni, saddādimattārammaṇarasāni, saddādiabhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānāni, saddārammaṇādīnaṃ kiriyamanodhātūnaṃ apagamapadaṭṭhānāni.

Herein, eye-consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing a visible form dependent on the eye, its function is to have merely a visible form as its object, it manifests as facing towards a visible form, and its proximate cause is the cessation of the functional mind-element that has a visible form as its object. Ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness have the characteristic of cognizing sounds and so on, dependent on the ear and so on; their function is to have merely a sound and so on as their object; they manifest as facing towards sounds and so on; and their proximate cause is the cessation of the functional mind-elements that have sound and so on as their objects.

Cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ anantaraṃ rūpādivijānanalakkhaṇā manodhātu, rūpādisampaṭicchanarasā, tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, cakkhuviññāṇādiapagamapadaṭṭhānā.

The mind-element has the characteristic of cognizing a visible form, etc., immediately after eye-consciousness and the others. Its function is to receive the visible form, etc. It manifests as the state of so doing. Its proximate cause is the cessation of eye-consciousness and the others.

Ahetukavipākā saḷārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇā duvidhāpi santīraṇādikiccā manoviññāṇadhātu, santīraṇādirasā, tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānā. Somanassupekkhāyogato pana dvipañcaṭṭhānabhedato ca tassā bhedo. Etāsu hi ekā ekantamiṭṭhārammaṇe pavattisabbhāvato somanassasampayuttā hutvā santīraṇatadārammaṇavasena pañcadvāre ceva javanāvasāne ca pavattanato dviṭṭhānā hoti. Ekā iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇe pavattisabbhāvato upekkhāsampayuttā hutvā santīraṇatadārammaṇapaṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasena pavattanato pañcaṭṭhānā hoti.

The two types of mind-consciousness-element that are rootless resultant have the characteristic of cognizing the six kinds of objects, the function of investigating and so on, they manifest as the state of so doing, and have the heart-base as their proximate cause. Their distinction, however, is due to their association with joy or equanimity, and to the difference in their occurring in two or five instances. For among these, one type, being associated with joy because it occurs with an exclusively desirable object, is of two instances, occurring by way of investigating at the five doors and by way of registration at the end of the javana process. The other type, being associated with equanimity because it occurs with a desirable or neutral object, is of five instances, occurring by way of investigating, registration, rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death.

Aṭṭhavidhampi cetaṃ ahetukavipākaviññāṇaṃ niyatāniyatārammaṇattā duvidhaṃ. Upekkhāsukhasomanassabhedato tividhaṃ. Viññāṇapañcakaṃ hettha niyatārammaṇaṃ yathākkamaṃ rūpādīsuyeva pavattito, sesaṃ aniyatārammaṇaṃ. Tatra hi manodhātu pañcasupi rūpādīsu pavattati, manoviññāṇadhātudvayaṃ chasūti. Kāyaviññāṇaṃ panettha sukhayuttaṃ, dviṭṭhānā manoviññāṇadhātu somanassayuttā, sesaṃ upekkhāyuttanti. Evaṃ tāva kusalavipākāhetukaṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ veditabbaṃ.

And these eight types of rootless resultant consciousness are twofold, on account of having a fixed or an unfixed object. They are threefold by distinction of equanimity, pleasure, and joy. Herein, the fivefold sense-consciousness has a fixed object, since it arises in sequence with respect to visible forms and so on; the rest have an unfixed object. For among them, the mind-element functions with respect to the five objects—visible forms and so on—while the two mind-consciousness-elements function with respect to the six. Herein, body-consciousness is associated with pleasure; the mind-consciousness-element that occurs in two instances is associated with joy; the remaining six are associated with equanimity. Thus, for now, the eightfold rootless wholesome-resultant consciousness should be understood.

Alobhādivipākahetusampayuttaṃ pana sahetukaṃ, taṃ kāmāvacarakusalaṃ viya somanassādi bhedato aṭṭhavidhaṃ. Yathā pana kusalaṃ dānādivasena [M 2.0086] chasu ārammaṇesu pavattati, na idaṃ tathā. Idañhi paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutitadārammaṇavasena parittadhammapariyāpannesuyeva chasu ārammaṇesu pavattati[V 2.0083]. Saṅkhārāsaṅkhārabhāvo panettha āgamanādivasena veditabbo. Sampayuttadhammānañca visese asatipi ādāsatalādīsu mukhanimittaṃ viya nirussāhaṃ vipākaṃ, mukhaṃ viya saussāhaṃ kusalanti veditabbaṃ.

However, that which is associated with resultant roots such as non-greed is resultant consciousness with roots. Like sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, it is eightfold by way of distinctions such as being accompanied by joy. But while wholesome consciousness occurs with the six objects by way of giving and so on, this is not so with the resultant. For this occurs only with the six objects that are included among limited phenomena, by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, death, and registration. Here, the distinction between prompted and unprompted should be understood by way of the textual tradition and so on. And although there is no difference in the associated mental factors, the resultant should be understood as effortless, like the reflection of a face in a mirror, while the wholesome should be understood as effortful, like the face itself.

Kevalaṃ hi akusalavipākaṃ ahetukameva, taṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇaṃ, sampaṭicchanakiccā manodhātu, santīraṇādikiccā pañcaṭṭhānā manoviññāṇadhātūti sattavidhaṃ. Taṃ lakkhaṇādito kusalāhetukavipāke vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Indeed, unwholesome resultant consciousness is exclusively rootless. It is sevenfold: eye-consciousness; ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness; the mind-element with the function of receiving; and the mind-consciousness-element that occurs in five instances with the function of investigating and so on. Its characteristics and so on should be understood in the same way as stated for the wholesome rootless resultant consciousness.

Kevalañhi kusalavipākāni iṭṭhaiṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇāni, imāni aniṭṭhaaniṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇāni. Tāni ca upekkhāsukhasomanassabhedato tividhāni, imāni dukkhaupekkhāvasena duvidhāni. Ettha hi kāyaviññāṇaṃ dukkhasahagatameva, sesāni upekkhāsahagatāni. Sā ca tesu upekkhā hīnā dukkhaṃ viya nātitikhiṇā, itaresu upekkhā paṇītā sukhaṃ viya nātitikhiṇā. Iti imesaṃ sattannaṃ akusalavipākānaṃ purimānañca soḷasannaṃ kusalavipākānaṃ vasena kāmāvacaraṃ vipākaviññāṇaṃ tevīsatividhaṃ.

Indeed, wholesome resultant consciousnesses have desirable or moderately desirable objects, while these have undesirable or moderately undesirable objects. And those are of three kinds, distinguished by equanimity, pleasure, or joy, while these are of two kinds, by way of pain or equanimity. Herein, body-consciousness is always accompanied by pain; the rest are accompanied by equanimity. And the equanimity in these is inferior, not very sharp like pain, while the equanimity in the others is superior, not very sharp like pleasure. Thus, by way of these seven unwholesome resultants and the previous sixteen wholesome resultants, the sense-sphere resultant consciousness is of twenty-three kinds.

Rūpāvacaraṃ pana kusalaṃ viya pañcavidhaṃ. Kusalaṃ pana samāpattivasena javanavīthiyaṃ pavattati. Idaṃ upapattiyaṃ paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasena. Yathā ca rūpāvacaraṃ, evaṃ arūpāvacarampi kusalaṃ viya catubbidhaṃ. Pavattibhedopissa rūpāvacare vuttanayo eva. Lokuttaravipākaṃ catumaggayuttacittaphalattā catubbidhaṃ, taṃ maggavīthivasena ceva samāpattivasena ca dvidhā pavattati. Evaṃ sabbampi catūsu bhūmīsu chattiṃsavidhaṃ vipākaviññāṇaṃ hoti.

The fine-material sphere resultant consciousness, however, is fivefold like the wholesome. But the wholesome consciousness occurs in the impulsion process by way of attainment; this resultant consciousness occurs in the new existence by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death. And just as the fine-material sphere, so too the immaterial sphere resultant consciousness is fourfold like the wholesome. The distinction in its occurrence is the same as the method stated for the fine-material sphere. The supramundane resultant is fourfold, as it is the fruit of the consciousnesses associated with the four paths. It occurs in two ways: by way of the path process and by way of attainment. Thus, in all four planes, resultant consciousness is of thirty-six kinds.

Kiriyaṃ pana bhūmibhedato tividhaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacarañca. Tattha kāmāvacaraṃ duvidhaṃ ahetukaṃ sahetukañca. Tattha alobhādikiriyahetuvirahitaṃ ahetukaṃ, taṃ manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātubhedato duvidhaṃ.

Functional consciousness, however, is of three kinds according to the distinction of plane: sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere. Herein, the sense-sphere functional consciousness is twofold: rootless and rooted. Herein, the rootless is that which is devoid of functional roots such as non-greed. It is of two kinds, distinguished as the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element.

Tattha cakkhuviññāṇādipurecararūpādivijānanalakkhaṇā manodhātu, āvajjanarasā, rūpādiabhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, bhavaṅgavicchedapadaṭṭhānā, sā upekkhāyuttāva hoti.

Herein, the mind-element has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms, etc., and of preceding eye-consciousness, etc. Its function is adverting. It is manifested as the state of facing towards visible forms, etc. Its proximate cause is the interruption of the life-continuum. It is always accompanied by equanimity.

Manoviññāṇadhātu [M 2.0087][V 2.0084] pana duvidhā sādhāraṇā asādhāraṇā ca. Tattha sādhāraṇā upekkhāsahagatāhetukakiriyā saḷārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇā, kiccavasena pañcadvāramanodvāresu voṭṭhabbanāvajjanarasā, tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, ahetukavipākamanoviññāṇadhātu bhavaṅgānaṃ aññatarāpagamapadaṭṭhānā.

The mind-consciousness-element, however, is of two kinds: common and uncommon. Herein, the common one is the rootless functional consciousness accompanied by equanimity. It has the characteristic of cognizing the six objects. By way of function, it has the function of determining in the five sense-doors and adverting in the mind-door. It is manifested as being that way. Its proximate cause is the cessation of one of the rootless resultant mind-consciousness-elements or of the life-continuum.

Asādhāraṇā somanassasahagatāhetukakiriyā saḷārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇā, kiccavasena arahataṃ anuḷāresu vatthūsu hasituppādanarasā, tathābhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, ekantato hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānāti. Iti kāmāvacarakiriyaṃ ahetukaṃ tividhaṃ.

The uncommon one is the rootless functional consciousness accompanied by joy. It has the characteristic of cognizing the six objects. By way of function, its function is to produce a smile for arahants regarding non-sublime matters. It is manifested as being that way. Its proximate cause is exclusively the heart-base. Thus, the rootless functional consciousness of the sense-sphere is of three kinds.

Sahetukaṃ pana somanassādibhedato kusalaṃ viya aṭṭhavidhaṃ. Kevalañhi kusalaṃ sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ uppajjati, idaṃ arahataṃyevāti ayamettha viseso. Evaṃ tāva kāmāvacaraṃ ekādasavidhaṃ.

The rooted functional consciousness, however, is eightfold, like the wholesome, with distinctions such as being accompanied by joy. Indeed, wholesome consciousness arises only for trainees and worldlings, while this functional consciousness arises only for arahants—this is the distinction here. Thus, so far, the sense-sphere functional consciousness is of eleven kinds.

Rūpāvacaraṃ pana arūpāvacarañca kusalaṃ viya pañcavidhaṃ catubbidhañca hoti. Arahataṃ uppattivaseneva cassa kusalato viseso veditabboti. Evaṃ sabbampi tīsu bhūmīsu vīsatividhaṃ kiriyaviññāṇaṃ hoti.

The fine-material sphere and immaterial sphere functional consciousness, however, are fivefold and fourfold respectively, like the wholesome. And its distinction from the wholesome should be understood as arising only for arahants. Thus, in all three planes, functional consciousness is of twenty kinds.

455. Iti ekavīsati kusalāni dvādasākusalāni chattiṃsa vipākāni vīsati kiriyānīti sabbānipi ekūnanavuti viññāṇāni honti. Yāni paṭisandhibhavaṅgāvajjanadassanasavanaghāyanasāyanaphusanasampaṭicchanasantīraṇavoṭṭhabbanajavanatadārammaṇacutivasena cuddasahi ākārehi pavattanti.

455. Thus, there are twenty-one wholesome, twelve unwholesome, thirty-six resultant, and twenty functional consciousnesses—in all, eighty-nine types of consciousness. These occur in fourteen modes: rebirth-linking, life-continuum, adverting, seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, receiving, investigating, determining, impulsion, registering, and death.

Kathaṃ? Yadā hi aṭṭhannaṃ kāmāvacarakusalānaṃ ānubhāvena devamanussesu sattā nibbattanti, tadā nesaṃ maraṇakāle paccupaṭṭhitaṃ kammakammanimittagatinimittānaṃ aññataraṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā aṭṭha sahetukakāmāvacaravipākāni, manussesu paṇḍakādibhāvaṃ āpajjamānānaṃ dubbaladvihetukakusalavipākaupekkhāsahagatāhetukavipākamanoviññāṇadhātu cāti paṭisandhivasena nava vipākacittāni pavattanti. Yadā rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakusalānubhāvena rūpārūpabhavesu nibbattanti[V 2.0085], tadā nesaṃ maraṇakāle paccupaṭṭhitaṃ kammanimittameva ārammaṇaṃ katvā nava rūpārūpāvacaravipākāni paṭisandhivasena pavattanti.

How so? When, through the power of the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, beings are reborn among devas and humans, then at the time of their death, taking as object one of the kamma, kamma-sign, or destiny-sign that is present, eight rooted sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses arise; and for those who attain existence as eunuchs and the like among humans, the rootless resultant mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity, which is the result of a weak two-rooted wholesome consciousness, arises. Thus, nine resultant consciousnesses occur by way of rebirth-linking. When, through the power of fine-material sphere and immaterial sphere wholesome consciousnesses, beings are reborn in the fine-material and immaterial realms, then at the time of their death, taking only the kamma-sign that is present as object, the nine fine-material and immaterial sphere resultant consciousnesses arise by way of rebirth-linking.

Yadā [M 2.0088] pana akusalānubhāvena apāye nibbattanti, tadā nesaṃ maraṇakāle paccupaṭṭhitaṃ kammakammanimittagatinimittānaṃ aññataraṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā ekā akusalavipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu paṭisandhivasena pavattatīti evaṃ tāvettha ekūnavīsatiyā vipākaviññāṇānaṃ paṭisandhivasena pavatti veditabbā.

But when they are reborn in the planes of deprivation through the power of unwholesome consciousness, then at the time of their death, taking as object one of the kamma, kamma-sign, or destiny-sign that is present, a single unwholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element arises by way of rebirth-linking. Thus, the occurrence of nineteen resultant consciousnesses by way of rebirth-linking should be understood.

Paṭisandhiviññāṇe pana niruddhe taṃ taṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇamanubandhamānaṃ tassa tasseva kammassa vipākabhūtaṃ tasmiññeva ārammaṇe tādisameva bhavaṅgaviññāṇaṃ nāma pavattati, punapi tādisanti evaṃ asati santānavinivattake aññasmiṃ cittuppāde nadīsotaṃ viya supinaṃ apassato niddokkamanakālādīsu aparimāṇasaṅkhyampi pavattatiyevāti evaṃ tesaññeva viññāṇānaṃ bhavaṅgavasenāpi pavatti veditabbā.

When the rebirth-linking consciousness has ceased, a life-continuum consciousness of the very same kind arises, following that rebirth-linking consciousness, being the result of that very same kamma, and having the very same object. Again and again, so long as no other consciousness arises to interrupt the continuity, it occurs a countless number of times, like the flow of a river, during dreamless sleep, when falling asleep, and so on. Thus, the occurrence of these same consciousnesses by way of the life-continuum should also be understood.

Evaṃ pavatte pana bhavaṅgasantāne yadā sattānaṃ indriyāni ārammaṇagahaṇakkhamāni honti, tadā cakkhussāpāthagate rūpe rūpaṃ paṭicca cakkhupasādassa ghaṭṭanā hoti, tato ghaṭṭanānubhāvena bhavaṅgacalanaṃ hoti, atha niruddhe bhavaṅge tadeva rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā bhavaṅgaṃ vicchindamānā viya āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā kiriyamanodhātu uppajjati. Sotadvārādīsupi eseva nayo. Manodvāre pana chabbidhepi ārammaṇe āpāthagate bhavaṅgacalanānantaraṃ bhavaṅgaṃ vicchindamānā viya āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā ahetukakiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu uppajjati upekkhāsahagatāti evaṃ dvinnaṃ kiriyaviññāṇānaṃ āvajjanavasena pavatti veditabbā.

Furthermore, when the stream of the life-continuum is thus proceeding, and the faculties of beings become capable of grasping an object, then when a form comes into the range of the eye, there is an impact on the eye-sensitivity on account of that form. Then, through the force of that impact, the life-continuum vibrates. Then, when the life-continuum has ceased, taking that very form as its object, the functional mind-element arises, accomplishing the function of adverting as if cutting off the life-continuum. This same method applies to the ear-door and so on. At the mind-door, however, when any of the six kinds of objects comes into range, immediately after the vibration of the life-continuum, the rootless functional mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity arises, accomplishing the function of adverting as if cutting off the life-continuum. Thus, the occurrence of the two functional consciousnesses by way of adverting should be understood.

Āvajjanānantaraṃ pana cakkhudvāre tāva dassanakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ cakkhupasādavatthukaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, sotadvārādīsu savanādikiccaṃ sādhayamānāni sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇāni pavattanti. Tāni iṭṭhaiṭṭhamajjhattesu visayesu kusalavipākāni, aniṭṭhaaniṭṭhamajjhattesu visayesu akusalavipākānīti evaṃ dasannaṃ vipākaviññāṇānaṃ dassanasavanaghāyanasāyanaphusanavasena pavatti veditabbā.

Furthermore, immediately after adverting, at the eye-door, eye-consciousness arises, which is based on the eye-sensitivity and accomplishes the function of seeing. At the ear-door and so on, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness arise, accomplishing the functions of hearing and so on. With desirable or moderately desirable objects, these are wholesome-resultant; with undesirable or moderately undesirable objects, they are unwholesome-resultant. Thus, the occurrence of the ten resultant consciousnesses by way of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching should be understood.

“Cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā [V 2.0086] uppajjitvā niruddhasamanantarā uppajjati cittaṃ mano mānasaṃ tajjā manodhātū”tiādivacanato (vibha. 184) pana cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ anantarā [M 2.0089] tesaññeva visayaṃ sampaṭicchamānā kusalavipākānantaraṃ kusalavipākā, akusalavipākānantaraṃ akusalavipākā manodhātu uppajjati. Evaṃ dvinnaṃ vipākaviññāṇānaṃ sampaṭicchanavasena pavatti veditabbā.

Furthermore, on account of such statements as (Vibhaṅga 184): 'Immediately after the eye-consciousness-element, having arisen, has ceased, there arises a mind, a mentation, a mental faculty, that is, the mind-element which is born of that,' the mind-element arises immediately after eye-consciousness and the others, receiving their very same object. After a wholesome-resultant, a wholesome-resultant mind-element arises; after an unwholesome-resultant, an unwholesome-resultant one arises. Thus, the occurrence of the two resultant consciousnesses by way of receiving should be understood.

“Manodhātuyāpi uppajjitvā niruddhasamanantarā uppajjati cittaṃ mano mānasaṃ tajjāmanoviññāṇadhātū”ti (vibha. 184) vacanato pana manodhātuyā sampaṭicchitameva visayaṃ santīrayamānā akusalavipākamanodhātuyā anantarā akusalavipākā, kusalavipākāya anantarā iṭṭhārammaṇe somanassasahagatā, iṭṭhamajjhatte upekkhāsahagatā uppajjati vipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātūti evaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vipākaviññāṇānaṃ santīraṇavasena pavatti veditabbā.

Furthermore, on account of the statement (Vibhaṅga 184), 'Immediately after the mind-element too, having arisen, has ceased, there arises a mind, a mentation, a mental faculty, that is, the mind-consciousness-element which is born of that,' the resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element arises, investigating the very object received by the mind-element. After an unwholesome-resultant mind-element, an unwholesome-resultant one arises. After a wholesome-resultant mind-element, with a desirable object, one accompanied by gladness arises; with a desirable-neutral object, one accompanied by equanimity arises. Thus, the occurrence of the three resultant consciousnesses by way of investigating should be understood.

Santīraṇānantaraṃ pana tameva visayaṃ vavatthāpayamānā uppajjati kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu upekkhāsahagatāti evaṃ ekasseva kiriyaviññāṇassa voṭṭhabbanavasena pavatti veditabbā.

Furthermore, immediately after investigating, the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element arises, accompanied by equanimity, determining that very same object. Thus, the occurrence of this single functional consciousness should be understood as occurring by way of determination.

Voṭṭhabbanānantaraṃ pana sace mahantaṃ hoti rūpādiārammaṇaṃ, atha yathāvavatthāpite visaye aṭṭhannaṃ vā kāmāvacarakusalānaṃ dvādasannaṃ vā akusalānaṃ navannaṃ vā avasesakāmāvacarakiriyānaṃ aññataravasena cha satta vā javanāni javanti, eso tāva pañcadvāre nayo.

Furthermore, immediately after determination, if the object such as a visible form is great, then in regard to the object that has been determined, six or seven impulsions of one of the eight sense-sphere wholesome, twelve unwholesome, or nine remaining sense-sphere functional consciousnesses run. This is the method at the five doors.

Manodvāre pana manodvārāvajjanānantaraṃ tāniyeva. Gotrabhuto uddhaṃ rūpāvacarato pañca kusalāni pañca kiriyāni, arūpāvacarato cattāri kusalāni cattāri kiriyāni, lokuttarato cattāri maggacittāni cattāri phalacittānīti imesu yaṃ yaṃ laddhapaccayaṃ hoti, taṃ taṃ javatīti evaṃ pañcapaññāsāya kusalākusalakiriyavipākaviññāṇānaṃ javanavasena pavatti veditabbā.

At the mind-door, however, immediately after mind-door adverting, those same impulsions occur. Beyond change-of-lineage, there are: from the fine-material sphere, five wholesome and five functional consciousnesses; from the immaterial sphere, four wholesome and four functional; and from the supramundane, four path consciousnesses and four fruition consciousnesses. Among these, whichever obtains the conditions, that one runs as impulsion. Thus, the occurrence of the fifty-five wholesome, unwholesome, functional, and resultant consciousnesses should be understood as occurring by way of impulsion.

Javanāvasāne pana sace pañcadvāre atimahantaṃ, manodvāre ca vibhūtamārammaṇaṃ hoti, atha kāmāvacarasattānaṃ kāmāvacarajavanāvasāne iṭṭhārammaṇādīnaṃ purimakammajavanacittādīnañca vasena yo yo paccayo laddho hoti, tassa tassa vasena aṭṭhasu sahetukakāmāvacaravipākesu tīsu [V 2.0087] vipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātūsu ca aññataraṃ paṭisotagataṃ nāvaṃ anubandhamānaṃ kiñci antaraṃ udakamiva bhavaṅgassārammaṇato aññasmiṃ ārammaṇe [M 2.0090] javitaṃ javanamanubandhaṃ dvikkhattuṃ sakiṃ vā vipākaviññāṇaṃ uppajjati. Tadetaṃ javanāvasāne bhavaṅgassa ārammaṇe pavattanārahaṃ samānaṃ tassa javanassa ārammaṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattattā tadārammaṇanti vuccati. Evaṃ ekādasannaṃ vipākaviññāṇānaṃ tadārammaṇavasena pavatti veditabbā.

At the end of the impulsion, however, if at the five doors the object is very great, or at the mind-door the object is clear, then for sense-sphere beings, at the end of a sense-sphere impulsion, according to whatever condition has been obtained by way of a desirable object, previous kamma, impulsion-moments, etc., one of the eight sense-sphere resultants with roots or three resultant rootless mind-consciousness-elements arises once or twice. It follows the impulsion that has run on an object different from that of the life-continuum, like a little water following a boat going upstream. This resultant consciousness, though fit to occur with the object of the life-continuum at the end of the impulsion, is called 'registering' because it occurs taking the object of that impulsion as its own object. Thus, the occurrence of the eleven resultant consciousnesses should be understood as occurring by way of registering.

Tadārammaṇāvasāne pana puna bhavaṅgameva pavattati, bhavaṅge vicchinne puna āvajjanādīnīti evaṃ laddhapaccayacittasantānaṃ bhavaṅgānantaraṃ āvajjanaṃ āvajjanānantaraṃ dassanādīnīti cittaniyamavaseneva punappunaṃ tāva pavattati, yāva ekasmiṃ bhave bhavaṅgassa parikkhayo. Ekasmiṃ hi bhave yaṃ sabbapacchimaṃ bhavaṅgacittaṃ, taṃ tato cavanattā cutīti vuccati. Tasmā tampi ekūnavīsatividhameva hoti. Evaṃ ekūnavīsatiyā vipākaviññāṇānaṃ cutivasena pavatti veditabbā.

At the end of registering, however, the life-continuum occurs again. When the life-continuum is interrupted, adverting and so on occur again. Thus the stream of consciousness, having obtained its conditions, proceeds again and again by way of the fixed order of consciousness: after the life-continuum, adverting; after adverting, seeing, etc. It occurs in this way repeatedly until the exhaustion of the life-continuum in a single existence. For in a single existence, the very last life-continuum consciousness is called 'death' because it is a falling away from that existence. Therefore, that too is of nineteen kinds. Thus, the occurrence of the nineteen resultant consciousnesses should be understood as occurring by way of death.

Cutito pana puna paṭisandhi, paṭisandhito puna bhavaṅganti evaṃ bhavagatiṭhitinivāsesu saṃsaramānānaṃ sattānaṃ avicchinnaṃ cittasantānaṃ pavattatiyeva. Yo panettha arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, tassa cuticitte niruddhe niruddhameva hotīti.

Furthermore, from death, rebirth-linking again; from rebirth-linking, the life-continuum again. Thus, for beings wandering in saṃsāra through becomings, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings, the unbroken stream of consciousness continues to occur. But for one who attains Arahantship here, when his death-consciousness has ceased, it has ceased completely.

Idaṃ viññāṇakkhandhe vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed explanation of the aggregate of consciousness.

Vedanākkhandhakathā

The Discourse on the Aggregate of Feeling

456. Idāni yaṃ vuttaṃ “yaṃkiñci vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekato katvā vedanākkhandho veditabbo”ti, etthāpi vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ nāma vedanāva. Yathāha – “vedayati vedayatīti kho āvuso, tasmā vedanāti vuccatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.450). Sā pana vedayitalakkhaṇena sabhāvato ekavidhāpi jātivasena tividhā hoti kusalā, akusalā, abyākatā cāti.

456. Now, as to what was said: ‘Whatever has the characteristic of being felt, all that, having been collected together, should be understood as the aggregate of feeling.’ Herein, that which has the characteristic of being felt is feeling itself. As it is said: ‘It feels, it feels, friend, therefore it is called feeling’ (MN 43). But that feeling, though it is onefold by nature in its characteristic of being felt, becomes threefold by way of class: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

Tattha kāmāvacaraṃ somanassupekkhāñāṇasaṅkhārabhedato aṭṭhavidhantiādinā nayena vuttena kusalaviññāṇena [V 2.0088] sampayuttā kusalā, akusalena sampayuttā akusalā, abyākatena sampayuttā abyākatāti veditabbā. Sā sabhāvabhedato pañcavidhā hoti – sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ somanassaṃ domanassaṃ upekkhāti.

Herein, it should be understood that feeling associated with wholesome consciousness is wholesome; associated with unwholesome consciousness, unwholesome; and associated with indeterminate consciousness, indeterminate, according to the method stated beginning with: ‘The sense-sphere wholesome consciousness is eightfold by the distinctions of being accompanied by joy or equanimity, associated with knowledge, and prompted or unprompted.’ By way of its intrinsic nature, feeling is fivefold: bodily pleasure, bodily pain, joy, sorrow, and equanimity.

Tattha [M 2.0091] kusalavipākena kāyaviññāṇena sampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ. Akusalavipākena dukkhaṃ. Kāmāvacarato catūhi kusalehi, catūhi sahetukavipākehi, ekena ahetukavipākena, catūhi sahetukakiriyehi, ekena ahetukakiriyena, catūhi akusalehi, rūpāvacarato ṭhapetvā pañcamajjhānaviññāṇaṃ catūhi kusalehi, catūhi vipākehi, catūhi kiriyehi, lokuttaraṃ pana yasmā ajhānikaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā aṭṭha lokuttarāni pañcannaṃ jhānānaṃ vasena cattālīsaṃ honti. Tesu ṭhapetvā aṭṭha pañcamajjhānikāni sesehi dvattiṃsāya kusalavipākehīti evaṃ somanassaṃ dvāsaṭṭhiyā viññāṇehi sampayuttaṃ. Domanassaṃ dvīhi akusalehi. Upekkhā avasesapañcapaññāsāya viññāṇehi sampayuttā.

Herein, bodily pleasure is that which is associated with wholesome-resultant body-consciousness. Bodily pain is that which is associated with unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness. Joy is associated with sixty-two consciousnesses: in the sense sphere, with four wholesome, four rooted resultant, one rootless resultant, four rooted functional, one rootless functional, and four unwholesome consciousnesses; in the form sphere, excluding the fifth-jhāna consciousnesses, with four wholesome, four resultant, and four functional consciousnesses; and in the supramundane sphere—since there is no non-jhānic type, the eight supramundane consciousnesses become forty by way of the five jhānas; excluding the eight fifth-jhāna types from these, joy is associated with the remaining thirty-two wholesome and resultant consciousnesses. Sorrow is associated with two unwholesome consciousnesses. Equanimity is associated with the remaining fifty-five consciousnesses.

Tattha iṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ sukhaṃ, sampayuttānaṃ upabrūhanarasaṃ, kāyikaassādapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, kāyindriyapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

Herein, bodily pleasure has the characteristic of experiencing a desirable tangible object, the function of intensifying associated states, manifestation as bodily relish, and the body faculty as its proximate cause.

Aniṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ dukkhaṃ, sampayuttānaṃ milāpanarasaṃ, kāyikābādhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, kāyindriyapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

Bodily pain has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable tangible object, the function of withering associated states, manifestation as bodily affliction, and the body faculty as its proximate cause.

Iṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ somanassaṃ, yathā tathā vā iṭṭhākārasambhogarasaṃ, cetasikaassādapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, passaddhipadaṭṭhānaṃ.

Joy has the characteristic of experiencing a desirable object, the function of partaking of the desirable aspect of an object in whatever way it is presented, manifestation as mental relish, and tranquility as its proximate cause.

Aniṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanalakkhaṇaṃ domanassaṃ, yathā tathā vā aniṭṭhākārasambhogarasaṃ, cetasikābādhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, ekanteneva hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ.

Sorrow has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable object, the function of partaking of the undesirable aspect of an object in whatever way it is presented, manifestation as mental affliction, and invariably the heart-base as its proximate cause.

Majjhattavedayitalakkhaṇā upekkhā, sampayuttānaṃ nātiupabrūhanamilāpanarasā, santabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, nippītikacittapadaṭṭhānāti.

Equanimity has the characteristic of being felt neutrally, the function of neither intensifying nor withering associated states, manifestation as a peaceful state, and consciousness devoid of zest as its proximate cause.

Idaṃ vedanākkhandhe vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed explanation of the aggregate of feeling.

Saññākkhandhakathā

The Discourse on the Aggregate of Perception

457. Idāni [V 2.0089] yaṃ vuttaṃ “yaṃkiñci sañjānanalakkhaṇaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekato katvā saññākkhandho veditabbo”ti, etthāpi sañjānanalakkhaṇaṃ nāma saññāva. Yathāha – “sañjānāti sañjānātīti kho, āvuso, tasmā saññāti vuccatī”ti [M 2.0092] (ma. ni. 1.450). Sā panesā sañjānanalakkhaṇena sabhāvato ekavidhāpi jātivasena tividhā hoti kusalā, akusalā, abyākatā ca.

457. Now, as to what was said: ‘Whatever has the characteristic of perceiving, all that, having been collected together, should be understood as the aggregate of perception.’ Herein, that which has the characteristic of perceiving is perception itself. As it is said: ‘It perceives, it perceives, friend, therefore it is called perception’ (MN 43). But this perception, though it is onefold by nature in its characteristic of perceiving, becomes threefold by way of class: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

Tattha kusalaviññāṇasampayuttā kusalā, akusalasampayuttā akusalā, abyākatasampayuttā abyākatā. Na hi taṃ viññāṇaṃ atthi, yaṃ saññāya vippayuttaṃ, tasmā yattako viññāṇassa bhedo, tattako saññāyāti.

Herein, perception associated with wholesome consciousness is wholesome; associated with unwholesome consciousness, unwholesome; associated with indeterminate consciousness, indeterminate. For there is no consciousness that is dissociated from perception. Therefore, the divisions of perception are as numerous as the divisions of consciousness.

Sā panesā evaṃ viññāṇena samappabhedāpi lakkhaṇādito sabbāva sañjānanalakkhaṇā, tadevetanti puna sañjānanapaccayanimittakaraṇarasā dāruādīsu tacchakādayo viya, yathāgahitanimittavasena abhinivesakaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānā hatthidassakaandhā (udā. 54) viya, yathāupaṭṭhitavisayapadaṭṭhānā tiṇapurisakesu migapotakānaṃ purisāti uppannasaññā viyāti.
