But although this perception has the same number of divisions as consciousness, in terms of characteristic, etc., all perception has the characteristic of perceiving; the function of making a sign as a condition for perceiving again that ‘this is the very same thing,’ like carpenters with wood; manifestation as the act of adhering by way of a sign as it has been grasped, like the blind men and the elephant (Ud 6.4); and an object as it has appeared as its proximate cause, like the perception ‘a man’ that arises in young deer with regard to a scarecrow.

Idaṃ saññākkhandhe vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed explanation of the aggregate of perception.

Saṅkhārakkhandhakathā

The Discourse on the Aggregate of Formations

458. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “yaṃkiñci abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ ekato katvā saṅkhārakkhandho veditabbo”ti, ettha abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ nāma rāsikaraṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti, saṅkhārāyeva. Yathāha – “saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharontīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā saṅkhārāti vuccantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.79). Te abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇā, āyūhanarasā, vipphārapaccupaṭṭhānā, sesakhandhattayapadaṭṭhānā.

458. As to what was said: ‘Whatever has the characteristic of forming, all that, having been collected together, should be understood as the aggregate of formations.’ Herein, the characteristic of forming means the characteristic of accumulating. But what is that? The formations themselves. As it is said: ‘They form the formed, bhikkhus, therefore they are called formations’ (SN 22.79). They have the characteristic of forming, the function of accumulating, manifestation as exertion, and the remaining three mental aggregates as their proximate cause.

Evaṃ lakkhaṇādito ekavidhāpi ca jātivasena tividhā kusalā, akusalā, abyākatāti[V 2.0090]. Tesu kusalaviññāṇasampayuttā kusalā. Akusalasampayuttā akusalā. Abyākatasampayuttā abyākatā.

Thus, though onefold from the point of view of characteristic, etc., they are threefold by way of class: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. Among these, those associated with wholesome consciousness are wholesome; those associated with unwholesome consciousness are unwholesome; and those associated with indeterminate consciousness are indeterminate.

Tattha kāmāvacarapaṭhamakusalaviññāṇasampayuttā tāva niyatā sarūpena āgatā sattavīsati, yevāpanakā cattāro, aniyatā pañcāti chattiṃsa. Tattha phasso, cetanā, vitakko, vicāro, pīti, vīriyaṃ, jīvitaṃ, samādhi, saddhā, sati, hirī, ottappaṃ, alobho, adoso, amoho, kāyapassaddhi, cittapassaddhi, kāyalahutā, cittalahutā, kāyamudutā, cittamudutā, kāyakammaññatā, cittakammaññatā, kāyapāguññatā, cittapāguññatā, kāyujukatā, cittujukatāti ime sarūpena [M 2.0093] āgatā sattavīsati (dha. sa. 1; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 yevāpanakavaṇṇanā). Chando, adhimokkho, manasikāro, tatramajjhattatāti ime yevāpanakā cattāro (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 yevāpanakavaṇṇanā). Karuṇā, muditā, kāyaduccaritavirati, vacīduccaritavirati, micchājīvaviratīti ime aniyatā pañca. Ete hi kadāci uppajjanti, uppajjamānāpi ca na ekato uppajjanti.

Herein, associated with the first sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, there are thirty-six formations: twenty-seven that arise fixedly in their own nature, four that are separable, and five that are occasional. The twenty-seven that arise fixedly are: contact, volition, initial application, sustained application, joy, energy, life faculty, concentration, faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, tranquility of body, tranquility of mind, lightness of body, lightness of mind, malleability of body, malleability of mind, wieldiness of body, wieldiness of mind, proficiency of body, proficiency of mind, rectitude of body, and rectitude of mind. The four separable factors are: zeal, decision, attention, and equanimity. The five occasional factors are: compassion, altruistic joy, abstinence from bodily misconduct, abstinence from verbal misconduct, and abstinence from wrong livelihood. For these arise only sometimes, and even when they arise, they do not all arise together.

459. Tattha phusatīti phasso. Svāyaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo. Saṅghaṭṭanaraso, sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno, āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhāno. Ayañhi arūpadhammopi samāno ārammaṇe phusanākāreneva pavattati. Ekadesena ca analliyamānopi rūpaṃ viya cakkhu, saddo viya ca sotaṃ cittaṃ ārammaṇañca saṅghaṭṭeti, tikasannipātasaṅkhātassa attano kāraṇassa vasena paveditattā sannipātapaccupaṭṭhāno. Tajjāsamannāhārena ceva indriyena ca parikkhate visaye anantarāyeneva uppajjanato āpāthagatavisayapadaṭṭhānoti vuccati. Vedanādhiṭṭhānabhāvato pana niccammagāvī (saṃ. ni. 2.63) viya daṭṭhabbo.

459. Herein, ‘it touches,’ thus it is contact. This has the characteristic of touching, the function of impinging, manifestation as coincidence, and an object that has entered the avenue of a sense faculty as its proximate cause. For although it is an immaterial state, it occurs in the mode of touching an object. And though it does not adhere in any part, just as form impinges on the eye and sound on the ear, so it makes the mind and its object impinge on each other. It has manifestation as coincidence because it is made known by its cause, which is designated as the coincidence of the three. It is said to have an object that has entered the avenue as its proximate cause because it arises without fail in an object that is determined by the sense faculty and by the appropriate attention born from that. And because it is the basis for feeling, it should be seen as being like a flayed cow.

460. Cetayatīti cetanā. Abhisandahatīti attho. Sā cetanābhāvalakkhaṇā, āyūhanarasā, saṃvidahanapaccupaṭṭhānā sakiccaparakiccasādhikā jeṭṭhasissamahāvaḍḍhakīādayo viya. Accāyikakammānussaraṇādīsu ca panāyaṃ sampayuttānaṃ ussahanabhāvena pavattamānā pākaṭā hoti.

460. ‘It wills,’ thus it is volition; the meaning is that it coordinates. It has the characteristic of the state of willing, the function of striving, and manifestation as coordinating, accomplishing its own task and the tasks of others, like a senior pupil or a master carpenter. Moreover, in such instances as the urgent recollection of a deed, this volition becomes manifest through its occurring with the nature of an urge to its associated states.

Vitakkavicārapītīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ pathavīkasiṇaniddese paṭhamajjhānavaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. 1.71) vuttameva.

Whatever should be said about initial application, sustained application, and joy, all that has already been said in the description of the first jhāna in the exposition of the earth kasiṇa.

461. Vīrabhāvo [V 2.0091] vīriyaṃ. Taṃ ussahanalakkhaṇaṃ, sahajātānaṃ upatthambhanarasaṃ, asaṃsīdanabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. “Saṃviggo yoniso padahatī”ti (a. ni. 4.113) vacanato saṃvegapadaṭṭhānaṃ, vīriyārambhavatthupadaṭṭhānaṃ vā, sammā āraddhaṃ sabbasampattīnaṃ mūlaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

461. The state of a hero is energy. It has the characteristic of exertion, the function of supporting co-nascent states, and manifestation as a state of non-collapse. As it is said, ‘Being stirred, one strives wisely,’ its proximate cause is a sense of urgency, or else the grounds for arousing energy. It should be seen that, when rightly aroused, it is the root of all accomplishments.

462. Jīvanti tena, sayaṃ vā jīvati, jīvanamattameva vā tanti jīvitaṃ. Lakkhaṇādīni panassa rūpajīvite vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Tañhi rūpadhammānaṃ jīvitaṃ, idaṃ arūpadhammānanti idamevettha nānākaraṇaṃ.

462. ‘One lives by means of it,’ or ‘it itself lives,’ or ‘it is mere living,’ thus it is the life faculty. Its characteristic and so on should be understood in the way stated for the material life faculty. For that is the life of material states, while this is the life of immaterial states—this alone is the difference here.

463. Ārammaṇe [M 2.0094] cittaṃ samaṃ ādhiyati, sammā vā ādhiyati, samādhānamattameva vā etaṃ cittassāti samādhi. So avisāralakkhaṇo, avikkhepalakkhaṇo vā, sahajātānaṃ sampiṇḍanaraso nhāniyacuṇṇānaṃ udakaṃ viya, upasamapaccupaṭṭhāno, visesato sukhapadaṭṭhāno, nivāte dīpaccīnaṃ ṭhiti viya cetaso ṭhitīti daṭṭhabbo.

463. ‘The mind is placed evenly on the object,’ or ‘is placed rightly,’ or ‘it is the mere placing of the mind,’ thus it is concentration. It has the characteristic of non-wandering, or of non-distraction; the function of unifying the co-nascent states, like water with bath powder; manifestation as tranquility; and its proximate cause is especially happiness. It should be seen as the stability of the mind, like the flame of a lamp in a windless place.

464. Saddahanti etāya, sayaṃ vā saddahati, saddahanamattameva vā esāti saddhā. Sā saddahanalakkhaṇā, okappanalakkhaṇā vā, pasādanarasā udakappasādakamaṇi viya, pakkhandanarasā vā oghuttaraṇo viya. Akālussiyapaccupaṭṭhānā, adhimuttipaccupaṭṭhānā vā, saddheyyavatthupadaṭṭhānā, saddhammassavanādisotāpattiyaṅga(dī. ni. 3.311; saṃ. ni. 5.1001) padaṭṭhānā vā, hatthavittabījāni viya daṭṭhabbā.

464. ‘One has faith by means of it,’ or ‘it has faith itself,’ or ‘it is simply the act of having faith’—this is faith. It has the characteristic of conviction, or of placing trust. Its function is to clarify, like a water-clearing gem, or to leap forward, like one crossing a flood. It is manifested as non-turbidity, or as resolution. Its proximate cause is an object of faith, or the factors of stream-entry such as listening to the good Dhamma. It should be seen as being like a hand, wealth, and a seed.

465. Saranti tāya, sayaṃ vā sarati saraṇamattameva vā esāti sati. Sā apilāpanalakkhaṇā, asammosarasā, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā, visayābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, thirasaññāpadaṭṭhānā, kāyādisatipaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānā vā. Ārammaṇe daḷhapatiṭṭhitattā pana esikā viya, cakkhudvārādirakkhaṇato dovāriko viya ca daṭṭhabbā.

465. ‘One remembers by means of it,’ or ‘it remembers by itself,’ or ‘it is simply the act of remembering’—this is mindfulness. It has the characteristic of not floating away, its function is non-confusion, and it is manifested as guarding, or as the state of facing the object. Its proximate cause is firm perception, or the foundations of mindfulness concerning the body, etc. Because it is firmly established on the object, it should be seen as like a pillar; and because it guards the eye-door and so on, it should be seen as like a gatekeeper.

466. Kāyaduccaritādīhi hiriyatīti hirī. Lajjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tehiyeva ottappatīti ottappaṃ. Pāpato ubbegassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tattha pāpato jigucchanalakkhaṇā hirī. Uttāsanalakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ. Lajjākārena pāpānaṃ akaraṇarasā hirī. Uttāsākārena ottappaṃ. Vuttappakāreneva [V 2.0092] ca pāpato saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānā etā, attagāravaparagāravapadaṭṭhānā. Attānaṃ garuṃ katvā hiriyā pāpaṃ jahāti kulavadhū viya. Paraṃ garuṃ katvā ottappena pāpaṃ jahāti vesiyā viya. Ime ca pana dve dhammā lokapālakāti (a. ni. 2.9) daṭṭhabbā.

466. ‘One is ashamed of bodily misconduct and so on,’ thus it is moral shame (hirī). This is a designation for shame. ‘One is apprehensive of those very things,’ thus it is moral dread (ottappa). This is a designation for anxiety about evil. Herein, moral shame has the characteristic of being disgusted with evil. Moral dread has the characteristic of being fearful of it. Moral shame has the function of not doing evil out of shame; moral dread has the function of not doing it out of fear. They are manifested as shrinking away from evil. Their proximate cause is respect for oneself and respect for others. Having respect for oneself, one abandons evil through moral shame, like a woman of good family. Having respect for others, one abandons evil through moral dread, like a courtesan. And these two qualities should be seen as the guardians of the world.

467. Na lubbhanti tena, sayaṃ vā na lubbhati, alubbhanamattameva vā tanti alobho. Adosāmohesupi eseva nayo. Tesu alobho ārammaṇe cittassa agedhalakkhaṇo, alaggabhāvalakkhaṇo vā kamaladale jalabindu viya. Apariggaharaso muttabhikkhu viya, anallīnabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno asucimhi patitapuriso viya.

467. ‘One is not greedy by means of it,’ or ‘one is not greedy oneself,’ or ‘it is simply the state of not being greedy’—this is non-greed. The same method applies to non-hatred and non-delusion. Among these, non-greed has the characteristic of the mind’s lack of greed for its object, or the characteristic of non-adherence, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. Its function is non-appropriation, like a liberated bhikkhu, and its manifestation is the state of non-adherence, like a person who has fallen into filth.

468. Adoso [M 2.0095] acaṇḍikkalakkhaṇo, avirodhalakkhaṇo vā anukūlamitto viya, āghātavinayaraso, pariḷāhavinayaraso vā candanaṃ viya, sommabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno puṇṇacando viya.

468. Non-hatred has the characteristic of lack of fierceness, or the characteristic of non-opposition, like a congenial friend. Its function is to remove vexation, or to subdue the fever of passion, like sandalwood. Its manifestation is a gentle state, like the full moon.

469. Amoho yathāsabhāvapaṭivedhalakkhaṇo, akkhalitapaṭivedhalakkhaṇo vā kusalissāsakhittausupaṭivedho viya, visayobhāsanaraso padīpo viya. Asammohapaccupaṭṭhāno araññagatasudesako viya. Tayopi cete sabbakusalānaṃ mūlabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

469. Non-delusion has the characteristic of penetrating things in their true nature, or the characteristic of unerring penetration, like the penetration of an arrow shot by a skilled archer. Its function is to illuminate the object, like a lamp. Its manifestation is non-confusion, like a good guide in a forest. And these three should be seen as the roots of all wholesome states.

470. Kāyassa passambhanaṃ kāyapassaddhi. Cittassa passambhanaṃ cittapassaddhi. Kāyoti cettha vedanādayo tayo khandhā. Ubhopi panetā ekato katvā kāyacittadarathavūpasamalakkhaṇā kāyacittapassaddhiyo, kāyacittadarathanimaddanarasā, kāyacittānaṃ aparipphandanasītibhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānaṃ avūpasamakarauddhaccādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

470. The calming of the mental body is bodily serenity. The calming of consciousness is mental serenity. Here, 'mental body' refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling. Both of these, taken together, have the characteristic of calming the agitation of the mental body and consciousness, the function of crushing the agitation of the mental body and consciousness, and the manifestation of non-trembling and coolness in the mental body and consciousness, with the mental body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be seen as the opponents of defilements, such as restlessness, that cause a lack of calm in the mental body and consciousness.

Kāyassa lahubhāvo kāyalahutā. Cittassa lahubhāvo cittalahutā. Tā kāyacittagarubhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā, kāyacittagarubhāvanimaddanarasā, kāyacittānaṃ adandhatāpaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānaṃ garubhāvakarathinamiddhādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The lightness of the mental body is bodily lightness. The lightness of consciousness is mental lightness. They have the characteristic of calming the heaviness of the mental body and consciousness, the function of crushing the heaviness of the mental body and consciousness, and the manifestation of non-sluggishness of the mental body and consciousness, with the mental body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be regarded as the opponents of the defilements that cause heaviness of the mental body and consciousness, such as sloth and torpor.

Kāyassa mudubhāvo kāyamudutā. Cittassa mudubhāvo cittamudutā. Tā kāyacittatthambhavūpasamalakkhaṇā[V 2.0093], kāyacittathaddhabhāvanimaddanarasā, appaṭighātapaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānaṃ thaddhabhāvakaradiṭṭhimānādikilesapaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The malleability of the mental body is bodily malleability. The malleability of consciousness is mental malleability. They have the characteristic of calming the rigidity of the mental body and consciousness, the function of crushing the stiffness of the mental body and consciousness, and the manifestation of non-resistance, with the mental body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be seen as the opponents of defilements, such as wrong view and conceit, that cause stiffness in the mental body and consciousness.

Kāyassa kammaññabhāvo kāyakammaññatā. Cittassa kammaññabhāvo cittakammaññatā. Tā kāyacittākammaññabhāvavūpasamalakkhaṇā, kāyacittākammaññabhāvanimaddanarasā, kāyacittānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇasampattipaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānaṃ akammaññabhāvakarāvasesanīvaraṇādipaṭipakkhabhūtā, pasādanīyavatthūsu pasādāvahā, hitakiriyāsu viniyogakkhamabhāvāvahā suvaṇṇavisuddhi viyāti daṭṭhabbā.

The workability of the mental body is bodily workability. The workability of consciousness is mental workability. They have the characteristic of calming the unworkability of the mental body and consciousness, the function of crushing the unworkability of the mental body and consciousness, and the manifestation of success in taking an object, with the mental body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be regarded as the opponents of the remaining hindrances that cause unworkability in the mental body and consciousness, as bringing serene confidence towards inspiring objects, and as bringing fitness for application to beneficial actions, like purified gold.

Kāyassa [M 2.0096] pāguññabhāvo kāyapāguññatā. Cittassa pāguññabhāvo cittapāguññatā. Tā kāyacittānaṃ agelaññabhāvalakkhaṇā, kāyacittagelaññanimaddanarasā, nirādīnavapaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānaṃ gelaññakaraasaddhiyādipaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The proficiency of the mental body is bodily proficiency. The proficiency of consciousness is mental proficiency. They have the characteristic of the healthiness of the mental body and consciousness, the function of crushing the sickness of the mental body and consciousness, and the manifestation of being without defect, with the mental body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be seen as the opponents of such things as lack of faith, which cause sickness in the mental body and consciousness.

Kāyassa ujukabhāvo kāyujukatā. Cittassa ujukabhāvo cittujukatā. Tā kāyacittaajjavalakkhaṇā, kāyacittakuṭilabhāvanimaddanarasā, ajimhatāpaccupaṭṭhānā, kāyacittapadaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittānaṃ kuṭilabhāvakaramāyāsāṭheyyādipaṭipakkhabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

The uprightness of the mental body is bodily uprightness. The uprightness of consciousness is mental uprightness. They have the characteristic of the straightness of the mental body and consciousness, the function of crushing the crookedness of the mental body and consciousness, and the manifestation of uncrookedness, with the mental body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be seen as the opponents of the defilements that cause crookedness of the mental body and consciousness, such as deceit and craftiness.

471. Chandoti kattukāmatāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā so kattukāmatālakkhaṇo chando, ārammaṇapariyesanaraso, ārammaṇena atthikatāpaccupaṭṭhāno, tadevassa padaṭṭhānaṃ. Ārammaṇaggahaṇe ayaṃ cetaso hatthappasāraṇaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo.

471. The term 'will' (chanda) is a designation for the wish to act. Therefore, that will has the characteristic of wishing to act, the function of seeking an object, and the manifestation of a need for the object. The object itself is its proximate cause. In grasping an object, this should be seen as the extending of the mind's hand.

472. Adhimuccanaṃ adhimokkho. So sanniṭṭhānalakkhaṇo, asaṃsappanaraso, nicchayapaccupaṭṭhāno, sanniṭṭheyyadhammapadaṭṭhāno, ārammaṇe niccalabhāvena indakhīlo viya daṭṭhabbo.

472. Resolution (adhimokkha) is the act of deciding. It has the characteristic of making a conclusion, the function of not wavering, and the manifestation of certainty. Its proximate cause is an object that can be decided upon. In relation to the object, it should be regarded as being as unshakable as a pillar.

473. Kiriyā kāro. Manamhi kāro manasikāro. Purimamanato visadisamanaṃ karotītipi manasikāro. Svāyaṃ ārammaṇapaṭipādako, vīthipaṭipādako, javanapaṭipādakoti tippakāro.

473. Kiriyā means 'doing' (kāro). Doing in the mind is attention (manasikāra). Attention is also so called because it makes the mind different from the preceding one. It is of three kinds: that which presents the object, that which presents the process, and that which presents the impulsion.

Tattha [V 2.0094] ārammaṇapaṭipādako manamhi kāroti manasikāro. So sāraṇalakkhaṇo, sampayuttānaṃ ārammaṇe saṃyojanaraso, ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno, ārammaṇapadaṭṭhāno. Saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpanno, ārammaṇapaṭipādakattena sampayuttānaṃ sārathi viya daṭṭhabbo. Vīthipaṭipādakoti pana pañcadvārāvajjanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Javanapaṭipādakoti manodvārāvajjanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Na te idha adhippetā.

Herein, the attention (manasikāra) that presents the object is the 'doing in the mind.' It has the characteristic of directing, the function of yoking the associated states to the object, and the manifestation of facing the object. Its proximate cause is the object. Included in the aggregate of formations, it should be seen as the charioteer of the associated states because it presents the object. However, 'that which presents the process' is a synonym for five-door adverting, and 'that which presents the impulsion' is a synonym for mind-door adverting. These are not intended here.

474. Tesu dhammesu majjhattatā tatramajjhattatā. Sā cittacetasikānaṃ samavāhitalakkhaṇā, ūnādhikatānivāraṇarasā, pakkhapātupacchedanarasā vā, majjhattabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, cittacetasikānaṃ ajjhupekkhanabhāvena samappavattānaṃ ājānīyānaṃ ajjhupekkhakasārathi viya daṭṭhabbā.

474. Neutrality towards those states is tatramajjhattatā. It has the characteristic of conveying consciousness and mental factors evenly, the function of preventing deficiency and excess or of cutting off partiality, and it is manifested as neutrality. It should be seen as a charioteer who looks on with equanimity at the thoroughbreds—consciousness and mental factors—proceeding evenly.

Karuṇāmuditā [M 2.0097] ca brahmavihāraniddese (visuddhi. 1.262) vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Kevalañhi tā appanāppattā rūpāvacarā, imā kāmāvacarāti ayameva viseso.

Compassion and sympathetic joy should be understood in the same way as explained in the exposition of the divine abidings. The only difference is that those, having reached absorption, are of the form sphere, while these are of the sense sphere.

Keci pana mettupekkhāyopi aniyatesu icchanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Atthato hi adosoyeva mettā, tatramajjhattupekkhāyeva upekkhāti.

Some, however, wish to include loving-kindness and equanimity among the indeterminate factors; this should not be accepted. For in reality, loving-kindness is simply non-hatred, and equanimity is simply tatramajjhattatā.

475. Kāyaduccaritato virati kāyaduccaritavirati. Esa nayo sesāsupi. Lakkhaṇādito panetā tissopi kāyaduccaritādivatthūnaṃ avītikkamalakkhaṇā, amaddanalakkhaṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāyaduccaritādivatthuto saṅkocanarasā, akiriyapaccupaṭṭhānā, saddhāhirottappaappicchatādiguṇapadaṭṭhānā, pāpakiriyato cittassa vimukhabhāvabhūtāti daṭṭhabbā.

475. Abstinence from bodily misconduct is kāyaduccaritavirati. The same method applies to the others. As to their characteristics and so on, all three have the characteristic of non-transgression regarding the occasions for bodily misconduct and so on; that is to say, they have the characteristic of not treading upon them. Their function is to shrink back from the occasions for bodily misconduct and so on. They are manifested as non-action. Their proximate cause is such qualities as faith, moral shame, moral dread, and fewness of wishes. They should be seen as being the state of the mind turning away from evil actions.

476. Iti imeva chattiṃsa saṅkhārā paṭhamena kāmāvacarakusalaviññāṇena sampayogaṃ gacchantīti veditabbā. Yathā ca paṭhamena, evaṃ dutiyenāpi. Sasaṅkhārabhāvamattameva hettha viseso.

476. Thus, it should be understood that these thirty-six formations are associated with the first wholesome sense-sphere consciousness. As with the first, so too with the second. The only difference here is that it is prompted.

Tatiyena pana ṭhapetvā amohaṃ avasesā veditabbā. Tathā catutthena. Sasaṅkhārabhāvamattameva hettha viseso.

With the third consciousness, however, the remaining factors should be understood, with the exception of non-delusion. Likewise with the fourth. Here too, the only difference is that it is prompted.

Paṭhame [V 2.0095] vuttesu pana ṭhapetvā pītiṃ avasesā pañcamena sampayogaṃ gacchanti. Yathā ca pañcamena, evaṃ chaṭṭhenāpi. Sasaṅkhārabhāvamattameva hettha viseso. Sattamena ca pana ṭhapetvā amohaṃ avasesā veditabbā. Tathā aṭṭhamena. Sasaṅkhārabhāvamattameva hettha viseso.

But among those stated in the first, excepting joy, the remaining associate with the fifth. Just as with the fifth, so also with the sixth; here the only difference is the fact of its being prompted. And with the seventh, excepting non-delusion, the remaining should be understood. Similarly with the eighth; here the only difference is the fact of its being prompted.

Paṭhame vuttesu ṭhapetvā viratittayaṃ sesā rūpāvacarakusalesu paṭhamena sampayogaṃ gacchanti. Dutiyena tato vitakkavajjā. Tatiyena tato vicāravajjā. Catutthena tato pītivajjā. Pañcamena tato aniyatesu karuṇāmuditāvajjā. Teyeva catūsu āruppakusalesu. Arūpāvacarabhāvoyeva hi ettha viseso.

Among those stated in the first, excepting the three abstinences, the remaining factors associate with the first of the fine-material sphere wholesome consciousnesses. With the second, they are the same but without initial application. With the third, without sustained application. With the fourth, without joy. With the fifth, without compassion and sympathetic joy from among the indeterminates. These same factors are found in the four immaterial-sphere wholesome consciousnesses, for here the only difference is the fact of their belonging to the immaterial sphere.

Lokuttaresu paṭhamajjhānike tāva maggaviññāṇe paṭhamarūpāvacaraviññāṇe vuttanayena, dutiyajjhānikādibhede dutiyarūpāvacaraviññāṇādīsu vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Karuṇāmuditānaṃ pana abhāvo, niyataviratitā[M 2.0098], lokuttaratā cāti ayamettha viseso. Evaṃ tāva kusalāyeva saṅkhārā veditabbā.

In the supramundane consciousnesses, the factors in the path consciousness of the first jhānic level should be understood in the way stated for the first fine-material sphere consciousness. And in the divisions beginning with the second jhānic level, they should be understood in the way stated for the second fine-material sphere consciousnesses and so on. However, the differences here are the absence of compassion and sympathetic joy, the fact that the abstinences are definite, and their supramundane nature. Thus should the wholesome formations be understood.

477. Akusalesu lobhamūle paṭhamākusalasampayuttā tāva niyatā sarūpena āgatā terasa, yevāpanakā cattāroti sattarasa. Tattha phasso, cetanā, vitakko, vicāro, pīti, vīriyaṃ, jīvitaṃ, samādhi, ahirikaṃ, anottappaṃ, lobho, moho, micchādiṭṭhīti ime sarūpena āgatā terasa (dha. sa. 365; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 365). Chando, adhimokkho, uddhaccaṃ, manasikāroti ime yevāpanakā cattāro (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 365).

477. Among the unwholesome states, in those rooted in greed, associated with the first unwholesome consciousness, there are seventeen factors: thirteen definite factors that arise in their own nature, and four adventitious factors. The thirteen definite factors are: contact, volition, initial application, sustained application, joy, energy, life faculty, concentration, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, greed, delusion, and wrong view. The four adventitious factors are: desire-to-do, decision, restlessness, and attention.

478. Tattha na hiriyatīti ahiriko. Ahirikassa bhāvo ahirikaṃ. Na otappatīti anottappaṃ. Tesu ahirikaṃ kāyaduccaritādīhi ajigucchanalakkhaṇaṃ, alajjālakkhaṇaṃ vā. Anottappaṃ teheva asārajjalakkhaṇaṃ, anuttāsalakkhaṇaṃ vā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana hirottappānaṃ vuttapaṭipakkhavasena veditabbo.

478. Herein, 'one is not ashamed' (na hiriyati), thus one is shameless (ahiriko); the state of a shameless one is shamelessness (ahirikaṃ). 'One has no moral dread' (na otappati), thus it is fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappaṃ). Among these, shamelessness has the characteristic of not being disgusted by bodily misconduct and so on, or the characteristic of immodesty. Fearlessness of wrongdoing has the characteristic of not being horrified by those same things, or the characteristic of lack of dread. This is a summary. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood by way of the opposite of what was said for shame and moral dread.

479. Lubbhanti tena, sayaṃ vā lubbhati, lubbhanamattameva vā tanti lobho. Muyhanti tena, sayaṃ vā muyhati, muyhanamattameva vā tanti moho. Tesu lobho ārammaṇaggahaṇalakkhaṇo makkaṭālepo viya, abhisaṅgaraso tattakapāle khittamaṃsapesi viya. Apariccāgapaccupaṭṭhāno telañjanarāgo [V 2.0096] viya. Saṃyojaniyadhammesu assādadassanapadaṭṭhāno. Taṇhānadībhāvena vaḍḍhamāno sīghasotā nadī iva mahāsamuddaṃ apāyameva gahetvā gacchatīti daṭṭhabbo.

479. 'They are greedy' (lubbhanti) because of it, or it is greedy, or it is simply the act of being greedy; thus it is greed (lobha). 'They are deluded' (muyhanti) because of it, or it is deluded, or it is simply the act of being deluded; thus it is delusion (moha). Among these, greed has the characteristic of grasping an object, like monkey-lime; its function is to cling, like a piece of meat thrown on a hot pan. It is manifested as not giving up, like a stain from lampblack. Its proximate cause is seeing gratification in things that fetter. It should be seen as swelling up like a river of craving, which, like a swift current, sweeps one away to the great ocean, that is, to the plane of misery.

480. Moho cittassa andhabhāvalakkhaṇo, aññāṇalakkhaṇo vā, asampaṭivedharaso, ārammaṇasabhāvacchādanaraso vā, asammāpaṭipattipaccupaṭṭhāno, andhakārapaccupaṭṭhāno vā, ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhāno, sabbākusalānaṃ mūlanti daṭṭhabbo.

480. Delusion has the characteristic of mental blindness, or the characteristic of ignorance. Its function is non-penetration, or concealing the intrinsic nature of the object. It is manifested as wrong practice, or as darkness. Its proximate cause is unwise attention. It should be regarded as the root of all unwholesome states.

481. Micchā passanti tāya, sayaṃ vā micchā passati, micchādassanamattaṃ vā esāti micchādiṭṭhi. Sā ayoniso abhinivesalakkhaṇā, parāmāsarasā, micchābhinivesapaccupaṭṭhānā, ariyānaṃ adassanakāmatādipadaṭṭhānā, paramaṃ vajjanti daṭṭhabbā.

481. 'They see wrongly' (micchā passanti) by means of it, or it sees wrongly, or it is simply wrong seeing; thus it is wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). It has the characteristic of unwise interpretation; its function is misapprehension; it is manifested as wrong adherence; its proximate cause is the unwillingness to see the noble ones, etc. It should be regarded as the supreme fault.

482. Uddhatabhāvo [M 2.0099] uddhaccaṃ. Taṃ avūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ vātābhighātacalajalaṃ viya, anavaṭṭhānarasaṃ vātābhighātacaladhajapaṭākā viya, bhantattapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ pāsāṇābhighātasamuddhatabhasmaṃ viya, cetaso avūpasame ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ, cittavikkhepoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sesā kusale vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Akusalabhāvoyeva hi akusalabhāvena ca lāmakattaṃ etesaṃ tehi viseso.

482. The state of being agitated is restlessness (uddhacca). It has the characteristic of non-tranquility, like water ruffled by the wind; its function is unsteadiness, like a banner fluttering in the wind; it is manifested as turmoil, like ashes scattered by a stone striking them. Its proximate cause is unwise attention to mental non-tranquility. It should be seen as mental agitation. The remaining factors should be understood in the way stated for the wholesome. The difference from those, however, is their unwholesome nature and their baseness on account of being unwholesome.

483. Iti ime sattarasa saṅkhārā paṭhamena akusalaviññāṇena sampayogaṃ gacchantīti veditabbā. Yathā ca paṭhamena, evaṃ dutiyenāpi. Sasaṅkhāratā panettha thinamiddhassa ca aniyatatā viseso.

483. Thus, it should be understood that these seventeen formations associate with the first unwholesome consciousness. As with the first, so also with the second. The difference here is its being prompted and the fact that sloth and torpor are indeterminate.

Tattha thinanatā thinaṃ. Middhanatā middhaṃ. Anussāhasaṃhananatā asattivighāto cāti attho. Thinañca middhañca thinamiddhaṃ. Tattha thinaṃ anussāhalakkhaṇaṃ, vīriyavinodanarasaṃ, saṃsīdanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Middhaṃ akammaññatālakkhaṇaṃ, onahanarasaṃ, līnatāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, pacalāyikāniddāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Ubhayampi arativijambhikādīsu ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānaṃ.

Herein, the state of being sluggish is sloth (thīna). The state of being torpid is torpor (middha). The meaning is lack of drive and impairment of energy. Sloth and torpor together are sloth-and-torpor. Herein, sloth has the characteristic of lack of drive, the function of dispelling energy, and it is manifested as sinking. Torpor has the characteristic of unwieldiness, the function of enveloping, and it is manifested as shrinking, or as nodding and sleepiness. The proximate cause of both is unwise attention to discontent, listlessness, yawning, and so on.

Tatiyena paṭhame vuttesu ṭhapetvā micchādiṭṭhiṃ avasesā veditabbā. Māno panettha aniyato [V 2.0097] hoti. Ayaṃ viseso, so uṇṇatilakkhaṇo, sampaggaharaso, ketukamyatāpaccupaṭṭhāno, diṭṭhivippayuttalobhapadaṭṭhāno, ummādo viya daṭṭhabbo.

With the third consciousness, the remaining factors among those stated for the first should be understood, but with the exclusion of wrong view. Here, conceit is an indeterminate factor. This is the difference. Conceit has the characteristic of haughtiness, its function is self-exaltation, it is manifested as a desire for prominence, its proximate cause is greed dissociated from views, and it should be regarded as being like madness.

Catutthena dutiye vuttesu ṭhapetvā micchādiṭṭhiṃ avasesā veditabbā. Etthāpi ca māno aniyatesu hotiyeva. Paṭhame vuttesu pana ṭhapetvā pītiṃ avasesā pañcamena sampayogaṃ gacchanti. Yathā ca pañcamena, evaṃ chaṭṭhenāpi. Sasaṅkhāratā panettha thinamiddhassa ca aniyatabhāvo viseso. Sattamena pañcame vuttesu ṭhapetvā diṭṭhiṃ avasesā veditabbā. Māno panettha aniyato hoti. Aṭṭhamena chaṭṭhe vuttesu ṭhapetvā diṭṭhiṃ avasesā veditabbā. Etthāpi ca māno aniyatesu hotiyevāti.

With the fourth consciousness, the remaining factors among those stated for the second should be understood, but with the exclusion of wrong view; and here too, conceit is indeed among the indeterminate factors. Furthermore, with the fifth, the remaining factors among those stated for the first associate, but with the exclusion of joy. As with the fifth, so also with the sixth; the difference here is its being prompted and the indeterminacy of sloth and torpor. With the seventh, the remaining factors among those stated for the fifth should be understood, but with the exclusion of view; here, conceit is an indeterminate factor. With the eighth, the remaining factors among those stated for the sixth should be understood, but with the exclusion of view; and here too, conceit is indeed among the indeterminate factors.

484. Dosamūlesu pana dvīsu paṭhamasampayuttā tāva niyatā sarūpena āgatā ekādasa, yevāpanakā cattāro, aniyatā tayoti aṭṭhārasa[M 2.0100]. Tattha phasso, cetanā, vitakko, vicāro, vīriyaṃ, jīvitaṃ, samādhi, ahirikaṃ, anoppattaṃ, doso, mohoti ime sarūpena āgatā ekādasa (dha. sa. 413; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 413). Chando, adhimokkho, uddhaccaṃ, manasikāroti ime yevāpanakā cattāro (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 413). Issā, macchariyaṃ, kukkuccanti ime aniyatā tayo (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 413).

484. Now, in the two consciousnesses rooted in hatred, those associated with the first are eighteen in total: eleven definite factors that arise in their own nature, four adventitious factors, and three indeterminate factors. Herein, the eleven definite factors that arise in their own nature are: contact, volition, initial application, sustained application, energy, life faculty, concentration, shamelessness, recklessness of wrongdoing, hatred, and delusion (Dhs §413; Dhs-a 413). The four adventitious factors are: desire-to-do, decision, restlessness, and attention (Dhs-a 413). The three indeterminate factors are: envy, stinginess, and worry (Dhs-a 413).

485. Tattha dussanti tena, sayaṃ vā dussati, dussanamattameva vā tanti doso. So caṇḍikkalakkhaṇo pahaṭāsīviso viya, visappanaraso visanipāto viya, attano nissayadahanaraso vā dāvaggi viya. Dūsanapaccupaṭṭhāno laddhokāso viya sapatto, āghātavatthupadaṭṭhāno, visasaṃsaṭṭhapūtimuttaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo.

485. Herein, 'they are corrupted' (dussanti) by it, or it itself is corrupted, or it is simply corruption; thus it is hatred (dosa). It has the characteristic of ferocity, like a struck venomous snake; its function is to spread, like a dose of poison, or to burn up its own support, like a forest fire. It is manifested as causing destruction, like an enemy who has found an opportunity. Its proximate cause is a ground for vexation. It should be regarded as being like putrid urine mixed with poison.

486. Issāyanā issā. Sā parasampattīnaṃ usūyanalakkhaṇā. Tattheva anabhiratirasā, tato vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, parasampattipadaṭṭhānā, saṃyojananti daṭṭhabbā.

486. The act of envying is envy (issā). It has the characteristic of being jealous of others' success. Its function is to be displeased with that very success. It is manifested as turning away from it. Its proximate cause is others' success. It should be regarded as a fetter.

487. Maccharabhāvo macchariyaṃ. Taṃ laddhānaṃ vā labhitabbānaṃ vā attano sampattīnaṃ nigūhanalakkhaṇaṃ, tāsaṃyeva parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaakkhamanarasaṃ, saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, kaṭukañcukatāpaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā, attasampattipadaṭṭhānaṃ, cetaso virūpabhāvoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

487. The state of being a miser is stinginess (macchariya). It has the characteristic of concealing one's own success, whether attained or to be attained. Its function is being unable to bear the sharing of that very success with others. It is manifested as shrinking, or as sour-facedness. Its proximate cause is one's own success. It should be regarded as a disfigurement of the mind.

488. Kucchitaṃ [V 2.0098] kataṃ kukataṃ. Tassa bhāvo kukkuccaṃ. Taṃ pacchānutāpalakkhaṇaṃ, katākatānusocanarasaṃ, vippaṭisārapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, katākatapadaṭṭhānaṃ, dāsabyamiva daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sesā vuttappakārāyevāti.

488. A contemptible deed is a wrong deed (kukata). The state of that is worry (kukkucca). It has the characteristic of subsequent regret; its function is to sorrow over what has been done and what has not been done; it is manifested as remorse; its proximate cause is what has been done and what has not been done. It should be regarded as being like slavery. The remaining factors are just as stated.

Iti ime aṭṭhārasa saṅkhārā paṭhamena dosamūlena sampayogaṃ gacchantīti veditabbā. Yathā ca paṭhamena, evaṃ dutiyenāpi. Sasaṅkhāratā pana aniyatesu ca thinamiddhasambhavova viseso.

Thus, it should be understood that these eighteen formations are associated with the first consciousness rooted in hatred. As with the first, so also with the second. The difference, however, is its being prompted and the possible arising of sloth and torpor among the indeterminate factors.

489. Mohamūlesu dvīsu vicikicchāsampayuttena tāva phasso, cetanā, vitakko, vicāro, vīriyaṃ, jīvitaṃ, cittaṭṭhiti, ahirikaṃ, anottappaṃ[M 2.0101], moho, vicikicchāti sarūpena āgatā ekādasa (dha. sa. 422; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 422), uddhaccaṃ, manasikāroti yevāpanakā dve cāti terasa.

489. In the two consciousnesses rooted in delusion, with the one associated with doubt there are thirteen factors: eleven that arise in their own nature, and two adventitious factors. The eleven are: contact, volition, initial application, sustained application, energy, life faculty, steadiness of mind, shamelessness, recklessness of wrongdoing, delusion, and doubt (Dhs §422; Dhs-a 422). The two adventitious factors are restlessness and attention.

490. Tattha cittaṭṭhitīti pavattiṭṭhitimatto dubbalo samādhi. Vigatā cikicchāti vicikicchā. Sā saṃsayalakkhaṇā, kampanarasā, anicchayapaccupaṭṭhānā, anekaṃsagāhapaccupaṭṭhānā vā, vicikicchāyaṃ ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhānā, paṭipattiantarāyakarāti daṭṭhabbā. Sesā vuttappakārāyeva.

490. Herein, 'steadiness of mind' (cittaṭṭhiti) is a weak concentration that is a mere stability of occurrence. Doubt (vicikicchā) is so called because it is a state 'without a cure' (vigatā cikicchā). It has the characteristic of uncertainty, the function of wavering, and manifests as indecisiveness or as taking up various sides. Its proximate cause is unwise attention, and it should be seen as an obstacle to the practice. The remaining factors are just as already described.

Uddhaccasampayuttena vicikicchāsampayutte vuttesu ṭhapetvā vicikicchaṃ sesā dvādasa. Vicikicchāya abhāvena panettha adhimokkho uppajjati. Tena saddhiṃ teraseva, adhimokkhasabbhāvato ca balavataro samādhi hoti. Yañcettha uddhaccaṃ, taṃ sarūpeneva āgataṃ. Adhimokkhamanasikārā yevāpanakavasenāti evaṃ akusalasaṅkhārā veditabbā.

With the consciousness associated with restlessness, of the factors mentioned in connection with the consciousness associated with doubt, the remaining twelve are found, setting aside doubt. Here, because of the absence of doubt, decision arises. Together with that, there are just thirteen factors. And because of the presence of decision, the concentration is stronger. The restlessness here is included by its own nature. Decision and attention are included by way of being adventitious. In this way, the unwholesome formations should be understood.

491. Abyākatesu vipākābyākatā tāva ahetukasahetukabhedato duvidhā. Tesu ahetukavipākaviññāṇasampayuttā ahetukā. Tattha kusalākusalavipākacakkhuviññāṇasampayuttā tāva phasso, cetanā, jīvitaṃ, cittaṭṭhitīti sarūpena āgatā cattāro (dha. sa. 431; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 431), yevāpanako manasikāroyevāti pañca. Sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇasampayuttāpi eteyeva. Ubhayavipākamanodhātuyā ete ceva vitakkavicārādhimokkhā cāti [V 2.0099] aṭṭha, tathā tividhāyapi ahetukamanoviññāṇadhātuyā. Yā panettha somanassasahagatā, tāya saddhiṃ pīti adhikā hotīti veditabbā.

491. Among the indeterminate states, the resultant-indeterminate are twofold: rootless and with roots. Among them, those associated with rootless resultant consciousness are the rootless ones. Here, associated with wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness are: contact, volition, life, and steadiness of mind—these four come by their own nature (Dhs. 431; Dhs. Aṭṭha. 431)—and with attention as the one adventitious factor, they make five. These same factors are also associated with ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness. In the mind-element which is the result of both, there are these same factors plus initial application, sustained application, and decision, making eight. It is the same for the threefold rootless mind-consciousness-element. It should be known, however, that in the one that is accompanied by gladness, joy is also present.

Sahetukavipākaviññāṇasampayuttā pana sahetukā. Tesu aṭṭhakāmāvacaravipākasampayuttā tāva aṭṭhahi kāmāvacarakusalehi sampayuttasaṅkhārasadisāyeva. Yā pana tā aniyatesu karuṇāmuditā, tā sattārammaṇattā vipākesu na santi. Ekantaparittārammaṇā hi kāmāvacaravipākā. Na kevalañca karuṇāmuditā, viratiyopi vipākesu na santi. “Pañca sikkhāpadā kusalāyevā”ti hi vuttaṃ.

The formations associated with resultant consciousness with roots, however, are the ones with roots. Among them, those associated with the eight sense-sphere resultants are just like the formations associated with the eight sense-sphere wholesome types of consciousness. However, compassion and appreciative joy, which are among the indeterminate factors, are not found in resultants because they take a being as their object. For sense-sphere resultants have an exclusively limited object. Not only compassion and appreciative joy, but the abstinences too are not found in resultants, for it is said: 'The five training rules are exclusively wholesome.'

Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaralokuttaravipākaviññāṇasampayuttā [M 2.0102] pana tesaṃ kusalaviññāṇasampayuttasaṅkhārehi sadisā eva.

Furthermore, the formations associated with the resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the supramundane are just like the formations associated with their respective wholesome consciousnesses.

492. Kiriyābyākatāpi ahetukasahetukabhedato duvidhā. Tesu ahetukakiriyaviññāṇasampayuttā ahetukā. Te ca kusalavipākamanodhātuahetukamanoviññāṇadhātudvayayuttehi samānā. Manoviññāṇadhātudvaye pana vīriyaṃ adhikaṃ. Vīriyasabbhāvato balappatto samādhi hoti. Ayamettha viseso.

492. The functional-indeterminate formations are also twofold, distinguished as rootless and with roots. Among them, those associated with rootless functional consciousness are the rootless ones. These are similar to the formations associated with the wholesome-resultant mind-element and the two wholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness-elements. However, in the two functional mind-consciousness-elements, energy is additional. Because of the presence of energy, concentration becomes strong. This is the difference here.

Sahetukakiriyaviññāṇasampayuttā pana sahetukā. Tesu aṭṭhakāmāvacarakiriyaviññāṇasampayuttā tāva ṭhapetvā viratiyo aṭṭhahi kāmāvacarakusalehi sampayuttasaṅkhārasadisā. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakiriyasampayuttā pana sabbākārenapi tesaṃ kusalaviññāṇasampayuttasadisāyevāti evaṃ abyākatāpi saṅkhārā veditabbāti.

Furthermore, the formations associated with functional consciousness with roots are the ones with roots. Among these, firstly, the formations associated with the eight sense-sphere functional consciousnesses, excluding the abstinences, are similar to the formations associated with the eight sense-sphere wholesome consciousnesses. The formations associated with the functional consciousness of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, however, are in all respects indeed similar to those associated with their wholesome consciousness. Thus the indeterminate formations should also be understood.

Idaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhe vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed exposition on the aggregate of formations.

Idaṃ tāva abhidhamme padabhājanīyanayena khandhesu vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This, then, is the introduction to the detailed exposition on the aggregates in the Abhidhamma according to the method of the Padabhājanīya.

Atītādivibhāgakathā

The Exposition on the Division into Past, etc.

493. Bhagavatā [V 2.0100] pana –

493. Furthermore, the Blessed One:

“Yaṃkiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, tadekajjhaṃ abhisaṃyūhitvā abhisaṅkhipitvā ayaṃ vuccati rūpakkhandho. Yā kāci vedanā… yā kāci saññā… ye keci saṅkhārā… yaṃkiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… abhisaṅkhipitvā ayaṃ vuccati viññāṇakkhandho”ti (vibha. 2,26) –

"Whatever material form there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all this, having been heaped together and compressed, is called the aggregate of material form. Whatever feeling... whatever perception... whatever formations... Whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present... having been heaped together and compressed, is called the aggregate of consciousness." (Vibh 2:2, 26)

Evaṃ khandhā vitthāritā.

Thus the aggregates have been expounded in detail.

Tattha yaṃkiñcīti anavasesapariyādānaṃ. Rūpanti atippasaṅganiyamanaṃ. Evaṃ padadvayenāpi rūpassa anavasesapariggaho kato hoti. Athassa atītādinā [M 2.0103] vibhāgaṃ ārabhati. Tañhi kiñci atītaṃ, kiñci anāgatādibhedanti. Esa nayo vedanādīsu.

Herein, 'whatever' signifies exhaustive inclusion. 'Form' is a restriction to prevent over-extension. Thus by these two terms an exhaustive comprehension of form is effected. Then its division by way of past, etc., is undertaken. For some of it is past, and some is of the division of future, etc. This is the method for feeling and the other aggregates.

494. Tattha rūpaṃ tāva addhāsantatisamayakhaṇavasena catudhā atītaṃ nāma hoti. Tathā anāgatapaccuppannaṃ.

494. Herein, form, in the first place, is called 'past' in four ways: by way of lifetime, continuity, occasion, and moment. Similarly with 'future' and 'present'.

Tattha addhāvasena tāva ekassa ekasmiṃ bhave paṭisandhito pubbe atītaṃ, cutito uddhaṃ anāgataṃ, ubhinnamantare paccuppannaṃ.

Herein, firstly, by way of lifetime: for a single being in a single existence, what is prior to rebirth-linking is past; what is subsequent to death is future; what is in between the two is present.

Santativasena sabhāgaekautusamuṭṭhānaṃ ekāhārasamuṭṭhānañca pubbāpariyavasena vattamānampi paccuppannaṃ, tato pubbe visabhāgautuāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ. Cittajaṃ ekavīthiekajavanaekasamāpattisamuṭṭhānaṃ paccuppannaṃ, tato pubbe atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ. Kammasamuṭṭhānassa pāṭiyekkaṃ santativasena atītādibhedo natthi, tesaññeva pana utuāhāracittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ upatthambhakavasena tassa atītādibhāvo veditabbo.

By way of continuity: what is presently occurring in sequence, arisen from a single homogeneous temperature and a single portion of nutriment, is present; what arose before from a dissimilar temperature and nutriment is past; what will arise after is future. What is mind-born, arisen within a single cognitive process, a single impulsion, or a single attainment, is present; what was before is past; what will be after is future. For what is kamma-born, there is individually no division into past, etc., by way of continuity; but its being past, etc., should be understood by way of its being a support for those same things born of temperature, nutriment, and mind.

Samayavasena [V 2.0101] ekamuhuttapubbaṇhasāyanharattindivādīsu samayesu santānavasena pavattamānaṃ taṃ taṃ samayaṃ paccuppannaṃ nāma, tato pubbe atītaṃ, pacchā anāgataṃ.

By way of occasion: what occurs by way of continuity on such occasions as a single muhutta, morning, evening, night, day, etc., is called present for that particular occasion; what was before is past; what will be after is future.

Khaṇavasena uppādādikhaṇattayapariyāpannaṃ paccuppannaṃ, tato pubbe anāgataṃ, pacchā atītaṃ. Apica atikkantahetupaccayakiccaṃ atītaṃ, niṭṭhitahetukiccaṃ aniṭṭhitapaccayakiccaṃ paccuppannaṃ, ubhayakiccaṃ asampattaṃ anāgataṃ. Sakiccakkhaṇe vā paccuppannaṃ, tato pubbe anāgataṃ, pacchā atītaṃ. Ettha ca khaṇādikathāva nippariyāyā. Sesā sapariyāyā.

By way of moment: what is comprised in the triad of moments—arising, etc.—is present; what is before that is future; what is after is past. Furthermore, what has passed beyond the function of its cause and condition is past; what has completed the function of its cause but not completed the function of its condition is present; what has not yet reached the function of both is future. Or, what is at the moment of its own function is present; what is before that is future; what is after is past. And herein, only the exposition concerning the moment and function is of direct meaning; the remaining expositions are of indirect meaning.

495. Ajjhattabahiddhābhedo vuttanayo eva. Apica idha niyakajjhattampi ajjhattaṃ parapuggalikampi ca bahiddhāti veditabbaṃ. Oḷārikasukhumabhedo vuttanayova.

495. The division into internal and external is just as has been stated. Moreover, here it should be understood that what is one's own internally is 'internal,' and what belongs to another person is 'external.' The division into gross and subtle is just as has been stated.

496. Hīnapaṇītabhedo duvidho pariyāyato nippariyāyato ca. Tattha akaniṭṭhānaṃ rūpato sudassīnaṃ rūpaṃ hīnaṃ. Tadeva sudassānaṃ rūpato paṇītaṃ. Evaṃ yāva narakasattānaṃ rūpaṃ, tāva pariyāyato hīnapaṇītatā veditabbā. Nippariyāyato pana yattha akusalavipākaṃ uppajjati, taṃ hīnaṃ. Yattha kusalavipākaṃ, taṃ paṇītaṃ.

496. The division into inferior and superior is twofold: by way of indirect meaning and by way of direct meaning. Herein, by way of indirect meaning, the form of the Sudassī devas is inferior to the form of the Akaniṭṭha devas. That same form is superior to the form of the Sudassa devas. In this way, down to the form of beings in hell, inferiority and superiority are to be understood. By way of direct meaning, however, a form in relation to which an unwholesome resultant consciousness arises is inferior; a form in relation to which a wholesome resultant consciousness arises is superior.

Dūre [M 2.0104] santiketi idampi vuttanayameva. Apica okāsatopettha upādāyupādāya dūrasantikatā veditabbā.

This matter of 'far' and 'near' is also just as has been stated. Moreover, here farness and nearness should also be understood relatively with respect to location.

497. Tadekajjhaṃ abhisaṃyūhitvā abhisaṅkhipitvāti taṃ atītādīhi padehi visuṃ visuṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ rūpaṃ sabbaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇasaṅkhāte ekavidhabhāve paññāya rāsiṃ katvā rūpakkhandhoti vuccatīti ayamettha attho. Etena sabbampi rūpaṃ ruppanalakkhaṇe rāsibhāvūpagamanena rūpakkhandhoti dassitaṃ hoti. Na hi rūpato añño rūpakkhandho nāma atthi.

497. As to 'having heaped it all together and compressed it': the meaning here is that all that form, indicated separately by the terms 'past,' etc., is made into a single mass by wisdom within the single state designated as the characteristic of being afflicted, and is thus called 'the aggregate of form.' By this it is shown that all form becomes the aggregate of form by being gathered into a mass that has the characteristic of being afflicted. For there is indeed no aggregate of form apart from form itself.

498. Yathā ca rūpaṃ, evaṃ vedanādayopi vedayitalakkhaṇādīsu rāsibhāvūpagamanena. Na hi vedanādīhi aññe vedanākkhandhādayo nāma atthi.

498. And just as with form, so too feeling and the other aggregates are so called by their being gathered into a mass that has the characteristic of experiencing, and so on. For there are indeed no aggregates of feeling, etc., apart from feeling, etc., themselves.

Atītādivibhāge [V 2.0102] panettha santativasena khaṇādivasena ca vedanāya atītānāgatapaccuppannabhāvo veditabbo. Tattha santativasena ekavīthiekajavanaekasamāpattipariyāpannā ekavīthivisayasamāyogappavattā ca paccuppannā, tato pubbe atītā, pacchā anāgatā. Khaṇādivasena khaṇattayapariyāpannā pubbantāparantamajjhattagatā sakiccañca kurumānā vedanā paccuppannā, tato pubbe atītā, pacchā anāgatā. Ajjhattabahiddhābhedo niyakajjhattavasena veditabbo.

Here, in the division into past, etc., the state of feeling as past, future, and present should be understood by way of continuity and by way of moment, etc. Herein, by way of continuity: feeling comprised within a single cognitive process, a single impulsion, or a single attainment, and feeling occurring in connection with an object of a single kind, is present. What was before is past; what will be after is future. By way of moment, etc.: feeling comprised in the triad of moments, situated in the middle between the past and the future, and performing its own function, is present. What is before that is future; what is after is past. The division into internal and external should be understood by way of what is one's own and internal.

499. Oḷārikasukhumabhedo “akusalā vedanā oḷārikā, kusalābyākatā vedanā sukhumā”tiādinā (vibha. 11) nayena vibhaṅge vuttena jātisabhāvapuggalalokiyalokuttaravasena veditabbo. Jātivasena tāva akusalā vedanā sāvajjakiriyahetuto, kilesasantāpabhāvato ca avūpasantavuttīti kusalavedanāya oḷārikā, sabyāpārato, saussāhato, savipākato, kilesasantāpabhāvato, sāvajjato ca vipākābyākatāya oḷārikā, savipākato, kilesasantāpabhāvato, sabyābajjhato, sāvajjato ca kiriyābyākatāya oḷārikā. Kusalābyākatā pana vuttavipariyāyato akusalāya sukhumā. Dvepi kusalākusalavedanā sabyāpārato, saussāhato, savipākato ca yathāyogaṃ duvidhāyapi abyākatāya oḷārikā[M 2.0105], vuttavipariyāyena duvidhāpi abyākatā tāhi sukhumā. Evaṃ tāva jātivasena oḷārikasukhumatā veditabbā.

499. The distinction between gross and subtle, as stated in the Vibhaṅga by the method, ‘Unwholesome feeling is gross; wholesome and indeterminate feelings are subtle,’ etc., should be understood in terms of class, intrinsic nature, individual, worldly, and supramundane. In terms of class, unwholesome feeling is gross compared to wholesome feeling because it is a cause for blameworthy action and has the nature of the torment of defilements, its occurrence being unpacified. It is gross compared to resultant-indeterminate feeling because it is active, energetic, productive of a result, has the nature of the torment of defilements, and is blameworthy. It is also gross compared to functional-indeterminate feeling because it is productive of a result, has the nature of the torment of defilements, is connected with affliction, and is blameworthy. Wholesome and indeterminate feelings, however, are subtle compared to unwholesome feeling for the opposite reasons. Both wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross compared to both types of indeterminate feeling because they are active, energetic, and productive of a result, as is appropriate. Conversely, both types of indeterminate feeling are subtle compared to them for the opposite reasons. Thus, in the first place, grossness and subtlety should be understood in terms of class.

500. Sabhāvavasena pana dukkhā vedanā nirassādato, savipphārato, khobhakaraṇato, ubbejanīyato, abhibhavanato ca itarāhi dvīhi oḷārikā, itarā pana dve sātato, santato, paṇītato, manāpato, majjhattato ca yathāyogaṃ dukkhāya sukhumā. Ubho pana sukhadukkhā savipphārato, khobhakaraṇato, pākaṭato ca adukkhamasukhāya oḷārikā, sā vuttavipariyāyena tadubhayato sukhumā. Evaṃ sabhāvavasena oḷārikasukhumatā veditabbā.

500. In terms of intrinsic nature, painful feeling is gross compared to the other two because it is without gratification, with perturbation, agitating, alarming, and overwhelming. The other two are subtle compared to painful feeling because they are, as appropriate, gratifying, peaceful, superior, agreeable, and neutral. Both pleasant and painful feelings are gross compared to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling because they are with perturbation, agitating, and manifest. The latter, for the opposite reasons, is subtle compared to both. Thus, grossness and subtlety should be understood in terms of intrinsic nature.

501. Puggalavasena pana asamāpannassa vedanā nānārammaṇe vikkhittabhāvato samāpannassa vedanāya oḷārikā, vipariyāyena itarā sukhumā. Evaṃ puggalavasena oḷārikasukhumatā veditabbā.

501. In terms of the individual, the feeling of a person who has not attained absorption is gross in comparison with that of one who has attained absorption because it is scattered among various objects; conversely, the latter feeling is subtle. Thus, grossness and subtlety should be understood in terms of the individual.

Lokiyalokuttaravasena [V 2.0103] pana sāsavā vedanā lokiyā, sā āsavuppattihetuto, oghaniyato, yoganiyato, ganthaniyato, nīvaraṇiyato, upādāniyato, saṃkilesikato, puthujjanasādhāraṇato ca anāsavāya oḷārikā. Sā vipariyāyena sāsavāya sukhumā. Evaṃ lokiyalokuttaravasena oḷārikasukhumatā veditabbā.

In terms of worldly and supramundane, feeling with taints is worldly; it is gross in comparison with taintless feeling because it is a cause for the arising of taints, is an object for the floods, yokes, bodily ties, hindrances, and clinging, is conducive to defilement, and is common to worldlings. Conversely, taintless feeling is subtle in comparison with tainted feeling. Thus, grossness and subtlety should be understood in terms of worldly and supramundane.

502. Tattha jātiādivasena sambhedo pariharitabbo. Akusalavipākakaāyaviññāṇasampayuttā hi vedanā jātivasena abyākatattā sukhumāpi samānā sabhāvādivasena oḷārikā hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ “abyākatā vedanā sukhumā. Dukkhā vedanā oḷārikā. Samāpannassa vedanā sukhumā. Asamāpannassa vedanā oḷārikā. Sāsavā vedanā oḷārikā. Anāsavā vedanā sukhumā”ti (vibha. 11). Yathā ca dukkhā vedanā, evaṃ sukhādayopi jātivasena oḷārikā sabhāvādivasena sukhumā honti. Tasmā yathā jātiādivasena sambhedo na hoti, tathā vedanānaṃ oḷārikasukhumatā veditabbā. Seyyathidaṃ – abyākatā jātivasena kusalākusalāhi sukhumā. Tattha katamā abyākatā? Kiṃ dukkhā? Kiṃ sukhā? Kiṃ samāpannassa? Kiṃ asamāpannassa? Kiṃ sāsavā[M 2.0106]? Kiṃ anāsavāti? Evaṃ sabhāvādibhedo na parāmasitabbo. Esa nayo sabbattha.

502. Here, confusion based on class and so on should be avoided. For the feeling associated with unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness, though it is subtle in terms of class because it is indeterminate, is gross in terms of intrinsic nature and so on. For it is said: ‘Indeterminate feeling is subtle. Painful feeling is gross. The feeling of one who has attained absorption is subtle. The feeling of one who has not attained absorption is gross. Tainted feeling is gross. Taintless feeling is subtle.’ And just as painful feeling, so too pleasant feelings and others, though gross in terms of class, are subtle in terms of intrinsic nature and so on. Therefore, the grossness and subtlety of feelings should be understood in such a way that there is no confusion based on class and so on. This is as follows: when it is said that indeterminate feeling is subtle in terms of class compared with wholesome and unwholesome feelings, one should not then consider the distinctions based on intrinsic nature, etc., by asking: ‘Which indeterminate feeling? Is it painful? Is it pleasant? Is it of one who has attained absorption? Is it of one who has not attained absorption? Is it tainted? Is it taintless?’ This method applies everywhere.

Apica taṃ taṃ vā pana vedanaṃ upādāyupādāya vedanā oḷārikasukhumā daṭṭhabbāti vacanato akusalādīsupi lobhasahagatāya dosasahagatā vedanā aggi viya attano nissayadahanato oḷārikā, lobhasahagatā sukhumā. Dosasahagatāpi niyatā oḷārikā, aniyatā sukhumā. Niyatāpi kappaṭṭhitikā oḷārikā, itarā sukhumā. Kappaṭṭhitikāsupi asaṅkhārikā oḷārikā, itarā sukhumā. Lobhasahagatā pana diṭṭhisampayuttā oḷārikā, itarā sukhumā. Sāpi niyatā kappaṭṭhitikā asaṅkhārikā oḷārikā, itarā sukhumā. Avisesena ca akusalā bahuvipākā oḷārikā, appavipākā sukhumā. Kusalā pana appavipākā oḷārikā, bahuvipākā sukhumā.

Moreover, in accordance with the saying, ‘Grossness and subtlety of feeling should be seen by comparing them one with another,’ even among unwholesome feelings and so on, feeling accompanied by hatred is gross in comparison with feeling accompanied by greed because it burns up its own basis like a fire; feeling accompanied by greed is subtle. Even among feelings accompanied by hatred, that which is fixed in its result is gross, the unfixed is subtle. Even among the fixed, that which lasts for an aeon is gross, the other is subtle. Even among those that last for an aeon, the unprompted is gross, the prompted is subtle. As to feeling accompanied by greed, that associated with wrong view is gross, the other is subtle. Of that too, the fixed, aeon-lasting, and unprompted is gross, the other is subtle. And in general, unwholesome feeling that is powerful in its result is gross, that which is weak in its result is subtle. But wholesome feeling that is weak in its result is gross, that which is powerful in its result is subtle.

Apica kāmāvacarakusalā oḷārikā. Rūpāvacarā sukhumā. Tato arūpāvacarā. Tato lokuttarā. Kāmāvacarā dānamayā oḷārikā. Sīlamayā sukhumā. Tato bhāvanāmayā. Bhāvanāmayāpi duhetukā oḷārikā. Tihetukā sukhumā. Tihetukāpi sasaṅkhārikā oḷārikā. Asaṅkhārikā sukhumā. Rūpāvacarā ca paṭhamajjhānikā oḷārikā…pe… pañcamajjhānikā [V 2.0104] sukhumā. Arūpāvacarā ca ākāsānañcāyatanasampayuttā oḷārikā…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasampayuttā sukhumāva. Lokuttarā ca sotāpattimaggasampayuttā oḷārikā…pe… arahattamaggasampayuttā sukhumāva. Esa nayo taṃ taṃ bhūmivipākakiriyavedanāsu ca dukkhādiasamāpannādisāsavādivasena vuttavedanāsu ca.

Furthermore, wholesome sense-sphere feeling is gross; form-sphere feeling is subtle; subtler than that is formless-sphere feeling; subtler still is supramundane feeling. Among sense-sphere feelings, that based on giving is gross; that based on moral discipline is subtle; subtler than that is feeling based on mental development. Among feelings based on mental development, the two-rooted is gross, the three-rooted is subtle. Among the three-rooted, the prompted is gross, the unprompted is subtle. Among form-sphere feelings, that of the first jhāna is gross … that of the fifth jhāna is subtle. Among formless-sphere feelings, that associated with the base of the infinity of space is gross … that associated with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subtle indeed. Among supramundane feelings, that associated with the path of stream-entry is gross … that associated with the path of arahantship is subtle indeed. This same method applies to the resultant and functional feelings of the various planes, and to the feelings described above in terms of painful etc., of one who has not attained absorption etc., and of the tainted etc.

Okāsavasena cāpi niraye dukkhā oḷārikā. Tiracchānayoniyaṃ sukhumā…pe… paranimmitavasavattīsu sukhumāva. Yathā ca dukkhā, evaṃ sukhāpi sabbattha yathānurūpaṃ yojetabbā. Vatthuvasena cāpi hīnavatthukā yā kāci vedanā oḷārikā, paṇītavatthukā sukhumā.

Also in terms of location: painful feeling in hell is gross. In the animal realm it is subtle … up to that in the realm of those who wield power over others’ creations it is subtle indeed. And just as painful feeling, so too pleasant feeling should be connected everywhere as is appropriate. Also in terms of the object: any feeling that has an inferior object is gross; one that has a superior object is subtle.

Hīnapaṇītabhede yā oḷārikā, sā hīnā. Yā ca sukhumā, sā paṇītāti daṭṭhabbā.

In the distinction between inferior and superior, it should be understood that what is gross is inferior, and what is subtle is superior.

503. Dūrapadaṃ pana “akusalā vedanā kusalābyākatāhi vedanāhi dūre”. Santikepadaṃ “akusalā vedanā akusalāya vedanāya santike”tiādinā [M 2.0107] nayena vibhaṅge vibhattaṃ. Tasmā akusalā vedanā visabhāgato, asaṃsaṭṭhato, asarikkhato ca kusalābyākatāhi dūre, tathā kusalābyākatā akusalāya. Esa nayo sabbavāresu. Akusalā pana vedanā sabhāgato, sarikkhato ca akusalāya santiketi. Idaṃ vedanākkhandhassa atītādivibhāge vitthārakathāmukhaṃ. Taṃtaṃvedanāsampayuttānaṃ pana saññādīnampi evameva veditabbaṃ.

503. Furthermore, the term ‘distant’ is analyzed in the Vibhaṅga by the method beginning: ‘Unwholesome feeling is far from wholesome and indeterminate feelings.’ The term ‘near’ is analyzed by the method beginning: ‘Unwholesome feeling is near to unwholesome feeling,’ and so on. Therefore, unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings in terms of dissimilarity, non-association, and non-resemblance; likewise, wholesome and indeterminate feelings are distant from unwholesome feeling. This method applies in all cases. But unwholesome feeling is near to unwholesome feeling in terms of similarity and resemblance. This is the introduction to the detailed exposition of the division of past, etc., in the feeling aggregate. This should be understood in the same way for perception and other states associated with each respective feeling.

Kamādivinicchayakathā

Discourse on Ascertaining Sequence, etc.

504. Evaṃ viditvā ca puna etesveva –

504. Having understood this, and again regarding these very things—

Khandhesu ñāṇabhedatthaṃ, kamatotha visesato;

Anūnādhikato ceva, upamāto tatheva ca.

To distinguish the kinds of knowledge regarding the aggregates,

By sequence, and then by distinction;

And also by neither deficient nor excessive,

And likewise by simile.

Daṭṭhabbato dvidhā evaṃ, passantassatthasiddhito;

Vinicchayanayo sammā, viññātabbo vibhāvinā.

By being seen thus in two ways,

And by the achievement of the goal for one who sees;

The method of determination should be rightly

Understood by the discerning one.

Tattha [V 2.0105] kamatoti idha uppattikkamo, pahānakkamo, paṭipattikkamo, bhūmikkamo, desanākkamoti bahuvidho kamo.

Here, as to 'by sequence,' this means sequence of arising, sequence of abandoning, sequence of practice, sequence of planes, and sequence of teaching; thus, sequence is of many kinds.

Tattha “paṭhamaṃ kalalaṃ hoti, kalalā hoti abbuda”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.235) evamādi uppattikkamo. “Dassanena pahātabbā dhammā, bhāvanāya pahātabbā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 8) evamādi pahānakkamo. “Sīlavisuddhi, cittavisuddhī”ti (ma. ni. 1.259; paṭi. ma. 3.41) evamādi paṭipattikkamo. “Kāmāvacarā, rūpāvacarā”ti (dha. sa. 987) evamādi bhūmikkamo. “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā”ti (dī. ni. 3.145) vā, “dānakathaṃ, sīlakatha”nti (dī. ni. 1.298) vā evamādi desanākkamo. Tesu idha uppattikkamo tāva na yujjati, kalalādīnaṃ viya khandhānaṃ pubbāpariyavavatthānena anuppattito. Na pahānakkamo, kusalābyākatānaṃ appahātabbato. Napaṭipattikkamo, akusalānaṃ appaṭipajjanīyato. Na bhūmikkamo, vedanādīnaṃ catubhūmipariyāpannattā. Desanākkamo pana yujjati.

Therein, the sequence of arising is such as: “First there is the embryo, from the embryo the fetus arises” (SN 1.206), and so on. The sequence of abandoning is such as: “dhammas to be abandoned by seeing, dhammas to be abandoned by development” (Dhs-mātikā §8), and so on. The sequence of practice is such as: “purification of virtue, purification of mind” (MN 24; Paṭis I 21), and so on. The sequence of planes is such as: “of the sense sphere, of the form sphere” (Dhs §987), and so on. The sequence of teaching is such as: “the four establishments of mindfulness, the four right strivings” (DN 33), or “talk on giving, talk on virtuous behavior” (DN 1), and so on. Among these, the sequence of arising is not appropriate here, because the aggregates do not arise in a fixed succession of earlier and later like the embryo, etc. Nor is the sequence of abandoning, because wholesome and indeterminate states are not to be abandoned. Nor is the sequence of practice, because unwholesome states are not to be practiced. Nor is the sequence of planes, because feeling, etc., are included in the four planes. But the sequence of teaching is appropriate.

Abhedena hi pañcasu khandhesu attagāhapatitaṃ veneyyajanaṃ samūhaghanavinibbhogadassanena attagāhato mocetukāmo bhagavā hitakāmo [M 2.0108] tassa tassa janassa sukhagahaṇatthaṃ cakkhuādīnampi visayabhūtaṃ oḷārikaṃ paṭhamaṃ rūpakkhandhaṃ desesi. Tato iṭṭhāniṭṭharūpasaṃvedanikaṃ vedanaṃ. “Yaṃ vedayati, taṃ sañjānātī”ti evaṃ vedanāvisayassa ākāragāhikaṃ saññaṃ. Saññāvasena abhisaṅkhārake saṅkhāre. Tesaṃ vedanādīnaṃ nissayaṃ adhipatibhūtañca nesaṃ viññāṇanti evaṃ tāva kamato vinicchayanayo viññātabbo.

For, wishing to free the trainable persons who have fallen into the grasp of self with respect to the five aggregates taken without distinction—to free them from that grasp of self by showing them the dispersion of the solid mass—and desiring the welfare of each and every person for the sake of their easy comprehension, the Blessed One first taught the material form aggregate, which is gross and the object of the eye, etc. Then he taught feeling, which experiences agreeable and disagreeable material form. Then, in the sense of “What one feels, that one perceives,” he taught perception, which grasps the features of the object of feeling. Then, by way of perception, the constructing formations. And then consciousness, which is the support for and dominant over feeling, etc. Thus, for now, the method of determination by way of sequence should be understood.

505. Visesatoti khandhānañca upādānakkhandhānañca visesato. Ko pana nesaṃ viseso, khandhā tāva avisesato vuttā. Upādānakkhandhā sāsavaupādāniyabhāvena visesetvā. Yathāha –

505. As to 'by distinction,' this means by the distinction between the aggregates and the clinging-aggregates. Now, what is the distinction between them? The aggregates are spoken of without distinction, while the clinging-aggregates are distinguished by being with taints and objects of clinging. As it is said:

“Pañca ceva vo, bhikkhave, khandhe desessāmi pañcupādānakkhandhe ca, taṃ suṇātha. Katame ca, bhikkhave, pañcakkhandhā, yaṃkiñci, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… santike vā, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, rūpakkhandho. Yā [V 2.0106] kāci vedanā…pe… yaṃkiñci viññāṇaṃ…pe… santike vā, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, viññāṇakkhandho. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, pañcakkhandhā. Katame ca, bhikkhave, pañcupādānakkhandhā. Yaṃkiñci, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ…pe… santike vā sāsavaṃ upādāniyaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, rūpupādānakkhandho. Yā kāci vedanā…pe… yaṃkiñci viññāṇaṃ…pe… santike vā sāsavaṃ upādāniyaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, pañcupādānakkhandhā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.48).

“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the five aggregates and the five clinging-aggregates. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates? Whatever kind of material form there is, whether past, future, or present… whether near or far: this is called the material form aggregate. Whatever kind of feeling… perception… formations… consciousness there is… whether near or far: this is called the consciousness aggregate. These, bhikkhus, are called the five aggregates. And what, bhikkhus, are the five clinging-aggregates? Whatever kind of material form there is… whether near or far, which is accompanied by taints and is an object of clinging: this is called the material form clinging-aggregate. Whatever kind of feeling… perception… formations… consciousness there is… whether near or far, which is accompanied by taints and is an object of clinging: this is called the consciousness clinging-aggregate. These, bhikkhus, are called the five clinging-aggregates.” (SN 22.48)

Ettha ca yathā vedanādayo anāsavāpi atthi, na evaṃ rūpaṃ. Yasmā panassa rāsaṭṭhena khandhabhāvo yujjati, tasmā khandhesu vuttaṃ. Yasmā rāsaṭṭhena ca sāsavaṭṭhena ca upādānakkhandhabhāvo yujjati, tasmā upādānakkhandhesu vuttaṃ. Vedanādayo pana anāsavāva khandhesu vuttā. Sāsavā upādānakkhandhesu. Upādānakkhandhāti cettha upādānagocarā khandhā upādānakkhandhāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Idha pana sabbepete ekajjhaṃ katvā khandhāti adhippetā.

Here, while there are taintless feeling, etc., this is not so for material form. But since its being an aggregate is appropriate in the sense of a heap, it is spoken of among the aggregates. And since its being a clinging-aggregate is appropriate in the sense of a heap and in the sense of being with taints, it is spoken of among the clinging-aggregates. Feeling, etc., however, are spoken of among the aggregates only when they are taintless; when with taints, they are spoken of among the clinging-aggregates. Here, 'clinging-aggregates' should be understood to mean 'aggregates that are the range of clinging are clinging-aggregates.' In this context, however, all these, having been taken together, are intended as 'aggregates.'

506. Anūnādhikatoti kasmā pana bhagavatā pañceva khandhā vuttā anūnā anadhikāti. Sabbasaṅkhatasabhāgekasaṅgahato attattaniyagāhavatthussa etaparamato aññesañca tadavarodhato. Anekappabhedesu hi saṅkhatadhammesu [M 2.0109] sabhāgavasena saṅgayhamānesu rūpampi rūpasabhāgekasaṅgahavasena eko khandho hoti. Vedanā vedanāsabhāgekasaṅgahavasena eko khandho hoti. Esa nayo saññādīsu. Tasmā sabbasaṅkhatasabhāgekasaṅgahato pañceva vuttā. Etaparamañcetaṃ attattaniyagāhavatthu yadidaṃ rūpādayo pañca. Vuttañhetaṃ “rūpe kho, bhikkhave, sati rūpaṃ upādāya rūpaṃ abhinivissa evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjati ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti. Vedanāya, saññāya, saṅkhāresu, viññāṇe sati viññāṇaṃ upādāya viññāṇaṃ abhinivissa evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajjati ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.207). Tasmā attattaniyagāhavatthussa etaparamatopi pañceva vuttā. Yepi caññe sīlādayo pañca dhammakkhandhā vuttā, tepi saṅkhārakkhandhe pariyāpannattā ettheva avarodhaṃ gacchanti. Tasmā aññesaṃ tadavarodhatopi pañceva vuttāti evaṃ anūnādhikato vinicchayanayo viññātabbo.

506. As to 'by neither deficient nor excessive': Now why were just five aggregates spoken of by the Blessed One, neither fewer nor more? Because of the inclusion of all conditioned things of a similar nature in one, because this is the ultimate basis for the grasp of self and what belongs to self, and because others are included therein. For among the many divisions of conditioned things, when being collected by way of similar nature, material form becomes one aggregate by being included in the one class of material form. Feeling becomes one aggregate by being included in the one class of feeling. The same method applies to perception and the rest. Thus, because of the inclusion of all conditioned things of a similar nature in one, just five were spoken of. Moreover, this is the ultimate basis for the grasp of self and what belongs to self, namely, these five: material form and the rest. For it is said: “Bhikkhus, when there is material form, by clinging to material form, by adhering to material form, such a view arises: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ When there is feeling… perception… formations… consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, by adhering to consciousness, such a view arises: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’” (SN 22.122). Therefore, because this is the ultimate basis for the grasp of self and what belongs to self, just five were spoken of. And whatever other five aggregates of dhammas have been spoken of, such as virtue, etc., they too are included right here since they are comprised in the formations aggregate. Therefore, because others are included therein, just five were spoken of. Thus the method of determination as 'by neither deficient nor excessive' should be understood.

507. Upamātoti ettha hi gilānasālupamo rūpupādānakkhandho, gilānupamassa viññāṇupādānakkhandhassa [V 2.0107] vatthudvārārammaṇavasena nivāsaṭṭhānato. Gelaññupamo vedanupādānakkhandho, ābādhakattā. Gelaññasamuṭṭhānupamo saññupādānakkhandho, kāmasaññādivasena rāgādisampayuttavedanāsabbhāvā. Asappāyasevanupamo saṅkhārupādānakkhandho, vedanāgelaññassa nidānattā. “Vedanaṃ vedanatthāya abhisaṅkharontī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.79) hi vuttaṃ. Tathā “akusalassa kammassa katattā upacitattā vipākaṃ kāyaviññāṇaṃ uppannaṃ hoti dukkhasahagata”nti (dha. sa. 556). Gilānupamo viññāṇupādānakkhandho, vedanāgelaññena aparimuttattā. Apica cārakakāraṇaaparādhakāraṇakārakaaparādhikupamā ete bhājanabhojanabyañjanaparivesakabhuñjakūpamā cāti evaṃ upamāto vinicchayanayo viññātabbo.

507. As to 'by simile': Here the aggregate of clinging to material form is like a sick-hall, because it is the dwelling place—by way of physical basis, door, and object—for the aggregate of clinging to consciousness, which is like a sick person. The aggregate of clinging to feeling is like the illness, because it is an affliction. The aggregate of clinging to perception is like the cause of the illness, because of the existence of feeling connected with lust, etc., by way of sensual perception, etc. The aggregate of clinging to formations is like the partaking of what is unsuitable, because it is the source of the illness of feeling. For it is said: “They generate formations for the purpose of feeling” (SN 22.81). And similarly: “Because of unwholesome kamma that has been done and accumulated, resultant body-consciousness accompanied by pain arises” (Dhs §556). The aggregate of clinging to consciousness is like the sick person, because it is not freed from the illness of feeling. Moreover, these are like the prison, the torture, the crime, the torturer, and the criminal; and like the bowl, the food, the curry, the server, and the eater.
