Thus the method of determination by way of simile should be understood.

508. Daṭṭhabbato dvidhāti saṅkhepato vitthārato cāti evaṃ dvidhā daṭṭhabbatopettha vinicchayanayo viññātabbo. Saṅkhepato hi pañcupādānakkhandhā āsīvisūpame (saṃ. ni. 4.238) vuttanayena ukkhittāsikapaccatthikato, bhārasuttavasena (saṃ. ni. 3.22) bhārato, khajjanīyapariyāyavasena (saṃ. ni. 3.79) khādakato, yamakasuttavasena (saṃ. ni. 3.85) aniccadukkhānattasaṅkhatavadhakato daṭṭhabbā. Vitthārato panettha pheṇapiṇḍo viya rūpaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, parimaddanāsahanato. Udakapubbuḷaṃ viya [M 2.0110] vedanā, muhuttaramaṇīyato. Marīcikā viya saññā, vippalambhanato. Kadalikkhandho viya saṅkhārā, asārakato. Māyā viya viññāṇaṃ, vañcakato. Visesato ca suḷārampi ajjhattikaṃ rūpaṃ asubhanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vedanā tīhi dukkhatāhi avinimuttato dukkhāti. Saññāsaṅkhārā avidheyyato anattāti. Viññāṇaṃ udayabbayadhammato aniccanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

508. As to 'by what is to be seen, in two ways': the method of determination should be understood here as to be seen in two ways, that is, in brief and in detail. In brief, the five aggregates of clinging should be seen as an enemy with sword upraised, in the way stated in the Simile of the Vipers (SN 35.238); as a burden, in accordance with the Burden Sutta (SN 22.22); as a devourer, in accordance with the Discourse on Devouring (SN 22.79); and as a killer that is impermanent, suffering, not-self, and conditioned, in accordance with the Yamaka Sutta (SN 22.85). In detail, here material form should be seen as like a lump of foam, because it cannot withstand rubbing. Feeling should be seen as like a water bubble, because it is pleasant for a moment. Perception should be seen as like a mirage, because it deludes. Formations should be seen as like a banana trunk, because they are without substance. Consciousness should be seen as like a magical illusion, because it deceives. And specifically, even gross internal material form should be seen as foul. Feeling should be seen as suffering because it is not free from the three kinds of suffering. Perception and formations should be seen as not-self because they are uncontrollable. Consciousness should be seen as impermanent because its nature is to arise and pass away.

509. Evaṃ passantassatthasiddhitoti evañca saṅkhepavitthāravasena dvidhā passato yā atthasiddhi hoti, tatopi vinicchayanayo viññātabbo. Seyyathidaṃ – saṅkhepato tāva pañcupādānakkhandhe ukkhittāsikapaccatthikādibhāvena passanto khandhehi na vihaññati. Vitthārato pana rūpādīni pheṇapiṇḍādisadisabhāvena passanto na asāresu sāradassī hoti.

509. As to 'from the achievement of the goal for one who sees thus': the method of determination should also be understood from the achievement of the goal that occurs for one who sees in two ways, in brief and in detail. That is as follows: Briefly, one who sees the five aggregates of clinging as an enemy with sword upraised, etc., is not tormented by the aggregates. In detail, however, one who sees material form, etc., as similar to a lump of foam, etc., does not see a substance in what is without substance.

Visesato ca ajjhattikarūpaṃ asubhato passanto kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ parijānāti, asubhe subhanti vipallāsaṃ pajahati. Kāmoghaṃ uttarati, kāmayogena visaṃyujjati, kāmāsavena anāsavo hoti, abhijjhākāyaganthaṃ bhindati, kāmupādānaṃ na upādiyati.

In particular, one who sees internal form as foul fully comprehends the nutriment of edible food, abandons the perversion of perceiving the attractive in the foul, crosses the flood of sensual desire, is freed from the yoke of sensual desire, becomes free from the taint of sensual desire, breaks the bodily tie of covetousness, and does not cling with the clinging to sensual pleasures.

Vedanaṃ [V 2.0108] dukkhato passanto phassāhāraṃ parijānāti, dukkhe sukhanti vipallāsaṃ pajahati, bhavoghaṃ uttarati, bhavayogena visaṃyujjati, bhavāsavena anāsavo hoti, byāpādakāyaganthaṃ bhindati, sīlabbatupādānaṃ na upādiyati.

One who sees feeling as suffering fully comprehends contact as nutriment, abandons the perversion of perceiving happiness in suffering, crosses the flood of becoming, is freed from the yoke of becoming, becomes free from the taint of becoming, breaks the bodily tie of ill will, and does not cling with the clinging to rules and vows.

Saññaṃ saṅkhāre ca anattato passanto manosañcetanāhāraṃ parijānāti, anattani attāti vipallāsaṃ pajahati, diṭṭhoghaṃ uttarati, diṭṭhiyogena visaṃyujjati, diṭṭhāsavena anāsavo hoti. Idaṃsaccābhinivesakāyaganthaṃ bhindati, attavādupādānaṃ na upādiyati.

By seeing perception and formations as not-self, one fully comprehends mental volition as nutriment; one abandons the perversion of perceiving self in what is not-self. One crosses over the flood of views, is released from the yoke of views, and becomes free from the taint of views. One breaks the bodily tie of insistence that 'this alone is truth' and does not cling with the clinging to a doctrine of self.

Viññāṇaṃ aniccato passanto viññāṇāhāraṃ parijānāti, anicce niccanti vipallāsaṃ pajahati, avijjoghaṃ uttarati, avijjāyogena visaṃyujjati, avijjāsavena anāsavo hoti, sīlabbataparāmāsakāyaganthaṃ bhindati, diṭṭhupādānaṃ na upādiyati.

By seeing consciousness as impermanent, one fully comprehends consciousness as nutriment; one abandons the perversion of perceiving permanence in the impermanent. One crosses over the flood of ignorance, is freed from the yoke of ignorance, and becomes free from the taint of ignorance. One breaks the bodily tie of adherence to rules and vows and does not cling with the clinging to views.

Evaṃ [M 2.0111] mahānisaṃsaṃ, vadhakādivasena dassanaṃ yasmā;

Tasmā khandhe dhīro, vadhakādivasena passeyyāti.

Since seeing them in terms of murderers, etc., has such great benefits, therefore the wise one should regard the aggregates in terms of murderers, etc.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, composed for the gladdening of good people,

Paññābhāvanādhikāre

In the Section on the Development of Wisdom,

Khandhaniddeso nāma

the chapter named the Exposition of the Aggregates,

Cuddasamo paricchedo.

is the Fourteenth Chapter.

15. Āyatanadhātuniddeso

15. Exposition of the Bases and Elements

Āyatanavitthārakathā

The Detailed Discourse on the Bases

510. Āyatanānīti [M 2.0112][V 2.0109] dvādasāyatanāni – cakkhāyatanaṃ, rūpāyatanaṃ, sotāyatanaṃ, saddāyatanaṃ, ghānāyatanaṃ, gandhāyatanaṃ, jivhāyatanaṃ, rasāyatanaṃ, kāyāyatanaṃ, phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ, manāyatanaṃ, dhammāyatananti. Tattha –

510. “Bases” means the twelve bases: the eye-base, form-base, ear-base, sound-base, nose-base, odor-base, tongue-base, taste-base, body-base, tangible-base, mind-base, and mind-object-base. Therein:

Attha lakkhaṇa tāvatva, kama saṅkhepa vitthārā;

Tathā daṭṭhabbato ceva, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Meaning, characteristic, enumeration, order, summary, and detail; and also by way of how they should be seen, the analysis should be understood.

Tattha visesato tāva cakkhatīti cakkhu, rūpaṃ assādeti vibhāveti cāti attho. Rūpayatīti rūpaṃ, vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti attho. Suṇātīti sotaṃ. Sappatīti saddo, udāhariyatīti attho. Ghāyatīti ghānaṃ. Gandhayatīti gandho. Attano vatthuṃ sūcayatīti attho. Jīvitaṃ avhayatīti jivhā. Rasanti taṃ sattāti raso, assādentīti attho. Kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ āyoti kāyo. Āyoti uppattideso. Phusiyatīti phoṭṭhabbaṃ. Munātīti mano. Attano lakkhaṇaṃ dhārentīti dhammā.

Therein, firstly in particular: ‘It sees,’ thus it is the eye (cakkhu), meaning it savors and clarifies form. ‘It is manifested,’ thus it is form (rūpa), meaning it reveals the state that has gone to the heart by undergoing change of color. ‘It hears,’ thus it is the ear (sota). ‘It is sounded,’ thus it is sound (sadda), meaning it is uttered. ‘It smells,’ thus it is the nose (ghāna). ‘It indicates,’ thus it is odor (gandha), meaning it indicates its own basis. ‘It calls for life,’ thus it is the tongue (jivhā). ‘Beings taste it,’ thus it is taste (rasa), meaning they savor it. ‘It is a source of contemptible, tainted states,’ thus it is the body (kāya). ‘Source’ means place of origin. ‘It is touched,’ thus it is the tangible (phoṭṭhabba). ‘It knows,’ thus it is the mind (mano). ‘They bear their own characteristics,’ thus they are dhammas.

511. Avisesato pana āyatanato, āyānaṃ tananato, āyatassa ca nayanato āyatananti veditabbaṃ. Cakkhurūpādīsu hi taṃtaṃdvārārammaṇā cittacetasikā dhammā sena sena anubhavanādinā kiccena āyatanti uṭṭhahanti ghaṭanti, vāyamantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Te ca āyabhūte dhamme etāni tanonti, vitthārentīti vuttaṃ hoti, idañca anamatagge saṃsāre pavattaṃ atīva āyataṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ yāva na nivattati, tāva nayanteva, pavattayantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Iti [V 2.0110] sabbepime dhammā āyatanato, āyānaṃ tananato, āyatassa ca nayanato āyatanaṃ āyatananti vuccanti.

511. But in general, it should be understood as ‘base’ (āyatana) because it is a place of exertion (āyatanato), because it extends the arrivals (āyānaṃ tananato), and because it leads on the long-drawn-out (āyatassa nayanato). For in the case of the eye, form, and so on, the mental states—consciousness and its concomitants—that have their respective doors and objects exert themselves (āyatanti), that is, they arise, endeavor, and strive with their own respective functions of experiencing, etc. This is what is meant. And these bases extend (tanonti), that is, they stretch forth, those states that are arrivals (āya). This is what is meant. And for as long as this exceedingly long-drawn-out (āyata) suffering of saṃsāra, which has been occurring in a round with no conceivable beginning, does not cease, they just lead it on (nayanteva), that is, they cause it to proceed. This is what is meant. Thus, all these phenomena are called ‘base’ (āyatana) because they are a place of exertion, because they extend the arrivals, and because they lead on the long-drawn-out.

512. Apica nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ākaraṭṭhena samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhena sañjātidesaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhena ca āyatanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi loke “issarāyatanaṃ vāsudevāyatana”ntiādīsu nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ āyatananti [M 2.0113] vuccati. “Suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ rajatāyatana”ntiādīsu ākaro. Sāsane pana “manoramme āyatane sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.38) samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. “Dakkhiṇāpatho gunnaṃ āyatana”ntiādīsu sañjātideso. “Tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati satiāyatane”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.102) kāraṇaṃ.

512. Furthermore, ‘base’ (āyatana) should be understood in the sense of a dwelling place, a mine, a meeting place, a place of origin, and a cause. For in the world, in such phrases as ‘the lord’s domain’ (issarāyatana) and ‘Vāsudeva’s domain’ (vāsudevāyatana), ‘āyatana’ is used for a dwelling place. In ‘a gold mine’ (suvaṇṇāyatana) and ‘a silver mine’ (rajatāyatana), it is used for a mine. In the Dispensation, in ‘Birds resort to a delightful resort (āyatane)’ (AN 5.38), it is used for a meeting place. In ‘The southern region is the birthplace (āyatana) of cattle,’ it is used for a place of origin. In ‘He attains the state of being able to witness it in this or that respect whenever there is a cause (sati satiāyatane)’ (AN 3.102), it is used for a cause.

Cakkhuādīsu cāpi te te cittacetasikā dhammā nivasanti tadāyattavuttitāyāti cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ. Cakkhādīsu ca te ākiṇṇā tannissitattā tadārammaṇattā cāti cakkhādayo nesaṃ ākaro. Cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha tattha vatthudvārārammaṇavasena samosaraṇato. Cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ sañjātideso, tannissayārammaṇabhāvena tattheva uppattito. Cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ kāraṇaṃ, tesaṃ abhāve abhāvatoti. Iti nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena, ākaraṭṭhena, samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhena, sañjātidesaṭṭhena, kāraṇaṭṭhenacāti imehipi kāraṇehi ete dhammā āyatanaṃ āyatananti vuccanti.

And in the case of the eye, etc., those several kinds of consciousness and mental states dwell, since their occurrence is dependent on them; thus the eye, etc., are their dwelling place. And they are abundant in the eye, etc., because they are dependent on them and have them as object; thus the eye, etc., are their mine. And the eye, etc., are their meeting place, because they meet there by way of basis, door, and object. And the eye, etc., are their place of origin, because they arise right there by being their support and object. And the eye, etc., are their cause, because they do not exist in their absence. Thus, for these reasons too—in the sense of a dwelling place, a mine, a meeting place, a place of origin, and a cause—these states are called ‘bases’ (āyatana).

Tasmā yathāvuttena atthena cakkhu ca taṃ āyatanañcāti cakkhāyatanaṃ…pe… dhammā ca te āyatanañcāti dhammāyatananti evaṃ tāvettha atthato viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Therefore, in accordance with the meaning given, ‘it is the eye and it is a base, thus it is the eye-base’ (cakkhāyatana)... ‘they are dhammas and they are a base, thus it is the dhamma-base’ (dhammāyatana). In this way, the analysis should first be understood here in terms of meaning.

513. Lakkhaṇāti cakkhādīnaṃ lakkhaṇatopettha viññātabbo vinicchayo. Tāni ca pana tesaṃ lakkhaṇāni khandhaniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

513. As to characteristics: here the analysis should be understood in terms of the characteristics of the eye and so on. And their characteristics should be understood in the way stated in the Exposition of the Aggregates.

Tāvatvatoti tāvabhāvato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – cakkhādayopi hi dhammā eva, evaṃ sati dhammāyatanamicceva avatvā kasmā dvādasāyatanānīti vuttānīti ce. Chaviññāṇakāyuppattidvārārammaṇavavatthānato idha channaṃ viññāṇakāyānaṃ dvārabhāvena ārammaṇabhāvena ca vavatthānato ayametesaṃ bhedo hotīti dvādasa vuttāni, cakkhuviññāṇavīthipariyāpannassa hi viññāṇakāyassa [V 2.0111] cakkhāyatanameva uppattidvāraṃ, rūpāyatanameva cārammaṇaṃ, tathā itarāni itaresaṃ. Chaṭṭhassa pana bhavaṅgamanasaṅkhāto manāyatanekadesova uppattidvāraṃ, asādhāraṇameva ca dhammāyatanaṃ ārammaṇanti[M 2.0114]. Iti channaṃ viññāṇakāyānaṃ uppattidvārārammaṇavavatthānato dvādasa vuttānīti evamettha tāvatvato viññātabbo vinicchayo.

As to enumeration: this means their numerical determination. This is what is meant: The eye, etc., are also simply dhammas. That being so, if it is asked why the twelve bases are mentioned instead of just the mind-object base, it is because of the establishment of the doors and objects for the arising of the six classes of consciousness. Because they are established here as the doors and objects for the six classes of consciousness, this distinction among them comes about, and so twelve are mentioned. For the class of consciousness included in the eye-consciousness process, the eye-base is the door of origin and the form-base is the object; likewise for the others in each case. But for the sixth, a part of the mind-base reckoned as the life-continuum mind is the door of origin, and the mind-object base is its unique object. Thus, because of the establishment of the doors and objects for the arising of the six classes of consciousness, twelve are mentioned. In this way, the analysis should be understood here in terms of enumeration.

514. Kamatoti idhāpi pubbe vuttesu uppattikkamādīsu desanākkamova yujjati. Ajjhattikesu hi āyatanesu sanidassanasappaṭighavisayattā cakkhāyatanaṃ pākaṭanti paṭhamaṃ desitaṃ, tato anidassanasappaṭighavisayāni sotāyatanādīni. Atha vā dassanānuttariyasavanānuttariyahetubhāvena bahūpakārattā ajjhattikesu cakkhāyatanasotāyatanāni paṭhamaṃ desitāni, tato ghānāyatanādīni tīṇi, pañcannampi gocaravisayattā ante manāyatanaṃ, cakkhāyatanādīnaṃ pana gocarattā tassa tassa antarantarāni bāhiresu rūpāyatanādīni. Apica viññāṇuppattikāraṇavavatthānatopi ayametesaṃ kamo veditabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇa”nti (ma. ni. 3.421; saṃ. ni. 2.43). Evaṃ kamatopettha viññātabbo vinicchayo.

514. As to order: here too, of the kinds of order mentioned before, such as the order of arising, the order of teaching is applicable. Among the internal bases, the eye-base is taught first because it is prominent, its object being visible and having impact. Then come the ear-base and so on, whose objects are invisible and have impact. Or alternatively, the internal eye-base and ear-base are taught first because they are of great service as the cause for the supreme seeing and supreme hearing, and then the three beginning with the nose-base. The mind-base is last because its object is the domain of all five. Furthermore, the external bases, beginning with the form-base, are taught immediately after their corresponding internal bases, since they are their respective objects. Furthermore, this order should be understood from the establishment of the conditions for the arising of consciousness. For it is said: 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises... dependent on the mind and dhammas, mind-consciousness arises' (MN 148; SN 12.43). In this way, the analysis should be understood here in terms of order.

515. Saṅkhepavitthārāti saṅkhepato hi manāyatanassa ceva dhammāyatanekadesassa ca nāmena tadavasesānañca āyatanānaṃ rūpena saṅgahitattā dvādasāpi āyatanāni nāmarūpamattameva honti. Vitthārato pana ajjhattikesu tāva cakkhāyatanaṃ jātivasena cakkhupasādamattameva, paccayagatinikāyapuggalabhedato pana anantappabhedaṃ. Tathā sotāyatanādīni cattāri. Manāyatanaṃ kusalākusalavipākakiriyaviññāṇabhedena ekūnanavutippabhedaṃ ekavīsuttarasatappabhedañca. Vatthupaṭipadādibhedato pana anantappabhedaṃ. Rūpasaddagandharasāyatanāni visabhāgapaccayādibhedato anantappabhedāni. Phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ pathavīdhātutejodhātuvāyodhātuvasena tippabhedaṃ. Paccayādibhedato anekappabhedaṃ. Dhammāyatanaṃ vedanāsaññāsaṅkhārakkhandhasukhumarūpanibbānānaṃ sabhāvanānattabhedato anekappabhedanti. Evaṃ saṅkhepavitthārā viññātabbo vinicchayo.

515. As for conciseness and detail: Briefly, since the mind-base and a portion of the dhamma-base are included under 'name,' while the remaining bases are included under 'form,' all twelve bases are merely name-and-form. In detail, however, among the internal bases, the eye-base is simply eye-sensitivity by way of its intrinsic nature, but it becomes infinitely varied when classified by conditions, destinies, groups, and individuals. Similarly, the four bases beginning with the ear-base are also infinitely varied. The mind-base has eighty-nine or one hundred twenty-one types when classified by wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional consciousness, and becomes infinitely varied when classified by physical base, practice, and so on. The form, sound, smell, and taste bases are infinitely varied when classified by dissimilar conditions and so on. The tangible-object base has three types—the earth element, fire element, and air element—and becomes manifold when classified by conditions and so on. The dhamma-base is manifold due to the inherent diversity of the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, subtle form, and Nibbāna. Thus the analysis should be understood in terms of conciseness and detail.

516. Daṭṭhabbatoti ettha pana sabbāneva saṅkhatāni āyatanāni anāgamanato aniggamanato ca daṭṭhabbāni. Na hi tāni pubbe udayā kutoci āgacchanti, napi uddhaṃ vayā [V 2.0112] kuhiñci gacchanti, atha kho pubbe udayā appaṭiladdhasabhāvāni[M 2.0115], uddhaṃ vayā paribhinnasabhāvāni, pubbantāparantavemajjhe paccayāyattavuttitāya avasāni pavattanti. Tasmā anāgamanato aniggamanato ca daṭṭhabbāni. Tathā nirīhakato abyāpārato ca. Na hi cakkhurūpādīnaṃ evaṃ hoti “aho vata amhākaṃ sāmaggiyaṃ viññāṇaṃ nāma uppajjeyyā”ti, na ca tāni viññāṇuppādanatthaṃ dvārabhāvena vatthubhāvena ārammaṇabhāvena vā īhanti, na byāpāramāpajjanti, atha kho dhammatāvesā, yaṃ cakkhurūpādisāmaggiyaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīni sambhavantīti. Tasmā nirīhakato abyāpārato ca daṭṭhabbāni. Apica ajjhattikāni suññagāmo viya daṭṭhabbāni, dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahitattā. Bāhirāni gāmaghātakacorā viya, ajjhattikānaṃ abhighātakattā. Vuttañhetaṃ “cakkhu, bhikkhave, haññati manāpāmanāpehi rūpehī”ti vitthāro. Apica ajjhattikāni cha pāṇakā viya daṭṭhabbāni, bāhirāni tesaṃ gocarā viyāti. Evamettha daṭṭhabbato viññātabbo vinicchayo.

516. As to how they should be seen: Here, all conditioned bases should be seen as without coming and without going. For they do not come from anywhere before arising, nor do they go anywhere after ceasing. Rather, before arising they have not acquired an own-nature, and after ceasing their own-nature has perished. In the interval, their occurrence is dependent on conditions and they proceed powerlessly. Therefore they should be seen as without coming and without going. Likewise, they should be seen as without striving and without activity. For it is not the case that the eye, forms, etc., think: ‘Oh, may consciousness arise from our conjunction!’ Nor do they strive or engage in activity for the purpose of producing consciousness by serving as a door, a base, or an object. Rather, it is simply by natural law that when there is a conjunction of eye, form, etc., eye-consciousness and so on arise. Therefore they should be seen as without striving and without activity. Furthermore, the internal bases should be seen as like an empty village, since they are devoid of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self. The external bases should be seen as like village-plundering robbers, since they assault the internal ones. For it is said: ‘Bhikkhus, the eye is struck by agreeable and disagreeable forms,’ and so on in detail. Moreover, the internal bases should be seen as like six animals, and the external bases as their pasture. Thus the analysis should be understood in terms of how they are to be seen.

Idaṃ tāva āyatanānaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This, for now, is the introduction to the detailed exposition of the bases.

Dhātuvitthārakathā

The Detailed Exposition of the Elements

517. Tadanantarā pana dhātuyoti aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo – cakkhudhātu, rūpadhātu, cakkhuviññāṇadhātu, sotadhātu, saddadhātu, sotaviññāṇadhātu, ghānadhātu, gandhadhātu, ghānaviññāṇadhātu, jivhādhātu, rasadhātu, jivhāviññāṇadhātu, kāyadhātu, phoṭṭhabbadhātu, kāyaviññāṇadhātu, manodhātu, dhammadhātu, manoviññāṇadhātūti. Tattha –

517. Next, as to the elements, there are eighteen elements: the eye-element, the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element; the ear-element, the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element; the nose-element, the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element; the tongue-element, the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element; the body-element, the tangible-element, the body-consciousness-element; the mind-element, the dhamma-element, and the mind-consciousness-element. Therein:

Atthato lakkhaṇādīhi, kama tāvatvasaṅkhato;

Paccayā atha daṭṭhabbā, veditabbo vinicchayo.

The analysis is to be understood by way of meaning; characteristics and so on; sequence, number, and enumeration; conditions; and how they are to be seen.

Tattha atthatoti cakkhatīti cakkhu. Rūpayatīti rūpaṃ. Cakkhussa viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇanti evamādinā tāva nayena cakkhādīnaṃ visesatthato veditabbo vinicchayo. Avisesena pana vidahati, dhīyate, vidhānaṃ, vidhīyate etāya, ettha vā dhīyatīti dhātu. Lokiyā hi dhātuyo kāraṇabhāvena vavatthitā hutvā suvaṇṇarajatādidhātuyo viya suvaṇṇarajatādiṃ[V 2.0113], anekappakāraṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ vidahanti. Bhārahārehi ca bhāro viya, sattehi [M 2.0116] dhīyante, dhāriyantīti attho. Dukkhavidhānamattameva cesā, avasavattanato. Etāhi ca karaṇabhūtāhi saṃsāradukkhaṃ sattehi anuvidhīyati. Tathāvihitañca taṃ etāsveva dhīyati, ṭhapiyatīti attho. Iti cakkhādīsu ekeko dhammo yathāsambhavaṃ vidahati, dhīyatītiādinā atthavasena dhātūti vuccati.

Therein, as to meaning: ‘It indicates’ (cakkhati), thus it is the eye (cakkhu). ‘It manifests’ (rūpayati), thus it is form (rūpa). ‘Consciousness of the eye is eye-consciousness.’ In this way, for now, the analysis of the eye and so on should be understood in their specific meanings. In a general sense, however, it is an ‘element’ (dhātu) because it lays down (vidahati), or is borne (dhīyate); it is a laying down (vidhānaṃ); or by it one is made to undergo (vidhīyate etāya), or in it something is borne (ettha vā dhīyate). For worldly elements, being established as causes, lay down the manifold suffering of saṃsāra, just as elements such as gold and silver produce gold, silver, and so on. And like a burden by burden-bearers, they are borne (dhīyante) by beings—that is, they are carried (dhāriyanti). They are merely a laying down of suffering, because they proceed powerlessly. And through these as instruments, beings are made to undergo the suffering of saṃsāra. And that suffering, thus laid down, is borne within these very elements; that is, it is placed there. Thus each phenomenon among the eye, etc., according as is possible, is called an ‘element’ in the sense that it lays down, is borne, etc.

518. Apica yathā titthiyānaṃ attā nāma sabhāvato natthi, na evametā, etā pana attano sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhātuyo. Yathā loke vicittā haritālamanosilādayo selāvayavā dhātuyoti vuccanti, evametāpi dhātuyo viya dhātuyo. Vicittā hete ñāṇañeyyāvayavāti. Yathā vā sarīrasaṅkhātassa samudāyassa avayavabhūtesu rasasoṇitādīsu aññamaññavisabhāgalakkhaṇaparicchinnesu dhātusamaññā, evametesupi pañcakkhandhasaṅkhātassa attabhāvassa avayavesu dhātusamaññā veditabbā. Aññamaññavisabhāgalakkhaṇaparicchinnā hete cakkhādayoti. Apica dhātūti nijjīvamattassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tathā hi bhagavā “cha dhāturo ayaṃ bhikkhu puriso”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.344) jīvasaññāsamūhananatthaṃ dhātudesanaṃ akāsīti.

518. Furthermore, just as for the adherents of other schools a self does not exist in its own nature, it is not so with these; rather, because they bear their own nature, they are elements. Just as in the world various mineral components of rock such as orpiment and realgar are called ‘elements,’ so too these are elements like those mineral elements, for these are the diverse components of cognition and the cognizable. Or, just as the term ‘element’ is applied to the components of the collection called the body—such as lymph, blood, etc.—which are defined by mutually dissimilar characteristics, so too the term ‘element’ should be understood in regard to the components of the individual existence comprised of the five aggregates. For these—the eye, etc.—are defined by mutually dissimilar characteristics. Moreover, ‘element’ is a designation for what is merely soulless. For the Blessed One gave the discourse on the elements—as in, ‘Bhikkhu, this person consists of six elements’—in order to eradicate the perception of a soul.

Tasmā yathāvuttena atthena cakkhu ca taṃ dhātu ca cakkhudhātu…pe… manoviññāṇañca taṃ dhātu ca manoviññāṇadhātūti. Evaṃ tāvettha atthato veditabbo vinicchayo.

Therefore, in the sense explained: it is the eye and it is an element, thus 'eye-element'… and so on down to… it is mind-consciousness and it is an element, thus 'mind-consciousness-element'. Thus, for now, the analysis should be understood here in terms of meaning.

519. Lakkhaṇāditoti cakkhādīnaṃ lakkhaṇāditopettha veditabbo vinicchayo. Tāni ca pana nesaṃ lakkhaṇādīni khandhaniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

519. As to characteristics, etc.: Here the analysis should be understood in terms of the characteristics, etc., of the eye and so on. And their characteristics, etc., should be understood in the same way as was stated in the exposition of the aggregates.

Kamatoti idhāpi pubbe vuttesu uppattikkamādīsu desanākkamova yujjati. So ca panāyaṃ hetuphalānupubbavavatthānavasena vutto. Cakkhudhātu rūpadhātūti idañhi dvayaṃ hetu, cakkhuviññāṇadhātūti phalaṃ. Evaṃ sabbattha.

As to sequence: Here too, of the sequences mentioned before, such as the sequence of arising, the sequence of teaching is the one that is appropriate. And this is stated based on the established succession of cause and effect. For these two, the eye-element and the form-element, are the cause; the eye-consciousness-element is the fruit. So it is in all cases.

520. Tāvatvatoti [M 2.0117] tāvabhāvato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tesu tesu hi suttābhidhammappadesesu “ābhādhātu, subhadhātu, ākāsānañcāyatanadhātu, viññāṇañcāyatanadhātu, ākiñcaññāyatanadhātu, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanadhātu, saññāvedayitanirodhadhātu” (saṃ. ni. 2.95), “kāmadhātu[V 2.0114], byāpādadhātu, vihiṃsādhātu, nekkhammadhātu, abyāpādadhātu, avihiṃsādhātu” (vibha. 182; dī. ni. 3.305; ma. ni. 3.125), “sukhadhātu, dukkhadhātu, somanassadhātu, domanassadhātu, upekkhādhātu, avijjādhātu” (vibha. 180; ma. ni. 3.125), “ārambhadhātu, nikkamadhātu, parakkamadhātu” (saṃ. ni. 5.183), “hīnadhātu, majjhimadhātu, paṇītadhātu” (dī. ni. 3.305), “pathavīdhātu, āpodhātu, tejodhātu, vāyodhātu (dī. ni. 3.311), ākāsadhātu, viññāṇadhātu” (ma. ni. 3.125; vibha. 172), “saṅkhatadhātu, asaṅkhatadhātu” (ma. ni. 3.125), “anekadhātu nānādhātu loko”ti (dī. ni. 2.366; ma. ni. 1.148) evamādayo aññāpi dhātuyo dissanti. Evaṃ sati sabbāsaṃ vasena paricchedaṃ akatvā kasmā aṭṭhārasāti ayameva paricchedo katoti ce. Sabhāvato vijjamānānaṃ sabbadhātūnaṃ tadantogadhattā.

520. As to number: This means their amount. This is what is said: In various passages of the Suttas and Abhidhamma, other elements are seen, such as: the lustre element, the beauty element, the element of the base of the infinity of space, the element of the base of the infinity of consciousness, the element of the base of nothingness, the element of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the element of the cessation of perception and feeling; the element of sensual desire, the element of ill will, the element of cruelty, the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill will, the element of non-cruelty; the element of pleasure, the element of pain, the element of joy, the element of sorrow, the element of equanimity, the element of ignorance; the element of initiative, the element of exertion, the element of striving; the inferior element, the middling element, the superior element; the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, the consciousness element; the conditioned element, the unconditioned element; and in such statements as ‘the world has many elements, various elements.’ This being so, if it is asked why this classification into just eighteen has been made, without making a classification that includes all of them, it is because all elements that exist in their own nature are included within them.

Rūpadhātuyeva hi ābhādhātu, subhadhātu pana rūpādipaṭibaddhā. Kasmā, subhanimittattā. Subhanimittañhi subhadhātu. Tañca rūpādivinimuttaṃ na vijjati. Kusalavipākārammaṇā vā rūpādayo eva subhadhātūti rūpādimattamevesā. Ākāsānañcāyatanadhātuādīsu cittaṃ manoviññāṇadhātuyeva, sesā dhammadhātu. Saññāvedayitanirodhadhātu pana sabhāvato natthi. Dhātudvayanirodhamattameva hi sā.

For the lustre element is just the form-element. The beauty element, however, is connected with form, etc. Why? Because it is the sign of beauty. For the sign of beauty is the beauty element, and that is not found apart from form, etc. Or, form, etc., themselves, being the objects of wholesome resultant consciousness, are the beauty element; thus it is merely form, etc. In the case of the element of the base of the infinity of space and so on, the consciousness is just the mind-consciousness-element; the remaining factors are the dhamma-element. The element of the cessation of perception and feeling, however, does not exist in its own nature, for it is merely the cessation of two elements.

Kāmadhātu dhammadhātumattaṃ vā hoti. Yathāha – “tattha katamā kāmadhātu? Kāmapaṭisaṃyutto takko vitakko micchāsaṅkappo”ti (vibha. 182). Aṭṭhārasāpi vā dhātuyo. Yathāha – “heṭṭhato avīcinirayaṃ pariyantaṃ karitvā uparito paranimmitavasavattī deve antokaritvā yaṃ etasmiṃ antare etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannā khandhadhātuāyatanā rūpā vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati kāmadhātū”ti (vibha. 182).

The sensual-sphere element is sometimes merely the dhamma-element. As it is said: “Therein, what is the sensual-sphere element? Thought, initial application, and wrong intention connected with sensual desire.” Or it is the eighteen elements. As it is said: “Having made the Avīci hell the lower limit and having included the devas of the sphere of Paranimmita-vasavatti as the upper limit, whatever aggregates, elements, and bases are within this interval, moving within this sphere, included in this sphere—form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness—this is called the sensual-sphere element.”

Nekkhammadhātu [M 2.0118] dhammadhātu eva, “sabbepi kusalā dhammā nekkhammadhātū”ti (vibha. 182) vacanato manoviññāṇadhātupi hotiyeva. Byāpādavihiṃsā-abyāpāda-avihiṃsāsukha-dukkha-somanassa-domanassupekkhā-avijjāārambha-nikkama-parakkamadhātuyo dhammadhātuyeva.

The element of renunciation is just the dhamma-element, for it is said: “All wholesome states are the element of renunciation”; thus the mind-consciousness element is also included. The elements of ill will, cruelty, non-ill will, non-cruelty, pleasure, pain, joy, grief, equanimity, ignorance, initiative, exertion, and striving are all just the dhamma-element.

Hīnamajjhimapaṇītadhātuyo aṭṭhārasa dhātumattameva. Hīnā hi cakkhādayo hīnā dhātu, majjhimapaṇītā [V 2.0115] majjhimā ceva paṇītā ca. Nippariyāyena pana akusalā dhammadhātumanoviññāṇadhātuyo hīnadhātu, lokiyā kusalābyākatā ubhopi cakkhudhātuādayo ca majjhimadhātu, lokuttarā pana dhammadhātumanoviññāṇadhātuyo paṇītadhātu.

The inferior, middling, and superior elements are merely a classification of the eighteen elements. For when the eye element and so on are inferior, they are the inferior element; when middling and superior, they are the middling and superior elements respectively. But unequivocally, the unwholesome dhamma-element and mind-consciousness-element are the inferior element; the mundane wholesome and indeterminate dhamma-element and mind-consciousness-element, and also the eye-element and so on, are the middling element; but the supramundane dhamma-element and mind-consciousness-element are the superior element.

Pathavītejovāyodhātuyo phoṭṭhabbadhātuyeva, āpodhātu ākāsadhātu ca dhammadhātuyeva. Viññāṇadhātu cakkhuviññāṇādisattaviññāṇadhātusaṅkhepoyeva.

The earth, fire, and air elements are just the tangible-object element. The water element and the space element are just the dhamma-element. The consciousness element is just a summary of the seven consciousness elements beginning with eye-consciousness.

Sattarasa dhātuyo dhammadhātuekadeso ca saṅkhatadhātu, asaṅkhatā pana dhātu dhammadhātuekadesova. Anekadhātunānādhātuloko pana aṭṭhārasa dhātuppabhedamattamevāti. Iti sabhāvato vijjamānānaṃ sabbadhātūnaṃ tadantogadhattā aṭṭhāraseva vuttāti.

Seventeen elements and a part of the dhamma-element are the conditioned element, but the unconditioned element is just a part of the dhamma-element. The world of many elements and various elements is merely the classification of the eighteen elements. Thus, because all elements that exist by their own nature are included within these, only eighteen are stated.

521. Apica vijānanasabhāve viññāṇe jīvasaññīnaṃ saññāsamūhananatthampi aṭṭhāraseva vuttā. Santi hi sattā vijānanasabhāve viññāṇe jīvasaññino, tesaṃ cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyamanodhātumanoviññāṇadhātubhedena tassa anekataṃ cakkhurūpādipaccayāyattavuttitāya aniccatañca pakāsetvā dīgharattānusayitaṃ jīvasaññaṃ samūhanitukāmena bhagavatā aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo pakāsitā. Kiñca bhiyyo tathā veneyyajjhāsayavasena ca. Ye ca imāya anatisaṅkhepavitthārāya desanāya veneyyasattā, tadajjhāsayavasena ca aṭṭhāraseva pakāsitā.

521. Moreover, the eighteen elements are also taught in order to uproot the perception of a living being in consciousness, which has the nature of cognizing. For there are beings who perceive a living being in consciousness, which has the nature of cognizing. Wishing to uproot their long-ingrained perception of a living being, the Blessed One proclaimed the eighteen elements by showing the multiplicity of that consciousness through its divisions into the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mind-consciousness elements, and by showing its impermanence due to its occurrence being dependent on conditions such as the eye and forms. And what is more? They were also taught according to the disposition of those to be trained. And for those beings who were to be trained by this teaching that is neither too brief nor too detailed, the eighteen elements were proclaimed according to their disposition.

Saṅkhepavitthāranayena tathā tathā hi,

Dhammaṃ pakāsayati esa yathā yathāssa;

Saddhammatejavihataṃ vilayaṃ khaṇena,

Veneyyasattahadayesu tamo payātīti.

By methods brief and detailed, in this way and that,

He clarifies the Dhamma as befits each one;

Struck by the power of the good Dhamma,

The darkness in the hearts of those to be trained

Is instantly dispersed and comes to naught.

Evamettha tāvatvato veditabbo vinicchayo.

Thus the analysis here should be understood in terms of their quantity.

522. Saṅkhatoti [M 2.0119] cakkhudhātu tāva jātito eko dhammotveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati cakkhupasādavasena, tathā sotaghānajivhākāyarūpasaddagandharasadhātuyo sotappasādādivasena, phoṭṭhabbadhātu pana pathavītejovāyovasena tayo dhammāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Cakkhuviññāṇadhātu kusalākusalavipākavasena [V 2.0116] dve dhammāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati, tathā sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇadhātuyo. Manodhātu pana pañcadvārāvajjanakusalākusalavipākasampaṭicchanavasena tayo dhammāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Dhammadhātu tiṇṇaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ soḷasannaṃ sukhumarūpānaṃ asaṅkhatāya ca dhātuyā vasena vīsati dhammāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Manoviññāṇadhātu sesakusalākusalābyākataviññāṇavasena chasattati dhammāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Evamettha saṅkhatopi veditabbo vinicchayo.

522. In terms of reckoning: The eye-element is reckoned as one state by way of eye-sensitivity. Similarly, the ear, nose, tongue, and body elements, and the form, sound, odor, and taste elements, are each reckoned as one state by way of ear-sensitivity and so on. The tangible-object element, however, is reckoned as three states by way of earth, fire, and air. The eye-consciousness element is reckoned as two states, namely, the wholesome-resultant and the unwholesome-resultant. The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body-consciousness elements. The mind-element is reckoned as three states, namely, the five-door-adverting consciousness and the two kinds of receiving consciousness (wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant). The dhamma-element is reckoned as twenty states by way of the three formless aggregates, the sixteen subtle material phenomena, and the unconditioned element. The mind-consciousness element is reckoned as seventy-six states by way of the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate consciousness. Thus the analysis here should also be understood in terms of reckoning.

523. Paccayāti ettha ca cakkhudhātu tāva cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā vippayuttapurejātaatthiavigatanissayindriyapaccayānaṃ vasena chahi paccayehi paccayo hoti, rūpadhātu purejātaatthiavigatārammaṇapaccayānaṃ vasena catūhi paccayehi paccayo hoti. Evaṃ sotaviññāṇadhātuādīnaṃ sotadhātusaddadhātuādayo. Pañcannaṃ pana nesaṃ āvajjanamanodhātu anantarasamanantaranatthivigatānantarūpanissayavasena pañcahi paccayehi paccayo hoti, tā ca pañcapi sampaṭicchanamanodhātuyā. Tathā sampaṭicchanamanodhātu santīraṇamanoviññāṇadhātuyā, sā ca voṭṭhabbanamanoviññāṇadhātuyā, voṭṭhabbanamanoviññāṇadhātu ca javanamanoviññāṇadhātuyā. Javanamanoviññāṇadhātu pana anantarāya javanamanoviññāṇadhātuyā tehi ceva pañcahi āsevanapaccayena cāti chahi paccayehi paccayo hoti. Esa tāva pañcadvāre nayo.

523. In terms of conditions: Herein, the eye-element is a condition for the eye-consciousness element in six ways: by way of dissociation, prenascent, presence, non-disappearance, dependence, and faculty conditions. The form-element is a condition in four ways: by way of prenascent, presence, non-disappearance, and object conditions. The same applies to the ear-consciousness element and so on in relation to the ear-element, sound-element, and so on. Furthermore, for the five consciousness elements, the adverting mind-element is a condition in five ways: by way of contiguity, immediate contiguity, absence, disappearance, and contiguity-strong-dependence; and they in turn are conditions for the receiving mind-element. Likewise, the receiving mind-element is a condition for the investigating mind-consciousness element; that for the determining mind-consciousness element; and the determining mind-consciousness element for the impulsion mind-consciousness element. An impulsion mind-consciousness element, however, is a condition for a subsequent impulsion mind-consciousness element in six ways: by those same five conditions and by the repetition condition. This, for now, is the method regarding the five doors.

Manodvāre pana bhavaṅgamanoviññāṇadhātu āvajjanamanoviññāṇadhātuyā. Āvajjanamanoviññāṇadhātu ca javanamanoviññāṇadhātuyā purimehi pañcahi paccayehi paccayo hoti. Dhammadhātu pana sattannampi viññāṇadhātūnaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatādīhi bahudhā paccayo hoti. Cakkhudhātuādayo pana ekaccā ca dhammadhātu ekaccāya manoviññāṇadhātuyā ārammaṇapaccayādīhipi paccayā honti. Cakkhuviññāṇadhātuādīnañca na kevalaṃ cakkhurūpādayo paccayā honti, atha kho ālokādayopi. Tenāhu pubbācariyā –

At the mind door, however, the life-continuum mind-consciousness element is a condition for the adverting mind-consciousness element, and the adverting mind-consciousness element is a condition for the impulsion mind-consciousness element by the aforesaid five conditions. The dhamma-element, however, is a condition in many ways for all seven consciousness elements through conascence, mutuality, dependence, association, presence, non-disappearance, and other conditions. Furthermore, the eye-element and so on, and certain parts of the dhamma-element, are conditions for a certain mind-consciousness element by way of object condition and so on. And for the eye-consciousness element and so on, not only are the eye, form, etc., conditions, but so too are light, etc. Therefore the ancient teachers said:

“Cakkhurūpālokamanasikāre [M 2.0120] paṭicca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Sotasaddavivaramanasikāre paṭicca uppajjati sotaviññāṇaṃ. Ghānagandhavāyumanasikāre paṭicca uppajjati ghānaviññāṇaṃ. Jivhārasaāpamanasikāre paṭicca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇaṃ. Kāyaphoṭṭhabbapathavīmanasikāre paṭicca uppajjati kāyaviññāṇaṃ. Bhavaṅgamanadhammamanasikāre paṭicca uppajjati manoviññāṇa”nti.

“Dependent on the eye, forms, light, and attention, eye-consciousness arises. Dependent on the ear, sounds, the aperture, and attention, ear-consciousness arises. Dependent on the nose, odors, air, and attention, nose-consciousness arises. Dependent on the tongue, tastes, the water element, and attention, tongue-consciousness arises. Dependent on the body, tangibles, the earth element, and attention, body-consciousness arises. Dependent on the life-continuum mind, dhammas, and attention, mind-consciousness arises.”

Ayamettha [V 2.0117] saṅkhepo. Vitthārato pana paccayappabhedo paṭiccasamuppādaniddese āvibhavissatīti evamettha paccayatopi veditabbo vinicchayo.

This is the summary here. The detailed classification of conditions will become clear in the exposition of dependent origination. Thus the analysis here should also be understood in terms of conditions.

524. Daṭṭhabbatoti daṭṭhabbatopettha vinicchayo veditabboti attho. Sabbā eva hi saṅkhatadhātuyo pubbantāparantavivittato dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvasuññato paccayāyattavuttito ca daṭṭhabbā.

524. “In terms of how they should be seen”: this means the analysis here should be understood in terms of how they are to be seen. For all conditioned elements should be seen as devoid of a past end and a future end, as void of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self, and as having their occurrence dependent on conditions.

Visesato panettha bheritalaṃ viya cakkhudhātu daṭṭhabbā, daṇḍo viya rūpadhātu, saddo viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Tathā ādāsatalaṃ viya cakkhudhātu, mukhaṃ viya rūpadhātu, mukhanimittaṃ viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Atha vā ucchutilā viya cakkhudhātu, yantacakkayaṭṭhi viya rūpadhātu, ucchurasatelāni viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Tathā adharāraṇī viya cakkhudhātu, uttarāraṇī viya rūpadhātu, aggi viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Esa nayo sotadhātuādīsu.

Specifically, herein, the eye-element should be seen as like the surface of a drum, the form-element as like the drumstick, and the eye-consciousness element as like the sound. Similarly, the eye-element is like the surface of a mirror, the form-element is like the face, and the eye-consciousness element is like the reflection of the face. Or, the eye-element is like sugarcane and sesame seeds, the form-element is like the rod of the press, and the eye-consciousness element is like sugarcane juice and sesame oil. Likewise, the eye-element is like the lower fire-stick, the form-element is like the upper fire-stick, and the eye-consciousness element is like the fire. This is the method for the ear-element and so on.

Manodhātu pana yathāsambhavato cakkhuviññāṇadhātuādīnaṃ purecarānucarā viya daṭṭhabbā.

The mind-element, however, should be seen as like a forerunner and a follower of the eye-consciousness element and the others, as the case may be.

Dhammadhātuyā vedanākkhandho sallamiva sūlamiva ca daṭṭhabbo. Saññāsaṅkhārakkhandhā vedanāsallasūlayogāāturā viya, puthujjanānaṃ vā saññā āsādukkhajananato rittamuṭṭhi viya. Ayathābhuccanimittagāhakato vanamigo viya. Saṅkhārā paṭisandhiyaṃ pakkhipanato aṅgārakāsuyaṃ khipanakapurisā viya. Jāti dukkhānubandhato rājapurisānubandhacorā viya. Sabbānatthāvahassa khandhasantānassa hetuto visarukkhabījāni viya. Rūpaṃ nānāvidhupaddavanimittato khuracakkaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Asaṅkhatā pana dhātu amatato santato khemato ca daṭṭhabbā. Kasmā? Sabbānatthāvahassa paṭipakkhabhūtattā.

Within the dhamma-element, the feeling aggregate should be seen as a dart and as a stake. The perception and formations aggregates, because of their connection with the dart and stake of feeling, are like a sick person. Or, for worldlings, perception is like an empty fist because it generates the suffering of longing; because it grasps signs incorrectly, it is like a forest deer. Volitional formations, because they cast one into rebirth-linking, are like men who throw someone into a pit of embers; because they are followed by the suffering of birth, they are like thieves pursued by the king's men; because they are the cause of the continuity of aggregates which brings every kind of ruin, they are like the seeds of a poison tree. Material form should be seen as a razor-wheel because it is a sign of various calamities. But the unconditioned element should be seen as deathless, peaceful, and secure. Why? Because it is the opposite of all that brings ruin.

Manoviññāṇadhātu [M 2.0121] ārammaṇesu vavatthānābhāvato araññamakkaṭo viya, duddamanato assakhaḷuṅko viya, yatthakāmanipātito vehāsakkhittadaṇḍo viya, lobhadosādinānappakārakilesavesayogato raṅganaṭo viya daṭṭhabbāti.

The mind-consciousness element should be seen as a forest monkey because it does not stay settled on its objects; as an untamed colt because it is difficult to tame; as a stick thrown into the air because it falls wherever it wants; and as an actor on a stage because it is associated with the guises of various defilements such as greed and hatred.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, made for the purpose of gladdening good people,

Paññābhāvanādhikāre

In the Section on the Development of Wisdom,

Āyatanadhātuniddeso nāma

The Exposition of the Bases and Elements,

Pannarasamo paricchedo.

The Fifteenth Chapter.

16. Indriyasaccaniddeso

16. The Exposition of the Faculties and Truths

Indriyavitthārakathā

Detailed Account of the Faculties

525. Dhātūnaṃ [M 2.0122][V 2.0118] anantaraṃ uddiṭṭhāni pana indriyānīti bāvīsatindriyāni – cakkhundriyaṃ sotindriyaṃ ghānindriyaṃ jivhindriyaṃ kāyindriyaṃ manindriyaṃ itthindriyaṃ purisindriyaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ sukhindriyaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ somanassindriyaṃ domanassindriyaṃ upekkhindriyaṃ saddhindriyaṃ vīriyindriyaṃ satindriyaṃ samādhindriyaṃ paññindriyaṃ anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ aññindriyaṃ aññātāvindriyanti. Tattha –

525. Now, the faculties were pointed out immediately after the elements. There are twenty-two faculties: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, mind faculty; the femininity faculty, masculinity faculty; the life faculty; the pleasure faculty, pain faculty, joy faculty, displeasure faculty, equanimity faculty; the faith faculty, energy faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty; the faculty 'I shall come to know the unknown,' the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has final knowledge. Herein—

Atthato lakkhaṇādīhi, kamato ca vijāniyā;

Bhedābhedā tathā kiccā, bhūmito ca vinicchayaṃ.

The determination should be known by meaning, by characteristics and so on, and by order; likewise by division and non-division, by function, and by plane.

Tattha cakkhādīnaṃ tāva cakkhatīti cakkhūtiādinā nayena attho pakāsito. Pacchimesu pana tīsu paṭhamaṃ pubbabhāge anaññātaṃ amataṃ padaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ vā jānissāmīti evaṃ paṭipannassa uppajjanato indriyaṭṭhasambhavato ca anaññātaññassāmītindriyanti vuttaṃ. Dutiyaṃ ājānanato indriyaṭṭhasambhavato ca aññindriyaṃ. Tatiyaṃ aññātāvino catūsu saccesu niṭṭhitaññāṇakiccassa khīṇāsavassa uppajjanato indriyaṭṭhasambhavato ca aññātāvindriyaṃ.

Herein, first, the meaning of the eye and so on has been explained by the method 'it sees, thus it is the eye,' and so on. But as to the last three, the first is called the faculty 'I shall come to know the unknown' because it arises in one who is practicing thus: 'I shall know the previously unknown deathless state or the Dhamma of the four truths,' and because the meaning of 'faculty' is present. The second is the faculty of final knowledge because of knowing and because the meaning of 'faculty' is present. The third is the faculty of one who has final knowledge because it arises in one who has final knowledge, an arahant whose task of knowing in regard to the four truths is completed, and because the meaning of 'faculty' is present.

Ko pana nesaṃ indriyaṭṭho nāmāti? Indaliṅgaṭṭho indriyaṭṭho. Indadesitaṭṭho indriyaṭṭho. Indadiṭṭhaṭṭho indriyaṭṭho. Indasiṭṭhaṭṭho indriyaṭṭho. Indajuṭṭhaṭṭho indriyaṭṭho. So sabbopi idha yathāyogaṃ yujjati. Bhagavā hi sammāsambuddho paramissariyabhāvato indo. Kusalākusalañca kammaṃ, kammesu kassaci issariyābhāvato. Tenevettha kammasañjanitāni tāva indriyāni kusalākusalakammaṃ [V 2.0119] ulliṅgenti. Tena ca siṭṭhānīti indaliṅgaṭṭhena indasiṭṭhaṭṭhena ca indriyāni. Sabbāneva panetāni bhagavatā yathābhūtato pakāsitāni abhisambuddhāni cāti indadesitaṭṭhena indadiṭṭhaṭṭhena ca indriyāni. Teneva bhagavatā munindena kānici gocarāsevanāya kānici bhāvanāsevanāya sevitānīti indajuṭṭhaṭṭhenāpi indriyāni.

But what is the meaning of 'faculty'? The meaning of 'faculty' is the meaning of being a mark of Inda (a lord). The meaning of 'faculty' is the meaning of being taught by Inda. The meaning of 'faculty' is the meaning of being seen by Inda. The meaning of 'faculty' is the meaning of being created by Inda. The meaning of 'faculty' is the meaning of being resorted to by Inda. All this is applicable here as is fitting. For the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is Inda because of his state of supreme sovereignty. And wholesome and unwholesome kamma is Inda, since no one else has sovereignty over kamma. Therefore, here, the faculties produced by kamma, for one, indicate wholesome and unwholesome kamma, and they are created by it; thus they are faculties in the sense of being a mark of Inda and in the sense of being created by Inda. Furthermore, all these have been declared and fully understood as they really are by the Blessed One; thus they are faculties in the sense of being taught by Inda and seen by Inda. And by that same Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, some were resorted to by way of attending to objects and some by way of development; thus they are also faculties in the sense of being resorted to by Inda.

Apica [M 2.0123] ādhipaccasaṅkhātena issariyaṭṭhenāpi etāni indriyāni. Cakkhuviññāṇādippavattiyañhi cakkhādīnaṃ siddhaṃ ādhipaccaṃ, tasmiṃ tikkhe tikkhattā mande ca mandattāti. Ayaṃ tāvettha atthato vinicchayo.

Moreover, these are faculties also in the sense of sovereignty, which is termed dominance. For in the occurrence of eye-consciousness and so on, the dominance of the eye faculty and so on is established; for when the faculty is keen, the consciousness is keen, and when it is dull, the consciousness is dull. This, first, is the determination by way of meaning.

Lakkhaṇādīhīti lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānehipi cakkhādīnaṃ vinicchayaṃ vijāniyāti attho. Tāni ca nesaṃ lakkhaṇādīni khandhaniddese vuttāneva. Paññindriyādīni hi cattāri atthato amohoyeva. Sesāni tattha sarūpeneva āgatāni.

'By characteristics, etc.' means that one should know the determination of the eye faculty and so on also by their characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause. And these characteristics, etc., of theirs have already been stated in the Exposition of the Aggregates. For the four faculties beginning with the wisdom faculty are in essence non-delusion. The remaining ones are included there in their own form.

526. Kamatoti ayampi desanākkamova. Tattha ajjhattadhamme pariññāya ariyabhūmipaṭilābho hotīti attabhāvapariyāpannāni cakkhundriyādīni paṭhamaṃ desitāni. So pana attabhāvo yaṃ dhammaṃ upādāya itthīti vā purisoti vā saṅkhaṃ gacchati, ayaṃ soti nidassanatthaṃ tato itthindriyaṃ purisindriyañca. So duvidhopi jīvitindriyapaṭibaddhavuttīti ñāpanatthaṃ tato jīvitindriyaṃ. Yāva tassa pavatti, tāva etesaṃ vedayitānaṃ anivatti. Yañca kiñci vedayitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ dukkhanti ñāpanatthaṃ tato sukhindriyādīni. Taṃnirodhatthaṃ pana ete dhammā bhāvetabbāti paṭipattidassanatthaṃ tato saddhādīni. Imāya paṭipattiyā esa dhammo paṭhamaṃ attani pātubhavatīti paṭipattiyā amoghabhāvadassanatthaṃ tato anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ. Tasseva phalattā tato anantaraṃ bhāvetabbato ca tato aññindriyaṃ. Tato paraṃ bhāvanāya imassa adhigamo, adhigate ca pana imasmiṃ natthi kiñci uttari karaṇīyanti ñāpanatthaṃ ante paramassāsabhūtaṃ aññātāvindriyaṃ desitanti ayamettha kamo.

526. 'By order': this too is the order of the teaching. Herein, since the attainment of the noble plane comes through fully understanding internal phenomena, the eye faculty and so on, which are included in the individual existence, are taught first. To show that this individual existence is the phenomenon by reason of which one is reckoned as 'woman' or 'man,' the femininity and masculinity faculties are taught next. To show that both kinds have their continuity bound up with the life faculty, the life faculty is taught next. To show that as long as that continues, there is no cessation of these feelings, and that whatever is felt is all suffering, the faculties of pleasure and so on are taught next. To show the practice—that for the sake of their cessation these states should be developed—the faculties of faith and so on are taught next. To show the unfailing nature of the practice—that through this practice this state first appears in oneself—the faculty 'I shall come to know the unknown' is taught next. Because it is the fruit of that and because it should be developed immediately after, the faculty of final knowledge is taught next. To show that after that its attainment comes through development, and that when this is attained there is nothing further to be done, the faculty of one who has final knowledge, which is the ultimate consolation, is taught at the end. This is the order here.

Bhedābhedāti jīvitindriyasseva cettha bhedo. Tañhi rūpajīvitindriyaṃ arūpajīvitindriyanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Sesānaṃ abhedoti evamettha bhedābhedato vinicchayaṃ vijāniyā.

'By division and non-division': Here there is division only of the life faculty. For it is twofold: the material life faculty and the immaterial life faculty. Of the rest there is no division. Thus one should know the determination here by way of division and non-division.

527. Kiccāti [V 2.0120] kiṃ indriyānaṃ kiccanti ce. Cakkhundriyassa tāva “cakkhāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ indriyapaccayena paccayo”ti vacanato yaṃ taṃ indriyapaccayabhāvena sādhetabbaṃ attano tikkhamandādibhāvena cakkhuviññāṇādidhammānaṃ tikkhamandādisaṅkhātaṃ attākārānuvattāpanaṃ, idaṃ kiccaṃ. Evaṃ sotaghānajivhākāyānaṃ. Manindriyassa pana [M 2.0124] sahajātadhammānaṃ attano vasavattāpanaṃ. Jīvitindriyassa sahajātadhammānupālanaṃ. Itthindriyapurisindriyānaṃ itthipurisaliṅganimittakuttākappākārānuvidhānaṃ. Sukhadukkhasomanassadomanassindriyānaṃ sahajātadhamme abhibhavitvā yathāsakaṃ oḷārikākārānupāpanaṃ. Upekkhindriyassa santapaṇītamajjhattākārānupāpanaṃ. Saddhādīnaṃ paṭipakkhābhibhavanaṃ sampayuttadhammānañca pasannākārādibhāvasampāpanaṃ. Anaññātaññassāmītindriyassa saṃyojanattayappahānañceva sampayuttānañca tappahānābhimukhabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Aññindriyassa kāmarāgabyāpādāditanukaraṇappahānañceva sahajātānañca attano vasānuvattāpanaṃ. Aññātāvindriyassa sabbakiccesu ussukkappahānañceva amatābhimukhabhāvapaccayatā ca sampayuttānanti evamettha kiccato vinicchayaṃ vijāniyā.

527. 'By function': If it is asked, what is the function of the faculties? First, for the eye faculty, according to the text, 'The eye base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element and for the states associated with it by way of faculty condition.' Thus its function is that which has to be accomplished by its being a faculty condition, namely, making the eye-consciousness and other states conform to its own nature, that is, to its being keen, dull, and so on. The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties. The function of the mind faculty is making its co-nascent states subject to its control. The function of the life faculty is the guarding of its co-nascent states. The function of the femininity and masculinity faculties is the producing of the aspects of female and male characteristics, signs, deportment, and appearance. The function of the faculties of pleasure, pain, joy, and displeasure is overpowering their co-nascent states and imparting their own respective gross aspects. The function of the equanimity faculty is imparting a peaceful, sublime, and neutral aspect. The function of the faculties of faith and so on is overcoming their opposites and endowing the associated states with the quality of confidence and so on. The function of the faculty 'I shall come to know the unknown' is the abandoning of the three fetters and making its associated states face toward their abandonment. The function of the faculty of gnosis is the abandoning by attenuation of sensual lust, ill will, and so on, and making its co-nascent states conform to its own control. The function of the faculty of one who has final knowledge is the abandoning of concern in all tasks and being a condition for its associated states to face the deathless. Thus one should know the determination here by way of function.

528. Bhūmitoti cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyaitthipurisasukhadukkhadomanassindriyāni cettha kāmāvacarāneva. Manindriyajīvitindriyaupekkhindriyāni saddhāvīriyasatisamādhipaññindriyāni ca catubhūmipariyāpannāni. Somanassindriyaṃ kāmāvacararūpāvacaralokuttaravasena bhūmittayapariyāpannaṃ. Avasāne tīṇi lokuttarānevāti evamettha bhūmitopi vinicchayaṃ vijāneyya. Evaṃ hi vijānanto –

528. 'By plane': Here, the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, femininity, masculinity, pleasure, pain, and displeasure belong only to the sense sphere. The faculties of mind, life, and equanimity, and the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are included in the four planes. The faculty of joy is included in three planes: the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the supramundane. The final three are only supramundane. Thus one should know the determination here by way of plane. For one who knows thus—

Saṃvegabahulo bhikkhu, ṭhito indriyasaṃvare;

Indriyāni pariññāya, dukkhassantaṃ karissatīti.

A bhikkhu full of spiritual urgency, established in restraint of the faculties, having fully understood the faculties, will make an end of suffering.

Idaṃ indriyānaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed account of the faculties.

Saccavitthārakathā

A Detailed Exposition of the Truths

529. Tadanantarāni pana saccānīti cattāri ariyasaccāni – dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhasamudayo [V 2.0121] ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodho ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccanti. Tattha –

529. Next are the truths, that is, the Four Noble Truths: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Herein—

Vibhāgato [M 2.0125] nibbacana, lakkhaṇādippabhedato;

Atthatthuddhārato ceva, anūnādhikato tathā.

By way of division and definition, by way of distinction by characteristic, etc.; by way of meaning and the extraction of the term, and likewise by being neither deficient nor excessive.

Kamato jātiādīnaṃ, nicchayā ñāṇakiccato;

Antogadhānaṃ pabhedā, upamāto catukkato.

By sequence, by the determination of birth and so on, by the function of knowledge; by the classification of what is included, by simile, and by the fourfold method.

Suññatekavidhādīhi, sabhāgavisabhāgato;

Vinicchayo veditabbo, viññunā sāsanakkame.

This determination should be understood by the wise one according to the order of the Teaching: by way of emptiness, the onefold method, and so on, and by way of what is similar and dissimilar.

Tattha vibhāgatoti dukkhādīnaṃ hi cattāro cattāro atthā vibhattā tathā avitathā anaññathā, ye dukkhādīni abhisamentehi abhisametabbā. Yathāha – “dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho, ime cattāro dukkhassa dukkhaṭṭhā tathā avitathā anaññathā. Samudayassa āyūhanaṭṭho nidānaṭṭho saṃyogaṭṭho palibodhaṭṭho. Nirodhassa nissaraṇaṭṭho vivekaṭṭho asaṅkhataṭṭho amataṭṭho. Maggassa niyyānaṭṭho hetuṭṭho dassanaṭṭho adhipateyyaṭṭho. Ime cattāro maggassa maggaṭṭhā tathā avitathā anaññathā”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.8). Tathā “dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho abhisamayaṭṭho”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.11) evamādi. Iti evaṃ vibhattānaṃ catunnaṃ catunnaṃ atthānaṃ vasena dukkhādīni veditabbānīti. Ayaṃ tāvettha vibhāgato vinicchayo.

Herein, as to 'by division': for suffering and the others, four meanings each are distinguished—actual, unfailing, not otherwise—which are to be fully understood by those who fully understand suffering and the others. As it is said: “For suffering, there is the meaning of affliction, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of torment, and the meaning of change. These four are the meanings of suffering as suffering, actual, unfailing, not otherwise. For the origin, there is the meaning of accumulation, the meaning of source, the meaning of bondage, and the meaning of impediment. For cessation, there is the meaning of escape, the meaning of seclusion, the meaning of the unconditioned, and the meaning of the deathless. For the path, there is the meaning of outlet, the meaning of cause, the meaning of vision, and the meaning of dominance. These four are the meanings of the path as the path, actual, unfailing, not otherwise” (PṭsM 2.8). And similarly: “For suffering, there is the meaning of affliction, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of torment, the meaning of change, and the meaning of full understanding” (PṭsM 2.11), and so on. Thus, suffering and the others should be understood by way of these four meanings each that have been distinguished. This, in the first place, is the determination by way of division.

530. Nibbacanalakkhaṇādippabhedatoti ettha pana nibbacanato tāva idha du-iti ayaṃ saddo kucchite dissati. Kucchitaṃ hi puttaṃ dupputtoti vadanti. Khaṃ-saddo pana tucche. Tucchaṃ hi ākāsaṃ “kha”nti vuccati. Idañca paṭhamasaccaṃ kucchitaṃ anekaupaddavādhiṭṭhānato. Tucchaṃ bālajanaparikappitadhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahitato. Tasmā kucchitattā tucchattā ca dukkhanti vuccati.

530. Herein, as to the phrase 'by distinction of definition, characteristic, etc.': First, by way of etymology, the sound 'du-' here is seen in the sense of 'contemptible.' For a contemptible son is called a 'dupputta' (bad son). The sound 'khaṃ,' however, is in the sense of 'empty.' For empty space is called 'kha.' And this first truth is contemptible because it is the basis for many afflictions. It is empty because it is devoid of the permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood imagined by foolish people. Therefore, because it is contemptible and empty, it is called 'dukkha.'

Saṃ-iti [V 2.0122] ca ayaṃ saddo “samāgamo sameta”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.396; vibha. 199) saṃyogaṃ dīpeti. U-iti ayaṃ “uppannaṃ udita”ntiādīsu (dha. sa. 1; mahāva. 84) uppattiṃ. Aya-saddo kāraṇaṃ dīpeti. Idañcāpi dutiyasaccaṃ avasesapaccayasamāyoge sati dukkhassuppattikāraṇaṃ. Iti dukkhassa saṃyoge uppattikāraṇattā dukkhasamudayanti vuccati.

The sound 'saṃ' indicates connection, as in such phrases as 'samāgamo sameta' (DN 2.396; Vbh 199). The sound 'u' indicates arising, as in such phrases as 'uppannaṃ udita' (Dhs 1; Mv 84). The word 'aya' indicates cause. This second truth, too, when the remaining conditions are conjoined, is the cause for the arising of suffering. Thus, because it is the cause for the arising of suffering through connection, it is called 'dukkhasamudaya' (origin of suffering).

Tatiyasaccaṃ [M 2.0126] pana yasmā ni-saddo abhāvaṃ, rodha-saddo ca cārakaṃ dīpeti. Tasmā abhāvo ettha saṃsāracārakasaṅkhātassa dukkharodhassa sabbagatisuññattā, samadhigate vā tasmiṃ saṃsāracārakasaṅkhātassa dukkharodhassa abhāvo hoti, tappaṭipakkhattātipi dukkhanirodhanti vuccati. Dukkhassa vā anuppādanirodhapaccayattā dukkhanirodhanti.

As for the third truth, since the sound 'ni-' indicates absence and the word 'rodha' indicates a prison, it is called 'dukkhanirodha' because here there is the absence of the prison of suffering—called the prison of saṃsāra—due to its being empty of all destinations. Or, when that has been attained, there is an absence of the prison of suffering—called the prison of saṃsāra—and also because it is the opposite of that, it is called 'dukkhanirodha'. Or, because it is a condition for the non-arising cessation of suffering, it is called 'dukkhanirodha'.

Catutthasaccaṃ pana yasmā etaṃ dukkhanirodhaṃ gacchati ārammaṇavasena tadabhimukhabhūtattā, paṭipadā ca hoti dukkhanirodhappattiyā. Tasmā dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti vuccati.

As for the fourth truth, since it proceeds to the cessation of suffering by taking it as its object and being directed towards it, and since it is the path for the attainment of the cessation of suffering, it is therefore called 'the path of practice leading to the cessation of suffering.'

531. Yasmā panetāni buddhādayo ariyā paṭivijjhanti, tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccanti. Yathāha “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, ariyasaccāni. Katamāni…pe… imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri ariyasaccāni. Ariyā imāni paṭivijjhanti, tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccantī”ti. Apica ariyassa saccānītipi ariyasaccāni. Yathāha “sadevake, bhikkhave, loke…pe… manussāya tathāgato ariyo, tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1098). Atha vā etesaṃ abhisambuddhattā ariyabhāvasiddhitopi ariyasaccāni. Yathāha – “imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ abhisambuddhattā tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho ariyoti vuccatī”ti. Apica kho pana ariyāni saccānītipi ariyasaccāni. Ariyānīti tathāni avitathāni avisaṃvādakānīti attho. Yathāha – “imāni kho, bhikkhave, cattāri ariyasaccāni tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni, tasmā ariyasaccānīti vuccantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1097) evamettha nibbacanato vinicchayo veditabbo.

531. Because noble ones, such as the Buddhas, penetrate these, they are called noble truths. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, there are these four noble truths. What four? … These, bhikkhus, are the four noble truths. The noble ones penetrate them, therefore they are called noble truths.' Furthermore, they are noble truths because they are the truths of the Noble One. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas … the Tathāgata is the Noble One; therefore they are called noble truths.' Alternatively, they are noble truths because the state of a noble one is achieved through full awakening to them. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, it is because he has been fully awakened to these four noble truths as they really are that the Tathāgata is called the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the Noble One.' Moreover, they are noble truths because they are truths that are noble. 'Noble' means actual, not false, and non-deceptive. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, these four noble truths are actual, not false, not otherwise; therefore they are called noble truths.' Thus the determination here should be understood by way of the word's meaning.

532. Kathaṃ lakkhaṇādippabhedato? Ettha hi bādhanalakkhaṇaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, santāpanarasaṃ, pavattipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Pabhavalakkhaṇaṃ samudayasaccaṃ, anupacchedakaraṇarasaṃ, palibodhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Santilakkhaṇaṃ [V 2.0123] nirodhasaccaṃ, accutirasaṃ, animittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Niyyānalakkhaṇaṃ maggasaccaṃ, kilesappahānarasaṃ, vuṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Apica pavattipavattananivattinivattanalakkhaṇāni paṭipāṭiyā. Tathā saṅkhatataṇhā asaṅkhatadassanalakkhaṇāni cāti evamettha lakkhaṇādippabhedato vinicchayo veditabbo.

532. How by way of distinction of characteristic, etc.? Herein, the truth of suffering has the characteristic of affliction, the function of tormenting, and manifestation as occurrence. The truth of the origin has the characteristic of originating, the function of preventing interruption, and manifestation as an impediment. The truth of cessation has the characteristic of peace, the function of being deathless, and manifestation as the signless. The truth of the path has the characteristic of leading out, the function of abandoning the defilements, and manifestation as emergence. Moreover, their characteristics in sequence are: occurrence, causing to occur, cessation, and causing to cease. Likewise, their characteristics are the conditioned, craving, the unconditioned, and vision. Thus the determination should be understood here by way of distinction of characteristic, etc.

533. Atthatthuddhārato [M 2.0127] cevāti ettha pana atthato tāva ko saccaṭṭhoti ce? Yo paññācakkhunā upaparikkhamānānaṃ māyāva viparīto, marīciva visaṃvādako, titthiyānaṃ attāva anupalabbhasabhāvo ca na hoti, atha kho bādhanappabhavasantiniyyānappakārena tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvena ariyañāṇassa gocaro hotiyeva. Esa aggilakkhaṇaṃ viya, lokapakati viya ca tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvo saccaṭṭhoti veditabbo. Yathāha – “idaṃ dukkhanti, bhikkhave, tathametaṃ avitathametaṃ anaññathameta”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.1090) vitthāro. Apica –

533. As to 'by meaning and by extraction of the term': Herein, first, as to meaning, if it is asked, 'What is the meaning of truth?' It is that which, for those who investigate with the eye of wisdom, is not perverse like an illusion, not deceptive like a mirage, and not of an imperceptible nature like the self of the sectarians; but rather, by its nature of being actual, not perverse, and real, in the modes of affliction, originating, peace, and leading out, it does indeed become the domain of noble knowledge. This nature of being actual, not perverse, and real, like the characteristic of fire and the nature of the world, should be understood as the meaning of truth. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, "this is suffering"—this is actual, this is not false, this is not otherwise,' and so on in detail. Moreover:

Nābādhakaṃ yato dukkhaṃ, dukkhā aññaṃ na bādhakaṃ;

Bādhakattaniyāmena, tato saccamidaṃ mataṃ.

Since suffering is never non-afflicting, and nothing other than suffering afflicts; by the principle of its being the afflicter, this is therefore considered a truth.

Taṃ vinā nāññato dukkhaṃ, na hoti na ca taṃ tato;

Dukkhahetuniyāmena, iti saccaṃ visattikā.

Without it, suffering arises from no other cause, nor is it that suffering does not arise from it; by the principle of being suffering's cause, craving is thus considered a truth.

Nāññā nibbānato santi, santaṃ na ca na taṃ yato;

Santabhāvaniyāmena, tato saccamidaṃ mataṃ.

Since there is no peace apart from Nibbāna, and it is not that it is not peace; by the principle of its nature as peace, this is therefore considered a truth.

Maggā aññaṃ na niyyānaṃ, aniyyāno na cāpi so;

Tacchaniyyānabhāvattā, iti so saccasammato.

There is no escape other than the Path, nor is the Path a non-escape; because its nature is true escape, it is thus regarded as a truth.

Iti tacchāvipallāsa, bhūtabhāvaṃ catūsvapi;

Dukkhādīsvavisesena, saccaṭṭhaṃ āhu paṇḍitāti.

Thus the wise declare that the meaning of truth, without distinction in all four beginning with suffering, is their nature of being actual, unperverted, and real.

Evaṃ atthato vinicchayo veditabbo.

Thus the determination by way of meaning should be understood.

534. Kathaṃ [V 2.0124] atthuddhārato? Idhāyaṃ sacca-saddo anekesu atthesu dissati. Seyyathidaṃ – “saccaṃ bhaṇe na kujjheyyā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 224) vācāsacce. “Sacce ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā cā”tiādīsu (jā. 2.21.433) viratisacce. “Kasmā nu saccāni vadanti nānā pavādiyāse kusalāvadānā”tiādīsu (su. ni. 891) diṭṭhisacce. “Ekaṃ hi saccaṃ na dutiya”ntiādīsu (su. ni. 890) paramatthasacce nibbāne ceva magge ca. “Catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ kati kusalā”tiādīsu (vibha. 216) ariyasacce. Svāyamidhāpi ariyasacce vattatīti evamettha atthuddhāratopi vinicchayo veditabbo.

534. How by extraction of the term? Here this word 'truth' (sacca) is seen in many senses. For example: in 'One should speak the truth, one should not be angry' (Dhp 224), it means verbal truth. In 'Ascetics and brahmins established in truth' (Ja 2.21.433), it means the truth of abstinence. In 'Why do the various disputants say that the truths are many?' (Sn 891), it means the truth of views. In 'Truth is one, there is no second' (Sn 890), it means ultimate truth, that is, Nibbāna and the path. In 'Among the four noble truths, how many are wholesome?' (Vbh 216), it means the noble truths. Here, too, this word applies in the sense of the noble truths. Thus the determination should be understood here also by way of extraction of the term.

535. Anūnādhikatoti [M 2.0128] kasmā pana cattāreva ariyasaccāni vuttāni anūnāni anadhikānīti ce? Aññassāsambhavato aññatarassa ca apaneyyābhāvato. Na hi etehi aññaṃ adhikaṃ vā, etesaṃ vā ekampi apanetabbaṃ sambhoti. Yathāha – “idha, bhikkhave, āgaccheyya samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ‘netaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, aññaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ. Ahametaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ paññapessāmī’ti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”tiādi. Yathā cāha – “yo hi koci, bhikkhave, samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃ vadeyya ‘netaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭhamaṃ ariyasaccaṃ yaṃ samaṇena gotamena desitaṃ, ahametaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭhamaṃ ariyasaccaṃ paccakkhāya aññaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭhamaṃ ariyasaccaṃ paññapessāmī’ti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.1086).

535. Why, it may be asked, were exactly Four Noble Truths stated—no fewer and no more? Because no other is possible, and because none of them can be removed. For it is not possible that there should be another in addition to these, or that even one of these should be removed. As it is said: 'Here, bhikkhus, should any ascetic or brahmin come and say, "This is not the Noble Truth of Suffering; the Noble Truth of Suffering is something else. Having set aside this Noble Truth of Suffering, I will proclaim another Noble Truth of Suffering," that is not possible,' and so on. And as it is said: 'Bhikkhus, if any ascetic or brahmin should say, "This is not the first Noble Truth of Suffering taught by the ascetic Gotama; having rejected this first Noble Truth of Suffering, I will proclaim another first Noble Truth of Suffering," that is not possible,' and so on (Saṃ. ni. 5.1086).

Apica pavattimācikkhanto bhagavā sahetukaṃ ācikkhi, nivattiñca saupāyaṃ. Iti pavattinivattitadubhayahetūnaṃ etaparamato cattāreva vuttāni. Tathā pariññeyyapahātabbasacchikātabbabhāvetabbānaṃ, taṇhāvatthutaṇhātaṇhānirodhataṇhānirodhupāyānaṃ, ālayaālayārāmatāālayasamugghātaālayasamugghātupāyānañca vasenāpi cattāreva vuttānīti evamettha anūnādhikato vinicchayo veditabbo.

Furthermore, when the Blessed One explained the process of existence, he explained it with its cause; and when he explained cessation, he explained it with its means. Thus, since the process of existence, its cause, cessation, and its means constitute the full extent, only four truths were stated. Likewise, only four were stated in terms of what is to be fully understood, what is to be abandoned, what is to be realized, and what is to be developed; in terms of the basis of craving, craving, the cessation of craving, and the means to the cessation of craving; and in terms of attachment, delight in attachment, the uprooting of attachment, and the means to the uprooting of attachment. Thus the analysis here should be understood as being neither deficient nor excessive.

536. Kamatoti ayampi desanākkamova. Ettha ca oḷārikattā, sabbasattasādhāraṇattā ca suviññeyyanti dukkhasaccaṃ paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasseva hetudassanatthaṃ tadanantaraṃ samudayasaccaṃ. Hetunirodhā phalanirodhoti ñāpanatthaṃ tato nirodhasaccaṃ. Tadadhigamupāyadassanatthaṃ ante maggasaccaṃ. Bhavasukhassādagadhitānaṃ vā sattānaṃ saṃvegajananatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ dukkhamāha. Taṃ neva akataṃ āgacchati[V 2.0125], na issaranimmānādito hoti, ito pana hotīti ñāpanatthaṃ tadanantaraṃ samudayaṃ. Tato sahetukena dukkhena abhibhūtattā saṃviggamānasānaṃ dukkhanissaraṇagavesīnaṃ nissaraṇadassanena assāsajananatthaṃ nirodhaṃ. Tato nirodhādhigamatthaṃ nirodhasampāpakaṃ magganti evamettha kamato vinicchayo veditabbo.

536. As to order: this too is the order of the teaching. Here, the truth of suffering was stated first because it is gross, common to all beings, and easily understood. Immediately after, the truth of the origin was stated to show its cause. Then, the truth of cessation was stated to make it known that with the cessation of the cause there is the cessation of the effect. Finally, the truth of the path was stated to show the means for attaining that cessation. Alternatively, to arouse a sense of spiritual urgency in beings greedy for the pleasure of existence, he first stated suffering. Then, to make it known that this suffering does not come about without a cause, nor does it arise from the creation of a lord, but that it arises from this, he stated the origin. Then, to bring comfort to those who are overwhelmed by suffering with its cause, whose minds are agitated and who are seeking an escape from suffering, by showing them the escape, he stated cessation. Then, for the purpose of attaining cessation, he stated the path that leads to cessation. Thus the analysis concerning the order should be understood.

537. Jātiādīnaṃ nicchayāti ye te ariyasaccāni niddisantena bhagavatā “jātipi dukkhā, jarāpi dukkhā, maraṇampi dukkhaṃ, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsāpi dukkhā, appiyehi sampayogo dukkho, piyehi [M 2.0129] vippayogo dukkho, yampicchaṃ na labhati tampi dukkhaṃ, saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti (vibha. 190) dukkhaniddese dvādasa dhammā, “yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobbhavikā nandīrāgasahagatā tatratatrābhinandinī. Seyyathidaṃ, kāmataṇhā, bhavataṇhā, vibhavataṇhā”ti (vibha. 203) samudayaniddese tividhā taṇhā, “yo tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodho cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo”ti (vibha. 204) evaṃ nirodhaniddese atthato ekameva nibbānaṃ, “katamaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminīpaṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ, ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo.
