Seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhī”ti (vibha. 205) evaṃ magganiddese aṭṭha dhammāti iti catunnaṃ saccānaṃ niddese jātiādayo dhammā vuttā, tesaṃ jātiādīnaṃ nicchayāpi ettha vinicchayo veditabbo.

537. As to the ascertainment of birth and so on: When the Blessed One pointed out the Noble Truths, in the exposition of suffering he mentioned twelve items: 'Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the unloved is suffering, separation from the loved is suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering; in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.' In the exposition of the origin, he mentioned the threefold craving: 'It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.' In the exposition of cessation, he mentioned what is in meaning Nibbāna alone: 'It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it.' In the exposition of the path, he mentioned eight factors: 'What is the Noble Truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view ... right concentration.' Thus, in the exposition of the four truths, phenomena such as birth have been stated. Herein, the analysis should also be understood as the ascertainment of these phenomena such as birth.

Dukkhaniddesakathā

The Discourse on the Exposition of Suffering

Jātiniddeso

Exposition of Birth

Seyyathidaṃ, ayañhi jāti-saddo anekattho. Tathā hesa “ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo”ti (dī. ni. 1.244; pārā. 12) ettha bhave āgato. “Atthi, visākhe, nigaṇṭhā nāma samaṇajātī”ti (a. ni. 3.71) ettha nikāye. “Jāti dvīhi khandhehi saṅgahitā”ti (dhātu. 71) ettha saṅkhatalakkhaṇe. “Yaṃ mātukucchismiṃ paṭhamaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ, paṭhamaṃ viññāṇaṃ pātubhūtaṃ, tadupādāya sāvassa jātī”ti (mahāva. 124) ettha paṭisandhiyaṃ. “Sampatijāto, ānanda, bodhisatto”ti (ma. ni. 3.207) ettha pasūtiyaṃ. “Akkhitto anupakuṭṭho jātivādenā”ti (dī. ni. 1.331) ettha kule. “Yatohaṃ, bhagini, ariyāya jātiyā jāto”ti (ma. ni. 2.351) ettha ariyasīle.

That is to say, this word 'birth' has many meanings. For it occurs in the sense of existence, as in 'one birth, two births'; in the sense of a group, as in 'There is, Visākha, a class of ascetics called the Nigaṇṭhas'; in the sense of a conditioned characteristic, as in 'Birth is comprised by two aggregates'; in the sense of rebirth-linking, as in 'Whatever is the first mind arisen, the first consciousness manifested in the mother's womb, from that point on is his birth'; in the sense of parturition, as in 'The Bodhisatta has just been born, Ānanda'; in the sense of lineage, as in 'not reviled, not scorned on account of birth'; and in the sense of noble virtue, as in 'Sister, from when I was born with the noble birth'.

538. Svāyamidha [V 2.0126] gabbhaseyyakānaṃ paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya yāva mātukucchimhā nikkhamanaṃ, tāva pavattesu khandhesu. Itaresaṃ paṭisandhikhandhesvevāti daṭṭhabbo. Ayampi ca pariyāyakathāva. Nippariyāyato pana tattha tattha nibbattamānānaṃ sattānaṃ ye ye khandhā pātubhavanti, tesaṃ tesaṃ paṭhamapātubhāvo jāti nāma.

538. Herein, for womb-born beings, it should be understood as applying to the aggregates in continuity from rebirth-linking up to the emergence from the mother's womb. For other beings, it should be understood as applying only to the aggregates at rebirth-linking. This, too, is a figurative explanation. But in the ultimate sense, for beings reborn here and there, the first appearance of whichever aggregates manifest is called birth.

Sā [M 2.0130] panesā tattha tattha bhave paṭhamābhinibbattilakkhaṇā, niyyātanarasā, atītabhavato idha ummujjanapaccupaṭṭhānā, dukkhavicittatāpaccupaṭṭhānā vā.

This birth has the characteristic of initial generation in various kinds of existence, the function of launching into a new existence, and it is manifested as emerging here from a past existence, or as the diversity of suffering.

539. Kasmā panesā dukkhāti ce? Anekesaṃ dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvato. Anekāni hi dukkhāni. Seyyathidaṃ – dukkhadukkhaṃ, vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ, saṅkhāradukkhaṃ, paṭicchannadukkhaṃ, appaṭicchannadukkhaṃ, pariyāyadukkhaṃ, nippariyāyadukkhanti.

539. But why is it suffering? Because it is the basis for many kinds of suffering. For there are many kinds of suffering, namely: suffering as suffering, suffering due to change, suffering due to formations, concealed suffering, unconcealed suffering, indirect suffering, and direct suffering.

Tattha kāyikacetasikā dukkhā vedanāsabhāvato ca nāmato ca dukkhattā dukkhadukkhanti vuccati.

Herein, painful bodily and mental feelings are called 'suffering as suffering' because they are suffering both in their intrinsic nature and in name.

Sukhā vedanā vipariṇāmena dukkhuppattihetuto vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ.

Pleasant feeling is 'suffering due to change' because it is a cause for the arising of suffering when it changes.

Upekkhā vedanā ceva avasesā ca tebhūmakā saṅkhārā udayabbayappaṭipīḷitattā saṅkhāradukkhaṃ. Kaṇṇasūladantasūlarāgajapariḷāhadosajapariḷāhādi kāyikacetasiko ābādho pucchitvā jānitabbato upakkamassa ca apākaṭabhāvato paṭicchannadukkhaṃ nāma. Apākaṭadukkhantipi vuccati.

Neutral feeling and the remaining formations pertaining to the three planes are 'suffering due to formations' because they are oppressed by arising and passing away. Bodily and mental afflictions such as earache, toothache, the fever born of lust, and the fever born of hate, are called 'concealed suffering' because they can only be known by asking and because their cause is not manifest. It is also called 'non-manifest suffering.'

Dvattiṃsakammakāraṇādisamuṭṭhāno ābādho apucchitvāva jānitabbato upakkamassa ca pākaṭabhāvato appaṭicchannadukkhaṃ nāma. Pākaṭadukkhantipi vuccati.

An affliction originating from such things as the thirty-two kinds of torture is called 'unconcealed suffering' because it can be known without asking and because its cause is manifest. It is also called 'manifest suffering.'

Ṭhapetvā dukkhadukkhaṃ sesaṃ dukkhasaccavibhaṅge āgataṃ jātiādi sabbampi tassa tassa dukkhassa vatthubhāvato pariyāyadukkhaṃ. Dukkhadukkhaṃ pana nippariyāyadukkhanti vuccati.

Excluding suffering-as-suffering, all the rest, such as birth and so on, which is mentioned in the Analysis of the Truth of Suffering, is suffering in a figurative sense because it is the basis for this or that suffering. Suffering-as-suffering, however, is called suffering in a direct sense.

Tatrāyaṃ [V 2.0127] jāti yaṃ taṃ bālapaṇḍitasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 3.246 ādayo) bhagavatāpi upamāvasena pakāsitaṃ āpāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ, yañca sugatiyampi manussaloke gabbhokkantimūlakādibhedaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, tassa vatthubhāvato dukkhā.

Herein, this birth is suffering because it is the basis for the suffering in the plane of misery—which the Blessed One has explained by way of similes in the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta and other discourses—and for the suffering that arises even in a good destination, in the human world, which is of different kinds beginning with that rooted in conception in the womb.

540. Tatridaṃ gabbhokkantimūlakādibhedaṃ dukkhaṃ – ayaṃ hi satto mātukucchimhi nibbattamāno na uppalapadumapuṇḍarīkādīsu nibbattati, atha kho heṭṭhā āmāsayassa upari pakkāsayassa udarapaṭalapiṭṭhikaṇṭakānaṃ vemajjhe paramasambādhe tibbandhakārenānākuṇapagandhaparibhāvitaparamaduggandhapavanavicarite adhimattajegucche kucchipadese pūtimacchapūtikummāsacandanikādīsu kimi viya nibbattati. So tattha nibbatto dasa māse mātukucchisambhavena usmanā puṭapākaṃ viya paccamāno piṭṭhapiṇḍi viya sediyamāno samiñjanapasāraṇādirahito adhimattaṃ dukkhamanubhotīti, idaṃ tāva gabbhokkantimūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

540. Herein, this suffering rooted in conception in the womb and so on is as follows: This being, when reborn in the mother's womb, is not reborn in a blue, red, or white lotus. Rather, it is reborn in a place of extreme confinement and utter darkness, below the stomach, above the rectum, between the belly-lining and the backbone—a most foul-smelling place pervaded by various stenches and foul airs, an exceedingly disgusting region of the belly, like a worm in rotting fish, putrid gruel, a cesspool, and the like. Having been reborn there, for ten months it is cooked by the heat originating in the mother's womb like a pudding being cooked in a leaf-wrap, steamed like a lump of dough, and being unable to stretch or bend, it experiences extreme suffering. This, then, is the suffering rooted in conception in the womb.

Yaṃ [M 2.0131] pana so mātu sahasā upakkhalanagamananisīdanavuṭṭhānaparivattanādīsu surādhuttahatthagato eḷako viya ahituṇḍikahatthagato sappapotako viya ca ākaḍḍhanaparikaḍḍhanaodhūnananiddhūnanādinā upakkamena adhimattaṃ dukkhamanubhavati, yañca mātu sītūdakapānakāle sītanarakupapanno viya, uṇhayāgubhattādiajjhoharaṇakāle aṅgāravuṭṭhisamparikiṇṇo viya, loṇambilādiajjhoharaṇakāle khārāpaṭicchakādikammakāraṇapatto viya tibbaṃ dukkhamanubhoti, idaṃ gabbhapariharaṇamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

Furthermore, when that being, due to the mother’s sudden stumbling, walking, sitting, rising, turning, and so on, is subjected to actions like being dragged towards, dragged all around, shaken down, and shaken out, like a ram in the hands of a drunkard or a young snake in the hands of a snake charmer, it experiences extreme suffering. And when the mother drinks cold water, it feels as if it has fallen into a cold hell. When she consumes hot gruel, rice, and so on, it feels as if it is being showered with a rain of embers. When she eats salty, sour, and other such foods, it feels as if it is being subjected to a punishment with caustic liquids, and it experiences intense suffering. This is the suffering rooted in being carried in the womb.

Yaṃ panassa mūḷhagabbhāya mātuyā mittāmaccasuhajjādīhipi adassanārahe dukkhuppattiṭṭhāne chedanaphālanādīhi dukkhaṃ uppajjati, idaṃ gabbhavipattimūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

Furthermore, whatever suffering arises for this being from cutting, splitting, and the like, when its mother has an obstructed labor, in a place where suffering arises that is unfit to be seen even by friends, companions, and loved ones—this is the suffering rooted in a calamity in the womb.

Yaṃ vijāyamānāya mātuyā kammajehi vātehi parivattetvā narakapapātaṃ viya atibhayānakaṃ yonimaggaṃ paṭipātiyamānassa paramasambādhena yonimukhena tāḷacchiggaḷena viya nikkaḍḍhiyamānassa mahānāgassa narakasattassa viya ca saṅghātapabbatehi vicuṇṇiyamānassa dukkhaṃ uppajjati, idaṃ vijāyanamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

The suffering that arises for the being who, while its mother is giving birth, is turned around by the kamma-born winds and pushed down the extremely terrifying birth canal as if into a precipice in hell; who is dragged out through the extremely constricted mouth of the womb as if a great elephant through a keyhole; and who is crushed as if by the clashing mountains like a being in hell—this is the suffering rooted in parturition.

Yaṃ pana jātassa taruṇavaṇasadisasukhumālasarīrassa hatthagahaṇanahāpanadhovanacoḷaparimajjanādikāle [V 2.0128] sūcimukhakhuradhārāhi vijjhanaphālanasadisaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, idaṃ mātukucchito bahinikkhamanamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ.

Furthermore, the suffering that arises for the newborn, whose body is delicate and tender like a fresh wound, when, at the time of being held by the hand, bathed, washed, wiped with a cloth, and so on, it feels a pain like being pierced by needle points and cut by razor blades—this is the suffering rooted in exiting from the mother's womb.

Yaṃ tato paraṃ pavattiyaṃ attanāva attānaṃ vadhentassa acelakavatādivasena ātāpanaparitāpanānuyogamanuyuttassa, kodhavasena abhuñjantassa, ubbandhantassa ca dukkhaṃ uppajjati, idaṃ attūpakkamamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ pana parato vadhabandhanādīni anubhavantassa uppajjati, idaṃ parūpakkamamūlakaṃ dukkhanti.

The suffering that arises thereafter in the course of life for one who torments oneself, for one who engages in the practice of mortification and torment by such means as the vow of nakedness, for one who does not eat out of anger, and for one who hangs oneself—this is suffering rooted in one's own assault. But the suffering that arises when one experiences execution, imprisonment, and the like from others—this is suffering rooted in the assault of others.

Iti imassa sabbassāpi dukkhassa ayaṃ jāti vatthumeva hoti.

Thus, this birth is indeed the basis for all this suffering.

541. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

541. Therefore it is said:

Jāyetha no ce narakesu satto,

Tattaggidāhādikamappasayhaṃ;

Labhetha dukkhaṃ nu kuhiṃ patiṭṭhaṃ,

Iccāha dukkhāti munīdha jātiṃ.

If a being were not born in the hells, where indeed could the unbearable suffering from the burning of hot fire and so on find a footing? Thus the Sage here has declared birth to be suffering.

Dukkhaṃ [M 2.0132] tiracchesu kasāpatoda-

Daṇḍābhighātādibhavaṃ anekaṃ;

Yaṃ taṃ kathaṃ tattha bhaveyya jātiṃ,

Vinā tahiṃ jāti tatopi dukkhā.

The manifold suffering in the animal realm, arising from whips, goads, beatings with sticks, and so on—how could that be there without birth? Therefore, birth is also suffering.

Petesu dukkhaṃ pana khuppipāsā-

Vātātapādippabhavaṃ vicittaṃ;

Yasmā ajātassa na tattha atthi,

Tasmāpi dukkhaṃ muni jātimāha.

Furthermore, the diverse suffering among the petas, originating from hunger and thirst, wind and sun, and so on—since this does not exist for one who is not born there, therefore, too, the Sage has declared birth to be suffering.

Tibbandhakāre [V 2.0129] ca asayhasīte,

Lokantare yaṃ asuresu dukkhaṃ;

Na taṃ bhave tattha na cassa jāti,

Yato ayaṃ jāti tatopi dukkhā.

The suffering in the Lokantarika hell, with its intense darkness and unbearable cold, and that among the asuras—that suffering would not exist if there were no birth there. Therefore, this birth is also suffering.

Yañcāpi gūthanarake viya mātugabbhe,

Satto vasaṃ ciramato bahi nikkhamañca;

Pappoti dukkhamatighoramidampi natthi,

Jātiṃ vinā itipi jāti ayañhi dukkhā.

And the extremely horrible suffering that a being obtains by dwelling for a long time in the mother's womb, which is like a cesspool hell, and then by exiting from it—this too does not exist without birth. Thus, indeed, this birth is suffering.

Kiṃ bhāsitena bahunā nanu yaṃ kuhiñci,

Atthīdha kiñcidapi dukkhamidaṃ kadāci;

Nevatthi jātivirahena yato mahesi,

Dukkhāti sabbapaṭhamaṃ imamāha jātinti.

What is the use of saying much? Surely, whatever suffering of any kind exists here anywhere at any time, it does not exist in the absence of birth. Therefore the Great Sage declared this birth, first of all, to be suffering.

Ayaṃ tāva jātiyaṃ vinicchayo.

This, for now, is the determination of birth.

Jarāniddeso

Exposition of Aging

542. Jarāpi dukkhāti ettha duvidhā jarā saṅkhatalakkhaṇañca, khaṇḍiccādisammato santatiyaṃ ekabhavapariyāpannakhandhapurāṇabhāvo ca, sā idha adhippetā. Sā panesā jarā khandhaparipākalakkhaṇā, maraṇūpanayanarasā, yobbanavināsapaccupaṭṭhānā. Dukkhā saṅkhāradukkhabhāvato ceva dukkhavatthuto ca[M 2.0133]. Yaṃ hi aṅgapaccaṅgasithilībhāvaindriyavikāravirūpatāyobbanavināsabalūpaghātasatimativippavāsaparaparibhavādianekapaccayaṃ kāyikacetasikadukkhaṃ uppajjati, jarā tassa vatthu. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

542. “Aging, too, is suffering.” Here, aging is of two kinds: the characteristic of conditioned phenomena, and the state of the aggregates included in a single lifetime becoming old, conventionally known as having broken teeth and so on. The latter type is intended here. This aging has the characteristic of the maturing of the aggregates, its function is to lead to death, and its manifestation is the destruction of youth. It is suffering both because it is the suffering inherent in formations and because it is a basis for suffering. For whatever physical and mental suffering arises due to many causes—such as the loosening of the limbs, the impairment of the faculties, disfigurement, the destruction of youth, the decline of strength, the loss of memory and intelligence, and contempt from others—aging is the basis for it. Therefore it is said:

“Aṅgānaṃ sithilībhāvā, indriyānaṃ vikārato;

Yobbanassa vināsena, balassa upaghātato.

“From the loosening of the limbs, from the impairment of the faculties, from the destruction of youth, from the decline of strength,

“Vippavāsā [V 2.0130] satādīnaṃ, puttadārehi attano;

Apasādanīyato ceva, bhiyyo bālattapattiyā.

From the loss of memory and so on, from being rejected by one’s own children and wife, and from frequently lapsing into childishness,

“Pappoti dukkhaṃ yaṃ macco, kāyikaṃ mānasaṃ tathā;

Sabbametaṃ jarāhetu, yasmā tasmā jarā dukhā”ti.

Whatever suffering a mortal encounters, both bodily and mental, all this has aging as its cause; therefore, aging is suffering.”

Ayaṃ jarāyaṃ vinicchayo.

This is the determination on aging.

Maraṇaniddeso

Exposition on Death

543. Maraṇampi dukkhanti etthāpi duvidhaṃ maraṇaṃ saṅkhatalakkhaṇañca, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “jarāmaraṇaṃ dvīhi khandhehi saṅgahita”nti (dhātu. 71). Ekabhavapariyāpannajīvitindriyappabandhavicchedo ca, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “niccaṃ maraṇato bhaya”nti (su. ni. 581). Taṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Jātipaccayā maraṇaṃ upakkamamaraṇaṃ sarasamaraṇaṃ āyukkhayamaraṇaṃ puññakkhayamaraṇantipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Tayidaṃ cutilakkhaṇaṃ, viyogarasaṃ, gativippavāsapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Dukkhassa pana vatthubhāvato dukkhanti veditabbaṃ. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

543. Death, too, is suffering. Here, death is of two kinds: the characteristic of the conditioned—with reference to which it is said, “aging and death are included in two aggregates”—and the cutting off of the continuity of the life faculty within a single existence—with reference to which it is said, “there is always fear of death.” The latter is intended here. Death conditioned by birth, untimely death, natural death, death due to the exhaustion of the life-span, and death due to the exhaustion of merit are also its names. It has the characteristic of passing away, the function of separation, and manifests as departure from the present destination. It should be understood as suffering because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, it is said:

“Pāpassa pāpakammādi-nimittamanupassato;

Bhaddassāpasahantassa, viyogaṃ piyavatthukaṃ;

Mīyamānassa yaṃ dukkhaṃ, mānasaṃ avisesato.

For the evil person who sees the sign of his evil deeds and so on, and for the good person who cannot bear separation from what is dear, there is the mental suffering of one who is dying.

Sabbesañcāpi yaṃ sandhi-bandhanacchedanādikaṃ;

Vitujjamānamammānaṃ, hoti dukkhaṃ sarīrajaṃ.

And for all without distinction, there is the bodily suffering that occurs from the cutting of joints and ligaments and so on, and from the piercing of vital spots.

Asayhamappatikāraṃ, dukkhassetassidaṃ yato;

Maraṇaṃ vatthu tenetaṃ, dukkhamicceva bhāsita”nti.

Since death is the basis for this unbearable and irremediable suffering, therefore it is called suffering.

Ayaṃ maraṇe vinicchayo.

This is the determination on death.

Sokādiniddesā

Expositions on Sorrow and So On

544. Sokādīsu [M 2.0134][V 2.0131] soko nāma ñātibyasanādīhi phuṭṭhassa cittasantāpo. So kiñcāpi atthato domanassameva hoti. Evaṃ santepi antonijjhānalakkhaṇo, cetaso parijjhāpanaraso, anusocanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Dukkho pana dukkhadukkhato dukkhavatthuto ca. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

544. Among sorrow and so on, sorrow is the mental scorching of one affected by the loss of relatives and the like. Although in meaning it is just grief, it has the characteristic of inward burning, the function of scorching the mind, and manifests as repeated grieving. It is suffering both because it is suffering as pain and because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, it is said:

“Sattānaṃ hadayaṃ soko, visasallaṃva tujjati;

Aggitattova nārāco, bhusaṃva dahate puna.

Sorrow pierces the hearts of beings like a poisoned arrow; like a fire-heated iron dart, it burns them fiercely again.

“Samāvahati ca byādhi-jarāmaraṇabhedanaṃ;

Dukkhampi vividhaṃ yasmā, tasmā dukkhoti vuccatī”ti.

And since it brings on sickness, aging, death, and ruin, and also various kinds of suffering, therefore it is called suffering.

Ayaṃ soke vinicchayo.

This is the determination on sorrow.

Paridevo

Lamentation

545. Paridevo nāma ñātibyasanādīhi phuṭṭhassa vacīpalāpo. So lālappanalakkhaṇo, guṇadosakittanaraso, sambhamapaccupaṭṭhāno. Dukkho pana saṅkhāradukkhabhāvato dukkhavatthuto ca. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

545. Lamentation is the verbal wailing of one affected by the loss of relatives and the like. It has the characteristic of wailing, the function of proclaiming virtues and faults, and manifests as bewilderment. It is suffering because it is suffering due to formations and because it is a basis for suffering. Therefore, it is said:

“Yaṃ sokasallavihato paridevamāno,

Kaṇṭhoṭṭhatālutalasosajamappasayhaṃ;

Bhiyyodhimattamadhigacchatiyeva dukkhaṃ,

Dukkhoti tena bhagavā paridevamāhā”ti.

Struck by the arrow of sorrow, one who is lamenting, unable to bear the dryness arising in the throat, lips, and palate, only attains suffering to a greater degree; therefore the Blessed One has declared lamentation to be suffering.

Ayaṃ parideve vinicchayo.

This is the determination on lamentation.

Dukkhaṃ

Pain

546. Dukkhaṃ [V 2.0132] nāma kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ, taṃ kāyapīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ, duppaññānaṃ domanassakaraṇarasaṃ, kāyikābādhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Dukkhaṃ pana dukkhadukkhato mānasadukkhāvahanato ca. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

546. Pain means bodily pain. It has the characteristic of oppressing the body, the function of causing grief to the unwise, and manifests as bodily affliction. It is suffering because it is suffering as pain and because it brings on mental suffering. Hence it is said:

“Pīḷeti kāyikamidaṃ, dukkhañca mānasaṃ bhiyyo;

Janayati yasmā tasmā, dukkhanti visesato vutta”nti.

Since this bodily pain oppresses and generates further mental suffering, therefore it is specifically called pain.

Ayaṃ dukkhe vinicchayo.

This is the determination on pain.

Domanassaṃ

Grief

547. Domanassaṃ [M 2.0135] nāma mānasaṃ dukkhaṃ. Taṃ cittapīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ, manovighātarasaṃ, mānasabyādhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Dukkhaṃ pana dukkhadukkhato kāyikadukkhāvahanato ca. Cetodukkhasamappitā hi kese pakiriya kandanti, urāni paṭipisanti, āvaṭṭanti, vivaṭṭanti, uddhaṃpādaṃ papatanti, satthaṃ āharanti, visaṃ khādanti, rajjuyā ubbandhanti, aggiṃ pavisantīti taṃ nānappakārakaṃ dukkhamanubhavanti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

547. Grief is mental suffering. It has the characteristic of oppressing the mind, the function of mental affliction, and manifests as mental illness. It is suffering because it is suffering as pain and because it brings on bodily suffering. For those overcome by mental pain tear their hair and weep, beat their breasts, toss about, fall headlong, take up a weapon, eat poison, hang themselves with a rope, or enter a fire, thus experiencing various kinds of suffering. Therefore, it is said:

“Pīḷeti yato cittaṃ, kāyassa ca pīḷanaṃ samāvahati;

Dukkhanti domanassaṃ, vidomanassā tato āhū”ti.

Since it oppresses the mind and brings on oppression of the body, therefore those who are free from grief have called it suffering.

Ayaṃ domanasse vinicchayo.

This is the determination on grief.

Upāyāso

Despair

548. Upāyāso nāma ñātibyasanādīhi phuṭṭhassa adhimattacetodukkhappabhāvito dosoyeva. Saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpanno eko dhammoti eke. So cittaparidahanalakkhaṇo, nitthunanaraso[V 2.0133], visādapaccupaṭṭhāno. Dukkho pana saṅkhāradukkhabhāvato cittaparidahanato kāyavisādanato ca. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

548. Despair is a form of aversion produced by excessive mental suffering in one affected by the loss of relatives and the like. Some say it is a single state included in the aggregate of formations. It has the characteristic of scorching the mind, the function of groaning, and manifests as dejection. It is suffering because it is suffering due to formations, because of the scorching of the mind, and because of the collapse of the body. Therefore, it is said:

“Cittassa ca paridahanā, kāyassa visādanā ca adhimattaṃ;

Yaṃ dukkhamupāyāso, janeti dukkho tato vutto”ti.

Since despair generates extreme suffering from the scorching of the mind and the collapse of the body, it is therefore called suffering.

Ayaṃ upāyāse vinicchayo.

This is the determination on despair.

Ettha ca mandagginā antobhājane pāko viya soko. Tikkhagginā paccamānassa bhājanato bahinikkhamanaṃ viya paridevo. Bahinikkhantāvasesassa nikkhamituṃ appahontassa antobhājaneyeva yāva parikkhayā pāko viya upāyāso daṭṭhabbo.

Here, sorrow should be seen as being like cooking in a pot over a slow fire. Lamentation is like boiling over from the pot when cooking over a fierce fire. Despair should be seen as being like the cooking of the remainder inside the pot, which, being unable to escape, cooks until it is dried up.

Appiyasampayogo

Association with the Disagreeable

549. Appiyasampayogo nāma amanāpehi sattasaṅkhārehi samodhānaṃ. So aniṭṭhasamodhānalakkhaṇo, cittavighātakaraṇaraso, anatthabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. Dukkho pana dukkhavatthuto. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

549. Association with the disagreeable is meeting with disagreeable beings and formations. It has the characteristic of meeting with the undesirable, the function of causing mental affliction, and manifests as bringing about what is unbeneficial. It is suffering because it is a basis for suffering. Hence it is said:

“Disvāva [M 2.0136] appiye dukkhaṃ, paṭhamaṃ hoti cetasi;

Tadupakkamasambhūta-mathakāye yato idha.

Upon seeing the disagreeable, suffering first arises in the mind; then, from their actions, suffering arises in the body here.

“Tato dukkhadvayassāpi, vatthuto so mahesinā;

Dukkho vuttoti viññeyyo, appiyehi samāgamo”ti.

Therefore, since it is the basis of this twofold suffering, it should be understood that association with the disagreeable has been declared to be suffering by the Great Sage.

Ayaṃ appiyasampayoge vinicchayo.

This is the determination on association with the disagreeable.

Piyavippayogo

Separation from the Loved

550. Piyavippayogo nāma manāpehi sattasaṅkhārehi vinābhāvo. So iṭṭhavatthuviyogalakkhaṇo[V 2.0134], sokuppādanaraso, byasanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Dukkho pana sokadukkhassa vatthuto. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

550. Separation from the loved is separation from agreeable beings and formations. It has the characteristic of separation from a desirable object, the function of producing sorrow, and manifests as affliction. It is suffering because it is a basis for the suffering of sorrow. Hence it is said:

“Ñātidhanādiviyogā,

Sokasarasamappitā vitujjanti;

Bālā yato tato yaṃ,

Dukkhoti mato piyavippayogo”ti.

“Because fools, pierced by the arrow of sorrow on account of separation from relatives, wealth, and so on, are tormented, therefore this separation from the loved is considered to be suffering.”

Ayaṃ piyavippayoge vinicchayo.

This is the determination on separation from the loved.

Icchitālābho

Not obtaining what is wished for.

551. Yampicchaṃ na labhatīti ettha “aho vata mayaṃ na jātidhammā assāmā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.398; vibha. 201) alabbhaneyyavatthūsu icchāva yampicchaṃ na labhati, tampi dukkhanti vuttā. Sā alabbhaneyyavatthuicchanalakkhaṇā, tappariyesanarasā, tesaṃ appattipaccupaṭṭhānā. Dukkhā pana dukkhavatthuto. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

551. Herein, regarding the statement 'not getting what one wants is suffering': in such cases as the wish for unobtainable things, 'Oh, that we were not subject to birth!', the very wish is what is meant by 'not getting what one wants,' and that too is said to be suffering. It has the characteristic of wishing for what is unobtainable, its function is to search for that, and its manifestation is the non-attainment of that. It is suffering because it is a basis for suffering. Hence it is said:

“Taṃ taṃ patthayamānānaṃ, tassa tassa alābhato;

Yaṃ vighātamayaṃ dukkhaṃ, sattānaṃ idha jāyati.

“For beings here who are longing for this and that, from the non-attainment of this and that, the suffering that consists of frustration arises.”

“Alabbhaneyyavatthūnaṃ, patthanā tassa kāraṇaṃ;

Yasmā tasmā jino dukkhaṃ, icchitālābhamabravī”ti.

“Because the longing for unobtainable things is the cause of that, therefore the Conqueror declared not obtaining what is wished for to be suffering.”

Ayaṃ icchitālābhe vinicchayo.

This is the determination on not obtaining what is wished for.

Pañcupādānakkhandhā

The five aggregates subject to clinging.

552. Saṃkhittena [M 2.0137] pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhāti ettha pana –

552. Herein, regarding the statement, 'In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering'—

Jātippabhutikaṃ [V 2.0135] dukkhaṃ, yaṃ vuttamidha tādinā;

Avuttaṃ yañca taṃ sabbaṃ, vinā ete na vijjati.

The suffering beginning with birth, which was stated here by the Such One, and whatever was unstated—all that does not exist apart from these aggregates.

Yasmā tasmā upādāna-kkhandhā saṅkhepato ime;

Dukkhāti vuttā dukkhanta-desakena mahesinā.

Therefore, these aggregates subject to clinging were concisely said to be suffering by the Great Sage, the expounder of the end of suffering.

Tathā hi indhanamiva pāvako, lakkhamiva paharaṇāni, gorūpaṃ viya ḍaṃsamakasādayo, khettamiva lāyakā, gāmaṃ viya gāmaghātakā upādānakkhandhapañcakameva jātiādayo nānappakārehi vibādhentā tiṇalatādīni viya bhūmiyaṃ, pupphaphalapallavāni viya rukkhesu upādānakkhandhesuyeva nibbattanti. Upādānakkhandhānañca ādidukkhaṃ jāti, majjhedukkhaṃ jarā, pariyosānadukkhaṃ maraṇaṃ, māraṇantikadukkhābhighātena pariḍayhanadukkhaṃ soko, tadasahanato lālappanadukkhaṃ paridevo, tato dhātukkhobhasaṅkhātaaniṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbasamāyogato kāyassa ābādhanadukkhaṃ dukkhaṃ, tena bādhiyamānānaṃ puthujjanānaṃ tattha paṭighuppattito cetobādhanadukkhaṃ domanassaṃ, sokādivuddhiyā janitavisādānaṃ anutthunanadukkhaṃ upāyāso, manorathavighātappattānaṃ icchāvighātadukkhaṃ icchitālābhoti evaṃ nānappakārato upaparikkhiyamānā upādānakkhandhāva dukkhāti. Yadetaṃ ekamekaṃ dassetvā vuccamānaṃ anekehipi kappehi na sakkā asesato vattuṃ, tasmā taṃ sabbampi dukkhaṃ ekajalabindumhi sakalasamuddajalarasaṃ viya yesu kesuci pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu saṃkhipitvā dassetuṃ “saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti bhagavā avocāti. Ayaṃ upādānakkhandhesu vinicchayo.

For just as fire afflicts fuel, weapons a target, gadflies and mosquitoes a cow, reapers a field, and village-plunderers a village, so too birth and the other kinds of suffering, while afflicting the five aggregates subject to clinging in many ways, arise right in those aggregates, just as grass and creepers arise on the earth, and flowers, fruits, and new leaves on trees. And for the aggregates subject to clinging, birth is the initial suffering, aging is the suffering in the middle, and death is the final suffering. Sorrow is the suffering of being consumed by the affliction of the pain of approaching death. Lamentation is the suffering of wailing from being unable to bear that. Bodily suffering is the suffering of the body’s affliction due to contact with disagreeable tangible objects, which constitutes a disturbance of the elements. Grief is the suffering of mental affliction due to the arising of aversion in worldlings who are afflicted by that. Despair is the suffering of groaning for those in dejection generated by the increase of sorrow and the like. Not getting what one wants is the suffering of the frustration of a wish for those who have met with the frustration of their desire. Thus, when examined in these various ways, it is the aggregates subject to clinging themselves that are suffering. What is being pointed out one by one here could not be stated completely even in many eons. Therefore, to show all that suffering summarized in the five aggregates subject to clinging—just as the taste of all the water in the ocean can be found in a single drop of water—the Blessed One said: ‘In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.’ This is the determination on the aggregates subject to clinging.

Ayaṃ tāva dukkhaniddese nayo.

This, for now, is the method in the exposition of suffering.

Samudayaniddesakathā

The Discourse on the Exposition of the Origin.

553. Samudayaniddese pana yāyaṃ taṇhāti yā ayaṃ taṇhā. Ponobbhavikāti punabbhavakaraṇaṃ punobbhavo, punobbhavo sīlametissāti [M 2.0138] ponobbhavikā. Nandīrāgena sahagatāti nandīrāgasahagatā, nandīrāgena saddhiṃ atthato ekattameva gatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatra tatrābhinandinīti yatra yatra attabhāvo nibbattati, tatra tatrābhinandinī. Seyyathidanti nipāto[V 2.0136], tassa sā katamāti ceti attho. Kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā vibhavataṇhāti imā paṭiccasamuppādaniddese āvibhavissanti. Idha panāyaṃ tividhāpi dukkhasaccassa nibbattakaṭṭhena ekattaṃ upanetvā dukkhasamudayaṃ ariyasaccanti vuttāti veditabbā.

553. In the exposition of the origin, the phrase 'this craving' refers to this very craving. 'Leading to renewed existence' (ponobbhavikā): renewed existence (punabbhavo) is the producing of a new existence; it is called 'leading to renewed existence' because renewed existence is its nature. 'Accompanied by delight and lust' (nandīrāgasahagatā): this means it has gone to oneness in meaning with delight and lust. 'Delighting here and there' (tatra tatrābhinandinī): wherever an individual existence is produced, there it delights. 'Seyyathidaṃ' is a particle; its meaning is 'namely, what is that?' Sensual craving, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—these will become clear in the exposition of dependent origination. Here, however, it should be understood that these three kinds, having been brought to unity on account of their being the producers of the truth of suffering, are called 'the noble truth of the origin of suffering'.

Ayaṃ samudayaniddese nayo.

This is the method in the exposition of the origin.

Nirodhaniddesakathā

Exposition of the Description of Cessation

554. Dukkhanirodhaniddese yo tassāyeva taṇhāyātiādinā nayena samudayanirodho vutto, so kasmāti ce? Samudayanirodhena dukkhanirodho. Samudayanirodhena hi dukkhaṃ nirujjhati, na aññathā. Tenāha –

554. In the exposition of the cessation of suffering, the cessation of the origin is stated by the method beginning with the words, “the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving.” Why is that? Because the cessation of suffering occurs through the cessation of its origin. For suffering ceases through the cessation of its origin, not otherwise. Therefore he said:

“Yathāpi mūle anupaddave daḷhe,

Chinnopi rukkho punadeva rūhati;

Evampi taṇhānusaye anūhate,

Nibbattatī dukkhamidaṃ punappuna”nti. (dha. pa. 338);

“Just as a tree, though cut down, grows again if its root is unharmed and firm, so too, if the underlying tendency to craving is not uprooted, this suffering arises again and again.”

Iti yasmā samudayanirodheneva dukkhaṃ nirujjhati, tasmā bhagavā dukkhanirodhaṃ desento samudayanirodheneva desesi. Sīhasamānavuttino hi tathāgatā. Te dukkhaṃ nirodhentā dukkhanirodhañca desentā hetumhi paṭipajjanti, na phale. Suvānavuttino pana titthiyā. Te dukkhaṃ nirodhentā dukkhanirodhañca desentā attakilamathānuyogadesanādīhi phale paṭipajjanti, na hetumhīti. Evaṃ tāva dukkhanirodhassa samudayanirodhavasena desanāya payojanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Thus, since suffering ceases only with the cessation of its origin, the Blessed One, in teaching the cessation of suffering, taught it through the cessation of the origin. For the Tathāgatas have the bearing of a lion. When causing suffering to cease and teaching its cessation, they proceed by way of the cause, not the result. But the sectarians, who have the bearing of dogs, proceed by way of the result—through teachings such as devotion to self-mortification—not by way of the cause. Thus the purpose of teaching the cessation of suffering in terms of the cessation of its origin should be understood.

555. Ayaṃ panattho – tassāyeva taṇhāyāti tassā “ponobbhavikā”ti vatvā kāmataṇhādivasena vibhattataṇhāya. Virāgo vuccati maggo. “Virāgā vimuccatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.245; saṃ. ni. 3.14) hi vuttaṃ. Virāgena nirodho virāganirodho. Anusayasamugghātato aseso virāganirodho asesavirāganirodho. Atha vā virāgoti pahānaṃ vuccati, tasmā aseso [M 2.0139] virāgo aseso nirodhoti evampettha yojanā daṭṭhabbā. Atthato pana sabbāneva [V 2.0137] etāni nibbānassa vevacanāni. Paramatthato hi dukkhanirodho ariyasaccanti nibbānaṃ vuccati. Yasmā pana taṃ āgamma taṇhā virajjati ceva nirujjhati ca, tasmā virāgoti ca nirodhoti ca vuccati. Yasmā ca tadeva āgamma tassā cāgādayo honti, kāmaguṇālayesu cettha ekopi ālayo natthi, tasmā “cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayo”ti vuccati.

555. This is the meaning: “of that very craving” refers to that craving which, after being described as “leading to renewed existence,” is analyzed by way of sensual craving and so on. “Dispassion” is a term for the path. For it is said: “Through dispassion one is liberated.” Cessation by means of dispassion is “dispassion-cessation.” Remainderless cessation by means of dispassion, owing to the eradication of the underlying tendencies, is “remainderless dispassion-cessation.” Or alternatively, “dispassion” is a term for abandonment; therefore, “remainderless dispassion, remainderless cessation”—this is how the connection should be understood here. But as to the meaning, all these are synonyms for Nibbāna. For in the ultimate sense, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering is called Nibbāna. And since by resorting to it craving fades away and ceases, it is called “dispassion” and “cessation.” And since by resorting to that same thing there occur the giving up of craving and so on, and since in this Nibbāna there is not a single attachment among the attachments to sensual pleasures, it is called “giving up, relinquishment, release, and non-attachment.”

556. Tayidaṃ santilakkhaṇaṃ, accutirasaṃ, assāsakaraṇarasaṃ vā, animittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, nippapañcapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ vā.

556. This has peace as its characteristic; its function is deathlessness, or its function is to provide relief; its manifestation is the signless, or its manifestation is non-proliferation.

Nibbānakathā

Discourse on Nibbāna

557. Nattheva nibbānaṃ, sasavisāṇaṃ viya anupalabbhanīyatoti ce? Na, upāyena upalabbhanīyato. Upalabbhati hi taṃ tadanurūpapaṭipattisaṅkhātena upāyena, cetopariyañāṇena paresaṃ lokuttaracittaṃ viya, tasmā “anupalabbhanīyato natthī”ti na vattabbaṃ. Na hi “yaṃ bālaputhujjanā na upalabhanti, taṃ natthī”ti vattabbaṃ.

557. Is it that Nibbāna does not exist at all, being unapprehendable like a rabbit's horn? No, for it is apprehendable by a means. It is apprehended by the means consisting of the practice appropriate to it, just as the supramundane consciousness of others is apprehended by the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others. Therefore it should not be said, “It does not exist because it is unapprehendable.” For it should not be said, “What foolish worldlings do not apprehend does not exist.”

558. Apica nibbānaṃ natthīti na vattabbaṃ, kasmā? Paṭipattiyā vañjhabhāvāpajjanato. Asati hi nibbāne sammādiṭṭhipurejavāya sīlādikhandhattayasaṅgahāya sammāpaṭipattiyā vañjhabhāvo āpajjati. Na cāyaṃ vañjhā, nibbānapāpanatoti. Na paṭipattiyā vañjhabhāvāpatti, abhāvapāpakattāti ce. Na, atītānāgatābhāvepi nibbānapattiyā abhāvato. Vattamānānampi abhāvo nibbānanti ce. Na, tesaṃ abhāvāsambhavato, abhāve ca avattamānabhāvāpajjanato, vattamānakkhandhanissitamaggakkhaṇe ca sopādisesanibbānadhātuppattiyā abhāvadosato. Tadā kilesānaṃ avattamānattā na dosoti ce. Na, ariyamaggassa niratthakabhāvāpajjanato. Evañhi sati ariyamaggakkhaṇato pubbepi kilesā na santīti ariyamaggassa niratthakabhāvo āpajjati. Tasmā akāraṇametaṃ.

558. Furthermore, it should not be said that Nibbāna does not exist. Why? Because the practice would become barren. For if Nibbāna did not exist, the right practice—which is comprised of the three aggregates beginning with virtue and is preceded by right view—would become barren. But it is not barren, since it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna. (Objection:) The practice does not become barren because it leads to non-existence. (Reply:) No, because there is no attainment of Nibbāna in the non-existence of what is past and future. (Objection:) The non-existence of what is present is Nibbāna. (Reply:) No, because their non-existence is impossible, and if they were non-existent they would cease to be present. Also, at the moment of the path, which is dependent on the present aggregates, there would be the fault of the non-attainment of the Nibbāna-element with residue. (Objection:) There is no fault, because at that time the defilements are not present. (Reply:) No, because the noble path would become pointless. For if this were so, the defilements would not exist even before the moment of the noble path, thus the noble path would be pointless. Therefore, this is not a valid reason.

559. “Yo kho, āvuso, rāgakkhayo”tiādivacanato (saṃ. ni. 4.315) “khayo nibbāna”nti ce. Na, arahattassāpi khayamattāpajjanato. Tampi hi [M 2.0140] “yo kho, āvuso[V 2.0138], rāgakkhayo”tiādinā (sa. ni. 4.315) nayena niddiṭṭhaṃ. Kiñca bhiyyo nibbānassa ittarakālādippattidosato. Evañhi sati nibbānaṃ ittarakālaṃ, saṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ, sammāvāyāmanirapekkhādhigamanīyabhāvañca āpajjati. Saṅkhatalakkhaṇattāyeva ca saṅkhatapariyāpannaṃ, saṅkhatapariyāpannattā rāgādīhi aggīhi ādittaṃ, ādittattā dukkhañcātipi āpajjati. Yasmā khayā paṭṭhāya na bhiyyo pavatti nāma hoti, tassa nibbānabhāvato na dosoti ce. Na, tādisassa khayassa abhāvato. Bhāvepi cassa vuttappakāradosānativattanato, ariyamaggassa ca nibbānabhāvāpajjanato. Ariyamaggo hi dose khīṇeti, tasmā khayoti vuccati. Tato ca paṭṭhāya na bhiyyo dosānaṃ pavattīti.

559. (Objection:) Based on the statement beginning, “Friend, the destruction of lust...” (SN 4.315), it is said that “destruction is Nibbāna.” (Reply:) No, because then Arahantship too would be mere destruction. For that too is indicated by the method beginning, “Friend, the destruction of lust....” Furthermore, Nibbāna would incur the faults of being temporary and so on. For if this were so, Nibbāna would become temporary, would have the characteristic of the conditioned, and would be attainable without depending on right effort. And just because it has the characteristic of the conditioned, it would be included in the conditioned; and because it is included in the conditioned, it would be ablaze with the fires of lust, hatred, and delusion, and being ablaze, it would also become suffering. (Objection:) There is no fault, because from the moment of destruction onwards there is no further occurrence. (Reply:) No, because such a destruction does not exist. And even if it did, it would not escape the faults mentioned, and the noble path itself would become Nibbāna. For the noble path is what destroys the defilements, which is why it is called “destruction,” and from that point onwards there is no further occurrence of the defilements.

Anuppattinirodhasaṅkhātassa pana khayassa pariyāyena upanissayattā, yassa upanissayo hoti tadupacārena “khayo”ti vuttaṃ. Sarūpeneva kasmā na vuttanti ce. Atisukhumattā. Atisukhumatā cassa bhagavato apposukkabhāvāvahanato, ariyena cakkhunā passitabbato ca siddhāti.

However, since [Nibbāna] is a decisive support for the destruction known as non-arising cessation, it is called 'destruction' by a figure of speech based on that for which it is a support. (Objection:) Why is it not described in terms of its own nature? (Reply:) Because of its extreme subtlety. And its extreme subtlety is established from its having led to the Blessed One's disinclination to teach and from its being visible only with the noble eye.

560. Tayidaṃ maggasamaṅginā pattabbato asādhāraṇaṃ, purimakoṭiyā abhāvato appabhavaṃ. Maggabhāve bhāvato na appabhavanti ce. Na, maggena anuppādanīyato. Pattabbameva hetaṃ maggena, na uppādetabbaṃ. Tasmā appabhavameva. Appabhavattā ajarāmaraṇaṃ. Pabhavajarāmaraṇānaṃ abhāvato niccaṃ.

560. This Nibbāna is to be attained by one endowed with the path, hence it is not common to all; because it has no first point, it is unoriginated. (Objection:) Since it comes to be when the path exists, it is not unoriginated. (Reply:) No, because it is not produced by the path. It is only to be attained by the path, not produced by it. Therefore, it is indeed unoriginated. Because it is unoriginated, it is without aging and death. Because of the absence of origination, aging, and death, it is permanent.

Nibbānasseva aṇuādīnampi niccabhāvāpattīti ce. Na, hetuno abhāvā. Nibbānassa niccattā te niccāti ce. Na, hetulakkhaṇassa anupapattito. Niccā uppādādīnaṃ abhāvato nibbānaṃ viyāti ce. Na, aṇuādīnaṃ asiddhattā.

(Objection:) Then atoms and so on would also have to be permanent. (Reply:) No, for want of a reason. (Objection:) They are permanent because Nibbāna is permanent. (Reply:) No, because the characteristic of a reason is not established. (Objection:) They are permanent, like Nibbāna, because they have no arising, etc. (Reply:) No, because atoms and so on are not proven to exist.

561. Yathāvuttayuttisabbhāvato pana idameva niccaṃ, rūpasabhāvātikkamato arūpaṃ. Buddhādīnaṃ niṭṭhāya visesābhāvato ekāva niṭṭhā. Yena bhāvanāya pattaṃ, tassa kilesavūpasamaṃ, upādisesañca upādāya paññāpanīyattā saha upādisesena paññāpiyatīti saupādisesaṃ. Yo cassa samudayappahānena upahatāyatikammaphalassa carimacittato ca uddhaṃ pavattikhandhānaṃ anuppādanato, uppannānañca antaradhānato upādisesābhāvo[M 2.0141], taṃ upādāya paññāpanīyato natthi ettha upādisesoti anupādisesaṃ.

561. But because of the validity of the reasoning just stated, this alone is permanent; because it transcends the intrinsic nature of form, it is formless. Since there is no difference in the final state for the Buddhas and others, the final state is one only. For one who has attained it through development, the stilling of the defilements is designated as 'with residue' (saupādisesa) because it is designated in dependence on the remaining aggregates. The absence of residue—which comes about for one whose future kamma-result is cut off through the abandoning of the origin, due to the non-arising of subsequent aggregates after the final consciousness, and the disappearance of those that have arisen—is designated as “without residue” (anupādisesa) because it is designated in dependence on this absence of residue.

Asithilaparakkamasiddhena [V 2.0139] ñāṇavisesena adhigamanīyato, sabbaññuvacanato ca paramatthena sabhāvato nibbānaṃ nāvijjamānaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “atthi, bhikkhave, ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhata”nti.

Because it is attainable by a special knowledge perfected through unfaltering effort, and because of the word of the Omniscient One, Nibbāna is not non-existent; in the ultimate sense, by its intrinsic nature, it exists. For this was said: “There is, bhikkhus, an unborn, unproduced, unmade, unconditioned.”

Idaṃ dukkhanirodhaniddese vinicchayakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the discourse on determination in the Exposition of the Cessation of Suffering.

Magganiddesakathā

The Discourse on the Exposition of the Path

562. Dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadāniddese vuttā pana aṭṭha dhammā kāmaṃ khandhaniddesepi atthato pakāsitāyeva, idha pana nesaṃ ekakkhaṇe pavattamānānaṃ visesāvabodhanatthaṃ vadāma. Saṅkhepato hi catusaccapaṭivedhāya paṭipannassa yogino nibbānārammaṇaṃ avijjānusayasamugghātakaṃ paññācakkhu sammādiṭṭhi. Sā sammā dassanalakkhaṇā, dhātuppakāsanarasā, avijjandhakāraviddhaṃsanapaccupaṭṭhānā. Tathā sampannadiṭṭhino taṃsampayuttaṃ micchāsaṅkappanighātakaṃ cetaso nibbānapadābhiniropanaṃ sammāsaṅkappo. So sammā cittābhiniropanalakkhaṇo, appanāraso, micchāsaṅkappappahānapaccupaṭṭhāno.

562. The eight factors mentioned in the Exposition of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering are, to be sure, also explained in substance in the Exposition of the Aggregates; here, however, we speak in order to make known the distinctions among them as they occur in a single moment. Briefly, for the yogin who has entered upon the path for the penetration of the four truths, right view is the eye of wisdom that has Nibbāna as its object and uproots the underlying tendency to ignorance. It has the characteristic of right seeing, its function is to illuminate the elements, and it is manifested as the dispelling of the darkness of ignorance. For one accomplished in such a view, the associated right intention is the directing of the mind onto the state of Nibbāna, which strikes down wrong intention. It has the characteristic of rightly directing the mind, its function is absorption, and it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong intention.

Tathā passato vitakkayato ca taṃsampayuttāva vacīduccaritasamugghātikā micchāvācāya virati sammāvācā nāma. Sā pariggahalakkhaṇā, viramaṇarasā, micchāvācāppahānapaccupaṭṭhānā. Tathā viramato taṃsampayuttāva micchākammantasamucchedikā pāṇātipātādivirati sammākammanto nāma. So samuṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇo, viramaṇaraso, micchākammantappahānapaccupaṭṭhāno. Yā panassa tesaṃ sammāvācākammantānaṃ visuddhibhūtā taṃsampayuttāva kuhanādiupacchedikā micchājīvavirati, so sammāājīvo nāma. So vodānalakkhaṇo, ñāyājīvapavattiraso, micchājīvappahānapaccupaṭṭhāno.

For one who sees and thinks thus, the associated abstinence from wrong speech, which eradicates verbal misconduct, is called right speech. It has the characteristic of encompassing, its function is abstaining, and it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong speech. For one who abstains thus, the associated abstinence from killing, etc., which cuts off wrong action, is called right action. It has the characteristic of originating, its function is abstaining, and it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong action. Further, for such a one, the associated abstinence from wrong livelihood—which is the purification of that right speech and right action and which cuts off scheming and the like—is called right livelihood. It has the characteristic of cleansing, its function is the pursuing of a proper livelihood, and it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong livelihood.

Athassa yo tassā sammāvācākammantājīvasaṅkhātāya sīlabhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhitassa tadanurūpo taṃsampayuttova kosajjasamucchedako vīriyārambho, esa sammāvāyāmo nāma. So paggahalakkhaṇo, anuppannaakusalānuppādanādiraso, micchāvāyāmappahānapaccupaṭṭhāno. Tassevaṃ vāyamato taṃsampayuttova micchāsativiniddhunano cetaso asammoso [M 2.0142] sammāsati nāma. Sā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇā, asammussanarasā, micchāsatippahānapaccupaṭṭhānā. Evaṃ anuttarāya satiyā saṃrakkhiyamānacittassa [V 2.0140] taṃsampayuttāva micchāsamādhividdhaṃsikā cittekaggatā sammāsamādhi nāma. So avikkhepalakkhaṇo, samādhānaraso, micchāsamādhippahānapaccupaṭṭhānoti. Ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadāniddese nayo. Evamettha jātiādīnaṃ vinicchayo veditabbo.

Then, for one established on the ground of virtue designated as right speech, right action, and right livelihood, the associated and suitable arousal of energy that cuts off laziness—this is called right effort. It has the characteristic of exertion, its function is the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states and so on, and it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong effort. For one striving thus, the associated non-delusion of mind that shakes off wrong mindfulness is called right mindfulness. It has the characteristic of establishing, its function is non-forgetfulness, and it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong mindfulness. Thus, for one whose mind is guarded by unsurpassed mindfulness, the associated one-pointedness of mind that demolishes wrong concentration is called right concentration. It has the characteristic of non-distraction, its function is unification, and it is manifested as the abandoning of wrong concentration. This is the method in the Exposition of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering. Thus the determination of birth and so on should be understood here.

563. Ñāṇakiccatoti saccañāṇassa kiccatopi vinicchayo veditabbo. Duvidhaṃ hi saccañāṇaṃ – anubodhañāṇaṃ paṭivedhañāṇañca. Tattha anubodhañāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ anussavādivasena nirodhe magge ca pavattati. Paṭivedhañāṇaṃ lokuttaraṃ nirodhamārammaṇaṃ katvā kiccato cattāri saccāni paṭivijjhati. Yathāha – “yo, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ passati, dukkhasamudayampi so passati, dukkhanirodhampi passati, dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadampi passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ. Taṃ panassa kiccaṃ ñāṇadassanavisuddhiyaṃ āvibhavissati.

563. The determination should also be understood by way of the function of knowledge. For the knowledge of the truths is twofold: knowledge as understanding and knowledge as penetration. Herein, knowledge as understanding is mundane and proceeds by way of hearsay and so on with regard to cessation and the path. Knowledge as penetration is supramundane; having taken cessation as its object, it penetrates the four truths by way of their functions. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, one who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, and also sees the path leading to the cessation of suffering.” The full passage should be quoted. But its function will become manifest in the Purification by Knowledge and Vision.

Yaṃ panetaṃ lokiyaṃ, tattha dukkhañāṇaṃ pariyuṭṭhānābhibhavavasena pavattamānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhiṃ nivatteti. Samudayañāṇaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ. Nirodhañāṇaṃ sassatadiṭṭhiṃ. Maggañāṇaṃ akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ. Dukkhañāṇaṃ vā dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvavirahitesu khandhesu dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvasaññāsaṅkhātaṃ phale vippaṭipattiṃ. Samudayañāṇaṃ issarapadhānakālasabhāvādīhi loko pavattatīti akāraṇe kāraṇābhimānappavattaṃ hetumhi vippaṭipattiṃ. Nirodhañāṇaṃ arūpalokalokathūpikādīsu apavaggagāhabhūtaṃ nirodhe vippaṭipattiṃ. Maggañāṇaṃ kāmasukhallikaattakilamathānuyogappabhede avisuddhimagge visuddhimaggagāhavasena pavattaṃ upāye vippaṭipattiṃ nivatteti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Now, as to that which is mundane: therein the knowledge of suffering, proceeding by way of overcoming obsessions, counteracts identity view. The knowledge of the origin counteracts the view of annihilationism. The knowledge of cessation counteracts the view of eternalism. The knowledge of the path counteracts the view of non-action. Or, the knowledge of suffering counteracts the misapprehension regarding the fruit, which is the perception of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self in the aggregates that are devoid of a permanent, beautiful, pleasant, and self-like nature. The knowledge of the origin counteracts the misapprehension regarding the cause, which proceeds from the conceit of a cause in what is not a cause, namely, that the world proceeds from a creator, a primal substance, time, intrinsic nature, and so on. The knowledge of cessation counteracts the misapprehension regarding cessation, which consists in grasping at the formless world, the peak of the world, etc., as liberation. The knowledge of the path counteracts the misapprehension regarding the means, which proceeds by way of grasping an impure path—distinguished as indulgence in sensual pleasures and the practice of self-mortification—as the pure path. Therefore it is said:

“Loke lokappabhave, lokatthagame sive ca tadupāye;

Sammuyhati tāva naro, na vijānāti yāva saccānī”ti.

“As long as a person does not know the truths, for so long are they deluded about the world, its origin, its cessation, the auspicious state, and the means to that.”

Evamettha ñāṇakiccatopi vinicchayo veditabbo.

Thus, the determination by way of the function of knowledge should also be understood here.

564. Antogadhānaṃ pabhedāti dukkhasaccasmiṃ hi ṭhapetvā taṇhañceva anāsavadhamme ca sesā sabbadhammā antogadhā. Samudayasacce chattiṃsa taṇhāvicaritāni. Nirodhasaccaṃ asammissaṃ. Maggasacce sammādiṭṭhimukhena vīmaṃsiddhipādapaññindriyapaññābaladhammavicayasambojjhaṅgāni. Sammāsaṅkappāpadesena tayo [M 2.0143] nekkhammavitakkādayo. Sammāvācāpadesena cattāri vacīsucaritāni[V 2.0141]. Sammākammantāpadesena tīṇi kāyasucaritāni. Sammājīvamukhena appicchatā santuṭṭhitā ca. Sabbesaṃyeva vā etesaṃ sammāvācākammantājīvānaṃ ariyakantasīlattā ariyakantasīlassa ca saddhāhatthena paṭiggahetabbattā tesaṃ atthitāya atthibhāvato saddhindriyasaddhābalachandiddhipādā. Sammāvāyāmāpadesena catubbidhasammappadhānavīriyindriyavīriyabalavīriyasambojjhaṅgāni. Sammāsatiapadesena catubbidhasatipaṭṭhānasatindriyasatibalasatisambojjhaṅgāni. Sammāsamādhiapadesena savitakkasavicārādayo tayo samādhī cittasamādhi samādhindriyasamādhibalapītipassaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgāni antogadhānīti evamettha antogadhānaṃ pabhedatopi vinicchayo veditabbo.

564. By way of the classification of what is included: In the truth of suffering, indeed, excepting craving and the untainted states, all remaining states are included. In the truth of the origin, the thirty-six courses of craving are included. The truth of cessation is unmixed. In the truth of the path, by way of right view are included the basis of success consisting of investigation, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and the enlightenment factor of discrimination of states. Under the heading of right intention, the three thoughts of renunciation and so on are included. Under the heading of right speech, the four kinds of good verbal conduct are included. Under the heading of right action, the three kinds of good bodily conduct are included. By way of right livelihood, fewness of wishes and contentment are included. Alternatively, since all these—right speech, right action, and right livelihood—are virtue dear to the noble ones, and since virtue dear to the noble ones is to be received by the hand of faith, from their existence there is the existence of the faculty of faith, the power of faith, and the basis of success consisting of zeal. Under the heading of right effort are included the four right strivings, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and the enlightenment factor of energy. Under the heading of right mindfulness are included the four establishments of mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. Under the heading of right concentration are included the three kinds of concentration such as that with initial and sustained application of thought, concentration of mind, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and the enlightenment factors of rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. Thus, the determination should be understood here also by way of the classification of what is included.

565. Upamātoti bhāro viya hi dukkhasaccaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, bhārādānamiva samudayasaccaṃ, bhāranikkhepanamiva nirodhasaccaṃ, bhāranikkhepanupāyo viya maggasaccaṃ. Rogo viya ca dukkhasaccaṃ, roganidānamiva samudayasaccaṃ, rogavūpasamo viya nirodhasaccaṃ, bhesajjamiva maggasaccaṃ. Dubbhikkhamiva vā dukkhasaccaṃ, dubbuṭṭhi viya samudayasaccaṃ, subhikkhamiva nirodhasaccaṃ, suvuṭṭhi viya maggasaccaṃ. Apica verī-veramūla-verasamugghāta-verasamugghātupāyehi, visarukkha-rukkhamūla-mūlupaccheda-tadupacchedupāyehi, bhaya-bhayamūla-nibbhaya-tadadhigamupāyehi, orimatīra-mahoghapārimatīra-taṃsampāpakavāyāmehi ca yojetvāpetāni upamāto veditabbānīti evamettha upamāto vinicchayo veditabbo.

565. By way of analogy: The truth of suffering should be seen as a burden, the truth of the origin as the taking up of the burden, the truth of cessation as the laying down of the burden, and the truth of the path as the means to lay down the burden. And the truth of suffering is like a disease, the truth of the origin like the cause of the disease, the truth of cessation like the subsiding of the disease, and the truth of the path like the medicine. Or the truth of suffering is like a famine, the truth of the origin like a drought, the truth of cessation like abundance, and the truth of the path like good rain. Furthermore, these truths should be understood by way of analogy by applying them to: an enemy, the root of the enemy, the eradication of the enemy, and the means to eradicate the enemy; a poisonous tree, the root of the tree, the cutting off of the root, and the means to cut it off; fear, the root of fear, fearlessness, and the means to attain it; and the near shore, the great flood, the far shore, and the effort to reach it. Thus, the determination should be understood here also by way of analogy.

566. Catukkatoti atthi cettha dukkhaṃ na ariyasaccaṃ, atthi ariyasaccaṃ na dukkhaṃ, atthi dukkhañceva ariyasaccañca, atthi neva dukkhaṃ na ariyasaccaṃ. Esa nayo samudayādīsu. Tattha maggasampayuttā dhammā sāmaññaphalāni ca “yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.15) vacanato saṅkhāradukkhatāya dukkhaṃ, na ariyasaccaṃ. Nirodho ariyasaccaṃ, na dukkhaṃ. Itaraṃ pana ariyasaccadvayaṃ siyā dukkhaṃ aniccato, na pana yassa pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathattena. Sabbākārena pana upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ dukkhañceva ariyasaccañca aññatra taṇhāya. Maggasampayuttā dhammā sāmaññaphalāni ca yassa pariññatthaṃ bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathattena neva dukkhaṃ na ariyasaccaṃ. Evaṃ samudayādīsupi yathāyogaṃ yojetvā catukkatopettha vinicchayo veditabbo.

566. By way of a fourfold method: Herein, there is suffering that is not a noble truth; there is a noble truth that is not suffering; there is that which is both suffering and a noble truth; and there is that which is neither suffering nor a noble truth. This same method applies to the origin and the rest. Herein, the states associated with the path and the fruits of the contemplative life are suffering due to being conditioned suffering, according to the statement, “What is impermanent is suffering,” but they are not a noble truth. Cessation is a noble truth, but not suffering. The other two noble truths might be suffering on account of impermanence, yet not in the real sense of that for the full understanding of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. However, in every way, the five aggregates subject to clinging, with the exception of craving, are both suffering and a noble truth. The states associated with the path and the fruits of the contemplative life, in the real sense of that for the full understanding of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One, are neither suffering nor a noble truth. Thus, the determination should be understood here also by way of the fourfold method, applying it to the origin and the rest as is appropriate.

567. Suññatekavidhādīhītiettha [M 2.0144][V 2.0142] suññato tāva paramatthena hi sabbāneva saccāni vedakakārakanibbutagamakābhāvato suññānīti veditabbāni. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

567. By way of emptiness, singularity, and so on: Herein, firstly as to emptiness, it should be understood that in the ultimate sense all the truths are empty because of the absence of an experiencer, a doer, one who is extinguished, and a goer. Therefore it is said:

“Dukkhameva hi, na koci dukkhito;

Kārako na, kiriyāva vijjati.

Atthi nibbuti, na nibbuto pumā;

Maggamatthi, gamako na vijjatī”ti.

“For there is only suffering, but none who suffers; No doer is there, but the deed is found. Extinction is, but no extinguished person; The path is, but no goer on it is found.”

Atha vā,

Alternatively:

Dhuvasubhasukhattasuññaṃ, purimadvayamattasuññamamatapadaṃ;

Dhuvasukhaattavirahito, maggoiti suññatā tesu.

“The first two truths are empty of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and self; The deathless state is empty of self; The path is devoid of permanence, pleasure, and self— Thus is the emptiness in them.”

Nirodhasuññāni vā tīṇi, nirodho ca sesattayasuñño. Phalasuñño vā ettha hetu samudaye dukkhassābhāvato, magge ca nirodhassa, na phalena sagabbho pakativādīnaṃ pakati viya. Hetusuññañca phalaṃ dukkhasamudayānaṃ nirodhamaggānañca asamavāyā, na hetusamavetaṃ hetuphalaṃ samavāyavādīnaṃ dviaṇukādi viya. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Or, the three truths are empty of cessation, and cessation is empty of the other three. Or, the cause is empty of the fruit, for in the origin suffering is absent and in the path cessation is absent; it is not pregnant with the fruit like the primordial nature of those who advocate a primordial nature. And the fruit is empty of the cause, owing to the non-concomitance of suffering and origin, and of cessation and path; the fruit of a cause is not inherent in the cause like the dyad, etc., of those who advocate inherence. Therefore it is said:

“Tayamidha nirodhasuññaṃ, tayena tenāpi nibbuti suññā;

Suñño phalena hetu, phalampi taṃhetunā suñña”nti.

“Here this triad is empty of cessation, and Nibbāna too is empty of that triad. The cause is empty of the fruit, and the fruit is empty of that cause.”

Evaṃ tāva suññato vinicchayo veditabbo.

Thus the determination in terms of emptiness should be understood.

Ekavidhādivinicchayakathā

Discourse on the Determination as Singlefold, etc.

568. Ekavidhādīhīti sabbameva cettha dukkhaṃ ekavidhaṃ pavattibhāvato. Duvidhaṃ nāmarūpato. Tividhaṃ kāmarūpārūpūpapattibhavabhedato. Catubbidhaṃ catuāhārabhedato. Pañcavidhaṃ pañcupādānakkhandhabhedato.

568. Regarding the singlefold and so on: Here, all suffering is singlefold because it has the nature of occurring. It is twofold in terms of name-and-form. It is threefold by the distinction of existence as rebirth in the sense-sphere, the form-sphere, and the formless-sphere. It is fourfold by the distinction of the four kinds of nutriment. It is fivefold by the distinction of the five aggregates subject to clinging.

Samudayopi [V 2.0143] ekavidho pavattakabhāvato. Duvidho diṭṭhisampayuttāsampayuttato. Tividho kāmabhavavibhavataṇhābhedato. Catubbidho catumaggappaheyyato. Pañcavidho rūpābhinandanādibhedato. Chabbidho chataṇhākāyabhedato.

The origin, too, is singlefold because it has the nature of originating. It is twofold as associated or unassociated with wrong view. It is threefold by the distinction of craving for sensual existence, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. It is fourfold as that which is to be abandoned by the four paths. It is fivefold by the distinction of delight in form, and so on. It is sixfold by the distinction of the six classes of craving.

Nirodhopi [M 2.0145] ekavidho asaṅkhatadhātubhāvato. Pariyāyena pana duvidho saupādisesaanupādisesabhedato. Tividho bhavattayavūpasamato. Catubbidho catumaggādhigamanīyato. Pañcavidho pañcābhinandanavūpasamato. Chabbidho chataṇhākāyakkhayabhedato.

Cessation, too, is singlefold because it is the unconditioned element. Figuratively, however, it is twofold by the distinction of that with residue remaining and that without residue remaining. It is threefold as the pacification of the three kinds of existence. It is fourfold as that which is to be realized by the four paths. It is fivefold as the pacification of the five kinds of delight. It is sixfold by the distinction of the destruction of the six classes of craving.

Maggopi ekavidho bhāvetabbato. Duvidho samathavipassanābhedato, dassanabhāvanābhedato vā. Tividho khandhattayabhedato. Ayañhi sappadesattā nagaraṃ viya rajjena nippadesehi tīhi khandhehi saṅgahito. Yathāha –

The path, too, is singlefold as that which is to be developed. It is twofold by the distinction of serenity and insight, or by the distinction of vision and development. It is threefold by the distinction of the three aggregates. For this path, being partial, is included by the three aggregates, which are complete, just as a city is by a kingdom. As it is said:

“Na kho, āvuso visākha, ariyena aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena tayo khandhā saṅgahitā, tīhi ca kho, āvuso visākha, khandhehi ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅgahito. Yā cāvuso visākha, sammāvācā, yo ca sammākammanto, yo ca sammāājīvo, ime dhammā sīlakkhandhe saṅgahitā. Yo ca sammāvāyāmo, yā ca sammāsati, yo ca sammāsamādhi, ime dhammā samādhikkhandhe saṅgahitā. Yā ca sammādiṭṭhi, yo ca sammāsaṅkappo, ime dhammā paññākkhandhe saṅgahitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.462).

“It is not the case, friend Visākha, that the three aggregates are included in the Noble Eightfold Path; on the contrary, friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is included in the three aggregates. Friend Visākha, whatever is right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these states are included in the aggregate of virtue. Whatever is right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these states are included in the aggregate of concentration. Whatever is right view and right intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom.”

Ettha hi sammāvācādayo tayo sīlameva, tasmā te sajātito sīlakkhandhena saṅgahitā. Kiñcāpi hi pāḷiyaṃ sīlakkhandheti bhummena niddeso kato, attho pana karaṇavaseneva veditabbo. Sammāvāyāmādīsu pana tīsu samādhi attano dhammatāya ārammaṇe ekaggabhāvena appetuṃ na sakkoti, vīriye pana paggahakiccaṃ sādhente satiyā ca apilāpanakiccaṃ sādhentiyā laddhupakāro hutvā sakkoti.

Here, the three beginning with right speech are virtue itself; therefore they are included in the aggregate of virtue by their common nature. And although in the Pāḷi text the designation is made in the locative case, as ‘in the aggregate of virtue,’ the meaning should be understood in an instrumental sense. But among the three beginning with right effort, concentration by its own nature is not able to apply itself to the object with one-pointedness; however, when it has received support from energy, which accomplishes the function of exertion, and from mindfulness, which accomplishes the function of non-superficiality, it becomes able to do so.

Tatrāyaṃ upamā – yathā hi nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmāti uyyānaṃ paviṭṭhesu tīsu sahāyesu eko supupphitaṃ campakarukkhaṃ disvā hatthaṃ ukkhipitvā gahetumpi na sakkuṇeyya. Athassa dutiyo onamitvā [V 2.0144] piṭṭhiṃ dadeyya, so tassa piṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhatvāpi kampamāno gahetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Athassa itaro aṃsakūṭaṃ upanāmeyya. So ekassa piṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhatvā ekassa aṃsakūṭaṃ olubbha yathāruci pupphāni ocinitvā piḷandhitvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷeyya. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here is a simile. Suppose three friends enter a park intending to celebrate a festival. One sees a champak tree in full bloom, but when he raises his hand he cannot reach the flowers. Then the second friend bends down and offers his back. Standing on his back, the first friend still trembles and cannot reach them. Then the other friend offers his shoulder. Standing on the one’s back and leaning on the other’s shoulder, he picks as many flowers as he likes, adorns himself with them, and celebrates the festival. This success should be understood in this way.

Ekato [M 2.0146] uyyānaṃ paviṭṭhā tayo sahāyā viya hi ekato jātā sammāvāyāmādayo tayo dhammā. Supupphitacampako viya ārammaṇaṃ. Hatthaṃ ukkhipitvāpi gahetuṃ asakkonto viya attano dhammatāya ārammaṇe ekaggabhāvena appetuṃ asakkonto samādhi. Piṭṭhiṃ datvā onatasahāyo viya vāyāmo. Aṃsakūṭaṃ datvā ṭhitasahāyo viya sati. Yathā tesu ekassa piṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhatvā ekassa aṃsakūṭaṃ olubbha itaro yathāruci pupphaṃ gahetuṃ sakkoti, evameva vīriye paggahakiccaṃ sādhente satiyā ca apilāpanakiccaṃ sādhentiyā laddhupakāro samādhi sakkoti ārammaṇe ekaggabhāvena appetuṃ. Tasmā samādhiyevettha sajātito samādhikkhandhena saṅgahito, vāyāmasatiyo pana kiriyato saṅgahitā honti.

For the three states beginning with right effort, which arise together, are like the three friends who entered the park together. The object is like the champak tree in full bloom. Concentration, unable by its own nature to apply itself to the object with one-pointedness, is like the one who was unable to reach though he raised his hand. Effort is like the friend who bent down and offered his back. Mindfulness is like the friend who stood and offered his shoulder. Just as the one friend, standing on another’s back and leaning on the other’s shoulder, was able to pick flowers as he liked, so too, when energy accomplishes the function of exertion and mindfulness accomplishes the function of non-superficiality, concentration, having received their support, is able to apply itself to the object with one-pointedness. Therefore, here concentration alone is included in the aggregate of concentration by its common nature, while effort and mindfulness are included by their function.

Sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappesupi paññā attano dhammatāya aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti ārammaṇaṃ nicchetuṃ na sakkoti. Vitakke pana ākoṭetvā ākoṭetvā dente sakkoti. Kathaṃ? Yathā hi heraññiko kahāpaṇaṃ hatthe ṭhapetvā sabbabhāgesu oloketukāmo samānopi na cakkhutaleneva parivattetuṃ sakkoti. Aṅgulipabbehi pana parivattetvā parivattetvā ito cito ca oloketuṃ sakkoti, evameva na paññā attano dhammatāya aniccādivasena ārammaṇaṃ nicchetuṃ sakkoti. Abhiniropanalakkhaṇena pana āhananapariyāhananarasena vitakkena ākoṭentena viya parivattentena viya ca ādāyādāya dinnameva nicchetuṃ sakkoti. Tasmā idhāpi sammādiṭṭhiyeva sajātito paññākkhandhena saṅgahitā, sammāsaṅkappo pana kiriyavasena saṅgahito hoti.

In the case of right view and right intention, too, wisdom by its own nature cannot determine the object as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. But it can do so when thought repeatedly strikes at it and presents it. How? Just as a money-changer, though wishing to examine all sides of a coin placed in his hand, cannot turn it over with his eye alone, but by repeatedly turning it over with his fingertips he can examine it on all sides; so too, wisdom by its own nature cannot determine the object as impermanent, etc. But by means of thought—which has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object and the function of striking and turning over, and which takes it up again and again—it can determine the object presented to it, as if striking it and turning it over. Therefore, here too, right view alone is included in the aggregate of wisdom by its common nature, while right intention is included by its function.

Iti imehi tīhi khandhehi maggo saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Tena vuttaṃ “tividho khandhattayabhedato”ti. Catubbidho sotāpattimaggādivaseneva.

Thus the path is included in these three aggregates. That is why it was said, ‘It is threefold by the distinction of the three aggregates.’ It is fourfold by way of the path of stream-entry and so on.

Apica sabbāneva saccāni ekavidhāni avitathattā, abhiññeyyattā vā. Duvidhāni lokiyalokuttarato, saṅkhatāsaṅkhatato vā. Tividhāni dassana-bhāvanāhi pahātabbato, appahātabbato ca. Catubbidhāni pariññeyyādibhedatoti evamettha ekavidhādīhi vinicchayo veditabbo.

Furthermore, all the truths are singlefold in that they are not unreal, or in that they are to be directly known. They are twofold as worldly and supramundane, or as conditioned and unconditioned. They are threefold as what is to be abandoned by vision, what is to be abandoned by development, and what is not to be abandoned. They are fourfold by the distinction of what is to be fully understood, and so on. Thus should the analysis here be understood in terms of the singlefold and so on.

569. Sabhāgavisabhāgatoti [M 2.0147][V 2.0145] sabbāneva saccāni aññamaññaṃ sabhāgāni avitathato attasuññato dukkarapaṭivedhato ca. Yathāha –

569. As to similarity and dissimilarity: All the truths are similar to one another in that they are not unreal, are void of self, and are difficult to penetrate. As it is said:

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, ānanda, katamaṃ nu kho dukkarataraṃ vā durabhisambhavataraṃ vā, yo vā dūratova sukhumena tāḷacchiggaḷena asanaṃ atipāteyya poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ avirādhitaṃ, yo vā satadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭivijjheyyāti? Etadeva, bhante, dukkaratarañceva durabhisambhavatarañca, yo vā satadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭivijjheyyāti. Tato kho te, ānanda, duppaṭivijjhataraṃ paṭivijjhanti. Ye idaṃ dukkhanti yathābhūtaṃ paṭivijjhanti…pe… ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti yathābhūtaṃ paṭivijjhantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1115).

“What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult, more difficult to accomplish: for one to shoot arrow after arrow from a distance through a tiny keyhole without missing, or for one to pierce the tip of a hair that has been split a hundred times with another tip?” “Venerable sir, it is more difficult, more difficult to accomplish, to pierce the tip of a hair that has been split a hundred times with another tip.” “Ānanda, those who penetrate as it really is, ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,’ penetrate something even more difficult to penetrate.”

Visabhāgāni salakkhaṇavavatthānato. Purimāni ca dve sabhāgāni duravagāhatthena gambhīrattā lokiyattā sāsavattā ca. Visabhāgāni phalahetubhedato pariññeyyappahātabbato ca. Pacchimānipi dve sabhāgāni gambhīrattena duravagāhattā lokuttarattā anāsavattā ca. Visabhāgāni visayavisayībhedato sacchikātabbabhāvetabbato ca. Paṭhamatatiyāni cāpi sabhāgāni phalāpadesato. Visabhāgāni saṅkhatāsaṅkhatato. Dutiyacatutthāni cāpi sabhāgāni hetuapadesato. Visabhāgāni ekantakusalākusalato. Paṭhamacatutthāni cāpi sabhāgāni saṅkhatato. Visabhāgāni lokiyalokuttarato. Dutiyatatiyāni cāpi sabhāgāni nevasekkhānāsekkhabhāvato. Visabhāgāni sārammaṇānārammaṇato.

They are dissimilar by the definition of their individual characteristics. The first two truths are similar in being profound in the sense of being difficult to fathom, in being worldly, and in being accompanied by taints. They are dissimilar by the distinction between fruit and cause, and between what is to be fully understood and what is to be abandoned. The last two truths are also similar in being profound and difficult to fathom, in being supramundane, and in being taintless. They are dissimilar by the distinction between object and subject, and between what is to be realized and what is to be developed. The first and third are also similar in being designated as fruit; they are dissimilar as conditioned and unconditioned. The second and fourth are also similar in being designated as cause; they are dissimilar as exclusively unwholesome and wholesome. The first and fourth are also similar in being conditioned; they are dissimilar as worldly and supramundane. The second and third are also similar in being states of neither-a-trainee-nor-one-beyond-training; they are dissimilar as being with an object and without an object.

Iti evaṃ pakārehi, nayehi ca vicakkhaṇo;

Vijaññā ariyasaccānaṃ, sabhāgavisabhāgatanti.

Thus, by these kinds and by these methods, a discerning person may understand the similarity and dissimilarity of the Noble Truths.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in The Path of Purification, composed for the gladdening of good people,

Paññābhāvanādhikāre

in the section on the Development of Wisdom,

Indriyasaccaniddeso nāma

the Exposition of the Faculties and Truths by name,

Soḷasamo paricchedo.

is the Sixteenth Chapter.

17. Paññābhūminiddeso

17. The Exposition of the Ground of Wisdom

Paṭiccasamuppādakathā

A Discussion of Dependent Origination

570. Idāni [M 2.0148][V 2.0146] “khandhāyatanadhātuindriyasaccapaṭiccasamuppādādibhedā dhammā bhūmī”ti evaṃ vuttesu imissā paññāya bhūmibhūtesu dhammesu yasmā paṭiccasamuppādoceva, ādisaddena saṅgahitā paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā ca avasesā honti, tasmā tesaṃ vaṇṇanākkamo anuppatto.

570. Now, it was said: 'The phenomena classified as aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, truths, dependent origination, etc., are the ground.' Since, among these phenomena that have become the ground for this wisdom, what remain are dependent origination itself and the dependently arisen phenomena included by the word 'etc.', the turn for their description has now come.

Tattha avijjādayo tāva dhammā paṭiccasamuppādoti veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Herein, the phenomena beginning with ignorance should first be understood as dependent origination. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādo?
