Avijjāpaccayā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ, saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ, upādānapaccayā bhavo, bhavapaccayā jāti, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādo”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.1).

"And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called dependent origination."

Jarāmaraṇādayo pana paṭiccasamuppannā dhammāti veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

But aging-and-death and so on should be understood as dependently arisen phenomena. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Katame ca, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā? Jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ khayadhammaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ nirodhadhammaṃ. Jāti, bhikkhave…pe… bhavo… upādānaṃ… taṇhā… vedanā… phasso… saḷāyatanaṃ… nāmarūpaṃ… viññāṇaṃ… saṅkhārā… avijjā, bhikkhave, aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā [V 2.0147] khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.20).

"And what, bhikkhus, are dependently arisen phenomena? Aging-and-death, bhikkhus, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Birth, bhikkhus… and so on… existence… clinging… craving… feeling… contact… the six sense bases… name-and-form… consciousness… volitional formations… Ignorance, bhikkhus, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. These, bhikkhus, are called dependently arisen phenomena."

571. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo. Paṭiccasamuppādoti paccayadhammā veditabbā. Paṭiccasamuppannā dhammāti tehi tehi paccayehi nibbattadhammā. Kathamidaṃ jānitabbanti [M 2.0149] ce? Bhagavato vacanena. Bhagavatā hi paṭiccasamuppādapaṭiccasamuppannadhammadesanāsutte –

571. This is the summary here. Dependent origination is to be understood as the conditioning phenomena. Dependently arisen phenomena are to be understood as the phenomena produced by those various conditions. If it is asked, 'How is this to be known?' By the word of the Blessed One. For in the Sutta on the Teaching of Dependent Origination and Dependently Arisen Phenomena, the Blessed One said:

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādo? Jātipaccayā, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇaṃ, uppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ anuppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ ṭhitāva sā dhātu dhammaṭṭhitatā dhammaniyāmatā idappaccayatā. Taṃ tathāgato abhisambujjhati abhisameti, abhisambujjhitvā abhisametvā ācikkhati deseti paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti, passathāti cāha. Jātipaccayā, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇaṃ. Bhavapaccayā, bhikkhave, jāti…pe… avijjāpaccayā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā uppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ…pe… uttānīkaroti passathāti cāha. Avijjāpaccayā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā. Iti kho, bhikkhave, yā tatra tathatā avitathatā anaññathatā idappaccayatā. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādo”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.20).

"And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? With birth as condition, bhikkhus, comes aging-and-death. Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, that element still stands, that stability of the Dhamma, that fixed course of the Dhamma, specific conditionality. The Tathāgata awakens to this and breaks through to it. Having awakened to it and broken through to it, he declares it, teaches it, clarifies it, establishes it, reveals it, analyzes it, makes it plain, and he says: ‘See! With birth as condition, bhikkhus, aging-and-death.’ With existence as condition, bhikkhus, birth… and so on… With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, volitional formations. Whether Tathāgatas arise… and so on… makes it plain, and he says: ‘See! With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, volitional formations.’ Thus, bhikkhus, that which therein is suchness, undeviatingness, unalterableness, specific conditionality: this is called dependent origination."

572. Evaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ desentena tathatādīhi vevacanehi paccayadhammāva paṭiccasamuppādoti vuttā. Tasmā jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ paccayalakkhaṇo paṭiccasamuppādo, dukkhānubandhanaraso, kummaggapaccupaṭṭhānoti veditabbo.

572. Thus, when teaching dependent origination with such synonyms as 'suchness,' etc., it was the conditioning phenomena themselves that were called dependent origination. Therefore, dependent origination should be understood as having the characteristic of being a condition for phenomena such as aging-and-death, as having the function of ensuring the continuation of suffering, and as having the manifestation of a wrong path.

So panāyaṃ tehi tehi paccayehi anūnādhikeheva tassa tassa dhammassa sambhavato tathatāti, sāmaggiṃ upagatesu paccayesu muhuttampi tato nibbattadhammānaṃ asambhavābhāvato avitathatāti, aññadhammapaccayehi aññadhammānuppattito anaññathatāti, yathāvuttānaṃ etesaṃ jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ paccayato vā paccayasamūhato vā idappaccayatāti vutto.

And this is called 'suchness' because of the arising of a specific phenomenon from its specific conditions without deficiency or excess. It is called 'undeviatingness' because when the conditions have come together, there is no non-arising, even for a moment, of the phenomena that should be produced from them. It is called 'unalterableness' because another phenomenon does not arise from the conditions for a different one. And it is called 'specific conditionality' because it is the condition, or the collection of conditions, for these phenomena mentioned, that is, aging-and-death, etc.

573. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho, imesaṃ paccayā idappaccayā. Idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā. Idappaccayānaṃ vā samūho idappaccayatā. Lakkhaṇaṃ panettha saddasatthato pariyesitabbaṃ.

573. Herein, this is the meaning of the expression: The conditions for these phenomena are 'this-conditions' (idappaccayā). 'This-conditionality' (idappaccayatā) is simply the state of being 'this-conditions.' Or 'this-conditionality' is the collection of 'this-conditions.' The grammatical formation here should be sought from the science of grammar.

574. Keci [V 2.0148] pana paṭicca sammā ca titthiyaparikappitapakatipurisādikāraṇanirapekkho uppādo paṭiccasamuppādoti evaṃ uppādamattaṃ paṭiccasamuppādoti vadanti[M 2.0150], taṃ na yujjati. Kasmā? Suttābhāvato, suttavirodhato, gambhīranayāsambhavato, saddabhedato ca. “Uppādamattaṃ paṭiccasamuppādo”ti hi suttaṃ natthi. Taṃ “paṭiccasamuppādo”ti ca vadantassa padesavihārasuttavirodho āpajjati. Kathaṃ? Bhagavato hi “atha kho bhagavā rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ anulomapaṭilomaṃ manasākāsī”ti (mahāva. 1) ādivacanato paṭiccasamuppādamanasikāro paṭhamābhisambuddhavihāro, padesavihāro ca tassekadesavihāro. Yathāha “yena svāhaṃ, bhikkhave, vihārena paṭhamābhisambuddho viharāmi, tassa padesena vihāsi”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.11). Tatra ca paccayākāradassanena vihāsi, na uppādamattadassanenāti. Yathāha “so evaṃ pajānāmi micchādiṭṭhipaccayāpi vedayitaṃ sammādiṭṭhipaccayāpi vedayitaṃ micchāsaṅkappapaccayāpi vedayita”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.11) sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Evaṃ uppādamattaṃ “paṭiccasamuppādo”ti vadantassa padesavihārasuttavirodho āpajjati. Tathā kaccānasuttavirodho.

574. Some, however, say that dependent origination is merely arising—that is, an arising that is dependent, right, and independent of causes such as primordial nature, a person, etc., fabricated by outsiders. That is not right. Why? Because there is no sutta for it, because it contradicts the suttas, because a profound method is impossible, and because of a grammatical violation. For there is no sutta that says, 'Dependent origination is merely arising.' And for one who says this, a contradiction with the Sutta on Partial Abiding arises. How? From the Blessed One's statement, 'Then, during the first watch of the night, the Blessed One gave attention to dependent origination in forward and reverse order,' it is clear that attention to dependent origination was his abiding immediately after full enlightenment, and the 'partial abiding' was an abiding in one part of that. As he said: 'Bhikkhus, I abide in a part of that abiding in which I abode when I was newly fully enlightened.' And there he abode by seeing the pattern of conditions, not by seeing mere arising. As he said: 'I understand thus: "There is feeling conditioned by wrong view, and there is feeling conditioned by right view; there is feeling conditioned by wrong thought..."' and so on in full. Thus, for one who says that dependent origination is merely arising, a contradiction with the Sutta on Partial Abiding arises. Likewise, a contradiction with the Kaccāna Sutta.

Kaccānasuttepi hi “lokasamudayaṃ kho, kaccāna, yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato yā loke natthitā, sā na hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.15) anulomapaṭiccasamuppādo lokapaccayato “lokasamudayo”ti ucchedadiṭṭhisamugghātatthaṃ pakāsito, na uppādamattaṃ. Na hi uppādamattadassanena ucchedadiṭṭhiyā samugghāto hoti. Paccayānuparamadassanena pana hoti. Paccayānuparame phalānuparamatoti. Evaṃ uppādamattaṃ “paṭiccasamuppādo”ti vadantassa kaccānasuttavirodhopi āpajjati.

In the Kaccāna Sutta, too, the forward-order dependent origination was shown as 'the origin of the world'—on account of the world's conditions—in order to eradicate the annihilationist view, not to show mere arising. For it is said: 'When, Kaccāna, one sees the origin of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, the view of non-existence in the world does not occur.' For the annihilationist view is not eradicated by seeing mere arising. But it is eradicated by seeing the non-cessation of conditions, because when the conditions do not cease, the result does not cease. Thus, for one who says that dependent origination is merely arising, a contradiction with the Kaccāna Sutta also arises.

Gambhīranayāsambhavatoti vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā “gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo gambhīrāvabhāso cā”ti (dī. ni. 2.95; saṃ. ni. 2.60). Gambhīrattañca nāma catubbidhaṃ, taṃ parato vaṇṇayissāma. Taṃ uppādamatte natthi. Catubbidhanayapaṭimaṇḍitañcetaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ vaṇṇayanti, tampi nayacatukkaṃ uppādamatte natthīti gambhīranayāsambhavatopi na uppādamattaṃ paṭiccasamuppādo.

Because a profound method is impossible: for this was said by the Blessed One: 'This dependent origination, Ānanda, is profound and it appears profound.' And profundity is fourfold, which we shall describe below. That does not exist in mere arising. They describe this dependent origination as adorned with a fourfold method, but that tetrad of methods, too, does not exist in mere arising. Therefore, also because a profound method is impossible, dependent origination is not mere arising.

575. Saddabhedatoti paṭiccasaddo ca panāyaṃ samāne kattari pubbakāle payujjamāno atthasiddhikaro [V 2.0149] hoti. Seyyathidaṃ, “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.43). Idha pana bhāvasādhanena uppādasaddena [M 2.0151] saddhiṃ payujjamāno samānassa kattu abhāvato saddabhedaṃ gacchati, na ca kiñci atthaṃ sādhetīti saddabhedatopi na uppādamattaṃ paṭiccasamuppādoti.

575. Because of a grammatical violation: for this word 'paṭicca,' when used with a common agent to denote a prior action, conveys its meaning. For example: 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises.' But here, when used with the word 'uppāda' in its abstract sense, it results in a grammatical violation because there is no common agent, and it does not establish any meaning. Therefore, also because of a grammatical violation, dependent origination is not mere arising.

Tattha siyā – “hoti-saddena saddhiṃ yojayissāma ‘paṭiccasamuppādo hotī’ti”, taṃ na yuttaṃ. Kasmā? Yogābhāvato ceva, uppādassa ca uppādapattidosato. “Paṭiccasamuppādaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādo…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādo”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.1). Imesu hi padesu ekenapi saddhiṃ hoti-saddo yogaṃ na gacchati, na ca uppādo hoti. Sace bhaveyya, uppādassāpi uppādo pāpuṇeyyāti.

Here it might be said: 'We shall connect it with the word 'hoti' (is), thus: 'paṭiccasamuppādo hoti' (dependent origination is).' That is not correct. Why? Both because of the lack of connection and because of the fault of an arising of arising. 'Bhikkhus, I will teach you dependent origination. And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? ... This, bhikkhus, is called dependent origination.' In these passages the word 'hoti' has no connection with any of them, nor does arising 'arise.' If it did, it would follow that arising itself has an arising.

576. Yepi maññanti “idappaccayānaṃ bhāvo idappaccayatā, bhāvo ca nāma yo ākāro avijjādīnaṃ saṅkhārādipātubhāve hetu, so. Tasmiñca saṅkhāravikāre paṭiccasamuppādasaññā”ti, tesaṃ taṃ na yujjati. Kasmā? Avijjādīnaṃ hetuvacanato. Bhagavatā hi “tasmātiha, ānanda, eseva hetu, etaṃ nidānaṃ, esa samudayo, esa paccayo jarāmaraṇassa yadidaṃ jāti…pe… saṅkhārānaṃ, yadidaṃ avijjā”ti (dī. ni. 2.98 ādayo) evaṃ avijjādayova hetūti vuttā, na tesaṃ vikāro. Tasmā “paṭiccasamuppādoti paccayadhammā veditabbā”ti iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ sammā vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

576. As for those who think: 'The state of these conditions is specific conditionality, and "state" refers to the mode that is the cause for the manifestation of volitional formations, etc., on the part of ignorance, etc. And in that modification of them, there is the designation of dependent origination'—that is not tenable for them. Why? Because ignorance and so on are stated as the cause. For the Blessed One has said: 'Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for aging-and-death, that is, birth… for volitional formations, that is, ignorance.' Thus ignorance and so on are stated as the causes, not their modification. Therefore, what was said—'Dependent origination is to be understood as the conditioning phenomena'—should be understood as rightly spoken.

577. Yā panettha “paṭiccasamuppādo”ti imāya byañjanacchāyāya uppādoyevāyaṃ vuttoti saññā uppajjati, sā imassa padassa evamatthaṃ gahetvā vūpasametabbā. Bhagavatā hi,

577. The perception that might arise here—that by this verbal formulation 'dependent origination' only an arising is spoken of—should be allayed by grasping the meaning of this term in this way. For the Blessed One has said:

Dvedhā tato pavatte, dhammasamūhe yato idaṃ vacanaṃ;

Tappaccayo tatoyaṃ, phalopacārena iti vutto.

Since this statement is twofold

Regarding the group of phenomena proceeding from that,

Therefore this, its condition, is so called

By a figurative usage for the fruit.

Yo hi ayaṃ paccayatāya pavatto dhammasamūho, tattha paṭiccasamuppādoti idaṃ vacanaṃ dvidhā icchanti. So hi yasmā patīyamāno hitāya sukhāya ca saṃvattati, tasmā paccetumarahanti [V 2.0150] naṃ paṇḍitāti paṭicco. Uppajjamāno ca saha sammā ca uppajjati, na ekekato, nāpi ahetutoti samuppādo. Evaṃ paṭicco ca so samuppādo cāti paṭiccasamuppādo[M 2.0152]. Apica saha uppajjatīti samuppādo, paccayasāmaggiṃ pana paṭicca apaccakkhāyāti evampi paṭiccasamuppādo. Tassa cāyaṃ hetusamūho paccayoti tappaccayattā ayampi, yathā loke semhassa paccayo guḷo semho guḷoti vuccati, yathā ca sāsane sukhappaccayo buddhānaṃ uppādo “sukho buddhānaṃ uppādo”ti vuccati, tathā paṭiccasamuppādo icceva phalavohārena vuttoti veditabbo.

Regarding this group of phenomena that proceeds by way of conditionality, the statement 'dependent origination' is intended in two ways. Because, when approached, it conduces to welfare and happiness, the wise are fit to approach it; hence paṭicca (dependent). And because it arises together and rightly, not singly nor without a cause, it is samuppāda (origination). Thus, it is paṭicca and it is samuppāda, hence paṭiccasamuppāda. Moreover, because it arises together, it is samuppāda; and because it does so dependent on an assemblage of conditions without rejecting any, thus too it is paṭiccasamuppāda. And since this group of causes is a condition, because of its being a condition for this, this too—just as in the world molasses, a condition for phlegm, is called 'phlegm,' and just as in the Dispensation the arising of the Buddhas, a condition for happiness, is called 'the happy arising of the Buddhas'—so too, it should be understood that 'dependent origination' is spoken of by a designation for the fruit.

578. Atha vā,

578. Or alternatively:

Paṭimukhamitoti vutto, hetusamūho ayaṃ paṭiccoti;

Sahite uppādeti ca, iti vutto so samuppādo.

This group of causes is called paṭicca

Because it is said to have 'gone towards';

And because it produces things that are together,

It is therefore called samuppāda.

Yo hi esa saṅkhārādīnaṃ pātubhāvāya avijjādiekekahetusīsena niddiṭṭho hetusamūho, so sādhāraṇaphalanipphādakaṭṭhena avekallaṭṭhena ca sāmaggiaṅgānaṃ aññamaññena paṭimukhaṃ ito gatoti katvā paṭiccoti vuccati. Svāyaṃ sahiteyeva aññamaññaṃ avinibbhogavuttidhamme uppādetīti samuppādotipi vutto. Evampi paṭicco ca so samuppādo cāti paṭiccasamuppādo.

This group of causes, which is indicated with ignorance and so on as the head of each single cause for the manifestation of volitional formations and so on, is called paṭicca because the components of the assemblage have 'gone towards' each other face to face, in the sense of producing a common result and in the sense of completeness. And this same group is also called samuppāda because it produces only together states whose functions are inseparable from each other. Thus too, it is paṭicca and it is samuppāda, hence paṭiccasamuppāda.

579. Aparo nayo –

579. Another method:

Paccayatā aññoññaṃ, paṭicca yasmā samaṃ saha ca dhamme;

Ayamuppādeti tatopi, evamidha bhāsitā muninā.

Because this conditionality produces

Phenomena dependently on each other,

Completely and together, therefore

It was spoken thus here by the Sage.

Avijjādisīsena niddiṭṭhapaccayesu hi ye paccayā yaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ dhammaṃ uppādenti, na te aññamaññaṃ apaṭicca aññamaññavekalle sati uppādetuṃ samatthāti. Tasmā paṭicca samaṃ saha ca na ekekadesaṃ, nāpi pubbāparabhāvena ayaṃ paccayatā dhamme uppādetīti atthānusāravohārakusalena muninā evamidha bhāsitā, paṭiccasamuppādotveva bhāsitāti attho.

For among the conditions indicated with ignorance and so on as their head, those conditions that produce a phenomenon such as volitional formations are not able to produce it without depending on each other, when there is a deficiency in regard to each other. Therefore, this conditionality produces phenomena dependently, completely, and together, not partially, nor in a sequence of before and after. Thus it was spoken here by the Sage, who is skilled in expression that accords with the meaning; that is, it was spoken of as 'dependent origination.' This is the meaning.

580. Evaṃ [V 2.0151] bhāsamānena ca,

580. And by speaking thus,

Purimena sassatādīna, mabhāvo pacchimena ca padena;

Ucchedādivighāto, dvayena paridīpito ñāyo.

By the first term, the absence of eternalism and so on,

And by the latter term, the demolition of annihilationism and so on;

By the two together the principle is clarified.

Purimenāti [M 2.0153] paccayasāmaggiparidīpakena paṭiccapadena pavattidhammānaṃ paccayasāmaggiyaṃ āyattavuttittā sassatāhetuvisamahetuvasavattivādappabhedānaṃ sassatādīnaṃ abhāvo paridīpito hoti? Kiṃ hi sassatānaṃ, ahetuādivasena vā pavattānaṃ paccayasāmaggiyāti? Pacchimena ca padenāti dhammānaṃ uppādaparidīpakena samuppādapadena paccayasāmaggiyaṃ dhammānaṃ uppattito vihatā ucchedanatthikaakiriyavādāti ucchedādivighāto paridīpito hoti. Purimapurimapaccayavasena hi punappunaṃ uppajjamānesu dhammesu kuto ucchedo, natthikākiriyavādā cāti. Dvayenāti sakalena paṭiccasamuppādavacanena tassā tassā paccayasāmaggiyā santatiṃ avicchinditvā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sambhavato majjhimā paṭipadā, “so karoti so paṭisaṃvedeti, añño karoti añño paṭisaṃvedetī”ti vādappahānaṃ, janapadaniruttiyā anabhiniveso, samaññāya anatidhāvananti ayaṃ ñāyo paridīpito hotīti ayaṃ tāva paṭiccasamuppādoti vacanamattassa attho.

'By the first term': By the term paṭicca, which clarifies the assemblage of conditions, the absence of eternalism and the like—that is, the various doctrines of eternalism, of causelessness, of uneven causes, and of a supreme creator—is clarified, since the occurrence of ongoing phenomena is dependent on an assemblage of conditions. For what has an assemblage of conditions to do with things that are eternal or that proceed from causelessness and so on? 'And by the latter term': By the term samuppāda, which clarifies the arising of phenomena, the demolition of annihilationism and so on—that is, the doctrines of annihilationism, nihilism, and inaction—is clarified, since phenomena originate from an assemblage of conditions. For when phenomena are arising again and again by the force of preceding conditions, whence can there be annihilationism, nihilism, or the doctrine of inaction? 'By the two together': By the whole expression 'dependent origination,' because of the occurrence of these and those phenomena without interrupting the continuity of this and that assemblage of conditions, this principle is clarified: the middle way; the abandonment of the doctrines 'He who acts is he who experiences' and 'One acts and another experiences'; non-adherence to provincial parlance; and not overrunning conventional usage. This, in the first place, is the meaning of the mere expression 'dependent origination'.

581. Yā panāyaṃ bhagavatā paṭiccasamuppādaṃ desentena “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā nayena nikkhittā tanti, tassā atthasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ karontena vibhajjavādimaṇḍalaṃ otaritvā ācariye anabbhācikkhantena sakasamayaṃ avokkamantena parasamayaṃ anāyūhantena suttaṃ appaṭibāhantena vinayaṃ anulomentena mahāpadese olokentena dhammaṃ dīpentena atthaṃ saṅgāhentena tamevatthaṃ punarāvattetvā aparehipi pariyāyantarehi niddisantena ca yasmā atthasaṃvaṇṇanā kātabbā hoti, pakatiyāpi ca dukkarāva paṭiccasamuppādassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanā. Yathāhu porāṇā –

581. Now, as to this textual formulation that was laid down by the Blessed One when he taught dependent origination by the method beginning, 'With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations,' an explanation of its meaning should be given by one who has entered the circle of the Analysts (Vibhajjavādins), who does not misrepresent the teachers, who does not abandon his own doctrine, who does not attack a rival doctrine, who does not reject the suttas, who conforms to the Vinaya, who looks to the Great Standards, who illuminates the Dhamma, who synthesizes the meaning, and who, after restating that same meaning, points it out by other alternative methods. And since, in the nature of things, an explanation of the meaning of dependent origination is difficult to make, as the ancients have said:

“Saccaṃ satto paṭisandhi, paccayākārameva ca;

Duddasā caturo dhammā, desetuṃ ca sudukkarā”ti.

Truth, a being, rebirth-linking,

And the structure of conditions too;

These four things are hard to see,

And to teach them is most difficult.

Tasmā [V 2.0152] aññatra āgamādhigamappattehi na sukarā paṭiccasamuppādassatthavaṇṇanāti paritulayitvā,

Therefore, having reflected that an explanation of the meaning of dependent origination is not easy for any except those who have attained the scriptures and realization,

Vattukāmo [M 2.0154] ahaṃ ajja, paccayākāravaṇṇanaṃ;

Patiṭṭhaṃ nādhigacchāmi, ajjhogāḷhova sāgaraṃ.

Wishing to speak today an explanation

Of the structure of conditions,

I find no footing, as if I were

One plunged into the ocean.

Sāsanaṃ panidaṃ nānā, desanānayamaṇḍitaṃ;

Pubbācariyamaggo ca, abbocchinno pavattati.

But this Dispensation is adorned

With many methods of teaching,

And the ancient teachers' path proceeds

Unbroken down to today.

Yasmā tasmā tadubhayaṃ, sannissāyatthavaṇṇanaṃ;

Ārabhissāmi etassa, taṃ suṇātha samāhitā.

Therefore, relying on them both,

I shall begin the explanation

Of its meaning. Now listen well

With minds attentive and composed.

Vuttañhetaṃ pubbācariyehi –

For it was said by the ancient teachers:

“Yo koci maṃ aṭṭhikatvā suṇeyya,

Labhetha pubbāpariyaṃ visesaṃ;

Laddhāna pubbāpariyaṃ visesaṃ,

Adassanaṃ maccurājassa gacche”ti.

Whoever listens to me with respect

Would gain a special distinction

In what precedes and what follows;

And gaining that, he would pass

Beyond the sight of the King of Death.

582. Iti avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārātiādīsu hi āditoyeva tāva,

582. So, in the sequence beginning, 'With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations,' first, at the very beginning,

Desanābhedato attha, lakkhaṇekavidhādito. Aṅgānañca vavatthānā, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

The exposition should be understood

From the division of the teaching,

From the meaning, characteristic, kinds, and so on,

And from the determination of the factors.

Tattha desanābhedatoti bhagavato hi vallihārakānaṃ catunnaṃ purisānaṃ valligahaṇaṃ viya ādito vā majjhato vā paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānaṃ, tathā pariyosānato vā majjhato vā paṭṭhāya yāva ādīti catubbidhā paṭiccasamuppādadesanā.

Herein, 'from the division of the teaching' means that the Blessed One's teaching of dependent origination is fourfold, like the grasping of a creeper by four men who are creeper-gatherers: from the beginning to the end, or from the middle to the end; likewise, from the end to the beginning, or from the middle to the beginning.

Yathā hi vallihārakesu catūsu purisesu eko valliyā mūlameva paṭhamaṃ passati, so taṃ mūle [V 2.0153] chetvā sabbaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā ādāya kamme upaneti, evaṃ bhagavā “iti kho, bhikkhave, avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā…pe… jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti (ma. ni. 1.402; saṃ. ni. 2.2) ādito paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānāpi paṭiccasamuppādaṃ deseti.

For just as among four creeper-gatherers, one first sees the root of the creeper, and cutting it at the root, he pulls the whole of it, takes it, and puts it to use; so the Blessed One teaches dependent origination from the beginning right up to the end: 'So, bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations… with birth as condition, there is aging-and-death' (MN 38; SN 12.1).

Yathā pana tesu purisesu eko valliyā majjhaṃ paṭhamaṃ passati, so majjhe chinditvā uparibhāgaññeva ākaḍḍhitvā ādāya kamme upaneti, evaṃ bhagavā “tassa taṃ vedanaṃ abhinandato abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato [M 2.0155] uppajjati nandī. Yā vedanāsu nandī, tadupādānaṃ. Tassupādānapaccayā bhavo, bhavapaccayā jātī”ti (ma. ni. 1.409; saṃ. ni. 3.5) majjhato paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānāpi deseti.

And just as among those men, one first sees the middle of the creeper, and cutting it in the middle, he pulls only the upper part, takes it, and puts it to use; so the Blessed One teaches from the middle to the end: 'For one who delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains holding to it, delight arises. Whatever delight there is in feelings is clinging. With clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth' (MN 38; SN 22.85).

Yathā ca tesu purisesu eko valliyā aggaṃ paṭhamaṃ passati, so agge gahetvā aggānusārena yāva mūlā sabbaṃ ādāya kamme upaneti, evaṃ bhagavā “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, jātipaccayā nu kho, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇaṃ no vā kathaṃ vo ettha hotīti? Jātipaccayā, bhante, jarāmaraṇaṃ. Evaṃ no ettha hoti jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti. Bhavapaccayā jāti…pe… avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, avijjāpaccayā nu kho, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā no vā kathaṃ vo ettha hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.403) pariyosānato paṭṭhāya yāva āditopi paṭiccasamuppādaṃ deseti.

And just as among those men, one first sees the tip of a creeper, takes hold of the tip, and following the tip all the way to the root, takes it all and applies it to his work, so the Blessed One says: ‘“With birth as condition, aging-and-death”—thus it was said. Now, bhikkhus, is aging-and-death conditioned by birth, or not? How does it appear to you in this matter?’ ‘With birth as condition, venerable sir, aging-and-death. Thus it appears to us in this matter: aging-and-death is conditioned by birth.’ ‘“With becoming as condition, birth”… “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations”—thus it was said. Now, bhikkhus, are volitional formations conditioned by ignorance, or not? How does it appear to you in this matter?’ (cf. MN 38). Thus he teaches dependent origination from the end back to the beginning.

Yathā panetesu purisesu eko valliyā majjhameva paṭhamaṃ passati, so majjhe chinditvā heṭṭhā otaranto yāva mūlā ādāya kamme upaneti, evaṃ bhagavā “ime ca, bhikkhave, cattāro āhārā kinnidānā, kiṃsamudayā, kiṃjātikā, kiṃpabhavā? Ime cattāro āhārā taṇhānidānā, taṇhāsamudayā, taṇhājātikā, taṇhāpabhavā. Taṇhā kinnidānā… vedanā… phasso… saḷāyatanaṃ… nāmarūpaṃ… viññāṇaṃ… saṅkhārā kinnidānā…pe… saṅkhārā avijjānidānā…pe… avijjāpabhavā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.11) majjhato paṭṭhāya yāva ādito deseti.

Again, just as one of these men first sees the middle of a creeper, cuts it in the middle and, going downwards, takes it as far as the root and applies it to his work, so the Blessed One teaches from the middle back to the beginning, saying: ‘And these four kinds of nutriment, bhikkhus—what is their source, what their origin, what their birth, what their provenance? These four kinds of nutriment have craving as their source, craving as their origin, craving as their birth, craving as their provenance. Craving—what is its source…? Feeling… Contact… The six sense bases… Name-and-form… Consciousness… Volitional formations—what is their source…? … Volitional formations have ignorance as their source… ignorance as their provenance’ (SN 12.11).

583. Kasmā panevaṃ desetīti? Paṭiccasamuppādassa samantabhaddakattā sayañca desanāvilāsappattattā. Samantabhaddako hi paṭiccasamuppādo, tato tato ñāyapaṭivedhāya saṃvattatiyeva[V 2.0154]. Desanāvilāsappatto ca bhagavā catuvesārajjapaṭisambhidāyogena catubbidhagambhīrabhāvappattiyā ca. So desanāvilāsappattattā nānānayeheva dhammaṃ deseti.

583. But why does he teach in this way? Because dependent origination is good all around, and because he himself has attained grace in exposition. For dependent origination is good all around, as it is conducive from any point to the penetration of the right method. And the Blessed One, having attained grace in exposition through his endowment with the four kinds of fearlessness and the analytical knowledges, and through his attainment of the fourfold profundity, teaches the Dhamma in various ways because of this attainment of grace in exposition.

Visesato panassa yā ādito paṭṭhāya anulomadesanā, sā pavattikāraṇavibhāgasaṃmūḷhaṃ veneyyajanaṃ samanupassato yathāsakehi kāraṇehi pavattisandassanatthaṃ uppattikkamasandassanatthañca pavattāti viññātabbā. Yā pariyosānato paṭṭhāya paṭilomadesanā, sā “kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko [M 2.0156] āpanno jāyati ca jīyati ca mīyati ca cavati ca upapajjati cā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.57; saṃ. ni. 2.4) nayena kicchāpannaṃ lokaṃ anuvilokayato pubbabhāgapaṭivedhānusārena tassa tassa jarāmaraṇādikassa dukkhassa attanā adhigatakāraṇasandassanatthaṃ. Yā majjhato paṭṭhāya yāva ādi pavattā, sā āhāranidānavavatthāpanānusārena yāva atītaṃ addhānaṃ atiharitvā puna atītaddhato pabhuti hetuphalapaṭipāṭisandassanatthaṃ. Yā pana majjhato paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānaṃ pavattā, sā paccuppanne addhāne anāgataddhahetusamuṭṭhānato pabhuti anāgataddhasandassanatthaṃ. Tāsu yā pavattikāraṇasammūḷhassa veneyyajanassa yathāsakehi kāraṇehi pavattisandassanatthaṃ uppattikkamasandassanatthañca ādito paṭṭhāya anulomadesanā vuttā, sā idha nikkhittāti veditabbā.

But specifically, it should be understood that his teaching in forward order from the beginning is intended for those persons to be trained who are confused about the analysis of the causes of the process of existence, for the purpose of showing them this process according to its respective causes and showing the sequence of arising. The teaching in reverse order from the end is for one who reflects on the world as having fallen into difficulty—‘Alas, this world has fallen into difficulty: it is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn’ (DN 14; SN 12.4)—for the purpose of showing, in accordance with his initial penetration, the causes that he himself discovered for such suffering as aging-and-death. The teaching that proceeds from the middle back to the beginning is for showing the sequence of cause and effect by tracing it back into the past in accordance with the establishment of nutriment as a condition, and then showing the sequence from the past onwards. The teaching that proceeds from the middle to the end is for showing the future, beginning from the arising of causes for the future in the present. Among these, it should be understood that the teaching presented here is the one in forward order from the beginning, which is intended for those confused about the causes of the process of existence, to show them this process and the sequence of arising according to its respective causes.

584. Kasmā panettha avijjā ādito vuttā, kiṃ pakativādīnaṃ pakati viya avijjāpi akāraṇaṃ mūlakāraṇaṃ lokassāti? Na akāraṇaṃ. “Āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.103) hi avijjāya kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Atthi pana pariyāyo yena mūlakāraṇaṃ siyā, ko pana soti? Vaṭṭakathāya sīsabhāvo.

584. But why is ignorance stated here as the beginning? Is it that, like the primal nature (pakati) of the primordialists, ignorance is an uncaused root cause of the world? No, it is not without a cause. For it is said, ‘With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance’ (MN 9), showing that ignorance has a cause. But there is a way in which it could be considered the root cause. What is it? It holds the principal place in the account of the round of existence.

Bhagavā hi vaṭṭakathaṃ kathento dve dhamme sīsaṃ katvā katheti, avijjaṃ vā. Yathāha – “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati avijjāya ‘ito pubbe avijjā nāhosi, atha pacchā samabhavī’ti, evañcetaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati, atha ca pana paññāyati idappaccayā avijjā”ti (a. ni. 10.61). Bhavataṇhaṃ vā. Yathāha – “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati bhavataṇhāya ‘ito pubbe bhavataṇhā nāhosi, atha pacchā samabhavī’ti, evañcetaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati, atha ca pana paññāyati idappaccayā bhavataṇhā”ti (a. ni. 10.62).

For when the Blessed One explains the round of existence, he makes two states primary in his explanation: either ignorance or craving for existence. As was said: ‘Bhikkhus, a first point of ignorance is not discerned, of which it might be said: “Before this, ignorance did not exist, and it came to be later.” And though this is said, bhikkhus, it is still discerned that ignorance has a specific condition.’ (AN 10.61). Or craving for existence. As was said: ‘Bhikkhus, a first point of craving for existence is not discerned, of which it might be said: “Before this, craving for existence did not exist, and it came to be later.” And though this is said, bhikkhus, it is still discerned that craving for existence has a specific condition.’ (AN 10.62).

585. Kasmā [V 2.0155] pana bhagavā vaṭṭakathaṃ kathento ime dve dhamme sīsaṃ katvā kathetīti? Sugatiduggatigāmino kammassa visesahetubhūtattā. Duggatigāmino hi kammassa visesahetu avijjā. Kasmā? Yasmā avijjābhibhūto puthujjano aggisantāpalaguḷābhighātaparissamābhibhūtā vajjhagāvī tāya parissamāturatāya nirassādampi attano anatthāvahampi ca uṇhodakapānaṃ [M 2.0157] viya kilesasantāpato nirassādampi duggatinipātanato ca attano anatthāvahampi pāṇātipātādiṃ anekappakāraṃ duggatigāmikammaṃ ārabhati. Sugatigāmino pana kammassa visesahetu bhavataṇhā. Kasmā? Yasmā bhavataṇhābhibhūto puthujjano sā vuttappakārā gāvī sītūdakataṇhāya saassādaṃ attano parissamavinodanañca sītūdakapānaṃ viya kilesasantāpavirahato saassādaṃ sugatisampāpanena attano duggatidukkhaparissamavinodanañca pāṇātipātā veramaṇiādiṃ anekappakāraṃ sugatigāmikammaṃ ārabhati.

585. But why does the Blessed One, when explaining the round of existence, make these two states primary? Because they are the special causes for kamma that leads to good and bad destinations. Ignorance is the special cause for kamma leading to bad destinations. Why? Because an uninstructed worldling, overwhelmed by ignorance—like a cow for slaughter that, overcome by the torment of being seared by fire and struck with a club, drinks hot water that is tasteless and harmful to it because it is afflicted by that torment—undertakes various kinds of kamma leading to a bad destination, such as the destruction of life, which is tasteless because of the torment of the defilements and harmful to himself because it leads to a fall into a bad destination. But craving for existence is the special cause for kamma leading to good destinations. Why? Because an uninstructed worldling, overwhelmed by craving for existence—like that same cow that, thirsting for cool water, drinks cool water that is pleasant and relieves its torment—undertakes various kinds of kamma leading to a good destination, such as abstaining from the destruction of life, which is pleasant because it is free from the torment of the defilements and which relieves the torment of suffering in a bad destination by bringing attainment of a good destination.

586. Etesu pana vaṭṭakathāya sīsabhūtesu dhammesu katthaci bhagavā ekadhammamūlikaṃ desanaṃ deseti. Seyyathidaṃ, “iti kho, bhikkhave, avijjūpanisā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārūpanisaṃ viññāṇa”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.23). Tathā “upādāniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati, taṇhāpaccayā upādāna”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.52). Katthaci ubhayamūlikampi. Seyyathidaṃ, “avijjānīvaraṇassa, bhikkhave, bālassa taṇhāya sampayuttassa evamayaṃ kāyo samudāgato. Iti ayañceva kāyo bahiddhā ca nāmarūpaṃ itthetaṃ dvayaṃ. Dvayaṃ paṭicca phasso saḷevāyatanāni, yehi phuṭṭho bālo sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedetī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.19). Tāsu desanāsu “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti ayamidha avijjāvasena ekadhammamūlikā desanāti veditabbā. Evaṃ tāvettha desanābhedato viññātabbo vinicchayo.

586. Among these states, which are primary in the account of the round of existence, the Blessed One sometimes gives a teaching with a single root. For instance: ‘Thus, bhikkhus, ignorance is the supporting condition for volitional formations; volitional formations are the supporting condition for consciousness….’ (SN 12.23). And: ‘Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are fuel for clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, there is clinging….’ (SN 12.52). Sometimes he gives a teaching with a double root. For instance: ‘Bhikkhus, for the fool, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has come to be. Thus there is this body and external name-and-form; so this is a dyad. With the dyad as condition, there is contact through the six sense bases; touched by them, the fool experiences pleasure and pain….’ (SN 12.19). Among these teachings, the one beginning ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations,’ should be understood here as a teaching with a single root, namely, ignorance. Thus the analysis should be understood according to the different kinds of teaching.

587. Atthatoti avijjādīnaṃ padānaṃ atthato. Seyyathidaṃ, pūretuṃ ayuttaṭṭhena kāyaduccaritādi avindiyaṃ nāma, aladdhabbanti attho. Taṃ avindiyaṃ vindatīti avijjā. Tabbiparītato kāyasucaritādi vindiyaṃ nāma, taṃ vindiyaṃ na vindatīti avijjā. Khandhānaṃ rāsaṭṭhaṃ, āyatanānaṃ āyatanaṭṭhaṃ, dhātūnaṃ suññaṭṭhaṃ, indriyānaṃ adhipatiyaṭṭhaṃ, saccānaṃ tathaṭṭhaṃ aviditaṃ karotītipi avijjā. Dukkhādīnaṃ pīḷanādivasena vuttaṃ catubbidhaṃ atthaṃ aviditaṃ karotītipi avijjā. Antavirahite saṃsāre sabbayonigatibhavaviññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsesu satte javāpetīti [V 2.0156] avijjā. Paramatthato avijjamānesu itthipurisādīsu javati, vijjamānesupi khandhādīsu na javatīti avijjā. Apica cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ [M 2.0158] vatthārammaṇānaṃ paṭiccasamuppādapaṭiccasamuppannānañca dhammānaṃ chādanatopi avijjā.

587. As to meaning: this is the meaning of the terms beginning with ignorance. For instance: bodily misconduct and so on are called ‘unobtainable’ (avindiya) in the sense that they are unfit to be pursued. Because it obtains (vindati) what is unobtainable (avindiya), it is called ignorance (avijjā). Conversely, bodily good conduct and so on are called ‘obtainable’ (vindiya). Because it does not obtain (na vindati) what is obtainable (vindiya), it is called ignorance (avijjā). Also, it is ignorance because it makes unknown the meaning of the aggregates as a heap, the meaning of the sense bases as sources, the meaning of the elements as voidness, the meaning of the faculties as sovereignty, and the meaning of the truths as reality. It is also ignorance because it makes unknown the fourfold meaning of suffering, etc., stated in terms of affliction, etc. It is ignorance because it makes beings run on in the beginningless round of existence through all destinations, planes of existence, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings. It is ignorance because it runs on with respect to what is non-existent in the ultimate sense, such as a woman or a man, but does not run on with respect to what is existent, such as the aggregates. Furthermore, it is ignorance because it conceals the bases and objects of such consciousnesses as eye-consciousness, and it conceals dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena.

Yaṃ paṭicca phalameti, so paccayo. Paṭiccāti na vinā apaccakkhatvāti attho. Etīti uppajjati ceva pavattati cāti attho. Apica upakārakaṭṭho paccayaṭṭho. Avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo. Tasmā avijjāpaccayā.

A condition (paccaya) is that depending on which a result comes to be. ‘Depending on’ (paṭicca) means not without, not separate from. ‘Comes to be’ (eti) means it both arises and continues. Furthermore, the meaning of ‘condition’ is that of a supporting factor. It is ignorance (avijjā) and it is a condition (paccayo), hence ‘ignorance-condition’ (avijjāpaccayo). Therefore, ‘on account of the ignorance-condition’ (avijjāpaccayā).

Saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharontīti saṅkhārā. Apica avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārasaddena āgatasaṅkhārāti duvidhā saṅkhārā. Tattha puññāpuññāneñjābhisaṅkhārā tayo, kāyavacīcittasaṅkhārā tayoti ime cha avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā. Te sabbepi lokiyakusalākusalacetanāmattameva honti.

‘They form the formed’ (saṅkhatam abhisaṅkharonti), thus they are called ‘formations’ (saṅkhārā). Furthermore, formations are of two kinds: those conditioned by ignorance, and those designated by the word ‘saṅkhāra’. Therein, there are the three formations—meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable—and the three formations—bodily, verbal, and mental. These six are the formations conditioned by ignorance. All of them are simply worldly wholesome and unwholesome volitions.

Saṅkhatasaṅkhāro, abhisaṅkhatasaṅkhāro, abhisaṅkharaṇakasaṅkhāro, payogābhisaṅkhāroti ime pana cattāro saṅkhāra-saddena āgatasaṅkhārā. Tattha “aniccā vata saṅkhārā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.221, 272; saṃ. ni. 1.186) vuttā sabbepi sappaccayā dhammā saṅkhatasaṅkhārā nāma. Kammanibbattā tebhūmakā rūpārūpadhammā abhisaṅkhatasaṅkhārāti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttā, tepi “aniccā vata saṅkhārā”ti (dī. ni. 2.221; 272; saṃ. ni. 1.186) ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Visuṃ pana nesaṃ āgataṭṭhānaṃ na paññāyati. Tebhūmikakusalākusalacetanā pana abhisaṅkharaṇakasaṅkhāroti vuccati, tassa “avijjāgatoyaṃ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo puññañceva saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharotī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.51) āgataṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati. Kāyikacetasikaṃ pana vīriyaṃ payogābhisaṅkhāroti vuccati, so “yāvatikā abhisaṅkhārassa gati, tāvatikā gantvā akkhāhataṃ maññe aṭṭhāsī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.15) āgato.

Furthermore, these four are the formations that come under the term 'formations': conditioned formations, specially conditioned formations, conditioning formations, and formations of exertion. Among these, all causally conditioned phenomena spoken of in passages such as, 'Impermanent, alas, are formations!' are called 'conditioned formations.' Material and immaterial phenomena in the three realms produced by kamma are called 'specially conditioned formations' in the commentaries, and they too are included right here in 'Impermanent, alas, are formations!' A separate textual source for them, however, is not apparent. Furthermore, wholesome and unwholesome volitions in the three realms are called 'conditioning formations'; their textual source is apparent in passages such as, 'Bhikkhus, this person, overcome by ignorance, conditions a meritorious formation.' Furthermore, bodily and mental energy is called 'formations of exertion'; it is found in passages such as, 'Having gone as far as the momentum of the conditioning force extends, it stood still, I suppose, as if fixed to an axle.'

Na kevalañca eteyeva, aññepi “saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpajjantassa kho, āvuso visākha, bhikkhuno paṭhamaṃ nirujjhati vacīsaṅkhāro, tato kāyasaṅkhāro, tato cittasaṅkhāro”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.464) nayena saṅkhāra-saddena āgatā aneke saṅkhārā. Tesu natthi so saṅkhāro, yo saṅkhatasaṅkhārehi saṅgahaṃ na gaccheyya, ito paraṃ saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇantiādīsu vuttaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

And it is not only these; there are also many other formations that come under the term 'formations' by the method beginning: 'For a bhikkhu, friend Visākha, who is attaining the cessation of perception and feeling, the verbal formation ceases first, then the bodily formation, then the mental formation.' Among these, there is no formation that would not be included under conditioned formations. Henceforth, what is stated in passages such as 'from formations as condition, consciousness arises' should be understood in the way already explained.

Avutte [M 2.0159][V 2.0157] pana vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ. Namatīti nāmaṃ. Ruppatīti rūpaṃ. Āye tanoti āyatañca nayatīti āyatanaṃ. Phusatīti phasso. Vedayatīti vedanā. Paritassatīti taṇhā. Upādiyatīti upādānaṃ. Bhavati bhāvayati cāti bhavo. Jananaṃ jāti. Jiraṇaṃ jarā. Maranti etenāti maraṇaṃ. Socanaṃ soko. Paridevanaṃ paridevo. Dukkhayatīti dukkhaṃ. Uppādaṭṭhitivasena vā dvidhā khaṇatītipi dukkhaṃ. Dummanabhāvo domanassaṃ. Bhuso āyāso upāyāso.

Furthermore, regarding the terms not yet explained: It is 'consciousness' because it cognizes. It is 'name' because it inclines. It is 'form' because it is afflicted. It is a 'base' because it extends what comes and leads on what is long. It is 'contact' because it touches. It is 'feeling' because it experiences. It is 'craving' because it thirsts. It is 'clinging' because it grasps. It is 'becoming' because it becomes and brings into being. Generation is 'birth.' Decaying is 'aging.' It is 'death' because they die by means of it. Sorrowing is 'sorrow.' Lamenting is 'lamentation.' It is 'suffering' because it causes suffering. Or it is also 'suffering' because it digs away in two ways: by way of arising and presence. The state of a troubled mind is 'grief.' Extreme fatigue is 'despair.'

Sambhavantīti abhinibbattanti. Na kevalañca sokādīheva, atha kho sabbapadehi sambhavanti-saddassa yojanā kātabbā. Itarathā hi “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti vutte kiṃ karontīti na paññāyeyya, sambhavantīti pana yojanāya sati avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo. Tasmā avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā sambhavantīti paccayapaccayuppannavavatthānaṃ kataṃ hoti. Esa nayo sabbattha.

'They come into being' means they are produced. The application of the word 'come into being' should be made not only with sorrow and the other terms, but with all the terms. For otherwise, when it is said, 'From ignorance as condition, formations,' it would not be apparent what they do. But when the application 'come into being' is present, then: 'it is ignorance and it is a condition, thus it is a condition of ignorance.' Therefore, by the statement 'From ignorance as condition, formations come into being,' the distinction between the condition and the conditionally arisen phenomenon is made. This is the method in all cases.

Evanti niddiṭṭhanayanidassanaṃ. Tena avijjādīheva kāraṇehi, na issaranimmānādīhīti dasseti. Etassāti yathāvuttassa. Kevalassāti asammissassa, sakalassa vā. Dukkhakkhandhassāti dukkhasamūhassa, na sattassa, na sukhasubhādīnaṃ. Samudayoti nibbatti. Hotīti sambhavati. Evamettha atthato viññātabbo vinicchayo.

The word 'Thus' is an indication of the method that has been explained. By it, the text shows that this occurs only from causes such as ignorance, not from a creator god or the like. 'Of this' means of what has been stated. 'Mere' means unmixed, or alternatively, whole. 'Mass of suffering' means the aggregate of suffering, not of a being, nor of pleasure, beauty, and so on. 'Origination' means arising. 'There is' means it comes to be. In this way, the definitive meaning should be understood here.

588. Lakkhaṇāditoti avijjādīnaṃ lakkhaṇādito. Seyyathidaṃ – aññāṇalakkhaṇā avijjā, sammohanarasā, chādanapaccupaṭṭhānā, āsavapadaṭṭhānā. Abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇā saṅkhārā, āyūhanarasā, cetanāpaccupaṭṭhānā, avijjāpadaṭṭhānā. Vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ viññāṇaṃ, pubbaṅgamarasaṃ, paṭisandhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, saṅkhārapadaṭṭhānaṃ, vatthārammaṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Namanalakkhaṇaṃ nāmaṃ, sampayogarasaṃ, avinibbhogapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, viññāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ, vikiraṇarasaṃ, abyākatapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, viññāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Āyatanalakkhaṇaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ, dassanādirasaṃ, vatthudvārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, nāmarūpapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Phusanalakkhaṇo phasso, saṅghaṭṭanaraso, saṅgatipaccupaṭṭhāno, saḷāyatanapadaṭṭhāno. Anubhavanalakkhaṇā vedanā, visayarasasambhogarasā, sukhadukkhapaccupaṭṭhānā, phassapadaṭṭhānā. Hetulakkhaṇā taṇhā, abhinandanarasā, atittabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, vedanāpadaṭṭhānā. Gahaṇalakkhaṇaṃ [M 2.0160] upādānaṃ, amuñcanarasaṃ, taṇhādaḷhattadiṭṭhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, taṇhāpadaṭṭhānaṃ. Kammakammaphalalakkhaṇo bhavo, bhāvanabhavanaraso, kusalākusalābyākatapaccupaṭṭhāno[V 2.0158], upādānapadaṭṭhāno. Jātiādīnaṃ lakkhaṇādīni saccaniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Evamettha lakkhaṇāditopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

588. By way of characteristic, etc.: This means by way of the characteristic, etc., of ignorance and the other links. That is: Ignorance has the characteristic of not knowing, the function of causing delusion, the manifestation of concealing, and the proximate cause of the taints. Formations have the characteristic of conditioning, the function of accumulating, the manifestation of volition, and the proximate cause of ignorance. Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing, the function of being the forerunner, the manifestation of rebirth-linking, and the proximate cause of formations, or alternatively, a base and an object. Name has the characteristic of inclining, the function of association, the manifestation of inseparability, and the proximate cause of consciousness. Form has the characteristic of being afflicted, the function of being scattered, the manifestation of being indeterminate, and the proximate cause of consciousness. The sixfold sense base has the characteristic of being a sphere of operation, the function of seeing, etc., the manifestation of being a physical base and a door, and the proximate cause of name-and-form. Contact has the characteristic of touching, the function of impinging, the manifestation of concurrence, and the proximate cause of the sixfold sense base. Feeling has the characteristic of being experienced, the function of enjoying the taste of the object, the manifestation of pleasure and pain, and the proximate cause of contact. Craving has the characteristic of being a cause of suffering, the function of delighting, the manifestation of insatiability, and the proximate cause of feeling. Clinging has the characteristic of grasping, the function of not letting go, the manifestation as the strengthening of craving and as wrong view, and the proximate cause of craving. Becoming has the characteristic of kamma and the result of kamma, the function of bringing to be and being, the manifestation as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, and the proximate cause of clinging. The characteristics, etc., of birth and the other links should be understood in the way stated in the Exposition of the Truths. Thus, the definitive meaning should be understood here also by way of characteristic, etc.

589. Ekavidhāditoti ettha avijjā aññāṇādassanamohādibhāvato ekavidhā. Appaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattito duvidhā. Tathā sasaṅkhārāsaṅkhārato. Vedanattayasampayogato tividhā. Catusaccapaṭivedhato catubbidhā. Gatipañcakādīnavacchādanato pañcavidhā. Dvārārammaṇato pana sabbesupi arūpadhammesu chabbidhatā veditabbā.

589. By way of being singlefold, etc.: Herein, ignorance is singlefold in that it is a state of not knowing, not seeing, delusion, and so on. It is twofold as non-comprehension and wrong comprehension. Likewise, it is twofold as prompted and unprompted. It is threefold by way of its association with the three kinds of feeling. It is fourfold by way of non-penetration of the four truths. It is fivefold by way of concealing the danger in the five destinations. Furthermore, its sixfold nature should be understood in relation to the doors and objects in all immaterial phenomena.

Saṅkhārā sāsavavipākadhammadhammādibhāvato ekavidhā. Kusalākusalato duvidhā. Tathā parittamahaggatahīnamajjhimamicchattaniyatāniyatato. Tividhā puññābhisaṅkhārādibhāvato. Catubbidhā catuyonisaṃvattanato. Pañcavidhā pañcagatigāmito.

Volitional formations are singlefold due to their nature as being with taints, as being phenomena that produce results, and so on. They are twofold by way of the wholesome and unwholesome. Similarly, they are twofold by way of the limited and exalted, the inferior and middling, and the wrongly-fixed and unfixed. They are threefold due to their nature as meritorious formations, and so on. They are fourfold as they cause rebirth in the four birth-origins. They are fivefold as they lead to the five destinations.

Viññāṇaṃ lokiyavipākādibhāvato ekavidhaṃ. Sahetukāhetukādito duvidhaṃ. Bhavattayapariyāpannato, vedanattayasampayogato, ahetukadvihetukatihetukato ca tividhaṃ. Yonigativasena catubbidhaṃ, pañcavidhañca.

Consciousness is of one kind due to its nature as worldly result, etc. It is of two kinds as with roots and without roots, etc. It is of three kinds as comprised in the three planes of existence, associated with the three feelings, and as rootless, with two roots, and with three roots. It is fourfold and fivefold according to birth-origin and destination.

Nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇasannissayato kammapaccayato ca ekavidhaṃ. Sārammaṇanārammaṇato duvidhaṃ. Atītādito tividhaṃ. Yonigativasena catubbidhaṃ, pañcavidhañca.

Name-and-form is of one kind as dependent on consciousness and conditioned by kamma. It is of two kinds as with an object and without an object. It is of three kinds as past, etc. It is fourfold and fivefold according to birth-origin and destination.

Saḷāyatanaṃ sañjātisamosaraṇaṭṭhānato ekavidhaṃ. Bhūtappasādaviññāṇādito duvidhaṃ. Sampattāsampattanobhayagocarato tividhaṃ. Yonigatipariyāpannato catubbidhaṃ pañcavidhañcāti iminā nayena phassādīnampi ekavidhādibhāvo veditabboti evamettha ekavidhāditopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

The six sense bases are singlefold as the place of arising and convergence. They are twofold by way of sensitive matter and consciousness, and so on. They are threefold by way of having an object that has arrived, has not arrived, or is neither of the two. They are fourfold and fivefold as comprised in the birth-origins and destinations. In this way, the singlefold nature and so on of contact and the rest should also be understood. Thus, the analysis here is to be understood by way of the singlefold, and so on.

590. Aṅgānañca vavatthānāti sokādayo cettha bhavacakkassa avicchedadassanatthaṃ vuttā. Jarāmaraṇabbhāhatassa hi bālassa te sambhavanti. Yathāha [M 2.0161] – “assutavā, bhikkhave, puthujjano sārīrikāya dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohamāpajjatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.252). Yāva ca tesaṃ pavatti, tāva avijjāyāti punapi [V 2.0159] avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti sambandhameva hoti bhavacakkaṃ. Tasmā tesaṃ jarāmaraṇeneva ekasaṅkhepaṃ katvā dvādaseva paṭiccasamuppādaṅgānīti veditabbāni. Evamettha aṅgānaṃ vavatthānatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

590. Regarding the demarcation of the factors: Herein, sorrow and so on are stated to show the uninterrupted nature of the cycle of existence. For they arise in a fool who is afflicted by aging and death. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, when an uninstructed ordinary person is touched by a painful bodily feeling, he sorrows, grieves, and laments; he beats his breast, wails, and becomes distraught.' And as long as these occur, so long does ignorance occur. Thus, again, with 'conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise,' the cycle of existence is indeed connected. Therefore, by grouping these together with aging and death, it should be understood that there are just twelve factors of dependent origination. Thus, the analysis here is also to be understood by way of the demarcation of the factors.

Ayaṃ tāvettha saṅkhepakathā.

This, for now, is the concise exposition here.

Avijjāpaccayāsaṅkhārapadakathā

The Exposition of the Phrase 'Conditioned by Ignorance, Volitional Formations'

561. Ayaṃ pana vitthāranayo – avijjāti suttantapariyāyena dukkhādīsu catūsu ṭhānesu aññāṇaṃ, abhidhammapariyāyena pubbantādīhi saddhiṃ aṭṭhasu. Vuttañhetaṃ “tattha katamā avijjā, dukkhe aññāṇaṃ…pe… dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya aññāṇaṃ, pubbante aññāṇaṃ, aparante, pubbantāparante, idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu aññāṇa”nti (dha. sa. 1106). Tattha kiñcāpi ṭhapetvā lokuttaraṃ saccadvayaṃ sesaṭṭhānesu ārammaṇavasena avijjā uppajjati, evaṃ santepi paṭicchādanavaseneva idha adhippetā. Sā hi uppannā dukkhasaccaṃ paṭicchādetvā tiṭṭhati, yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ na deti, tathā samudayaṃ, nirodhaṃ, maggaṃ, pubbantasaṅkhātaṃ atītaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ, aparantasaṅkhātaṃ anāgataṃ khandhapañcakaṃ, pubbantāparantasaṅkhātaṃ tadubhayaṃ, idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannadhammasaṅkhātaṃ idappaccayatañceva paṭiccasamuppannadhamme ca paṭicchādetvā tiṭṭhati. “Ayaṃ avijjā, ime saṅkhārā”ti evaṃ yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇamettha paṭivijjhituṃ na deti. Tasmā dukkhe aññāṇaṃ…pe… idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu aññāṇanti vuccati.

561. Now, this is the detailed explanation. Ignorance (avijjā), according to the Suttanta method, is the lack of knowledge in four instances beginning with suffering; according to the Abhidhamma method, it is the lack of knowledge in eight instances including the past ends. For it is said: 'Herein, what is ignorance? Lack of knowledge concerning suffering... lack of knowledge concerning the path leading to the cessation of suffering; lack of knowledge concerning the past end, the future end, both the past and future ends; lack of knowledge concerning this-conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.' Here, although ignorance arises by way of taking as object the remaining six instances, setting aside the two supramundane truths, it is nevertheless intended here only in the sense of concealment. For when it arises, it stands concealing the truth of suffering, not allowing its true, inherent characteristic to be penetrated. Similarly, it stands concealing the origin, cessation, and path; the past five aggregates reckoned as the past end; the future five aggregates reckoned as the future end; both of these reckoned as both the past and future ends; and both this-conditionality and the dependently arisen phenomena, which are reckoned as 'this-conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.' It does not allow one to penetrate herein their true, inherent characteristic, as in: 'This is ignorance, these are volitional formations.' Therefore, it is called 'lack of knowledge concerning suffering... lack of knowledge concerning this-conditionality and dependently arisen phenomena.'

592. Saṅkhārāti puññādayo tayo kāyasaṅkhārādayo tayoti evaṃ pubbe saṅkhepato vuttā cha, vitthārato panettha puññābhisaṅkhāro dānasīlādivasena pavattā aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacetanā ceva bhāvanāvasena pavattā pañca rūpāvacarakusalacetanā cāti terasa cetanā honti. Apuññābhisaṅkhāro pāṇātipātādivasena pavattā dvādasa akusalacetanā[M 2.0162]. Āneñjābhisaṅkhāro bhāvanāvaseneva pavattā catasso arūpāvacarakusalacetanā cāti tayopi saṅkhārā ekūnatiṃsa cetanā honti.

592. The formations (saṅkhārā) are the three, namely, meritorious formations and so on, and the three, namely, bodily formations and so on; thus, six were briefly stated before. But here in detail, the meritorious formation (puññābhisaṅkhāra) consists of thirteen volitions: the eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions occurring through giving, virtue, and so on, and the five wholesome form-sphere volitions occurring through meditation. The demeritorious formation (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) consists of the twelve unwholesome volitions occurring through killing living beings and so on. The imperturbable formation (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) consists of the four wholesome formless-sphere volitions occurring through meditation alone. Thus, these three formations amount to twenty-nine volitions.

Itaresu [V 2.0160] pana tīsu kāyasañcetanā kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīsañcetanā vacīsaṅkhāro, manosañcetanā cittasaṅkhāro. Ayaṃ tiko kammāyūhanakkhaṇe puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ dvārato pavattidassanatthaṃ vutto. Kāyaviññattiṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā hi kāyadvārato pavattā aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacetanā, dvādasa akusalacetanāti samavīsati cetanā kāyasaṅkhāro nāma. Tā eva vacīviññattiṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā vacīdvārato pavattā vacīsaṅkhāro nāma. Abhiññācetanā panettha parato viññāṇassa paccayo na hotīti na gahitā. Yathā ca abhiññācetanā, evaṃ uddhaccacetanāpi na hoti. Tasmā sāpi viññāṇassa paccayabhāve apanetabbā, avijjāpaccayā pana sabbāpetā honti. Ubhopi viññattiyo asamuṭṭhāpetvā manodvāre uppannā pana sabbāpi ekūnatiṃsati cetanā cittasaṅkhāroti. Iti ayaṃ tiko purimattikameva pavisatīti atthato puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃyeva vasena avijjāya paccayabhāvo veditabbo.

Furthermore, concerning the other three: bodily volition is the bodily formation, verbal volition is the verbal formation, and mental volition is the mental formation. This triad is stated to show the occurrence through the doors of the meritorious formations and so on at the moment of accumulating kamma. For, having produced bodily intimation, the twenty volitions that occur through the body-door—namely, the eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions and the twelve unwholesome volitions—are called the bodily formation. Those same volitions, having produced verbal intimation and occurring through the speech-door, are called the verbal formation. Herein, the volition of direct knowledge is not included because it is not a condition for consciousness hereafter. And just as the volition of direct knowledge, so too the volition of restlessness is not a condition. Therefore, it too should be removed when considering the conditions for consciousness. However, all these volitions are indeed conditioned by ignorance. Furthermore, all twenty-nine volitions that arise in the mind-door without producing either of the two intimations are called the mental formation. Thus, this triad is included in the previous triad. Therefore, in terms of meaning, the conditionality from ignorance should be understood only by way of the meritorious formations and so on.

593. Tattha siyā – kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ “ime saṅkhārā avijjā paccayā hontī”ti? Avijjābhāve bhāvato. Yassa hi dukkhādīsu avijjāsaṅkhātaṃ aññāṇaṃ appahīnaṃ hoti, so dukkhe tāva pubbantādīsu ca aññāṇena saṃsāradukkhaṃ sukhasaññāya gahetvā tasseva hetubhūte tividhepi saṅkhāre ārabhati. Samudaye aññāṇena dukkhahetubhūtepi taṇhāparikkhāre saṅkhāre sukhahetuto maññamāno ārabhati. Nirodhe pana magge ca aññāṇena dukkhassa anirodhabhūtepi gativisese dukkhanirodhasaññī hutvā nirodhassa ca amaggabhūtesupi yaññāmaratapādīsu nirodhamaggasaññī hutvā dukkhanirodhaṃ patthayamāno yaññāmaratapādimukhena tividhepi saṅkhāre ārabhati.

593. Here, it might be asked: “How is it to be known that ‘these formations are conditioned by ignorance’?” By their arising when ignorance is present. For one in whom the non-knowledge known as ignorance regarding suffering and so on is not abandoned, that person, firstly, due to ignorance regarding suffering, perceives the suffering of saṃsāra as pleasure and thus undertakes the threefold formations that are the cause of that very suffering. Due to ignorance regarding the origin, even though the formations, which are the accessories of craving, are causes of suffering, that person regards them as causes of happiness and thus undertakes them. Furthermore, regarding cessation and the path, due to ignorance, even in particular destinations that are not the cessation of suffering, that person perceives them as the cessation of suffering; and even in sacrifices, austerities, and so on, which are not the path to cessation, that person perceives them as the path to cessation. Desiring the cessation of suffering, that person undertakes the threefold formations by means of sacrifices, austerities, and so on.

Apica so tāya catūsu saccesu appahīnāvijjatāya visesato jātijarārogamaraṇādianekādīnavavokiṇṇampi puññaphalasaṅkhātaṃ dukkhaṃ dukkhato ajānanto tassa adhigamāya kāyavacīcittasaṅkhārabhedaṃ puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ [M 2.0163] ārabhati devaccharakāmako viya maruppapātaṃ. Sukhasammatassāpi ca tassa puññaphalassa ante mahāpariḷāhajanikaṃ vipariṇāmadukkhataṃ appassādatañca apassantopi tappaccayaṃ vuttappakārameva puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati salabho viya dīpasikhābhinipātaṃ, madhubindugiddho viya ca madhulittasatthadhārālehanaṃ. Kāmupasevanādīsu ca savipākesu ādīnavaṃ apassanto sukhasaññāya ceva kilesābhibhūtatāya ca dvārattayappavattampi apuññābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati, bālo viya gūthakīḷanaṃ, maritukāmo viya ca visakhādanaṃ. Āruppavipākesu [V 2.0161] cāpi saṅkhāravipariṇāmadukkhataṃ anavabujjhamāno sassatādivipallāsena cittasaṅkhārabhūtaṃ āneñjābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati, disāmūḷho viya pisācanagarābhimukhamaggagamanaṃ.

Furthermore, due to that unabandoned ignorance regarding the four truths, that person, not knowing as suffering the suffering known as the fruit of merit—even though it is especially intermingled with the many dangers of birth, aging, sickness, death, and so on—undertakes, for the attainment of that fruit, the meritorious formation, which is divided into bodily, verbal, and mental formations, like one desiring a celestial nymph who leaps from a cliff. And although that fruit of merit is considered to be happiness, not seeing at its end the great feverish burning, the suffering due to change, and its ungratifying nature, one undertakes the meritorious formation of the very kind described, which is the cause of that fruit, like a moth plunging into a flame, or like one greedy for a drop of honey licking a honey-smeared razor's edge. And not seeing the danger in sensual indulgence and so on, together with their results, through the perception of pleasure and through being overcome by defilements, one undertakes the demeritorious formation that proceeds through the three doors, like a fool playing with excrement, or like one who wishes to die eating poison. And also, not comprehending the suffering of formations and the suffering due to change in the results of the formless sphere, through the perversion of eternalism and so on, one undertakes the imperturbable formation, which is a mental formation, like one who has lost their way taking the road to a city of goblins.

Evaṃ yasmā avijjābhāvatova saṅkhārabhāvo, na abhāvato. Tasmā jānitabbametaṃ “ime saṅkhārā avijjāpaccayā hontī”ti. Vuttampi cetaṃ “avidvā, bhikkhave, avijjāgato puññābhisaṅkhārampi abhisaṅkharoti, apuññābhisaṅkhārampi abhisaṅkharoti, āneñjābhisaṅkhārampi abhisaṅkharoti. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno avijjā pahīnā, vijjā uppannā; so avijjāvirāgā vijjuppādā neva puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharotī”ti.

Thus, since the existence of formations is due to the presence of ignorance, and not to its absence, it should be known that: ‘These formations are conditioned by ignorance.’ And this has also been said: ‘Bhikkhus, an unwise person, possessed of ignorance, constructs the meritorious formation, constructs the demeritorious formation, and constructs the imperturbable formation. But when, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge has arisen, then through the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, he does not construct the meritorious formation...’

Paṭṭhānapaccayakathā

Exposition on the Paṭṭhāna Conditions

594. Etthāha – gaṇhāma tāva etaṃ avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayoti, idaṃ pana vattabbaṃ katamesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ kathaṃ paccayo hotīti? Tatridaṃ vuccati, bhagavatā hi “hetupaccayo, ārammaṇapaccayo, adhipatipaccayo, anantarapaccayo, samanantarapaccayo, sahajātapaccayo, aññamaññapaccayo, nissayapaccayo, upanissayapaccayo, purejātapaccayo, pacchājātapaccayo, āsevanapaccayo, kammapaccayo, vipākapaccayo, āhārapaccayo, indriyapaccayo, jhānapaccayo, maggapaccayo, sampayuttapaccayo, vippayuttapaccayo, atthipaccayo, natthipaccayo, vigatapaccayo, avigatapaccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.paccayuddesa) catuvīsati paccayā vuttā.

594. Here it is said: Let us first accept this: ignorance is a condition for formations. But then it should be stated: For which formations and how is it a condition? Herein, it is said that the Blessed One has stated twenty-four conditions: “Root-condition, object-condition, dominance-condition, immediate-condition, contiguous-condition, co-nascence-condition, reciprocity-condition, dependence-condition, decisive support-condition, pre-nascence-condition, post-nascence-condition, repetition-condition, kamma-condition, result-condition, nutriment-condition, faculty-condition, jhāna-condition, path-condition, association-condition, dissociation-condition, presence-condition, absence-condition, disappearance-condition, non-disappearance-condition.”

Tattha [M 2.0164] hetu ca so paccayo cāti hetupaccayo, hetu hutvā paccayo, hetubhāvena paccayoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ārammaṇapaccayādīsupi eseva nayo.

Herein, it is a root-condition (hetupaccayo) because it is a root and it is a condition. It is a condition by being a root; it is a condition by way of its nature as a root—thus it is said. This same method applies to the object-condition and so forth.

595. Tattha hetūti vacanāvayavakāraṇamūlānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. “Paṭiññā, hetū”tiādīsu hi loke vacanāvayavo hetūti vuccati. Sāsane pana “ye dhammā hetuppabhavā”tiādīsu (mahāva. 60) kāraṇaṃ. “Tayo kusalahetū, tayo akusalahetū”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1059) mūlaṃ hetūti vuccati, taṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Paccayoti ettha pana ayaṃ vacanattho, paṭicca etasmā etīti paccayo. Apaccakkhāya naṃ vattatīti attho. Yo hi dhammo yaṃ dhammaṃ apaccakkhāya tiṭṭhati vā uppajjati vā, so tassa [V 2.0162] paccayoti vuttaṃ hoti. Lakkhaṇato pana upakārakalakkhaṇo paccayo. Yo hi dhammo yassa dhammassa ṭhitiyā vā uppattiyā vā upakārako hoti, so tassa paccayoti vuccati. Paccayo, hetu, kāraṇaṃ, nidānaṃ, sambhavo, pabhavotiādi atthato ekaṃ, byañjanato nānaṃ. Iti mūlaṭṭhena hetu, upakārakaṭṭhena paccayoti saṅkhepato mūlaṭṭhena upakārako dhammo hetupaccayo.

595. Herein, the term ‘hetu’ is a designation for a component of speech, a cause, and a root. In the world, in such phrases as ‘the proposition, the reason,’ a component of speech is called a ‘hetu.’ But in the Dispensation, in such phrases as ‘those things that are of cause-origin,’ it means cause. In such phrases as ‘three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots,’ root is called ‘hetu,’ and that is what is intended here. As for ‘paccaya’ (condition), this is its verbal meaning: ‘dependent on this, it proceeds’ (paṭicca etasmā eti), thus it is a condition (paccayo). The meaning is that it proceeds without leaving it behind. For it is said that whatever phenomenon stands or arises without leaving another phenomenon behind, the latter is a condition for the former. By characteristic, however, a condition has the characteristic of being supportive. For it is said that whatever phenomenon is supportive of the stability or arising of another phenomenon, the former is called a condition for the latter. ‘Condition’ (paccayo), ‘root’ (hetu), ‘cause’ (kāraṇa), ‘source’ (nidāna), ‘origin’ (sambhava), ‘provenance’ (pabhavo), and so on are one in meaning but different in expression. Thus, it is a ‘hetu’ in the sense of root, and a ‘paccaya’ in the sense of being supportive. In brief, a phenomenon that is supportive in the sense of being a root is a root-condition.

So sāliādīnaṃ sālibījādīni viya, maṇipabhādīnaṃ viya ca maṇivaṇṇādayo kusalādīnaṃ kusalādibhāvasādhakoti ācariyānaṃ adhippāyo. Evaṃ sante pana taṃsamuṭṭhānarūpesu hetupaccayatā na sampajjati. Na hi so tesaṃ kusalādibhāvaṃ sādheti, na ca paccayo na hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ “hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.1). Ahetukacittānañca vinā etena abyākatabhāvo siddho, sahetukānampi ca yonisomanasikārādipaṭibaddho kusalādibhāvo, na sampayuttahetupaṭibaddho. Yadi ca sampayuttahetūsu sabhāvatova kusalādibhāvo siyā, sampayuttesu hetupaṭibaddho alobho kusalo vā siyā abyākato vā. Yasmā pana ubhayathāpi hoti, tasmā yathā sampayuttesu, evaṃ hetūsupi kusalāditā pariyesitabbā.

The teachers' view is that this root-condition establishes the state of being wholesome, etc., for wholesome states, etc., just as rice seeds, etc., do for rice plants, etc., and as the color of a gem, etc., does for the lustre of a gem, etc. However, if this were so, the nature of a root-condition would not be established in the case of material phenomena originated therefrom. For that root does not establish their state of being wholesome, etc., yet it is not that it is not a condition. For this has been stated: 'Roots are a condition for states associated with roots and for the material phenomena originated therefrom by way of root-condition' (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.1). Furthermore, for rootless consciousnesses, the indeterminate state is established without this root; and even for states with roots, the state of being wholesome, etc., is dependent on wise attention, etc., not on the associated root. And if the state of being wholesome, etc., were inherent in the associated roots, non-greed would be either wholesome or indeterminate. But since it is both, therefore, just as in the associated states, so too in the roots themselves, the nature of being wholesome, etc., must be sought.

Kusalādibhāvasādhanavasena [M 2.0165] pana hetūnaṃ mūlaṭṭhaṃ agahetvā suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanavasena gayhamāne na kiñci virujjhati. Laddhahetupaccayā hi dhammā virūḷhamūlā viya pādapā thirā honti suppatiṭṭhitā, ahetukā tilabījakādisevālā viya na suppatiṭṭhitā. Iti mūlaṭṭhena upakārakoti suppatiṭṭhitabhāvasādhanena upakārako dhammo hetupaccayoti veditabbo.

However, if the meaning of ‘root’ for the roots is taken not in the sense of establishing wholesome and other states, but in the sense of establishing firmness, then nothing is contradicted. For phenomena that have obtained the root-condition are firm and well-established, like trees with well-grown roots, whereas those without a root are not well-established, like duckweed the size of sesame seeds and the like. Thus, a phenomenon that is helpful by way of being a root—that is, helpful by establishing firmness—should be understood as the root-condition.

596. Tato paresu ārammaṇabhāvena upakārako dhammo ārammaṇapaccayo. So “rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.2) ārabhitvāpi “yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ ārabbha ye ye dhammā uppajjanti cittacetasikā dhammā, te te dhammā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.2) osāpitattā na koci dhammo na hoti. Yathā hi dubbalo puriso daṇḍaṃ vā rajjuṃ vā ālambitvāva uṭṭhahati ceva tiṭṭhati ca, evaṃ cittacetasikā dhammā rūpādiārammaṇaṃ ārabbheva uppajjanti ceva tiṭṭhanti ca. Tasmā sabbepi cittacetasikānaṃ ārammaṇabhūtā dhammā ārammaṇapaccayoti veditabbā.

596. Among the subsequent conditions, a phenomenon that is helpful by way of being an object is the object-condition. Since the teaching begins with “the form-sphere is a condition for the eye-consciousness element” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.2), and concludes with “whatever phenomena are taken as object, based on which whatever mental and mental-factor phenomena arise, those phenomena are a condition for those respective phenomena by way of object-condition” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.2), there is no phenomenon that is not an object-condition. Just as a weak person rises and stands only by leaning on a staff or a rope, so too do mental and mental-factor phenomena arise and persist only by taking an object such as form. Therefore, all phenomena that become objects for mental and mental-factor phenomena should be understood as the object-condition.

597. Jeṭṭhakaṭṭhena [V 2.0163] upakārako dhammo adhipatipaccayo, so sahajātārammaṇavasena duvidho. Tattha “chandādhipati chandasampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ adhipatipaccayena paccayo”tiādivacanato (paṭṭhā. 1.3.3) chandavīriyacittavīmaṃsāsaṅkhātā cattāro dhammā adhipatipaccayoti veditabbā, no ca kho ekato. Yadā hi chandaṃ dhuraṃ chandaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā cittaṃ pavattati, tadā chandova adhipati, na itare. Esa nayo sesesupi.

597. A phenomenon that is helpful by way of being foremost is the dominance-condition; it is twofold by way of co-nascence and object. Herein, from the statement, “Desire as dominance is a condition for the states associated with desire and for the material forms originating from them by way of dominance-condition” (Paṭṭhāna 1.3.3), it should be understood that the four phenomena—namely, desire, energy, consciousness, and investigation—are dominance-conditions, but not simultaneously. For when consciousness proceeds by making desire the principal thing, by making desire the foremost thing, then desire alone is the dominant factor, not the others. The same principle applies to the rest.

Yaṃ pana dhammaṃ garuṃ katvā arūpadhammā pavattanti, so nesaṃ ārammaṇādhipati. Tena vuttaṃ “yaṃ yaṃ dhammaṃ garuṃ katvā ye ye dhammā uppajjanti cittacetasikā dhammā, te te dhammā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ adhipatipaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.3).

Furthermore, whatever phenomenon is taken as important, based upon which immaterial phenomena proceed, that is their object-dominance condition. Hence it is said: “Whatever phenomena are taken as important, based on which whatever mental and mental-factor phenomena arise, those phenomena are a condition for those respective phenomena by way of dominance-condition” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.3).

598. Anantarabhāvena upakārako dhammo anantarapaccayo. Samanantarabhāvena upakārako dhammo samanantarapaccayo. Idañca paccayadvayaṃ [M 2.0166] bahudhā papañcayanti. Ayaṃ panettha sāro, yo hi esa cakkhuviññāṇānantarā manodhātu, manodhātuanantarā manoviññāṇadhātūtiādi cittaniyamo, so yasmā purimapurimacittavaseneva ijjhati, na aññathā, tasmā attano attano anantaraṃ anurūpassa cittuppādassa uppādanasamattho dhammo anantarapaccayo. Tenevāha – “anantarapaccayoti cakkhuviññāṇadhātu taṃsampayuttakā ca dhammā manodhātuyā taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ anantarapaccayena paccayo”tiādi (paṭṭhā. 1.1.4). Yo anantarapaccayo, sveva samanantarapaccayo. Byañjanamattameva hettha nānaṃ, upacayasantatīsu viya adhivacananiruttidukādīsu viya ca. Atthato pana nānaṃ natthi.

598. A phenomenon that is helpful by way of proximity is the proximity-condition. A phenomenon that is helpful by way of contiguity is the contiguity-condition. These two conditions are elaborated in many ways.
