Manodvārepi so tathāti manodvārepi hi tadārammaṇavasena pavattānaṃ kāmāvacaravipākavedanānaṃ so sahajātamanosamphassasaṅkhāto phasso tatheva aṭṭhadhā paccayo hoti, paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivasena pavattānaṃ tebhūmakavipākavedanānampi. Yā pana tā manodvāre tadārammaṇavasena [M 2.0202] pavattā kāmāvacaravedanā, tāsaṃ manodvārāvajjanasampayutto manosamphasso upanissayavasena ekadhāva paccayo hotīti.

“And so too at the mind-door” means that at the mind-door as well, for the sense-sphere resultant feelings occurring by way of that object, that contact known as co-nascent mind-contact is similarly a condition in eight ways, and also for the resultant feelings of the three planes occurring by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death. But as for those sense-sphere feelings occurring by way of that object at the mind-door, the mind-contact associated with mind-door adverting is a condition in only one way, by way of decisive support.

Ayaṃ “phassapaccayā vedanā”ti padasmiṃ vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed explanation on the phrase “feeling is conditioned by contact.”

Vedanāpaccayātaṇhāpadavitthārakathā

The Detailed Explanation of the Phrase “Craving is Conditioned by Feeling”

644. Vedanāpaccayā [V 2.0200] taṇhāpade –

644. In the phrase “craving is conditioned by feeling”:

Rūpataṇhādibhedena, cha taṇhā idha dīpitā;

Ekekā tividhā tattha, pavattākārato matā.

Here, six kinds of craving are shown, divided as craving for forms and so on; each of these is considered threefold according to its mode of occurrence.

Imasmiṃ hi pade seṭṭhiputto brāhmaṇaputtoti pitito nāmavasena putto viya “rūpataṇhā. Sadda… gandha… rasa… phoṭṭhabba… dhammataṇhā”ti (vibha. 232) ārammaṇato nāmavasena vibhaṅge cha taṇhā dīpitā.

Indeed, in this phrase, just as a son is named after his father as “son of a merchant” or “son of a brahmin,” so too in the Vibhaṅga six cravings are shown, named according to their object: “craving for forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.”

Tāsu pana taṇhāsu ekekā taṇhā pavattiākārato kāmataṇhā, bhavataṇhā, vibhavataṇhāti evaṃ tividhā matā. Rūpataṇhāyeva hi yadā cakkhussa āpāthamāgataṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ kāmassādavasena assādayamānā pavattati, tadā kāmataṇhā nāma hoti. Yadā tadevārammaṇaṃ “dhuvaṃ sassata”nti pavattāya sassatadiṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ pavattati, tadā bhavataṇhā nāma hoti. Sassatadiṭṭhisahagato hi rāgo bhavataṇhāti vuccati. Yadā pana tadevārammaṇaṃ “ucchijjati vinassatī”ti pavattāya ucchedadiṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ pavattati, tadā vibhavataṇhā nāma hoti. Ucchedadiṭṭhisahagato hi rāgo vibhavataṇhāti vuccati. Esa nayo saddataṇhādīsupīti. Etā aṭṭhārasa taṇhā honti.

Among these cravings, each is considered threefold according to its mode of occurrence: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. For when craving for forms occurs by savoring a form-object that has come into the range of the eye with the relish of sensual pleasure, it is called craving for sensual pleasures. When it occurs in connection with the eternalist view that that same object is “permanent, everlasting,” it is called craving for existence. For lust accompanied by the eternalist view is called craving for existence. But when it occurs in connection with the annihilationist view that that same object “is annihilated, it perishes,” it is called craving for non-existence. For lust accompanied by the annihilationist view is called craving for non-existence. This same method applies to craving for sounds and so on. These are the eighteen cravings.

Tā ajjhattarūpādīsu aṭṭhārasa, bahiddhā aṭṭhārasāti chattiṃsa. Iti atītā chattiṃsa, anāgatā chattiṃsa, paccuppannā chattiṃsāti aṭṭhasataṃ taṇhā honti. Tā puna saṅkheppamāṇā rūpādiārammaṇavasena cha, kāmataṇhādivasena vā tissova taṇhā hontīti veditabbā.

These eighteen cravings occur with regard to internal forms and so on, and eighteen with regard to external, making thirty-six. Thus, with thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present, there are one hundred and eight cravings. When summarized, these should be understood as six cravings by way of their objects—forms and so on—or as just three cravings: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.

Yasmā panime sattā puttaṃ assādetvā putte mamattena dhātiyā viya rūpādiārammaṇavasena uppajjamānaṃ vedanaṃ assādetvā vedanāya mamattena [M 2.0203] rūpādiārammaṇadāyakānaṃ cittakāra-gandhabba-gandhika-sūda-tantavāyarasāyanavidhāyakavejjādīnaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ karonti. Tasmā sabbāpesā vedanāpaccayā taṇhā hotīti veditabbā.

For just as these beings, having savored a son and cherishing him with a sense of “mine,” pay great honor to his wet-nurse, so too, having savored the feeling that arises by way of objects such as form and cherishing that feeling with a sense of “mine,” they pay great honor to the providers of those sense-objects, such as painters, musicians, perfumers, cooks, weavers, and physicians who prepare elixirs. Therefore, it should be understood that all this craving is conditioned by feeling.

Yasmā [V 2.0201] cettha adhippetā, vipākasukhavedanā;

Ekāva ekadhāvesā, tasmā taṇhāya paccayo.

Because here only the one pleasant resultant feeling is intended, it is therefore a condition for craving in only one way.

Ekadhāti upanissayapaccayeneva paccayo hoti. Yasmā vā,

“In one way” means that it is a condition only by way of decisive support condition. Or, because:

Dukkhī sukhaṃ patthayati, sukhī bhiyyopi icchati;

Upekkhā pana santattā, sukhamicceva bhāsitā.

One who suffers longs for happiness; one who is happy desires even more; but equanimity, since it is peaceful, is also spoken of as happiness.

Taṇhāya paccayā tasmā, honti tissopi vedanā;

Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā, iti vuttā mahesinā.

Therefore all three feelings become conditions for craving; thus the Great Sage has said: “Craving is conditioned by feeling.”

Vedanāpaccayā cāpi, yasmā nānusayaṃ vinā;

Hoti tasmā na sā hoti, brāhmaṇassa vusīmatoti.

And although craving is conditioned by feeling, since it does not occur without the underlying tendencies, it therefore does not arise for the brahmin who has lived the holy life.

Ayaṃ “vedanāpaccayā taṇhā”ti padasmiṃ vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed explanation on the phrase “craving is conditioned by feeling.”

Taṇhāpaccayāupādānapadavitthārakathā

The Detailed Explanation of the Phrase “Clinging is Conditioned by Craving”

645. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānapade –

645. In the phrase “clinging is conditioned by craving”:

Upādānāni cattāri, tāni atthavibhāgato;

Dhammasaṅkhepavitthārā, kamato ca vibhāvaye.

The four kinds of clinging should be clarified according to their analysis by meaning, according to the teaching in brief and in detail, and according to their sequence.

Tatrāyaṃ vibhāvanā – kāmupādānaṃ, diṭṭhupādānaṃ, sīlabbatupādānaṃ, attavādupādānanti imāni tāvettha cattāri upādānāni. Tesaṃ ayaṃ atthavibhāgo – vatthusaṅkhātaṃ kāmaṃ upādiyatīti kāmupādānaṃ, kāmo ca so upādānañcātipi kāmupādānaṃ. Upādānanti daḷhaggahaṇaṃ. Daḷhattho hettha upasaddo upāyāsaupakaṭṭhādīsu viya. Tathā diṭṭhi ca sā upādānañcāti diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Diṭṭhiṃ upādiyatīti vā diṭṭhupādānaṃ. “Sassato attā ca loko cā”tiādīsu [V 2.0202] (dī. ni. 1.31) hi purimadiṭṭhiṃ uttaradiṭṭhi upādiyati. Tathā sīlabbataṃ upādiyatīti sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Sīlabbatañca taṃ upādānañcātipi sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Gosīlagovatādīni hi “evaṃ suddhī”ti abhinivesato sayameva upādānāni. Tathā vadanti etenāti vādo. Upādiyanti [M 2.0204] etenāti upādānaṃ. Kiṃ vadanti, upādiyanti vā? Attānaṃ. Attano vādupādānaṃ attavādupādānaṃ. Attavādamattameva vā attāti upādiyanti etenāti attavādupādānaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva tesaṃ atthavibhāgo.

Here is the clarification: These are the four kinds of clinging in this context: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rites and rituals, and clinging to a doctrine of self. This is their analysis by meaning: one clings to sensual pleasure, which is reckoned as the object, thus it is “clinging to sensual pleasures”; or it is both sensual pleasure and clinging, thus “clinging to sensual pleasures.” “Clinging” means firm grasping. Here the prefix “upa-” has the sense of firmness, as in “upāyāsa” (intense trouble) and “upakaṭṭha” (very near). Similarly, it is both a view and clinging, thus “clinging to views”; or one clings to a view, thus “clinging to views.” For in such cases as “The self and the world are eternal,” a later view clings to a former view. Similarly, one clings to rites and rituals, thus “clinging to rites and rituals”; or it is both rites and rituals and clinging, thus “clinging to rites and rituals.” For practices like cow-vows and cow-observances become clingings in themselves through the adherence, “By this there is purification.” Further, “vādo” (doctrine) is that with which one asserts; “upādānaṃ” (clinging) is that with which one clings. What do they assert and cling to? The self. The clinging to a doctrine of self is “attavādupādānaṃ” (clinging to a doctrine of self). Or, it is “attavādupādānaṃ” because with it one clings to the mere doctrine of self as being the self. This, for now, is the analysis of their meaning.

Dhammasaṅkhepavitthāre pana kāmupādānaṃ tāva “tattha katamaṃ kāmupādānaṃ? Yo kāmesu kāmacchando kāmarāgo kāmanandī kāmataṇhā kāmasneho kāmapariḷāho kāmamucchā kāmajjhosānaṃ, idaṃ vuccati kāmupādāna”nti (dha. sa. 1220; vibha. 938) āgatattā saṅkhepato taṇhādaḷhattaṃ vuccati. Taṇhādaḷhattaṃ nāma purimataṇhāupanissayapaccayena daḷhasambhūtā uttarataṇhāva. Keci panāhu “appattavisayapatthanā taṇhā andhakāre corassa hatthappasāraṇaṃ viya, sampattavisayaggahaṇaṃ upādānaṃ tasseva bhaṇḍaggahaṇaṃ viya. Appicchatāsantuṭṭhitāpaṭipakkhā ca te dhammā. Tathā pariyesanārakkhadukkhamūlā”ti. Sesupādānattayaṃ pana saṅkhepato diṭṭhimattameva.

In the brief and detailed analysis of the Dhamma, first, regarding clinging to sensual pleasures, since it is stated: 'Herein, what is clinging to sensual pleasures? It is sensual desire, sensual passion, sensual delight, sensual craving, sensual affection, sensual fever, sensual infatuation, and sensual obsession—this is called clinging to sensual pleasures' (Dhs §1220; Vibh §938), in brief it is called the strengthening of craving. The strengthening of craving is the subsequent craving that arises strongly with previous craving as its decisive support condition. Some, however, say: 'Craving is the longing for an unattained object, like a thief stretching out his hand in the dark; clinging is the grasping of an attained object, like that same thief seizing the goods. These states are opposed to having few wishes and contentment, and are likewise the root of the suffering of seeking and protecting.' The remaining three kinds of clinging, in brief, are simply wrong view.

Vitthārato pana pubbe rūpādīsu vuttaaṭṭhasatappabhedāyapi taṇhāya daḷhabhāvo kāmupādānaṃ. Dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhi diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Yathāha – “tattha katamaṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ? Natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ…pe… sacchikatvā pavedentīti yā evarūpā diṭṭhi…pe… vipariyesaggāho. Idaṃ vuccati diṭṭhupādāna”nti (dha. sa. 1221; vibha. 938). Sīlabbatehi suddhīti parāmasanaṃ pana sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Yathāha – “tattha katamaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ? Sīlena suddhi, vatena suddhi, sīlabbatena suddhīti yā evarūpā diṭṭhi…pe… vipariyesaggāho. Idaṃ vuccati sīlabbatupādāna”nti (dha. sa. 1222; vibha. 938). Vīsativatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhi attavādupādānaṃ. Yathāha – “tattha katamaṃ attavādupādānaṃ? Idha assutavā puthujjano…pe… sappurisadhamme avinīto rūpaṃ attato samanupassati…pe… vipariyesaggāho, idaṃ vuccati attavādupādāna”nti (dha. sa. 1223; vibha. 938). Ayamettha dhammasaṅkhepavitthāro.

In detail, however, clinging to sensual pleasures is the strengthened state of the one hundred and eight kinds of craving previously mentioned in regard to forms and so on. Wrong view with its ten bases is clinging to views. As it is said: 'Herein, what is clinging to views? The view that there is nothing given, nothing offered… who declare it after having realized it for themselves… any such view… a perverted grasp. This is called clinging to views' (Dhs §1221; Vibh §938). The misapprehension that there is purification through rites and rituals is clinging to rites and rituals. As it is said: 'Herein, what is clinging to rites and rituals? The view that there is purification through a rite, through a ritual, through a rite and ritual… any such view… a perverted grasp. This is called clinging to rites and rituals' (Dhs §1222; Vibh §938). Identity view with its twenty bases is clinging to a doctrine of self. As it is said: 'Herein, what is clinging to a doctrine of self? Herein, an uninstructed worldling… untrained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, regards form as self… any such view… a perverted grasp. This is called clinging to a doctrine of self' (Dhs §1223; Vibh §938). This is the brief and detailed analysis of the Dhamma herein.

Kamatoti ettha pana tividho kamo uppattikkamo pahānakkamo desanākkamo ca. Tattha anamatagge [V 2.0203] saṃsāre imassa paṭhamaṃ uppattīti abhāvato kilesānaṃ nippariyāyena uppattikkamo na vuccati. Pariyāyena pana yebhuyyena ekasmiṃ bhave attaggāhapubbaṅgamo sassatucchedābhiniveso, tato “sassato ayaṃ attā”ti gaṇhato attavisuddhatthaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ, “ucchijjatī”ti gaṇhato paralokanirapekkhassa kāmupādānanti [M 2.0205] evaṃ paṭhamaṃ attavādupādānaṃ, tato diṭṭhisīlabbatakāmupādānānīti ayametesaṃ ekasmiṃ bhave uppattikkamo.

Herein, 'by sequence' refers to a threefold sequence: the sequence of arising, the sequence of abandoning, and the sequence of exposition. Among these, since in beginningless saṃsāra there is no 'first arising' of the defilements, the sequence of arising is not spoken of in an absolute sense. But in a relative sense, for the most part in a single existence, adherence to eternalism and annihilationism is preceded by the grasping of a self. Then, for one who holds 'this self is eternal,' clinging to rites and rituals arises for the sake of self-purification; for one who holds 'it is annihilated,' being indifferent to the next world, clinging to sensual pleasures arises. Thus, first comes clinging to a doctrine of self, then clinging to views, to rites and rituals, and to sensual pleasures—this is their sequence of arising in a single existence.

Diṭṭhupādānādīni cettha paṭhamaṃ pahīyanti sotāpattimaggavajjhattā. Kāmupādānaṃ pacchā, arahattamaggavajjhattāti ayametesaṃ pahānakkamo.

Herein, clinging to views and the others are abandoned first, as they are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry. Clinging to sensual pleasures is abandoned later, as it is to be abandoned by the path of arahantship. This is their sequence of abandonment.

Mahāvisayattā pana pākaṭattā ca etesu kāmupādānaṃ paṭhamaṃ desitaṃ. Mahāvisayaṃ hi taṃ aṭṭhacittasampayogā, appavisayāni itarāni catucittasampayogā, yebhuyyena ca ālayarāmattā pajāya pākaṭaṃ kāmupādānaṃ, na itarāni. Kāmupādāna vā kāmānaṃ samadhigamatthaṃ kotūhalamaṅgalādibahulo hoti, sāssa diṭṭhīti tadanantaraṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ, taṃ pabhijjamānaṃ sīlabbataattavādupādānavasena duvidhaṃ hoti. Tasmiṃ dvaye gokiriyaṃ kukkurakiriyaṃ vā disvāpi veditabbato oḷārikanti sīlabbatupādānaṃ paṭhamaṃ desitaṃ. Sukhumattā ante attavādupādānanti ayametesaṃ desanākkamo.

Due to its vast scope and prominence, clinging to sensual pleasures is taught first among these. For it has a vast scope, being associated with eight types of consciousness, whereas the others have a small scope, being associated with only four types of consciousness. Moreover, because people generally delight in attachments, clinging to sensual pleasures is manifest, but not the others. Or, one with clinging to sensual pleasures is much given to auspicious signs, ceremonies, and the like for the sake of attaining sensual pleasures; that is a wrong view, and therefore clinging to views is taught immediately after. When that is analyzed, it is twofold: clinging to rites and rituals and clinging to a doctrine of self. Between these two, since it can be known even by seeing cow-practices and dog-practices, clinging to rites and rituals is taught first because it is gross. Due to its subtlety, clinging to a doctrine of self is taught at the end. This is their sequence of exposition.

Taṇhā ca purimassettha, ekadhā hoti paccayo;

Sattadhā aṭṭhadhā vāpi, hoti sesattayassa sā.

Herein, craving is a condition for the first clinging in one way; for the remaining three, it is a condition in seven or even eight ways.

Ettha ca evaṃ desite upādānacatukke purimassa kāmupādānassa kāmataṇhā upanissayavasena ekadhāva paccayo hoti, taṇhābhinanditesu visayesu uppattito. Sesattayassa pana sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatahetuvasena sattadhā vā, upanissayena saha aṭṭhadhā vāpi paccayo hoti. Yadā ca sā upanissayavasena paccayo hoti, tadā asahajātāva hotīti.

Herein, in the fourfold clinging thus expounded, for the first, clinging to sensual pleasures, sensual craving is a condition in one way only, by way of decisive support, because of its arising in regard to objects delighted in through craving. But for the remaining three, it is a condition in seven ways—by way of conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root conditions—or even in eight ways together with decisive support. And when it is a condition by way of decisive support, it is non-conascent.

Ayaṃ “taṇhāpaccayā upādāna”nti padasmiṃ vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed explanation of the phrase 'With craving as condition, clinging.'

Upādānapaccayābhavapadavitthārakathā

Detailed Explanation of the Phrase 'With Clinging as Condition, Becoming'

646. Upādānapaccayā [V 2.0204] bhavapade –

646. In the phrase 'With clinging as condition, becoming':

Atthato dhammato ceva, sātthato bhedasaṅgahā;

Yaṃ yassa paccayo ceva, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

The determination should be understood: by meaning and by phenomenon, by its meaningfulness, by division and combination, and by what is a condition for what.

Tattha [M 2.0206] bhavatīti bhavo. So kammabhavo upapattibhavo cāti duvidho hoti. Yathāha – “bhavo duvidhena atthi kammabhavo, atthi upapattibhavo”ti (vibha. 234). Tattha kammameva bhavo kammabhavo, tathā upapattiyeva bhavo upapattibhavo. Ettha ca upapatti bhavatīti bhavo. Kammaṃ pana yathā sukhakāraṇattā “sukho buddhānaṃ uppādo”ti (dha. pa. 194) vutto, evaṃ bhavakāraṇattā phalavohārena bhavoti veditabbanti. Evaṃ tāvettha atthato viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Therein, 'it becomes,' thus it is becoming (bhava). It is twofold: kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming. As it is said: 'Becoming is twofold: there is kamma-becoming and there is rebirth-becoming' (Vibh §234). Therein, kamma itself is becoming, thus kamma-becoming; likewise, rebirth itself is becoming, thus rebirth-becoming. And herein, 'rebirth becomes,' thus it is becoming. But kamma, just as it is called 'happiness' because it is a cause of happiness—as stated, 'Happy is the arising of the Buddhas' (Dhp 194)—so too, because it is a cause of becoming, it should be understood as 'becoming' by way of the designation of its result. Thus, first, the determination should be understood here by way of meaning.

647. Dhammato pana kammabhavo tāva saṅkhepato cetanā ceva cetanāsampayuttā ca abhijjhādayo kammasaṅkhātā dhammā. Yathāha – “tattha katamo kammabhavo? Puññābhisaṅkhāro apuññābhisaṅkhāro āneñjābhisaṅkhāro (vibha. 234) parittabhūmako vā mahābhūmako vā, ayaṃ vuccati kammabhavo. Sabbampi bhavagāmikammaṃ kammabhavo”ti (vibha. 234). Ettha hi puññābhisaṅkhāroti terasa cetanā. Apuññābhisaṅkhāroti dvādasa. Āneñjābhisaṅkhāroti catasso cetanā. Evaṃ parittabhūmako vā mahābhūmako vāti etena tāsaṃyeva cetanānaṃ mandabahuvipākatā vuttā. Sabbampi bhavagāmikammanti iminā pana cetanāsampayuttā abhijjhādayo vuttā.

647. By way of phenomenon, however, kamma-becoming, in brief, is volition and the states associated with volition called kamma, such as covetousness and so on. As it is said: 'Herein, what is kamma-becoming? Meritorious formation, demeritorious formation, imperturbable formation, whether belonging to the limited sphere or the great sphere—this is called kamma-becoming. All kamma leading to becoming is kamma-becoming.' Here, 'meritorious formation' means thirteen volitions. 'Demeritorious formation' means twelve. 'Imperturbable formation' means four volitions. Thus, by 'whether belonging to the limited sphere or the great sphere,' the weakness or abundance of the results of those same volitions is stated. But by 'all kamma leading to becoming,' the states associated with volition, such as covetousness and so on, are stated.

Upapattibhavo pana saṅkhepato kammābhinibbattā khandhā, pabhedato navavidho hoti. Yathāha – “tattha katamo upapattibhavo? Kāmabhavo rūpabhavo arūpabhavo saññābhavo asaññābhavo nevasaññānāsaññābhavo, ekavokārabhavo catuvokārabhavo pañcavokārabhavo, ayaṃ vuccati upapattibhavo”ti (vibha. 234). Tattha kāmasaṅkhāto bhavo kāmabhavo. Esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesu. Saññāvataṃ bhavo, saññā vā ettha bhave atthīti saññābhavo. Vipariyāyena asaññābhavo. Oḷārikāya saññāya abhāvā sukhumāya ca bhāvā nevasaññā, nāsaññā asmiṃ [V 2.0205] bhaveti nevasaññānāsaññābhavo. Ekena rūpakkhandhena vokiṇṇo bhavo ekavokārabhavo. Eko vā vokāro assa bhavassāti ekavokārabhavo. Esa nayo catuvokārapañcavokārabhavesu. Tattha kāmabhavo pañca upādiṇṇakkhandhā. Tathā rūpabhavo. Arūpabhavo cattāro[M 2.0207], saññābhavo pañca. Asaññābhavo eko upādiṇṇakkhandho. Nevasaññānāsaññābhavo cattāro. Ekavokārabhavādayo ekacatupañcakkhandhā upādiṇṇakkhandhehīti evamettha dhammatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Rebirth-becoming, in brief, is the aggregates generated by kamma; in detail, it is of nine kinds. As it is said: 'Herein, what is rebirth-becoming? Sense-sphere becoming, form-sphere becoming, formless-sphere becoming, percipient becoming, non-percipient becoming, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient becoming, one-constituent becoming, four-constituent becoming, five-constituent becoming—this is called rebirth-becoming.' Herein, the becoming designated as 'sensual' is sense-sphere becoming. This is the method in the cases of form-sphere and formless-sphere becomings. The becoming of percipient beings, or 'perception exists in this becoming,' thus it is percipient becoming. Conversely, it is non-percipient becoming. Due to the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, in this becoming there is neither perception (gross) nor an absence of perception (subtle); thus, it is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient becoming. A becoming interspersed with one constituent, the form aggregate, is one-constituent becoming. Or, 'this becoming has one constituent,' thus it is one-constituent becoming. This is the method in the cases of four-constituent and five-constituent becomings. Therein, sense-sphere becoming is the five clung-to aggregates. Likewise form-sphere becoming. Formless-sphere becoming is four; percipient becoming is five. Non-percipient becoming is one clung-to aggregate. Neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient becoming is four. The one-constituent becoming and so on are the one, four, and five aggregates, by way of the clung-to aggregates. Thus the determination should be understood here also by way of phenomenon.

648. Sātthatoti yathā ca bhavaniddese, tatheva kāmaṃ saṅkhāraniddesepi puññābhisaṅkhārādayova vuttā, evaṃ santepi purime atītakammavasena idha paṭisandhiyā paccayattā, ime paccuppannakammavasena āyatiṃ paṭisandhiyā paccayattāti punavacanaṃ sātthakameva, pubbe vā “tattha katamo puññābhisaṅkhāro? Kusalā cetanā kāmāvacarā”ti (vibha. 226) evamādinā nayena cetanāva saṅkhārāti vuttā. Idha pana “sabbampi bhavagāmikamma”nti (vibha. 234) vacanato cetanāsampayuttāpi. Pubbe ca viññāṇapaccayameva kammaṃ “saṅkhārā”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni asaññābhavanibbattakampi. Kiṃ vā bahunā, “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti ettha puññābhisaṅkhārādayova kusalākusalā dhammā vuttā. “Upādānapaccayā bhavo”ti idha pana upapattibhavassāpi saṅgahitattā kusalākusalābyākatā dhammā vuttā. Tasmā sabbathāpi sātthakamevidaṃ punavacananti evamettha sātthatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

648. As to its meaningfulness: just as in the exposition of becoming, so too in the exposition of formations, meritorious formations and so on are indeed mentioned. Even so, since the former are a condition for rebirth here by way of past kamma, while these are a condition for future rebirth by way of present kamma, the repetition is indeed meaningful. Or, previously, it was said in the way beginning, 'Herein, what is meritorious formation? Wholesome volition pertaining to the sense-sphere,' that volition itself is formations. Here, however, on the authority of the statement 'All kamma leading to becoming,' what is associated with volition is also included. And previously, only kamma that is a condition for consciousness was called 'formations'; now, that which generates non-percipient becoming is also included. Or what is the need for much talk? In the phrase 'With ignorance as condition, formations,' only wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, which are meritorious formations and so on, are mentioned. But here, in the phrase 'With clinging as condition, becoming,' since rebirth-becoming is also included, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena are mentioned. Therefore, this repetition is in every way meaningful. Thus the determination should be understood here also by way of its meaningfulness.

649. Bhedasaṅgahāti upādānapaccayā bhavassa bhedato ceva saṅgahato ca. Yañhi kāmupādānapaccayā kāmabhavanibbattakaṃ kammaṃ karīyati, so kammabhavo. Tadabhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesu. Evaṃ kāmupādānapaccayā dve kāmabhavā, tadantogadhā ca saññābhavapañcavokārabhavā, dve rūpabhavā, tadantogadhā ca saññābhavaasaññābhavaekavokārabhavapañcavokārabhavā, dve arūpabhavā, tadantogadhā ca saññābhavanevasaññānāsaññābhavacatuvokārabhavāti saddhiṃ antogadhehi cha bhavā. Yathā ca kāmupādānapaccayā saddhiṃ antogadhehi cha bhavā. Tathā sesupādānapaccayāpīti evaṃ upādānapaccayā bhedato saddhiṃ antogadhehi catuvīsati bhavā.

649. As to division and inclusion: this refers to the division and inclusion of becoming conditioned by clinging. For whatever kamma is performed conditioned by clinging to sensual pleasures, which generates sense-sphere becoming, that is kamma-becoming. The aggregates generated by it are rebirth-becoming. This is the method in the cases of form-sphere and formless-sphere becomings. Thus, conditioned by clinging to sensual pleasures, there are two sense-sphere becomings, and included within them are percipient becoming and five-constituent becoming; two form-sphere becomings, and included within them are percipient becoming, non-percipient becoming, one-constituent becoming, and five-constituent becoming; two formless-sphere becomings, and included within them are percipient becoming, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient becoming, and four-constituent becoming—thus, there are six becomings together with those included. Just as there are six becomings conditioned by clinging to sensual pleasures, together with those included, so too are there for those conditioned by the remaining clingings. Thus, by way of division, there are twenty-four becomings conditioned by clinging, together with those included.

Saṅgahato pana kammabhavaṃ upapattibhavañca ekato katvā kāmupādānapaccayā saddhiṃ antogadhehi [V 2.0206] eko kāmabhavo. Tathā rūpārūpabhavāti tayo bhavā. Tathā sesupādānapaccayā pīti. Evaṃ upādānapaccayā saṅgahato saddhiṃ antogadhehi dvādasa bhavā. Apica [M 2.0208] avisesena upādānapaccayā kāmabhavūpagaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo. Tadabhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesu. Evaṃ upādānapaccayā saddhiṃ antogadhehi dve kāmabhavā, dve rūpabhavā, dve arūpabhavāti aparena pariyāyena saṅgahato cha bhavā. Kammabhavaupapattibhavabhedaṃ vā anupagamma saddhiṃ antogadhehi kāmabhavādivasena tayo bhavā honti. Kāmabhavādibhedampi anupagamma kammabhavaupapattibhavavasena dve bhavā honti. Kammupapattibhedañcāpi anupagamma upādānapaccayā bhavoti bhavavasena ekova bhavo hotīti evamettha upādānapaccayassa bhavassa bhedasaṅgahāpi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

By way of inclusion, however, having grouped kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming together, conditioned by clinging to sensual pleasures, there is one sense-sphere becoming, together with those included. Likewise form-sphere and formless-sphere becomings, making three becomings. So too for the remaining clingings. Thus, by way of inclusion, there are twelve becomings conditioned by clinging, together with those included. Furthermore, without distinction, kamma leading to the sense-sphere becoming, conditioned by clinging, is kamma-becoming. The aggregates generated by it are rebirth-becoming. This is the method in the cases of form-sphere and formless-sphere becomings. Thus, by another way of inclusion, there are six becomings conditioned by clinging, together with those included: two sense-sphere becomings, two form-sphere becomings, and two formless-sphere becomings. Or, without making the distinction between kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming, there are three becomings by way of sense-sphere becoming, etc., together with those included. Without making the distinction of sense-sphere becoming, etc., there are two becomings by way of kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming. And without making the distinction between kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming, conditioned by clinging, there is becoming; thus by way of becoming, there is just one becoming. In this way, the determination of the division and inclusion of becoming conditioned by clinging should also be understood.

650. Yaṃ yassa paccayo cevāti yañcettha upādānaṃ yassa paccayo hoti, tatopi viññātabbo vinicchayoti attho. Kiṃ panettha kassa paccayo hoti? Yaṃkiñci yassa kassaci paccayo hotiyeva. Ummattako viya hi puthujjano. So idaṃ yuttaṃ idaṃ ayuttanti avicāretvā yassa kassaci upādānassa vasena yaṃkiñci bhavaṃ patthetvā yaṃkiñci kammaṃ karotiyeva. Tasmā yadekacce sīlabbatupādānena rūpārūpabhavā na hontīti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Sabbena pana sabbo hotīti gahetabbaṃ.

650. As to 'And what is a condition for what': the meaning is that the determination should also be understood from which clinging here is a condition for which becoming. Herein, what is a condition for what? Anything whatsoever is a condition for anything whatsoever. For an ordinary person is like a madman. Without investigating 'this is proper, this is improper,' he desires any kind of becoming by way of any kind of clinging and performs any kind of kamma. Therefore, the statement of some that form-sphere and formless-sphere becomings do not come to be through clinging to rules and observances should not be accepted. Rather, it should be accepted that any becoming comes to be through any clinging.

Seyyathidaṃ – idhekacco anussavavasena vā diṭṭhānusārena vā “kāmā nāmete manussaloke ceva khattiyamahāsālakulādīsu, cha kāmāvacaradevaloke ca samiddhā”ti cintetvā tesaṃ adhigamatthaṃ asaddhammassavanādīhi vañcito “iminā kammena kāmā sampajjantī”ti maññamāno kāmupādānavasena kāyaduccaritādīnipi karoti, so duccaritapāripūriyā apāye upapajjati. Sandiṭṭhike vā pana kāme patthayamāno paṭiladdhe ca gopayamāno kāmupādānavasena kāyaduccaritādīni karoti, so duccaritapāripūriyā apāye upapajjati. Tatrāssa upapattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo. Kammābhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Saññābhavapañcavokārabhavā pana tadantogadhā eva.

For example, here a certain person, through hearsay or by following what has been seen, thinks: 'These sensual pleasures are abundant among humans in the world, in great families of nobles, and so on, and in the six sense-sphere deva worlds.' Desiring to attain them, deceived by listening to the false Dhamma and so on, and thinking, 'By this action sensual pleasures are achieved,' he engages in bodily misconduct and the like out of clinging to sensual pleasures. Due to the fulfillment of that misconduct, he is reborn in a plane of misery. Or else, desiring sensual pleasures in this very life and protecting them when they have been obtained, he engages in bodily misconduct and the like out of clinging to sensual pleasures. Due to the fulfillment of that misconduct, he is reborn in a plane of misery. Therein, the kamma that is the cause for his rebirth is kamma-becoming. The aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming. But perception-becoming and five-constituent becoming are included within that.

Aparo [M 2.0209] pana saddhammassavanādīhi upabrūhitañāṇo “iminā kammena kāmā sampajjantī”ti maññamāno kāmupādānavasena kāyasucaritādīni karoti. So sucaritapāripūriyā [V 2.0207] devesu vā manussesu vā upapajjati. Tatrāssa upapattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo. Kammābhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Saññābhavapañcavokārabhavā pana tadantogadhā eva. Iti kāmupādānaṃ sappabhedassa sāntogadhassa kāmabhavassa paccayo hoti.

Again, another person, whose knowledge is augmented by listening to the true Dhamma and so on, thinking, 'By this action sensual pleasures are achieved,' engages in bodily good conduct and the like out of clinging to sensual pleasures. Due to the fulfillment of good conduct, he is reborn among devas or human beings. Therein, the kamma that is the cause for his rebirth is kamma-becoming. The aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming. But perception-becoming and five-constituent becoming are included within that. Thus, clinging to sensual pleasures is a condition for sensual-sphere becoming with its subdivisions and inclusions.

Aparo “rūpārūpabhavesu tato samiddhatarā kāmā”ti sutvā parikappetvā vā kāmupādānavaseneva rūpārūpasamāpattiyo nibbattetvā samāpattibalena rūpārūpabrahmaloke upapajjati. Tatrāssa upapattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo. Kammābhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Saññā-asaññā-nevasaññānāsaññā-eka-catu-pañcavokārabhavā pana tadantogadhā eva. Iti kāmupādānaṃ sappabhedānaṃ sāntogadhānaṃ rūpārūpabhavānampi paccayo hoti.

Again, another person, having heard or conceived that 'in the form and formless becomings there are sensual pleasures more abundant than those,' generates the form and formless attainments solely out of clinging to sensual pleasures. By the power of these attainments, he is reborn in the form and formless brahma worlds. Therein, the kamma that is the cause for his rebirth is kamma-becoming. The aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming. But the perception-, non-perception-, neither-perception-nor-non-perception-, one-, four-, and five-constituent becomings are included within that. Thus, clinging to sensual pleasures is also a condition for the form and formless becomings with their subdivisions and inclusions.

Aparo “ayaṃ attā nāma kāmāvacarasampattibhave vā rūpārūpabhavānaṃ vā aññatarasmiṃ ucchinne suucchinno hotī”ti ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ upādāya tadupagaṃ kammaṃ karoti, tassa taṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo. Kammābhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Saññābhavādayo pana tadantogadhā eva. Iti diṭṭhupādānaṃ sappabhedānaṃ sāntogadhānaṃ tiṇṇampi kāmarūpārūpabhavānaṃ paccayo hoti.

Again, another person, clinging to the annihilationist view, thinks: 'This so-called self, when it is cut off in a state of becoming endowed with sensual-sphere fortune or in one of the form or formless becomings, is utterly annihilated.' He performs kamma that leads to that, and for him that kamma is kamma-becoming. The aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming. But perception-becoming and so on are included within that. Thus, clinging to views is a condition for all three becomings—sensual-sphere, form, and formless—with their subdivisions and inclusions.

Aparo “ayaṃ attā nāma kāmāvacarasampattibhave vā rūpārūpabhavānaṃ vā aññatarasmiṃ sukhī hoti vigatapariḷāho”ti attavādupādānena tadupagaṃ kammaṃ karoti, tassa taṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo. Tadabhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Saññābhavādayo pana tadantogadhā eva. Iti attavādupādānaṃ sappabhedānaṃ sāntogadhānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bhavānaṃ paccayo hoti.

Again, another person, through clinging to the doctrine of self, thinks: 'This so-called self is happy and free from torment, whether in a state of becoming endowed with sensual-sphere fortune or in one of the form or formless becomings.' He performs kamma that leads to that, and for him that kamma is kamma-becoming. The aggregates produced by it are rebirth-becoming. But perception-becoming and so on are included within that. Thus, clinging to the doctrine of self is a condition for the three becomings with their subdivisions and inclusions.

Aparo “idaṃ sīlabbataṃ nāma kāmāvacarasampattibhave vā rūpārūpabhavānaṃ vā aññatarasmiṃ paripūrentassa sukhaṃ pāripūriṃ gacchatī”ti sīlabbatupādānavasena tadupagaṃ kammaṃ karoti, tassa taṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo. Tadabhinibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo. Saññābhavādayo pana tadantogadhā eva. Iti sīlabbatupādānaṃ sappabhedānaṃ sāntogadhānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bhavānaṃ paccayo hoti. Evamettha yaṃ yassa paccayo hoti, tatopi viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Again, another person, through clinging to rules and observances, thinks: 'For one who perfects these so-called rules and observances, happiness reaches fulfillment, whether in a state of becoming endowed with sensual-sphere fortune or in one of the form or formless becomings.' He performs kamma that leads to that out of clinging to rules and observances, and for him that kamma is kamma-becoming. The aggregates produced by it are rebirth-becoming. But perception-becoming and so on are included within that. Thus, clinging to rules and observances is a condition for the three becomings with their subdivisions and inclusions. In this way, the determination should be understood from what is a condition for what.

Kiṃ panettha [M 2.0210] kassa bhavassa kathaṃ paccayo hotīti ce?

If it is asked: 'Herein, which clinging is a condition for which becoming, and how?'

Rūpārūpabhavānaṃ[V 2.0208], upanissayapaccayo upādānaṃ;

Sahajātādīhipi taṃ, kāmabhavassāti viññeyyaṃ.

For the form and formless becomings, clinging is a decisive support condition. It should be understood that for sensual-sphere becoming, it is a condition also through conascence and other conditions.

Rūpārūpabhavānaṃ hi, kāmabhavapariyāpannassa ca kammabhave kusalakammasseva, upapattibhavassa cetaṃ catubbidhampi upādānaṃ upanissayapaccayavasena ekadhāva paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave attanā sampayuttākusalakammabhavassa sahajātaaññamaññanissayasampayuttaatthiavigatahetupaccayappabhedehi sahajātādīhi paccayo hoti. Vippayuttassa pana upanissayapaccayenevāti.

Indeed, for the form and formless becomings, for the wholesome kamma of kamma-becoming included in the sensual sphere, and for rebirth-becoming, all four kinds of clinging are a condition in only one way: as a decisive support condition. For the unwholesome kamma-becoming in the sensual sphere with which it is associated, it is a condition through the modes beginning with conascence, that is, by way of conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, non-disappearance, and root conditions. But for what is dissociated, it is a condition only as a decisive support condition.

Ayaṃ “upādānapaccayā bhavo”ti padasmiṃ vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed exposition on the phrase, 'With clinging as condition, becoming.'

Bhavapaccayājātiādivitthārakathā

The Detailed Exposition on 'With Becoming as Condition, Birth,' etc.

651. Bhavapaccayā jātītiādīsu jātiādīnaṃ vinicchayo saccaniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Bhavoti panettha kammabhavova adhippeto. So hi jātiyā paccayo, na upapattibhavo. So ca pana kammapaccayaupanissayapaccayavasena dvedhā paccayo hotīti.

651. In the passage 'with becoming as condition, birth,' etc., the determination of birth and so on should be understood in the same way as stated in the Exposition of the Truths. Here, 'becoming' is intended only as kamma-becoming. For it is the condition for birth, not rebirth-becoming. And it is a condition in two ways: as kamma-condition and as decisive-support condition.

Tattha siyā – kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbaṃ bhavo jātiyā paccayoti ce? Bāhirapaccayasamattepi hīnapaṇītatādivisesadassanato. Bāhirānaṃ hi janakajananīsukkasoṇitāhārādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ samattepi sattānaṃ yamakānampi sataṃ hīnapaṇītatādiviseso dissati. So ca na ahetuko sabbadā ca sabbesañca abhāvato, na kammabhavato aññahetuko tadabhinibbattakasattānaṃ ajjhattasantāne aññassa kāraṇassa abhāvatoti kammabhavahetukova. Kammaṃ hi sattānaṃ hīnapaṇītatādivisesassa hetu. Tenāha bhagavā “kammaṃ satte vibhajati yadidaṃ hīnappaṇītatāyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.289). Tasmā jānitabbametaṃ “bhavo jātiyā paccayo”ti.

Here, one might ask: 'How then is it to be known that becoming is a condition for birth?' By the observation of distinctions such as inferiority and superiority even when external conditions are the same. For even when external conditions—such as the father and mother, their semen and blood, nutriment, etc.—are the same, distinctions of inferiority and superiority are seen among beings, even among twins. And this distinction is not uncaused, since it is not always and for all beings absent; nor is it caused by anything other than kamma-becoming, since there is no other cause to be found in the internal continuity of the beings so produced. Therefore, it has kamma-becoming as its cause. For kamma is the cause of the distinctions of inferiority and superiority among beings. Thus the Blessed One has said: 'Kamma divides beings, that is, by way of inferiority and superiority' (MN 135). Therefore it should be known: 'Becoming is a condition for birth.'

Yasmā ca asati jātiyā jarāmaraṇaṃ nāma, sokādayo vā dhammā na honti. Jātiyā pana sati jarāmaraṇañceva, jarāmaraṇasaṅkhātadukkhadhammaphuṭṭhassa ca bālajanassa jarāmaraṇābhisambandhā [V 2.0209] vā tena tena dukkhadhammena phuṭṭhassa [M 2.0211] anabhisambandhā vā sokādayo ca dhammā honti. Tasmā ayampi jāti jarāmaraṇassa ceva sokādīnañca paccayo hotīti veditabbā. Sā pana upanissayakoṭiyā ekadhāva paccayo hotīti.

And because, when there is no birth, there is no such thing as aging-and-death, nor are there states such as sorrow and the like. But when birth exists, there is aging-and-death; and for the foolish person afflicted by the painful states reckoned as aging-and-death, states such as sorrow and the like arise, whether connected with that aging-and-death or unconnected, when afflicted by this or that painful state. Therefore, this birth should be understood as a condition for both aging-and-death and for sorrow and the rest. But it is a condition in only one way, in the category of decisive support.

Ayaṃ “bhavapaccayā jātī”tiādīsu vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed explanation of 'with becoming as condition, birth,' and so on.

Bhavacakkakathā

Discourse on the Wheel of Becoming

652. Yasmā panettha sokādayo avasāne vuttā, tasmā yā sā avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti evametassa bhavacakkassa ādimhi vuttā, sā,

652. Since sorrow and the like are mentioned here at the end, therefore that ignorance which is stated at the beginning of this wheel of becoming in the words 'with ignorance as condition, formations'—that ignorance,

Sokādīhi avijjā, siddhā bhavacakkamaviditādimidaṃ;

Kārakavedakarahitaṃ, dvādasavidhasuññatāsuññaṃ.

Ignorance is established by sorrow and the like; this wheel of becoming has an unknown beginning, is devoid of a maker and an experiencer, and is empty with a twelvefold emptiness.

Satataṃ samitaṃ pavattatīti veditabbaṃ.

It should be understood that it turns constantly and perpetually.

Kathaṃ panettha sokādīhi avijjā siddhā, kathamidaṃ bhavacakkaṃ aviditādi, kathaṃ kārakavedakarahitaṃ, kathaṃ dvādasavidhasuññatāsuññanti ce? Ettha hi sokadomanassupāyāsā avijjāya aviyogino, paridevo ca nāma mūḷhassāti tesu tāva siddhesu siddhā hoti avijjā. Apica “āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.103) vuttaṃ. Āsavasamudayā cete sokādayo honti.

One might ask: How is ignorance established here through sorrow and the like? How does this wheel of becoming have an unknown beginning? How is it devoid of a maker and an experiencer? And how is it empty with a twelvefold emptiness? Here, sorrow, grief, and despair are inseparable from ignorance, and lamentation belongs to the deluded; thus, when these are established, ignorance is established. Moreover, it is said: 'With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance' (MN 9). And these states of sorrow and the like arise with the arising of the taints.

Kathaṃ? Vatthukāmaviyoge tāva soko kāmāsavasamudayā hoti. Yathāha –

How so? First, sorrow over separation from the objects of sensual pleasure arises from the arising of the taint of sensual desire. As it is said:

“Tassa ce kāmayānassa, chandajātassa jantuno;

Te kāmā parihāyanti, sallaviddhova ruppatī”ti. (su. ni. 773);

For the person who desires, for the being in whom longing has arisen, if those sensual pleasures are lost, he is tormented as if pierced by a dart.

Yathā cāha – “kāmato jāyati soko”ti. (Dha. pa. 215).

And as it is said: 'From sensual pleasure sorrow is born' (Dhp 215).

Sabbepi [V 2.0210] cete diṭṭhāsavasamudayā honti. Yathāha –

And all these states arise from the arising of the taint of views. As it is said:

“Tassa ‘ahaṃ rūpaṃ mama rūpa’nti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino rūpavipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.1).

For one who abides obsessed with the notion 'I am form, form is mine,' sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise from the change and alteration of form (SN 22.1).

Yathā ca diṭṭhāsavasamudayā, evaṃ bhavāsavasamudayāpi. Yathāha –

And just as they arise from the arising of the taint of views, so too they arise from the arising of the taint of becoming. As it is said:

“Yepi [M 2.0212] te devā dīghāyukā vaṇṇavanto sukhabahulā uccesu vimānesu ciraṭṭhitikā, tepi tathāgatassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā bhayaṃ santāsaṃ saṃvegamāpajjantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.78). Pañca pubbanimittāni disvā maraṇabhayena santajjitānaṃ devānaṃ viya.

'Even those devas who are long-lived, beautiful, abounding in happiness, dwelling for a long time in lofty mansions—even they, on hearing the Tathāgata's teaching of the Dhamma, fall into fear, terror, and agitation' (SN 22.78). This is like the devas who, on seeing the five preliminary signs, are terrified by the fear of death.

Yathā ca bhavāsavasamudayā, evaṃ avijjāsavasamudayāpi. Yathāha –

And just as they arise from the arising of the taint of becoming, so too they arise from the arising of the taint of ignorance. As it is said:

“Sa kho so, bhikkhave, bālo tividhaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedetī”ti (ma. ni. 3.246).

'That fool, monks, experiences threefold pain and grief in this very life' (MN 129).

Iti yasmā āsavasamudayā ete dhammā honti, tasmā ete sijjhamānā avijjāya hetubhūte āsave sādhenti. Āsavesu ca siddhesu paccayabhāve bhāvato avijjāpi siddhāva hotīti. Evaṃ tāvettha sokādīhi avijjā siddhā hotīti veditabbā.

Thus, since these states arise from the arising of the taints, when they are established, they establish the taints that are the cause of ignorance. And when the taints are established, because the effect exists when the condition is present, ignorance too is established. In this way it should be understood that here ignorance is established through sorrow and the like.

Yasmā pana evaṃ paccayabhāve bhāvato avijjāya siddhāya puna avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇanti evaṃ hetuphalaparamparāya pariyosānaṃ natthi. Tasmā taṃ hetuphalasambandhavasena pavattaṃ dvādasaṅgaṃ bhavacakkaṃ aviditādīti siddhaṃ hoti.

But since, with ignorance thus established because the effect exists when the condition is present, there are again 'with ignorance as condition, formations,' 'with formations as condition, consciousness,' and so on, there is no end to this series of cause and effect. Therefore, that twelve-linked wheel of becoming, which turns by way of this connection of cause and effect, is established as having an unknown beginning.

Evaṃ sati avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti idaṃ ādimattakathanaṃ virujjhatīti ce. Nayidaṃ ādimattakathanaṃ. Padhānadhammakathanaṃ panetaṃ. Tiṇṇannaṃ hi vaṭṭānaṃ avijjā padhānā. Avijjāggahaṇena hi avasesakilesavaṭṭañca kammādīni ca bālaṃ palibodhenti. Sappasiraggahaṇena sesasappasarīraṃ viya bāhaṃ. Avijjāsamucchede pana kate tehi vimokkho hoti[V 2.0211]. Sappasiracchede kate palibodhitabāhāvimokkho viya. Yathāha – “avijjāyatveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.1; mahāva. 1). Iti yaṃ gaṇhato bandho, muccato ca mokkho hoti, tassa padhānadhammassa kathanamidaṃ, na ādimattakathananti. Evamidaṃ bhavacakkaṃ aviditādīti veditabbaṃ.

If it is said: 'This being so, the statement "with ignorance as condition, formations" is a statement about a mere beginning, which is a contradiction,' we reply: this is not a statement about a mere beginning. Rather, it is a statement about the principal state. For ignorance is the principal state among the three rounds. By grasping ignorance, the remaining round of defilements and kamma, etc., entangle the fool, just as when one grasps a snake's head, the rest of its body entangles one's arm. But when ignorance is cut off, there is liberation from them, just as when the snake's head is cut off, the entangled arm is freed. As it is said: 'With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance comes the cessation of formations,' etc. (SN 12.1). Thus, this is a statement about the principal state, by grasping which there is bondage and by releasing which there is liberation; it is not a statement about a mere beginning. In this way, this wheel of becoming should be understood as having an unknown beginning.

Tayidaṃ [M 2.0213] yasmā avijjādīhi kāraṇehi saṅkhārādīnaṃ pavatti, tasmā tato aññena “brahmā mahābrahmā seṭṭho sajitā”ti (dī. ni. 1.42) evaṃ parikappitena brahmādinā vā saṃsārassa kārakena, “so kho pana me ayaṃ attā vado vedeyyo”ti evaṃ parikappitena attanā vā sukhadukkhānaṃ vedakena rahitaṃ. Iti kārakavedakarahitanti veditabbaṃ.

And since this process of formations and the rest occurs because of causes such as ignorance, it is therefore devoid of any maker of saṃsāra other than these—such as the imagined Brahmā, etc., about whom it is conceived: 'Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Best, the Creator...' (DN 1)—and it is devoid of any experiencer of pleasure and pain, such as the self about which it is conceived: 'This self of mine that speaks and feels...' Thus it should be understood as 'devoid of a maker and an experiencer.'

Yasmā panettha avijjā udayabbayadhammakattā dhuvabhāvena, saṃkiliṭṭhattā saṃkilesikattā ca subhabhāvena, udayabbayapaṭipīḷitattā sukhabhāvena, paccayāyattavuttittā vasavattanabhūtena attabhāvena ca suññā. Tathā saṅkhārādīnipi aṅgāni. Yasmā vā avijjā na attā, na attano, na attani, na attavatī. Tathā saṅkhārādīnipi aṅgāni. Tasmā dvādasavidhasuññatāsuññametaṃ bhavacakkanti veditabbaṃ.

Because here ignorance is empty of permanence, since it has the nature of arising and passing away; empty of beauty, since it is defiled and defiling; empty of pleasure, since it is oppressed by arising and passing away; and empty of self, since its occurrence is dependent on conditions and it is not subject to control. The same applies to the other links, such as formations. Or, because ignorance is not self, does not belong to a self, is not in a self, and does not have a self. The same applies to the other links, such as formations. Therefore this wheel of becoming should be understood as 'empty with the twelvefold emptiness.'

653. Evañca viditvā puna,

653. Having understood this, further:

Tassāvijjātaṇhā, mūlamatītādayo tayo kālā;

Dve aṭṭha dve eva ca, sarūpato tesu aṅgāni.

Its root is ignorance and craving; its times are the three—past and so on; its links are two, and eight, and two, respectively, in their own nature.

Tassa kho panetassa bhavacakkassa avijjā taṇhā cāti dve dhammā mūlanti veditabbā. Tadetaṃ pubbantāharaṇato avijjāmūlaṃ vedanāvasānaṃ, aparantasantānato taṇhāmūlaṃ jarāmaraṇāvasānanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha purimaṃ diṭṭhicaritavasena vuttaṃ, pacchimaṃ taṇhācaritavasena. Diṭṭhicaritānaṃ hi avijjā, taṇhācaritānañca taṇhā saṃsāranāyikā. Ucchedadiṭṭhisamugghātāya vā paṭhamaṃ, phaluppattiyā hetūnaṃ anupacchedappakāsanato, sassatadiṭṭhisamugghātāya dutiyaṃ, uppannānaṃ jarāmaraṇappakāsanato. Gabbhaseyyakavasena vā purimaṃ, anupubbapavattidīpanato, opapātikavasena pacchimaṃ, sahuppattidīpanato.

It should be understood that the root of this wheel of becoming is two things: ignorance and craving. This is twofold: when traced back to the past end, it is rooted in ignorance and ends with feeling; in the continuity of the future end, it is rooted in craving and ends with aging-and-death. Here, the former is stated for one of speculative temperament, the latter for one of craving temperament. For those of speculative temperament, ignorance is the leader in saṃsāra; for those of craving temperament, craving is the leader. Alternatively, the first is for the eradication of the annihilationist view, by showing the non-interruption of causes for the arising of fruit; the second is for the eradication of the eternalist view, by showing the aging-and-death of what has come to be. Or, the former is stated by way of womb-birth, showing a gradual process; the latter by way of spontaneous birth, showing simultaneous arising.

Atītapaccuppannānāgatā [V 2.0212] cassa tayo kālā. Tesu pāḷiyaṃ sarūpato āgatavasena “avijjā, saṅkhārā cā”ti dve aṅgāni atītakālāni. Viññāṇādīni bhavāvasānāni aṭṭha paccuppannakālāni. Jāti ceva jarāmaraṇañca dve anāgatakālānīti veditabbāni.

Its three times are past, present, and future. Among these, it should be understood that, according to what is given in its own nature in the Pāli text, the two links 'ignorance and formations' belong to the past time; the eight from consciousness to the end of becoming belong to the present time; and the two, 'birth and aging-and-death,' belong to the future time.

654. Puna[M 2.0214],

654. Again,

“Hetuphalahetupubbaka-tisandhicatubhedasaṅgahañcetaṃ;

Vīsati ākārāraṃ, tivaṭṭamanavaṭṭhitaṃ bhamati”.

With three connections preceded by cause, effect, and cause, and fourfold sections; with twenty spokes which are its aspects, and three rounds, it turns unceasingly.

Itipi veditabbaṃ.

This too should be understood.

Tattha saṅkhārānañca paṭisandhiviññāṇassa ca antarā eko hetuphalasandhi nāma. Vedanāya ca taṇhāya ca antarā eko phalahetusandhi nāma. Bhavassa ca jātiyā ca antarā eko hetuphalasandhīti evamidaṃ hetuphalahetupubbakatisandhīti veditabbaṃ.

Here, between formations and rebirth-consciousness is one connection, named the cause-effect connection. Between feeling and craving is one connection, named the effect-cause connection. Between becoming and birth is one connection, the cause-effect connection. Thus this should be understood as having three connections preceded by cause, effect, and cause.

Sandhīnaṃ ādipariyosānavavatthitā panassa cattāro saṅgahā honti. Seyyathidaṃ – avijjāsaṅkhārā eko saṅgaho. Viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanaphassavedanā dutiyo. Taṇhupādānabhavā tatiyo. Jātijarāmaraṇaṃ catutthoti. Evamidaṃ catubhedasaṅgahanti veditabbaṃ.

Now, its four groupings are established by the beginning and end of the connections. They are as follows: ignorance and formations are one group; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are the second; craving, clinging, and becoming are the third; birth and aging-and-death are the fourth. Thus this should be understood as having fourfold sections.

Atīte hetavo pañca, idāni phalapañcakaṃ;

Idāni hetavo pañca, āyatiṃ phalapañcakanti.

In the past there were five causes, at present a pentad of fruits; at present there are five causes, in the future a pentad of fruits.

Etehi pana vīsatiyā ākārasaṅkhātehi arehi vīsatiākārāranti veditabbaṃ. Tattha atīte hetavo pañcāti avijjā saṅkhārā cāti ime tāva dve vuttā eva. Yasmā pana avidvā paritassati, paritassito upādiyati, tassupādānapaccayā bhavo. Tasmā taṇhupādānabhavāpi gahitā honti. Tenāha “purimakammabhavasmiṃ moho avijjā, āyūhanā saṅkhārā, nikanti taṇhā, upagamanaṃ upādānaṃ, cetanā bhavoti ime pañca dhammā purimakammabhavasmiṃ idha paṭisandhiyā paccayā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.47).

Furthermore, by these twenty spokes, which are designated as aspects, this wheel should be understood as 'having twenty spokes which are its aspects.' Herein, regarding the words 'in the past there were five causes': two of these, ignorance and formations, have already been mentioned. But since one who is ignorant is anxious, and being anxious one clings, and with that clinging as condition there is becoming, craving, clinging, and becoming are also included. Hence it is said: 'In a previous kamma-becoming, delusion is ignorance; accumulation is formations; delight is craving; taking up is clinging; volition is becoming. These five things in a previous kamma-becoming are conditions for relinking here' (Paṭis I 47).

Tattha [V 2.0213] purimakammabhavasminti purime kammabhave, atītajātiyaṃ kammabhave kariyamāneti attho. Moho avijjāti yo tadā dukkhādīsu moho, yena mūḷho kammaṃ karoti, sā avijjā. Āyūhanā saṅkhārāti taṃ kammaṃ karoto yā purimacetanāyo, yathā “dānaṃ dassāmī”ti cittaṃ uppādetvā māsampi saṃvaccharampi dānupakaraṇāni sajjentassa uppannā purimacetanāyo. Paṭiggāhakānaṃ pana hatthe dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpayato cetanā bhavoti vuccati. Ekāvajjanesu vā chasu javanesu cetanā āyūhanā saṅkhārā nāma[M 2.0215]. Sattame bhavo. Yā kāci vā pana cetanā bhavo. Sampayuttā āyūhanā saṅkhārā nāma. Nikanti taṇhāti yā kammaṃ karontassa phale upapattibhave nikāmanā patthanā, sā taṇhā nāma. Upagamanaṃ upādānanti yaṃ kammabhavassa paccayabhūtaṃ “idaṃ katvā asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne kāme sevissāmi ucchijjissāmī”tiādinā nayena pavattaṃ upagamanaṃ gahaṇaṃ parāmasanaṃ, idaṃ upādānaṃ nāma. Cetanā bhavoti āyūhanāvasāne vuttā cetanā bhavoti evamattho veditabbo.

Herein, 'in a previous kamma-becoming' means in the previous kamma-becoming, that is, while kamma was being performed in a past birth. 'Delusion is ignorance' means the delusion concerning suffering, etc., at that time, through which a deluded person performs kamma; that is ignorance. 'Accumulation is formations' refers to the prior volitions of one performing that kamma, as when, having generated the thought, 'I will give a gift,' one spends a month or a year preparing the requisites for the gift; these are the prior volitions that have arisen. But the volition at the moment of placing the offering in the recipient's hand is called 'becoming.' Or, the volition in the six impulsions is called 'accumulation, that is, formations'; the seventh is 'becoming.' Or else, any volition is 'becoming'; its associated states are 'accumulation, that is, formations.' 'Delight is craving' means the fondness or aspiration for the fruit in a future rebirth-becoming while one is performing kamma; that is craving. 'Taking up is clinging' means the taking up, grasping, or adherence that occurs as a condition for kamma-becoming, in the manner of thinking, 'Having done this, I will enjoy sensual pleasures in such-and-such a place,' or 'I will be annihilated'; this is clinging. 'Volition is becoming'—the meaning should be understood thus: the volition mentioned at the conclusion of the accumulation is 'becoming.'

Idāni phalapañcakanti viññāṇādivedanāvasānaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgatameva. Yathāha – “idha paṭisandhi viññāṇaṃ, okkanti nāmarūpaṃ, pasādo āyatanaṃ, phuṭṭho phasso, vedayitaṃ vedanā, ime pañca dhammā idhūpapattibhavasmiṃ purekatassa kammassa paccayā”ti (paṭi. 1.47). Tattha paṭisandhi viññāṇanti yaṃ bhavantarapaṭisandhānavasena uppannattā paṭisandhīti vuccati, taṃ viññāṇaṃ. Okkanti nāmarūpanti yā gabbhe rūpārūpadhammānaṃ okkanti āgantvā pavisanaṃ viya, idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ. Pasādo āyatananti idaṃ cakkhādipañcāyatanavasena vuttaṃ. Phuṭṭho phassoti yo ārammaṇaṃ phuṭṭho phusanto uppanno, ayaṃ phasso. Vedayitaṃ vedanāti yaṃ paṭisandhiviññāṇena vā saḷāyatanapaccayena vā phassena saha uppannaṃ vipākavedayitaṃ, sā vedanāti evamattho veditabbo.

As to 'at present a pentad of fruits,' this, beginning with consciousness and ending with feeling, is indeed found in the Pāli. As it is said: 'Here, relinking is consciousness; descent is name-and-form; sensitivity is the sense base; what is touched is contact; what is felt is feeling. These five things in this rebirth-existence are the result of kamma done previously' (Paṭis I 47). Herein, 'relinking is consciousness' means the consciousness that is called 'relinking' because it has arisen by way of linking one existence to another. 'Descent is name-and-form' means the descent, like an arrival and entry, of material and immaterial states into the womb; this is name-and-form. 'Sensitivity is the sense base' is stated with reference to the five sense bases beginning with the eye. 'What is touched is contact' means the contact that has arisen touching, making impact with, the object. 'What is felt is feeling' means the resultant feeling that arises together with the relinking consciousness or with contact conditioned by the six sense bases; that is feeling. The meaning should be understood in this way.

Idāni hetavo pañcāti taṇhādayo pāḷiyaṃ āgatā taṇhupādānabhavā. Bhave pana gahite tassa pubbabhāgā taṃsampayuttā vā saṅkhārā gahitāva honti. Taṇhupādānaggahaṇena ca taṃsampayuttā, yāya vā mūḷho kammaṃ karoti, sā avijjā gahitāva hotīti. Evaṃ pañca. Tenāha “idha paripakkattā āyatanānaṃ moho avijjā, āyūhanā saṅkhārā, nikanti taṇhā, upagamanaṃ upādānaṃ, cetanā bhavoti ime pañca dhammā idha kammabhavasmiṃ āyatiṃ paṭisandhiyā paccayā”ti [V 2.0214] (paṭi. ma. 1.47). Tattha idha paripakkattā āyatanānanti paripakkāyatanassa kammakaraṇakāle sammoho dassito. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

As to 'at present there are five causes,' these are craving and so on, which are found in the Pāli as craving, clinging, and existence. Now, when existence is taken, the formations that are its prior phase or are associated with it are also included. And by the inclusion of craving and clinging, the ignorance that is associated with them, or through which a deluded person performs kamma, is also included. Thus there are five. Hence it is said: 'Here, owing to the maturity of the sense bases, delusion is ignorance; accumulation is formations; delight is craving; taking up is clinging; volition is existence. These five things in this kamma-existence are conditions for future relinking' (Paṭis I 47). Herein, by the words 'here, owing to the maturity of the sense bases,' the delusion at the time of performing kamma by one with mature sense bases is shown. The rest has a plain meaning.

Āyatiṃ phalapañcakanti viññāṇādīni pañca. Tāni jātiggahaṇena vuttāni. Jarāmaraṇaṃ pana tesaṃyeva jarāmaraṇaṃ. Tenāha – “āyatiṃ paṭisandhi viññāṇaṃ[M 2.0216], okkanti nāmarūpaṃ, pasādo āyatanaṃ, phuṭṭho phasso, vedayitaṃ vedanā, ime pañca dhammā āyatiṃ upapattibhavasmiṃ idha katassa kammassa paccayā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.47). Evamidaṃ vīsati ākārāraṃ hoti.

As to 'in the future a pentad of fruits,' this means the five beginning with consciousness. They are stated by the inclusion of birth. And aging-and-death is the aging-and-death of just these. Hence it is said: 'In the future, relinking is consciousness; descent is name-and-form; sensitivity is the sense base; what is touched is contact; what is felt is feeling. These five things in a future rebirth-existence are the result of kamma done here' (Paṭis I 47). Thus this comes to have twenty aspects as its spokes.

Tivaṭṭamanavaṭṭhitaṃ bhamatīti ettha pana saṅkhārabhavā kammavaṭṭaṃ, avijjātaṇhupādānāni kilesavaṭṭaṃ, viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanaphassavedanā vipākavaṭṭanti imehi tīhi vaṭṭehi tivaṭṭamidaṃ bhavacakkaṃ yāva kilesavaṭṭaṃ na upacchijjati, tāva anupacchinnapaccayattā anavaṭṭhitaṃ punappunaṃ parivattanato bhamatiyevāti veditabbaṃ.

Here, as to the statement that it revolves with three rounds, without stop: formations and existence are the round of kamma; ignorance, craving, and clinging are the round of defilements; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are the round of results. It should be understood that this wheel of existence has three rounds because of these three rounds. For as long as the round of defilements is not cut off, for so long, because its condition is not cut off, it revolves without stop, turning again and again.

655. Tayidamevaṃ bhamamānaṃ,

655. This very wheel of existence, thus revolving,

Saccappabhavato kiccā, vāraṇā upamāhi ca;

Gambhīranayabhedā ca, viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

Should be understood as is fitting: from its origin from the truths, from its function, from its prevention, by similes, and from the distinctions in its profound method.

Tattha yasmā kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ avisesena samudayasaccanti saccavibhaṅge vuttaṃ, tasmā avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti avijjāya saṅkhārā dutiyasaccappabhavaṃ dutiyasaccaṃ. Saṅkhārehi viññāṇaṃ dutiyasaccappabhavaṃ paṭhamasaccaṃ. Viññāṇādīhi [M 2.0217] nāmarūpādīni vipākavedanāpariyosānāni paṭhamasaccappabhavaṃ paṭhamasaccaṃ. Vedanāya taṇhā paṭhamasaccappabhavaṃ dutiyasaccaṃ. Taṇhāya upādānaṃ dutiyasaccappabhavaṃ dutiyasaccaṃ. Upādānato bhavo dutiyasaccappabhavaṃ paṭhamadutiyasaccadvayaṃ. Bhavato jāti dutiyasaccappabhavaṃ paṭhamasaccaṃ. Jātiyā jarāmaraṇaṃ paṭhamasaccappabhavaṃ paṭhamasaccanti evaṃ tāvidaṃ saccappabhavato viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

Herein, since it is said in the Saccavibhaṅga that wholesome and unwholesome kamma without distinction is the truth of the origin, therefore: 'With ignorance as condition, formations' means that from ignorance (the second truth) there arise formations (the second truth). From formations (the second truth) there arises consciousness (the first truth). From consciousness and so on (the first truth), there arise name-and-form and so on, ending with resultant feeling (the first truth). From feeling (the first truth) there arises craving (the second truth). From craving (the second truth) there arises clinging (the second truth). From clinging (the second truth) there arises existence (the pair of the first and second truths). From existence (the second truth) there arises birth (the first truth). From birth (the first truth) there arises aging-and-death (the first truth). Thus this should be understood as is fitting from the standpoint of its origin from the truths.

656. Yasmā panettha avijjā vatthūsu ca satte sammoheti, paccayo ca hoti saṅkhārānaṃ [V 2.0215] pātubhāvāya. Tathā saṅkhārā saṅkhatañca abhisaṅkharonti, paccayā ca honti viññāṇassa. Viññāṇampi vatthuñca paṭivijānāti, paccayo ca hoti nāmarūpassa. Nāmarūpampi aññamaññañca upatthambheti, paccayo ca hoti saḷāyatanassa. Saḷāyatanampi savisaye ca pavattati, paccayo ca hoti phassassa. Phassopi ārammaṇañca phusati, paccayo ca hoti vedanāya. Vedanāpi ārammaṇarasañca anubhavati, paccayo ca hoti taṇhāya. Taṇhāpi rajjanīye ca dhamme rajjati, paccayo ca hoti upādānassa. Upādānampi upādāniye ca dhamme upādiyati, paccayo ca hoti bhavassa. Bhavopi nānāgatīsu ca vikkhipati, paccayo ca hoti jātiyā. Jātipi khandhe ca janeti tesaṃ abhinibbattibhāvena pavattattā, paccayo ca hoti jarāmaraṇassa. Jarāmaraṇampi khandhānaṃ pākabhedabhāvañca adhitiṭṭhati, paccayo ca hoti bhavantarapātubhāvāya sokādīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānattā. Tasmā sabbapadesu dvedhā pavattikiccatopi idaṃ viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

656. Since, herein, ignorance both deludes beings in regard to things and is a condition for the appearance of formations. Likewise, formations both fashion the formed and are a condition for consciousness. Consciousness both cognizes the object and is a condition for name-and-form. Name-and-form both support each other and are a condition for the sixfold sense base. The sixfold sense base both operates in its own domain and is a condition for contact. Contact both touches the object and is a condition for feeling. Feeling both experiences the taste of the object and is a condition for craving. Craving both delights in desirable things and is a condition for clinging. Clinging both clings to things that can be clung to and is a condition for existence. Existence both casts beings into various destinies and is a condition for birth. Birth both generates the aggregates, since it occurs as their new production, and is a condition for aging-and-death. Aging-and-death both presides over the maturing and dissolution of the aggregates and is a condition for the appearance of a future existence, being the basis for sorrow and the like. Therefore, this should be understood as is fitting from the standpoint of its twofold function in all its parts.

657. Yasmā cettha avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti idaṃ kārakadassananivāraṇaṃ. Saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇanti attasaṅkantidassananivāraṇaṃ. Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti “attā”tiparikappitavatthubhedadassanato ghanasaññānivāraṇaṃ. Nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanantiādi attā passati…pe… vijānāti, phusati, vedayati, taṇhiyati, upādiyati, bhavati, jāyati, jīyati, mīyatītievamādidassananivāraṇaṃ. Tasmā micchādassananivāraṇatopetaṃ bhavacakkaṃ viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

657. Since, herein, the statement 'with ignorance as condition, formations' prevents the view of a creator. The statement 'with formations as condition, consciousness' prevents the view of a transmigrating self. The statement 'with consciousness as condition, name-and-form' prevents the perception of compactness by showing the division of the things conceived of as a 'self.' The statement 'with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold sense base,' and so on, prevents such views as 'the self sees... knows, contacts, feels, craves, clings, exists, is born, ages, and dies.' Therefore, this wheel of existence should also be understood, as is fitting, as a prevention of wrong views.

658. Yasmā [M 2.0218] panettha salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇavasena dhammānaṃ adassanato andho viya avijjā. Andhassa upakkhalanaṃ viya avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā. Upakkhalitassa patanaṃ viya saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ. Patitassa gaṇḍapātubhāvo viya viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ. Gaṇḍabhedapīḷakā viya nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ. Gaṇḍapīḷakāghaṭṭanaṃ viya saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso. Ghaṭṭanadukkhaṃ viya phassapaccayā vedanā, dukkhassa paṭikārābhilāso viya vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Paṭikārābhilāsena asappāyaggahaṇaṃ viya taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ. Upādiṇṇaasappāyālepanaṃ viya upādānapaccayā bhavo. Asappāyālepanena gaṇḍavikārapātubhāvo viya bhavapaccayā jāti. Gaṇḍavikārato gaṇḍabhedo viya jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ. Yasmā vā panettha avijjā appaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattibhāvena satte abhibhavati paṭalaṃ viya akkhīni[V 2.0216]. Tadabhibhūto ca bālo punabbhavikehi saṅkhārehi attānaṃ veṭheti kosakārakimi viya kosappadesehi. Saṅkhārapariggahitaṃ viññāṇaṃ gatīsu patiṭṭhaṃ labhati pariṇāyakapariggahito viya rājakumāro rajje. Upapattinimittaparikappanato viññāṇaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ anekappakāraṃ nāmarūpaṃ abhinibbatteti māyākāro viya māyaṃ. Nāmarūpe patiṭṭhitaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ pāpuṇāti subhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhito vanappagumbo viya. Āyatanaghaṭṭanato phasso jāyati araṇisahitābhimanthanato aggi viya. Phassena phuṭṭhassa vedanā pātubhavati agginā phuṭṭhassa dāho viya. Vedayamānassa taṇhā pavaḍḍhati loṇūdakaṃ pivato pipāsā viya. Tasito bhavesu abhilāsaṃ karoti pipāsito viya pānīye. Tadassupādānaṃ, upādānena bhavaṃ upādiyati āmisalobhena maccho baḷisaṃ viya. Bhave sati jāti hoti bīje sati aṅkuro viya. Jātassa avassaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ uppannassa rukkhassa patanaṃ viya. Tasmā evaṃ upamāhipetaṃ bhavacakkaṃ viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

658. Herein, because of not seeing phenomena according to their individual and general characteristics, ignorance is like a blind person. Formations conditioned by ignorance are like a blind person's stumbling. Consciousness conditioned by formations is like the falling of one who has stumbled. Name-and-form conditioned by consciousness is like the appearance of a boil on one who has fallen. The six sense bases conditioned by name-and-form are like a pustule on a boil about to burst. Contact conditioned by the six sense bases is like the striking of the boil and pustule. Feeling conditioned by contact is like the pain from that striking. Craving conditioned by feeling is like the desire for a remedy for the pain. Clinging conditioned by craving is like grasping an unsuitable remedy out of that desire. Becoming conditioned by clinging is like applying the unsuitable remedy that has been grasped. Birth conditioned by becoming is like the appearance of a corruption of the boil from the unsuitable application. Aging-and-death conditioned by birth is like the bursting of the boil from its corruption. Alternatively, herein ignorance overwhelms beings through non-attainment and wrong practice, like a film over the eyes. And being overcome by it, the fool entangles himself with formations that lead to renewed existence, like a cocoon-making worm with the parts of its cocoon. Consciousness, seized by formations, finds a footing in the destinations, like a prince established in the kingdom by his guardian. Through the mental construction of the sign of rebirth, consciousness at rebirth-linking generates name-and-form of many kinds, like a magician creating an illusion. Established in name-and-form, the six sense bases reach growth, increase, and expansion, like a grove of trees established in fertile soil. From the impact on the sense bases, contact arises, like fire from the friction of fire-sticks. For one touched by contact, feeling arises, like the burning for one touched by fire. For one who is feeling, craving increases, like the thirst of one drinking salt water. Being thirsty with craving, one desires states of existence, like a thirsty person desires water. That desire becomes its clinging. Through clinging, one grasps at becoming, like a fish seizes a hook out of greed for bait. When there is becoming, birth occurs, like a sprout when there is a seed. For one who is born, aging-and-death is inevitable, like the falling of a tree that has arisen. Therefore, this wheel of existence should also be understood, as is fitting, through these similes.

659. Yasmā ca bhagavatā atthatopi dhammatopi desanatopi paṭivedhatopi gambhīrabhāvaṃ sandhāya “gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo gambhīrāvabhāso cā”ti (dī. ni. 2.95; saṃ. ni. 2.60) vuttaṃ, tasmā gambhīrabhedatopetaṃ bhavacakkaṃ viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

659. And because the Blessed One, with reference to its profundity in terms of meaning, principle, teaching, and penetration, said, ‘This dependent origination, Ānanda, is profound and it appears profound,’ therefore this wheel of existence should also be understood, as is fitting, from the standpoint of its distinctions of profundity.

Tattha [M 2.0219] yasmā na jātito jarāmaraṇaṃ na hoti, na ca jātiṃ vinā aññato hoti, itthañca jātito samudāgacchatīti evaṃ jātipaccayasamudāgataṭṭhassa duravabodhanīyato jarāmaraṇassa jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho gambhīro. Tathā jātiyā bhavapaccaya…pe… saṅkhārānaṃ avijjāpaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho gambhīro. Tasmā idaṃ bhavacakkaṃ atthagambhīranti ayaṃ tāvettha atthagambhīratā. Hetuphalañhi atthoti vuccati. Yathāha – “hetuphale ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 720).

Herein, since it is not that aging-and-death does not arise from birth, nor does it arise from anything else apart from birth, and in this way it arises from birth—because this state of having arisen together from birth as its condition is difficult to comprehend, the nature of aging-and-death as having been produced and having arisen together from birth as its condition is profound. Likewise, the nature of birth as having been produced and having arisen together from becoming as its condition… and so on… the nature of formations as having been produced and having arisen together from ignorance as their condition is profound. Therefore, this wheel of existence is profound in meaning. This, for a start, is the profundity of meaning here. For the fruit of a cause is called 'meaning' (attha), as it is said: ‘Knowledge of the fruit of a cause is the analytical knowledge of meaning.’

Yasmā pana yenākārena yadavatthā ca avijjā tesaṃ tesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hoti, tassa duravabodhanīyato avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho gambhīro. Tathā saṅkhārānaṃ…pe… jātiyā jarāmaraṇassa paccayaṭṭho gambhīro, tasmā idaṃ bhavacakkaṃ dhammagambhīranti ayamettha dhammagambhīratā. Hetuno hi dhammoti nāmaṃ. Yathāha – “hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 720).

Furthermore, because the mode and the state in which ignorance is a condition for these and those formations are difficult to comprehend, the nature of ignorance as a condition for formations is profound. Likewise, the nature of formations as a condition… and so on… the nature of birth as a condition for aging-and-death is profound. Therefore, this wheel of existence is profound in principle. This is the profundity in principle here. For 'principle' (dhamma) is a name for the cause, as it is said: ‘Knowledge in the cause is the analytical knowledge of principle (dhamma).’

Yasmā [V 2.0217] cassa tena tena kāraṇena tathā tathā pavattetabbattā desanāpi gambhīrā, na tattha sabbaññutaññāṇato aññaṃ ñāṇaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ labhati. Tathāhetaṃ katthaci sutte anulomato, katthaci paṭilomato, katthaci anulomapaṭilomato, katthaci vemajjhato paṭṭhāya anulomato vā paṭilomato vā, katthaci tisandhicatusaṅkhepaṃ, katthaci dvisandhitisaṅkhepaṃ, katthaci ekasandhidvisaṅkhepaṃ desitaṃ, tasmā idaṃ bhavacakkaṃ desanāgambhīranti ayaṃ desanāgambhīratā.

Furthermore, because its teaching must be expounded in this way and that way for this reason and that, the teaching itself is profound; no knowledge other than the knowledge of omniscience gains a footing there. Thus it has been taught in some suttas in forward order; in some, in reverse order; in some, in both forward and reverse order; in some, beginning from the middle and proceeding either forwards or backwards; in some, with three connections and four sections; in some, with two connections and three sections; and in some, with one connection and two sections. Therefore, this wheel of existence is profound in its teaching. This is the profundity of its teaching.

Yasmā cettha yo so avijjādīnaṃ sabhāvo, yena paṭividdhena avijjādayo sammā salakkhaṇato paṭividdhā honti, so duppariyogāhattā gambhīro, tasmā idaṃ bhavacakkaṃ paṭivedhagambhīraṃ. Tathā hettha avijjāya aññāṇādassanasaccāsampaṭivedhaṭṭho gambhīro, saṅkhārānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇāyūhanasarāgavirāgaṭṭho, viññāṇassa suññataabyāpāraasaṅkantipaṭisandhipātubhāvaṭṭho, nāmarūpassa ekuppādavinibbhogāvinibbhoganamanaruppanaṭṭho, saḷāyatanassa adhipatilokadvārakhettavisayibhāvaṭṭho, phassassa phusanasaṅghaṭṭanasaṅgatisannipātaṭṭho[M 2.0220], vedanāya ārammaṇarasānubhavanasukhadukkhamajjhattabhāvanijjīvavedayitaṭṭho. Taṇhāya abhinanditajjhosānasaritālatānadītaṇhāsamuddaduppūraṭṭho, upādānassa ādānaggahaṇābhinivesaparāmāsaduratikkamaṭṭho, bhavassa āyūhanābhisaṅkharaṇayonigatiṭhitinivāsesukhipanaṭṭho, jātiyā jāti sañjāti okkanti nibbatti pātubhāvaṭṭho, jarāmaraṇassa khayavayabhedavipariṇāmaṭṭho gambhīroti ayamettha paṭivedhagambhīratā.

Furthermore, since the intrinsic nature of ignorance and the other factors—by the penetration of which ignorance and the other factors are rightly penetrated according to their individual characteristics—is profound because it is difficult to fathom, therefore this wheel of existence is profound in terms of what is to be penetrated. Herein, the profundity of ignorance lies in its meaning of non-knowing, not seeing, and not penetrating the truths. The profundity of formations lies in their meaning of forming, accumulating, being with passion, and being without passion. The profundity of consciousness lies in its meaning of being empty, inactive, non-transference, and manifestation as rebirth-linking. The profundity of name-and-form lies in its meaning of co-arising, being separable, being inseparable, inclining, and being afflicted. The profundity of the six sense bases lies in their meaning of being dominant, a world, a door, a field, and a sphere. The profundity of contact lies in its meaning of touching, impact, coming together, and concurrence.
