The profundity of feeling lies in its meaning of experiencing the flavour of an object, being pleasant, painful, or neutral, and being felt as lifeless. The profundity of craving lies in its meaning of delighting, adhering, being like a flowing stream, a creeper, a river, an ocean of craving, and being hard to fill. The profundity of clinging lies in its meaning of taking up, grasping, adherence, misapprehension, and being hard to get past. The profundity of becoming lies in its meaning of accumulating, forming, and projecting into wombs, destinations, stations, and abodes. The profundity of birth lies in its meaning of birth, generation, descent, production, and manifestation. The profundity of aging-and-death lies in its meaning of decay, fading, breaking up, and changing. This, herein, is the profundity in terms of what is to be penetrated.

660. Yasmā panettha ekattanayo, nānattanayo, abyāpāranayo, evaṃdhammatānayoti cattāro atthanayā honti, tasmā nayabhedatopetaṃ bhavacakkaṃ viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

660. Furthermore, since there are herein four modes of meaning—the mode of unity, the mode of diversity, the mode of non-agency, and the mode of suchness—therefore, this wheel of existence should also be understood by way of the distinctions of method, as is fitting.

Tattha avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇanti evaṃ bījassa aṅkurādibhāvena rukkhabhāvappatti viya santānānupacchedo ekattanayo nāma. Yaṃ sammā passanto hetuphalasambandhena santānassa anupacchedāvabodhato ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati. Micchā passanto hetuphalasambandhena pavattamānassa santānānupacchedassa ekattagahaṇato sassatadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

Herein, ‘With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness’—thus, the unbroken continuity, like a seed reaching the state of a tree by way of a sprout and so on, is called the mode of unity. One who sees this rightly abandons the annihilation view by understanding the unbrokenness of the continuum through the connection of cause and effect. One who sees wrongly adopts the eternalism view by grasping as a unity the unbroken continuity of the ongoing process connected by cause and effect.

Avijjādīnaṃ pana yathāsakaṃlakkhaṇavavatthānaṃ nānattanayo nāma. Yaṃ sammā passanto navanavānaṃ [V 2.0218] uppādadassanato sassatadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati. Micchā passanto ekasantānapatitassa bhinnasantānasseva nānattaggahaṇato ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

The establishment of the individual characteristics of ignorance and the other factors is the mode of diversity. One who sees this rightly abandons the eternalism view by seeing the arising of ever new phenomena. One who sees wrongly adopts the annihilation view by grasping the diversity that occurs within a single continuum as if it were a broken continuum.

Avijjāya saṅkhārā mayā uppādetabbā, saṅkhārānaṃ vā viññāṇaṃ amhehīti evamādibyāpārābhāvo abyāpāranayo nāma. Yaṃ sammā passanto kārakassa abhāvāvabodhato attadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati. Micchā passanto yo asatipi byāpāre avijjādīnaṃ sabhāvaniyamasiddho hetubhāvo, tassa aggahaṇato akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyati.

The absence of any agency such as ‘Formations are to be produced by me through ignorance’ or ‘Consciousness is to be produced by us through formations’ is the mode of non-agency. One who sees this rightly abandons the self-view by understanding the absence of a doer. One who sees wrongly, by not grasping that even without an agent there is a causal state for ignorance and the other factors established by the necessity of their own nature, adopts the view of non-action.

Avijjādīhi pana kāraṇehi saṅkhārādīnaṃyeva sambhavo khīrādīhi dadhiādīnaṃ viya, na aññesanti ayaṃ evaṃdhammatānayo nāma. Yaṃ sammā passanto paccayānurūpato phalāvabodhā ahetukadiṭṭhiṃ akiriyadiṭṭhiñca pajahati. Micchā passanto paccayānurūpaṃ phalappavattiṃ aggahetvā yato kutoci [M 2.0221] yassa kassaci asambhavaggahaṇato ahetukadiṭṭhiñceva niyatavādañca upādiyatīti evamidaṃ bhavacakkaṃ,

The arising of only formations and so on from conditions such as ignorance and so on—like the arising of only curds and so on from milk and so on, and not from other things—is the mode of suchness. One who sees rightly abandons the views of causelessness and inefficacy by understanding the result in accordance with its conditions. One who sees wrongly, by not grasping the occurrence of the result in accordance with its conditions and by grasping the impossible arising of anything whatsoever from anywhere whatsoever, adopts the view of causelessness and the doctrine of fatalism. Thus is this wheel of existence,

Saccappabhavato kiccā, vāraṇāupamāhi ca;

Gambhīranayabhedā ca, viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

From its source in the truths, from function, from prevention, and from similes; and from the distinctions of profundity and method, it should be understood as is fitting.

661. Idañhi atigambhīrato agādhaṃ. Nānānayagahanato duratiyānaṃ. Ñāṇāsinā samādhipavarasilāyaṃ sunisitena,

661. For this is unfathomable for its great depth, hard to traverse for its jungle of many methods. With the sword of wisdom, well-sharpened on the excellent stone of concentration,

Bhavacakkamapadāletvā, asanivicakkamiva niccanimmathanaṃ;

Saṃsārabhayamatīto, na koci supinantarepyatthi.

Without shattering the wheel of existence, there is no one, not even in a dream, who has passed beyond the fear of saṃsāra, which is ever-crushing like the wheel of a thunderbolt.

Vuttampi hetaṃ bhagavatā – “gambhīro cāyaṃ, ānanda, paṭiccasamuppādo gambhīrāvabhāso ca. Etassa cānanda, dhammassa ananubodhā appaṭivedhā evamayaṃ pajā tantākulakajātā kulāgaṇṭhikajātā muñjapabbajabhūtā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ saṃsāraṃ nātivattatī”ti (mahāva. 95; saṃ. ni. 2.60). Tasmā attano vā paresaṃ vā hitāya ca sukhāya ca paṭipanno avasesakiccāni pahāya,

This was also spoken by the Blessed One: 'Deep, Ānanda, is this dependent origination, and it appears deep. It is through not understanding and not penetrating this Dhamma, Ānanda, that this generation has become a tangled skein, a knotted ball of thread, like matted muñja and babbaja grass; it does not pass beyond the plane of misery, the bad destination, the nether world, saṃsāra' (DN 15.1; SN 12.60). Therefore, having abandoned other duties, one who is practicing for the welfare and happiness of oneself or others,

Gambhīre [V 2.0219] paccayākārappabhede idha paṇḍito;

Yathā gādhaṃ labhethevamanuyuñje sadā satoti.

A wise person here should always mindfully apply himself to the deep and diverse modes of the conditional structure, in order to find a firm footing.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, composed for the joy of good people,

Paññābhāvanādhikāre

in the chapter on the Development of Wisdom,

Paññābhūminiddeso nāma

the Exposition of the Ground of Wisdom by name,

Sattarasamo paricchedo.

is the Seventeenth Chapter.

18. Diṭṭhivisuddhiniddeso

18. The Exposition of the Purification of View

Nāmarūpapariggahakathā

The Discourse on the Comprehension of Mentality-Materiality

662. Idāni [M 2.0222][V 2.0220] yā “imesu bhūmibhūtesu dhammesu uggahaparipucchāvasena ñāṇaparicayaṃ katvā ‘sīlavisuddhi ceva cittavisuddhi cā’ti dve mūlabhūtā visuddhiyo sampādetabbā”ti vuttā. Tattha sīlavisuddhi nāma suparisuddhaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarādicatubbidhaṃ sīlaṃ, tañca sīlaniddese vitthāritameva. Cittavisuddhi nāma saupacārā aṭṭha samāpattiyo, tāpi cittasīsena vuttasamādhiniddese sabbākārena vitthāritā eva. Tasmā tā tattha vitthāritanayeneva veditabbā.

662. Now, it was said: 'Having gained acquaintance with knowledge of these states that are the ground by way of study and questioning, two purifications that are the root should be accomplished, namely, purification of virtue and purification of mind.' Herein, purification of virtue is the fourfold utterly pure virtue beginning with the Pātimokkha restraint, and that has been explained in detail in the Exposition of Virtue. Purification of mind is the eight attainments together with their access concentration, and these too have been explained in every way in the Exposition of Concentration, which was stated under the heading of mind. Therefore, they should be understood in the way they were explained in detail there.

Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “diṭṭhivisuddhi, kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi, maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi, paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi, ñāṇadassanavisuddhīti imā pana pañca visuddhiyo sarīra”nti, tattha nāmarūpānaṃ yāthāvadassanaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhi nāma.

But as to what was said: 'Purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of path and not-path, purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision—these five purifications are the body.' Herein, the seeing of mentality-materiality as it really is is called purification of view.

663. Taṃ sampādetukāmena samathayānikena tāva ṭhapetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ avasesarūpārūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ aññatarato vuṭṭhāya vitakkādīni jhānaṅgāni, taṃsampayuttā ca dhammā lakkhaṇarasādivasena pariggahetabbā. Pariggahetvā sabbampetaṃ ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ namanato namanaṭṭhena nāmanti vavatthapetabbaṃ.

663. A serenity-vehicle meditator who wishes to accomplish this should first, setting aside the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, emerge from any of the remaining fine-material or immaterial jhānas. Then the jhāna factors, such as applied thought, and the states associated with them, should be comprehended by way of their characteristic, function, etc. Having comprehended them, all this should be defined as 'mentality' on the ground of bending, in the sense of its inclining towards an object.

Tato yathā nāma puriso antogehe sappaṃ disvā taṃ anubandhamāno tassa āsayaṃ passati, evameva ayampi yogāvacaro taṃ nāmaṃ upaparikkhanto “idaṃ nāmaṃ kiṃ nissāya pavattatī”ti pariyesamāno tassa nissayaṃ hadayarūpaṃ passati. Tato hadayarūpassa nissayabhūtāni, bhūtanissitāni ca sesupādāyarūpānīti rūpaṃ pariggaṇhāti. So sabbampetaṃ ruppanato [V 2.0221] rūpanti vavatthapeti. Tato namanalakkhaṇaṃ nāmaṃ, ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpanti saṅkhepato nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapeti.

Then, just as a man who sees a snake in his house follows it and finds its lair, so too this meditator, while investigating that mentality and searching, 'On what does this mentality depend?' sees the heart-materiality as its support. Then he comprehends materiality, namely, the material phenomena that are the support for the heart-materiality and the remaining derived material phenomena that are dependent on the primary elements. He defines all this as 'materiality' on the ground of its being afflicted. Then, in brief, he defines mentality-materiality as 'mentality with the characteristic of bending' and 'materiality with the characteristic of being afflicted'.

664. Suddhavipassanāyāniko pana ayameva vā samathayāniko catudhātuvavatthāne vuttānaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ dhātupariggahamukhānaṃ aññataramukhavasena saṅkhepato vā vitthārato vā catasso dhātuyo pariggaṇhāti. Athassa yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇato āvibhūtāsu dhātūsu kammasamuṭṭhānamhi [M 2.0223] tāva kese “catasso dhātuyo, vaṇṇo, gandho, raso, ojā, jīvitaṃ, kāyappasādo”ti evaṃ kāyadasakavasena dasa rūpāni, tattheva bhāvassa atthitāya bhāvadasakavasena dasa, tattheva āhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ, utusamuṭṭhānaṃ, cittasamuṭṭhānanti aparānipi catuvīsatīti evaṃ catusamuṭṭhānesu catuvīsatikoṭṭhāsesu catucattālīsa catucattālīsa rūpāni, sedo, assu, kheḷo, siṅghāṇikāti imesu pana catūsu utucittasamuṭṭhānesu dvinnaṃ ojaṭṭhamakānaṃ vasena soḷasa soḷasa rūpāni, udariyaṃ, karīsaṃ, pubbo, muttanti imesu catūsu utusamuṭṭhānesu utusamuṭṭhānasseva ojaṭṭhamakassa vasena aṭṭha aṭṭha rūpāni pākaṭāni hontīti. Esa tāva dvattiṃsākāre nayo.

664. But a pure-insight-vehicle meditator, or this same serenity-vehicle meditator, comprehends the four great elements either briefly or in detail by one of the approaches to the comprehension of elements stated in the Definition of the Four Elements. Then, when the elements have become manifest to him with their individual characteristics as appropriate, there become evident to him: first, in the kamma-born hair of the head, ten material phenomena by way of the body-decad—'the four great elements, color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, life, and body-sensitivity'; and there also, because of the presence of sex-materiality, ten by way of the sex-decad; and there also, the nutriment-born, temperature-born, and consciousness-born octads with nutritive essence as the eighth, thus another twenty-four. So in each of the twenty-four parts with fourfold origination, there are forty-four material phenomena. But in these four—sweat, tears, saliva, and snot—which are born of temperature and consciousness, there are sixteen material phenomena each by way of two octads with nutritive essence as the eighth. And in these four—stomach contents, feces, pus, and urine—which are born of temperature only, there are eight material phenomena each by way of the temperature-born octad with nutritive essence as the eighth, become manifest. This, for now, is the method regarding the thirty-two parts.

Ye pana imasmiṃ dvattiṃsākāre āvibhūte apare dasa ākārā āvibhavanti. Tattha asitādiparipācake tāva kammaje tejokoṭṭhāsamhi ojaṭṭhamakañceva jīvitañcāti nava rūpāni, tathā cittaje assāsapassāsakoṭṭhāsepi ojaṭṭhamakañceva saddo cāti nava, sesesu catusamuṭṭhānesu aṭṭhasu jīvitanavakañceva tīṇi ca ojaṭṭhamakānīti tettiṃsa rūpāni pākaṭāni honti.

But when these thirty-two parts have become manifest, another ten parts become manifest. Therein, first, in the kamma-born fire-element part that digests what is eaten, drunk, etc., there are nine material phenomena: the octad with nutritive essence as the eighth and life. Similarly, in the consciousness-born in-and-out-breathing part, there are nine: the octad with nutritive essence as the eighth and sound. In the remaining eight parts with fourfold origination, thirty-three material phenomena become manifest: the life-nonad and three octads with nutritive essence as the eighth.

Tassevaṃ vitthārato dvācattālīsākāravasena imesu bhūtupādāyarūpesu pākaṭesu jātesu vatthudvāravasena pañca cakkhudasakādayo, hadayavatthudasakañcāti aparānipi saṭṭhirūpāni pākaṭāni honti. So sabbānipi tāni ruppanalakkhaṇena ekato katvā “etaṃ rūpa”nti passati.

When for him in this way, by way of the forty-two parts in detail, these primary and derived material phenomena have become manifest, then by way of the bases and doors, another sixty material phenomena also become manifest: the five decad-groups beginning with the eye-decad, and the heart-base-decad. Having grouped them all together by the characteristic of being afflicted, he sees: 'This is materiality.'

Tassevaṃ pariggahitarūpassa dvāravasena arūpadhammā pākaṭā honti. Seyyathidaṃ – dvepañcaviññāṇāni, tisso manodhātuyo, aṭṭhasaṭṭhi manoviññāṇadhātuyoti ekāsīti lokiyacittāni, avisesena ca tehi cittehi sahajāto phasso, vedanā, saññā, cetanā, jīvitaṃ, cittaṭṭhiti, manasikāroti ime satta satta cetasikāti. Lokuttaracittāni pana neva suddhavipassakassa[V 2.0222], na samathayānikassa pariggahaṃ gacchanti anadhigatattāti. So sabbepi te arūpadhamme namanalakkhaṇena ekato katvā “etaṃ nāma”nti passati. Evameko catudhātuvavatthānamukhena vitthārato nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapeti.

For one who has thus comprehended materiality, the immaterial phenomena become manifest by way of the doors. That is to say: the two sets of five consciousnesses, the three mind-elements, and the sixty-eight mind-consciousness-elements—thus eighty-one mundane consciousnesses; and, without exception, associated with these consciousnesses are these seven mental factors: contact, feeling, perception, volition, life, one-pointedness, and attention. However, the supramundane consciousnesses are not comprehended by either the pure-insight-vehicle meditator or the serenity-vehicle meditator because they have not been attained. Having grouped all these immaterial phenomena together by the characteristic of bending, he sees: 'This is mentality.' Thus someone defines mentality-materiality in detail by the approach of the definition of the four elements.

665. Aparo [M 2.0224] aṭṭhārasadhātuvasena. Kathaṃ? Idha bhikkhu atthi imasmiṃ attabhāve cakkhudhātu…pe… manoviññāṇadhātūti dhātuyo āvajjitvā yaṃ loko setakaṇhamaṇḍalavicittaṃ āyatavitthataṃ akkhikūpake nhārusuttakena ābaddhaṃ maṃsapiṇḍaṃ “cakkhū”ti sañjānāti, taṃ aggahetvā khandhaniddese upādārūpesu vuttappakāraṃ cakkhupasādaṃ “cakkhudhātū”ti vavatthapeti.

665. Another way is by means of the eighteen elements. How? Here, a bhikkhu adverts to the elements thus: 'In this individual existence there is the eye element... up to... the mind-consciousness element.' Having adverted to them, he does not take what the world perceives as the 'eye'—the variegated circle of white and black, long and broad, a ball of flesh bound by sinew-threads in the socket of the eye—but instead he defines as the 'eye element' the eye-sensitivity of the kind described in the Exposition of the Aggregates under Derived Materiality.

Yāni panassa nissayabhūtā catasso dhātuyo, parivārakāni cattāri vaṇṇa-gandha-rasa-ojā-rūpāni, anupālakaṃ jīvitindriyanti nava sahajātarūpāni, tattheva ṭhitāni kāyadasakabhāvadasakavasena vīsati kammajarūpāni, āhārasamuṭṭhānādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ojaṭṭhamakānaṃ vasena catuvīsati anupādinnarūpānīti evaṃ sesāni tepaṇṇāsa rūpāni honti, na tāni ca “cakkhudhātū”ti vavatthapeti. Esa nayo sotadhātuādīsupi. Kāyadhātuyaṃ pana avasesāni tecattālīsa rūpāni honti. Keci pana utucittasamuṭṭhānāni saddena saha nava nava katvā pañcacattālīsāti vadanti.

But the four great elements that are its support, the four surrounding material phenomena of color, odor, taste, and nutritive essence, and the life faculty that sustains them—these nine co-nascent material phenomena; and the twenty kamma-born material phenomena standing there by way of the body-decad and the sex-decad; and the twenty-four non-appropriated material phenomena by way of the three octads born of nutriment, etc.—thus the remaining fifty-three material phenomena are present, but he does not define these as the 'eye element.' This is the method for the ear element, etc., as well. In the case of the body element, however, the remaining material phenomena are forty-three. But some say forty-five, counting the temperature-born and consciousness-born groups as nine each together with sound.

Iti ime pañca pasādā, tesañca visayā rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbā pañcāti dasa rūpāni dasa dhātuyo honti. Avasesarūpāni dhammadhātuyeva honti. Cakkhuṃ pana nissāya rūpaṃ ārabbha pavattaṃ cittaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātu nāmāti evaṃ dvepañcaviññāṇāni pañca viññāṇadhātuyo honti. Tīṇi manodhātucittāni ekā manodhātu, aṭṭhasaṭṭhi manoviññāṇadhātucittāni manoviññāṇadhātūti sabbānipi ekāsīti lokiyacittāni satta viññāṇadhātuyo. Taṃsampayuttā phassādayo dhammadhātūti evamettha aḍḍhekādasa dhātuyo rūpaṃ, aḍḍhaṭṭhamā dhātuyo nāmanti evameko aṭṭhārasadhātuvasena nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapeti.

Thus these five sensitivities and their five objects—sights, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—are ten material phenomena, which are ten elements. The remaining material phenomena are the Dhamma-element. Consciousness that arises dependent on the eye and taking a sight as object is called the eye-consciousness element; thus the two sets of five consciousnesses are five consciousness elements. The three mind-element consciousnesses are one mind-element. The sixty-eight mind-consciousness-element consciousnesses are the mind-consciousness element. Thus all eighty-one mundane consciousnesses are seven consciousness elements. The associated mental factors beginning with contact are the Dhamma-element. Thus here, ten and a half elements are materiality, and seven and a half elements are mentality. In this way, one defines mentality-materiality by way of the eighteen elements.

666. Aparo dvādasāyatanavasena. Kathaṃ? Cakkhudhātuyaṃ vuttanayeneva ṭhapetvā tepaṇṇāsa rūpāni cakkhupasādamattaṃ “cakkhāyatana”nti vavatthapeti. Tattha vuttanayeneva ca sotaghānajivhākāyadhātuyo “sotaghānajivhākāyāyatanānī”ti, tesaṃ visayabhūte pañcadhamme “rūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbāyatanānī”ti[V 2.0223], lokiyasattaviññāṇadhātuyo “manāyatana”nti, taṃsampayuttā phassādayo sesarūpañca “dhammāyatana”nti evamettha [M 2.0225] aḍḍhekādasa āyatanāni rūpaṃ, diyaḍḍhaāyatanāni nāmanti evameko dvādasāyatanavasena nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapeti.

666. Another defines it by way of the twelve bases. How? In the same way as stated for the eye-element, setting aside the fifty-three material phenomena, one defines just the eye-sensitivity as the 'eye-base.' And in the same way as stated there, the ear, nose, tongue, and body elements are defined as the 'ear, nose, tongue, and body bases'; their five objective phenomena as the 'bases of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects'; the seven mundane consciousness-elements as the 'mind-base'; and the associated mental factors beginning with contact and the remaining material phenomena as the 'Dhamma-base.' Thus, here, ten and a half bases are materiality, and one and a half bases are mentality. In this way, one defines mentality-materiality by way of the twelve bases.

667. Aparo tato saṃkhittataraṃ khandhavasena vavatthapeti. Kathaṃ? Idha bhikkhu imasmiṃ sarīre catusamuṭṭhānā catasso dhātuyo, taṃnissito vaṇṇo, gandho, raso, ojā, cakkhupasādādayo pañca pasādā, vatthurūpaṃ, bhāvo, jīvitindriyaṃ, dvisamuṭṭhāno saddoti imāni sattarasa rūpāni sammasanupagāni nipphannāni rūparūpāni. Kāyaviññatti, vacīviññatti, ākāsadhātu, rūpassa lahutā, mudutā, kammaññatā, upacayo, santati, jaratā, aniccatāti imāni pana dasa rūpāni na sammasanupagāni, ākāravikāraantaraparicchedamattakāni, na nipphannarūpāni, na rūparūpāni. Apica kho rūpānaṃ ākāravikāraantaraparicchedamattato rūpanti saṅkhaṃ gatāni. Iti sabbāni petāni sattavīsati rūpāni rūpakkhandho, ekāsītiyā lokiyacittehi saddhiṃ uppannā vedanā vedanākkhandho, taṃsampayuttā saññā saññākkhandho, saṅkhārā saṅkhārakkhandho, viññāṇaṃ viññāṇakkhandhoti. Iti rūpakkhandho rūpaṃ, cattāro arūpino khandhā nāmanti evameko pañcakkhandhavasena nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapeti.

667. Another defines it more concisely by way of the aggregates. How? Here, a bhikkhu considers that in this body there are four elements arising from four sources. Dependent on these are color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, the five sensitivities such as the eye sensitivity, the heart-basis, gender, the life faculty, and sound arising from two sources—these seventeen types of material phenomena are produced, are materiality proper, and are accessible to comprehension. But bodily intimation, verbal intimation, the space element, lightness, softness, and wieldiness of materiality, along with its integration, continuation, decay, and impermanence—these ten types of material phenomena are not accessible to comprehension, being merely modes, alterations, or demarcations; they are not produced material phenomena, nor are they materiality proper. Yet they are counted as 'materiality' because they are merely modes, alterations, or demarcations of materiality. Thus, all these twenty-seven types of material phenomena constitute the materiality aggregate. The feeling that arises together with the eighty-one mundane consciousnesses is the feeling aggregate. The perception associated with them is the perception aggregate. The formations are the formations aggregate. The consciousness is the consciousness aggregate. Thus, the materiality aggregate is materiality, and the four immaterial aggregates are mentality. In this way, one defines mentality-materiality by way of the five aggregates.

668. Aparo “yaṃkiñci rūpaṃ sabbaṃ rūpaṃ cattāri mahābhūtāni catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpa”nti (ma. ni. 1.347; a. ni. 11.17) evaṃ saṃkhitteneva imasmiṃ attabhāve rūpaṃ pariggahetvā, tathā manāyatanañceva dhammāyatanekadesañca nāmanti pariggahetvā “iti idañca nāmaṃ idañca rūpaṃ, idaṃ vuccati nāmarūpa”nti saṅkhepato nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapeti.

668. Another, having briefly grasped materiality in this individual existence with the concise definition, 'Whatever materiality there is, all materiality is the four great elements and the materiality derived from the four great elements,' and having likewise grasped the mind-base and a portion of the Dhamma-base as mentality, defines mentality-materiality concisely thus: 'This is mentality and this is materiality; this is called mentality-materiality.'

669. Sace panassa tena tena mukhena rūpaṃ pariggahetvā arūpaṃ pariggaṇhato sukhumattā arūpaṃ na upaṭṭhāti, tena dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā rūpameva punappunaṃ sammasitabbaṃ manasikātabbaṃ pariggahetabbaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Yathā yathā hissa rūpaṃ suvikkhālitaṃ hoti nijjaṭaṃ suparisuddhaṃ, tathā tathā tadārammaṇā arūpadhammā sayameva pākaṭā honti.

669. But if, when grasping materiality through one or another of these approaches, he attempts to grasp the immaterial, and due to its subtlety the immaterial does not present itself to him, then without abandoning the task, he should repeatedly examine, attend to, grasp, and define materiality itself. For to the extent that materiality becomes well-washed, disentangled, and perfectly pure for him, to that same extent the immaterial phenomena that have it as their object will naturally become evident.

Yathā hi cakkhumato purisassa aparisuddhe ādāse mukhanimittaṃ olokentassa nimittaṃ na paññāyati, so “nimittaṃ na paññāyatī”ti na ādāsaṃ [M 2.0226] chaḍḍeti, atha kho naṃ punappunaṃ parimajjati[V 2.0224]. Tassa parisuddhe ādāse nimittaṃ sayameva pākaṭaṃ hoti. Yathā ca telatthiko tilapiṭṭhaṃ doṇiyaṃ ākiritvā udakena paripphosetvā ekavāraṃ dvevāraṃ pīḷanamattena tele anikkhamante na tilapiṭṭhaṃ chaḍḍeti, atha kho naṃ punappunaṃ uṇhodakena paripphosetvā madditvā pīḷeti. Tassevaṃ karoto vippasannaṃ tilatelaṃ nikkhamati. Yathā vā pana udakaṃ pasādetukāmo katakaṭṭhiṃ gahetvā antoghaṭe hatthaṃ otāretvā ekadvevāre ghaṃsanamattena udake avippasīdante na katakaṭṭhiṃ chaḍḍeti, atha kho naṃ punappunaṃ ghaṃsati. Tassevaṃ karontassa kalalakaddamaṃ sannisīdati. Udakaṃ acchaṃ hoti vippasannaṃ, evamevaṃ tena bhikkhunā dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā rūpameva punappunaṃ sammasitabbaṃ manasikātabbaṃ pariggahetabbaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ.

Just as when a man with good sight looks at the image of his face in a dirty mirror and the image is not clear, he does not discard the mirror thinking, 'The image is not clear.' Instead, he repeatedly cleans it. When the mirror is clean, the image naturally becomes clear. Or just as one wanting oil, having poured sesame flour into a trough and sprinkled it with water, does not discard the sesame flour when the oil does not come out by pressing it only once or twice; instead, he repeatedly sprinkles it with warm water, kneads it, and presses it. As he does so, the clear sesame oil emerges. Or just as one wishing to clarify water, taking a clearing-nut seed and putting his hand into the water pot, does not discard the seed when the water does not become clear by rubbing it only once or twice; instead, he rubs it repeatedly. As he does so, the silt and mud settle, and the water becomes clear and limpid. In the same way, that bhikkhu, without abandoning the task, should repeatedly examine, attend to, grasp, and define materiality itself.

Yathā yathā hissa rūpaṃ suvikkhālitaṃ hoti nijjaṭaṃ suparisuddhaṃ, tathā tathā tappaccanīkakilesā sannisīdanti, kaddamupari udakaṃ viya cittaṃ pasannaṃ hoti. Tadārammaṇā arūpadhammā sayameva pākaṭā honti. Evaṃ aññāhipi ucchucoragoṇadadhimacchādīhi upamāhi ayamattho pakāsetabbo.

For to the extent that materiality becomes well-washed, disentangled, and perfectly pure for him, to that same extent the opposing defilements subside, and the mind becomes serene like water above mud. The immaterial phenomena that have it as their object will naturally become evident. This meaning should also be illustrated by other similes, such as those of sugar cane, a thief, an ox, curds, and a fish.

Arūpadhammānaṃ upaṭṭhānākārakathā

The Explanation of the Manner of Appearance of Immaterial Phenomena

670. Evaṃ suvisuddharūpapariggahassa panassa arūpadhammā tīhi ākārehi upaṭṭhahanti phassavasena vā vedanāvasena vā viññāṇavasena vā. Kathaṃ? Ekassa tāva “pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”tiādinā nayena dhātuyo pariggaṇhantassa paṭhamābhinipāto phasso, taṃsampayuttā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, saddhiṃ phassena cetanā saṅkhārakkhandho, cittaṃ viññāṇakkhandhoti upaṭṭhāti. Tathā “kese pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā…pe… assāsapassāse pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”ti (visuddhi. 1.307) paṭhamābhinipāto phasso, taṃsampayuttā vedanā vedanākkhandho…pe… cittaṃ viññāṇakkhandhoti upaṭṭhāti. Evaṃ arūpadhammā phassavasena upaṭṭhahanti.

670. To one who has thus grasped materiality with thorough purity, immaterial phenomena become apparent in three ways: by way of contact, by way of feeling, or by way of consciousness. How so? For one who is grasping the elements by the method beginning, ‘The earth element has the characteristic of hardness,’ the initial impact is contact. The feeling associated with it is the feeling aggregate; perception is the perception aggregate; volition together with contact is the formations aggregate; and consciousness is the consciousness aggregate—thus they become apparent. Similarly, when considering, ‘In the hair of the head, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness… and so on … in the in-breaths and out-breaths, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness,’ the initial impact is contact. The feeling associated with it is the feeling aggregate… and so on … consciousness is the consciousness aggregate—thus they become apparent. In this way, immaterial phenomena become apparent by way of contact.

Ekassa “pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”ti tadārammaṇarasānubhavanakavedanā vedanākkhandho, taṃsampayuttā saññā saññākkhandho, taṃsampayutto phasso [M 2.0227] ca cetanā ca saṅkhārakkhandho, taṃsampayuttaṃ cittaṃ viññāṇakkhandhoti upaṭṭhāti. Tathā “kese pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā [V 2.0225] …pe… assāsapassāse pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”ti tadārammaṇarasānubhavanakavedanā vedanākkhandho…pe… taṃsampayuttaṃ cittaṃ viññāṇakkhandhoti upaṭṭhāti. Evaṃ vedanāvasena arūpadhammā upaṭṭhahanti.

For another, when considering, ‘The earth element has the characteristic of hardness,’ the feeling that experiences the flavor of that object is the feeling aggregate; the perception associated with it is the perception aggregate; the contact and volition associated with it are the formations aggregate; and the consciousness associated with it is the consciousness aggregate—thus they become apparent. Similarly, when considering, ‘In the hair of the head, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness… and so on … in the in-breaths and out-breaths, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness,’ the feeling that experiences the flavor of that object is the feeling aggregate… and so on … the consciousness associated with it is the consciousness aggregate—thus they become apparent. In this way, immaterial phenomena become apparent by way of feeling.

Aparassa “pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”ti ārammaṇapaṭivijānanaṃ viññāṇaṃ viññāṇakkhandho, taṃsampayuttā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, phasso ca cetanā ca saṅkhārakkhandhoti upaṭṭhāti. Tathā “kese pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā…pe… assāsapassāse pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”ti ārammaṇapaṭivijānanaṃ viññāṇaṃ viññāṇakkhandho, taṃsampayuttā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, phasso ca cetanā ca saṅkhārakkhandhoti upaṭṭhāti. Evaṃ viññāṇavasena arūpadhammā upaṭṭhahanti.

For yet another, when considering, ‘The earth element has the characteristic of hardness,’ the consciousness that cognizes the object is the consciousness aggregate; the feeling associated with it is the feeling aggregate; perception is the perception aggregate; and contact and volition are the formations aggregate—thus they become apparent. Similarly, when considering, ‘In the hair of the head, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness… and so on … in the in-breaths and out-breaths, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness,’ the consciousness that cognizes the object is the consciousness aggregate; the feeling associated with it is the feeling aggregate; perception is the perception aggregate; and contact and volition are the formations aggregate—thus they become apparent. In this way, immaterial phenomena become apparent by way of consciousness.

Eteneva upāyena “kammasamuṭṭhāne kese pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā”tiādinā nayena dvācattālīsāya dhātukoṭṭhāsesu catunnaṃ catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ vasena, sesesu ca cakkhudhātuādīsu rūpapariggahamukhesu sabbaṃ nayabhedaṃ anugantvā yojanā kātabbā.

By this same method, the application should be made by following every variation of the method in regard to the forty-two bodily parts by way of the four elements in each, beginning with the method, ‘In kamma-born hair of the head, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness’; and also in regard to the remaining gateways for grasping materiality, such as the eye-element and so on.

671. Yasmā ca evaṃ suvisuddharūpapariggahasseva tassa arūpadhammā tīhākārehi pākaṭā honti. Tasmā suvisuddharūpapariggaheneva arūpapariggahāya yogo kātabbo, na itarena. Sace hi ekasmiṃ vā rūpadhamme upaṭṭhite dvīsu vā rūpaṃ pahāya arūpapariggahaṃ ārabhati kammaṭṭhānato parihāyati, pathavīkasiṇabhāvanāya vuttappakārā pabbateyyā gāvī viya. Suvisuddharūpapariggahassa pana arūpapariggahāya yogaṃ karoto kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ pāpuṇāti.

671. And since it is for one who has thus grasped materiality with thorough purity that immaterial phenomena become manifest in these three ways, therefore one should undertake the effort to grasp the immaterial only after having grasped materiality with thorough purity, not otherwise. For if, while one or two material phenomena are still apparent, one abandons materiality and begins to grasp the immaterial, one falls away from the meditation subject, like the mountain cow of the kind told in connection with the development of the earth kasiṇa. But for one who undertakes the effort to grasp the immaterial after having grasped materiality with thorough purity, the meditation subject attains growth, development, and abundance.

So evaṃ phassādīnaṃ vasena upaṭṭhite cattāro arūpino khandhe nāmanti, tesaṃ ārammaṇabhūtāni cattāri mahābhūtāni, catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpaṃ rūpanti vavatthapeti. Iti aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo dvādasāyatanāni pañcakkhandhāti sabbepi tebhūmake dhamme khaggena samuggaṃ vivaramāno [M 2.0228] viya yamakatālakandaṃ phālayamāno viya ca nāmañca rūpañcāti dvedhā vavatthapeti. Nāmarūpamattato uddhaṃ añño satto vā puggalo vā devo vā brahmā vā natthīti niṭṭhaṃ gacchati.

He thus determines the four immaterial aggregates, which have become apparent by way of contact and so on, as ‘mentality’; and he determines the four great elements that are their object, along with the derived materiality dependent on the four great elements, as ‘materiality.’ Thus, like one opening a casket with a sword or splitting a twin palm shoot, he divides all these phenomena of the three planes—the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates—into two parts as ‘mentality and materiality.’ He comes to the conclusion: ‘Beyond mere mentality-and-materiality, there is no other being or person, no deva or brahmā.’

Sambahulasuttantasaṃsandanā

Correlation with Many Suttas

672. So [V 2.0226] evaṃ yāthāvasarasato nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā suṭṭhutaraṃ “satto puggalo”ti imissā lokasamaññāya pahānatthāya sattasammohassa samatikkamatthāya asammohabhūmiyaṃ cittaṃ ṭhapanatthāya sambahulasuttantavasena “nāmarūpamattamevidaṃ, na satto, na puggalo atthī”ti etamatthaṃ saṃsandetvā vavatthapeti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

672. Having thus determined mentality-and-materiality according to its true nature, in order to more thoroughly abandon the worldly convention ‘a being,’ ‘a person,’ in order to overcome the delusion about a being, and in order to establish the mind in the domain of non-delusion, he correlates this meaning with many suttas and determines it thus: ‘This is merely mentality-and-materiality; there is no being, no person.’ For it is said:

“Yathāpi aṅgasambhārā, hoti saddo ratho iti;

Evaṃ khandhesu santesu, hoti sattoti sammutī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.171);

“Just as with an assemblage of parts,

The word ‘chariot’ is used;

So, when the aggregates are present,

There is the convention ‘a being.’”

Aparampi vuttaṃ, “seyyathāpi, āvuso, kaṭṭhañca paṭicca valliñca paṭicca mattikañca paṭicca tiṇañca paṭicca ākāso parivārito agārantveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati, evameva kho, āvuso, aṭṭhiñca paṭicca nhāruñca paṭicca maṃsañca paṭicca cammañca paṭicca ākāso parivārito rūpantveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.306).

And again it is said: ‘Friends, just as, dependent on timber, creepers, clay, and grass, a space is enclosed and it comes to be reckoned as a “house,” so too, dependent on bones, sinews, flesh, and skin, a space is enclosed and it comes to be reckoned as “material form.”’

Aparampi vuttaṃ –

And again it is said:

“Dukkhameva hi sambhoti, dukkhaṃ tiṭṭhati veti ca;

Nāññatra dukkhā sambhoti, nāññaṃ dukkhā nirujjhatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.171);

“It is only suffering that comes to be,

Suffering that persists and passes away.

Nothing other than suffering comes to be,

Nothing other than suffering ceases.”

Upamāhi nāmarūpavibhāvanā

Elucidating Mentality-and-Materiality with Similes

673. Evaṃ anekasatehi suttantehi nāmarūpameva dīpitaṃ, na satto na puggalo. Tasmā yathā akkhacakkapañjaraīsādīsu aṅgasambhāresu ekenākārena saṇṭhitesu rathoti vohāramattaṃ hoti, paramatthato ekekasmiṃ aṅge upaparikkhiyamāne ratho nāma natthi. Yathā ca kaṭṭhādīsu gehasambhāresu ekenākārena ākāsaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitesu gehanti vohāramattaṃ hoti, paramatthato gehaṃ nāma natthi. Yathā ca aṅguliaṅguṭṭhādīsu ekenākārena ṭhitesu muṭṭhīti vohāramattaṃ [V 2.0227] hoti. Doṇitantiādīsu vīṇāti. Hatthiassādīsu senāti. Pākāragehagopurādīsu [M 2.0229] nagaranti. Khandhasākhāpalāsādīsu ekenākārena ṭhitesu rukkhoti vohāramattaṃ hoti, paramatthato ekekasmiṃ avayave upaparikkhiyamāne rukkho nāma natthi. Evamevaṃ pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu sati “satto, puggalo”ti vohāramattaṃ hoti, paramatthato ekekasmiṃ dhamme upaparikkhiyamāne “asmīti vā ahanti vā”ti gāhassa vatthubhūto satto nāma natthi. Paramatthato pana nāmarūpamattameva atthīti. Evaṃ passato hi dassanaṃ yathābhūtadassanaṃ nāma hoti.

673. Thus, in many hundreds of suttas, only name-and-form is illuminated, not a being or a person. Therefore, just as when the component parts of a chariot—such as the axle, wheels, frame, and pole—are assembled in a certain way, the mere designation 'chariot' arises, but in the ultimate sense, when each part is examined, there is no chariot to be found. And just as when the materials of a house—such as wood and so on—are arranged in a certain way to enclose space, the mere designation 'house' arises, but in the ultimate sense, there is no house. And just as when the fingers and thumb are brought together in a certain way, the mere designation 'fist' arises; with the soundbox, strings, and so on, 'lute'; with elephants, horses, and so on, 'army'; with walls, houses, and gate-towers, 'city'; with the trunk, branches, and leaves arranged in a certain way, the mere designation 'tree' arises, but in the ultimate sense, when each component is examined, there is no tree. In the same way, when the five aggregates subject to clinging are present, the mere designation 'being' or 'person' arises, but in the ultimate sense, when each phenomenon is examined, there is no being to be found as a basis for the grasping 'I am' or 'I.' In the ultimate sense, there is only name-and-form. For one who sees thus, that vision is called 'seeing things as they truly are.'

674. Yo panetaṃ yathābhūtadassanaṃ pahāya “satto atthī”ti gaṇhāti. So tassa vināsaṃ anujāneyya avināsaṃ vā. Avināsaṃ anujānanto sassate patati. Vināsaṃ anujānanto ucchede patati. Kasmā? Khīranvayassa dadhino viya tadanvayassa aññassa abhāvato. So “sassato satto”ti gaṇhanto olīyati nāma. “Ucchijjatī”ti gaṇhanto atidhāvati nāma. Tenāha bhagavā –

674. But whoever, having abandoned this vision of things as they truly are, grasps the view, 'A being exists,' must allow for either its destruction or its non-destruction. By allowing for its non-destruction, he falls into eternalism. By allowing for its destruction, he falls into annihilationism. Why? Because of the absence of anything else that follows from it in the way that curd follows from milk. One who grasps, 'The being is eternal,' is one who holds back. One who grasps, 'It is annihilated,' is one who overshoots. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Dvīhi, bhikkhave, diṭṭhigatehi pariyuṭṭhitā devamanussā olīyanti eke, atidhāvanti eke, cakkhumanto ca passanti.

"Bhikkhus, beset by two kinds of views, gods and humans are such that some hold back and some overshoot; but those with vision see."

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, olīyanti eke? Bhavārāmā, bhikkhave, devamanussā bhavaratā bhavasamuditā. Tesaṃ bhavanirodhāya dhamme desiyamāne cittaṃ na pakkhandati nappasīdati na santiṭṭhati nādhimuccati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, olīyanti eke.

"And how, bhikkhus, do some hold back? Bhikkhus, gods and humans delight in existence, are fond of existence, rejoice in existence. When the Dhamma is taught to them for the cessation of existence, their mind does not enter into it, does not gain confidence in it, does not settle upon it, and is not resolved upon it. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that some hold back."

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, atidhāvanti eke? Bhaveneva kho paneke aṭṭīyamānā harāyamānā jigucchamānā vibhavaṃ abhinandanti, yato kira bho ayaṃ attā kāyassa bhedā ucchijjati vinassati, na hoti paraṃmaraṇā, etaṃ santaṃ, etaṃ paṇītaṃ, etaṃ yāthāvanti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, atidhāvanti eke.

"And how, bhikkhus, do some overshoot? Some, being afflicted, humiliated, and disgusted by that very existence, delight in non-existence, thinking: 'Sirs, since this self is annihilated and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, this is peaceful, this is sublime, this is the truth!' It is in this way, bhikkhus, that some overshoot."

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, cakkhumanto passanti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhūtaṃ bhūtato [V 2.0228] passati, bhūtaṃ bhūtato disvā bhūtassa nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, cakkhumanto passantī”ti (itivu. 49).

"And how, bhikkhus, do those with vision see? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees what has come to be as what has come to be. Having seen what has come to be as what has come to be, he is practicing for disenchantment with, for dispassion toward, and for the cessation of what has come to be. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that those with vision see." (Itivuttaka 49)

675. Tasmā [M 2.0230] yathā dāruyantaṃ suññaṃ nijjīvaṃ nirīhakaṃ, atha ca pana dārurajjukasamāyogavasena gacchatipi tiṭṭhatipi. Saīhakaṃ sabyāpāraṃ viya khāyati, evamidaṃ nāmarūpampi suññaṃ nijjīvaṃ nirīhakaṃ, atha ca pana aññamaññasamāyogavasena gacchatipi tiṭṭhatipi. Saīhakaṃ sabyāpāraṃ viya khāyatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāhu porāṇā –

675. Therefore, just as a wooden automaton is empty, lifeless, and inert, yet by means of the connection of wood and strings it moves and stands and appears as if it has volition and is active, so too this name-and-form is empty, lifeless, and inert, yet by means of their mutual connection it moves and stands and appears as if it has volition and is active. Thus it should be understood. Therefore the ancients have said:

“Nāmañca rūpañca idhatthi saccato,

Na hettha satto manujo ca vijjati;

Suññaṃ idaṃ yantamivābhisaṅkhataṃ,

Dukkhassa puñjo tiṇakaṭṭhasādiso”ti.

"Here there truly are but name and form, / No being is found herein, no person; / This is void, constructed like an automaton, / A mass of suffering, like grass and sticks."

Na kevalañcetaṃ dāruyantupamāya, aññāhipi naḷakalāpīādīhi upamāhi vibhāvetabbaṃ – yathā hi dvīsu naḷakalāpīsu aññamaññaṃ nissāya ṭhapitāsu ekā ekissā upatthambho hoti, ekissā patamānāya itarāpi patati, evamevaṃ pañcavokārabhave nāmarūpaṃ aññamaññaṃ nissāya pavattati, ekaṃ ekassa upatthambho hoti. Maraṇavasena ekasmiṃ patamāne itarampi patati. Tenāhu porāṇā –

This should be elucidated not only by the simile of the wooden automaton but also by other similes such as that of the sheaves of reeds. For just as two sheaves of reeds stand by leaning against one another, so that one is the support for the other, and if one falls the other falls too; so too, in the five-constituent existence, name-and-form proceed in dependence on each other, one being a support for the other. When one falls by way of death, the other falls too. Therefore the ancients have said:

“Yamakaṃ nāmarūpañca, ubho aññoññanissitā;

Ekasmiṃ bhijjamānasmiṃ, ubho bhijjanti paccayā”ti.

"Name-and-form are a pair, both mutually dependent. When one is broken, both conditions break."

676. Yathā ca daṇḍābhihataṃ bheriṃ nissāya sadde pavattamāne aññā bherī, añño saddo, bherisaddā asammissā, bherī saddena suññā, saddo bheriyā suñño, evamevaṃ vatthudvārārammaṇasaṅkhātaṃ rūpaṃ nissāya nāme pavattamāne aññaṃ rūpaṃ, aññaṃ nāmaṃ, nāmarūpā asammissā, nāmaṃ rūpena suññaṃ, rūpaṃ nāmena suññaṃ, apica kho bheriṃ paṭicca saddo viya rūpaṃ paṭicca nāmaṃ pavattati. Tenāhu porāṇā –

676. And just as when a drum is struck with a stick, sound occurs in dependence on it, the drum is one thing and the sound another; the drum and sound are unmixed; the drum is void of sound, and the sound is void of the drum. So too, when name occurs in dependence on form—that is, the physical basis, door, and object—form is one thing and name another; name and form are unmixed; name is void of form, and form is void of name. And yet, just as sound occurs in dependence on a drum, so name occurs in dependence on form. Therefore the ancients have said:

“Na [V 2.0229] cakkhuto jāyare phassapañcamā,

Na rūpato no ca ubhinnamantarā;

Hetuṃ paṭiccappabhavanti saṅkhatā,

Yathāpi saddo pahaṭāya bheriyā.

"The mental states with contact as the fifth do not arise from the eye, nor from forms, nor from between the two. Formations arise in dependence on a cause, just as sound arises from a beaten drum."

“Na [M 2.0231] sotato jāyare phassapañcamā,

Na saddato no ca ubhinnamantarā…pe….

"The mental states with contact as the fifth do not arise from the ear, nor from sounds, nor from between the two…"

“Na ghānato jāyare phassapañcamā,

Na gandhato no ca ubhinnamantarā…pe….

"The mental states with contact as the fifth do not arise from the nose, nor from odors, nor from between the two…"

“Na jivhāto jāyare phassapañcamā,

Na rasato no ca ubhinnamantarā…pe….

"The mental states with contact as the fifth do not arise from the tongue, nor from tastes, nor from between the two…"

“Na kāyato jāyare phassapañcamā,

Na phassato no ca ubhinnamantarā…pe….

"The mental states with contact as the fifth do not arise from the body, nor from tangibles, nor from between the two…"

“Na vatthurūpā pabhavanti saṅkhatā,

Na cāpi dhammāyatanehi niggatā;

Hetuṃ paṭiccappabhavanti saṅkhatā,

Yathāpi saddo pahaṭāya bheriyā”ti.

"Formations do not arise from the physical basis, nor do they issue from the mind-object base. Formations arise in dependence on a cause, just as sound arises from a beaten drum."

677. Apicettha nāmaṃ nittejaṃ na sakena tejena pavattituṃ sakkoti, na khādati, na pivati, na byāharati, na iriyāpathaṃ kappeti. Rūpampi nittejaṃ na sakena tejena pavattituṃ sakkoti. Na hi tassā khāditukāmatā, nāpi pivitukāmatā, na byāharitukāmatā, na iriyāpathaṃ kappetukāmatā, atha kho nāmaṃ nissāya rūpaṃ pavattati, rūpaṃ nissāya nāmaṃ pavattati, nāmassa khāditukāmatāya pivitukāmatāya byāharitukāmatāya iriyāpathaṃ kappetukāmatāya sati rūpaṃ khādati, pivati, byāharati, iriyāpathaṃ kappeti.

677. Furthermore, in this context, name is powerless; it cannot proceed by its own power. It does not eat, or drink, or speak, or adopt a posture. Form, too, is powerless; it cannot proceed by its own power. For it has no desire to eat, or drink, or speak, or adopt a posture. But rather, form proceeds in dependence on name, and name proceeds in dependence on form. When there is in name the desire to eat, or drink, or speak, or adopt a posture, then form eats, drinks, speaks, and adopts a posture.

Imassa [V 2.0230] panatthassa vibhāvanatthāya imaṃ upamaṃ udāharanti – yathā jaccandho ca pīṭhasappī ca disāpakkamitukāmā assu, jaccandho pīṭhasappiṃ evamāha “ahaṃ kho bhaṇe, sakkomi pādehi pādakaraṇīyaṃ kātuṃ, natthi ca me cakkhūni yehi samavisamaṃ passeyya”nti. Pīṭhasappīpi jaccandhaṃ evamāha “ahaṃ kho bhaṇe, sakkomi cakkhunā cakkhukaraṇīyaṃ kātuṃ, natthi ca me pādāni yehi abhikkameyyaṃ vā paṭikkameyyaṃ vā”ti. So tuṭṭhahaṭṭho jaccandho pīṭhasappiṃ aṃsakūṭaṃ āropesi. Pīṭhasappī jaccandhassa aṃsakūṭe nisīditvā evamāha “vāmaṃ muñca dakkhiṇaṃ gaṇha, dakkhiṇaṃ muñca vāmaṃ gaṇhā”ti. Tattha jaccandhopi nittejo [M 2.0232] dubbalo na sakena tejena sakena balena gacchati, pīṭhasappīpi nittejo dubbalo na sakena tejena sakena balena gacchati, na ca tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ nissāya gamanaṃ nappavattati, evamevaṃ nāmampi nittejaṃ na sakena tejena uppajjati, na tāsu tāsu kiriyāsu pavattati. Rūpampi nittejaṃ na sakena tejena uppajjati, na tāsu tāsu kiriyāsu pavattati, na ca tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ nissāya uppatti vā pavatti vā na hoti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

To elucidate this meaning, they cite the following simile. Suppose a man born blind and a cripple wanted to go on a journey. The man born blind said to the cripple: 'Friend, I can do with my feet what needs to be done by feet, but I have no eyes with which to see the even and uneven ground.' The cripple, too, said to the man born blind: 'Friend, I can do with my eyes what needs to be done by eyes, but I have no feet with which to go forward or back.' The man born blind, glad and delighted, mounted the cripple on his shoulders. And the cripple, sitting on the shoulders of the man born blind, directed him, saying: 'Leave the left and take the right; leave the right and take the left.' Here, the man born blind is powerless and weak; he cannot go by his own power and strength. The cripple, too, is powerless and weak; he cannot go by his own power and strength. Yet it is not the case that their journey does not proceed when they are dependent on each other. In the same way, name is powerless; it cannot arise by its own power, nor can it proceed in this or that activity. Form, too, is powerless; it cannot arise by its own power, nor can it proceed in this or that activity. Yet it is not the case that their arising or proceeding does not happen when they are dependent on each other. Therefore it is said:

“Na sakena balena jāyare,

Nopi sakena balena tiṭṭhare;

Paradhammavasānuvattino,

Jāyare saṅkhatā attadubbalā.

"Not by their own strength are they born,

Nor by their own strength do they endure;

Subject to the power of other states,

Formations, weak in themselves, are born.

“Parapaccayato ca jāyare,

Paraārammaṇato samuṭṭhitā;

Ārammaṇapaccayehi ca,

Paradhammehi cime pabhāvitā.

"From other conditions are they born,

From other objects they arise;

By object-conditions and by other states

Are these things brought into being.

“Yathāpi nāvaṃ nissāya, manussā yanti aṇṇave;

Evameva rūpaṃ nissāya, nāmakāyo pavattati.

"Just as people travel on the ocean depending on a boat,

So too, the mental body proceeds depending on form.

“Yathā ca manusse nissāya, nāvā gacchati aṇṇave;

Evameva nāmaṃ nissāya, rūpakāyo pavattati.

"And just as a boat travels on the ocean depending on people,

So too, the material body proceeds depending on name.

“Ubho [V 2.0231] nissāya gacchanti, manussā nāvā ca aṇṇave;

Evaṃ nāmañca rūpañca, ubho aññoññanissitā”ti.

"Both travel in dependence, people and a boat upon the ocean;

So too name and form are both mutually dependent."

Evaṃ nānānayehi nāmarūpaṃ vavatthāpayato sattasaññaṃ abhibhavitvā asammohabhūmiyaṃ ṭhitaṃ nāmarūpānaṃ yāthāvadassanaṃ diṭṭhivisuddhīti veditabbaṃ. Nāmarūpavavatthānantipi saṅkhāraparicchedotipi etasseva adhivacanaṃ.

Thus, the seeing of name-and-form as it really is—by one who defines it in these various ways, has overcome the perception of a being, and is established in the domain of non-delusion—should be known as the purification of view. 'Definition of name-and-form' and 'delimitation of formations' are also designations for this very thing.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, composed for the gladdening of good people,

Paññābhāvanādhikāre

In the Section on the Development of Wisdom,

Diṭṭhivisuddhiniddeso nāma

The Exposition of the Purification of View,

Aṭṭhārasamo paricchedo.

Is the Eighteenth Chapter.

19. Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiniddeso

19. Exposition of the Purification by Overcoming Doubt

Paccayapariggahakathā

The Discourse on the Comprehension of Conditions

678. Etasseva [M 2.0233][V 2.0232] pana nāmarūpassa paccayapariggahaṇena tīsu addhāsu kaṅkhaṃ vitaritvā ṭhitaṃ ñāṇaṃ kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi nāma.

678. The knowledge that is established by having overcome doubt about the three periods of time through the comprehension of the conditions for this very name-and-form is called the purification by overcoming doubt.

Taṃ sampādetukāmo bhikkhu yathā nāma kusalo bhisakko rogaṃ disvā tassa samuṭṭhānaṃ pariyesati. Yathā vā pana anukampako puriso daharaṃ kumāraṃ mandaṃ uttānaseyyakaṃ rathikāya nipannaṃ disvā “kassa nu kho ayaṃ puttako”ti tassa mātāpitaro āvajjati, evameva tassa nāmarūpassa hetupaccayapariyesanaṃ āpajjati.

A bhikkhu who wishes to accomplish this undertakes the investigation of the causes and conditions of that name-and-form, just as a skilled physician, upon seeing a disease, seeks its origin; or just as a compassionate man who, upon seeing a tender, helpless infant lying on its back in the street, wonders, "Whose child is this?" and considers its parents.

So āditova iti paṭisañcikkhati “na tāvidhaṃ nāmarūpaṃ ahetukaṃ, sabbattha sabbadā sabbesañca ekasadisabhāvāpattito, na issarādihetukaṃ, nāmarūpato uddhaṃ issarādīnaṃ abhāvato. Yepi nāmarūpamattameva issarādayoti vadanti, tesaṃ issarādisaṅkhātanāmarūpassa ahetukabhāvappattito. Tasmā bhavitabbamassa hetupaccayehi, ke nu kho te”ti.

From the very beginning, he reflects thus: "This name-and-form is not without a cause, for that would entail that it would have a single, uniform nature everywhere, at all times, and for all beings. Nor is it caused by a creator god (Issara), etc., for there are no such creators apart from name-and-form. And for those who say that a creator, etc., is nothing but name-and-form, it would follow that the name-and-form designated as 'creator' is itself without a cause. Therefore, it must have causes and conditions. Now, what are they?"

679. So evaṃ nāmarūpassa hetupaccaye āvajjetvā imassa tāva rūpakāyassa evaṃ hetupaccaye pariggaṇhāti – “ayaṃ kāyo nibbattamāno neva uppalapadumapuṇḍarīkasogandhikādīnaṃ abbhantare nibbattati, na maṇimuttāhārādīnaṃ, atha kho āmāsayapakkāsayānaṃ antare udarapaṭalaṃ pacchato piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ purato katvā antaantaguṇaparivārito sayampi duggandhajegucchapaṭikkūlo duggandhajegucchapaṭikkūle paramasambādhe okāse pūtimacchapūtikummāsaoḷigallacandanikādīsu kimiva nibbattati. Tassevaṃ nibbattamānassa ‘avijjā taṇhā upādānaṃ kamma’nti ime cattāro dhammā nibbattakattā hetu, āhāro upatthambhakattā paccayoti pañca [V 2.0233] dhammā hetupaccayā honti. Tesupi avijjādayo tayo imassa kāyassa mātā viya dārakassa upanissayā honti. Kammaṃ pitā viya puttassa janakaṃ[M 2.0234]. Āhāro dhāti viya dārakassa sandhārako”ti. Evaṃ rūpakāyassa paccayapariggahaṃ katvā, puna “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.43) nayena nāmakāyassa paccayapariggahaṃ karoti.

679. Having thus adverted to the causes and conditions of name-and-form, he first comprehends the causes and conditions of this material body as follows: 'This body, when it is produced, is not produced inside a blue lotus, red lotus, white lotus, water lily, or the like, nor inside jewels, pearls, necklaces, or the like. Rather, it is produced between the stomach and the intestines, with the belly-lining behind and the backbone in front, surrounded by the entrails and mesentery, itself foul-smelling, disgusting, and repulsive, in an extremely confined, foul-smelling, disgusting, and repulsive place, like a worm in rotting fish, in putrid gruel, in a cesspool, or in a sewer. When it is thus produced, these four things—ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma—are its causes because they are its producers, while nutriment is its condition because it is its supporter. Thus, these five things are its causes and conditions. Among them, the three beginning with ignorance are the support for this body, like a mother is for her child. Kamma is the generator, like a father is for his son. Nutriment is the sustainer, like a wet-nurse is for the infant.' Having thus comprehended the conditions of the material body, he then comprehends the conditions of the mental body by the method beginning: 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises' (SN 12.43).

So evaṃ paccayato nāmarūpassa pavattiṃ disvā yathā idaṃ etarahi, evaṃ atītepi addhāne paccayato pavattittha, anāgatepi paccayato pavattissatīti samanupassati.

Having thus seen the occurrence of name-and-form from conditions, he understands that just as it occurs now from conditions, so too in the past it occurred from conditions, and in the future it will occur from conditions.

680. Tassevaṃ samanupassato yā sā pubbantaṃ ārabbha “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhānaṃ, na nu kho ahosiṃ atītamaddhānaṃ, kiṃ nu kho ahosiṃ atītamaddhānaṃ, kathaṃ nu kho ahosiṃ atītamaddhānaṃ, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) pañcavidhā vicikicchā vuttā, yāpi aparantaṃ ārabbha “bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, na nu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṃ, kiṃ nu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṃ, kathaṃ nu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṃ, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhāna”nti pañcavidhā vicikicchā vuttā, yāpi paccuppannaṃ ārabbha “etarahi vā pana paccuppannaṃ addhānaṃ ajjhattaṃ kathaṃkathī hoti – ahaṃ nu khosmi, no nu khosmi, kiṃ nu khosmi, kathaṃ nu khosmi, ayaṃ nu kho satto kuto āgato, so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.18) chabbidhā vicikicchā vuttā, sā sabbāpi pahīyati.

680. For one who understands in this way, the five kinds of doubt concerning the past, spoken of thus: 'Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past?' (MN 2); and the five kinds of doubt concerning the future, spoken of thus: 'Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I become in the future?'; and also the six kinds of doubt concerning the present, spoken of thus: 'Now, in the present time, he is inwardly perplexed: “Do I exist? Do I not exist? What am I? How am I? From where has this being come? Where will it go?”' (MN 2)—all this doubt is abandoned.

681. Aparo sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇavasena duvidhaṃ nāmassa paccayaṃ passati, kammādivasena catubbidhaṃ rūpassa. Duvidho hi nāmassa paccayo sādhāraṇo asādhāraṇo ca. Tattha cakkhādīni cha dvārāni, rūpādīni cha ārammaṇāni nāmassa sādhāraṇo paccayo, kusalādibhedato sabbappakārassāpi tato pavattito. Manasikārādiko asādhāraṇo. Yoniso manasikārasaddhammassavanādiko hi kusalasseva hoti, viparīto akusalassa, kammādiko vipākassa, bhavaṅgādiko kiriyassāti.

681. Another sees the condition for name as twofold, by way of common and uncommon, and for form as fourfold, by way of kamma, etc. For the condition for name is twofold: common and uncommon. Herein, the six doors beginning with the eye and the six objects beginning with forms are the common condition for name, since all kinds of it, distinguished as wholesome, etc., occur from them. Attention and so on is the uncommon condition. For wise attention, hearing the good Dhamma, and so on, are conditions only for the wholesome; the opposite for the unwholesome; kamma, etc., for the resultant; the life-continuum, etc., for the functional.

Rūpassa [V 2.0234] pana kammaṃ cittaṃ utu āhāroti ayaṃ kammādiko catubbidho paccayo. Tattha kammaṃ atītameva kammasamuṭṭhānassa rūpassa paccayo hoti[M 2.0235]. Cittaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānassa uppajjamānaṃ. Utuāhārā utuāhārasamuṭṭhānassa ṭhitikkhaṇe paccayā hontīti. Evameveko nāmarūpassa paccayapariggahaṃ karoti.

For form, the condition is fourfold: kamma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment. Herein, only past kamma is the condition for kamma-originated form. Consciousness, when arising, is the condition for consciousness-originated form. Temperature and nutriment are conditions for temperature-originated and nutriment-originated form at the moment of presence. In this way a certain one comprehends the conditions for name-and-form.

So evaṃ paccayato nāmarūpassa pavattiṃ disvā yathā idaṃ etarahi, evaṃ atītepi addhāne paccayato pavattittha, anāgatepi paccayato pavattissatīti samanupassati. Tassevaṃ samanupassato vuttanayeneva tīsupi addhāsu vicikicchā pahīyati.

Having thus seen the occurrence of name-and-form from conditions, he understands that just as it occurs now from conditions, so too in the past it occurred from conditions, and in the future it will occur from conditions. For one who understands thus, doubt concerning the three periods of time is abandoned in the way described.

682. Aparo tesaṃyeva nāmarūpasaṅkhātānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ jarāpattiṃ jiṇṇānañca bhaṅgaṃ disvā idaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ nāma jātiyā sati hoti, jāti bhave sati, bhavo upādāne sati, upādānaṃ taṇhāya sati, taṇhā vedanāya sati, vedanā phasse sati, phasso saḷāyatane sati, saḷāyatanaṃ nāmarūpe sati, nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇe sati, viññāṇaṃ saṅkhāresu sati, saṅkhārā avijjāya satīti evaṃ paṭilomapaṭiccasamuppādavasena nāmarūpassa paccayapariggahaṃ karoti. Athassa vuttanayeneva vicikicchā pahīyati.

682. Another, seeing the aging of those very formations reckoned as name-and-form, and the breaking up of the aged, comprehends the conditions for name-and-form by way of dependent origination in reverse order: 'This aging and death of formations occurs when there is birth; birth when there is becoming; becoming when there is clinging; clinging when there is craving; craving when there is feeling; feeling when there is contact; contact when there is the sixfold sense base; the sixfold sense base when there is name-and-form; name-and-form when there is consciousness; consciousness when there are formations; formations when there is ignorance.' Then his doubt is abandoned in the manner described.

683. Aparo “iti kho avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.2) pubbe vitthāretvā dassitaanulomapaṭiccasamuppādavaseneva nāmarūpassa paccayapariggahaṃ karoti. Athassa vuttanayeneva kaṅkhā pahīyati.

683. Another comprehends the conditions for name-and-form by way of dependent origination in forward order, as shown in detail before, beginning: 'Thus, with ignorance as condition, formations come to be' (SN 12.2). Then his doubt is abandoned in the manner described.

684. Aparo “purimakammabhavasmiṃ moho avijjā, āyūhanā saṅkhārā, nikanti taṇhā, upagamanaṃ upādānaṃ, cetanā bhavoti ime pañca dhammā purimakammabhavasmiṃ idha paṭisandhiyā paccayā, idha paṭisandhi viññāṇaṃ, okkanti nāmarūpaṃ, pasādo āyatanaṃ, phuṭṭho phasso, vedayitaṃ vedanāti ime pañca dhammā idhūpapattibhavasmiṃ purekatassa kammassa paccayā. Idha paripakkattā āyatanānaṃ moho avijjā…pe… cetanā bhavoti ime pañca dhammā idha kammabhavasmiṃ āyatiṃ paṭisandhiyā paccayā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.47) evaṃ kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭavasena nāmarūpassa paccayapariggahaṃ karoti.

684. Another comprehends the conditions for name-and-form by way of the round of kamma and the round of results, as follows: "In a previous kamma-existence, delusion was ignorance; accumulation was volitional formations; delight was craving; approaching was clinging; and volition was becoming. These five things in a previous kamma-existence were the conditions for rebirth-linking here. Here, in this resultant-existence, rebirth-linking is consciousness; descent is name-and-form; sensitivity is the sense base; the touched is contact; the felt is feeling. These five things are the result here of kamma done previously. Here, due to the maturing of the sense bases, delusion is ignorance… volition is becoming. These five things in this kamma-existence here are the conditions for future rebirth-linking" (Paṭis I 47).

685. Tattha [V 2.0235] catubbidhaṃ kammaṃ – diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ, upapajjavedanīyaṃ, aparāpariyavedanīyaṃ, ahosikammanti. Tesu ekajavanavīthiyaṃ sattasu cittesu kusalā [M 2.0236] vā akusalā vā paṭhamajavanacetanā diṭṭhidhammavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Taṃ imasmiññeva attabhāve vipākaṃ deti. Tathā asakkontaṃ pana “ahosikammaṃ nāhosi kammavipāko, na bhavissati kammavipāko, natthi kammavipāko”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.234) imassa tikassa vasena ahosikammaṃ nāma hoti. Atthasādhikā pana sattamajavanacetanā upapajjavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Taṃ anantare attabhāve vipākaṃ deti. Tathā asakkontaṃ vuttanayeneva ahosikammaṃ nāma hoti. Ubhinnaṃ antare pañca javanacetanā aparāpariyavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Taṃ anāgate yadā okāsaṃ labhati, tadā vipākaṃ deti. Sati saṃsārappavattiyā ahosikammaṃ nāma na hoti.

685. Herein, kamma is fourfold: immediately effective kamma, subsequently effective kamma, indefinitely effective kamma, and defunct kamma. Among these, the volition of the first impulsion in a single cognitive series of seven cittas, whether wholesome or unwholesome, is called immediately effective kamma. It yields its result in this very existence. If it is unable to do so, it becomes defunct kamma, in the sense of the triad: 'There was kamma, but there was no kamma-result, there will be no kamma-result, and there is no kamma-result.' The volition of the seventh impulsion that accomplishes its purpose is called subsequently effective kamma. It yields its result in the immediately following existence. If it is unable to do so, it becomes defunct kamma in the way just stated. The volitions of the five intermediate impulsions are called indefinitely effective kamma. They yield their result in the future whenever an opportunity arises. As long as the round of existence continues, this kamma does not become defunct.

686. Aparampi catubbidhaṃ kammaṃ – yaṃ garukaṃ, yaṃ bahulaṃ, yadāsannaṃ, kaṭattā vā pana kammanti. Tattha kusalaṃ vā hotu akusalaṃ vā, garukāgarukesu yaṃ garukaṃ mātughātādikammaṃ vā mahaggatakammaṃ vā, tadeva paṭhamaṃ vipaccati. Tathā bahulābahulesupi yaṃ bahulaṃ hoti susīlyaṃ vā dussīlyaṃ vā, tadeva paṭhamaṃ vipaccati. Yadāsannaṃ nāma maraṇakāle anussaritakammaṃ. Yañhi āsannamaraṇo anussarituṃ sakkoti, teneva upapajjati. Etehi pana tīhi muttaṃ punappunaṃ laddhāsevanaṃ kaṭattā vā pana kammaṃ nāma hoti, tesaṃ abhāve taṃ paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhati.

686. There is another fourfold classification of kamma: weighty kamma, habitual kamma, proximate kamma, and reserve kamma. Herein, whether wholesome or unwholesome, among weighty and non-weighty kammas, that which is weighty—such as matricide or a sublime kamma pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres—ripens first. Similarly, among habitual and non-habitual kammas, that which is habitual—whether virtuous or unvirtuous conduct—ripens first. Proximate kamma is that which is recollected at the time of death. For one is reborn by whatever kamma one who is near death is able to recollect. Apart from these three, kamma that has been repeatedly practiced is called reserve kamma. In the absence of the former three, it is this kamma that brings about rebirth-linking.

687. Aparampi catubbidhaṃ kammaṃ – janakaṃ, upatthambhakaṃ, upapīḷakaṃ, upaghātakanti. Tattha janakaṃ nāma kusalampi hoti akusalampi. Taṃ paṭisandhiyampi pavattepi rūpārūpavipākakkhandhe janeti. Upatthambhakaṃ pana vipākaṃ janetuṃ na sakkoti, aññena kammena dinnāya paṭisandhiyā janite vipāke uppajjamānakasukhadukkhaṃ upatthambheti, addhānaṃ pavatteti. Upapīḷakaṃ aññena kammena dinnāya paṭisandhiyā janite vipāke uppajjamānakasukhadukkhaṃ pīḷeti bādhati, addhānaṃ pavattituṃ na deti. Upaghātakaṃ pana sayaṃ kusalampi akusalampi samānaṃ aññaṃ dubbalakammaṃ ghātetvā tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karoti. Evaṃ pana kammena kate okāse taṃ vipākaṃ uppannaṃ nāma vuccati.

687. There is still another fourfold kamma: generative, supportive, oppressive, and destructive. Herein, generative kamma, which can be either wholesome or unwholesome, generates the material and immaterial resultant aggregates both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. Supportive kamma cannot generate a result itself; rather, when rebirth-linking has been given by another kamma, it supports and prolongs the pleasure and pain that arise in the generated result. Oppressive kamma oppresses and obstructs the pleasure and pain that arise in the result generated by another kamma, not allowing it to continue. Destructive kamma, being itself wholesome or unwholesome, destroys another weaker kamma, wards off its result, and creates an opportunity for its own result. When an opportunity has thus been created by a kamma, its result is said to have arisen.

Iti [M 2.0237] imesaṃ dvādasannaṃ kammānaṃ kammantarañceva vipākantarañca buddhānaṃ kammavipākañāṇasseva [V 2.0236] yāthāvasarasato pākaṭaṃ hoti, asādhāraṇaṃ sāvakehi. Vipassakena pana kammantarañca vipākantarañca ekadesato jānitabbaṃ. Tasmā ayaṃ mukhamattadassanena kammaviseso pakāsitoti.

Thus, the distinctions among these twelve kinds of kamma and the distinctions among their results are fully evident, in all their specific instances, only to the Buddhas' knowledge of kamma and its result, a knowledge not shared with the disciples. A meditator practicing insight, however, should understand the distinctions among kammas and the distinctions among their results in part. Therefore, this specific analysis of kamma has been set forth as a mere indication.

688. Iti imaṃ dvādasavidhaṃ kammaṃ kammavaṭṭe pakkhipitvā evaṃ eko kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭavasena nāmarūpassa paccayapariggahaṃ karoti. So evaṃ kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭavasena paccayato nāmarūpassa pavattiṃ disvā “yathā idaṃ etarahi, evaṃ atītepi addhāne kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭavasena paccayato pavattittha, anāgatepi kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭavaseneva paccayato pavattissatī”ti. Iti kammañceva kammavipāko ca, kammavaṭṭañca vipākavaṭṭañca, kammapavattañca vipākapavattañca, kammasantati ca vipākasantati ca, kiriyā ca kiriyāphalañca.

688. Thus, having included this twelvefold kamma in the round of kamma, one in this way discerns the conditions for name-and-form by way of the round of kamma and the round of result. Having seen the occurrence of name-and-form as conditioned by the round of kamma and the round of result, one understands: 'Just as it is now, so too in the past time it occurred conditioned by the round of kamma and the round of result; and in the future time it will occur conditioned by the round of kamma and the round of result.' Thus: kamma and kamma-result; the round of kamma and the round of result; the process of kamma and the process of result; the continuity of kamma and the continuity of result; action and the fruit of action.

Kammā vipākā vattanti, vipāko kammasambhavo;

Kammā punabbhavo hoti, evaṃ loko pavattatīti. –

From kamma results proceed, a result has kamma for its source;

From kamma comes renewed existence; thus the world revolves.

Samanupassati. Tassevaṃ samanupassato yā sā pubbantādayo ārabbha “ahosiṃ nu kho aha”ntiādinā nayena vuttā soḷasavidhā vicikicchā, sā sabbā pahīyati. Sabbabhavayonigatiṭṭhitinivāsesu hetuphalasambandhavasena pavattamānaṃ nāmarūpamattameva khāyati. So neva kāraṇato uddhaṃ kārakaṃ passati, na vipākappavattito uddhaṃ vipākapaṭisaṃvedakaṃ. Kāraṇe pana sati “kārako”ti, vipākappavattiyā sati “paṭisaṃvedako”ti samaññāmattena paṇḍitā voharanticcevassa sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hoti.

He sees this. For one who sees in this way, the sixteen kinds of doubt concerning the past, etc., stated in the way beginning, 'Did I exist in the past?' are all abandoned. In all kinds of existence, generation, destiny, station, and abode, only mere name-and-form is apparent, occurring by way of the connection between cause and effect. He sees no doer apart from the condition, no experiencer apart from the occurrence of the result. And it is well seen by him with right wisdom that the wise use mere conventional expressions when, there being a condition, they speak of a 'doer,' and when, there being an occurrence of a result, they speak of an 'experiencer.'

689. Tenāhu porāṇā –

689. Therefore the ancients have said:

“Kammassa kārako natthi, vipākassa ca vedako;

Suddhadhammā pavattanti, evetaṃ sammadassanaṃ.

No doer of the kamma can be found, no one who reaps the fruit of it; mere phenomena flow on—this is right seeing.

“Evaṃ kamme vipāke ca, vattamāne sahetuke;

Bījarukkhādikānaṃva, pubbā koṭi na nāyati;

Anāgatepi saṃsāre, appavattaṃ na dissati.

With kamma and result thus turning, together with their causal source, like seeds and trees and so on, no first beginning can be known. And in the future round of births, non-occurrence is not seen.

“Etamatthaṃ [M 2.0238][V 2.0237] anaññāya, titthiyā asayaṃvasī;

Sattasaññaṃ gahetvāna, sassatucchedadassino;

Dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhanti, aññamaññavirodhitā.

Not understanding this point, sectarians without self-mastery, grasping the perception of a 'being,' and views of eternalism and annihilation, adopt the sixty-two wrong views, in conflict with one another.

“Diṭṭhibandhanabaddhā te, taṇhāsotena vuyhare;

Taṇhāsotena vuyhantā, na te dukkhā pamuccare.

Bound by the fetters of wrong views, they are carried by craving's stream; and being carried by that stream, they are not freed from suffering.

“Evametaṃ abhiññāya, bhikkhu buddhassa sāvako;

Gambhīraṃ nipuṇaṃ suññaṃ, paccayaṃ paṭivijjhati.

But having understood this well, a bhikkhu, the Buddha's disciple, penetrates the conditionality that is profound, subtle, and void.

“Kammaṃ natthi vipākamhi, pāko kamme na vijjati;

Aññamaññaṃ ubho suññā, na ca kammaṃ vinā phalaṃ.

In the result no kamma is found, nor is the fruit found in the kamma; they are both void of one another, yet no fruit is without the kamma.

“Yathā na sūriye aggi, na maṇimhi na gomaye;

Na tesaṃ bahi so atthi, sambhārehi ca jāyati.

Just as fire is not in the sun, nor in the crystal, nor in cow dung; nor does it exist outside of them, but is born from their components.

“Tathā na anto kammassa, vipāko upalabbhati;

Bahiddhāpi na kammassa, na kammaṃ tattha vijjati.

So too, a result is not found within the kamma, nor outside it; and the kamma is not found within the result that has arisen.

“Phalena suññaṃ taṃ kammaṃ, phalaṃ kamme na vijjati;

Kammañca kho upādāya, tato nibbattate phalaṃ.

That kamma is empty of its fruit, and in the kamma no fruit is found; but depending on that very kamma, the fruit from it is brought to be.

“Na hettha devo brahmā vā, saṃsārassatthikārako;

Suddhadhammā pavattanti, hetusambhārapaccayā”ti.

There is no god or Brahmā here who is the maker of this round; mere phenomena flow on, conditioned by their causal base.

690. Tassevaṃ kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭavasena nāmarūpassa paccayapariggahaṃ katvā tīsu addhāsu pahīnavicikicchassa sabbe atītānāgatapaccuppannadhammā cutipaṭisandhivasena viditā honti, sāssa hoti ñātapariññā.

690. For one who has thus discerned the conditions of name-and-form by way of the round of kamma and the round of result, and who has abandoned doubt concerning the three periods of time, all past, future, and present phenomena become known by way of death and rebirth-linking. This is his full understanding of the known.

So [V 2.0238] evaṃ pajānāti – ye atīte kammapaccayā nibbattā khandhā, te tattheva niruddhā, atītakammapaccayā pana imasmiṃ bhave aññe nibbattā, atītabhavato imaṃ bhavaṃ āgato ekadhammopi natthi, imasmimpi bhave kammapaccayena nibbattā khandhā nirujjhissanti, punabbhave aññe nibbattissanti, imamhā bhavā punabbhavaṃ ekadhammopi na gamissati. Apica kho yathā na ācariyamukhato sajjhāyo antevāsikassa mukhaṃ pavisati, na ca tappaccayā tassa [M 2.0239] mukhe sajjhāyo na vattati, na dūtena mantodakaṃ pītaṃ rogino udaraṃ pavisati, na ca tassa tappaccayā rogo na vūpasammati, na mukhe maṇḍanavidhānaṃ ādāsatalādīsu mukhanimittaṃ gacchati, na ca tattha tappaccayā maṇḍanavidhānaṃ na paññāyati, na ekissā vaṭṭiyā dīpasikhā aññaṃ vaṭṭiṃ saṅkamati, na ca tattha tappaccayā dīpasikhā na nibbattati, evameva na atītabhavato imaṃ bhavaṃ, ito vā punabbhavaṃ koci dhammo saṅkamati, na ca atītabhave khandhāyatanadhātupaccayā idha, idha vā khandhāyatanadhātupaccayā punabbhave khandhāyatanadhātuyo na nibbattantīti.

He understands thus: 'The aggregates that were produced in the past conditioned by kamma ceased right there. But conditioned by past kamma, other aggregates have been produced in this existence. Not a single phenomenon has come from the past existence to this existence. And the aggregates produced in this existence conditioned by kamma will cease, and other aggregates will be produced in a future existence. Not a single phenomenon will go from this existence to a future existence.' Moreover, just as a teacher's recitation does not pass into the student's mouth, and yet because of it the recitation occurs in the student's mouth; just as consecrated water drunk by a messenger does not enter the patient's stomach, and yet because of it the patient's illness is cured; just as the decoration on a face does not pass to its reflection in a mirror, and yet because of it the decoration appears there; and just as the flame from one wick does not transmigrate to another wick, and yet because of it a flame is produced on the other wick—so too, no phenomenon transmigrates from a past existence to this one, or from this one to a future existence. And yet, it is not the case that aggregates, bases, and elements are not produced here conditioned by the aggregates, bases, and elements in the past, or that they will not be produced in a future existence conditioned by the aggregates, bases, and elements here.

Yatheva cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, manodhātuanantaraṃ;

Na ceva āgataṃ nāpi, na nibbattaṃ anantaraṃ.

Just as eye-consciousness arises immediately after the mind-element; it has not come from it, and yet it is not that it does not arise in succession.

Tatheva paṭisandhimhi, vattate cittasantati;

Purimaṃ bhijjate cittaṃ, pacchimaṃ jāyate tato.

So too at rebirth-linking does the stream of consciousness proceed; the prior consciousness dissolves, and from it is the next one born.

Tesaṃ antarikā natthi, vīci tesaṃ na vijjati;

Na cito gacchati kiñci, paṭisandhi ca jāyatīti.

Between them is no interval, no wave is found to pass between; nothing goes from this life to the next, and yet rebirth-linking takes place.

691. Evaṃ cutipaṭisandhivasena viditasabbadhammassa sabbākārena nāmarūpassa paccayapariggahañāṇaṃ thāmagataṃ hoti, soḷasavidhā kaṅkhā suṭṭhutaraṃ pahīyati. Na kevalañca sā eva, “satthari kaṅkhatī”ti (dha. sa. 1008) ādinayappavattā aṭṭhavidhāpi kaṅkhā pahīyatiyeva, dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni vikkhambhanti. Evaṃ nānānayehi nāmarūpapaccayapariggahaṇena tīsu addhāsu kaṅkhaṃ vitaritvā ṭhitaṃ ñāṇaṃ kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhīti veditabbaṃ. Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇantipi yathābhūtañāṇantipi sammādassanantipi etassevādhivacanaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

691. Thus, for one who has understood all phenomena by way of death and rebirth-linking, the knowledge that comprehends the conditions of mentality-materiality in all its aspects becomes strong, and the sixteen kinds of doubt are thoroughly abandoned. Not only these, but the eight kinds of doubt that occur in the way beginning, 'He doubts the Teacher' (Dhs. 1008), are also abandoned, and the sixty-two wrong views are suppressed.
