In this way, the knowledge that stands firm, having overcome doubt about the three periods of time by comprehending the conditions of mentality-materiality in various ways, is to be known as the purification by overcoming doubt. Knowledge of the stability of phenomena, knowledge of things as they actually are, and right view are also designations for this. For this was said:

“Avijjā [V 2.0239] paccayo, saṅkhārā paccayasamuppannā. Ubhopete dhammā paccayasamuppannāti paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.46).

'Ignorance is a condition; formations are dependently arisen. Both these phenomena are dependently arisen.'—The wisdom in comprehending the conditions is knowledge of the stability of phenomena. (Paṭis I 46)

“Aniccato manasikaronto katame dhamme yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, kathaṃ sammādassanaṃ hoti, kathaṃ tadanvayena sabbe saṅkhārā aniccato sudiṭṭhā honti, kattha kaṅkhā pahīyati? Dukkhato…pe… anattato manasikaronto katame dhamme yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati…pe… kattha kaṅkhā pahīyatīti?

'By giving attention to impermanence, what phenomena does one know and see as they actually are? How does right view come to be? How, in consequence of that, are all formations well seen as impermanent? Where is doubt abandoned? By giving attention to suffering...pe... by giving attention to non-self, what phenomena does one know and see as they actually are?...pe... Where is doubt abandoned?'

“Aniccato [M 2.0240] manasikaronto nimittaṃ yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, tena vuccati sammādassanaṃ. Evaṃ tadanvayena sabbe saṅkhārā aniccato sudiṭṭhā honti. Ettha kaṅkhā pahīyati. Dukkhato manasikaronto pavattaṃ yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati…pe… anattato manasikaronto nimittañca pavattañca yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, tena vuccati sammādassanaṃ. Evaṃ tadanvayena sabbe dhammā anattato sudiṭṭhā honti. Ettha kaṅkhā pahīyati.

'By giving attention to impermanence, one knows and sees the sign as it actually is; because of that, it is called right view. In this way, in consequence of that, all formations are well seen as impermanent. Here doubt is abandoned. By giving attention to suffering, one knows and sees the occurrence as it actually is...pe... By giving attention to non-self, one knows and sees both the sign and the occurrence as they actually are; because of that, it is called right view. In this way, in consequence of that, all phenomena are well seen as non-self. Here doubt is abandoned.'

“Yañca yathābhūtañāṇaṃ yañca sammādassanaṃ yā ca kaṅkhāvitaraṇā, ime dhammā nānatthā ceva nānābyañjanā ca, udāhu ekatthā byañjanameva nānanti? Yañca yathābhūtañāṇaṃ yañca sammādassanaṃ yā ca kaṅkhāvitaraṇā, ime dhammā ekatthā, byañjanameva nāna”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.227).

'The knowledge of things as they actually are, right view, and the overcoming of doubt—are these phenomena different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they the same in meaning and different only in phrasing? The knowledge of things as they actually are, right view, and the overcoming of doubt—these phenomena are the same in meaning, different only in phrasing.' (Paṭis I 227)

Iminā pana ñāṇena samannāgato vipassako buddhasāsane laddhassāso laddhapatiṭṭho niyatagatiko cūḷasotāpanno nāma hoti.

Endowed with this knowledge, the insight meditator gains confidence and a firm footing in the Buddha's Dispensation. He is fixed in his destiny and is called a 'lesser stream-enterer.'

Tasmā bhikkhu sadā sato, nāmarūpassa sabbaso;

Paccaye pariggaṇheyya, kaṅkhāvitaraṇatthikoti.

Therefore a bhikkhu, ever mindful,

Of mentality-materiality in every way,

Should comprehend its conditions,

If he would overcome his doubt.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, composed for the gladdening of good people,

Paññābhāvanādhikāre

in the section on the Development of Wisdom,

Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiniddeso nāma

the Explanation of the Purification by Overcoming Doubt,

Ekūnavīsatimo paricchedo.

the nineteenth chapter, is concluded.

20. Maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso

20. Explanation of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of Path and Not-Path

Sammasanañāṇakathā

The Discussion on the Knowledge of Comprehension

692. Ayaṃ [M 2.0241][V 2.0240] maggo, ayaṃ na maggoti evaṃ maggañca amaggañca ñatvā ṭhitaṃ ñāṇaṃ pana maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi nāma.

692. The knowledge that stands firm, having known the path and the not-path thus, 'This is the path, this is not the path,' is called the purification by knowledge and vision of path and not-path.

Taṃ sampādetukāmena kalāpasammasanasaṅkhātāya nayavipassanāya tāva yogo karaṇīyo. Kasmā? Āraddhavipassakassa obhāsādisambhave maggāmaggañāṇasambhavato. Āraddhavipassakassa hi obhāsādīsu sambhūtesu maggāmaggañāṇaṃ hoti, vipassanāya ca kalāpasammasanaṃ ādi. Tasmā etaṃ kaṅkhāvitaraṇānantaraṃ uddiṭṭhaṃ. Apica yasmā tīraṇapariññāya vattamānāya maggāmaggañāṇaṃ uppajjati, tīraṇapariññā ca ñātapariññānantarā, tasmāpi taṃ maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiṃ sampādetukāmena kalāpasammasane tāva yogo kātabbo.

To accomplish that, one who wishes to do so should first apply himself to the methodical insight known as the comprehension of groups (kalāpasammasana). Why? Because for an insight meditator who has undertaken the practice, the knowledge of path and not-path arises with the occurrence of illumination and so on. For when illumination, etc., have occurred for an insight meditator who has undertaken the practice, the knowledge of path and not-path arises, and comprehension of groups is the beginning of insight. That is why this was described immediately after the overcoming of doubt. Furthermore, since the knowledge of path and not-path arises while full understanding by scrutinizing is occurring, and full understanding by scrutinizing is subsequent to full understanding as the known, therefore one who wishes to accomplish that purification by knowledge and vision of path and not-path should first apply himself to the comprehension of groups.

693. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – tisso hi lokiyapariññā ñātapariññā tīraṇapariññā pahānapariññā ca. Yā sandhāya vuttaṃ “abhiññāpaññā ñātaṭṭhe ñāṇaṃ. Pariññāpaññā tīraṇaṭṭhe ñāṇaṃ. Pahānapaññā pariccāgaṭṭhe ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.75). Tattha “ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ, vedayitalakkhaṇā vedanā”ti evaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paccattalakkhaṇasallakkhaṇavasena pavattā paññā ñātapariññā nāma. “Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ, vedanā aniccā”tiādinā nayena tesaṃyeva dhammānaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā pavattā lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanā paññā tīraṇapariññā nāma. Tesuyeva pana dhammesu niccasaññādipajahanavasena pavattā lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanā paññā pahānapariññā nāma.

693. Herein, this is the detailed analysis: There are three mundane kinds of full understanding: full understanding as the known, full understanding by scrutinizing, and full understanding by abandoning. With reference to this it is said: 'Wisdom of direct knowledge is knowledge in the sense of the known. Wisdom of full understanding is knowledge in the sense of scrutinizing. Wisdom of abandoning is knowledge in the sense of relinquishing' (Paṭis I 75). Herein, the wisdom that proceeds by way of discerning the individual characteristics of the several phenomena, such as 'Form has the characteristic of being afflicted, feeling has the characteristic of being felt,' is called full understanding as the known. The wisdom of insight that has the characteristics of phenomena as its object, which proceeds by ascribing the general characteristics to those same phenomena in the way beginning, 'Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent,' is called full understanding by scrutinizing. The wisdom of insight that has the characteristics of phenomena as its object, which proceeds by way of abandoning the perception of permanence, etc., in those same phenomena, is called full understanding by abandoning.

Tattha saṅkhāraparicchedato paṭṭhāya yāva paccayapariggahā ñātapariññāya bhūmi. Etasmiṃ hi antare [V 2.0241] dhammānaṃ paccattalakkhaṇapaṭivedhasseva ādhipaccaṃ hoti. Kalāpasammasanato pana paṭṭhāya yāva udayabbayānupassanā tīraṇapariññāya bhūmi. Etasmiṃ hi antare sāmaññalakkhaṇapaṭivedhasseva ādhipaccaṃ hoti. Bhaṅgānupassanaṃ ādiṃ katvā upari pahānapariññāya bhūmi[M 2.0242]. Tato paṭṭhāya hi aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahati, dukkhato anupassanto sukhasaññaṃ, anattato anupassanto attasaññaṃ, nibbindanto nandiṃ, virajjanto rāgaṃ, nirodhento samudayaṃ, paṭinissajjanto ādānaṃ pajahatīti (paṭi. ma. 1.52) evaṃ niccasaññādipahānasādhikānaṃ sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ ādhipaccaṃ. Iti imāsu tīsu pariññāsu saṅkhāraparicchedassa ceva paccayapariggahassa ca sādhitattā iminā yoginā ñātapariññāva adhigatā hoti, itarā ca adhigantabbā. Tena vuttaṃ “yasmā tīraṇapariññāya vattamānāya maggāmaggañāṇaṃ uppajjati, tīraṇapariññā ca ñātapariññānantarā, tasmāpi taṃ maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiṃ sampādetukāmena kalāpasammasane tāva yogo kātabbo”ti.

Herein, from the delimitation of formations up to the comprehension of conditions is the domain of full understanding as the known. In this interval, the penetration of the individual characteristics of phenomena is predominant. From the comprehension of groups up to the contemplation of rise and fall is the domain of full understanding by scrutinizing. In this interval, the penetration of the general characteristics is predominant. From the contemplation of dissolution onwards is the domain of full understanding by abandoning. From that point on, 'contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence; contemplating as suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure; contemplating as non-self, one abandons the perception of self; becoming disenchanted, one abandons delight; becoming dispassionate, one abandons lust; causing to cease, one abandons arising; relinquishing, one abandons grasping' (Paṭis I 52). Thus the seven contemplations that accomplish the abandoning of the perception of permanence, etc., are predominant. Therefore, among these three kinds of full understanding, since the delimitation of formations and the comprehension of conditions have been accomplished, this meditator has attained only full understanding as the known, while the others remain to be attained. Hence it was said: 'Since the knowledge of path and not-path arises while full understanding by scrutinizing is occurring, and full understanding by scrutinizing is subsequent to full understanding as the known, therefore one who wishes to accomplish the purification by knowledge and vision of path and not-path should first apply himself to the comprehension of groups.'

694. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

694. Herein is the Pāli text:

“Kathaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhipitvā vavatthāne paññā sammasane ñāṇaṃ? Yaṃkiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā…pe… yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aniccato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Dukkhato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Anattato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Yā kāci vedanā…pe… yaṃkiñci viññāṇaṃ…pe… anattato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasanaṃ.

'How is there wisdom in defining by summarizing, and knowledge in comprehending, past, future, and present phenomena? Whatever form—past, future, or present, internal or...pe... far or near—all form he defines as impermanent; this is one comprehension. He defines it as suffering; this is one comprehension. He defines it as non-self; this is one comprehension. Whatever feeling...pe... whatever consciousness...pe... he defines as non-self; this is one comprehension.'

“Cakkhuṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Dukkhato anattato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasanaṃ.

'The eye...pe... aging-and-death—past, future, and present—he defines as impermanent: this is one comprehension. He defines it as suffering and as non-self: this is one comprehension.'

“Rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena, dukkhaṃ bhayaṭṭhena, anattā asārakaṭṭhenāti saṅkhipitvā vavatthāne paññā sammasane ñāṇaṃ. Vedanaṃ… viññāṇaṃ… cakkhuṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ…pe… sammasane ñāṇaṃ.

'Form—past, future, and present—is impermanent in the sense of decay, suffering in the sense of fear, non-self in the sense of being without substance': wisdom in defining by summarizing thus, knowledge in comprehending. Feeling... consciousness... the eye...pe... aging-and-death...pe... knowledge in comprehending.

“Rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ khayadhammaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ [V 2.0242] nirodhadhammanti saṅkhipitvā vavatthāne paññā sammasane ñāṇaṃ. Vedanaṃ… viññāṇaṃ… cakkhuṃ… jarāmaraṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ…pe… nirodhadhammanti saṅkhipitvā vavatthāne paññā sammasane ñāṇaṃ.

'Form—past, future, and present—is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to decay, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation': wisdom in defining by summarizing thus, knowledge in comprehending. Feeling... consciousness... the eye... aging-and-death—past, future, and present—is impermanent, conditioned...pe... subject to cessation: wisdom in defining by summarizing thus, knowledge in comprehending.

“Jātipaccayā [M 2.0243] jarāmaraṇaṃ, asati jātiyā natthi jarāmaraṇanti saṅkhipitvā vavatthāne paññā sammasane ñāṇaṃ. Atītampi addhānaṃ, anāgatampi addhānaṃ jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ, asati jātiyā natthi jarāmaraṇanti saṅkhipitvā vavatthāne paññā sammasane ñāṇaṃ. Bhavapaccayā jāti…pe… avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, asati avijjāya natthi saṅkhārāti saṅkhipitvā vavatthāne paññā sammasane ñāṇaṃ. Atītampi addhānaṃ, anāgatampi addhānaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā, asati avijjāya natthi saṅkhārāti saṅkhipitvā vavatthāne paññā sammasane ñāṇaṃ.

'With birth as condition, there is aging and death; when there is no birth, there is no aging and death': wisdom in defining by summarizing thus, knowledge in comprehending. 'In the past time and in the future time, with birth as condition, there is aging and death; when there is no birth, there is no aging and death': wisdom in defining by summarizing thus, knowledge in comprehending. 'With existence as condition, birth... with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; when there is no ignorance, there are no volitional formations': wisdom in defining by summarizing thus, knowledge in comprehending. 'In the past time and in the future time, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; when there is no ignorance, there are no volitional formations': wisdom in defining by summarizing thus, knowledge in comprehending.

“Taṃ ñātaṭṭhena ñāṇaṃ. Pajānanaṭṭhena paññā. Tena vuccati atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhipitvā vavatthāne paññā sammasane ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.48).

It is knowledge in the sense of knowing. It is wisdom in the sense of discerning. Therefore it is said: 'The wisdom that defines past, future, and present phenomena by summarizing them is the knowledge of comprehension.' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.48)

Ettha ca cakkhuṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇanti iminā peyyālena dvārārammaṇehi saddhiṃ dvārappavattā dhammā, pañcakkhandhā, cha dvārāni, cha ārammaṇāni, cha viññāṇāni, cha phassā, cha vedanā, cha saññā, cha cetanā, cha taṇhā, cha vitakkā, cha vicārā, cha dhātuyo, dasa kasiṇāni, dvattiṃsakoṭṭhāsā, dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo, bāvīsati indriyāni, tisso dhātuyo, nava bhavā, cattāri jhānāni, catasso appamaññā, catasso samāpattiyo, dvādasa paṭiccasamuppādaṅgānīti ime dhammarāsayo saṃkhittāti veditabbā.

Here, by this abbreviation 'the eye… aging-and-death,' it should be understood that the following collections of phenomena are condensed: phenomena that occur at the doors along with their objects, the five aggregates, the six sense doors, the six objects, the six consciousnesses, the six contacts, the six feelings, the six perceptions, the six volitions, the six cravings, the six initial applications of mind, the six sustained applications of mind, the six elements, the ten kasiṇas, the thirty-two parts of the body, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the twenty-two faculties, the three elements, the nine kinds of existence, the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the twelve links of dependent origination.

Vuttaṃ hetaṃ abhiññeyyaniddese –

For this was stated in the Exposition of What Is to Be Directly Known:

“Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññeyyaṃ. Kiñca, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ abhiññeyyaṃ? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, abhiññeyyaṃ. Rūpā… cakkhuviññāṇaṃ… cakkhusamphasso… yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā, tampi [V 2.0243] abhiññeyyaṃ. Sotaṃ…pe… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā, tampi abhiññeyyaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, all is to be directly known. And what, bhikkhus, is the all that is to be directly known? The eye, bhikkhus, is to be directly known. Forms… eye-consciousness… eye-contact… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is to be directly known. The ear… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is to be directly known.

“Rūpaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ… cakkhu…pe… mano… rūpā…pe… dhammā… cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manoviññāṇaṃ… cakkhusamphasso…pe… manosamphasso….

“Form… consciousness… eye… mind… forms… mental phenomena… eye-consciousness… mind-consciousness… eye-contact… mind-contact….

“Cakkhusamphassajā [M 2.0244] vedanā…pe… manosamphassajā vedanā… rūpasaññā…pe… dhammasaññā… rūpasañcetanā…pe… dhammasañcetanā… rūpataṇhā…pe… dhammataṇhā… rūpavitakko…pe… dhammavitakko… rūpavicāro…pe… dhammavicāro….

“Feeling born of eye-contact… feeling born of mind-contact… perception of forms… perception of mental phenomena… volition regarding forms… volition regarding mental phenomena… craving for forms… craving for mental phenomena… initial thought about forms… initial thought about mental phenomena… sustained thought about forms… sustained thought about mental phenomena….

“Pathavīdhātu…pe… viññāṇadhātu… pathavīkasiṇaṃ…pe… viññāṇakasiṇaṃ… kesā…pe… muttaṃ… matthaluṅgaṃ….

“The earth element… the consciousness element… the earth kasiṇa… the consciousness kasiṇa… hair of the head… urine… the brain….

“Cakkhāyatanaṃ…pe… dhammāyatanaṃ… cakkhudhātu…pe… manodhātu… manoviññāṇadhātu… cakkhundriyaṃ…pe… aññātāvindriyaṃ….

“The eye base… the mental-phenomena base… the eye element… the mind element… the mind-consciousness element… the eye faculty… the faculty of one who has final knowledge….

“Kāmadhātu… rūpadhātu… arūpadhātu… kāmabhavo… rūpabhavo… arūpabhavo… saññābhavo… asaññābhavo… nevasaññānāsaññābhavo… ekavokārabhavo… catuvokārabhavo… pañcavokārabhavo….

“The sense-sphere realm… the form realm… the formless realm… sensual existence… form existence… formless existence… existence with perception… existence without perception… existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception… one-constituent existence… four-constituent existence… five-constituent existence….

“Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ… mettācetovimutti…pe… upekkhācetovimutti… ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpatti…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpatti… avijjā abhiññeyyā…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ abhiññeyya”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.3; saṃ. ni. 4.46).

“The first jhāna… the fourth jhāna… the mind-deliverance of loving-kindness… the mind-deliverance of equanimity… the attainment of the base of infinite space… the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception… ignorance is to be directly known… aging and death are to be directly known.” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.3; SN 35.23)

Taṃ tattha evaṃ vitthārena vuttattā idha sabbaṃ peyyālena saṃkhittaṃ. Evaṃ saṃkhitte panettha ye lokuttarā dhammā āgatā, te asammasanupagattā imasmiṃ adhikāre na gahetabbā. Yepi ca sammasanupagā[V 2.0244], tesu ye yassa pākaṭā honti sukhena pariggahaṃ gacchanti, tesu tena sammasanaṃ ārabhitabbaṃ.

Since this was stated there in detail, here it is all condensed by abbreviation. In this condensed version, those supramundane phenomena that are included should not be taken up in this section, as they are not subject to comprehension. But among those that are subject to comprehension, one should begin the comprehension with those that are evident to oneself and easily grasped.

695. Tatrāyaṃ khandhavasena ārabbhavidhānayojanā – yaṃkiñci rūpaṃ…pe… sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aniccato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Dukkhato anattato vavatthapeti, ekaṃ sammasananti. Ettāvatā ayaṃ bhikkhu “yaṃkiñci rūpa”nti evaṃ aniyamaniddiṭṭhaṃ sabbampi rūpaṃ atītattikena ceva catūhi ca ajjhattādidukehīti ekādasahi okāsehi paricchinditvā sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aniccato vavatthapeti, aniccanti sammasati.

695. Herein, this is the application of the method for undertaking it by way of the aggregates: ‘Whatever form there is… he determines all form as impermanent—this is one comprehension. He determines it as suffering and as non-self—this is one comprehension.’ To this extent, this bhikkhu, having delimited all form—even that which is indefinitely indicated by the expression ‘whatever form’—in eleven cases, namely, by the triad of time and by the four dyads beginning with ‘internal,’ determines all form as impermanent, comprehending it as ‘impermanent.’

Kathaṃ[M 2.0245]? Parato vuttanayena. Vuttañhetaṃ – “rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhenā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.48).

How? According to the method stated hereafter. For it was said: “Form—past, future, or present—is impermanent in the sense of perishing.” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.48)

Tasmā esa yaṃ atītaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ yasmā atīteyeva khīṇaṃ, nayimaṃ bhavaṃ sampattanti aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena.

Therefore, as to past form, since it perished in the past itself and did not reach this present existence, he comprehends it as impermanent in the sense of perishing.

Yaṃ anāgataṃ anantarabhave nibbattissati, tampi tattheva khīyissati, na tato paraṃ bhavaṃ gamissatīti aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena.

As to future form that will be produced in the immediately following existence, that too will perish right there; it will not go to a further existence. Thus he comprehends it as impermanent in the sense of perishing.

Yaṃ paccuppannaṃ rūpaṃ, tampi idheva khīyati, na ito gacchatīti aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena.

As to present form, that too perishes right here; it does not go from here. Thus he comprehends it as impermanent in the sense of perishing.

Yaṃ ajjhattaṃ, tampi ajjhattameva khīyati, na bahiddhābhāvaṃ gacchatīti aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena.

Whatever is internal, that too perishes internally; it does not pass into an external state. Thus he comprehends it as impermanent in the sense of perishing.

Yaṃ bahiddhā…pe… oḷārikaṃ…pe… sukhumaṃ…pe… hīnaṃ…pe… paṇītaṃ…pe… dūre…pe… santike, tampi tattheva khīyati, na dūrabhāvaṃ gacchatīti aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhenāti sammasati.

Whatever is external… coarse… subtle… inferior… superior… far… near, that too perishes right there; it does not pass into a state of being far away. Thus he comprehends that it is impermanent in the sense of perishing.

Idaṃ sabbampi “aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhenā”ti etassa vasena ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Bhedato pana ekādasavidhaṃ hoti.

All this, by way of “impermanent in the sense of perishing,” is one comprehension. But by way of distinction, it becomes elevenfold.

Sabbameva ca taṃ dukkhaṃ bhayaṭṭhena. Bhayaṭṭhenāti sappaṭibhayatāya. Yañhi aniccaṃ, taṃ bhayāvahaṃ hoti sīhopamasutte (saṃ. ni. 3.78; a. ni. 4.33) devānaṃ viya. Iti [V 2.0245] idampi “dukkhaṃ bhayaṭṭhenā”ti etassa vasena ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Bhedato pana ekādasavidhaṃ hoti.

And all of that is suffering in the sense of fear. ‘In the sense of fear’ means because it is frightening. For whatever is impermanent is fear-inspiring, as it was for the devas in the Sīhopama Sutta. Thus this too, by way of “suffering in the sense of fear,” is one comprehension. But by way of distinction, it becomes elevenfold.

Yathā ca dukkhaṃ, evaṃ sabbampi taṃ anattā asārakaṭṭhena. Asārakaṭṭhenāti “attā nivāsī kārako vedako sayaṃvasī”ti evaṃ parikappitassa attasārassa abhāvena. Yañhi aniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ, taṃ attanopi aniccataṃ vā udayabbayapīḷanaṃ vā vāretuṃ na sakkoti, kuto tassa kārakādibhāvo. Tenāha – “rūpañca hidaṃ, bhikkhave, attā abhavissa. Nayidaṃ rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvatteyyā”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 3.59). Iti idampi “anattā asārakaṭṭhenā”ti [M 2.0246] etassa vasena ekaṃ sammasanaṃ. Bhedato pana ekādasavidhaṃ hoti. Esa nayo vedanādīsu.

And just as it is suffering, so all of it is non-self in the sense of being essenceless. ‘In the sense of being essenceless’ means because of the absence of a self-essence conceived as ‘a resident, a doer, an experiencer, one who is self-governing.’ For whatever is impermanent and suffering cannot ward off its own impermanence or the oppression of arising and passing away, so how could it have the status of a doer, etc.? Therefore the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, if this form were self, this form would not lead to affliction,” and so on. Thus this too, by way of “non-self in the sense of being essenceless,” is one comprehension. But by way of distinction, it becomes elevenfold. This is the method for feeling and the other aggregates.

696. Yaṃ pana aniccaṃ, taṃ yasmā niyamato saṅkhatādibhedaṃ hoti. Tenassa pariyāyadassanatthaṃ, nānākārehi vā manasikārappavattidassanatthaṃ “rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ khayadhammaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ nirodhadhamma”nti puna pāḷi vuttā. Esa nayo vedanādīsūti.

696. Moreover, whatever is impermanent is necessarily differentiated as conditioned, etc. Therefore, to show its various aspects, or to show the occurrence of attention in various ways, the Pāḷi is stated again: “Form—past, future, or present—is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to perishing, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation.” This is the method for feeling and the other aggregates.

Cattārīsākāraanupassanākathā

The Discourse on Contemplation by Forty Aspects

697. So tasseva pañcasu khandhesu aniccadukkhānattasammasanassa thirabhāvatthāya, yaṃ taṃ bhagavatā “katamehi cattārīsāya ākārehi anulomikaṃ khantiṃ paṭilabhati, katamehi cattārīsāya ākārehi sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamatī”ti etassa vibhaṅge –

697. For the sake of making firm the contemplation of the five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and not-self, in the analysis of what was said by the Blessed One: 'By what forty aspects does one acquire conformity acceptance? By what forty aspects does one enter the fixed course of rightness?'—

“Pañcakkhandhe aniccato, dukkhato, rogato, gaṇḍato, sallato, aghato, ābādhato, parato, palokato, ītito, upaddavato, bhayato, upasaggato, calato, pabhaṅguto, addhuvato, atāṇato, aleṇato, asaraṇato, rittato, tucchato, suññato, anattato, ādīnavato, vipariṇāmadhammato, asārakato, aghamūlato, vadhakato, vibhavato, sāsavato, saṅkhatato, mārāmisato, jātidhammato, jarādhammato, byādhidhammato, maraṇadhammato[V 2.0246], sokadhammato, paridevadhammato, upāyāsadhammato, saṃkilesikadhammato”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.37) –

‘The five aggregates as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as perishable, as a calamity, as a disaster, as fearful, as a menace, as unstable, as crumbling, as transient, as without protection, as without shelter, as without refuge, as empty, as hollow, as void, as not-self, as perilous, as subject to change, as essenceless, as the root of misery, as a slayer, as subject to destruction, as with taints, as conditioned, as Māra’s bait, as subject to birth, as subject to aging, as subject to illness, as subject to death, as subject to sorrow, as subject to lamentation, as subject to despair, as of a nature to be defiled’—

Cattārīsāya ākārehi,

By forty aspects,

“Pañcakkhandhe aniccato passanto anulomikaṃ khantiṃ paṭilabhati. Pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ nirodho niccaṃ nibbānanti passanto sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamatī”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 3.38) nayena,

‘One who sees the five aggregates as impermanent obtains conformity acceptance. One who sees that the cessation of the five aggregates is permanent, Nibbāna, enters the fixed course of rightness’—by the method beginning thus,

Anulomañāṇaṃ vibhajantena pabhedato aniccādisammasanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassāpi vasena ime pañcakkhandhe sammasati.

When analyzing conformity knowledge, the contemplation of impermanence and so forth is explained in detail. And by means of that too, one contemplates these five aggregates.

698. Kathaṃ[M 2.0247]? So hi ekekaṃ khandhaṃ anaccantikatāya, ādiantavantatāya ca aniccato. Uppādavayapaṭipīḷanatāya, dukkhavatthutāya ca dukkhato. Paccayayāpanīyatāya, rogamūlatāya ca rogato. Dukkhatāsūlayogitāya, kilesāsucipaggharaṇatāya, uppādajarābhaṅgehi uddhumātaparipakkapabhinnatāya ca gaṇḍato. Pīḷājanakatāya, antotudanatāya, dunnīharaṇīyatāya ca sallato. Vigarahaṇīyatāya, avaḍḍhiāvahanatāya, aghavatthutāya ca aghato. Aseribhāvajanakatāya, ābādhapadaṭṭhānatāya ca ābādhato. Avasatāya, avidheyyatāya ca parato. Byādhijarāmaraṇehi palujjanatāya palokato. Anekabyasanāvahanatāya ītito. Aviditānaṃyeva vipulānaṃ anatthānaṃ āvahanato, sabbupaddavavatthutāya ca upaddavato. Sabbabhayānaṃ ākaratāya, dukkhavūpasamasaṅkhātassa paramassāsassa paṭipakkhabhūtatāya ca bhayato. Anekehi anatthehi anubaddhatāya, dosūpasaṭṭhatāya, upasaggo viya anadhivāsanārahatāya ca upasaggato. Byādhijarāmaraṇehi ceva lābhālābhādīhi ca lokadhammehi pacalitatāya calato. Upakkamena ceva sarasena ca pabhaṅgupagamanasīlatāya pabhaṅguto. Sabbāvatthanipātitāya, thirabhāvassa ca abhāvatāya addhuvato. Atāyanatāya ceva, alabbhaneyyakhematāya ca atāṇato. Allīyituṃ anarahatāya, allīnānampi ca leṇakiccākāritāya aleṇato. Nissitānaṃ bhayasārakattābhāvena asaraṇato. Yathāparikappitehi dhuvasubhasukhattabhāvehi rittatāya rittato. Rittatāyeva tucchato appakattā vā, appakampi hi loke tucchanti vuccati. Sāmi-nivāsi-kāraka-vedakādhiṭṭhāyakavirahitatāya [V 2.0247] suññato. Sayañca assāmikabhāvāditāya anattato. Pavattidukkhatāya, dukkhassa ca ādīnavatāya ādīnavato, atha vā ādīnaṃ vāti gacchati pavattatīti ādīnavo, kapaṇamanussassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, khandhāpi ca kapaṇāyevāti ādīnavasadisatāya ādīnavato. Jarāya ceva maraṇena cāti dvedhā pariṇāmapakatitāya vipariṇāmadhammato. Dubbalatāya, pheggu viya sukhabhañjanīyatāya ca asārakato. Aghahetutāya aghamūlato. Mittamukhasapatto [M 2.0248] viya vissāsaghātitāya vadhakato. Vigatabhavatāya, vibhavasambhūtatāya ca vibhavato. Āsavapadaṭṭhānatāya sāsavato. Hetupaccayehi abhisaṅkhatatāya saṅkhatato. Maccumārakilesamārānaṃ āmisabhūtatāya mārāmisato. Jāti-jarā-byādhimaraṇapakatitāya jāti-jarā-byādhi-maraṇadhammato. Soka-parideva-upāyāsahetutāya soka-paridevaupāyāsadhammato. Taṇhādiṭṭhiduccaritasaṃkilesānaṃ visayadhammatāya saṃkilesikadhammatoti evaṃ pabhedato vuttassa aniccādisammasanassa vasena sammasati.

698. How? For he contemplates each aggregate as impermanent because it is not everlasting and has a beginning and an end; as suffering because it is oppressed by arising and passing away and is a basis for suffering; as a disease because it must be maintained by conditions and is the root of disease; as a tumor because it is connected with the stake of suffering, oozes with the impurity of defilements, and is swollen, festered, and burst by arising, aging, and breaking up; as a dart because it generates affliction, pricks within, and is hard to extract; as misery because it is reprehensible, brings decline, and is a basis for misery; as an affliction because it produces a state of non-independence and is a ground for ailments; as alien because it is uncontrollable and ungovernable; as perishable because it is shattered by sickness, aging, and death; as a calamity because it brings many misfortunes; as a disaster because it brings vast, unknown harms and is a basis for all troubles; as fearful because it is a source of all fears and is the opponent of the supreme solace called the appeasement of suffering; as a menace because it is bound to many harms, afflicted by faults, and unworthy of endurance like an attack; as unstable because it is shaken by sickness, aging, and death, and by the worldly conditions beginning with gain and loss; as crumbling because it is prone to breaking up by assault and by its own nature; as transient because it falls apart in all states and lacks a stable nature; as without protection because it offers no protection and because safety from it is unobtainable; as without shelter because it is unfit to cling to and does not perform the function of a shelter even for those who cling to it; as without refuge because it does not ward off fear for those who depend on it; as empty because it is devoid of the imagined qualities of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self; as hollow because of its very emptiness, or because of its insignificance, for in the world what is insignificant is called 'hollow'; as void because it is devoid of an owner, indweller, maker, experiencer, or one who exercises control; as not-self because it is itself without a master and so on; as perilous because it is the suffering of existence and a danger of suffering, or because it leads to misery, like a wretched person, for the aggregates too are wretched and thus resemble what is perilous; as subject to change because it has the nature of changing in two ways: through aging and death; as essenceless because it is weak and easily broken like pith; as the root of misery because it is the cause of misery; as a slayer because it betrays trust like an enemy with the face of a friend; as subject to passing away because it is devoid of being and arises from non-being; as with taints because it is a proximate cause for the taints; as conditioned because it is formed by causes and conditions; as Māra’s bait because it is the bait for the Māra of death and the Māra of defilements; as subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death because it has the nature of birth, aging, sickness, and death; as subject to sorrow, lamentation, and despair because it is a cause of sorrow, lamentation, and despair; as of a nature to be defiled because it is an object for the defilements of craving, views, and misconduct. Thus one contemplates by way of the contemplation of impermanence and so on, which has been explained in detail.

Ettha hi aniccato, palokato, calato, pabhaṅguto, addhuvato, vipariṇāmadhammato, asārakato, vibhavato, saṅkhatato, maraṇadhammatoti ekekasmiṃ khandhe dasa dasa katvā paññāsa aniccānupassanāni. Parato, rittato, tucchato, suññato, anattatoti ekekasmiṃ khandhe pañca pañca katvā pañcavīsati anattānupassanāni. Sesāni dukkhato, rogatotiādīni ekekasmiṃ khandhe pañcavīsati pañcavīsati katvā pañcavīsatisataṃ dukkhānupassanānīti.

Herein, the ten aspects for each aggregate—as impermanent, as perishable, as unstable, as crumbling, as transient, as subject to change, as essenceless, as subject to passing away, as conditioned, and as subject to death—make fifty contemplations of impermanence. The five aspects for each aggregate—as alien, as empty, as hollow, as void, and as not-self—make twenty-five contemplations of not-self. The remaining twenty-five aspects for each aggregate—as suffering, as a disease, and so on—make one hundred and twenty-five contemplations of suffering.

Iccassa iminā dvisatabhedena aniccādisammasanena pañcakkhandhe sammasato taṃ nayavipassanāsaṅkhātaṃ aniccadukkhānattasammasanaṃ thiraṃ hoti. Idaṃ tāvettha pāḷinayānusārena sammasanārambhavidhānaṃ.

Thus, for one who contemplates the five aggregates with this contemplation of impermanence and so on in its two hundred divisions, that contemplation of impermanence, suffering, and not-self, known as insight by way of method, becomes firm. This, now, is the procedure for beginning contemplation according to the canonical method.

Indriyatikkhakāraṇanavakakathā

The Discourse on the Nine Causes for the Sharpness of the Faculties

699. Yassa pana evaṃ nayavipassanāya yogaṃ karotopi nayavipassanā na sampajjati, tena “navahākārehi indriyāni tikkhāni bhavanti – uppannuppannānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ khayameva passati, tattha ca sakkaccakiriyāya sampādeti, sātaccakiriyāya sampādeti, sappāyakiriyāya sampādeti, samādhissa ca nimittaggāhena, bojjhaṅgānañca anupavattanatāya, kāye ca jīvite ca [V 2.0248] anapekkhataṃ upaṭṭhāpeti, tattha ca abhibhuyya nekkhammena, antarā ca abyosānenā”ti evaṃ vuttānaṃ navannaṃ ākārānaṃ vasena indriyāni tikkhāni katvā pathavīkasiṇaniddese vuttanayena satta asappāyāni vajjetvā satta sappāyāni sevamānena kālena rūpaṃ sammasitabbaṃ, kālena arūpaṃ. Rūpaṃ sammasantena rūpassa nibbatti passitabbā.

699. But for one who, though practicing methodical insight in this way, does not succeed in it, the faculties should be sharpened by nine methods. It is said: 'The faculties become sharp by nine factors: one sees only the destruction of formations as they arise; one accomplishes this with reverence; one accomplishes this with perseverance; one accomplishes this with suitable application; by grasping the sign of concentration; by the continuous application of the enlightenment factors; one establishes non-attachment to the body and life; by overcoming through renunciation; and by not flagging in the interim.' Having sharpened the faculties by means of these nine factors as stated, and having avoided the seven unsuitable things and cultivated the seven suitable ones in the way described in the exposition on the earth kasiṇa, one should contemplate materiality at the appropriate time and immateriality at the appropriate time. While contemplating materiality, one should perceive the origination of materiality.

Rūpanibbattipassanākārakathā

The Discourse on the Mode of Contemplating the Origination of Materiality

700. Seyyathidaṃ [M 2.0249] – idaṃ rūpaṃ nāma kammādivasena catūhi kāraṇehi nibbattati. Tattha sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ rūpaṃ nibbattamānaṃ paṭhamaṃ kammato nibbattati. Paṭisandhikkhaṇeyeva hi gabbhaseyyakānaṃ tāva tisantativasena vatthu-kāya-bhāvadasakasaṅkhātāni tiṃsa rūpāni nibbattanti, tāni ca kho paṭisandhicittassa uppādakkhaṇeyeva. Yathā ca uppādakkhaṇe, tathā ṭhitikkhaṇepi bhaṅgakkhaṇepi.

700. It is as follows: this so-called materiality arises from four causes, beginning with kamma. Therein, for all beings, when materiality arises, it first arises from kamma. For at the very moment of rebirth-linking, in the case of womb-born beings, thirty material phenomena—reckoned as the base-decad, the body-decad, and the sex-decad—arise by way of three decads. And they arise at the very arising-moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness. And just as at the arising-moment, so too at the presence-moment and the dissolution-moment.

Tattha rūpaṃ dandhanirodhaṃ garuparivatti, cittaṃ khippanirodhaṃ lahuparivatti. Tenāha – “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, citta”nti (a. ni. 1.48). Rūpe dharanteyeva hi soḷasavāre bhavaṅgacittaṃ uppajjitvā nirujjhati. Cittassa uppādakkhaṇopi ṭhitikkhaṇopi bhaṅgakkhaṇopi ekasadisā. Rūpassa pana uppādabhaṅgakkhaṇāyeva lahukā, tehi sadisā. Ṭhitikkhaṇo pana mahā, yāva soḷasa cittāni uppajjitvā nirujjhanti, tāva vattati. Paṭisandhicittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ ṭhānappattaṃ purejātaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya dutiyaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ uppajjati. Tena saddhiṃ uppannaṃ ṭhānappattaṃ purejātaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya tatiyaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ uppajjati. Iminā nayena yāvatāyukaṃ cittappavatti veditabbā. Āsannamaraṇassa pana ekameva ṭhānappattaṃ purejātaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya soḷasa cittāni uppajjanti.

Therein, materiality is slow to cease and heavy in its turning, while consciousness is quick to cease and light in its turning. Therefore, it is said: 'Bhikkhus, I do not see a single thing that turns so quickly as this consciousness, bhikkhus.' For while one material phenomenon endures, the life-continuum consciousness arises and ceases sixteen times. The arising-moment, presence-moment, and dissolution-moment of consciousness are of equal duration. For materiality, however, only the arising- and dissolution-moments are brief, like those of consciousness. But its presence-moment is long, lasting for as long as sixteen consciousnesses arise and cease. The second consciousness, the life-continuum, arises depending on the pre-arisen physical base that arose at the arising-moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness and has reached its presence-moment. The third consciousness, the life-continuum, arises depending on the pre-arisen physical base that arose together with the second and has reached its presence-moment. In this way, the process of consciousness should be understood to continue for the entire lifespan. But for one nearing death, sixteen consciousnesses arise depending on a single pre-arisen physical base that has reached its presence-moment.

Paṭisandhicittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ rūpaṃ paṭisandhicittato uddhaṃ soḷasamena cittena saddhiṃ nirujjhati. Ṭhānakkhaṇe uppannaṃ sattarasamassa uppādakkhaṇena saddhiṃ nirujjhati. Bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannaṃ sattarasamassa ṭhānakkhaṇaṃ patvā nirujjhati. Yāva pavatti nāma atthi, evameva pavattati. Opapātikānampi sattasantativasena sattati rūpāni evameva pavattanti.

The materiality that arose at the arising-moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases together with the sixteenth consciousness subsequent to the rebirth-linking consciousness. That which arose at the presence-moment ceases together with the arising-moment of the seventeenth subsequent consciousness. That which arose at the dissolution-moment ceases upon reaching the presence-moment of the seventeenth subsequent consciousness. As long as the process of existence continues, it proceeds in just this manner. For spontaneously born beings as well, seventy material phenomena, by way of seven series of decads, proceed in just this way.

701. Tattha [V 2.0249] kammaṃ, kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kammapaccayaṃ, kammapaccayacittasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kammapaccayaāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ, kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānanti esa vibhāgo veditabbo. Tattha kammaṃ nāma kusalākusalacetanā. Kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma vipākakkhandhā ca, cakkhudasakādi samasattatirūpañca. Kammapaccayaṃ nāma tadeva, kammaṃ hi kammasamuṭṭhānassa upatthambhakapaccayopi hoti. Kammapaccayacittasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma vipākacittasamuṭṭhānaṃ rūpaṃ. Kammapaccayaāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma kammasamuṭṭhānarūpesu [M 2.0250] ṭhānappattā ojā aññaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, tatrāpi ojā ṭhānaṃ patvā aññanti evaṃ catasso vā pañca vā pavattiyo ghaṭeti. Kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma kammajatejodhātu ṭhānappattā utusamuṭṭhānaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, tatrāpi utu aññaṃ ojaṭṭhamakanti evaṃ catasso vā pañca vā pavattiyo ghaṭeti. Evaṃ tāva kammajarūpassa nibbatti passitabbā.

701. Herein, the following distinction should be understood: kamma, kamma-originated, kamma-as-condition, kamma-conditioned-consciousness-originated, kamma-conditioned-nutriment-originated, and kamma-conditioned-temperature-originated. Herein, kamma is wholesome and unwholesome volition. Kamma-originated are the resultant aggregates and the seventy kinds of materiality beginning with the eye-decad. Kamma-as-condition is that very same thing, for kamma is also a supporting condition for what is kamma-originated. Kamma-conditioned-consciousness-originated is materiality originated by resultant consciousness. Kamma-conditioned-nutriment-originated is when the nutritive essence that has reached its presence-moment in kamma-originated materiality generates another octad with nutritive essence as the eighth; there too, the nutritive essence, having reached its presence-moment, generates another—thus it produces four or five successions. Kamma-conditioned-temperature-originated is when the kamma-born heat element that has reached its presence-moment generates a temperature-originated octad with nutritive essence as the eighth; there too, the temperature generates another octad—thus it produces four or five successions. In this way, first, the origination of kamma-born materiality should be seen.

702. Cittajesupi cittaṃ, cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ, cittapaccayaṃ, cittapaccayaāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ, cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhānanti esa vibhāgo veditabbo. Tattha cittaṃ nāma ekūnanavuticittāni.

702. Among the consciousness-born phenomena, too, the following distinction should be understood: consciousness, consciousness-originated, consciousness-as-condition, consciousness-conditioned-nutriment-originated, and consciousness-conditioned-temperature-originated. Herein, consciousness refers to the eighty-nine kinds of consciousness.

Tesu dvattiṃsa cittāni, chabbīsekūnavīsati;

Soḷasa rūpiriyāpathaviññattijanakā matā.

Among these, thirty-two, twenty-six, nineteen, and sixteen consciousnesses are known with respect to the generation of materiality, posture, and intimation.

Kāmāvacarato hi aṭṭha kusalāni, dvādasākusalāni, manodhātuvajjā dasa kiriyā, kusalakiriyato dve abhiññācittānīti dvattiṃsa cittāni rūpaṃ, iriyāpathaṃ, viññattiñca janenti. Vipākavajjāni sesadasarūpāvacarāni, aṭṭha arūpāvacarāni, aṭṭha lokuttaracittānīti chabbīsati cittāni rūpaṃ, iriyāpathañca janayanti, na viññattiṃ. Kāmāvacare dasa bhavaṅgacittāni, rūpāvacare pañca, tisso manodhātuyo, ekā vipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātusomanassasahagatāti ekūnavīsati cittāni rūpameva janayanti, na iriyāpathaṃ, na viññattiṃ. Dvepañcaviññāṇāni, sabbasattānaṃ paṭisandhicittaṃ, khīṇāsavānaṃ cuticittaṃ, cattāri āruppavipākānīti soḷasa cittāni neva rūpaṃ janayanti, na iriyāpathaṃ, na viññattiṃ. Yāni cettha rūpaṃ janenti, tāni na ṭhitikkhaṇe, bhaṅgakkhaṇe vā, tadā hi cittaṃ dubbalaṃ hoti. Uppādakkhaṇe pana balavaṃ, tasmā taṃ tadā purejātaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti.

For, from the sense-sphere, eight wholesome, twelve unwholesome, ten functional (excluding the mind-element), and two consciousnesses of supernormal knowledge—these thirty-two types of consciousness produce materiality, posture, and intimation. The ten non-resultant fine-material-sphere consciousnesses, the eight non-resultant immaterial-sphere consciousnesses, and the eight supramundane consciousnesses—these twenty-six types of consciousness produce materiality and posture, but not intimation. The ten sense-sphere life-continuum consciousnesses, the five fine-material-sphere ones, the three mind-elements, and the one joy-accompanied resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element—these nineteen types of consciousness produce only materiality, not posture or intimation. The two sets of five sense-consciousnesses, the rebirth-linking consciousness of all beings, the death consciousness of the arahants, and the four immaterial resultants—these sixteen types of consciousness produce neither materiality, nor posture, nor intimation. Among these, those that do produce materiality do not do so at the presence-moment or the dissolution-moment, for then the consciousness is weak. But at the arising-moment it is strong; therefore, at that time, it generates materiality depending on the pre-arisen physical base.

Cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0250] nāma tayo arūpino khandhā, “saddanavakaṃ, kāyaviññatti, vacīviññatti, ākāsadhātu, lahutā, mudutā, kammaññatā, upacayo, santatī”ti sattarasavidhaṃ rūpañca. Cittapaccayaṃ nāma “pacchājātā cittacetasikā dhammā purejātassa imassa kāyassā”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.11) evaṃ vuttaṃ catusamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ. Cittapaccayaāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma cittasamuṭṭhānarūpesu ṭhānappattā [M 2.0251] ojā aññaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, evaṃ dve tisso pavattiyo ghaṭeti. Cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma cittasamuṭṭhāno utu ṭhānappatto aññaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, evaṃ dve tisso pavattiyo ghaṭeti. Evaṃ cittajarūpassa nibbatti passitabbā.

What is called ‘consciousness-originated’ comprises the three immaterial aggregates and seventeen kinds of materiality, namely: the sound-nonad, bodily intimation, verbal intimation, the space element, lightness, softness, wieldiness, growth, and continuity. What is called ‘consciousness-as-condition’ is the materiality originated from the four sources, as it is said: ‘Subsequently arisen consciousness and mental factors are a condition for this pre-arisen body’ (Paᅩᅩh. 1.1.11). What is called ‘consciousness-conditioned-nutriment-originated’ is when the nutritive essence that has reached its presence-moment in consciousness-originated materiality generates another octad with nutritive essence as the eighth; in this way, it connects two or three successions. What is called ‘consciousness-conditioned-temperature-originated’ is when the temperature originated by consciousness has reached its presence-moment and generates another octad with nutritive essence as the eighth; in this way, it connects two or three successions. Thus, the arising of consciousness-born materiality should be seen.

703. Āhārajesupi āhāro, āhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ, āhārapaccayaṃ, āhārapaccayaāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ, āhārapaccayautusamuṭṭhānanti esa vibhāgo veditabbo. Tattha āhāro nāma kabaḷīkāro āhāro. Āhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma upādiṇṇaṃ kammajarūpaṃ paccayaṃ labhitvā tattha patiṭṭhāya ṭhānappattāya ojāya samuṭṭhāpitaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ, ākāsadhātu, lahutā, mudutā, kammaññatā, upacayo, santatīti cuddasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ. Āhārapaccayaṃ nāma “kabaḷīkāro āhāro imassa kāyassa āhārapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.15) evaṃ vuttaṃ catusamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ. Āhārapaccayaāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma āhārasamuṭṭhānesu rūpesu ṭhānappattā ojā aññaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, tatrāpi ojā aññanti evaṃ dasadvādasavāre pavattiṃ ghaṭeti. Ekadivasaṃ paribhuttāhāro sattāhampi upatthambheti. Dibbā pana ojā ekamāsaṃ dvemāsampi upatthambheti. Mātarā paribhuttāhāropi dārakassa sarīraṃ pharitvā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Sarīre makkhitāhāropi rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Kammajāhāro upādiṇṇakāhāro nāma. Sopi ṭhānappatto rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, tatrāpi ojā aññaṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti evaṃ catasso vā pañca vā pavattiyo ghaṭeti. Āhārapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma āhārasamuṭṭhānā tejodhātu ṭhānappattā utusamuṭṭhānaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tatrāyaṃ āhāro āhārasamuṭṭhānānaṃ janako hutvā paccayo hoti, sesānaṃ nissayāhāraatthiavigatavasenāti evaṃ āhārajarūpassa nibbatti passitabbā.

703. Regarding things born of nutriment, this distinction should be understood: nutriment, nutriment-originated, conditioned by nutriment, nutriment-conditioned and nutriment-originated, and nutriment-conditioned and temperature-originated. Herein, ‘nutriment’ means edible food. ‘Nutriment-originated’ refers to the fourteen kinds of material form—the nutritive-essence-octad, the space element, lightness, softness, wieldiness, growth, and continuity—produced by the nutritive essence that has reached its presence-moment, having obtained as its support the clung-to kamma-born matter and become established therein. ‘Conditioned by nutriment’ refers to the material form with four origins, as stated: “Edible food is a condition for this body by way of nutriment condition.” ‘Nutriment-conditioned and nutriment-originated’ means that the nutritive essence, having reached its presence-moment among nutriment-originated material forms, produces another nutritive-essence-octad; and there too, the nutritive essence produces another—thus it sets the process in motion for ten or twelve rounds. Food consumed in a single day supports for up to seven days. But divine nutritive essence supports for one or two months. The food consumed by a mother also pervades the child’s body and produces material form. Even food smeared on the body produces material form. The nutritive essence in kamma-born matter is called ‘nutriment in what is clung-to.’ That too, having reached its presence-moment, produces material form; and there too, the nutritive essence produces another—thus it sets in motion four or five processes. ‘Nutriment-conditioned and temperature-originated’ means that the heat element from nutriment-originated matter, having reached its presence-moment, produces a temperature-originated nutritive-essence-octad. Herein, this nutriment becomes a condition by being a generator of nutriment-originated phenomena; for the others, it is a condition by way of dependence, nutriment, presence, and non-disappearance. Thus the arising of nutriment-born material form should be seen.

704. Utujesupi utu, utusamuṭṭhānaṃ, utupaccayaṃ, utupaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ, utupaccayaāhārasamuṭṭhānanti esa vibhāgo veditabbo. Tattha utu nāma catusamuṭṭhānā tejodhātu, uṇhautu sītautūti evaṃ panesa duvidho hoti. Utusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma catusamuṭṭhāno utu upādiṇṇakaṃ paccayaṃ labhitvā ṭhānappatto sarīre rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Taṃ saddanavakaṃ, ākāsadhātu[M 2.0252][V 2.0251], lahutā, mudutā, kammaññatā, upacayo, santatīti pannarasavidhaṃ hoti. Utupaccayaṃ nāma utu catusamuṭṭhānikarūpānaṃ pavattiyā ca vināsassa ca paccayo hoti. Utupaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma utusamuṭṭhānā tejodhātu ṭhānappattā aññaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, tatrāpi utu aññanti evaṃ dīghampi addhānaṃ anupādiṇṇapakkhe ṭhatvāpi utusamuṭṭhānaṃ pavattatiyeva. Utupaccayaāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma utusamuṭṭhānā ṭhānappattā ojā aññaṃ ojaṭṭhamakaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, tatrāpi ojā aññanti evaṃ dasadvādasavāre pavattiṃ ghaṭeti. Tatrāyaṃ utu utusamuṭṭhānānaṃ janako hutvā paccayo hoti, sesānaṃ nissayaatthiavigatavasenāti evaṃ utujarūpassa nibbatti passitabbā. Evañhi rūpassa nibbattiṃ passanto kālena rūpaṃ sammasati nāma.

704. Regarding things born of temperature, this distinction should be understood: temperature, temperature-originated, conditioned by temperature, temperature-conditioned and temperature-originated, and temperature-conditioned and nutriment-originated. Herein, ‘temperature’ refers to the heat element with four origins; it is twofold, as heat-temperature and cold-temperature. ‘Temperature-originated’ means that the temperature with four origins, having obtained the clung-to as its support and reached its presence-moment, produces material form in the body. This comprises fifteen kinds: the sound-nonad, the space element, lightness, softness, wieldiness, growth, and continuity. ‘Conditioned by temperature’ means that temperature is a condition for the occurrence and cessation of the material forms with four origins. ‘Temperature-conditioned and temperature-originated’ means that the heat element from temperature-originated matter, having reached its presence-moment, produces another nutritive-essence-octad; and there too, the temperature produces another. Thus, temperature-originated phenomena continue to occur even over a long period in the non-clung-to sphere. ‘Temperature-conditioned and nutriment-originated’ means that the nutritive essence from temperature-originated matter, having reached its presence-moment, produces another nutritive-essence-octad; and there too, the nutritive essence produces another—thus it sets the process in motion for ten or twelve rounds. Herein, this temperature becomes a condition by being a generator of temperature-originated phenomena; for the others, it is a condition by way of dependence, presence, and non-disappearance. Thus the arising of temperature-born material form should be seen. For one who sees the arising of material form in this way is called one who contemplates material form at the proper time.

Arūpanibbattipassanākārakathā

The Exposition on the Way of Seeing the Arising of the Immaterial

705. Yathā ca rūpaṃ sammasantena rūpassa, evaṃ arūpaṃ sammasantenapi arūpassa nibbatti passitabbā. Sā ca kho ekāsīti lokiyacittuppādavaseneva.

705. Just as one contemplating material form should see the arising of material form, so too one contemplating the immaterial should see the arising of the immaterial. And this occurs by way of the eighty-one kinds of mundane consciousness.

Seyyathidaṃ – idañhi arūpaṃ nāma purimabhave āyūhitakammavasena paṭisandhiyaṃ tāva ekūnavīsaticittuppādappabhedaṃ nibbattati. Nibbattanākāro panassa paṭiccasamuppādaniddese vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Tadeva paṭisandhicittassa anantaracittato paṭṭhāya bhavaṅgavasena, āyupariyosāne cutivasena. Yaṃ tattha kāmāvacaraṃ, taṃ chasu dvāresu balavārammaṇe tadārammaṇavasena.

That is to say, this so-called immaterial first arises at rebirth-linking, due to kamma accumulated in a previous existence, as the nineteen kinds of consciousness. The manner of its arising should be understood in the way explained in the Exposition of Dependent Origination. That same consciousness, from the consciousness immediately following the rebirth-linking consciousness, proceeds by way of the life-continuum, and at the end of the lifespan, by way of the death consciousness. Whatever among this is of the sense sphere, that arises by way of registering consciousness at the six doors when the object is strong.

Pavatte pana asambhinnattā cakkhussa āpāthagatattā rūpānaṃ ālokasannissitaṃ manasikārahetukaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ nibbattati saddhiṃ sampayuttadhammehi. Cakkhupasādassa hi ṭhitikkhaṇe ṭhitippattameva rūpaṃ cakkhuṃ ghaṭṭeti. Tasmiṃ ghaṭṭite dvikkhattuṃ bhavaṅgaṃ uppajjitvā nirujjhati. Tato tasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjati. Tadanantaraṃ tadeva rūpaṃ passamānaṃ kusalavipākaṃ akusalavipākaṃ vā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tato tadeva rūpaṃ sampaṭicchamānā vipākamanodhātu. Tato tadeva rūpaṃ santīrayamānā vipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu. Tato tadeva rūpaṃ vavatthāpayamānā kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu [V 2.0252] upekkhāsahagatā[M 2.0253]. Tato paraṃ kāmāvacarakusalākusalakiriyacittesu ekaṃ vā upekkhāsahagatāhetukaṃ cittaṃ pañca satta vā javanāni. Tato kāmāvacarasattānaṃ ekādasasu tadārammaṇacittesu javanānurūpaṃ yaṃkiñci tadārammaṇanti. Esa nayo sesadvāresupi. Manodvāre pana mahaggatacittānipi uppajjantīti. Evaṃ chasu dvāresu arūpassa nibbatti passitabbā. Evañhi arūpassa nibbattiṃ passanto kālena arūpaṃ sammasati nāma.

But during the course of existence, when the eye is not impaired and a form has come into its focus, eye-consciousness arises, supported by light and caused by attention, together with its associated mental states. For a form that has reached its static phase impinges on the eye sensitivity at its static moment. When it has impinged, the life-continuum arises and ceases twice. Then, performing the function of adverting to that same object, the functional mind-element arises. Immediately after, seeing that same form, eye-consciousness, which is either wholesome-resultant or unwholesome-resultant, arises. Then, receiving that same form, the resultant mind-element arises. Then, investigating that same form, the resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element arises. Then, determining that same form, the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element accompanied by equanimity arises. After that, one of the sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, or functional consciousnesses runs for five or seven moments as impulsion; or a rootless consciousness accompanied by equanimity arises. Then, for sense-sphere beings, from among the eleven registering consciousnesses, a certain registering consciousness suitable to the impulsion arises. This is the method in the remaining doors as well. In the mind door, however, even sublime consciousnesses arise. Thus the arising of the immaterial should be seen in the six doors. For one who sees the arising of the immaterial in this way is called one who at times contemplates the immaterial.

Evaṃ kālena rūpaṃ kālena arūpaṃ sammasitvāpi tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā anukkamena paṭipajjamāno eko paññābhāvanaṃ sampādeti.

Thus, by contemplating material form at times and the immaterial at other times, and having applied the three characteristics, a certain one who practices in sequence accomplishes the development of wisdom.

Rūpasattakasammasanakathā

The Discussion on the Sevenfold Contemplation of Form

706. Aparo rūpasattakaarūpasattakavasena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhāre sammasati. Tattha ādānanikkhepanato, vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamato, āhāramayato, utumayato, kammajato, cittasamuṭṭhānato, dhammatārūpatoti imehi ākārehi āropetvā sammasanto rūpasattakavasena āropetvā sammasati nāma. Tenāhu porāṇā –

706. Another person contemplates formations by applying the three characteristics by way of the sevenfold contemplation of form and the sevenfold contemplation of the immaterial. Herein, one who contemplates by applying the characteristics through these modes—(1) by taking up and laying down, (2) by aging and dissolution, (3) as nutriment-originated, (4) as temperature-originated, (5) as kamma-born, (6) as mind-originated, and (7) as form by its intrinsic nature—is said to contemplate by applying them by way of the sevenfold contemplation of form. Thus the ancients have said:

“Ādānanikkhepanato, vayovuḍḍhatthagāmito;

Āhārato ca ututo, kammato cāpi cittato;

Dhammatārūpato satta, vitthārena vipassatī”ti.

“By taking up and laying down, by aging and dissolution; by nutriment and temperature, by kamma and also by mind; as form by its intrinsic nature—these seven, one contemplates in detail.”

Tattha ādānanti paṭisandhi. Nikkhepananti cuti. Iti yogāvacaro imehi ādānanikkhepehi ekaṃ vassasataṃ paricchinditvā saṅkhāresu tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti. Kathaṃ? Etthantare sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā. Kasmā? Uppādavayavattito, vipariṇāmato, tāvakālikato, niccapaṭikkhepato ca. Yasmā pana uppannā saṅkhārā ṭhitiṃ pāpuṇanti, ṭhitiyaṃ jarāya kilamanti, jaraṃ patvā avassaṃ bhijjanti, tasmā abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanato, dukkhamato dukkhavatthuto, sukhapaṭikkhepato ca dukkhā. Yasmā ca “uppannā saṅkhārā ṭhitiṃ mā pāpuṇantu, ṭhānappattā mā jīrantu, jarappattā mā bhijjantū”ti imesu tīsu [M 2.0254] ṭhānesu kassaci vasavattibhāvo [V 2.0253] natthi, suññā tena vasavattanākārena, tasmā suññato, assāmikato, avasavattito, attapaṭikkhepato ca anattāti.

Herein, 'taking up' means relinking, and 'laying down' means death. Thus the practitioner, having delimited a span of a hundred years by this taking up and laying down, applies the three characteristics to formations. How? Within this interval, all formations are impermanent. Why? Because they are subject to arising and passing away, because they change, because they are temporary, and because they are the opposite of the permanent. Furthermore, since arisen formations attain a static phase, are afflicted by aging in that phase, and having reached old age, inevitably break up, they are suffering on account of constant oppression, because they are suffering, because they are a basis for suffering, and because they are the opposite of pleasure. And since no one has any power of control over these three states—'May arisen formations not attain a static phase; may those that have attained a static phase not age; may those that have reached old age not break up!'—they are empty of this characteristic of control. Therefore, because they are empty, masterless, and uncontrollable, and because they are the opposite of a self, they are not-self.

707. Evaṃ ādānanikkhepanavasena vassasataparicchinne rūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā tato paraṃ vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamato āropeti. Tattha vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamo nāma vayavasena vuḍḍhassa vaḍḍhitassa rūpassa atthaṅgamo. Tassa vasena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetīti attho.

707. In this way, having applied the three characteristics to form delimited by a hundred years by way of taking up and laying down, thereafter one applies them by way of aging and dissolution. Herein, 'aging and dissolution' means the dissolution of form that has grown and aged by way of age. The meaning is that one applies the three characteristics by means of this.

Kathaṃ? So tameva vassasataṃ paṭhamavayena majjhimavayena pacchimavayenāti tīhi vayehi paricchindati. Tattha ādito tettiṃsa vassāni paṭhamavayo nāma. Tato catuttiṃsa majjhimavayo nāma. Tato tettiṃsa pacchimavayo nāmāti. Iti imehi tīhi vayehi paricchinditvā, “paṭhamavaye pavattaṃ rūpaṃ majjhimavayaṃ appatvā tattheva nirujjhati, tasmā taṃ aniccaṃ. Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Majjhimavaye pavattarūpampi pacchimavayaṃ appatvā tattheva nirujjhati, tasmā tampi aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā. Pacchimavaye tettiṃsa vassāni pavattarūpampi maraṇato paraṃ gamanasamatthaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā tampi aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

How? He delimits that same hundred years by three ages: the first age, the middle age, and the last age. Herein, the first thirty-three years are called the first age; the next thirty-four years, the middle age; and the subsequent thirty-three years, the last age. Thus, having delimited it by these three ages, he applies the three characteristics: “The form that occurred in the first age ceases right there without reaching the middle age; therefore it is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. The form that occurred in the middle age also ceases right there without reaching the last age; therefore it too is impermanent, suffering, and not-self. Even the form that occurred during the thirty-three years of the last age is in no way capable of continuing on beyond death; therefore it too is impermanent, suffering, and not-self.”

708. Evaṃ paṭhamavayādivasena vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamato tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā puna “mandadasakaṃ, khiḍḍādasakaṃ, vaṇṇadasakaṃ, baladasakaṃ, paññādasakaṃ, hānidasakaṃ, pabbhāradasakaṃ, vaṅkadasakaṃ, momūhadasakaṃ, sayanadasaka”nti imesaṃ dasannaṃ dasakānaṃ vasena vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamato tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

708. Thus having applied the three characteristics by way of aging and dissolution based on the stages of life beginning with the first age, he again applies the three characteristics by way of aging and dissolution based on these ten decades: the decade of infancy, the decade of play, the decade of beauty, the decade of strength, the decade of wisdom, the decade of decline, the decade of stooping, the decade of crookedness, the decade of dotage, and the decade of lying down.

Tattha dasakesu tāva vassasatajīvino puggalassa paṭhamāni dasa vassāni mandadasakaṃ nāma, tadā hi so mando hoti capalo kumārako. Tato parāni dasa khiḍḍādasakaṃ nāma, tadā hi so khiḍḍāratibahulo hoti. Tato parāni dasa vaṇṇadasakaṃ nāma, tadā hissa vaṇṇāyatanaṃ vepullaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tato parāni dasa baladasakaṃ nāma, tadā hissa balañca thāmo ca vepullaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tato parāni dasa paññādasakaṃ nāma, tadā hissa paññā suppatiṭṭhitā hoti, pakatiyā kira dubbalapaññassāpi [M 2.0255] tasmiṃ kāle appamattakā paññā uppajjatiyeva. Tato parāni dasa hānidasakaṃ nāma, tadā hissa khiḍḍārativaṇṇabalapaññā parihāyanti. Tato parāni [V 2.0254] dasa pabbhāradasakaṃ nāma, tadā hissa attabhāvo purato pabbhāro hoti. Tato parāni dasa vaṅkadasakaṃ nāma, tadā hissa attabhāvo naṅgalakoṭi viya vaṅko hoti. Tato parāni dasa momūhadasakaṃ nāma. Tadā hi so momūho hoti, kataṃ kataṃ pamussati. Tato parāni dasa sayanadasakaṃ nāma, vassasatiko hi sayanabahulova hoti.

Herein, among the decades, for a person who lives a hundred years, the first ten years are called the decade of infancy, for then he is a dull and fickle boy. The next ten years are called the decade of play, for then he is much given to play and amusement. The next ten years are called the decade of beauty, for then his beauty reaches its peak. The next ten years are called the decade of strength, for then his strength and stamina reach their peak. The next ten years are called the decade of wisdom, for then his wisdom becomes well-established; indeed, it is said that even for one naturally weak in wisdom, some small measure of wisdom arises at that time. The next ten years are called the decade of decline, for then his delight in play, his beauty, strength, and wisdom all decline. The next ten years are called the decade of stooping, for then his body stoops forward. The next ten years are called the decade of crookedness, for then his body becomes crooked like the tip of a plough. The next ten years are called the decade of dotage, for then he becomes muddled and forgets what he has done. The next ten years are called the decade of lying down, for a centenarian is indeed much given to lying down.

Tatrāyaṃ yogī etesaṃ dasakānaṃ vasena vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamato tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetuṃ iti paṭisañcikkhati – “paṭhamadasake pavattarūpaṃ dutiyadasakaṃ appatvā tattheva nirujjhati, tasmā taṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā. Dutiyadasake…pe… navamadasake pavattarūpaṃ dasamadasakaṃ appatvā tattheva nirujjhati. Dasamadasake pavattarūpaṃ punabbhavaṃ appatvā idheva nirujjhati, tasmā tampi aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

Herein, this practitioner reflects thus to apply the three characteristics by way of aging and dissolution based on these ten decades: “The form that occurred in the first decade ceases right there without reaching the second decade; therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and not-self. The form that occurred in the second decade… and so on… the form that occurred in the ninth decade ceases right there without reaching the tenth decade. The form that occurred in the tenth decade ceases right here without reaching a new existence; therefore, it too is impermanent, suffering, and not-self.” Thus he applies the three characteristics.

709. Evaṃ dasakavasena vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamato tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā puna tadeva vassasataṃ pañcapañcavassavasena vīsatikoṭṭhāse katvā vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamato tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti. Kathaṃ? So hi iti paṭisañcikkhati – “paṭhame vassapañcake pavattarūpaṃ dutiyaṃ vassapañcakaṃ appatvā tattheva nirujjhati, tasmā taṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā. Dutiye vassapañcake pavattarūpaṃ tatiyaṃ…pe… ekūnavīsatime vassapañcake pavattarūpaṃ vīsatimaṃ vassapañcakaṃ appatvā tattheva nirujjhati. Vīsatime vassapañcake pavattarūpaṃ maraṇato paraṃ gamanasamatthaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā tampi aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti.

709. Thus, having applied the three characteristics by way of aging and dissolution based on the decades, he again divides that same hundred years into twenty portions of five years each and applies the three characteristics by way of aging and dissolution. How? He reflects thus: “The form that occurred in the first five-year period ceases right there without reaching the second five-year period; therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and not-self. The form that occurred in the second five-year period… and so on… the form that occurred in the nineteenth five-year period ceases right there without reaching the twentieth five-year period. The form that occurred in the twentieth five-year period is in no way capable of continuing on beyond death; therefore, it too is impermanent, suffering, and not-self.”

Evaṃ vīsatikoṭṭhāsavasena vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamato tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā puna pañcavīsati koṭṭhāse katvā catunnaṃ catunnaṃ vassānaṃ vasena āropeti. Tato tettiṃsa koṭṭhāse katvā tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vassānaṃ vasena, paññāsa koṭṭhāse katvā dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ vassānaṃ vasena, sataṃ koṭṭhāse katvā ekekavassavasena. Tato ekaṃ vassaṃ tayo [M 2.0256] koṭṭhāse katvā vassānahemantagimhesu tīsu utūsu ekekautuvasena tasmiṃ vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

Thus, having applied the three characteristics by way of aging and dissolution based on the twenty portions, he again applies them by making twenty-five portions of four years each; then by making thirty-three portions of three years each; then by making fifty portions of two years each; and then by making a hundred portions of single years. Then, dividing one year into three portions, he applies the three characteristics to that form subject to aging and dissolution by way of each single season among the three seasons—the rainy season, winter, and summer.

Kathaṃ? “Vassāne catumāsaṃ pavattarūpaṃ hemantaṃ appatvā tattheva niruddhaṃ. Hemante pavattarūpaṃ gimhaṃ appatvā tattheva niruddhaṃ. Gimhe pavattarūpaṃ puna vassānaṃ appatvā tattheva niruddhaṃ, tasmā taṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti. Evaṃ āropetvā puna ekaṃ vassaṃ cha koṭṭhāse katvā – “vassāne [V 2.0255] dvemāsaṃ pavattarūpaṃ saradaṃ appatvā tattheva niruddhaṃ. Sarade pavattarūpaṃ hemantaṃ. Hemante pavattarūpaṃ sisiraṃ. Sisire pavattarūpaṃ vasantaṃ. Vasante pavattarūpaṃ gimhaṃ. Gimhe pavattarūpaṃ puna vassānaṃ appatvā tattheva niruddhaṃ, tasmā aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti evaṃ tasmiṃ vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

How? “The form that occurred for four months in the rainy season has ceased right there without reaching winter. The form that occurred in winter has ceased right there without reaching summer. The form that occurred in summer has ceased right there without reaching the rainy season again; therefore it is impermanent, suffering, and not-self.” Having applied the characteristics thus, he again divides one year into six portions: “The form that occurred for two months in the rainy season has ceased right there without reaching autumn. The form that occurred in autumn has ceased without reaching winter. The form that occurred in winter has ceased without reaching the cool season. The form that occurred in the cool season has ceased without reaching spring. The form that occurred in spring has ceased without reaching summer. The form that occurred in summer has ceased right there without reaching the rainy season again; therefore it is impermanent, suffering, and not-self.” In this way he applies the three characteristics to that form subject to aging and dissolution.

Evaṃ āropetvā tato kāḷajuṇhavasena – “kāḷe pavattarūpaṃ juṇhaṃ appatvā. Juṇhe pavattarūpaṃ kāḷaṃ appatvā tattheva niruddhaṃ, tasmā aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti. Tato rattindivavasena – “rattiṃ pavattarūpaṃ divasaṃ appatvā tattheva niruddhaṃ. Divasaṃ pavattarūpampi rattiṃ appatvā tattheva niruddhaṃ, tasmā aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti. Tato tadeva rattindivaṃ pubbaṇhādivasena cha koṭṭhāse katvā – “pubbaṇhe pavattarūpaṃ majjhanhaṃ appatvā. Majjhanhe pavattarūpaṃ sāyanhaṃ. Sāyanhe pavattarūpaṃ paṭhamayāmaṃ. Paṭhamayāme pavattarūpaṃ majjhimayāmaṃ. Majjhimayāme pavattarūpaṃ pacchimayāmaṃ appatvā tattheva niruddhaṃ. Pacchimayāme pavattarūpaṃ puna pubbaṇhaṃ appatvā tattheva niruddhaṃ, tasmā aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

Having applied it thus, then by way of the dark and bright fortnights: ‘The form that occurred in the dark fortnight, not having reached the bright fortnight, ceases right there. The form that occurred in the bright fortnight, not having reached the dark fortnight, ceases right there; therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and not-self’—he applies the three characteristics. Then by way of night and day: ‘The form that occurred at night, not having reached the day, ceases right there. And the form that occurred during the day, not having reached the night, ceases right there; therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and not-self’—he applies the three characteristics. Then, having divided that same night and day into six parts by way of the forenoon and so on: ‘The form that occurred in the forenoon, not having reached midday… The form that occurred at midday, not having reached the evening… The form that occurred in the evening, not having reached the first watch… The form that occurred in the first watch, not having reached the middle watch… The form that occurred in the middle watch, not having reached the last watch, ceases right there. The form that occurred in the last watch, not having reached the forenoon again, ceases right there; therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and not-self’—he applies the three characteristics.

710. Evaṃ āropetvā puna tasmiṃyeva rūpe abhikkamapaṭikkamaālokanavilokanasamiñjanapasāraṇavasena – “abhikkame pavattarūpaṃ paṭikkamaṃ appatvā tattheva nirujjhati. Paṭikkame pavattarūpaṃ ālokanaṃ. Ālokane pavattarūpaṃ vilokanaṃ. Vilokane pavattarūpaṃ samiñjanaṃ. Samiñjane pavattarūpaṃ pasāraṇaṃ appatvā tattheva nirujjhati. Tasmā aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

710. Having applied it thus, again on that very materiality, by way of advancing, retreating, looking ahead, looking around, bending, and stretching: ‘Materiality that arises in advancing, not having reached retreating, ceases right there. Materiality that arises in retreating, not having reached looking ahead… Materiality that arises in looking ahead, not having reached looking around… Materiality that arises in looking around, not having reached bending… Materiality that arises in bending, not having reached stretching, ceases right there. Therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self’—he applies the three characteristics.

Tato ekapadavāraṃ uddharaṇa atiharaṇavītiharaṇavossajjanasannikkhepanasannirumbhanavasena cha koṭṭhāse karoti.

Then he divides the section on a single footstep into six parts by way of: lifting up, carrying forward, moving aside, lowering, placing down, and pressing firmly.

Tattha [M 2.0257] uddharaṇaṃ nāma pādassa bhūmito ukkhipanaṃ. Atiharaṇaṃ nāma purato haraṇaṃ. Vītiharaṇaṃ nāma khāṇukaṇṭakadīghajātiādīsu kiñcideva disvā ito cito ca pādasañcāraṇaṃ. Vossajjanaṃ nāma pādassa heṭṭhā oropanaṃ. Sannikkhepanaṃ nāma pathavītale ṭhapanaṃ. Sannirumbhanaṃ nāma puna pāduddharaṇakāle pādassa pathaviyā saddhiṃ abhinippīḷanaṃ. Tattha uddharaṇe pathavīdhātu [V 2.0256] āpodhātūti dve dhātuyo omattā honti mandā, itarā dve adhimattā honti balavatiyo. Tathā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesu. Vossajjane tejodhātu vāyodhātūti dve dhātuyo omattā honti mandā, itarā dve adhimattā honti balavatiyo. Tathā sannikkhepanasannirumbhanesu. Evaṃ cha koṭṭhāse katvā tesaṃ vasena tasmiṃ vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

Herein, ‘lifting up’ is the lifting of the foot from the ground. ‘Carrying forward’ is the carrying of it forward. ‘Moving aside’ is the moving of the foot here and there on seeing something like a stump, thorn, or snake. ‘Lowering’ is the placing of the foot down. ‘Placing down’ is the setting of it on the surface of the earth. ‘Pressing firmly’ is the firm pressing of the foot against the earth at the time of lifting the foot again. Therein, during lifting up, the earth element and the water element are deficient and weak, while the other two elements are excessive and strong. It is similar during carrying forward and moving aside. During lowering, the fire element and the air element are deficient and weak, while the other two elements are excessive and strong. It is similar during placing down and pressing firmly. Having thus made six divisions, by means of them he applies the three characteristics to that materiality subject to growth and decline.

Kathaṃ? So iti paṭisañcikkhati – “yā uddharaṇe pavattā dhātuyo, yāni ca tadupādāyarūpāni, sabbe te dhammā atiharaṇaṃ appatvā ettheva nirujjhanti, tasmā aniccā dukkhā anattā. Tathā atiharaṇe pavattā vītiharaṇaṃ. Vītiharaṇe pavattā vossajjanaṃ. Vossajjane pavattā sannikkhepanaṃ. Sannikkhepane pavattā sannirumbhanaṃ appatvā ettheva nirujjhanti. Iti tattha tattha uppannā itaraṃ itaraṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ appatvā tattha tattheva pabbaṃ pabbaṃ sandhi sandhi odhi odhi hutvā tattakapāle pakkhittatilā viya taṭataṭāyantā saṅkhārā bhijjanti. Tasmā aniccā dukkhā anattā”ti. Tassevaṃ pabbapabbagate saṅkhāre vipassato rūpasammasanaṃ sukhumaṃ hoti.

How? He reflects thus: ‘The elements that have arisen in lifting, and the materiality derived from them—all these phenomena, not having reached carrying forward, cease right there; therefore they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Similarly, those that have arisen in carrying forward, not having reached moving aside… those that have arisen in moving aside, not having reached lowering… those that have arisen in lowering, not having reached placing down… those that have arisen in placing down, not having reached pressing firmly, cease right there. Thus what has arisen in each case, not having reached the next division, breaks up right there. Section by section, joint by joint, limit by limit, the formations break apart, crackling like sesame seeds thrown on a hot pan. Therefore they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self.’ For one who thus sees with insight the formations proceeding section by section, the comprehension of materiality becomes subtle.

711. Sukhumatte ca panassa idaṃ opammaṃ. Eko kira dārutiṇukkādīsu kataparicayo adiṭṭhapubbapadīpo paccantavāsiko nagaramāgamma antarāpaṇe jalamānaṃ padīpaṃ disvā ekaṃ purisaṃ pucchi ambho “kiṃ nāmetaṃ evaṃ manāpa”nti? Tamenaṃ so āha “kimettha manāpaṃ, padīpo nāmesa telakkhayena vaṭṭikkhayena ca gatamaggopissa na paññāyissatī”ti. Tamañño evamāha “idaṃ oḷārikaṃ, imissā hi vaṭṭiyā anupubbena ḍayhamānāya tatiyabhāge tatiyabhāge jālā itarītaraṃ padesaṃ appatvāva nirujjhissatī”ti.
