Tamañño evamāha “idampi oḷārikaṃ, imissā hi aṅgulaṅgulantare aḍḍhaṅgulaḍḍhaṅgulantare [M 2.0258] tantumhi tantumhi aṃsumhi aṃsumhi jālā itarītaraṃ aṃsuṃ appatvāva nirujjhissati. Aṃsuṃ pana muñcitvā na sakkā jālaṃ paññāpetu”nti.

711. On the subtlety of this, there is this simile. It is said that a certain border-dweller, who was familiar with wood, grass, torches, and the like, but had never before seen a lamp, came to the city. Seeing a burning lamp in the market street, he asked a man, ‘Friend, what is this so pleasing?’ That one told him: ‘What is pleasing about this? This is called a lamp. When the oil and the wick are exhausted, even the path it has taken will not be known.’ Another told him: ‘That is coarse. For as this wick burns down successively, in each third part the flame will cease without ever reaching the other part.’ Yet another told him: ‘This too is coarse. For in this, in each finger-breadth, in each half finger-breadth, in each thread, and in each fiber, the flame will cease without ever reaching the next fiber. But apart from the fiber, it is not possible to point out the flame.’

Tattha “telakkhayena vaṭṭikkhayena ca padīpassa gatamaggopi na paññāyissatī”ti purisassa ñāṇaṃ viya yogino ādānanikkhepanato vassasatena paricchinnarūpe tilakkhaṇāropanaṃ. “Vaṭṭiyā tatiyabhāge tatiyabhāge jālā itarītaraṃ padesaṃ appatvāva nirujjhissatī”ti [V 2.0257] purisassa ñāṇaṃ viya yogino vassasatassa tatiyakoṭṭhāsaparicchinne vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamarūpe tilakkhaṇāropanaṃ. “Aṅgulaṅgulantare jālā itarītaraṃ appatvāva nirujjhissatī”ti purisassa ñāṇaṃ viya yogino dasavassa pañcavassa catuvassa tivassa dvivassa ekavassa paricchinne rūpe tilakkhaṇāropanaṃ. “Aḍḍhaṅgulaḍḍhaṅgulantare jālā itarītaraṃ appatvāva nirujjhissatī”ti purisassa ñāṇaṃ viya yogino ekekautuvasena ekaṃ vassaṃ tidhā, chadhā ca vibhajitvā catumāsa-dvimāsaparicchinne rūpe tilakkhaṇāropanaṃ. “Tantumhi tantumhi jālā itarītaraṃ appatvāva nirujjhissatī”ti purisassa ñāṇaṃ viya yogino kāḷajuṇhavasena, rattindivavasena, ekarattindivaṃ cha koṭṭhāse katvā pubbaṇhādivasena ca paricchinne rūpe tilakkhaṇāropanaṃ. “Aṃsumhi aṃsumhi jālā itarītaraṃ appatvāva nirujjhissatī”ti purisassa ñāṇaṃ viya yogino abhikkamādivasena ceva uddharaṇādīsu ca ekekakoṭṭhāsavasena paricchinne rūpe tilakkhaṇāropananti.

Herein, the yogi’s application of the three characteristics to materiality limited by a hundred years from its taking up and laying down is like the man’s knowledge that ‘when the oil and the wick are exhausted, even the path the lamp has taken will not be known.’ The yogi’s application of the three characteristics to materiality subject to growth and decline, limited by a third of a hundred years, is like the man’s knowledge that ‘in each third part of the wick, the flame will cease without ever reaching the other part.’ The yogi’s application of the three characteristics to materiality limited by ten years, five years, four years, three years, two years, and one year is like the man’s knowledge that ‘in each finger-breadth, the flame will cease without reaching the other.’ The yogi’s application of the three characteristics to materiality limited by four months and two months—by dividing a single year into three or six parts by way of the seasons—is like the man’s knowledge that ‘in each half finger-breadth, the flame will cease without reaching the other.’ The yogi’s application of the three characteristics to materiality limited by way of the dark and bright fortnights, by way of night and day, and by way of the forenoon, etc., having divided a single night and day into six parts, is like the man’s knowledge that ‘in each thread, the flame will cease without reaching the other.’ The yogi’s application of the three characteristics to materiality limited by way of each single division in advancing, etc., and in lifting, etc., is like the man’s knowledge that ‘in each fiber, the flame will cease without reaching the other.’

712. So evaṃ nānākārehi vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā puna tadeva rūpaṃ visaṅkharitvā āhāramayādivasena cattāro koṭṭhāse katvā ekekakoṭṭhāse tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti. Tatrāssa āhāramayaṃ rūpaṃ chātasuhitavasena pākaṭaṃ hoti. Chātakāle samuṭṭhitaṃ rūpaṃ hi jhattaṃ hoti kilantaṃ, jhāmakhāṇuko viya, aṅgārapacchiyaṃ nilīnakāko viya ca dubbaṇṇaṃ dussaṇṭhitaṃ. Suhitakāle samuṭṭhitaṃ dhātaṃ pīṇitaṃ mudu siniddhaṃ phassavantaṃ hoti. So taṃ pariggahetvā “chātakāle [M 2.0259] pavattarūpaṃ suhitakālaṃ appatvā ettheva nirujjhati. Suhitakāle samuṭṭhitampi chātakālaṃ appatvā ettheva nirujjhati, tasmā taṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti evaṃ tattha tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

712. Having thus in various ways applied the three characteristics to materiality subject to growth and decline, he again dismantles that same materiality, and having made four divisions by way of what is nutriment-originated and so on, he applies the three characteristics to each division. Therein, for him, nutriment-originated materiality becomes manifest by way of hunger and satiety. For materiality that arises at a time of hunger is withered and weary, like a burnt stump, and like a crow hiding in a basket of coals it is discolored and ill-formed. Materiality that arises at a time of satiety is supported, plump, soft, smooth, and pleasant to touch. Having grasped this, he applies the three characteristics to it thus: ‘Materiality that arises at a time of hunger, not having reached a time of satiety, ceases right there. And what arises at a time of satiety, not having reached a time of hunger, ceases right there; therefore it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.’

713. Utumayaṃ sītuṇhavasena pākaṭaṃ hoti. Uṇhakāle samuṭṭhitaṃ rūpaṃ hi jhattaṃ hoti kilantaṃ dubbaṇṇaṃ. Sītautunā samuṭṭhitaṃ rūpaṃ dhātaṃ pīṇitaṃ siniddhaṃ hoti. So taṃ pariggahetvā “uṇhakāle pavattarūpaṃ sītakālaṃ appatvā ettheva nirujjhati. Sītakāle pavattarūpaṃ uṇhakālaṃ appatvā ettheva nirujjhati, tasmā taṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti evaṃ tattha tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

713. What is temperature-originated becomes manifest by way of cold and heat. For materiality that arises at a time of heat is withered, weary, and discolored. Materiality that arises from cold temperature is supported, plump, and smooth. Having grasped this, he applies the three characteristics to it thus: ‘Materiality that arises at a time of heat, not having reached a time of cold, ceases right there. Materiality that arises at a time of cold, not having reached a time of heat, ceases right there; therefore it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.’

714. Kammajaṃ āyatanadvāravasena pākaṭaṃ hoti. Cakkhudvārasmiṃ hi cakkhukāyabhāvadasakavasena [V 2.0258] tiṃsa kammajarūpāni, upatthambhakāni pana tesaṃ utucittāhārasamuṭṭhānāni catuvīsatīti catupaṇṇāsa honti. Tathā sotaghānajivhādvāresu. Kāyadvāre kāyabhāvadasakavasena ceva utusamuṭṭhānādivasena ca catucattālīsa. Manodvāre hadayavatthukāyabhāvadasakavasena ceva utusamuṭṭhānādivasena ca catupaṇṇāsameva.

714. What is kamma-originated becomes manifest by way of the sense-base doors. In the eye-door, there are thirty kamma-originated material phenomena by way of the eye-decad, body-decad, and sex-decad. The supporting phenomena for them, arisen from temperature, consciousness, and nutriment, are twenty-four, thus there are fifty-four. It is similar in the ear, nose, and tongue doors. In the body-door, by way of the body-decad and sex-decad, and by way of what is arisen from temperature and so on, there are forty-four. In the mind-door, by way of the heart-base-decad, body-decad, and sex-decad, and by way of what is arisen from temperature and so on, there are likewise fifty-four.

So sabbampi taṃ rūpaṃ pariggahetvā “cakkhudvāre pavattarūpaṃ sotadvāraṃ appatvā ettheva nirujjhati. Sotadvāre pavattarūpaṃ ghānadvāraṃ. Ghānadvāre pavattarūpaṃ jivhādvāraṃ. Jivhādvāre pavattarūpaṃ kāyadvāraṃ. Kāyadvāre pavattarūpaṃ manodvāraṃ appatvā ettheva nirujjhati, tasmā taṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti evaṃ tattha tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

Having grasped all that materiality, he applies the three characteristics to it thus: ‘The materiality arising at the eye-door, not reaching the ear-door, ceases right there. The materiality arising at the ear-door, not reaching the nose-door, ceases right there. The materiality arising at the nose-door, not reaching the tongue-door, ceases right there. The materiality arising at the tongue-door, not reaching the body-door, ceases right there. The materiality arising at the body-door, not reaching the mind-door, ceases right there; therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.’

715. Cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ somanassitadomanassitavasena pākaṭaṃ hoti, somanassitakāle uppannaṃ hi rūpaṃ siniddhaṃ mudu pīṇitaṃ phassavantaṃ hoti. Domanassitakāle uppannaṃ jhattaṃ kilantaṃ dubbaṇṇaṃ hoti. So taṃ pariggahetvā “somanassitakāle pavattarūpaṃ domanassitakālaṃ appatvā ettheva nirujjhati. Domanassitakāle pavattarūpaṃ somanassitakālaṃ appatvā ettheva nirujjhati, tasmā taṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti evaṃ tattha tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti.

715. Mind-originated materiality becomes manifest by way of joy and sadness. For the materiality that arises at a time of joy is smooth, soft, plump, and pleasant to touch, while the materiality that arises at a time of sadness is withered, weary, and discolored. Having grasped this, he applies the three characteristics to it thus: ‘The materiality that arises during a time of joy ceases right there without reaching a time of sadness. The materiality that arises during a time of sadness ceases right there without reaching a time of joy; therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self.’

Tassevaṃ [M 2.0260] cittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ pariggahetvā tattha tilakkhaṇaṃ āropayato ayamattho pākaṭo hoti –

For one who thus grasps mind-originated materiality and applies the three characteristics to it, this meaning becomes manifest:

Jīvitaṃ attabhāvo ca, sukhadukkhā ca kevalā;

Ekacittasamāyuttā, lahuso vattate khaṇo.

Life, individuality, and happiness and suffering entire, are conjoined with a single consciousness; the moment passes swiftly.

Cullāsīti sahassāni, kappaṃ tiṭṭhanti ye marū;

Na tveva tepi tiṭṭhanti, dvīhi cittehi samohitā.

Those gods who live for eighty-four thousand aeons, even they do not endure endowed with two consciousnesses.

Ye niruddhā marantassa, tiṭṭhamānassa vā idha;

Sabbeva sadisā khandhā, gatā appaṭisandhikā.

Those aggregates that have ceased for one who is dying, or for one who is living here—all are alike, gone without relinking in rebirth.

Anantarā [V 2.0259] ca ye bhaggā, ye ca bhaggā anāgate;

Tadantarā niruddhānaṃ, vesamaṃ natthi lakkhaṇe.

Of those that broke up in the immediate past and those that will break up in the future, and of those ceasing in between, there is no difference in their characteristic.

Anibbattena na jāto, paccuppannena jīvati;

Cittabhaṅgā mato loko, paññatti paramatthiyā.

One is not born from the unproduced; one lives by the present. With the breakup of consciousness, the world is dead: this is a designation in the ultimate sense.

Anidhānagatā bhaggā, puñjo natthi anāgate;

Nibbattā yepi tiṭṭhanti, āragge sāsapūpamā.

Having broken up, they are not stored away; no heap exists for the future. Even those that have arisen and exist are like a mustard seed on an awl's point.

Nibbattānañca dhammānaṃ, bhaṅgo nesaṃ purakkhato;

Palokadhammā tiṭṭhanti, purāṇehi amissitā.

For phenomena that have arisen, their breakup is imminent. They exist as things of a perishable nature, unmixed with the old.

Adassanato āyanti, bhaggā gacchantudassanaṃ;

Vijjuppādova ākāse, uppajjanti vayanti cāti. (mahāni. 10);

From an unseen state they come; having broken up, they go to an unseen state. Like a flash of lightning in the sky, they arise and pass away.

716. Evaṃ āhāramayādīsu tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā puna dhammatārūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti. Dhammatārūpaṃ nāma bahiddhā anindriyabaddhaṃ ayalohatipusīsasuvaṇṇarajatamuttāmaṇiveḷuriyasaṅkhasilāpavāḷalohitaṅgamasāragallabhūmipāsāṇapabbatatiṇarukkhalatādibhedaṃ vivaṭṭakappato paṭṭhāya uppajjanakarūpaṃ. Tadassa asokaṅkurādivasena pākaṭaṃ hoti.

716. Thus, having applied the three characteristics to nutriment-originated materiality and the others, he then applies the three characteristics to materiality as a natural process. Materiality as a natural process is external materiality not bound up with the faculties, of such kinds as iron, bronze, tin, lead, gold, silver, pearls, gems, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystal, coral, rubies, cat's-eye gems, earth, stones, mountains, grass, trees, and creepers—materiality that has been arising since the aeon of evolution. This becomes manifest to him by way of the Ashoka sprout and so on.

Asokaṅkuraṃ hi āditova tanurattaṃ hoti, tato dvīhatīhaccayena ghanarattaṃ, puna dvīhatīhaccayena mandarattaṃ, tato taruṇapallavavaṇṇaṃ, tato [M 2.0261] pariṇatapallavavaṇṇaṃ, tato haritapaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ. Tato nīlapaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ. Tato nīlapaṇṇavaṇṇakālato paṭṭhāya sabhāgarūpasantatimanuppabandhāpayamānaṃ saṃvaccharamattena paṇḍupalāsaṃ hutvā vaṇṭato chijjitvā patati.

For the Ashoka sprout is at first light red; then after two or three days it becomes deep red; again after two or three days it becomes pale red; then the color of a young shoot; then the color of a mature shoot; then the color of a green leaf; then the color of a dark leaf. Then, from the time it has the color of a dark leaf, maintaining a continuity of similar materiality, after about a year it becomes a yellow leaf and, breaking off from the stalk, it falls.

So taṃ pariggahetvā “tanurattakāle pavattarūpaṃ ghanarattakālaṃ appatvā nirujjhati. Ghanarattakāle pavattarūpaṃ mandarattakālaṃ. Mandarattakāle pavattarūpaṃ taruṇapallavavaṇṇakālaṃ. Taruṇapallavavaṇṇakāle pavattaṃ pariṇatapallavavaṇṇakālaṃ. Pariṇatapallavavaṇṇakāle pavattaṃ haritapaṇṇavaṇṇakālaṃ[V 2.0260]. Haritapaṇṇakāle pavattaṃ nīlapaṇṇavaṇṇakālaṃ. Nīlapaṇṇavaṇṇakāle pavattaṃ paṇḍupalāsakālaṃ. Paṇḍupalāsakāle pavattaṃ vaṇṭato chijjitvā patanakālaṃ appatvāva nirujjhati, tasmā taṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropeti, evaṃ tattha tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā iminā nayena sabbampi dhammatārūpaṃ sammasati.

Having grasped that, he reflects: 'The form that arises at the time it is light red ceases without reaching the time it is deep red. The form that arises at the time it is deep red ceases without reaching the time it is pale red. The form that arises at the time it is pale red ceases without reaching the time it is the color of a young shoot. The form that arises at the time it is the color of a young shoot ceases without reaching the time it is the color of a mature shoot. The form that arises at the time it is the color of a mature shoot ceases without reaching the time it is the color of a green leaf. The form that arises at the time it is the color of a green leaf ceases without reaching the time it is the color of a dark leaf. The form that arises at the time it is the color of a dark leaf ceases without reaching the time it is a yellow leaf. The form that arises at the time it is a yellow leaf ceases without even reaching the time it breaks from the stalk and falls. Therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and not-self.' Thus he applies the three characteristics to it. Having applied the three characteristics to it in this way, by this method he contemplates all natural materiality.

Evaṃ tāva rūpasattakavasena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhāre sammasati.

Thus far one contemplates formations by applying the three characteristics by way of the sevenfold materiality.

Arūpasattakasammasanakathā

Discourse on the Sevenfold Contemplation of the Immaterial

717. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “arūpasattakavasenā”ti, tattha ayaṃ mātikā – kalāpato, yamakato, khaṇikato, paṭipāṭito, diṭṭhiugghāṭanato, mānasamugghāṭanato, nikantipariyādānatoti.

717. Now, as to what was said, "by way of the sevenfold immaterial," this is the outline: by groups, by pairs, by moments, in sequence, by uprooting view, by thoroughly uprooting conceit, and by the complete exhaustion of delight.

Tattha kalāpatoti phassapañcamakā dhammā. Kathaṃ kalāpato sammasatīti? Idha bhikkhu iti paṭisañcikkhati – “ye ime ‘kesā aniccā dukkhā anattā’ti sammasane uppannā phassapañcamakā dhammā, ye ca ‘lomā…pe… matthaluṅgaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā’ti sammasane uppannā phassapañcamakā dhammā, sabbe te itarītaraṃ appatvā pabbaṃpabbaṃ odhiodhi hutvā tattakapāle pakkhittatilā viya taṭataṭāyantā vinaṭṭhā, tasmā aniccā dukkhā anattā”ti. Ayaṃ tāva visuddhikathāyaṃ nayo.

Herein, "by groups" refers to the phenomena in the group of five with contact as the fifth. How does one contemplate by groups? Here, a bhikkhu reflects thus: "Those phenomena in the group of five with contact as the fifth that arose during the contemplation 'Hairs of the head are impermanent, suffering, not-self,' and those phenomena in the group of five with contact as the fifth that arose during the contemplation 'Hairs of the body ... the brain in the head is impermanent, suffering, not-self'—all these have perished without reaching one another, having become separated section by section, boundary by boundary, crackling like sesame seeds thrown on a hot pan. Therefore, they are impermanent, suffering, and not-self." This, for now, is the method in the Discourse on Purification.

Ariyavaṃsakathāyaṃ pana “heṭṭhā rūpasattake sattasu ṭhānesu ‘rūpaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā’ti pavattaṃ cittaṃ aparena cittena ‘aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā’ti sammasanto ‘kalāpato [M 2.0262] sammasatī’ti” vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttataraṃ. Tasmā sesānipi teneva nayena vibhajissāma.

However, in the Discourse on the Noble Lineages it is said: 'When one contemplates with a subsequent mind, as "impermanent, suffering, not-self," the mind that had occurred in the seven instances of the sevenfold materiality below while contemplating "materiality is impermanent, suffering, not-self," this is called "contemplating by groups."' This is more suitable. Therefore, we will analyze the remaining items by this same method.

718. Yamakatoti idha bhikkhu ādānanikkheparūpaṃ “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti sammasitvā tampi cittaṃ aparena cittena “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti sammasati. Vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamarūpaṃ, āhāramayaṃ, utumayaṃ, kammajaṃ, cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ, dhammatārūpaṃ “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti [V 2.0261] sammasitvā tampi cittaṃ aparena cittena “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti sammasati. Evaṃ yamakato sammasati nāma.

718. As to 'by pairs': here a bhikkhu, having contemplated the materiality of taking up and putting down as "impermanent, suffering, not-self," then contemplates that very mind with a subsequent mind as "impermanent, suffering, not-self." Having contemplated the materiality of aging, growth, and passing away; materiality produced by nutriment, by temperature, by kamma, by mind; and natural materiality as "impermanent, suffering, not-self," he then contemplates that very mind with a subsequent mind as "impermanent, suffering, not-self." Thus is it called contemplating by pairs.

719. Khaṇikatoti idha bhikkhu ādānanikkheparūpaṃ “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti sammasitvā taṃ paṭhamacittaṃ dutiyacittena, dutiyaṃ tatiyena, tatiyaṃ catutthena, catutthaṃ pañcamena “etampi aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti sammasati. Vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamarūpaṃ, āhāramayaṃ, utumayaṃ, kammajaṃ, cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ, dhammatārūpaṃ “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti sammasitvā taṃ paṭhamacittaṃ dutiyacittena, dutiyaṃ tatiyena, tatiyaṃ catutthena, catutthaṃ pañcamena “etampi aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti sammasati. Evaṃ rūpapariggāhakacittato paṭṭhāya cattāri cattāri cittāni sammasanto khaṇikato sammasati nāma.

719. As to 'by moments': here a bhikkhu, having contemplated the materiality of taking up and putting down as "impermanent, suffering, not-self," contemplates that first mind with a second mind, the second with a third, the third with a fourth, and the fourth with a fifth, as "this too is impermanent, suffering, not-self." Having contemplated the materiality of aging, growth, and passing away; materiality produced by nutriment, by temperature, by kamma, by mind; and natural materiality as "impermanent, suffering, not-self," he contemplates that first mind with a second mind, the second with a third, the third with a fourth, and the fourth with a fifth, as "this too is impermanent, suffering, not-self." Thus, starting from the mind that grasps materiality, by contemplating the minds four times in this manner, this is called contemplating by moments.

720. Paṭipāṭitoti ādānanikkheparūpaṃ “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti sammasitvā taṃ paṭhamacittaṃ dutiyacittena, dutiyaṃ tatiyena, tatiyaṃ catutthena…pe… dasamaṃ ekādasamena “etampi aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti sammasati. Vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamarūpaṃ, āhāramayaṃ, utumayaṃ, kammajaṃ, cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ, dhammatārūpaṃ “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti sammasitvā taṃ paṭhamacittaṃ dutiyacittena, dutiyaṃ tatiyena, tatiyaṃ catutthena…pe… dasamaṃ ekādasamena “etampi aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti evaṃ vipassanā paṭipāṭiyā sakalampi divasabhāgaṃ sammasituṃ vaṭṭeyya. Yāva dasamacittasammasanā pana rūpakammaṭṭhānampi arūpakammaṭṭhānampi paguṇaṃ hoti. Tasmā dasameyeva ṭhapetabbanti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sammasanto paṭipāṭito sammasati nāma.

720. As to 'in sequence': having contemplated the materiality of taking up and putting down as "impermanent, suffering, not-self," one contemplates that first mind with a second mind, the second with a third, the third with a fourth ... the tenth with an eleventh, as "this too is impermanent, suffering, not-self." Having contemplated the materiality of aging, growth, and passing away; materiality produced by nutriment, by temperature, by kamma, by mind; and natural materiality as "impermanent, suffering, not-self," one contemplates that first mind with a second mind, the second with a third, the third with a fourth ... the tenth with an eleventh, as "this too is impermanent, suffering, not-self." In this way, by the sequence of insight, one could contemplate for an entire portion of the day. However, up to the contemplation of the tenth mind, both the material meditation subject and the immaterial meditation subject become proficient. Therefore, it is said that one should stop at the tenth. Contemplating in this way is called contemplating in sequence.

721. Diṭṭhiugghāṭanato mānaugghāṭanato nikantipariyādānatoti imesu tīsu visuṃ sammasananayo nāma natthi. Yaṃ panetaṃ heṭṭhā [M 2.0263] rūpaṃ, idha ca arūpaṃ pariggahitaṃ, taṃ passanto rūpārūpato uddhaṃ aññaṃ sattaṃ nāma na passati. Sattassa adassanato paṭṭhāya sattasaññā ugghāṭitā hoti. Sattasaññaṃ ugghāṭitacittena saṅkhāre pariggaṇhato diṭṭhi nuppajjati. Diṭṭhiyā anuppajjamānāya diṭṭhi ugghāṭitā nāma hoti. Diṭṭhiugghāṭitacittena saṅkhāre pariggaṇhato māno nuppajjati. Māne anuppajjante māno samugghāṭito nāma hoti. Mānasamugghāṭitacittena saṅkhāre pariggaṇhato taṇhā nuppajjati. Taṇhāya anuppajjantiyā nikanti pariyādiṇṇā nāma hotīti idaṃ tāva visuddhikathāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

721. As for 'by the uprooting of view, by the thorough uprooting of conceit, and by the complete exhaustion of delight,' there is no separate method of contemplation for these three. Rather, having apprehended the materiality below and the immateriality here, one does not perceive any being beyond materiality and immateriality. From the non-perception of a being, the perception of a being is uprooted. When, with a mind from which the perception of a being is uprooted, one apprehends formations, no view arises. When no view arises, view is said to be uprooted. When, with a mind from which view is uprooted, one apprehends formations, no conceit arises. When no conceit arises, conceit is said to be thoroughly uprooted. When, with a mind from which conceit is thoroughly uprooted, one apprehends formations, no craving arises. When no craving arises, delight is said to be completely exhausted. This, for now, has been stated in the Discourse on Purification.

Ariyavaṃsakathāyaṃ [V 2.0262] pana “diṭṭhiugghāṭanato mānasamugghāṭanato nikantipariyādānato”ti mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā ayaṃ nayo dassito.

However, in the discourse on the noble lineage, having laid down the matrix: 'from the uprooting of view, from the uprooting of conceit, from the complete abandoning of delight,' this method is shown.

“Ahaṃ vipassāmi, mama vipassanā”ti gaṇhato hi diṭṭhisamugghāṭanaṃ nāma na hoti. “Saṅkhārāva saṅkhāre vipassanti sammasanti vavatthapenti pariggaṇhanti paricchindantī”ti gaṇhato pana diṭṭhiugghāṭanaṃ nāma hoti.

For one who grasps, 'I contemplate, it is my contemplation,' there is no uprooting of view. But for one who grasps, 'It is only formations that contemplate formations, comprehend, determine, apprehend, and delimit them,' there is the uprooting of view.

“Suṭṭhu vipassāmi, manāpaṃ vipassāmī”ti gaṇhato mānasamugghāṭo nāma na hoti. “Saṅkhārāva saṅkhāre vipassanti sammasanti vavatthapenti pariggaṇhanti paricchindantī”ti gaṇhato pana mānasamugghāṭo nāma hoti.

For one who grasps, 'I contemplate well, I contemplate delightfully,' there is no uprooting of conceit. But for one who grasps, 'It is only formations that contemplate formations, comprehend, determine, apprehend, and delimit them,' there is the uprooting of conceit.

“Vipassituṃ sakkomī”ti vipassanaṃ assādentassa nikantipariyādānaṃ nāma na hoti. “Saṅkhārāva saṅkhāre vipassanti sammasanti vavatthapenti pariggaṇhanti paricchindantī”ti gaṇhato pana nikantipariyādānaṃ nāma hoti.

For one who savors insight, thinking, 'I am able to contemplate,' there is no complete abandoning of delight. But for one who grasps, 'It is only formations that contemplate formations, comprehend, determine, apprehend, and delimit them,' there is the complete abandoning of delight.

Sace saṅkhārā attā bhaveyyuṃ, attāti gahetuṃ vaṭṭeyyuṃ, anattā ca pana attāti gahitā, tasmā te avasavattanaṭṭhena anattā, hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā, uppādavayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhāti passato diṭṭhiugghāṭanaṃ nāma hoti.

If formations were self, it would be proper to take them as self. But what is non-self is taken as self. Therefore, for one who sees them as non-self in the sense of being uncontrollable, as impermanent in the sense of ceasing to be after having come to be, and as suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, the uprooting of view occurs.

Sace saṅkhārā niccā bhaveyyuṃ, niccāti gahetuṃ vaṭṭeyyuṃ, aniccā ca pana niccāti gahitā, tasmā te hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā, uppādavayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhā, avasavattanaṭṭhena anattāti passato mānasamugghāṭo nāma hoti.

If formations were permanent, it would be proper to take them as permanent. But what is impermanent is taken as permanent. Therefore, for one who sees them as impermanent in the sense of ceasing to be after having come to be, as suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, and as non-self in the sense of being uncontrollable, the uprooting of conceit occurs.

Sace [M 2.0264] saṅkhārā sukhā bhaveyyuṃ, sukhāti gahetuṃ vaṭṭeyyuṃ, dukkhā ca pana sukhāti gahitā, tasmā te uppādavayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhā, hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā, avasavattanaṭṭhena anattāti passato nikantipariyādānaṃ nāma hoti.

If formations were pleasant, it would be proper to take them as pleasant. But what is suffering is taken as pleasant. Therefore, for one who sees them as suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, as impermanent in the sense of ceasing to be after having come to be, and as non-self in the sense of being uncontrollable, the complete abandoning of delight occurs.

Evaṃ saṅkhāre anattato passantassa diṭṭhisamugghāṭanaṃ nāma hoti. Aniccato passantassa mānasamugghāṭanaṃ [V 2.0263] nāma hoti. Dukkhato passantassa nikantipariyādānaṃ nāma hoti. Iti ayaṃ vipassanā attano attano ṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhatīti.

Thus, for one who sees formations as non-self, the uprooting of view occurs. For one who sees them as impermanent, the uprooting of conceit occurs. For one who sees them as suffering, the complete abandoning of delight occurs. Thus this insight stands in its own proper place.

Evaṃ arūpasattakavasenāpi tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhāre sammasati. Ettāvatā panassa rūpakammaṭṭhānampi arūpakammaṭṭhānampi paguṇaṃ hoti.

In this way, one also comprehends formations by applying the three characteristics by way of the sevenfold comprehension of mentality. With this, both one's form meditation subject and mentality meditation subject become proficient.

722. So evaṃ paguṇarūpārūpakammaṭṭhāno yā upari bhaṅgānupassanato paṭṭhāya pahānapariññāvasena sabbākārato pattabbā aṭṭhārasa mahāvipassanā, tāsaṃ idheva tāva ekadesaṃ paṭivijjhanto tappaṭipakkhe dhamme pajahati.

722. Thus, one who has mastered the meditation subjects of form and mentality, while penetrating here a portion of the eighteen great insights—which are to be attained in all aspects by way of the full understanding of abandoning, beginning from the contemplation of dissolution upwards—abandons the opposing states.

Aṭṭhārasa mahāvipassanā nāma aniccānupassanādikā paññā. Yāsu aniccānupassanaṃ bhāvento niccasaññaṃ pajahati, dukkhānupassanaṃ bhāvento sukhasaññaṃ pajahati, anattānupassanaṃ bhāvento attasaññaṃ pajahati, nibbidānupassanaṃ bhāvento nandiṃ pajahati, virāgānupassanaṃ bhāvento rāgaṃ pajahati, nirodhānupassanaṃ bhāvento samudayaṃ pajahati, paṭinissaggānupassanaṃ bhāvento ādānaṃ pajahati, khayānupassanaṃ bhāvento ghanasaññaṃ pajahati, vayānupassanaṃ bhāvento āyūhanaṃ pajahati, vipariṇāmānupassanaṃ bhāvento dhuvasaññaṃ pajahati, animittānupassanaṃ bhāvento nimittaṃ pajahati, appaṇihitānupassanaṃ bhāvento paṇidhiṃ pajahati, suññatānupassanaṃ bhāvento abhinivesaṃ pajahati, adhipaññādhammavipassanaṃ bhāvento sārādānābhinivesaṃ pajahati, yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ bhāvento sammohābhinivesaṃ pajahati, ādīnavānupassanaṃ bhāvento ālayābhinivesaṃ pajahati, paṭisaṅkhānupassanaṃ bhāvento appaṭisaṅkhaṃ pajahati, vivaṭṭānupassanaṃ bhāvento saṃyogābhinivesaṃ pajahati.

The eighteen great insights are wisdoms such as the contemplation of impermanence. By developing the contemplation of impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence. By developing the contemplation of suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure. By developing the contemplation of non-self, one abandons the perception of self. By developing the contemplation of disenchantment, one abandons delight. By developing the contemplation of dispassion, one abandons passion. By developing the contemplation of cessation, one abandons origination. By developing the contemplation of relinquishment, one abandons grasping. By developing the contemplation of destruction, one abandons the perception of compactness. By developing the contemplation of passing away, one abandons accumulation. By developing the contemplation of change, one abandons the perception of stability. By developing the contemplation of the signless, one abandons the sign. By developing the contemplation of the desireless, one abandons desire. By developing the contemplation of emptiness, one abandons adherence. By developing the higher-wisdom-insight into phenomena, one abandons adherence to grasping at a core. By developing the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, one abandons adherence to delusion. By developing the contemplation of danger, one abandons adherence to clinging. By developing the contemplation of reflection, one abandons non-reflection. By developing the contemplation of turning away, one abandons adherence to the fetters.

Tāsu [M 2.0265] yasmā iminā aniccādilakkhaṇattayavasena saṅkhārā diṭṭhā, tasmā anicca-dukkha-anattānupassanā paṭividdhā honti. Yasmā ca “yā ca aniccānupassanā yā ca animittānupassanā, ime dhammā ekatthā, byañjanameva nānaṃ”. Tathā “yā ca dukkhānupassanā yā ca appaṇihitānupassanā, ime dhammā ekatthā, byañjanameva nānaṃ”. “Yā ca anattānupassanā yā ca suññatānupassanā, ime dhammā ekatthā, byañjanameva nāna”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.227) vuttaṃ. Tasmā tāpi paṭividdhā honti.

Among these, because formations have been seen by way of these three characteristics of impermanence and so forth, the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, and non-self are penetrated. And because it is said: 'The contemplation of impermanence and the contemplation of the signless are the same in meaning, differing only in expression. Similarly, the contemplation of suffering and the contemplation of the desireless are the same in meaning, differing only in expression. The contemplation of non-self and the contemplation of emptiness are the same in meaning, differing only in expression' (Paṭisambhidāmagga I 227), these too are penetrated.

Adhipaññādhammavipassanā [V 2.0264] pana sabbāpi vipassanā. Yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiyā eva saṅgahitaṃ. Iti idampi dvayaṃ paṭividdhameva hoti. Sesesu vipassanāñāṇesu kiñci paṭividdhaṃ, kiñci appaṭividdhaṃ, tesaṃ vibhāgaṃ parato āvikarissāma.

The higher-wisdom-insight into phenomena, however, is all insight. The knowledge and vision of things as they really are is included in the purification by overcoming doubt itself. Thus, this pair is also penetrated. Among the remaining insight-knowledges, some are penetrated and some are not; we will make their distinction clear later.

Yadeva hi paṭividdhaṃ, taṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ “evaṃ paguṇarūpārūpakammaṭṭhāno yā upari bhaṅgānupassanato paṭṭhāya pahānapariññāvasena sabbākārato pattabbā aṭṭhārasa mahāvipassanā. Tāsaṃ idheva tāva ekadesaṃ paṭivijjhanto tappaṭipakkhe dhamme pajahatī”ti.

It is with reference to what has been penetrated that this was said: 'Thus, one who has mastered the meditation subjects of form and mentality, while penetrating here a portion of the eighteen great insights—which are to be attained in all aspects by way of the full understanding of abandoning, beginning from the contemplation of dissolution upwards—abandons the opposing states.'

Udayabbayañāṇakathā

The Explanation of the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away

723. So evaṃ aniccānupassanādipaṭipakkhānaṃ niccasaññādīnaṃ pahānena visuddhañāṇo sammasanañāṇassa pāraṃ gantvā, yaṃ taṃ sammasanañāṇānantaraṃ “paccuppannānaṃ dhammānaṃ vipariṇāmānupassane paññā udayabbayānupassane ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. mātikā 1.6) udayabbayānupassanaṃ vuttaṃ, tassa adhigamāya yogaṃ ārabhati. Ārabhamāno ca saṅkhepato tāva ārabhati. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

723. Thus, with his knowledge purified by abandoning the perception of permanence and so on, the counterparts of the contemplation of impermanence and so on, and having gone beyond the knowledge of comprehension, he undertakes the practice to attain the contemplation of arising and passing away. This, which follows the knowledge of comprehension, is spoken of as 'wisdom in contemplating the alteration of present phenomena, knowledge in the contemplation of arising and passing away' (Paṭis. M. 1:6). When undertaking this, he begins at first in brief. Here is the Pāli text:

“Kathaṃ paccuppannānaṃ dhammānaṃ vipariṇāmānupassane paññā udayabbayānupassane ñāṇaṃ? Jātaṃ rūpaṃ paccuppannaṃ, tassa nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ udayo, vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ vayo, anupassanā ñāṇaṃ. Jātā vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ… jātaṃ cakkhu…pe… jāto bhavo paccuppanno, tassa nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ udayo, vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ vayo, anupassanā ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.49).

'How is there wisdom in contemplating the alteration of present phenomena, knowledge in contemplating arising and passing away? Arisen form is present; its characteristic of production is arising, its characteristic of alteration is passing away; the contemplation of this is knowledge. Arisen feeling… perception… formations… consciousness… arisen eye… up to… arisen becoming is present; its characteristic of production is arising, its characteristic of alteration is passing away; the contemplation of this is knowledge' (Paṭis. M. 1:49).

So [M 2.0266] iminā pāḷinayena jātassa nāmarūpassa nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ jātiṃ uppādaṃ abhinavākāraṃ “udayo”ti, vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ khayaṃ bhaṅgaṃ “vayo”ti samanupassati. So evaṃ pajānāti “imassa nāmarūpassa uppattito pubbe anuppannassa rāsi vā nicayo vā natthi, uppajjamānassāpi rāsito vā nicayato vā āgamanaṃ nāma natthi, nirujjhamānassāpi disāvidisāgamanaṃ nāma natthi, niruddhassāpi ekasmiṃ ṭhāne rāsito nicayato nidhānato avaṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0265] nāma natthi. Yathā pana vīṇāya vādiyamānāya uppannasaddassa neva uppattito pubbe sannicayo atthi, na uppajjamāno sannicayato āgato, na nirujjhamānassa disāvidisāgamanaṃ atthi, na niruddho katthaci sannicito tiṭṭhati, atha kho vīṇañca upavīṇañca purisassa ca tajjaṃ vāyāmaṃ paṭicca ahutvā sambhoti, hutvā paṭiveti. Evaṃ sabbepi rūpārūpino dhammā ahutvā sambhonti, hutvā paṭiventī”ti.

Thus, by this Pāli method, he contemplates the characteristic of origination of arisen name-and-form—birth, arising, a fresh state—as 'arising,' and the characteristic of alteration—dissolution, breaking apart—as 'passing away.' He understands thus: 'Before the arising of this name-and-form, there was no mass or accumulation of the unarisen. When arising, there is no coming from a mass or accumulation. When ceasing, there is no going to any direction. When ceased, there is no remaining as a mass, accumulation, or deposit in any place. Just as when a lute is played, the sound that arises has no prior accumulation before its arising, nor does it come from an accumulation when arising, nor does it go to any direction when ceasing, nor does it remain accumulated anywhere when ceased—but rather, dependent on the lute, the plectrum, and the man's appropriate effort, it comes to be from not having been, and having been, it ceases. So too, all material and immaterial phenomena come to be from not having been, and having been, they cease.'

724. Evaṃ saṅkhepato udayabbayamanasikāraṃ katvā puna yāni etasseva udayabbayañāṇassa vibhaṅge –

724. Having thus briefly attended to arising and passing away, again, in the analysis of this very knowledge of arising and passing away:

“Avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. Taṇhāsamudayā… kammasamudayā… āhārasamudayā rūpasamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. Nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. Rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passanto imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni passati.

'With the arising of ignorance, the arising of form'—he sees the arising of the form aggregate in terms of the arising of conditions. 'With the arising of craving… kamma… nutriment, the arising of form'—he sees the arising of the form aggregate in terms of the arising of conditions. Even when seeing the characteristic of production, he sees the arising of the form aggregate. Seeing the arising of the form aggregate, he sees these five characteristics.

“Avijjānirodhā rūpanirodhoti paccayanirodhaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Taṇhānirodhā… kammanirodhā… āhāranirodhā rūpanirodhoti paccayanirodhaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passantopi imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni passati” (paṭi. ma. 1.50).

'With the cessation of ignorance, form ceases'—he sees the passing away of the form aggregate in terms of the cessation of conditions. 'With the cessation of craving… of kamma… of nutriment, form ceases'—he sees the passing away of the form aggregate in terms of the cessation of conditions. Even when seeing the characteristic of alteration, he sees the passing away of the form aggregate. Even when seeing the passing away of the form aggregate, he sees these five characteristics' (Paṭis. M. 1:50).

Tathā “avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. Taṇhāsamudayā… kammasamudayā… phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. Nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi vedanākkhandhassa [M 2.0267] udayaṃ passati. Vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passanto imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni passati. Avijjānirodhā… taṇhānirodhā… kammanirodhā… phassanirodhā vedanānirodhoti paccayanirodhaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passanto imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni passati” (paṭi. ma. 1.50).

Similarly: 'With the arising of ignorance, the arising of feeling'—he sees the arising of the feeling aggregate in terms of the arising of conditions. 'With the arising of craving… with the arising of kamma… with the arising of contact, the arising of feeling'—he sees the arising of the feeling aggregate in terms of the arising of conditions. Even when seeing the characteristic of production, he sees the arising of the feeling aggregate. Seeing the arising of the feeling aggregate, he sees these five characteristics. 'With the cessation of ignorance… with the cessation of craving… with the cessation of kamma… with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling'—he sees the passing away of the feeling aggregate in terms of the cessation of conditions. Even when seeing the characteristic of alteration, he sees the passing away of the feeling aggregate. Seeing the passing away of the feeling aggregate, he sees these five characteristics' (Paṭis. M. 1:50).

Vedanākkhandhassa [V 2.0266] viya ca saññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇakkhandhānaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso, viññāṇakkhandhassa phassaṭṭhāne “nāmarūpasamudayā, nāmarūpanirodhā”ti –

For the aggregates of perception, formations, and consciousness, it is like for the feeling aggregate. However, there is this distinction: for the consciousness aggregate, in place of 'contact' it is said: 'With the arising of name-and-form... with the cessation of name-and-form...'

Evaṃ ekekassa khandhassa udayabbayadassane dasa dasa katvā paññāsa lakkhaṇāni vuttāni. Tesaṃ vasena evampi rūpassa udayo evampi rūpassa vayo, evampi rūpaṃ udeti, evampi rūpaṃ vetīti paccayato ceva khaṇato ca vitthārena manasikāraṃ karoti.

Thus, for each aggregate, fifty characteristics are spoken of for the seeing of arising and passing away, ten for each. Based on these, he attends in detail to: 'In this way there is the arising of form, in this way its passing away; in this way form arises, in this way it passes away,' considering this both in terms of conditions and in terms of moments.

725. Tassevaṃ manasikaroto “iti kirime dhammā ahutvā sambhonti, hutvā paṭiventī”ti ñāṇaṃ visadataraṃ hoti. Tassevaṃ paccayato ceva khaṇato ca dvedhā udayabbayaṃ passato saccapaṭiccasamuppādanayalakkhaṇabhedā pākaṭā honti.

725. As he thus attends, his knowledge becomes clearer: 'Indeed, these phenomena, not having been, come into being; and having been, they vanish.' For him who thus sees arising and passing away in two ways—by way of conditions and by way of moments—the distinctions concerning the truths, dependent origination, the method, and characteristics become manifest.

726. Yañhi so avijjādisamudayā khandhānaṃ samudayaṃ, avijjādinirodhā ca khandhānaṃ nirodhaṃ passati, idamassa paccayato udayabbayadassanaṃ. Yaṃ pana nibbattilakkhaṇavipariṇāmalakkhaṇāni passanto khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ passati, idamassa khaṇato udayabbayadassanaṃ, uppattikkhaṇeyeva hi nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ. Bhaṅgakkhaṇe ca vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ.

726. For when he sees the arising of the aggregates due to the arising of ignorance and so on, and the cessation of the aggregates due to the cessation of ignorance and so on, this is his seeing of arising and passing away in terms of conditions. But when he sees the arising and passing away of the aggregates by observing the characteristics of production and alteration, this is his seeing of arising and passing away in terms of moments. For the characteristic of production is at the moment of arising, and the characteristic of alteration is at the moment of dissolution.

727. Iccassevaṃ paccayato ceva khaṇato ca dvedhā udayabbayaṃ passato paccayato udayadassanena samudayasaccaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti janakāvabodhato. Khaṇato udayadassanena dukkhasaccaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti jātidukkhāvabodhato. Paccayato vayadassanena nirodhasaccaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti paccayānuppādena paccayavataṃ anuppādāvabodhato. Khaṇato vayadassanena dukkhasaccameva pākaṭaṃ hoti maraṇadukkhāvabodhato. Yañcassa [M 2.0268] udayabbayadassanaṃ, maggovāyaṃ lokikoti maggasaccaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti tatra sammohavighātato.

727. Thus, for one who sees arising and passing away in these two ways—by way of conditions and by way of moments—the truth of origination becomes evident through seeing arising by way of conditions, by comprehending the generative cause. The truth of suffering becomes evident through seeing arising by way of moments, by comprehending the suffering of birth. The truth of cessation becomes evident through seeing passing away by way of conditions, by comprehending the non-arising of things dependent on conditions through the non-arising of their conditions. The truth of suffering becomes evident again through seeing passing away by way of moments, by comprehending the suffering of death. And that seeing of arising and passing away, which is the mundane path, makes the truth of the path evident by dispelling delusion therein.

728. Paccayato cassa udayadassanena anulomo paṭiccasamuppādo pākaṭo hoti, “imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotī”ti (ma. ni. 1.404; saṃ. ni. 2.21; udā. 1) avabodhato. Paccayato vayadassanena paṭilomo paṭiccasamuppādo pākaṭo hoti, “imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.406; saṃ. ni. 2.21; udā. 2) avabodhato[V 2.0267]. Khaṇato pana udayabbayadassanena paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā pākaṭā honti saṅkhatalakkhaṇāvabodhato. Udayabbayavanto hi saṅkhatā, te ca paṭiccasamuppannāti.

728. Furthermore, for one who sees arising by way of conditions, dependent origination in forward order becomes clear, through comprehending, 'When this is, that comes to be' (M I 404; S II 21; Ud 1). By seeing passing away by way of conditions, dependent origination in reverse order becomes clear, through comprehending, 'With the cessation of this, that ceases' (M I 406; S II 21; Ud 2). But by seeing arising and passing away by way of moments, dependently arisen phenomena become clear through comprehending the characteristic of the conditioned. For things that possess arising and passing away are conditioned, and those are dependently arisen.

729. Paccayato cassa udayadassanena ekattanayo pākaṭo hoti hetuphalasambandhena santānassa anupacchedāvabodhato. Atha suṭṭhutaraṃ ucchedadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati. Khaṇato udayadassanena nānattanayo pākaṭo hoti navanavānaṃ uppādāvabodhato. Atha suṭṭhutaraṃ sassatadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati. Paccayato cassa udayabbayadassanena abyāpāranayo pākaṭo hoti dhammānaṃ avasavattibhāvāvabodhato. Atha suṭṭhutaraṃ attadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati. Paccayato pana udayadassanena evaṃdhammatānayo pākaṭo hoti paccayānurūpena phalassa uppādāvabodhato. Atha suṭṭhutaraṃ akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ pajahati.

729. Furthermore, for one who sees arising by way of conditions, the method of unity becomes clear through comprehending the non-interruption of the continuity by the connection of cause and result. Then one thoroughly abandons the view of annihilation. By seeing arising by way of moments, the method of diversity becomes clear through comprehending the arising of ever new phenomena. Then one thoroughly abandons the view of eternalism. Furthermore, by seeing arising and passing away by way of conditions, the method of non-agency becomes clear through comprehending the state of phenomena being beyond control. Then one thoroughly abandons the view of self. But by seeing arising by way of conditions, the method of thusness becomes clear through comprehending the arising of the result in conformity with the condition. Then one thoroughly abandons the view of non-action.

730. Paccayato cassa udayadassanena anattalakkhaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti dhammānaṃ nirīhakattapaccayapaṭibaddhavuttitāvabodhato. Khaṇato udayabbayadassanena aniccalakkhaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti hutvā abhāvāvabodhato, pubbantāparantavivekāvabodhato ca. Dukkhalakkhaṇampi pākaṭaṃ hoti udayabbayehi paṭipīḷanāvabodhato. Sabhāvalakkhaṇampi pākaṭaṃ hoti udayabbayaparicchinnāvabodhato. Sabhāvalakkhaṇe saṅkhatalakkhaṇassa tāvakālikattampi pākaṭaṃ hoti udayakkhaṇe vayassa, vayakkhaṇe ca udayassa abhāvāvabodhatoti.

730. Furthermore, by seeing arising by way of conditions, the characteristic of not-self becomes clear through comprehending that phenomena are without an agent and their occurrence is bound to conditions. By seeing arising and passing away by way of moments, the characteristic of impermanence becomes clear through comprehending their non-existence after having come to be, and through comprehending their voidness of a past and a future. The characteristic of suffering also becomes clear through comprehending the oppression by arising and passing away. The characteristic of own-nature also becomes clear through comprehending that it is defined by arising and passing away. Within the characteristic of own-nature, the temporariness of the characteristic of the conditioned also becomes clear through comprehending the absence of passing away at the moment of arising, and the absence of arising at the moment of passing away.

731. Tassevaṃ pākaṭībhūtasaccapaṭiccasamuppādanayalakkhaṇabhedassa “evaṃ kira nāmime dhammā anuppannapubbā uppajjanti, uppannā nirujjhantī”ti niccanavāva hutvā saṅkhārā [M 2.0269] upaṭṭhahanti. Na kevalañca niccanavā, sūriyuggamane ussāvabindu viya udakabubbuḷo viya udake daṇḍarāji viya āragge sāsapo viya vijjuppādo viya ca parittaṭṭhāyino. Māyāmarīcisupinantaalātacakkagandhabbanagarapheṇakadaliādayo viya assārā nissārāti cāpi upaṭṭhahanti.

731. To one for whom the distinctions of the truths, dependent origination, methods, and characteristics have thus become manifest, formations appear as ever new, in the sense: 'Indeed, these phenomena, not having arisen before, arise; and having arisen, they cease.' And not only as ever new, but they also appear as lasting for a short time, like a dewdrop at sunrise, a bubble on water, a line drawn on water, a mustard seed on the point of an awl, or a flash of lightning. They also appear as coreless and essenceless, like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a whirling firebrand, a city of gandhabbas, foam, a plantain trunk, and so on.

Ettāvatānena “vayadhammameva uppajjati, uppannañca vayaṃ upetī”ti iminā ākārena samapaññāsa lakkhaṇāni paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitaṃ udayabbayānupassanaṃ nāma taruṇavipassanāñāṇaṃ adhigataṃ hoti, yassādhigamā āraddhavipassakoti saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

By this much, having penetrated the fifty characteristics in this manner—'Only that which is of a vanishing nature arises, and what has arisen goes to vanishing'—one has attained the tender insight-knowledge called 'contemplation of arising and passing away.' Through its attainment, one is reckoned as 'one who has commenced insight.'

Vipassanupakkilesakathā

The Account of the Corruptions of Insight

732. Athassa [V 2.0268] imāya taruṇavipassanāya āraddhavipassakassa dasa vipassanupakkilesā uppajjanti. Vipassanupakkilesā hi paṭivedhappattassa ariyasāvakassa ceva vippaṭipannakassa ca nikkhittakammaṭṭhānassa kusītapuggalassa nuppajjanti. Sammāpaṭipannakassa pana yuttapayuttassa āraddhavipassakassa kulaputtassa uppajjantiyeva.

732. Then, for this one who has commenced insight with this tender insight, ten corruptions of insight arise. For the corruptions of insight do not arise for a noble disciple who has attained penetration, nor for one who is practicing wrongly, nor for one who has laid aside his meditation subject, nor for a lazy person. But they do indeed arise for a son of good family who is practicing rightly, is properly engaged, and has commenced insight.

Katame pana te dasa upakkilesāti? Obhāso, ñāṇaṃ, pīti, passaddhi, sukhaṃ, adhimokkho, paggaho, upaṭṭhānaṃ, upekkhā, nikantīti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Now, what are these ten corruptions? Illumination, knowledge, rapture, tranquility, happiness, resolution, exertion, establishment, equanimity, and delight. For it has been said:

“Kathaṃ dhammuddhaccaviggahitamānasaṃ hoti? Aniccato manasikaroto obhāso uppajjati, ‘obhāso dhammo’ti obhāsaṃ āvajjati, tato vikkhepo uddhaccaṃ. Tena uddhaccena viggahitamānaso aniccato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Dukkhato… anattato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti”.

'How is it that the mind becomes seized by agitation over phenomena? For one attending to impermanence, an illumination arises. One adverts to the illumination, thinking, 'This illumination is the Dhamma.' From that, distraction and agitation arise. With a mind seized by that agitation, one does not know as it really is the establishing of mindfulness on impermanence... on suffering... on not-self.'

Tathā “aniccato manasikaroto ñāṇaṃ uppajjati…pe… pīti… passaddhi… sukhaṃ… adhimokkho… paggaho… upaṭṭhānaṃ… upekkhā… nikanti uppajjati, ‘nikanti dhammo’ti nikantiṃ āvajjati, tato vikkhepo uddhaccaṃ. Tena uddhaccena viggahitamānaso aniccato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Dukkhato… anattato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātī”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.6).

Similarly: 'For one attending to impermanence, knowledge arises... rapture... tranquility... happiness... resolution... exertion... establishment... equanimity... delight arises. One adverts to the delight, thinking, "This delight is the Dhamma." From that, distraction and agitation arise. With a mind seized by that agitation, one does not know as it really is the establishing of mindfulness on impermanence... on suffering... on not-self' (Paṭis II 6).

733. Tattha [M 2.0270] obhāsoti vipassanobhāso. Tasmiṃ uppanne yogāvacaro “na vata me ito pubbe evarūpo obhāso uppannapubbo, addhā maggappattosmi phalapattosmī”ti amaggameva “maggo”ti, aphalameva ca “phala”nti gaṇhāti. Tassa amaggaṃ “maggo”ti aphalaṃ “phala”nti gaṇhato vipassanāvīthi ukkantā nāma hoti. So attano mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā obhāsameva assādento nisīdati.

733. Herein, illumination means the illumination of insight. When it arises, the meditator thinks: 'Indeed, never before has such an illumination arisen in me. Surely, I have attained the path, I have attained the fruit!' He grasps what is not the path as 'path' and what is not the fruit as 'fruit.' For him who thus grasps the non-path as path and the non-fruit as fruit, the course of insight is said to have gone astray. Abandoning his basic meditation subject, he sits down just enjoying the illumination.

So kho panāyaṃ obhāso kassaci bhikkhuno pallaṅkaṭṭhānamattameva obhāsento uppajjati. Kassaci [V 2.0269] antogabbhaṃ. Kassaci bahigabbhampi. Kassaci sakalavihāraṃ, gāvutaṃ, aḍḍhayojanaṃ, yojanaṃ, dviyojanaṃ, tiyojanaṃ…pe… kassaci pathavītalato yāva akaniṭṭhabrahmalokā ekālokaṃ kurumāno. Bhagavato pana dasasahassilokadhātuṃ obhāsento udapādi.

Now this illumination arises for a certain bhikkhu illuminating only the space of his seat. For another, the inner chamber. For another, the exterior of the chamber too. For another, the entire monastery, a gāvuta, half a yojana, a yojana, two yojanas, three yojanas... For another, it makes a single light from the surface of the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world. But for the Blessed One, it arose illuminating the ten-thousand-world-system.

Evaṃ vemattatāya cassa idaṃ vatthu – cittalapabbate kira dvikuṭṭagehassa anto dve therā nisīdiṃsu. Taṃdivasañca kāḷapakkhuposatho hoti, meghapaṭalacchannā disā, rattibhāge caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ tamaṃ pavattati. Atheko thero āha – “bhante, mayhaṃ idāni cetiyaṅgaṇamhi sīhāsane pañcavaṇṇāni kusumāni paññāyantī”ti. Taṃ itaro āha – “anacchariyaṃ, āvuso, kathesi, mayhaṃ panetarahi mahāsamuddamhi yojanaṭṭhāne macchakacchapā paññāyantī”ti.

And on its diversity, this is a story. On Cittalapabbata, it seems, two elders were sitting inside a two-storied house. That day was the Uposatha of the dark fortnight, the quarters were covered by a veil of clouds, and in the night a four-factored darkness prevailed. Then one elder said: 'Venerable sir, just now five-colored flowers on the lion-throne in the shrine courtyard are visible to me.' The other said to him: 'You say nothing wonderful, friend. But to me, just now, fish and turtles a yojana away in the great ocean are visible.'

Ayaṃ pana vipassanupakkileso yebhuyyena samathavipassanālābhino uppajjati. So samāpattivikkhambhitānaṃ kilesānaṃ asamudācārato “arahā aha”nti cittaṃ uppādeti uccavālikavāsī mahānāgatthero viya haṃkanakavāsī mahādattatthero viya cittalapabbate niṅkapeṇṇakapadhānagharavāsī cūḷasumanatthero viya ca.

This corruption of insight, however, arises for the most part in one who has obtained both serenity and insight. Because the defilements suppressed by the attainment do not manifest, he generates the thought, 'I am an arahant,' like the Elder Mahānāga, a resident of Uccavālika, or the Elder Mahādatta, a resident of Haṃkanaka, or the Elder Cūḷasumana, a resident of the Niṅkapeṇṇaka meditation house on Cittalapabbata.

Tatridaṃ ekavatthuparidīpanaṃ – talaṅgaravāsī dhammadinnatthero kira nāma eko pabhinnapaṭisambhido mahākhīṇāsavo mahato bhikkhusaṅghassa ovādadāyako [M 2.0271] ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ attano divāṭṭhāne nisīditvā “kinnu kho amhākaṃ ācariyassa uccavālikavāsīmahānāgattherassa samaṇabhāvakiccaṃ matthakaṃ pattaṃ, no”ti āvajjanto puthujjanabhāvamevassa disvā “mayi agacchante puthujjanakālakiriyameva karissatī”ti ca ñatvā iddhiyā vehāsaṃ uppatitvā divāṭṭhāne nisinnassa therassa samīpe orohitvā vanditvā vattaṃ dassetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. “Kiṃ, āvuso dhammadinna, akāle āgatosī”ti ca vutte “pañhaṃ, bhante, pucchituṃ āgatomhī”ti āha. Tato “pucchāvuso, jānamānā kathayissāmā”ti vutte pañhasahassaṃ pucchi.

Herein, this is an illustration with one story. It seems there was an elder named Dhammadinna, a resident of Talaṅgara, a great arahant who had attained the analytical knowledges and was an advisor to a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus. One day, while sitting in his daytime quarters, he adverted: 'Has our teacher, the Elder Mahānāga of Uccavālika, reached the culmination of the task of a recluse, or not?' Seeing that he was still a worldling, and knowing, 'If I do not go, he will die as a worldling,' he rose into the air by psychic power, descended near the elder who was seated in his daytime quarters, paid homage, showed his respects, and sat down to one side. When he was asked, 'Why have you come at the wrong time, friend Dhammadinna?' he replied, 'I have come to ask a question, venerable sir.' Then, when told, 'Ask, friend; if we know, we shall say,' he asked a thousand questions.

Thero pucchitapucchitaṃ asajjamānova kathesi. Tato “atitikkhaṃ vo, bhante, ñāṇaṃ, kadā tumhehi ayaṃ dhammo adhigato”ti vutte “ito saṭṭhivassakāle, āvuso”ti āha. Samādhimpi, bhante, vaḷañjethāti, na yidaṃ, āvuso, bhāriyanti. Tena hi, bhante, ekaṃ hatthiṃ māpethāti[V 2.0270]. Thero sabbasetaṃ hatthiṃ māpesi. Idāni, bhante, yathā ayaṃ hatthī añcitakaṇṇo pasāritanaṅguṭṭho soṇḍaṃ mukhe pakkhipitvā bheravaṃ koñcanādaṃ karonto tumhākaṃ abhimukho āgacchati, tathā naṃ karothāti. Thero tathā katvā vegena āgacchato hatthissa bheravaṃ ākāraṃ disvā uṭṭhāya palāyituṃ āraddho. Tamenaṃ khīṇāsavatthero hatthaṃ pasāretvā cīvarakaṇṇe gahetvā “bhante, khīṇāsavassa sārajjaṃ nāma hotī”ti āha.

The elder answered each question he was asked without hesitating. Then, when asked, 'Your knowledge is exceedingly sharp, venerable sir. When did you attain this Dhamma?' he replied, 'Sixty years ago, friend.' 'Do you still practice concentration, venerable sir?' 'Friend, that is not a difficult task.' 'In that case, venerable sir, create an elephant.' The elder created an all-white elephant. 'Now, venerable sir, make it come towards you with its ears bent back, its tail outstretched, and its trunk placed in its mouth, making a terrifying trumpeting sound.' The elder did so, but on seeing the terrifying appearance of the elephant coming at him with speed, he got up and started to flee. The elder who was an arahant stretched out his hand, grabbed him by the corner of his robe, and said: 'Venerable sir, can one whose cankers are destroyed have fear?'

So tamhi kāle attano puthujjanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “avassayo me, āvuso, dhammadinna hohī”ti vatvā pādamūle ukkuṭikaṃ nisīdi. “Bhante, tumhākaṃ avassayo bhavissāmiccevāhaṃ āgato, mā cintayitthā”ti kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Thero kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā caṅkamaṃ āruyha tatiye padavāre aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Thero kira dosacarito ahosi. Evarūpā bhikkhū obhāse kampanti.

At that moment, realizing his own state as a worldling, he said, 'Friend Dhammadinna, be my refuge!' and sat down on his heels at his feet. 'Venerable sir, it is precisely to become your refuge that I have come. Do not worry.' And he gave him a meditation subject. The elder took the meditation subject, mounted the meditation walk, and at the third step attained the supreme fruit, arahantship. It seems the elder was of a hateful temperament. Such bhikkhus are shaken by the illumination.

734. Ñāṇanti vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Tassa kira rūpārūpadhamme tulayantassa tīrentassa vissaṭṭhaindavajiramiva avihatavegaṃ tikhiṇaṃ sūraṃ ativisadaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati.

734. Knowledge means insight knowledge. It is said that for one who is weighing and judging material and immaterial phenomena, there arises a knowledge that is sharp, brave, and exceedingly clear, with its speed unimpeded like the thunderbolt of Indra that has been released.

Pītīti [M 2.0272] vipassanāpīti. Tassa kira tasmiṃ samaye khuddakāpīti, khaṇikāpīti, okkantikāpīti, ubbegāpīti, pharaṇāpītīti ayaṃ pañcavidhā pīti sakalasarīraṃ pūrayamānā uppajjati.

Rapture means insight-rapture. It is said that at that time these five kinds of rapture arise, filling his entire body: minor rapture, momentary rapture, showering rapture, uplifting rapture, and pervading rapture.

Passaddhīti vipassanāpassaddhi. Tassa kira tasmiṃ samaye rattiṭṭhāne vā divāṭṭhāne vā nisinnassa kāyacittānaṃ neva daratho, na gāravaṃ, na kakkhaḷatā, na akammaññatā, na gelaññaṃ, na vaṅkatā hoti, atha kho panassa kāyacittāni passaddhāni lahūni mudūni kammaññāni suvisadāni ujukāniyeva honti. So imehi passaddhādīhi anuggahitakāyacitto tasmiṃ samaye amānusiṃ nāma ratiṃ anubhavati. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

Tranquility means insight-tranquility. It is said that at that time, for one sitting in his night quarters or day quarters, there is no distress, heaviness, rigidity, unwieldiness, sickness, or crookedness of body and mind. Instead, his body and mind are tranquil, light, malleable, wieldy, proficient, and straight. With his body and mind aided by these qualities beginning with tranquility, at that time he experiences a superhuman delight. In reference to this it has been said:

“Suññāgāraṃ paviṭṭhassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno;

Amānusī rati hoti, sammā dhammaṃ vipassato.

For a bhikkhu who has entered an empty abode,

Whose mind is peaceful,

There is a superhuman delight

As he rightly discerns the Dhamma.

“Yato [V 2.0271] yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 373-374);

"Whenever he comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates, he finds rapture and joy: that is the deathless for those who know." (Dhp. 374)

Evamassa imaṃ amānusiṃ ratiṃ sādhayamānā lahutādisampayuttā passaddhi uppajjati.

Thus, for him, tranquility arises, which, being endowed with lightness and other such qualities, brings about this superhuman delight.

Sukhanti vipassanāsukhaṃ. Tassa kira tasmiṃ samaye sakalasarīraṃ abhisandayamānaṃ atipaṇītaṃ sukhaṃ uppajjati.

"Sukha" means the happiness of insight. For at that time, an extremely refined happiness arises in him, suffusing his entire body.

Adhimokkhoti saddhā. Vipassanāsampayuttāyeva hissa cittacetasikānaṃ atisayapasādabhūtā balavatī saddhā uppajjati.

"Adhimokkha" means faith. For a powerful faith associated only with insight arises in him, which is an exceptional clarity concerning the mind and mental factors.

Paggahoti vīriyaṃ. Vipassanāsampayuttameva hissa asithilaṃ anaccāraddhaṃ supaggahitaṃ vīriyaṃ uppajjati.

"Paggaha" means energy. For energy associated only with insight arises in him that is not lax, not over-exerted, and well-sustained.

Upaṭṭhānanti sati. Vipassanāsampayuttāyeva hissa supaṭṭhitā supatiṭṭhitā nikhātā acalā pabbatarājasadisā sati uppajjati. So yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ āvajjati samannāharati manasikaroti paccavekkhati, taṃ taṃ ṭhānamassa okkhanditvā pakkhanditvā dibbacakkhuno paraloko viya satiyā upaṭṭhāti.

"Upaṭṭhāna" means mindfulness. For mindfulness associated only with insight arises in him that is well-established, firmly founded, dug in, unshakable, like a king of mountains. Whatever object he adverts to, considers, gives attention to, or reviews, that very object presents itself to his mindfulness, leaping and jumping upon it, like another world to the divine eye.

Upekkhāti [M 2.0273] vipassanupekkhā ceva āvajjanupekkhā ca. Tasmiṃ hissa samaye sabbasaṅkhāresu majjhattabhūtā vipassanupekkhāpi balavatī uppajjati. Manodvāre āvajjanupekkhāpi. Sā hissa taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ āvajjantassa vissaṭṭhaindavajiramiva pattapuṭe pakkhitta tattanārāco viya ca sūrā tikhiṇā hutvā vahati.

"Upekkhā" means both the equanimity of insight and the equanimity of adverting. At that time, a powerful equanimity of insight, which is a state of neutrality towards all formations, arises in him, as does the equanimity of adverting at the mind-door. For him, as he adverts to this or that object, the latter proceeds valiantly and sharply, like a discharged thunderbolt of Inda or like a heated iron arrow placed in a leaf-cup.

Nikantīti vipassanānikanti. Evaṃ obhāsādipaṭimaṇḍitāya hissa vipassanāya ālayaṃ kurumānā sukhumā santākārā nikanti uppajjati. Yā nikanti kilesoti pariggahetumpi na sakkā hoti.

"Nikanti" means delight in insight. For as he forms an attachment to the insight adorned with light and so on, a subtle delight of peaceful appearance arises in him. This delight is such that it cannot even be grasped as a defilement.

Yathā [V 2.0272] ca obhāse, evaṃ etesupi aññatarasmiṃ uppanne yogāvacaro “na vata me ito pubbe evarūpaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppannapubbaṃ, evarūpā pīti, passaddhi, sukhaṃ, adhimokkho, paggaho, upaṭṭhānaṃ, upekkhā, nikanti uppannapubbā, addhā maggappattosmi phalappattosmī”ti amaggameva “maggo”ti aphalameva ca “phala”nti gaṇhāti. Tassa amaggaṃ “maggo”ti aphalaṃ “phala”nti gaṇhato vipassanāvīthi ukkantā nāma hoti. So attano mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā nikantimeva assādento nisīdatīti.

Just as with the light, so too, when any of these others has arisen, the yogi thinks: "Surely, never before has such knowledge arisen in me, nor such joy, tranquility, happiness, resolution, exertion, mindfulness, equanimity, or delight. I have certainly attained the path, I have attained the fruit!" Thus he grasps what is not the path as the path and what is not the fruit as the fruit. For one who grasps the non-path as the path and the non-fruit as the fruit, the course of insight is said to have gone astray. Having abandoned his basic meditation subject, he sits savoring that very delight.

735. Ettha ca obhāsādayo upakkilesavatthutāya upakkilesāti vuttā, na akusalattā. Nikanti pana upakkileso ceva upakkilesavatthu ca. Vatthuvaseneva cete dasa. Gāhavasena pana samatiṃsa honti. Kathaṃ? “Mama obhāso uppanno”ti gaṇhato hi diṭṭhigāho hoti, “manāpo vata obhāso uppanno”ti gaṇhato mānagāho, obhāsaṃ assādayato taṇhāgāho, iti obhāse diṭṭhimānataṇhāvasena tayo gāhā. Tathā sesesupīti evaṃ gāhavasena samatiṃsa upakkilesā honti. Tesaṃ vasena akusalo abyatto yogāvacaro obhāsādīsu kampati vikkhipati. Obhāsādīsu ekekaṃ “etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti (ma. ni. 1.241) samanupassati. Tenāhu porāṇā –

735. Herein, light and the others are called corruptions because they are the basis for corruption, not because they are unwholesome. Delight, however, is both a corruption and a basis for corruption. By way of their basis, they are ten. But by way of grasping, they become thirty. How so? For one who grasps thinking, "Light has arisen for me," there is grasping by view. For one who grasps thinking, "Ah, how pleasing is the light that has arisen," there is grasping by conceit. For one who savors the light, there is grasping by craving. Thus, in the case of light, there are three kinds of grasping: by view, conceit, and craving. The same applies to the rest. In this way, by way of grasping, there are thirty corruptions. Because of them, the unskilled, inexpert yogi trembles and is distracted by light and the others. He regards each of them, from light onwards, thus: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self." Therefore the ancients said:

“Obhāse ceva ñāṇe ca, pītiyā ca vikampati;

Passaddhiyā sukhe ceva, yehi cittaṃ pavedhati.

"At light and knowledge, and at joy, he trembles; at tranquility and happiness, by which the mind is shaken.

“Adhimokkhe [M 2.0274] ca paggāhe, upaṭṭhāne ca kampati;

Upekkhāvajjanāyañca, upekkhāya nikantiyā”ti. (paṭi. ma. 2.7);

"At resolution and exertion, and at mindfulness, he trembles; at the equanimity of adverting, at equanimity, and at delight."

Maggāmaggavavatthānakathā

The Discourse on the Determination of Path and Not-Path

736. Kusalo pana paṇḍito byatto buddhisampanno yogāvacaro obhāsādīsu uppannesu “ayaṃ kho me obhāso uppanno, so kho panāyaṃ anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno khayadhammo vayadhammo virāgadhammo nirodhadhammo”ti iti vā taṃ paññāya paricchindati upaparikkhati. Atha vā panassa evaṃ hoti, “sace obhāso attā bhaveyya, ‘attā’ti gahetuṃ [V 2.0273] vaṭṭeyya. Anattā ca panāyaṃ ‘attā’ti gahito. Tasmā so avasavattanaṭṭhena anattā, hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena anicco, uppādavayapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkho”ti sabbaṃ arūpasattake vuttanayena vitthāretabbaṃ. Yathā ca obhāse, evaṃ sesesupi.

736. But the skilled, wise, expert, and intelligent yogi, when light and the others arise, defines and investigates them with wisdom thus: "This light has arisen in me. But it is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, of a nature to be destroyed, of a nature to vanish, of a nature to fade away, of a nature to cease." Or it occurs to him thus: "If light were self, it would be right to take it as 'self.' But it is non-self, though taken as 'self.' Therefore, because it is not subject to one's will, it is non-self; because it ceases after having come to be, it is impermanent; because it is oppressed by arising and passing away, it is suffering." All this should be elaborated in the way stated in the sevenfold analysis of the formless. And as with light, so with the rest.

So evaṃ upaparikkhitvā obhāsaṃ “netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā”ti (ma. ni. 1.241) samanupassati. Ñāṇaṃ…pe… nikantiṃ “netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā”ti (ma. ni. 1.241) samanupassati. Evaṃ samanupassanto obhāsādīsu na kampati na vedhati. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Having investigated in this way, he regards light thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self." He regards knowledge... he regards delight thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self." Regarding them thus, he does not tremble or shake on account of light and the others. Therefore the ancients said:

“Imāni dasa ṭhānāni, paññāyassa pariccitā;

Dhammuddhaccakusalo hoti, na ca vikkhepaṃ gacchatī”ti. (paṭi. ma. 2.7);

"When these ten instances are defined by one's wisdom, one becomes skilled in regard to agitation over phenomena and does not fall into distraction."

So evaṃ vikkhepaṃ agacchanto taṃ samatiṃsavidhaṃ upakkilesajaṭaṃ vijaṭetvā obhāsādayo dhammā na maggo. Upakkilesavimuttaṃ pana vīthipaṭipannaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ maggoti maggañca amaggañca vavatthapeti. Tassevaṃ “ayaṃ maggo, ayaṃ na maggo”ti maggañca amaggañca ñatvā ṭhitaṃ ñāṇaṃ maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhīti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, not falling into distraction and having disentangled the thirty-fold tangle of corruptions, he determines what is the path and what is not the path, knowing: "Light and the other states are not the path; but the insight knowledge that is free from the corruptions and has entered upon the right course—that is the path." The knowledge that is established by knowing, "This is the path, this is not the path," should be understood as the purification by knowledge and vision of path and not-path.

Ettāvatā ca pana tena tiṇṇaṃ saccānaṃ vavatthānaṃ kataṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? Diṭṭhivisuddhiyaṃ tāva nāmarūpassa vavatthāpanena dukkhasaccassa vavatthānaṃ kataṃ. Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiyaṃ paccayapariggahaṇena samudayasaccassa vavatthānaṃ. Imissaṃ maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiyaṃ sammāmaggassa avadhāraṇena maggasaccassa vavatthānaṃ [M 2.0275] katanti, evaṃ lokiyeneva tāva ñāṇena tiṇṇaṃ saccānaṃ vavatthānaṃ kataṃ hoti.

And by this much, a determination of the three truths has been made by him. How? Firstly, in the purification of view, by determining mentality-materiality, a determination of the truth of suffering is made. In the purification by overcoming doubt, by comprehending conditions, a determination of the truth of the origin is made. In this purification by knowledge and vision of path and not-path, by ascertaining the right path, a determination of the truth of the path is made. Thus, by means of mundane knowledge alone, a determination of the three truths has been made.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, composed for the gladdening of good people,

Paññābhāvanādhikāre

in the Section on the Development of Wisdom,

Maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso nāma

the exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of Path and Not-Path,

Vīsatimo paricchedo.

the Twentieth Chapter.

21. Paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso

21. Exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way

Upakkilesavimuttaudayabbayañāṇakathā

Discourse on the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away Freed from Corruptions

737. Aṭṭhannaṃ [M 2.0276][V 2.0274] pana ñāṇānaṃ vasena sikhāppattā vipassanā, navamañca saccānulomikañāṇanti ayaṃ paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi nāma. Aṭṭhannanti cettha upakkilesavimuttaṃ vīthipaṭipannavipassanāsaṅkhātaṃ udayabbayānupassanāñāṇaṃ, bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇaṃ, bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ, ādīnavānupassanāñāṇaṃ, nibbidānupassanāñāṇaṃ, muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ, paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ, saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇanti imāni aṭṭha ñāṇāni veditabbāni. Navamaṃ saccānulomikañāṇanti anulomassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmā taṃ sampādetukāmena upakkilesavimuttaṃ udayabbayañāṇaṃ ādiṃ katvā etesu ñāṇesu yogo karaṇīyo.

737. Insight that has reached its culmination by means of the eight knowledges, and the ninth, the knowledge in conformity with the truths—this is called the purification by knowledge and vision of the way. Herein, the eight knowledges are to be understood as: the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away, which is free from corruptions and reckoned as insight that has entered the path; the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution; the knowledge of the appearance of terror; the knowledge of contemplation of danger; the knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment; the knowledge of desire for deliverance; the knowledge of contemplation of reflection; and the knowledge of equanimity towards formations. The ninth, the knowledge in conformity with the truths, is a designation for conformity knowledge. Therefore, one who wishes to accomplish this should make an effort in these knowledges, beginning with the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away, which is free from corruptions.

738. Puna udayabbayañāṇe yogo kimatthiyoti ce? Lakkhaṇasallakkhaṇattho. Udayabbayañāṇaṃ hi heṭṭhā dasahi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭhaṃ hutvā yāthāvasarasato tilakkhaṇaṃ sallakkhetuṃ nāsakkhi. Upakkilesavimuttaṃ pana sakkoti. Tasmā lakkhaṇasallakkhaṇatthamettha puna yogo karaṇīyo.

738. And why make effort again in the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away? For the purpose of discerning the characteristics. For the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away, having been previously defiled by the ten corruptions, was unable to discern the three characteristics as they really are. But when freed from the corruptions, it is able to. Therefore, effort must be made here again for the purpose of discerning the characteristics.

739. Lakkhaṇāni pana kissa amanasikārā kena paṭicchannattā na upaṭṭhahanti? Aniccalakkhaṇaṃ tāva udayabbayānaṃ amanasikārā santatiyā paṭicchannattā na upaṭṭhāti. Dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanassa amanasikārā iriyāpathehi paṭicchannattā na upaṭṭhāti. Anattalakkhaṇaṃ nānādhātuvinibbhogassa amanasikārā ghanena paṭicchannattā na upaṭṭhāti. Udayabbayampana pariggahetvā santatiyā vikopitāya aniccalakkhaṇaṃ yāthāvasarasato upaṭṭhāti. Abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanaṃ manasikatvā iriyāpathe ugghāṭite dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ yāthāvasarasato upaṭṭhāti. Nānādhātuyo vinibbhujitvā ghanavinibbhoge kate anattalakkhaṇaṃ yāthāvasarasato upaṭṭhāti.

739. But due to not attending to what, and due to being concealed by what, do the characteristics not appear? The characteristic of impermanence, in the first place, does not appear because of not attending to arising and passing away and because it is concealed by continuity. The characteristic of suffering does not appear because of not attending to constant oppression and because it is concealed by the postures. The characteristic of not-self does not appear because of not attending to the analysis of the various elements and because it is concealed by compactness. But when arising and passing away are comprehended and continuity is disrupted, the characteristic of impermanence appears as it really is. When constant oppression is attended to and the postures are exposed, the characteristic of suffering appears as it really is. When the various elements are analyzed and compactness is broken down, the characteristic of not-self appears as it really is.

740. Ettha [V 2.0275] ca aniccaṃ, aniccalakkhaṇaṃ, dukkhaṃ, dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ, anattā, anattalakkhaṇanti ayaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo. Tattha aniccanti khandhapañcakaṃ. Kasmā? Uppādavayaññathattabhāvā[M 2.0277], hutvā abhāvato vā. Uppādavayaññathattaṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ hutvā abhāvasaṅkhāto vā ākāravikāro.

740. Herein, this distinction is to be understood: the impermanent and the characteristic of impermanence; suffering and the characteristic of suffering; not-self and the characteristic of not-self. Therein, 'the impermanent' refers to the five aggregates. Why? Because of their arising, passing away, and altering, or because they cease to be after having been. Arising, passing away, and alteration is the characteristic of impermanence; or it is the change of mode reckoned as ceasing to be after having been.

“Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.15) vacanato pana tadeva khandhapañcakaṃ dukkhaṃ. Kasmā? Abhiṇhapaṭipīḷanā, abhiṇhapaṭipīḷanākāro dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ.

But in accordance with the text, 'What is impermanent is suffering' (SN 22.15), those same five aggregates are suffering. Why? Because of constant oppression. The mode of constant oppression is the characteristic of suffering.

“Yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.15) pana vacanato tadeva khandhapañcakaṃ anattā. Kasmā? Avasavattanato, avasavattanākāro anattalakkhaṇaṃ.

And in accordance with the text, 'What is suffering, that is not-self' (SN 22.15), those same five aggregates are not-self. Why? Because they are not subject to control. The mode of being not subject to control is the characteristic of not-self.

Tayidaṃ sabbampi ayaṃ yogāvacaro upakkilesavimuttena vīthipaṭipannavipassanāsaṅkhātena udayabbayānupassanāñāṇena yāthāvasarasato sallakkheti.

This meditator discerns all this as it really is with the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away, which is free from corruptions and reckoned as insight that has entered the path.

Upakkilesavimuttaudayabbayañāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away free from corruptions is concluded.

Bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇakathā

Discourse on the Knowledge of Contemplation of Dissolution

741. Tassevaṃ sallakkhetvā punappunaṃ “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti rūpārūpadhamme tulayato tīrayato taṃ ñāṇaṃ tikkhaṃ hutvā vahati, saṅkhārā lahuṃ upaṭṭhahanti, ñāṇe tikkhe vahante saṅkhāresu lahuṃ upaṭṭhahantesu uppādaṃ vā ṭhitiṃ vā pavattaṃ vā nimittaṃ vā na sampāpuṇāti. Khayavayabhedanirodheyeva sati santiṭṭhati. Tassa “evaṃ uppajjitvā evaṃ nāma saṅkhāragataṃ nirujjhatī”ti passato etasmiṃ ṭhāne bhaṅgānupassanaṃ nāma vipassanāñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

741.
