For one who has thus discerned, as he repeatedly weighs and judges material and immaterial states as 'impermanent, suffering, not-self,' that knowledge becomes sharp and proceeds swiftly, and formations appear readily. When his knowledge proceeds sharply and formations appear readily, his mind does not alight on their arising, or standing, or occurrence, or sign. His mindfulness is established only on their destruction, passing away, breaking up, and cessation. For him who sees, 'Having thus arisen, the aggregate of formations thus ceases,' at that point the insight knowledge called 'contemplation of dissolution' arises. In reference to this it was said:

“Kathaṃ ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhā bhaṅgānupassane paññā vipassane ñāṇaṃ? Rūpārammaṇatā cittaṃ uppajjitvā bhijjati, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhā tassa cittassa bhaṅgaṃ anupassati[V 2.0276]. Anupassatīti kathaṃ anupassati? Aniccato anupassati no niccato, dukkhato anupassati no sukhato, anattato anupassati no attato, nibbindati no nandati, virajjati no rajjati, nirodheti no samudeti, paṭinissajjati no ādiyati.

"How is wisdom in the contemplation of dissolution by reflecting on the object, which is knowledge in insight? A mind having form as its object arises and breaks up. Having reflected on that object, one contemplates the dissolution of that mind. How does one contemplate? One contemplates it as impermanent, not as permanent; as suffering, not as pleasant; as not-self, not as self. One becomes disenchanted, one does not delight; one becomes dispassionate, one is not impassioned; one brings it to cessation, one does not cause it to originate; one relinquishes, one does not grasp.

“Aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahati. Dukkhato anupassanto sukhasaññaṃ, anattato anupassanto attasaññaṃ, nibbindanto [M 2.0278] nandiṃ, virajjanto rāgaṃ, nirodhento samudayaṃ paṭinissajjanto ādānaṃ pajahati.

"Contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence. Contemplating as suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure. Contemplating as not-self, one abandons the perception of self. Becoming disenchanted, one abandons delight. Becoming dispassionate, one abandons lust. Bringing to cessation, one abandons origination. Relinquishing, one abandons grasping."

“Vedanārammaṇatā…pe… saññārammaṇatā… saṅkhārārammaṇatā… viññāṇārammaṇatā… cakkhārammaṇatā…pe… jarāmaraṇārammaṇatā cittaṃ uppajjitvā bhijjati…pe… paṭinissajjanto ādānaṃ pajahati.

“A mind having feeling as its object... perception as its object... formations as its object... consciousness as its object... the eye as its object... aging-and-death as its object arises and breaks up... By relinquishing, one abandons grasping.”

“Vatthusaṅkamanā ceva, paññāya ca vivaṭṭanā;

Āvajjanābalañceva, paṭisaṅkhāvipassanā.

“Transition of the basis, turning away of wisdom, and the power of adverting: this is insight of reflection.”

“Ārammaṇaanvayena, ubho ekavavatthanā;

Nirodhe adhimuttatā, vayalakkhaṇavipassanā.

“By following the object, the determination of both as one, and resolve upon cessation: this is insight into the characteristic of passing away.”

“Ārammaṇañca paṭisaṅkhā, bhaṅgañca anupassati;

Suññato ca upaṭṭhānaṃ, adhipaññāvipassanā.

“Reflection on the object, contemplation of its dissolution, and its appearance as empty: this is insight of higher wisdom.”

“Kusalo tīsu anupassanāsu, catasso ca vipassanāsu;

Tayo upaṭṭhāne kusalatā, nānādiṭṭhīsu na kampatī”ti.

“Skilled in the three contemplations and in the four insights; through skill in the three establishments, one is not shaken by various views.”

“Taṃ ñātaṭṭhena ñāṇaṃ, pajānanaṭṭhena paññā, tena vuccati ‘ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhā bhaṅgānupassane paññā vipassane ñāṇa’”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.51-52).

“It is knowledge in the sense of knowing, wisdom in the sense of discerning. Therefore it is said: ‘Wisdom in the contemplation of dissolution by reflecting on the object is knowledge in insight.’”

742. Tattha [V 2.0277] ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhāti yaṃkiñci ārammaṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhāya jānitvā, khayato vayato disvāti attho. Bhaṅgānupassane paññāti tassa, ārammaṇaṃ khayato vayato paṭisaṅkhāya uppannassa ñāṇassa bhaṅgaṃ anupassane yā paññā, idaṃ vipassane ñāṇanti vuttaṃ. Taṃ kathaṃ hotīti ayaṃ tāva kathetukamyatāpucchāya attho. Tato yathā taṃ hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “rūpārammaṇatā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

742. Herein, ‘by reflecting on the object’ means: having known whatever object by reflecting on it, having seen it as subject to destruction and passing away. ‘Wisdom in the contemplation of dissolution’ means: the wisdom in contemplating the dissolution of the knowledge that has arisen by reflecting on the object as subject to destruction and passing away; this is called ‘knowledge in insight.’ ‘How does this come to be?’—this is the meaning of the question expressing the desire to explain. Then, to show how it comes to be, ‘the state of having form as object,’ etc., was said.

Tattha rūpārammaṇatā cittaṃ uppajjitvā bhijjatīti rūpārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ uppajjitvā bhijjati. Atha vā rūpārammaṇabhāve cittaṃ uppajjitvā bhijjatīti attho. Taṃ ārammaṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhāti taṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhāya jānitvā, khayato vayato disvāti attho. Tassa cittassa bhaṅgaṃ anupassatīti yena cittena taṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ khayato vayato diṭṭhaṃ, tassa cittassa aparena cittena bhaṅgaṃ anupassatīti attho. Tenāhu porāṇā “ñātañca ñāṇañca ubhopi vipassatī”ti.

Herein, ‘a mind in the state of having form as its object arises and breaks up’ means a mind with a form as its object arises and breaks up. Or the meaning is that a mind arises in the state of having a form as its object and breaks up. ‘Having reflected on that object’ means: having known that form-object by reflecting on it, having seen it as subject to destruction and passing away. ‘One contemplates the dissolution of that mind’ means: with a subsequent mind one contemplates the dissolution of that mind by which the form-object was seen as subject to destruction and passing away. Hence the ancients said: ‘One has insight into both the known and the knowledge.’”

Ettha [M 2.0279] ca anupassatīti anu anu passati, anekehi ākārehi punappunaṃ passatīti attho. Tenāha – “anupassatīti kathaṃ anupassati. Aniccato anupassatī”tiādi.

Herein, ‘contemplates’ (anupassati) means sees again and again (anu anu passati); the meaning is that one sees repeatedly in many aspects. Hence it was said: ‘“How does one contemplate?” “One contemplates as impermanent,”’ and so on.

Tattha yasmā bhaṅgo nāma aniccatāya paramā koṭi, tasmā so bhaṅgānupassako yogāvacaro sabbaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ aniccato anupassati, no niccato. Tato aniccassa dukkhattā, dukkhassa ca anattattā tadeva dukkhato anupassati, no sukhato. Anattato anupassati no attato.

Herein, since dissolution is the highest point of impermanence, that meditator who contemplates dissolution contemplates all conditioned phenomena as impermanent, not as permanent. Then, because what is impermanent is suffering, and what is suffering is not-self, he contemplates that same thing as suffering, not as pleasant, and as not-self, not as self.

Yasmā pana yaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā, na taṃ abhinanditabbaṃ. Yañca anabhinanditabbaṃ, na tattha rajjitabbaṃ. Tasmā etasmiṃ bhaṅgānupassanānusārena “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti diṭṭhe saṅkhāragate nibbindati, no nandati. Virajjati, no rajjati. So evaṃ arajjanto lokikeneva tāva ñāṇena rāgaṃ nirodheti, no samudeti. Samudayaṃ na karotīti attho.

Furthermore, since what is impermanent, suffering, and not-self should not be delighted in, and one should not have passion for what should not be delighted in, therefore, in accordance with the contemplation of dissolution, with regard to conditioned phenomena seen as ‘impermanent, suffering, and not-self,’ one becomes disenchanted, one does not delight; one becomes dispassionate, one is not impassioned. Thus, by not being impassioned, one brings lust to cessation for the time being with merely mundane knowledge; one does not cause it to originate. The meaning is that one does not produce its origination.

Atha vā so evaṃ viratto yathā diṭṭhaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ, tathā adiṭṭhampi anvayañāṇavasena nirodheti[V 2.0278], no samudeti. Nirodhatova manasikaroti. Nirodhamevassa passati, no samudayanti attho.

Alternatively, being thus dispassionate, just as he brings to cessation the conditioned phenomena that are seen, so too, by way of inferential knowledge, he brings to cessation those that are unseen; he does not cause them to originate. He attends only to cessation. The meaning is that he sees only their cessation, not their origination.

So evaṃ paṭipanno paṭinissajjati, no ādiyati. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Ayampi aniccādianupassanā tadaṅgavasena saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilesānaṃ pariccajanato, saṅkhatadosadassanena ca tabbiparīte nibbāne tanninnatāya pakkhandanato pariccāgapaṭinissaggo ceva pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo cāti vuccati. Tasmā tāya samannāgato bhikkhu yathāvuttena nayena kilese pariccajati, nibbāne ca pakkhandati. Nāpi nibbattanavasena kilese ādiyati, na adosadassitāvasena saṅkhatārammaṇaṃ. Tena vuccati “paṭinissajjati no ādiyatī”ti.

Practicing thus, one relinquishes, one does not grasp. What is meant by this? This contemplation of impermanence, etc., is called both ‘relinquishment by abandoning’—because, by way of temporary abandonment, one abandons the defilements together with the formations of the aggregates—and ‘relinquishment by proceeding’—because, by seeing the danger in the conditioned, one proceeds towards its opposite, Nibbāna, with an inclination for it. Therefore, a bhikkhu endowed with this abandons the defilements in the aforesaid manner and proceeds towards Nibbāna. He neither grasps the defilements by way of generating them, nor a conditioned object by way of not seeing its danger. Hence it is said: ‘He relinquishes, he does not grasp.’

743. Idānissa tehi ñāṇehi yesaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānaṃ hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha nandinti sappītikaṃ taṇhaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

743. Now, to show the abandoning of those states that is effected by these knowledges, it is said: ‘Contemplating things as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence,’ and so on. Herein, ‘delight’ means craving accompanied by zest. The rest is as has been explained.

744. Gāthāsu [M 2.0280] pana vatthusaṅkamanāti rūpassa bhaṅgaṃ disvā puna yena cittena bhaṅgo diṭṭho, tassāpi bhaṅgadassanavasena purimavatthuto aññavatthusaṅkamanā. Paññāya ca vivaṭṭanāti udayaṃ pahāya vaye santiṭṭhanā. Āvajjanābalañcevāti rūpassa bhaṅgaṃ disvā puna bhaṅgārammaṇassa cittassa bhaṅgadassanatthaṃ anantarameva āvajjanasamatthatā. Paṭisaṅkhāvipassanāti esā ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhābhaṅgānupassanā nāma.

744. But in the verses, ‘transition of the basis’ means this: having seen the dissolution of form, one then sees the dissolution of the very mind by which that dissolution was seen; this is a transition from the former basis to another basis. And ‘the turning away of wisdom’ means that, having abandoned arising, one becomes established in dissolution. And ‘the power of adverting’ is the ability, immediately after seeing the dissolution of form, to advert in order to see the dissolution of the mind that had dissolution as its object. ‘Insight by reflection’ is this contemplation of dissolution by reflecting upon the object.

745. Ārammaṇaanvayena ubho ekavavatthanāti paccakkhato diṭṭhassa ārammaṇassa anvayena anugamanena yathā idaṃ, tathā atītepi saṅkhāragataṃ bhijjittha, anāgatepi bhijjissatīti evaṃ ubhinnaṃ ekasabhāveneva vavatthāpananti attho.

745. ‘The determination of both as one by following the object’ means this: by sequentially following the object that has been directly seen, one determines both past and future phenomena as having the very same nature, thus: ‘Just as this present formation broke up, so too did conditioned things in the past break up, and so will they break up in the future.’

Vuttampi cetaṃ porāṇehi –

This was also said by the ancients:

“Saṃvijjamānamhi visuddhadassano,

Tadanvayaṃ neti atītanāgate;

Sabbepi [V 2.0279] saṅkhāragatā palokino,

Ussāvabindū sūriyeva uggate”ti.

“One with purified vision of the present, infers accordingly for the past and future. All conditioned things are perishable, like dewdrops when the sun has risen.”

Nirodhe adhimuttatāti evaṃ ubhinnaṃ bhaṅgavasena ekavavatthānaṃ katvā tasmiññeva bhaṅgasaṅkhāte nirodhe adhimuttatā taggarutā tanninnatā tappoṇatā tappabbhāratāti attho. Vayalakkhaṇavipassanāti esā vayalakkhaṇavipassanā nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Being resolved on cessation' means this: having thus determined both as one by way of dissolution, one is resolved on, gives gravity to, inclines towards, converges upon, and leans towards that very cessation, which is reckoned as dissolution. This is the meaning. This is what is meant by 'insight into the characteristic of vanishing.'

746. Ārammaṇañca paṭisaṅkhāti purimañca rūpādiārammaṇaṃ jānitvā. Bhaṅgañca anupassatīti tassārammaṇassa bhaṅgaṃ disvā tadārammaṇassa cittassa bhaṅgaṃ anupassati. Suññato ca upaṭṭhānanti tassevaṃ bhaṅgaṃ anupassato “saṅkhārāva bhijjanti, tesaṃ bhedo maraṇaṃ, na añño koci atthī”ti suññato upaṭṭhānaṃ ijjhati.

746. 'And one reflects on the object' means: having known the previous object, such as form. 'And one contemplates dissolution' means: having seen the dissolution of that object, one contemplates the dissolution of the mind that had that as its object. 'And the appearance as empty' means: for one who contemplates dissolution in this way, the appearance as empty succeeds, thus: 'It is only formations that break up; their breaking up is death; there is no other being.'

Tenāhu [M 2.0281] porāṇā –

Therefore the ancients have said:

“Khandhā nirujjhanti na catthi añño,

Khandhāna bhedo maraṇanti vuccati;

Tesaṃ khayaṃ passati appamatto,

Maṇiṃva vijjhaṃ vajirena yoniso”ti.

“The aggregates cease; there is no other being. The breakup of the aggregates is called death. The heedful one, wisely, sees their destruction, like piercing a gem with a diamond.”

Adhipaññāvipassanāti yā ca ārammaṇapaṭisaṅkhā yā ca bhaṅgānupassanā yañca suññato upaṭṭhānaṃ, ayaṃ adhipaññāvipassanā nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Insight of higher wisdom' means this: the reflection on the object, the contemplation of dissolution, and the appearance as empty—this is what is called 'insight of higher wisdom.'

747. Kusalo tīsu anupassanāsūti aniccānupassanādīsu tīsu cheko bhikkhu. Catasso ca vipassanāsūti nibbidādīsu ca catūsu vipassanāsu. Tayo upaṭṭhāne kusalatāti khayato vayato suññatoti imasmiñca tividhe upaṭṭhāne kusalatāya. Nānādiṭṭhīsu na kampatīti sassatadiṭṭhiādīsu nānappakārāsu diṭṭhīsu na vedhati.

747. 'Skilled in the three contemplations' means a bhikkhu is adept in the three contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence. 'And in the four insights' means in the four insights beginning with disenchantment. 'Skill in the three appearances' means skill in this threefold appearance: as destruction, as vanishing, and as empty. 'Is not shaken by diverse views' means one does not waver amidst the various kinds of views, such as the view of eternalism.

748. So evaṃ avedhamāno “aniruddhameva nirujjhati, abhinnameva bhijjatī”ti pavattamanasikāro [V 2.0280] dubbalabhājanassa viya bhijjamānassa, sukhumarajasseva vippakiriyamānassa, tilānaṃ viya bhajjiyamānānaṃ sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ uppādaṭṭhitipavattanimittaṃ vissajjetvā bhedameva passati. So yathā nāma cakkhumā puriso pokkharaṇītīre vā nadītīre vā ṭhito thūlaphusitake deve vassante udakapiṭṭhe mahantamahantāni udakabubbuḷakāni uppajjitvā uppajjitvā sīghaṃ sīghaṃ bhijjamānāni passeyya, evameva sabbe saṅkhārā bhijjanti bhijjantīti passati. Evarūpaṃ hi yogāvacaraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ bhagavatā –

748. Thus, not wavering, with his attention proceeding as 'what has not yet ceased is ceasing, what has not yet broken is breaking,' he abandons the sign of arising, presence, and occurrence of all formations—which are like a weak vessel being broken, like fine dust being scattered, like sesame seeds being roasted—and sees only their breakup. Just as a person with good sight standing on the bank of a pond or a river when it is raining with heavy drops would see large bubbles arising and quickly breaking up on the surface of the water, so too he sees: 'All formations are breaking up, breaking up.' It was with reference to such a meditator that the Blessed One said:

“Yathā bubbuḷakaṃ passe, yathā passe marīcikaṃ;

Evaṃ lokaṃ avekkhantaṃ, maccurājā na passatī”ti. (dha. pa. 170);

“As one would see a bubble, and as one would see a mirage, so the King of Death does not see one who looks upon the world.”

749. Tassevaṃ “sabbe saṅkhārā bhijjanti bhijjantī”ti abhiṇhaṃ passato aṭṭhānisaṃsaparivāraṃ bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇaṃ balappattaṃ hoti. Tatrime aṭṭhānisaṃsā – bhavadiṭṭhippahānaṃ, jīvitanikantipariccāgo, sadāyuttapayuttatā, visuddhājīvitā, ussukkappahānaṃ, vigatabhayatā, khantisoraccapaṭilābho, aratiratisahanatāti.

749. For one who repeatedly sees in this way, 'All formations are breaking up, breaking up,' the knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution, endowed with eight benefits, becomes powerful. These are the eight benefits: the abandoning of the view of being, the relinquishing of craving for life, being always yoked and diligent, purity of livelihood, the abandoning of anxiety, freedom from fear, the acquisition of patience and gentleness, and the endurance of discontent and delight.

Tenāhu [M 2.0282] porāṇā –

Therefore the ancients have said:

“Imāni aṭṭhagguṇamuttamāni,

Disvā tahiṃ sammasate punappunaṃ;

Ādittacelassirasūpamo muni,

Bhaṅgānupassī amatassa pattiyā”ti.

“Having seen these eight supreme benefits, he reflects on them again and again. The sage, like one whose clothes or head are on fire, contemplates dissolution for the attainment of the Deathless.”

Bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The knowledge of the contemplation of dissolution is concluded.

Bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇakathā

Discourse on the Knowledge of Appearance as Terror

750. Tassevaṃ sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ khayavayabhedanirodhārammaṇaṃ bhaṅgānupassanaṃ āsevantassa bhāventassa [V 2.0281] bahulīkarontassa sabbabhavayonigatiṭhitisattāvāsesu pabhedakā saṅkhārā sukhena jīvitukāmassa bhīrukapurisassa sīhabyagghadīpiacchataracchayakkharakkhasacaṇḍagoṇacaṇḍakukkurapabhinnamadacaṇḍahatthighoraāsīvisaasanivicakkasusānaraṇabhūmijalitaaṅgārakāsuādayo viya mahābhayaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Tassa “atītā saṅkhārā niruddhā, paccuppannā nirujjhanti, anāgate nibbattanakasaṅkhārāpi evameva nirujjhissantī”ti passato etasmiṃ ṭhāne bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ nāma uppajjati.

750. As he thus cultivates, develops, and makes much of this contemplation of dissolution—which has as its object the destruction, passing away, breaking up, and cessation of all formations—the formations that bring about distinction in all kinds of becoming, birth-places, destinies, stations, and abodes of beings appear to him as a great terror, just as lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, yakkhas, raksasas, fierce bulls, savage dogs, fierce elephants in rut, terrible venomous snakes, thunderbolts, charnel grounds, battlefields, and blazing pits of embers appear to a timid man who wishes to live in comfort. When he sees, “Past formations have ceased, present ones are ceasing, and future formations that would be generated will also cease in just the same way,” at this stage the knowledge called ‘appearance as terror’ arises in him.

Tatrāyaṃ upamā – ekissā kira itthiyā tayo puttā rājaparādhikā, tesaṃ rājā sīsacchedaṃ āṇāpesi. Sā puttehi saddhiṃ āghātanaṃ agamāsi. Athassā jeṭṭhaputtassa sīsaṃ chinditvā majjhimassa chindituṃ ārabhiṃsu. Sā jeṭṭhassa sīsaṃ chinnaṃ majjhimassa ca chijjamānaṃ disvā kaniṭṭhamhi ālayaṃ vissajji “ayampi etesaññeva sadiso bhavissatī”ti. Tattha tassā itthiyā jeṭṭhaputtassa chinnasīsadassanaṃ viya yogino atītasaṅkhārānaṃ nirodhadassanaṃ, majjhimassa chijjamānasīsadassanaṃ viya paccuppannānaṃ nirodhadassanaṃ, “ayampi etesaññeva sadiso bhavissatī”ti kaniṭṭhaputtamhi ālayavissajjanaṃ viya “anāgatepi nibbattanakasaṅkhārā bhijjissantī”ti anāgatānaṃ nirodhadassanaṃ. Tassevaṃ passato etasmiṃ ṭhāne uppajjati bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ.

Here is a simile: It is said that a certain woman had three sons who were offenders against the king, and the king ordered their beheading. She went to the execution ground with her sons. There, they cut off the head of the eldest son and began to cut off the middle one’s. Seeing the eldest son’s head already severed and the middle one’s being cut, she relinquished attachment to the youngest, thinking, 'This one too will meet the same fate.' Herein, the woman seeing the eldest son’s severed head is like a yogi’s seeing the cessation of past formations. Seeing the middle son’s head being cut is like seeing the cessation of present formations. Relinquishing attachment to the youngest son, thinking, 'This one too will meet the same fate,' is like seeing the cessation of future formations, thinking, 'Future formations that would be generated will also break apart.' When one sees thus, at this stage the knowledge of appearance as terror arises.

Aparāpi upamā – ekā kira pūtipajā itthī dasa dārake vijāyi. Tesu nava matā, eko hatthagato marati, aparo kucchiyaṃ. Sā nava dārake [M 2.0283] mate dasamañca mīyamānaṃ disvā kucchigate ālayaṃ vissajji “ayampi etesaññeva sadiso bhavissatī”ti. Tattha tassā itthiyā navannaṃ dārakānaṃ maraṇānussaraṇaṃ viya yogino atītasaṅkhārānaṃ nirodhadassanaṃ, hatthagatassa mīyamānabhāvadassanaṃ viya yogino paccuppannānaṃ nirodhadassanaṃ, kucchigate ālayavissajjanaṃ viya anāgatānaṃ nirodhadassanaṃ. Tassevaṃ passato etasmiṃ khaṇe uppajjati bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ.

Another simile: It is said that a certain woman whose children were prone to die gave birth to ten children. Nine of them died, one was dying in her arms, and another was in her womb. Seeing the nine dead and the tenth dying, she relinquished attachment to the one in her womb, thinking, “This one too will have the same fate.” Herein, the woman’s recollection of the death of the nine children is like a yogi’s seeing the cessation of past formations. Seeing the one in her arms in the process of dying is like a yogi’s seeing the cessation of present formations. Relinquishing attachment to the one in her womb is like the yogi's seeing of the cessation of future formations. When one sees thus, the knowledge of appearance as terror arises at that moment.

751. Bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ pana bhāyati na bhāyatīti? Na bhāyati. Tañhi atītā saṅkhārā niruddhā, paccuppannā nirujjhanti, anāgatā nirujjhissantīti tīraṇamattameva hoti. Tasmā yathā nāma cakkhumā puriso nagaradvāre tisso aṅgārakāsuyo olokayamāno sayaṃ na bhāyati, kevalaṃ hissa “ye ye ettha nipatissanti, sabbe anappakaṃ dukkhamanubhavissantī”ti tīraṇamattameva hoti. Yathā vā pana cakkhumā puriso khadirasūlaṃ ayosūlaṃ suvaṇṇasūlanti paṭipāṭiyā [V 2.0282] ṭhapitaṃ sūlattayaṃ olokayamāno sayaṃ na bhāyati, kevalaṃ hissa “ye ye imesu sūlesu nipatissanti, sabbe anappakaṃ dukkhamanubhavissantī”ti tīraṇamattameva hoti, evameva bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ sayaṃ na bhāyati, kevalaṃ hissa aṅgārakāsuttayasadisesu, sūlattayasadisesu ca tīsu bhavesu “atītā saṅkhārā niruddhā, paccuppannā nirujjhanti, anāgatā nirujjhissantī”ti tīraṇamattameva hoti. Yasmā panassa kevalaṃ sabbabhavayonigatiṭhitinivāsagatā saṅkhārā byasanāpannā sappaṭibhayā hutvā bhayato upaṭṭhahanti, tasmā bhayatupaṭṭhānanti vuccati.

751. Now, does the knowledge of appearance as terror fear, or does it not? It does not fear. It is merely a judgment that past formations have ceased, present ones are ceasing, and future ones will cease. Just as a man with eyesight, seeing three pits of burning coals at the city gate, does not fear for himself but merely judges, 'Whoever falls here will suffer greatly.' Or like a man with eyesight seeing three stakes—an acacia stake, an iron stake, and a golden stake—arranged in a row, who does not fear for himself but merely judges, 'Whoever falls upon these stakes will suffer greatly.' Similarly, the knowledge of appearance as terror does not itself fear. It is merely a judgment concerning the three kinds of existence, which are like the three pits of burning coals or the three stakes, that 'past formations have ceased, present ones are ceasing, and future ones will cease.' However, because all formations belonging to every becoming, birth-place, destiny, station, and abode appear to him as calamitous and perilous, as a terror, it is called the knowledge of appearance as terror.

Evaṃ bhayato upaṭṭhāne panassa ayaṃ pāḷi –

Thus, concerning its appearance as terror, this is the canonical text:

“Aniccato manasikaroto kiṃ bhayato upaṭṭhāti? Dukkhato. Anattato manasikaroto kiṃ bhayato upaṭṭhātīti? Aniccato manasikaroto nimittaṃ bhayato upaṭṭhāti. Dukkhato manasikaroto pavattaṃ bhayato upaṭṭhāti. Anattato manasikaroto nimittañca pavattañca bhayato upaṭṭhātī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.227).

“When one attends to impermanence, what appears as terror? When one attends to suffering, what appears as terror? When one attends to non-self, what appears as terror? When one attends to impermanence, the sign appears as terror. When one attends to suffering, the ongoing process appears as terror. When one attends to non-self, both the sign and the ongoing process appear as terror.”

Tattha [M 2.0284] nimittanti saṅkhāranimittaṃ. Atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ saṅkhārānamevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Aniccato manasikaronto hi saṅkhārānaṃ maraṇameva passati, tenassa nimittaṃ bhayato upaṭṭhāti. Pavattanti rūpārūpabhavapavatti. Dukkhato manasikaronto hi sukhasammatāyapi pavattiyā abhiṇhapaṭipīḷanabhāvameva passati, tenassa pavattaṃ bhayato upaṭṭhāti. Anattato manasikaronto pana ubhayampetaṃ suññagāmaṃ viya marīcigandhabbanagarādīni viya ca rittaṃ tucchaṃ suññaṃ assāmikaṃ apariṇāyakaṃ passati. Tenassa nimittañca pavattañca ubhayaṃ bhayato upaṭṭhātīti.

Herein, ‘sign’ means the sign of formations. This is a designation for past, future, and present formations. For one who attends to impermanence sees only the death of formations; thus the sign appears to him as terror. ‘Ongoing process’ means the ongoing process of material and immaterial existence. For one who attends to suffering sees only the state of constant oppression even in the ongoing process that is considered to be pleasant; thus the ongoing process appears to him as terror. But one who attends to non-self sees both of these as void, hollow, and empty, without an owner or governor, like an empty village, a mirage, a celestial city, and so on. Thus, both the sign and the ongoing process appear to him as terror.

Bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Knowledge of Appearance as Terror is concluded.

Ādīnavānupassanāñāṇakathā

Discourse on the Knowledge of Contemplation of Danger

752. Tassa taṃ bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ āsevantassa bhāventassa bahulīkarontassa sabbabhavayonigatiṭhitisattāvāsesu [V 2.0283] neva tāṇaṃ, na leṇaṃ, na gati, nappaṭisaraṇaṃ paññāyati. Sabbabhavayonigatiṭhitinivāsagatesu saṅkhāresu ekasaṅkhārepi patthanā vā parāmāso vā na hoti. Tayo bhavā vītaccikaṅgārapuṇṇaaṅgārakāsuyo viya, cattāro mahābhūtā ghoravisaāsīvisā viya, pañcakkhandhā ukkhittāsikavadhakā viya, cha ajjhattikāyatanāni suññagāmo viya, cha bāhirāyatanāni gāmaghātakacorā viya, satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo, nava ca sattāvāsā ekādasahi aggīhi ādittā sampajjalitā sajotibhūtā viya ca, sabbe saṅkhārā gaṇḍabhūtā rogabhūtā sallabhūtā aghabhūtā ābādhabhūtā viya ca nirassādā nirasā mahāādīnavarāsibhūtā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti.

752. For one who resorts to, develops, and cultivates that knowledge of appearance as terror, no protection, shelter, refuge, or resort is discerned in any becoming, birth-place, destiny, station, or abode of beings. In regard to the formations found in any becoming, birth-place, destiny, station, or abode, there is not even in a single formation any longing or grasping. The three kinds of existence appear like a pit of glowing embers; the four great elements like terribly venomous serpents; the five aggregates like slayers with raised swords; the six internal sense bases like an empty village; the six external sense bases like village-plundering robbers; the seven stations of consciousness and the nine abodes of beings like what is ablaze, burning, and has become a mass of flames from the eleven fires; and all formations present themselves as being like a boil, a disease, a dart, a calamity, and an affliction, as being tasteless, sapless, a great mass of danger.

Kathaṃ? Sukhena jīvitukāmassa bhīrukapurisassa ramaṇīyākārasaṇṭhitampi savāḷakamiva vanagahanaṃ, sasaddūlā viya guhā, sagāharakkhasaṃ viya udakaṃ, samussitakhaggā viya paccatthikā, savisaṃ viya bhojanaṃ, sacoro viya maggo, ādittamiva agāraṃ, uyyuttasenā viya raṇabhūmi. Yathā hi so puriso etāni savāḷakavanagahanādīni āgamma bhīto saṃviggo lomahaṭṭhajāto samantato ādīnavameva passati, evamevāyaṃ yogāvacaro [M 2.0285] bhaṅgānupassanāvasena sabbasaṅkhāresu bhayato upaṭṭhitesu samantato nirasaṃ nirassādaṃ ādīnavameva passati. Tassevaṃ passato ādīnavañāṇaṃ nāma uppannaṃ hoti. Yaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ –

How so? For a timid person who desires to live in comfort, even a delightfully configured forest thicket is like one with beasts of prey; a cave is like one with tigers; a body of water is like one with a water-demon; enemies are like those with raised swords; food is like that mixed with poison; a road is like one with a robber; a house is like one on fire; a battlefield is like one with an army arrayed for battle. Just as that person, having come to that forest thicket with beasts of prey and so on, becomes frightened, agitated, with his hair standing on end, and sees only danger all around, just so this meditator, by means of contemplating dissolution, when all formations have appeared as terror, sees on all sides only what is sapless, tasteless, and dangerous. For one who sees thus, the knowledge of danger arises. It is with reference to this that it was said:

“Kathaṃ bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā ādīnave ñāṇaṃ? Uppādo bhayanti bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā ādīnave ñāṇaṃ. Pavattaṃ bhayanti… nimittaṃ bhayanti… āyūhanā bhayanti… paṭisandhi bhayanti… gati bhayanti… nibbatti bhayanti… upapatti bhayanti… jāti bhayanti… jarā bhayanti… byādhi bhayanti… maraṇaṃ bhayanti… soko bhayanti… paridevo bhayanti… upāyāso bhayanti bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā ādīnave ñāṇaṃ. Anuppādo khemanti santipade ñāṇaṃ. Appavattaṃ…pe… anupāyāso khemanti santipade ñāṇaṃ. Uppādo bhayaṃ, anuppādo khemanti santipade ñāṇaṃ. Pavattaṃ…pe… upāyāso bhayaṃ, anupāyāso khemanti santipade ñāṇaṃ.

“How is wisdom in the appearance of fear knowledge of danger? ‘Arising is fear’—this is wisdom in the appearance of fear, knowledge of danger. ‘Occurrence is fear’ … ‘the sign is fear’ … ‘volitional formation is fear’ … ‘rebirth-linking is fear’ … ‘destiny is fear’ … ‘generation is fear’ … ‘reappearance is fear’ … ‘birth is fear’ … ‘aging is fear’ … ‘illness is fear’ … ‘death is fear’ … ‘sorrow is fear’ … ‘lamentation is fear’ … ‘despair is fear’—this is wisdom in the appearance of fear, knowledge of danger. ‘Non-arising is security’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Non-occurrence …pe… non-despair is security’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Arising is fear, non-arising is security’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Occurrence …pe… despair is fear, non-despair is security’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state.”

“Uppādo dukkhanti bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā ādīnave ñāṇaṃ. Pavattaṃ…pe… upāyāso dukkhanti bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā ādīnave ñāṇaṃ. Anuppādo sukhanti santipade [V 2.0284] ñāṇaṃ. Appavattaṃ…pe… anupāyāso sukhanti santipade ñāṇaṃ. Uppādo dukkhaṃ, anuppādo sukhanti santipade ñāṇaṃ. Pavattaṃ…pe… upāyāso dukkhaṃ, anupāyāso sukhanti santipade ñāṇaṃ.

“‘Arising is suffering’—this is wisdom in the appearance of fear, knowledge of danger. ‘Occurrence …pe… despair is suffering’—this is wisdom in the appearance of fear, knowledge of danger. ‘Non-arising is happiness’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Non-occurrence …pe… non-despair is happiness’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Arising is suffering, non-arising is happiness’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Occurrence …pe… despair is suffering, non-despair is happiness’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state.”

“Uppādo sāmisanti bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā ādīnave ñāṇaṃ. Pavattaṃ…pe… upāyāso sāmisanti bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā ādīnave ñāṇaṃ. Anuppādo nirāmisanti santipade ñāṇaṃ. Appavattaṃ…pe… anupāyāso nirāmisanti santipade ñāṇaṃ. Uppādo sāmisaṃ, anuppādo nirāmisanti santipade ñāṇaṃ. Pavattaṃ…pe… upāyāso sāmisaṃ, anupāyāso nirāmisanti santipade ñāṇaṃ.

“‘Arising is with bait’—this is wisdom in the appearance of fear, knowledge of danger. ‘Occurrence …pe… despair is with bait’—this is wisdom in the appearance of fear, knowledge of danger. ‘Non-arising is without bait’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Non-occurrence …pe… non-despair is without bait’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Arising is with bait, non-arising is without bait’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Occurrence …pe… despair is with bait, non-despair is without bait’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state.”

Uppādo [M 2.0286] “saṅkhārāti bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā ādīnave ñāṇaṃ. Pavattaṃ…pe… upāyāso saṅkhārāti bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā ādīnave ñāṇaṃ. Anuppādo nibbānanti santipade ñāṇaṃ. Appavattaṃ…pe… anupāyāso nibbānanti santipade ñāṇaṃ. Uppādo saṅkhārā, anuppādo nibbānanti santipade ñāṇaṃ. Pavattaṃ…pe… upāyāso saṅkhārā, anupāyāso nibbānanti santipade ñāṇaṃ.

“‘Arising is formations’—this is wisdom in the appearance of fear, knowledge of danger. ‘Occurrence …pe… despair is formations’—this is wisdom in the appearance of fear, knowledge of danger. ‘Non-arising is Nibbāna’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Non-occurrence …pe… non-despair is Nibbāna’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Arising is formations, non-arising is Nibbāna’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state. ‘Occurrence …pe… despair is formations, non-despair is Nibbāna’—this is knowledge in the peaceful state.”

“Uppādañca pavattañca, nimittaṃ dukkhanti passati;

Āyūhanaṃ paṭisandhiṃ, ñāṇaṃ ādīnave idaṃ.

“One sees arising, occurrence, the sign, / volitional formation, and rebirth-linking as suffering; / this is the knowledge of danger.

“Anuppādaṃ appavattaṃ, animittaṃ sukhanti ca;

Anāyūhanā appaṭisandhi, ñāṇaṃ santipade idaṃ.

“And non-arising, non-occurrence, the signless, / non-volitional-formation, and non-rebirth-linking / as happiness: this is the knowledge in the peaceful state.

“Idaṃ ādīnave ñāṇaṃ, pañcaṭhānesu jāyati;

Pañcaṭhāne santipade, dasa ñāṇe pajānāti;

Dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ kusalatā, nānādiṭṭhīsu na kampatī”ti.

“This knowledge of danger / arises in five instances; / in the peaceful state, in five instances, / one fully understands ten knowledges. / Through skill in the two knowledges / one does not waver among various views.”

“Taṃ ñātaṭṭhena ñāṇaṃ. Pajānanaṭṭhena paññā. Tena vuccati “bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā ādīnave ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.53).

That is knowledge in the sense of knowing it; it is wisdom in the sense of discerning it. Therefore it is said: ‘Wisdom in the appearance of fear is knowledge of danger’.

753. Tattha [V 2.0285] uppādoti purimakammapaccayā idha uppatti. Pavattanti tathā uppannassa pavatti. Nimittanti sabbampi saṅkhāranimittaṃ. Āyūhanāti āyatiṃ paṭisandhihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ. Paṭisandhīti āyatiṃ uppatti. Gatīti yāya gatiyā sā paṭisandhi hoti. Nibbattīti khandhānaṃ nibbattanaṃ. Upapattīti “samāpannassa vā upapannassa vā”ti (dha. sa. 1289, 1291) evaṃ vuttā vipākappavatti. Jātīti jarādīnaṃ paccayabhūtā bhavapaccayā jāti. Jarāmaraṇādayo pākaṭā eva. Ettha ca uppādādayo pañceva ādīnavañāṇassa vatthuvasena vuttā. Sesā tesaṃ vevacanavasena. Nibbatti jātīti idañhi dvayaṃ uppādassa ceva paṭisandhiyā ca vevacanaṃ. Gati upapattīti idaṃ dvayaṃ pavattassa. Jarādayo nimittassāti. Tenāha –

753. Herein, arising is generation here conditioned by past kamma. Occurrence is the occurrence of what has been thus generated. Sign is the sign that is all formations. Volitional formation is the kamma that is the cause for future rebirth-linking. Rebirth-linking is future generation. Destiny is the destiny in which that rebirth-linking occurs. Generation is the generation of the aggregates. Reappearance is the occurrence of the result as stated: ‘of one who has attained or has reappeared’. Birth is the birth conditioned by existence that is the condition for aging, etc. Aging, death, and so on are self-evident. Here, the five terms beginning with ‘arising’ are stated as the objects for the knowledge of danger. The others are stated as their synonyms. For ‘generation’ and ‘birth’ are synonyms for ‘arising’ and ‘rebirth-linking.’ ‘Destiny’ and ‘reappearance’ are synonyms for ‘occurrence.’ Aging and so on are synonyms for ‘sign.’ Hence he said:

“Uppādañca pavattañca, nimittaṃ dukkhanti passati;

Āyūhanaṃ paṭisandhiṃ, ñāṇaṃ ādīnave ida”nti ca.

“Idaṃ ādīnave ñāṇaṃ, pañcaṭhānesu jāyatī”ti ca.

“One sees arising, occurrence, the sign, / volitional formation, and rebirth-linking as suffering; / this is the knowledge of danger.” And: “This knowledge of danger / arises in five instances.”

Anuppādo [M 2.0287] khemanti santipade ñāṇantiādi pana ādīnavañāṇassa paṭipakkhañāṇadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhayatupaṭṭhānena vā ādīnavaṃ disvā ubbiggahadayānaṃ abhayampi atthi khemaṃ nirādīnavanti assāsajananatthampi etaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā vā panassa uppādādayo bhayato sūpaṭṭhitā honti, tassa tappaṭipakkhaninnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmā bhayatupaṭṭhānavasena siddhassa ādīnavañāṇassa ānisaṃsadassanatthampetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

However, the passage beginning ‘“Non-arising is security”—this is knowledge in the peaceful state’ was stated to show the knowledge that is the counterpart to the knowledge of danger. Or it was stated to give reassurance to those with agitated hearts who have seen the danger through the appearance of fear, telling them: ‘There is also the fearless, the secure, the free from danger.’ Or else, since for this meditator arising and so on have become well-manifest as fearful, his mind inclines to their counterpart. Therefore, it should be understood that this was also stated to show the benefit of the knowledge of danger, which is perfected by means of the appearance of fear.

Ettha ca yaṃ bhayaṃ, taṃ yasmā niyamato dukkhaṃ. Taṃ vaṭṭāmisalokāmisakilesāmisehi avippamuttattā sāmisameva. Yañca sāmisaṃ, taṃ saṅkhāramattameva. Tasmā “uppādo dukkhanti bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā ādīnave ñāṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ santepi bhayākārena dukkhākārena sāmisākārenāti evaṃ ākāranānattato pavattivasenevettha nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Here, whatever is fear is necessarily suffering. Because it is not liberated from the bait of the round, the bait of the world, and the bait of the defilements, it is itself with bait. And whatever is with bait is a mere formation. Therefore it was said: ‘“Arising is suffering”—this is wisdom in the appearance of fear, knowledge of danger,’ and so on. This being so, the diversity here should be understood as due to the process of occurrence with its variety of aspects, that is, the aspect of fear, the aspect of suffering, and the aspect of being with bait.

Dasañāṇe pajānātīti ādīnavañāṇaṃ pajānanto uppādādivatthukāni pañca, anuppādādivatthukāni pañcāti dasa ñāṇāni pajānāti paṭivijjhati sacchikaroti. Dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ kusalatāti ādīnavañāṇassa ceva santipadañāṇassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ kusalatāya. Nānādiṭṭhīsu [V 2.0286] na kampatīti paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānādivasena pavattāsu diṭṭhīsu na vedhati. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

As to ‘one fully understands ten knowledges’: while fully understanding the knowledge of danger, one fully understands, penetrates, and realizes ten knowledges, that is, the five that have arising and so on as their object, and the five that have non-arising and so on as their object. As to ‘through skill in the two knowledges’: this means by skill in these two, that is, the knowledge of danger and the knowledge of the peaceful state. As to ‘one does not waver among various views’: one does not tremble at views that proceed in such ways as ‘the supreme Nibbāna visible in this very life.’ The rest here is self-evident.

Ādīnavānupassanāñāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Knowledge of Contemplation of Danger is concluded.

Nibbidānupassanāñāṇakathā

An Explanation of the Knowledge of Contemplation of Disenchantment

754. So evaṃ sabbasaṅkhāre ādīnavato passanto sabbabhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsagate sabhedake saṅkhāragate nibbindati ukkaṇṭhati nābhiramati.

754. Thus, seeing all formations as dangerous, he becomes disenchanted with, is wearied by, and does not delight in the entire conditioned realm, which is subject to breaking up—in all kinds of existence, origins, destinies, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings.

Seyyathāpi nāma, cittakūṭapabbatapādābhirato suvaṇṇarājahaṃso asucimhi caṇḍālagāmadvāraāvāṭe nābhiramati, sattasu mahāsaresuyeva abhiramati, evameva ayampi yogīrājahaṃso suparidiṭṭhādīnave sabhedake saṅkhāragate nābhiramati. Bhāvanārāmatāya pana bhāvanāratiyā samannāgatattā sattasu anupassanāsuyeva ramati.

Just as a golden royal swan that delights at the foot of Mount Cittakūṭa does not delight in a filthy cesspool at the gate of an outcaste village but delights only in the seven great lakes, so too this royal swan of a yogi, having clearly seen the danger in the conditioned realm that is subject to breaking up, does not delight in it. But because he is endowed with delight in development and joy in development, he delights only in the seven contemplations.

Yathā [M 2.0288] ca suvaṇṇapañjare pakkhitto sīho migarājā nābhiramati, tiyojanasahassavitthate pana himavanteyeva ramati, evamayaṃ yogīsīho tividhe sugatibhavepi nābhiramati, tīsu pana anupassanāsuyeva ramati.

And just as a lion, the king of beasts, put into a golden cage does not delight, but delights only in the Himalayas that stretch for three thousand leagues, so too this yogi-lion does not delight even in the threefold happy existence, but delights only in the three contemplations.

Yathā ca sabbaseto sattapatiṭṭho iddhimā vehāsaṅgamo chaddanto nāgarājā nagaramajjhe nābhiramati, himavati chaddantadahagahaneyeva abhiramati, evamayaṃ yogīvaravāraṇo sabbasmimpi saṅkhāragate nābhiramati, anuppādo khemantiādinā nayena diṭṭhe santipadeyeva abhiramati, tanninnatappoṇatappabbhāramānaso hotīti.

And just as the elephant king Chaddanta, an all-white elephant with seven points of support, endowed with psychic power, a sky-goer, does not delight in the middle of a city but delights only in the thickets by Lake Chaddanta in the Himalayas, so too this excellent yogi-elephant does not delight in the entire conditioned realm. He delights only in the state of peace, seen in accordance with the principle 'Non-arising is security,' and his mind inclines, slopes, and leans towards it.

Nibbidānupassanāñāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Knowledge of Contemplation of Disenchantment is finished.

755. Taṃ panetaṃ purimena ñāṇadvayena atthato ekaṃ. Tenāhu porāṇā –

755. This knowledge, however, is one in meaning with the two preceding knowledges. Therefore the ancients have said:

“Bhayatupaṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0287] ekameva tīṇi nāmāni labhati, sabbasaṅkhāre bhayato addasāti bhayatupaṭṭhānaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Tesuyeva saṅkhāresu ādīnavaṃ uppādetīti ādīnavānupassanā nāma jātaṃ. Tesuyeva saṅkhāresu nibbindamānaṃ uppannanti nibbidānupassanā nāma jāta”nti.

‘The knowledge of appearance as fearful is one and the same, but it receives three names. Because one has seen all formations as fearful, it is called “knowledge of appearance as fearful.” Because it arouses the perception of danger in regard to those same formations, it is called “contemplation of danger.” Because it arises as disenchantment in regard to those same formations, it is called “contemplation of disenchantment.”’

Pāḷiyampi vuttaṃ – “yā ca bhayatupaṭṭhāne paññā, yañca ādīnave ñāṇaṃ, yā ca nibbidā, ime dhammā ekatthā, byañjanameva nāna”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.227).

It is also said in the Pāḷi: ‘The wisdom in the appearance as fearful, the knowledge of danger, and disenchantment—these states are one in meaning; only the phrasing is different’ (Paṭis.m. I, 227).

Muñcitukamyatāñāṇakathā

An Explanation of the Knowledge of the Wish for Deliverance

756. Iminā pana nibbidāñāṇena imassa kulaputtassa nibbindantassa ukkaṇṭhantassa anabhiramantassa sabbabhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsagatesu sabhedakesu saṅkhāresu ekasaṅkhārepi cittaṃ na sajjati, na laggati, na bajjhati, sabbasmā saṅkhāragatā muccitukāmaṃ nissaritukāmaṃ hoti. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā nāma jālabbhantaragato maccho, sappamukhagato maṇḍūko, pañjarapakkhitto vanakukkuṭo, daḷhapāsavasagato migo, ahituṇḍikahatthagato sappo, mahāpaṅkapakkhando kuñjaro, supaṇṇamukhagato [M 2.0289] nāgarājā, rāhumukhappaviṭṭho cando, sapattaparivārito purisoti evamādayo tato tato muccitukāmā nissaritukāmāva honti, evaṃ tassa yogino cittaṃ sabbasmā saṅkhāragatā muccitukāmaṃ nissaritukāmaṃ hoti. Athassa evaṃ sabbasaṅkhāresu vigatālayassa sabbasmā saṅkhāragatā muccitukāmassa uppajjati muñcitukamyatā ñāṇanti.

756. Now, through this knowledge of disenchantment, the mind of this clansman—who is becoming disenchanted, wearied, and finds no delight—does not cling to, adhere to, or get bound by even a single formation among all the formations subject to breaking up, in all kinds of existence, origins, destinies, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings. His mind desires to be delivered and to escape from the entire conditioned realm. How so? Just as a fish that has gotten into a net, a frog in a snake’s mouth, a wild fowl put in a cage, a deer caught in a strong snare, a snake in a snake-charmer’s hand, an elephant that has plunged into a great mire, a Nāga king in a supaṇṇa’s mouth, the moon that has entered Rāhu’s mouth, or a man surrounded by his enemies—just as these all desire to be delivered and to escape from their respective situations, so the yogi’s mind desires to be delivered and to escape from the entire conditioned realm. Then, for one who is thus without attachment to all formations and who desires deliverance from the entire conditioned realm, there arises the knowledge of the wish for deliverance.

Muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Knowledge of the Wish for Deliverance is finished.

Paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇakathā

An Explanation of the Knowledge of Contemplation by Reflection

757. So evaṃ sabbabhavayonigatiṭṭhitinivāsagatehi sabhedakehi saṅkhārehi muccitukāmo sabbasmā saṅkhāragatā muccituṃ puna te evaṃ saṅkhāre paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā pariggaṇhāti.

757. Thus, wishing to be delivered from formations that are subject to breaking up—in all kinds of existence, origins, destinies, stations, and abodes—in order to be delivered from the entire conditioned realm, he again comprehends those same formations by means of the knowledge of contemplation by reflection, applying the three characteristics to them.

So [V 2.0288] sabbasaṅkhāre anaccantikato, tāvakālikato, uppādavayaparicchinnato, palokato, calato, pabhaṅguto, addhuvato, vipariṇāmadhammato, assārakato, vibhavato, saṅkhatato, maraṇadhammatotiādīhi kāraṇehi aniccāti passati.

He sees all formations as impermanent for such reasons as: because they are not lasting, because they are temporary, because they are limited by arising and passing away, because they are perishable, because they are trembling, because they are breaking up, because they are unstable, because they are subject to change, because they are essenceless, because they are subject to destruction, because they are conditioned, and because they are subject to death.

Abhiṇhapaṭipīḷanato, dukkhamato, dukkhavatthuto, rogato, gaṇḍato, sallato, aghato, ābādhato, ītito, upaddavato, bhayato, upasaggato, atāṇato, aleṇato, asaraṇato, ādīnavato, aghamūlato, vadhakato, sāsavato, mārāmisato, jātidhammato, jarādhammato, byādhidhammato, sokadhammato, paridevadhammato, upāyāsadhammato, saṃkilesikadhammatotiādīhi kāraṇehi dukkhāti passati.

He sees them as suffering for such reasons as: because they are a constant oppression, suffering itself, a basis for suffering, a disease, a boil, a dart, misery, an affliction, a calamity, a distress, a fear, a danger, without protection, without shelter, without refuge, fraught with danger, the root of misery, a killer, tainted, Māra’s bait, subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to sickness, subject to sorrow, subject to lamentation, subject to despair, and subject to defilement.

Ajaññato, duggandhato, jegucchato, paṭikkūlato, amaṇḍanārahato, virūpato, bībhacchatotiādīhi kāraṇehi dukkhalakkhaṇassa parivārabhūtato asubhato passati.

He sees them as foul because they are an accessory to the characteristic of suffering, and for such reasons as: because they are base, foul-smelling, disgusting, repulsive, unworthy of adornment, ugly, and loathsome.

Parato, rittato, tucchato, suññato, assāmikato, anissarato, avasavattitotiādīhi kāraṇehi anattato passati.

He sees them as not-self for such reasons as: because they are other, empty, vain, void, masterless, without a ruler, and uncontrollable.

758. Evañhi [M 2.0290] passatānena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhārā pariggahitā nāma honti. Kasmā panāyamete evaṃ pariggaṇhātīti? Muñcanassa upāyasampādanatthaṃ.

758. When one sees in this way, it is said that formations have been comprehended by applying the three characteristics. But why does he comprehend them in this way? For the purpose of providing the means for deliverance.

Tatrāyaṃ upamā – eko kira puriso “macche gahessāmī”ti macchakhippaṃ gahetvā udake oḍḍāpesi so khippamukhena hatthaṃ otāretvā antoudake sappaṃ gīvāya gahetvā “maccho me gahito”ti attamano ahosi. So “mahā vata mayā maccho laddho”ti ukkhipitvā passanto sovatthikattayadassanena sappoti sañjānitvā bhīto ādīnavaṃ disvā gahaṇe nibbinno muñcitukāmo hutvā muñcanassa upāyaṃ karonto agganaṅguṭṭhato paṭṭhāya hatthaṃ nibbeṭhetvā bāhuṃ ukkhipitvā uparisīse dve tayo vāre āvijjhitvā sappaṃ dubbalaṃ katvā “gaccha duṭṭha sappā”ti nissajjitvā vegena taḷākapāḷiṃ āruyha “mahantassa vata bho sappassa mukhato muttomhī”ti āgatamaggaṃ olokayamāno aṭṭhāsi.

Here is a simile. A man, it seems, thinking, ‘I will catch a fish,’ took a fish-trap and cast it in the water. Putting his hand in through the trap’s mouth, he caught a snake by the neck inside the water and was delighted, thinking, ‘I have caught a fish.’ Thinking, ‘What a big fish I’ve got!’ he lifted it up to look. But on seeing the three marks on its neck, he recognized it was a snake. He became frightened, saw the danger, and grew disenchanted with what he had caught. Wishing to release it, he devised a means for its release: starting from the tip of its tail, he unwound his hand, raised his arm, and whirled the snake over his head two or three times. Having thus weakened it, he threw it away, saying, ‘Go, you vile snake!’ Then he quickly climbed up on the bank of the pond and stood there looking back along the way he had come, thinking, ‘Sirs, I have escaped from the mouth of a great snake!’

Tattha [V 2.0289] tassa purisassa “maccho”ti sappaṃ gīvāya gahetvā tuṭṭhakālo viya imassāpi yogino āditova attabhāvaṃ paṭilabhitvā tuṭṭhakālo, tassa khippamukhato sīsaṃ nīharitvā sovatthikattayadassanaṃ viya imassa ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā saṅkhāresu tilakkhaṇadassanaṃ, tassa bhītakālo viya imassa bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ. Tato ādīnavadassanaṃ viya ādīnavānupassanāñāṇaṃ, gahaṇe nibbindanaṃ viya nibbidānupassanāñāṇaṃ. Sappaṃ muñcitukāmatā viya muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ, muñcanassa upāyakaraṇaṃ viya paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇena saṅkhāresu tilakkhaṇāropanaṃ. Yathā hi so puriso sappaṃ āvijjhitvā dubbalaṃ katvā nivattetvā ḍaṃsituṃ asamatthabhāvaṃ pāpetvā sumuttaṃ muñcati, evamayaṃ yogāvacaro tilakkhaṇāropanena saṅkhāre āvijjhitvā dubbale katvā puna niccasukhasubhaattākārena upaṭṭhātuṃ asamatthataṃ pāpetvā sumuttaṃ muñcati. Tena vuttaṃ “muñcanassa upāyasampādanatthaṃ evaṃ pariggaṇhātī”ti.

Herein, the time of the man’s delight on catching the snake by the neck, thinking it was a fish, is like the time of this yogi’s delight on first obtaining an individual existence. The man’s seeing the three marks on its neck after pulling the snake’s head out of the trap’s mouth is like this yogi’s seeing the three characteristics in formations after having broken down their compactness. The time of the man’s fear is like this yogi’s knowledge of appearance as fearful. His seeing the danger is like the knowledge of contemplation of danger. His disenchantment with his catch is like the knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment. His wish to release the snake is like the knowledge of the wish for deliverance. His devising a means for its release is like the applying of the three characteristics to formations by means of the knowledge of contemplation by reflection. For just as that man, by whirling the snake, weakening it, and rendering it incapable of biting back, releases it well, so this yogi, by applying the three characteristics, whirls formations, weakens them, and renders them incapable of appearing again in the guise of permanence, pleasure, beauty, or self, and so releases them well. Therefore it was said: ‘For the purpose of providing the means for deliverance, he comprehends them in this way.’

759. Ettāvatā tassa uppannaṃ hoti paṭisaṅkhāñāṇaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

759. By this much the knowledge of reflection has arisen in him. With reference to this it is said:

“Aniccato [M 2.0291] manasikaroto kiṃ paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇaṃ uppajjati? Dukkhato. Anattato manasikaroto kiṃ paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇaṃ uppajjati? Aniccato manasikaroto nimittaṃ paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Dukkhato manasikaroto pavattaṃ paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Anattato manasikaroto nimittañca pavattañca paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇaṃ uppajjatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.227).

‘When one gives attention to impermanence, what knowledge of reflection arises? Knowledge of reflection on suffering. When one gives attention to not-self, what knowledge of reflection arises? When one gives attention to impermanence, the knowledge of reflection on the sign arises. When one gives attention to suffering, the knowledge of reflection on the occurrence arises. When one gives attention to not-self, the knowledge of reflection on both the sign and the occurrence arises’ (Paṭis.m. I, 227).

Ettha ca nimittaṃ paṭisaṅkhāti saṅkhāranimittaṃ “addhuvaṃ tāvakālika”nti aniccalakkhaṇavasena jānitvā. Kāmañca na paṭhamaṃ jānitvā pacchā ñāṇaṃ uppajjati, vohāravasena pana “manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇa”ntiādīni (ma. ni. 3.421) viya evaṃ vuccati. Ekattanayena vā purimañca pacchimañca ekaṃ katvā evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Iminā nayena itarasmimpi padadvaye attho veditabboti.

Herein, ‘reflects on the sign’ means knowing the sign of formations as ‘unstable, temporary’ by way of the characteristic of impermanence. And it is not that one first knows and then knowledge arises afterward; rather, this is said as a matter of convention, like the passage beginning, ‘Dependent on the mind and on phenomena, mind-consciousness arises’ (MN 148). Or it should be understood that this is said by unifying the former and the latter according to the principle of oneness. The meaning of the other two phrases should be understood in the same way.

Paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Knowledge of Contemplation by Reflection is finished.

Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇakathā

Discourse on the Knowledge of Equanimity Towards Formations

760. So [V 2.0290] evaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇena “sabbe saṅkhārā suññā”ti pariggahetvā puna “suññamidaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā”ti (ma. ni. 3.69) dvikoṭikaṃ suññataṃ pariggaṇhāti. So evaṃ neva attānaṃ, na paraṃ kiñci attano parikkhārabhāve ṭhitaṃ disvā puna “nāhaṃ kvacani, kassaci kiñcanatasmiṃ, na ca mama kvacani, kismiñci kiñcanatatthī”ti yā ettha catukoṭikā suññatā kathitā, taṃ pariggaṇhāti.

760. Having thus grasped with the knowledge of contemplation by reflection that 'all formations are empty,' he further grasps the twofold emptiness: 'This is empty of self or of what belongs to self.' Seeing that neither a self nor anything other exists as a possession of his, he then grasps the fourfold emptiness stated here: 'I am not anywhere, nor am I anyone's possession in any way; and there is nothing of mine anywhere, nor is there for me any possession in anything.'

Kathaṃ? Ayañhi nāhaṃ kvacanīti kvaci attānaṃ na passati. Kassaci kiñcanatasminti attano attānaṃ kassaci parassa kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ na passati. Bhātiṭṭhānevā bhātaraṃ, sahāyaṭṭhāne vā sahāyaṃ, parikkhāraṭṭhāne vā parikkhāraṃ maññitvā upanetabbaṃ na passatīti attho. Na ca mama kvacanīti ettha mama-saddaṃ tāva ṭhapetvā na ca kvacanīti parassa ca attānaṃ kvaci napassatīti [M 2.0292] ayamattho. Idāni mama-saddaṃ āharitvā mama kismiñci kiñcanatatthīti so parassa attā mama kismiñci kiñcanabhāve atthīti na passatīti. Attano bhātiṭṭhāne vā bhātaraṃ, sahāyaṭṭhāne vā sahāyaṃ parikkhāraṭṭhāne vā parikkhāranti kismiñci ṭhāne parassa attānaṃ iminā kiñcanabhāvena upanetabbaṃ na passatīti attho. Evamayaṃ yasmā neva katthaci attānaṃ passati, na taṃ parassa kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ passati, na parassa attānaṃ passati, na parassa attānaṃ attano kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ passati. Tasmānena catukoṭikā suññatā pariggahitā hotīti.

How? 'I am not anywhere' means he does not see a self anywhere. 'Nor am I anyone's possession in any way' means he does not see his own self as something to be brought into a state of possession for any other person. That is, he does not see it as something to be brought over, thinking of it as a brother in the place of a brother, a friend in the place of a friend, or a possession in the place of a possession. As for 'and there is nothing of mine anywhere, nor is there for me any possession in anything,' here, setting aside the word 'mine' for a moment, 'and not anywhere' means he does not see another’s self anywhere. Now, bringing in the word 'mine,' 'nor is there for me any possession in anything' means he does not see that another's self exists for him in any state of possession. That is, he does not see another’s self as something to be brought into a state of possession for himself, such as a brother in the place of a brother, a friend in the place of a friend, or a possession in the place of a possession. Thus, because he neither sees a self anywhere, nor sees that self as something to be brought into a state of possession for another, nor sees another’s self, nor sees another’s self as something to be brought into a state of possession for himself, therefore this fourfold emptiness is grasped by him.

761. Evaṃ catukoṭikaṃ suññataṃ pariggahetvā puna chahākārehi suññataṃ pariggaṇhāti. Kathaṃ? Cakkhu suññaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā niccena vā dhuvena vā sassatena vā avipariṇāmadhammena vā…pe… mano suñño. Rūpā suññā…pe… dhammā suññā. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manoviññāṇaṃ. Cakkhusamphassoti evaṃ yāva jarāmaraṇā nayo netabbo.

761. Having thus grasped the fourfold emptiness, he further grasps emptiness in six aspects. How? The eye is empty of self, or of what belongs to self, or of permanence, or of stability, or of eternity, or of an unchanging nature… up to… the mind is empty. Forms are empty… up to… mental phenomena are empty. Eye-consciousness… up to… mind-consciousness. Eye-contact… thus the method should be applied all the way up to aging and death.

762. Evaṃ chahākārehi suññataṃ pariggahetvā puna aṭṭhahākārehi pariggaṇhāti. Seyyathidaṃ – rūpaṃ asāraṃ nissāraṃ sārāpagataṃ niccasārasārena vā dhuvasārasārena vā sukhasārasārena [V 2.0291] vā attasārasārena vā niccena vā dhuvena vā sassatena vā avipariṇāmadhammena vā. Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ… cakkhu…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ asāraṃ nissāraṃ sārāpagataṃ niccasārasārena vā dhuvasārasārena vā sukhasārasārena vā attasārasārena vā niccena vā dhuvena vā sassatena vā avipariṇāmadhammena vā. Yathā naḷo asāro nissāro sārāpagato. Yathā eraṇḍo… yathā udumbaro… yathā setavaccho… yathā pāḷibhaddako… yathā pheṇapiṇḍo… yathā udakabubbuḷaṃ… yathā marīci… yathā kadalikkhandho… yathā māyā asārā nissārā sārāpagatā, evameva rūpaṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ asāraṃ nissāraṃ sārāpagataṃ niccasārasārena vā…pe… avipariṇāmadhammena vāti (cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 88).

762. Having comprehended emptiness in these six ways, one then comprehends it in eight ways. Namely: form is without essence, devoid of essence, with essence departed; it is empty of an essence of permanence, an essence of stability, an essence of happiness, or an essence of self; and it is empty of being permanent, stable, eternal, or of an unchanging nature. Feeling… perception… formations… consciousness… the eye… up to… aging-and-death is without essence, devoid of essence, with essence departed... Just as a reed is without essence, devoid of essence, with essence departed; just as a castor-oil plant… just as a fig tree… just as a setavaccha tree… just as a coral tree… just as a ball of foam… just as a water bubble… just as a mirage… just as a plantain trunk… just as a magical illusion is without essence, devoid of essence, with essence departed—so too is form… up to… aging-and-death without essence, devoid of essence, with essence departed; empty of an essence of permanence… up to… or of an unchanging nature.

763. So [M 2.0293] evaṃ aṭṭhahākārehi suññataṃ pariggahetvā puna dasahākārehi pariggaṇhāti, rūpaṃ rittato passati. Tucchato… suññato… anattato… anissariyato… akāmakāriyato… alabbhanīyato… avasavattakato… parato… vivittato passati. Vedanaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ rittato…pe… vivittato passatīti.

763. Having thus apprehended emptiness in these eight aspects, one further apprehends it in ten aspects: one sees form as empty… as hollow… as void… as not-self… as masterless… as unable to be willed… as unobtainable… as uncontrollable… as other… as secluded. One sees feeling… up to… consciousness as empty… up to… as secluded.

764. Evaṃ dasahākārehi suññataṃ pariggahetvā puna dvādasahākārehi pariggaṇhāti. Seyyathidaṃ – rūpaṃ na satto, na jīvo, na naro, na māṇavo, na itthī, na puriso, na attā, na attaniyaṃ. Nāhaṃ, na mama, na aññassa, na kassaci. Vedanā…pe… viññāṇaṃ na kassacīti (cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 88).

764. Having comprehended emptiness in these ten ways, one then comprehends it in twelve ways. Namely: form is not a being, not a living principle, not a man, not a youth, not a woman, not a male, not a self, not what belongs to a self. Not ‘I,’ not ‘mine,’ not ‘another's,’ not ‘anyone's.’ Feeling... up to... consciousness is not ‘anyone's.’

765. Evaṃ dvādasahākārehi suññataṃ pariggaṇhitvā puna tīraṇapariññāvasena dvācattālīsāya ākārehi suññataṃ pariggaṇhāti, rūpaṃ aniccato… dukkhato… rogato… gaṇḍato… sallato… aghato… ābādhato… parato… palokato… ītito… upaddavato… bhayato… upasaggato… calato… pabhaṅguto… addhuvato… atāṇato… aleṇato… asaraṇato… asaraṇībhūtato… rittato… tucchato… suññato… anattato… anassādato… ādīnavato… vipariṇāmadhammato… assārakato… aghamūlato… vadhakato… vibhavato… sāsavato… saṅkhatato… mārāmisato… jātidhammato… jarādhammato… byādhidhammato… maraṇadhammato… sokaparidevadukkhadomanassaupāyāsadhammato… samudayato… atthaṅgamato… anassādato [V 2.0292]… ādīnavato… nissaraṇato passati. Vedanaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ aniccato…pe… nissaraṇato passati.

765. Having comprehended emptiness in these twelve ways, one then comprehends it in forty-two ways through full understanding by investigation: one sees form as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as other, as dissolving, as a scourge, as a calamity, as a terror, as a vexation, as unstable, as crumbling, as not lasting, as without protection, as without shelter, as without refuge, as refuge-less, as empty, as hollow, as void, as not-self, as without gratification, as dangerous, as subject to change, as pithless, as a root of misery, as a slayer, as liable to destruction, as with taints, as conditioned, as Māra's bait, as subject to birth, as subject to aging, as subject to illness, as subject to death, as subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, as arising, as vanishing, as without gratification, as dangerous, as an escape. One sees feeling... up to... consciousness as impermanent... up to... as an escape.

Vuttampi cetaṃ – “rūpaṃ aniccato…pe… nissaraṇato passanto suññato lokaṃ avekkhati. Vedanaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ aniccato…pe… nissaraṇato passanto suññato lokaṃ avekkhati”.

And this has been said: 'Seeing form as impermanent… up to… as an escape, one regards the world as empty. Seeing feeling… up to… consciousness as impermanent… up to… as an escape, one regards the world as empty.'

“Suññato lokaṃ avekkhassu, mogharāja sadā sato;

Attānudiṭṭhiṃ ūhacca, evaṃ maccutaro siyā;

Evaṃ lokaṃ avekkhantaṃ, maccurājā na passatī”ti. (su. ni. 1125; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 88);

'Regard the world as empty, Mogharāja, ever mindful; having uprooted the view of self, one may thus cross beyond death. The King of Death does not see one who regards the world in this way.'

766. Evaṃ [M 2.0294] suññato disvā tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā saṅkhāre pariggaṇhanto bhayañca nandiñca vippahāya saṅkhāresu udāsīno ahosi majjhatto, ahanti vā mamanti vā na gaṇhāti vissaṭṭhabhariyo viya puriso.

766. Seeing them thus as empty and applying the three characteristics, while comprehending formations, he abandons fear and delight. He becomes indifferent and neutral towards formations, not grasping at 'I' or 'mine,' like a man who has repudiated his wife.

Yathā nāma purisassa bhariyā bhaveyya iṭṭhā kantā manāpā, so tāya vinā muhuttampi adhivāsetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya, ativiya naṃ mamāyeyya, so taṃ itthiṃ aññena purisena saddhiṃ ṭhitaṃ vā nisinnaṃ vā kathentiṃ vā hasantiṃ vā disvā kupito assa anattamano, adhimattaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeyya. So aparena samayena tassā itthiyā dosaṃ disvā muñcitukāmo hutvā taṃ vissajjeyya, na naṃ mamāti gaṇheyya. Tato paṭṭhāya taṃ yenakenaci saddhiṃ yaṃkiñci kurumānaṃ disvāpi neva kuppeyya, na domanassaṃ āpajjeyya, aññadatthu udāsīnova bhaveyya majjhatto. Evamevāyaṃ sabbasaṅkhārehi muñcitukāmo hutvā paṭisaṅkhānupassanāya saṅkhāre pariggaṇhanto ahaṃ mamāti gahetabbaṃ adisvā bhayañca nandiñca vippahāya sabbasaṅkhāresu udāsīno hoti majjhatto.

Just as a man might have a wife who is desired, lovely, and pleasing, so that he could not endure even for a moment without her and would be exceedingly attached to her; if he were to see that woman standing, sitting, talking, or laughing with another man, he would become angry and displeased, and would experience extreme grief. But at a later time, having seen a fault in that woman and wishing to be free from her, he would repudiate her and no longer regard her as his. From then on, even seeing her doing anything with anyone else, he would neither be angry nor experience grief; instead, he would remain indifferent and neutral. In the same way, this person, wishing to be free from all formations, comprehending formations through reflective contemplation, not seeing anything to be grasped as 'I' or 'mine,' and having abandoned fear and delight, becomes indifferent and neutral towards all formations.

Tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato tīsu bhavesu catūsu yonīsu pañcasu gatīsu sattasu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu [V 2.0293] navasu sattāvāsesu cittaṃ patilīyati patikuṭati pativattati na sampasāriyati, upekkhā vā pāṭikulyatā vā saṇṭhāti.

For one who knows thus and sees thus, his mind shrinks back, recoils, and turns away from the three realms of existence, the four modes of generation, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings. It does not expand, but settles in equanimity or repugnance.

Seyyathāpi nāma padumapalāse īsakapoṇe udakaphusitāni patilīyanti patikuṭanti pativattanti na sampasāriyanti, evameva…pe… seyyathāpi nāma kukkuṭapattaṃ vā nahārudaddulaṃ vā aggimhi pakkhittaṃ patilīyati patikuṭati pativattati na sampasāriyati (a. ni. 7.49), evameva tassa tīsu bhavesu cittaṃ…pe… upekkhā vā pāṭikulyatā vā saṇṭhāti. Iccassa saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ nāma uppannaṃ hoti.

Just as water droplets on a slightly tilted lotus leaf shrink back, curl back, and roll back, and do not spread out; and just as a chicken feather or a piece of sinew thrown into a fire shrinks, curls, and rolls back, and does not spread out, even so his mind... stays in either equanimity or repugnance regarding the three realms of existence. Thus, the knowledge of equanimity toward formations has arisen in him.

767. Taṃ panetaṃ sace santipadaṃ nibbānaṃ santato passati, sabbaṃ saṅkhārappavattaṃ vissajjetvā nibbānameva pakkhandati. No ce nibbānaṃ santato [M 2.0295] passati, punappunaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇameva hutvā pavattati sāmuddikānaṃ disākāko viya. Sāmuddikā kira vāṇijakā nāvaṃ ārohantā disākākaṃ nāma gaṇhanti, te yadā nāvā vātakkhittā videsaṃ pakkhandati, tīraṃ na paññāyati, tadā disākākaṃ vissajjenti. So kūpakayaṭṭhito ākāsaṃ laṅghitvā sabbā disā ca vidisā ca anugantvā sace tīraṃ passati, tadabhimukhova gacchati. No ce passati, punappunaṃ āgantvā kūpakayaṭṭhiṃyeva allīyati. Evameva sace saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ santipadaṃ nibbānaṃ santato passati, sabbaṃ saṅkhārappavattaṃ vissajjetvā nibbānameva pakkhandati. No ce passati, punappunaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇameva hutvā pavattati.

767. If this knowledge of equanimity towards formations sees Nibbāna, the peaceful state, as peaceful, it abandons the entire stream of formations and leaps into Nibbāna alone. If it does not see Nibbāna as peaceful, it occurs again and again with formations as its object, like the direction-crow of seafarers. It is said that seafaring merchants, when boarding a ship, take a direction-crow with them. When their ship, tossed by the wind, is driven to a foreign region and the shore is no longer visible, they release the direction-crow. It soars into the sky from the mast, flies around all the directions and intermediate directions, and if it sees a shore, it goes straight towards it. If it does not see a shore, it returns again and again and settles on the mast itself. In the same way, if the knowledge of equanimity towards formations sees Nibbāna, the peaceful state, as peaceful, it abandons the entire stream of formations and leaps into Nibbāna alone. If it does not see it, it occurs again and again with formations as its object.

Tadidaṃ suppagge piṭṭhaṃ vaṭṭayamānaṃ viya. Nibbaṭṭitakappāsaṃ vihanamānaṃ viya nānappakārato saṅkhāre pariggahetvā bhayañca nandiñca pahāya saṅkhāravicinane majjhattaṃ hutvā tividhānupassanāvasena tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tividhavimokkhamukhabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā sattaariyapuggalavibhāgāya paccayo hoti.

This knowledge, becoming subtle like flour being sifted on a tray or like ginned cotton being carded, comprehends formations in various ways, abandons both fear and delight, and becomes neutral in the investigation of formations; thus it abides by way of the threefold contemplation. So abiding, it reaches the state of being a gateway to the threefold liberation and becomes a condition for the classification of the seven noble individuals.

768. Tatridaṃ tividhānupassanāvasena pavattanato tiṇṇaṃ indriyānaṃ ādhipateyyavasena tividhavimokkhamukhabhāvaṃ āpajjati nāma. Tisso hi anupassanā tīṇi vimokkhamukhānīti vuccanti. Yathāha –

768. Herein, it is said that this knowledge attains the state of being a threefold gateway to liberation because it proceeds by way of the threefold contemplation and by way of the dominance of the three faculties. For the three contemplations are called the three gateways to liberation. As it was said:

“Tīṇi [V 2.0294] kho panimāni vimokkhamukhāni lokaniyyānāya saṃvattanti, sabbasaṅkhāre paricchedaparivaṭumato samanupassanatāya, animittāya ca dhātuyā cittasampakkhandanatāya, sabbasaṅkhāresu manosamuttejanatāya, appaṇihitāya ca dhātuyā cittasampakkhandanatāya, sabbadhamme parato samanupassanatāya, suññatāya ca dhātuyā cittasampakkhandanatāya, imāni tīṇi vimokkhamukhāni lokaniyyānāya saṃvattantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.219).

“These three gateways to liberation, indeed, conduce to the escape from the world: through contemplating all formations as delimited and circumscribed, and through the mind’s leaping into the signless element; through stimulating the mind in regard to all formations, and through the mind’s leaping into the desireless element; through contemplating all things as other, and through the mind’s leaping into the emptiness element. These three gateways to liberation conduce to the escape from the world.”

Tattha paricchedaparivaṭumatoti udayabbayavasena paricchedato ceva parivaṭumato ca. Aniccānupassanaṃ hi “udayato pubbe saṅkhārā natthī”ti paricchinditvā tesaṃ gatiṃ samannesamānaṃ “vayato paraṃ na gacchanti, ettheva antaradhāyantī”ti parivaṭumato samanupassati. Manosamuttejanatāyāti cittasaṃvejanatāya[M 2.0296]. Dukkhānupassanena hi saṅkhāresu cittaṃ saṃvejeti. Parato samanupassanatāyāti “nāhaṃ, na mamā”ti evaṃ anattato samanupassanatāya. Iti imāni tīṇi padāni aniccānupassanādīnaṃ vasena vuttānīti veditabbāni. Teneva tadanantare pañhavissajjane vuttaṃ – “aniccato manasikaroto khayato saṅkhārā upaṭṭhahanti. Dukkhato manasikaroto bhayato saṅkhārā upaṭṭhahanti. Anattato manasikaroto suññato saṅkhārā upaṭṭhahantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.219).

Here, ‘as delimited and circumscribed’ means by way of delimiting and circumscribing through arising and passing away. For the contemplation of impermanence, having delimited by thinking, ‘Before their arising, formations do not exist,’ and while investigating their course, contemplates them as circumscribed by thinking, ‘After passing away, they do not go anywhere—they vanish right here.’ ‘Stimulation of the mind’ means for the sake of stirring a sense of urgency in the mind. For, through the contemplation of suffering, one stirs a sense of urgency in the mind regarding formations. ‘Contemplating as other’ means contemplating as not-self, thus: ‘This is not I, this is not mine.’ Thus, these three phrases should be understood as spoken in connection with the contemplation of impermanence and so on. For this reason, in the answer to the question that immediately follows, it is said: ‘To one who attends to them as impermanent, formations appear as perishing. To one who attends to them as suffering, formations appear as fearful. To one who attends to them as not-self, formations appear as empty.’”

769. Katame pana te vimokkhā, yesaṃ imāni anupassanāni mukhānīti? Animitto, appaṇihito, suññatoti ete tayo. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ “aniccato manasikaronto adhimokkhabahulo animittaṃ vimokkhaṃ paṭilabhati. Dukkhato manasikaronto passaddhibahulo appaṇihitaṃ vimokkhaṃ paṭilabhati. Anattato manasikaronto vedabahulo suññatavimokkhaṃ paṭilabhatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.223).

769. But what are those liberations for which these contemplations are the gateways? They are these three: the signless, the desireless, and the empty. For it has been said: ‘One who attends to impermanence, being abundant in resolve, attains the signless liberation. One who attends to suffering, being abundant in tranquility, attains the desireless liberation. One who attends to not-self, being abundant in knowledge, attains the empty liberation.’”

Ettha ca animitto vimokkhoti animittākārena nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavatto ariyamaggo. So hi animittāya dhātuyā uppannattā animitto. Kilesehi ca vimuttattā vimokkho. Eteneva nayena appaṇihitākārena nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavatto appaṇihito. Suññatākārena nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavatto suññatoti veditabbo.

Herein, the signless liberation is the noble path that proceeds having taken Nibbāna as its object in its signless aspect. For it is ‘signless’ because it has arisen in the signless element, and it is ‘liberation’ because it is liberated from the defilements. By this same method, that which proceeds having taken Nibbāna as its object in its desireless aspect is the desireless liberation. That which proceeds having taken Nibbāna as its object in its emptiness aspect is to be understood as the empty liberation.

770. Yaṃ pana abhidhamme “yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāveti niyyānikaṃ apacayagāmiṃ [V 2.0295] diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāya paṭhamāya bhūmiyā pattiyā vivicceva kāmehi paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati appaṇihitaṃ suññata”nti (dha. sa. 343 ādayo) evaṃ vimokkhadvayameva vuttaṃ, taṃ nippariyāyato vipassanāgamanaṃ sandhāya. Vipassanāñāṇaṃ hi kiñcāpi paṭisambhidāmagge –

770. However, in the Abhidhamma, where it is said: ‘At the time when one develops the supramundane jhāna that is emancipating, that leads to the undoing of the round, for the abandonment of views, for the attainment of the first stage, having, quite secluded from sensual pleasures… entered upon and abided in the first jhāna, which is desireless and empty’ (Dhs. §343ff.), only two liberations are mentioned. This is stated directly with reference to the approach of insight. For although insight knowledge in the Paṭisambhidāmagga—

“Aniccānupassanāñāṇaṃ niccato abhinivesaṃ muñcatīti suññato vimokkho. Dukkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ sukhato abhinivesaṃ. Anattānupassanāñāṇaṃ attato abhinivesaṃ muñcatīti [M 2.0297] suññato vimokkho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.229) evaṃ abhinivesaṃ muñcanavasena suññato vimokkhoti ca,

is called empty liberation by way of releasing adherence, thus: ‘The knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence releases adherence to permanence, thus it is empty liberation. The knowledge of the contemplation of suffering [releases adherence] to pleasure… The knowledge of the contemplation of not-self releases adherence to self, thus it is empty liberation’ (Paṭis I 229); and

“Aniccānupassanāñāṇaṃ niccato nimittaṃ muñcatīti animitto vimokkho. Dukkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ sukhato nimittaṃ, anattānupassanāñāṇaṃ attato nimittaṃ muñcatīti animitto vimokkho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.229) evaṃ nimittaṃ muñcanavasena animitto vimokkhoti ca,

is called signless liberation by way of releasing the sign, thus: ‘The knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence releases the sign of permanence, thus it is signless liberation. The knowledge of the contemplation of suffering [releases the sign] of pleasure… The knowledge of the contemplation of not-self releases the sign of self, thus it is signless liberation’ (Paṭis I 229); and

“Aniccānupassanāñāṇaṃ niccato paṇidhiṃ muñcatīti appaṇihito vimokkho. Dukkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ sukhato paṇidhiṃ. Anattānupassanāñāṇaṃ attato paṇidhiṃ muñcatīti appaṇihito vimokkho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.229) evaṃ paṇidhiṃ muñcanavasena appaṇihito vimokkhoti ca –

‘The knowledge of contemplating impermanence releases the aspiration for permanence, thus it is desireless liberation. The knowledge of contemplating suffering releases the aspiration for pleasure. The knowledge of contemplating non-self releases the aspiration for self, thus it is desireless liberation.’ (Paṭis. I 229) In this way, by way of releasing aspiration, it is called desireless liberation.

Vuttaṃ. Tathāpi taṃ saṅkhāranimittassa avijahanato na nippariyāyena animittaṃ. Nippariyāyena pana suññatañceva appaṇihitañca. Tassa ca āgamanavasena ariyamaggakkhaṇe vimokkho uddhaṭo. Tasmā appaṇihitaṃ suññatanti vimokkhadvayameva vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāvettha vimokkhakathā.

It is said. Nevertheless, because it does not abandon the sign of formations, it is not signless in the absolute sense. In the absolute sense, however, it is both empty and desireless. And its liberation is expounded at the moment of the noble path by way of its approach. Therefore, it should be understood that only the two liberations—the desireless and the empty—are spoken of. This, to this extent, is the discussion on liberation here.

771. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “sattaariyapuggalavibhāgāya paccayo hotī”ti, tattha saddhānusārī, saddhāvimutto, kāyasakkhi, ubhatobhāgavimutto, dhammānusārī, diṭṭhippatto, paññāvimuttoti [V 2.0296] ime tāva satta ariyapuggalā, tesaṃ vibhāgāya idaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ paccayo hoti.

771. As for what was said, ‘It is a condition for the classification of the seven noble individuals,’ in that context: the faith-follower, the faith-emancipated, the body-witness, the one liberated both ways, the Dhamma-follower, the view-attainer, and the wisdom-emancipated—these are indeed the seven noble individuals.
