For their classification, this knowledge of equanimity regarding formations is a condition.

772. Yo hi aniccato manasikaronto adhimokkhabahulo saddhindriyaṃ paṭilabhati, so sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe saddhānusārī hoti. Sesesu sattasu ṭhānesu saddhāvimutto.

772. For one who attends to impermanence, being abundant in conviction, attains the faculty of faith. At the moment of the path of stream-entry, they are a faith-follower. In the remaining seven instances, they are faith-emancipated.

773. Yo pana dukkhato manasikaronto passaddhibahulo samādhindriyaṃ paṭilabhati, so sabbattha kāyasakkhi nāma hoti. Arūpajjhānaṃ pana patvā aggaphalappatto ubhatobhāgavimutto nāma hoti.

773. One who attends to suffering, being abundant in tranquility, attains the faculty of concentration; they are called a body-witness in all instances. But having attained the formless jhānas and reached the supreme fruit, one is called liberated both ways.

774. Yo [M 2.0298] pana anattato manasikaronto vedabahulo paññindriyaṃ paṭilabhati, so sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe dhammānusārī hoti. Chasu ṭhānesu diṭṭhippatto aggaphale paññāvimuttoti.

774. One who attends to non-self, being abundant in knowledge, attains the faculty of wisdom; they are a Dhamma-follower at the moment of the path of stream-entry. In six instances, they are a view-attainer; in the highest fruition, wisdom-emancipated.

775. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ –

775. For this has been said:

“Aniccato manasikaroto saddhindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti. Saddhindriyassa adhimattattā sotāpattimaggaṃ paṭilabhati, tena vuccati saddhānusārī”ti.

‘By attending to impermanence, the faculty of faith becomes predominant. Because of the predominance of the faculty of faith, one attains the path of stream-entry; therefore, one is called a faith-follower.’

Tathā “aniccato manasikaroto saddhindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti, saddhindriyassa adhimattattā sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchikataṃ hoti, tena vuccati saddhāvimutto”tiādi (paṭi. ma. 1.221).

Similarly, ‘When one attends to impermanence, the faculty of faith becomes predominant. Due to the predominance of the faculty of faith, the fruit of stream-entry is realized; therefore, one is called faith-emancipated,’ and so on (Paṭis. I 221).

776. Aparampi vuttaṃ –

776. Further, it is said:

“Saddahanto vimuttoti saddhāvimutto. Phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikatoti kāyasakkhi. Diṭṭhantaṃ pattoti diṭṭhippatto. Saddahanto vimuccatīti saddhāvimutto. Jhānaphassaṃ paṭhamaṃ phusati pacchā nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikarotīti kāyasakkhi. ‘Dukkhā saṅkhārā, sukho nirodho’ti ñātaṃ hoti diṭṭhaṃ viditaṃ sacchikataṃ phusitaṃ paññāyāti diṭṭhippatto”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.221).

‘One who is liberated through faith is called faith-emancipated. One who has directly experienced what is to be touched is called a body-witness. One who has attained what is to be seen is called a view-attainer. One who is liberated through faith is called faith-emancipated. One who first experiences the contact of jhāna and later directly experiences cessation, Nibbāna, is called a body-witness. ‘Formations are suffering, cessation is bliss’—this is known, seen, understood, directly experienced, and touched by wisdom; thus, one is called a view-attainer’ (Paṭis. I 221).

777. Itaresu [V 2.0297] pana catūsu saddhaṃ anusarati, saddhāya vā anusarati gacchatīti saddhānusārī. Tathā paññāsaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ anusarati, dhammena vā anusaratīti dhammānusārī. Arūpajjhānena ceva ariyamaggena cāti ubhatobhāgena vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimutto. Pajānanto vimuttoti paññāvimuttoti evaṃ vacanattho veditabboti.

777. As for the other four: one follows faith, or proceeds by means of faith—thus, one is a 'faith-follower.' Similarly, one follows the Dhamma reckoned as wisdom, or proceeds by means of the Dhamma—thus, one is a 'Dhamma-follower.' One is liberated by both parts—by the formless jhānas and by the noble path—thus, one is 'liberated both ways.' One is liberated through understanding—thus, one is 'liberated by wisdom.' In this way, the meaning of the terms should be understood.

Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ.

The knowledge of equanimity regarding formations.

778. Taṃ panetaṃ purimena ñāṇadvayena atthato ekaṃ. Tenāhu porāṇā – “idaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ ekameva tīṇi nāmāni labhati, heṭṭhā [M 2.0299] muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ nāma jātaṃ, majjhe paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇaṃ nāma, ante ca sikhāppattaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ nāma”.

778. That knowledge, however, is one in meaning with the two preceding knowledges. Therefore, the ancients said: "This knowledge of equanimity towards formations is one, but obtains three names: at the beginning, it comes to be called 'knowledge of the desire for release'; in the middle, 'knowledge of reflective contemplation'; and at the end, 'knowledge of equanimity towards formations, having reached the summit.'"

779. Pāḷiyampi vuttaṃ –

779. It is also stated in the canonical text:

“Kathaṃ muñcitukamyatā-paṭisaṅkhā-santiṭṭhanā paññā saṅkhārupekkhāsu ñāṇaṃ? Uppādaṃ muñcitukamyatā-paṭisaṅkhā-santiṭṭhanā paññā saṅkhārupekkhāsu ñāṇaṃ. Pavattaṃ…pe… nimittaṃ…pe… upāyāsaṃ muñcitukamyatāpaṭisaṅkhā-santiṭṭhanā paññā saṅkhārupekkhāsu ñāṇaṃ. Uppādo dukkhanti…pe… bhayanti…pe… sāmisanti…pe… uppādo saṅkhārāti…pe… upāyāso saṅkhārāti muñcitukamyatā-paṭisaṅkhā-santiṭṭhanā paññā saṅkhārupekkhāsu ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.54).

"How is wisdom, the knowledge of equanimity regarding formations, characterized by the desire for release, reflection, and steadiness? Wisdom regarding arising is the knowledge of equanimity towards formations characterized by the desire for release, reflection, and steadiness. Wisdom regarding continuation... the sign... distress is the knowledge of equanimity towards formations characterized by the desire for release, reflection, and steadiness. 'Arising is suffering'... 'fearsome'... 'with attachment'... 'arising is formations'... 'distress is formations'—wisdom is the knowledge of equanimity towards formations characterized by the desire for release, reflection, and steadiness" (Paṭis. I 54).

780. Tattha muñcitukamyatā ca sā paṭisaṅkhā ca santiṭṭhanā cāti muñcitukamyatā-paṭisaṅkhā-santiṭṭhanā. Iti pubbabhāge nibbidāñāṇena nibbinnassa uppādādīni pariccajitukāmatā muñcitukāmatā. Muñcanassa upāyakaraṇatthaṃ majjhe paṭisaṅkhānaṃ paṭisaṅkhā. Muñcitvā avasāne ajjhupekkhanaṃ santiṭṭhanā. Yaṃ sandhāya “uppādo saṅkhārā, te saṅkhāre ajjhupekkhatīti saṅkhārupekkhā”tiādi (paṭi. ma. 1.54) vuttaṃ. Evaṃ ekamevidaṃ ñāṇaṃ.

780. Herein, the desire for deliverance, reflection, and remaining steady—these are called 'the desire for deliverance, reflection, and remaining steady.' Thus, in the preliminary stage, the desire to abandon arising and so on, of one who is disenchanted by the knowledge of disenchantment, is the desire for deliverance. In the middle, reflection is the consideration for making a means of deliverance. At the end, the equanimity of overlooking after deliverance is remaining steady. Regarding this, it is said: "Arising is formations; one remains equanimous toward those formations—thus, it is called 'equanimity toward formations,'" and so on (Paṭis. I 54). In this way, this is indeed one knowledge.

781. Apica imāyapi pāḷiyā idaṃ ekamevāti veditabbaṃ. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ – “yā ca muñcitukamyatā, yā ca paṭisaṅkhānupassanā, yā ca saṅkhārupekkhā, ime dhammā ekatthā, byañjanameva nāna”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.227).

781. Moreover, from this canonical passage, it should be understood that this is just one. For it was said: "The wish to be liberated, reflective insight, and equanimity towards formations—these qualities have the same meaning, only the wording is different" (Paṭis. I 227).

782. Evaṃ [V 2.0298] adhigatasaṅkhārupekkhassa pana imassa kulaputtassa vipassanā sikhāppattā vuṭṭhānagāminī hoti. Sikhāppattā vipassanāti vā vuṭṭhānagāminīti vā saṅkhārupekkhādiñāṇattayasseva etaṃ nāmaṃ. Sā hi sikhaṃ uttamabhāvaṃ pattattā sikhāppattā. Vuṭṭhānaṃ gacchatīti vuṭṭhānagāminī. Vuṭṭhānaṃ vuccati bahiddhānimittabhūtato abhiniviṭṭhavatthuto ceva ajjhattapavattato ca vuṭṭhahanato maggo, taṃ gacchatīti vuṭṭhānagāminī, maggena saddhiṃ ghaṭiyatīti attho.

782. For this clansman who has thus attained equanimity towards formations, insight, having reached its peak, becomes emergence-leading. 'Insight that has reached its peak' or 'emergence-leading' are names for the threefold knowledge beginning with equanimity towards formations. For it is called 'having reached its peak' because it has reached the peak, the supreme state. It is called 'emergence-leading' because it goes to emergence. The path is called 'emergence' because it emerges from the object of adherence which has become an external sign, and from internal occurrence. Because it goes to that, it is 'emergence-leading'; the meaning is that it connects with the path.

783. Tatrāyaṃ abhinivesavuṭṭhānānaṃ āvibhāvatthāya mātikā – ajjhattaṃ abhinivisitvā ajjhattā vuṭṭhāti, ajjhattaṃ abhinivisitvā bahiddhā vuṭṭhāti[M 2.0300], bahiddhā abhinivisitvā bahiddhā vuṭṭhāti, bahiddhā abhinivisitvā ajjhattā vuṭṭhāti, rūpe abhinivisitvā rūpā vuṭṭhāti, rūpe abhinivisitvā arūpā vuṭṭhāti, arūpe abhinivisitvā arūpā vuṭṭhāti, arūpe abhinivisitvā rūpā vuṭṭhāti, ekappahārena pañcahi khandhehi vuṭṭhāti, aniccato abhinivisitvā aniccato vuṭṭhāti, aniccato abhinivisitvā dukkhato, anattato vuṭṭhāti, dukkhato abhinivisitvā dukkhato, aniccato, anattato vuṭṭhāti, anattato abhinivisitvā anattato, aniccato, dukkhato vuṭṭhāti.

783. Here, to make clear the initial applications and the emergences, is the matrix: Having initially contemplated the internal, one emerges from the internal. Having initially contemplated the internal, one emerges from the external. Having initially contemplated the external, one emerges from the external. Having initially contemplated the external, one emerges from the internal. Having initially contemplated form, one emerges from form. Having initially contemplated form, one emerges from the formless. Having initially contemplated the formless, one emerges from the formless. Having initially contemplated the formless, one emerges from form. One emerges from the five aggregates all at once. Having initially contemplated by way of impermanence, one emerges by way of impermanence. Having initially contemplated by way of impermanence, one emerges by way of suffering or by way of non-self. Having initially contemplated by way of suffering, one emerges by way of suffering, by way of impermanence, or by way of non-self. Having initially contemplated by way of non-self, one emerges by way of non-self, by way of impermanence, or by way of suffering.

784. Kathaṃ? Idhekacco āditova ajjhattasaṅkhāresu abhinivisati, abhinivisitvā te passati. Yasmā pana na suddhaajjhattadassanamatteneva maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, bahiddhāpi daṭṭhabbameva, tasmā parassa khandhepi anupādiṇṇasaṅkhārepi aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti passati. So kālena ajjhattaṃ sammasati, kālena bahiddhā. Tassevaṃ sammasato ajjhattaṃ sammasanakāle vipassanā maggena saddhiṃ ghaṭiyati. Ayaṃ ajjhattaṃ abhinivisitvā ajjhattā vuṭṭhāti nāma.

784. How so? Here, a certain person from the very beginning initially contemplates internal formations; having initially contemplated them, he sees them. But since the emergence of the path does not come about merely by seeing what is purely internal—the external must also be seen—he therefore sees as impermanent, suffering, and non-self the aggregates of others and formations not appropriated by clinging. At times he contemplates the internal, at other times the external. As he is contemplating in this way, at the time of contemplating the internal, his insight connects with the path. This one is called: 'having initially contemplated the internal, he emerges from the internal.'

Sace panassa bahiddhā sammasanakāle vipassanā maggena saddhiṃ ghaṭiyati, ayaṃ ajjhattaṃ abhinivisitvā bahiddhā vuṭṭhāti nāma. Esa nayo bahiddhā abhinivisitvā bahiddhā ca ajjhattā ca vuṭṭhānepi.

But if his insight connects with the path at the time of contemplating the external, this one is called: 'having initially contemplated the internal, he emerges from the external.' This is also the method in the case of emerging from the external and from the internal after having initially contemplated the external.

785. Aparo āditova rūpe abhinivisati, abhinivisitvā bhūtarūpañca upādārūpañca rāsiṃ katvā passati. Yasmā pana na suddharūpadassanamatteneva vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, arūpampi daṭṭhabbameva. Tasmā taṃ rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannaṃ vedanaṃ saññaṃ saṅkhāre viññāṇañca “idaṃ arūpa”nti arūpaṃ passati. So kālena rūpaṃ sammasati, kālena arūpaṃ[V 2.0299]. Tassevaṃ sammasato rūpasammasanakāle vipassanā maggena saddhiṃ ghaṭiyati, ayaṃ rūpe abhinivisitvā rūpā vuṭṭhāti nāma.

785. Another person from the very beginning initially contemplates form; having initially contemplated it, he sees primary matter and derived matter, having grouped them together. But since emergence does not come about merely by seeing form alone—the formless must also be seen—he therefore takes that form as object and sees the arisen feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as 'this is the formless.' At times he contemplates form, at other times the formless. As he is contemplating in this way, at the time of contemplating form, his insight connects with the path. This one is called: 'having initially contemplated form, he emerges from form.'

Sace panassa arūpasammasanakāle vipassanā maggena saddhiṃ ghaṭiyati, ayaṃ arūpe abhinivisitvā arūpā vuṭṭhāti nāma. Esa nayo arūpe abhinivisitvā arūpā ca rūpā ca vuṭṭhānepi.

But if his insight connects with the path at the time of contemplating the formless, this one is called: 'having initially contemplated form, he emerges from the formless.' This is also the method in the case of emerging from the formless and from form after having initially contemplated the formless.

786. “Yaṃkiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti (dī. ni. 1.298) evaṃ abhinivisitvā evameva vuṭṭhānakāle pana ekappahārena pañcahi khandhehi vuṭṭhāti nāma.

786. Having initially contemplated thus: 'Whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of ceasing,' then at the time of emergence, in this very way, one is said to emerge from the five aggregates all at once.

787. Eko [M 2.0301] āditova aniccato saṅkhāre sammasati. Yasmā pana na aniccato sammasanamatteneva vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, dukkhatopi anattatopi sammasitabbameva, tasmā dukkhatopi anattatopi sammasati. Tassevaṃ paṭipannassa aniccato sammasanakāle vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, ayaṃ aniccato abhinivisitvā aniccato vuṭṭhāti nāma.

787. A certain person from the very beginning contemplates formations by way of impermanence. But since emergence does not come about merely by contemplating by way of impermanence, they must also be contemplated by way of suffering and non-self. Therefore, he contemplates them by way of suffering and non-self. For one practicing in this way, emergence occurs at the time of contemplating by way of impermanence. This one is called: 'having initially contemplated by way of impermanence, he emerges by way of impermanence.'

Sace panassa dukkhato anattato sammasanakāle vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, ayaṃ aniccato abhinivisitvā dukkhato, anattato vuṭṭhāti nāma. Esa nayo dukkhato anattato abhinivisitvā sesavuṭṭhānesupi.

But if for him emergence occurs at the time of contemplating by way of suffering or by way of non-self, this one is called: 'having initially contemplated by way of impermanence, he emerges by way of suffering, or by way of non-self.' This is also the method for the remaining emergences after having initially contemplated by way of suffering and by way of non-self.

788. Ettha ca yopi aniccato abhiniviṭṭho, yopi dukkhato, yopi anattato, vuṭṭhānakāle ca aniccato vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tayopi janā adhimokkhabahulā honti, saddhindriyaṃ paṭilabhanti, animittavimokkhena vimuccanti, paṭhamamaggakkhaṇe saddhānusārino honti, sattasu ṭhānesu saddhāvimuttā. Sace pana dukkhato vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tayopi janā passaddhibahulā honti, samādhindriyaṃ paṭilabhanti, appaṇihitavimokkhena vimuccanti, sabbattha kāyasakkhino honti. Yassa panettha arūpajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ, so aggaphale ubhatobhāgavimutto hoti. Atha nesaṃ anattato vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tayopi janā vedabahulā honti, paññindriyaṃ paṭilabhanti, suññatavimokkhena vimuccanti, paṭhamamaggakkhaṇe dhammānusārino honti, chasu ṭhānesu diṭṭhippattā aggaphale paññāvimuttāti.

788. Herein, whether one has initially focused on impermanence, on suffering, or on non-self, if at the time of emergence there is emergence by way of impermanence, all three types of persons abound in conviction, obtain the faith faculty, are liberated by the signless liberation, are faith-followers at the moment of the first path, and are faith-liberated in the seven instances. But if there is emergence by way of suffering, all three types of persons abound in tranquility, obtain the concentration faculty, are liberated by the desireless liberation, and are in all cases body-witnesses. Among them, one for whom an immaterial absorption is the basis becomes one liberated in both ways at the highest fruition. Then, if for them there is emergence by way of non-self, all three types of persons abound in knowledge, obtain the wisdom faculty, are liberated by the emptiness liberation, are Dhamma-followers at the moment of the first path, are attainers-of-view in the six instances, and are wisdom-liberated at the highest fruition.

789. Idāni [V 2.0300] saddhiṃ purimapacchimañāṇehi imissā vuṭṭhānagāminiyā vipassanāya āvibhāvatthaṃ dvādasa upamā veditabbā. Tāsaṃ idaṃ uddānaṃ –

789. Now, to make clear this emergence-leading insight, together with the preceding and subsequent knowledges, twelve similes are to be understood. Of these, this is the summary verse:

“Vaggulī kaṇhasappo ca, gharaṃ go yakkhi dārako;

Khuddaṃ pipāsaṃ sītuṇhaṃ, andhakāraṃ visena cā”ti.

The bat and the black snake, the house, the cow, the ogress, the child; hunger, thirst, cold and heat, darkness, and with poison.

Imā ca upamā bhayatupaṭṭhānato pabhuti yattha katthaci ñāṇe ṭhatvā āharituṃ vaṭṭeyyuṃ. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne āhariyamānāsu bhayatupaṭṭhānato yāva phalañāṇaṃ sabbaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, tasmā idheva āharitabbāti vuttā.

These similes could be adduced in connection with any knowledge whatsoever, beginning with the knowledge of the appearance as terror. But when they are adduced in this context, everything from the knowledge of the appearance as terror up to the knowledge of fruition becomes manifest. Therefore, it is said that they should be adduced right here.

790. Vaggulīti [M 2.0302] ekā kira vaggulī “ettha pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā labhissāmī”ti pañcasākhe madhukarukkhe nilīyitvā ekaṃ sākhaṃ parāmasitvā na tattha kiñci pupphaṃ phalaṃ vā gayhupagaṃ addasa. Yathā ca ekaṃ, evaṃ dutiyaṃ, tatiyaṃ, catutthaṃ. Pañcamampi sākhaṃ parāmasitvā nāddasa. Sā “aphalo vatāyaṃ rukkho, natthettha kiñci gayhupaga”nti tasmiṃ rukkhe ālayaṃ vissajjetvā ujukāya sākhāya āruyha viṭapantarena sīsaṃ nīharitvā uddhaṃ ulloketvā ākāse uppatitvā aññasmiṃ phalarukkhe nilīyati.

790. Regarding the bat: It is said that a certain bat, thinking, “Here I shall find flowers or fruit,” settled on a five-branched madhuka tree. Having examined one branch, it saw no flower or fruit there fit to be taken. And as with the first, so it was with the second, third, and fourth. Having examined the fifth branch also, it saw nothing. Thinking, “Alas, this tree is fruitless; there is nothing here fit to be taken,” it abandoned its attachment to that tree, climbed up a straight branch, put its head out from between the branches, looked up, flew up into the sky, and settled on another fruit-bearing tree.

Tattha vagguli viya yogāvacaro daṭṭhabbo, pañcasākho madhukarukkho viya pañcupādānakkhandhā, tattha vagguliyā nilīyanaṃ viya yogino khandhapañcake abhiniveso, tassā ekekaṃ sākhaṃ parāmasitvā kiñci gayhupagaṃ adisvā avasesasākhāparāmasanaṃ viya yogino rūpakkhandhaṃ sammasitvā tattha kiñci gayhupagaṃ adisvā avasesakkhandhasammasanaṃ, tassā “aphalo vatāyaṃ rukkho”ti rukkhe ālayavissajjanaṃ viya yogino pañcasupi khandhesu aniccalakkhaṇādidassanavasena nibbinnassa muñcitukamyatādiñāṇattayaṃ, tassā ujukāya sākhāya upari ārohanaṃ viya yogino anulomaṃ, sīsaṃ nīharitvā uddhaṃ ullokanaṃ viya gotrabhuñāṇaṃ, ākāse uppatanaṃ viya maggañāṇaṃ, aññasmiṃ phalarukkhe nilīyanaṃ viya phalañāṇaṃ.

In this simile, the meditator is to be seen as the bat; the five aggregates subject to clinging as the five-branched madhuka tree. The bat’s settling on it is like the meditator’s adherence to the five aggregates. The bat’s examining each branch and, seeing nothing fit to be taken, examining the remaining branches, is like the meditator’s contemplating the aggregate of form and, seeing nothing fit to be grasped, contemplating the remaining aggregates. The bat’s thinking, “Alas, this tree is fruitless,” and abandoning its attachment to the tree, is like the threefold knowledge—beginning with the desire for deliverance—of the meditator who has become disenchanted by seeing the characteristic of impermanence, etc., in all five aggregates. The bat’s climbing up the straight branch is like the meditator’s adaptation knowledge. Its putting its head out and looking up is like change-of-lineage knowledge. Its flying up into the sky is like path knowledge. Its settling on another fruit-bearing tree is like fruition knowledge.

791. Kaṇhasappupamā paṭisaṅkhāñāṇe vuttāva. Upamāsaṃsandane panettha sappavissajjanaṃ viya [V 2.0301] gotrabhuñāṇaṃ, muñcitvā āgatamaggaṃ olokentassa ṭhānaṃ viya maggañāṇaṃ, gantvā abhayaṭṭhāne ṭhānaṃ viya phalañāṇanti ayaṃ viseso.

791. The simile of the black snake has already been stated in connection with the knowledge of reflection. Here, in the application of the simile, the releasing of the snake is like change-of-lineage knowledge; the standing and looking at the path one has come by after releasing it is like path knowledge; and the standing in a place of safety after having gone is like fruition knowledge. This is the distinction.

792. Gharanti gharasāmike kira sāyaṃ bhuñjitvā sayanaṃ āruyha niddaṃ okkante gharaṃ ādittaṃ, so pabujjhitvā aggiṃ disvā “bhīto sādhu vatassa sace aḍayhamāno nikkhameyya”nti olokayamāno maggaṃ disvā nikkhamitvā vegena khemaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā ṭhito. Tattha gharasāmikassa bhuñjitvā sayanaṃ āruyha niddokkamanaṃ viya bālaputhujjanassa khandhapañcake “ahaṃ mamā”ti gahaṇaṃ. Pabujjhitvā aggiṃ disvā bhītakālo viya sammāpaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjitvā lakkhaṇaṃ disvā bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ, nikkhamanamaggaṃ olokanaṃ viya muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ[M 2.0303], maggadassanaṃ viya anulomaṃ, nikkhamanaṃ viya gotrabhuñāṇaṃ, vegena gamanaṃ viya maggañāṇaṃ, khemaṭṭhāne ṭhānaṃ viya phalañāṇaṃ.

792. Regarding the house: It is said that while a householder, having eaten his evening meal and gone to bed, was fast asleep, his house caught fire. Waking up and seeing the fire, he was terrified. Thinking, “It would be good indeed if I could escape without being burned!” he looked for an exit, saw one, and got out. He then went quickly to a place of safety and stood there. In this simile, the householder’s having eaten, gone to bed, and fallen asleep is like the foolish worldling’s grasping of the five aggregates as “I” and “mine.” The time of terror on waking and seeing the fire is like the knowledge of the appearance as terror, which arises for one who, having undertaken the right practice, sees the characteristics. Looking for the way of exit is like the knowledge of desire for deliverance. Seeing the way is like adaptation knowledge. Getting out is like change-of-lineage knowledge. Going quickly is like path knowledge. Standing in a place of safety is like fruition knowledge.

793. Goti ekassa kira kassakassa rattibhāge niddaṃ okkantassa vajaṃ bhinditvā goṇā palātā, so paccūsasamaye tattha gantvā olokento tesaṃ palātabhāvaṃ ñatvā anupadaṃ gantvā rañño goṇe addasa. Te “mayhaṃ goṇā”ti sallakkhetvā āharanto pabhātakāle “na ime mayhaṃ goṇā, rañño goṇā”ti sañjānitvā “yāva maṃ ‘coro aya’nti gahetvā rājapurisā na anayabyasanaṃ pāpenti, tāvadeva palāyissāmī”ti bhīto goṇe pahāya vegena palāyitvā nibbhayaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Tattha “mayhaṃ goṇā”ti rājagoṇānaṃ gahaṇaṃ viya bālaputhujjanassa “ahaṃ mamā”ti khandhānaṃ gahaṇaṃ, pabhāte “rājagoṇā”ti sañjānanaṃ viya yogino tilakkhaṇavasena khandhānaṃ “aniccā dukkhā anattā”ti sañjānanaṃ, bhītakālo viya bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇaṃ, vissajjitvā gantukāmatā viya muñcitukamyatā, vissajjanaṃ viya gotrabhu, palāyanaṃ viya maggo, palāyitvā abhayadese ṭhānaṃ viya phalaṃ.

793. Regarding the oxen: It is said that while a certain farmer was asleep at night, his oxen broke out of their pen and fled. At dawn, he went to the pen, and realizing they had fled, he followed their tracks and came upon the king’s oxen. Thinking, “These are my oxen,” he began leading them away. But when it grew light, he realized, “These are not my oxen; they are the king’s oxen!” He became afraid, thinking, “Before the king’s men seize me as a thief and bring me to ruin, I must flee.” So he abandoned the oxen, fled quickly, and stood in a place of safety. In this simile, the taking of the king’s oxen as “my oxen” is like the foolish worldling’s grasping of the aggregates as “I” and “mine.” The realization when it grew light that they were the king’s oxen is like the meditator’s discerning, by means of the three characteristics, that the aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and non-self. The time of fear is like the knowledge of the appearance as terror. The wish to release them and go is like the desire for deliverance. The act of releasing them is like change-of-lineage knowledge. The fleeing is like the path. Standing in a place of safety after fleeing is like the fruition.

794. Yakkhīti eko kira puriso yakkhiniyā saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappesi, sā rattibhāge “sutto aya”nti mantvā āmakasusānaṃ gantvā manussamaṃsaṃ khādati. So “kuhiṃ esā gacchatī”ti anubandhitvā manussamaṃsaṃ khādamānaṃ disvā tassā amanussibhāvaṃ ñatvā “yāva maṃ na khādati, tāva palāyissāmī”ti bhīto vegena palāyitvā khemaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Tattha yakkhiniyā saddhiṃ saṃvāso viya khandhānaṃ “ahaṃ mamā”ti gahaṇaṃ, susāne manussamaṃsaṃ khādamānaṃ [V 2.0302] disvā “yakkhinī aya”nti jānanaṃ viya khandhānaṃ tilakkhaṇaṃ disvā aniccādibhāvajānanaṃ, bhītakālo viya bhayatupaṭṭhānaṃ, palāyitukāmatā viya muñcitukamyatā, susānavijahanaṃ viya gotrabhu, vegena palāyanaṃ viya maggo, abhayadese ṭhānaṃ viya phalaṃ.

794. Regarding the female yakkha: It is said that a certain man cohabited with a female yakkha. At night, thinking, “He is asleep,” she would go to a charnel ground for uncremated bodies and devour human flesh. He, wondering, “Where does she go?” followed her and saw her eating human flesh. Realizing her non-human nature, he thought in terror, “I must flee before she devours me!” He fled quickly and stood in a place of safety. In this simile, cohabiting with the female yakkha is like grasping the aggregates as “I” and “mine.” Seeing her devouring human flesh in the charnel ground and recognizing, “This is a female yakkha,” is like seeing the three characteristics of the aggregates and knowing their nature as impermanent, and so on. The time of terror is like the knowledge of the appearance as terror. The desire to flee is like the desire for deliverance. The abandoning of the charnel ground is like change-of-lineage knowledge. Fleeing swiftly is like the path. Standing in a place of safety is like the fruition.

795. Dārakoti ekā kira puttagiddhinī itthī, sā uparipāsāde nisinnāva antaravīthiyaṃ dārakasaddaṃ sutvā “putto nu kho me kenaci viheṭhiyatī”ti vegasā gantvā “attano putto”ti saññāya paraputtaṃ aggahesi. Sā “paraputto aya”nti sañjānitvā ottappamānā ito cito [M 2.0304] ca oloketvā “mā heva maṃ koci ‘dārakacorī aya’nti vadeyyā”ti dārakaṃ tattheva oropetvā puna vegasā pāsādaṃ āruyha nisīdi. Tattha attano puttasaññāya paraputtassa gahaṇaṃ viya “ahaṃ mamā”ti pañcakkhandhagahaṇaṃ, “paraputto aya”nti sañjānanaṃ viya tilakkhaṇavasena “nāhaṃ, na mamā”ti sañjānanaṃ, ottappanaṃ viya bhayatupaṭṭhānaṃ, ito cito ca olokanaṃ viya muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ, tattheva dārakassa oropanaṃ viya anulomaṃ, oropetvā antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhitakālo viya gotrabhu, pāsādārūhanaṃ viya maggo, āruyha nisīdanaṃ viya phalaṃ.

795. It is said that there was once a woman deeply attached to her son. While sitting in an upper story of a mansion, she heard the sound of a child in the street. Thinking, “Could my son be being harmed by someone?” she went down in haste and, perceiving him to be her own son, took up another’s child. When she realized, “This is another’s child,” she became alarmed. Looking here and there, lest someone should say of her, “This is a child-thief,” she set the child down right there and, returning with haste, ascended the mansion and sat down. Herein, the taking up of another’s child with the perception that it is one’s own son is like the grasping of the five aggregates as “I” and “mine.” The realization, “This is another’s child,” is like the realization by means of the three characteristics that “This is not I, this is not mine.” The alarm is like the knowledge of the appearance of terror. The looking here and there is like the knowledge of the desire for deliverance. The setting down of the child right there is like conformity knowledge. The moment of being in the street after having set him down is like change-of-lineage knowledge. The ascent to the mansion is like the path. Having ascended and being seated is like fruition.

796. Khuddaṃ pipāsaṃ sītuṇhaṃ, andhakāraṃ visena cāti imā pana cha upamā vuṭṭhānagāminiyā vipassanāya ṭhitassa lokuttaradhammābhimukhaninnapoṇapabbhārabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttā. Yathā hi khuddāya abhibhūto sujighacchito puriso sādurasaṃ bhojanaṃ pattheti, evamevāyaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭajighacchāya phuṭṭho yogāvacaro amatarasaṃ kāyagatāsatibhojanaṃ pattheti.

796. Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, darkness, and poison—these six similes are spoken to show the state of one established in insight leading to emergence, whose mind is inclined, sloping, and bent toward the supramundane Dhamma. For just as a person overwhelmed by hunger, being extremely famished, desires delicious food, so too this meditator, afflicted by the hunger of the round of existence, desires the food of mindfulness directed to the body, which has the taste of the Deathless.

Yathā ca pipāsito puriso parisussamānakaṇṭhamukho anekaṅgasambhāraṃ pānakaṃ pattheti, evamevāyaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭapipāsāya phuṭṭho yogāvacaro ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikamaggapānakaṃ pattheti.

Just as a thirsty person with a parched throat and mouth longs for a drink with many ingredients, so too does this meditator, afflicted by the thirst of the round of existence, long for the Noble Eightfold Path as a drink.

Yathā pana sītasamphuṭṭho puriso uṇhaṃ pattheti, evamevāyaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭe taṇhāsinehasītena phuṭṭho yogāvacaro kilesasantāpakaṃ maggatejaṃ pattheti.

Just as a person touched by cold longs for warmth, so too does this meditator, touched by the cold of craving’s moisture in the cycle of existence, long for the fiery power of the Path that burns away the defilements.

Yathā ca uṇhasamphuṭṭho puriso sītaṃ pattheti, evamevāyaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭe ekādasaggisantāpasantatto yogāvacaro ekādasaggivūpasamaṃ nibbānaṃ pattheti.

Just as a person scorched by heat longs for coolness, so too does this meditator, tormented by the elevenfold fires in this round of existence, long for Nibbāna, the stilling of the elevenfold fires.

Yathā [V 2.0303] pana andhakārapareto puriso ālokaṃ pattheti, evamevāyaṃ avijjandhakārena onaddhapariyonaddho yogāvacaro ñāṇālokaṃ maggabhāvanaṃ pattheti.

Just as a man surrounded by darkness longs for light, so too does this meditator, completely enveloped and overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance, long for the development of the path, the light of knowledge.

Yathā ca visasamphuṭṭho puriso visaghātanaṃ bhesajjaṃ pattheti, evamevāyaṃ kilesavisasamphuṭṭho yogāvacaro kilesavisanimmathanaṃ amatosadhaṃ nibbānaṃ pattheti. Tena vuttaṃ – “tassevaṃ jānato evaṃ passato [M 2.0305] tīsu bhavesu…pe… navasu sattāvāsesu cittaṃ patilīyati patikuṭati pativattati na sampasāriyati. Upekkhā vā pāṭikulyatā vā saṇṭhāti. Seyyathāpi nāma padumapalāse īsakapoṇe”ti sabbaṃ pubbe vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Just as a person struck by poison seeks an antidote to eliminate the poison, so too does this meditator, afflicted by the poison of defilements, seek the Deathless medicine of Nibbāna, which crushes the poison of defilements. Therefore, it is said: “For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind shrinks back, recoils, and turns away from the three realms of existence… from the nine abodes of beings. It does not expand. Either equanimity or disgust becomes established. Just as, for example, on a slightly curved lotus leaf…” All should be understood in the same way as previously stated.

797. Ettāvatā ca panesa patilīnacaro nāma hoti, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

797. By this much, he is called one of withdrawn conduct, in reference to whom it was said:

“Patilīnacarassa bhikkhuno,

Bhajamānassa vivittamāsanaṃ;

Sāmaggiyamāhu tassa taṃ,

Yo attānaṃ bhavane na dassaye”ti. (su. ni. 816; mahāni. 45);

“For a monk of withdrawn conduct,

Frequenting a solitary seat,

It is fitting for him, they say,

That he not show himself in any state of existence.”

Evamidaṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ yogino patilīnacarabhāvaṃ niyametvā uttari ariyamaggassāpi bojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānaṅgapaṭipadāvimokkhavisesaṃ niyameti. Keci hi therā bojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānaṅgānaṃ visesaṃ pādakajjhānaṃ niyametīti vadanti. Keci vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā khandhā niyamentīti vadanti. Keci puggalajjhāsayo niyametīti vadanti. Tesampi vādesu ayaṃ pubbabhāgavuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāva niyametīti veditabbā.

Thus, this knowledge of equanimity towards formations, having determined the yogi’s state of withdrawn conduct, further determines the specific qualities of the noble path: the enlightenment factors, path factors, jhāna factors, modes of practice, and liberations. For some elders say that the foundational jhāna determines the specific qualities of the enlightenment factors, path factors, and jhāna factors. Some say that the aggregates, which are the object of insight, determine them. Others say that the individual’s underlying disposition determines them. Yet, among these views, it should be understood that it is this preliminary insight leading to emergence that determines them.

798. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – vipassanāniyamena hi sukkhavipassakassa uppannamaggopi, samāpattilābhino jhānaṃ pādakaṃ akatvā uppannamaggopi, paṭhamajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā pakiṇṇakasaṅkhāre sammasitvā uppāditamaggopi paṭhamajjhānikāva honti. Sabbesu satta bojjhaṅgāni aṭṭha maggaṅgāni pañca jhānaṅgāni honti. Tesaṃ hi pubbabhāgavipassanā somanassasahagatāpi upekkhāsahagatāpi hutvā vuṭṭhānakāle saṅkhārupekkhābhāvaṃ patvā somanassasahagatā [V 2.0304] hoti. Pañcakanaye dutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānāni pādakāni katvā uppāditamaggesu yathākkameneva jhānaṃ caturaṅgikaṃ tivaṅgikaṃ duvaṅgikañca hoti. Sabbesu pana satta maggaṅgāni honti. Catutthe cha bojjhaṅgāni. Ayaṃ viseso pādakajjhānaniyamena ceva vipassanāniyamena ca hoti. Tesampi hi pubbabhāgavipassanā somanassasahagatāpi upekkhāsahagatāpi hoti. Vuṭṭhānagāminī somanassasahagatāva. Pañcamajjhānaṃ [M 2.0306] pādakaṃ katvā nibbattitamagge pana upekkhācittekaggatāvasena dve jhānaṅgāni bojjhaṅgamaggaṅgāni cha satta ceva. Ayampi viseso ubhayaniyamavasena hoti. Imasmiṃ hi naye pubbabhāgavipassanā somanassasahagatā vā upekkhāsahagatā vā hoti. Vuṭṭhānagāminī upekkhāsahagatāva. Arūpajjhānāni pādakaṃ katvā uppāditamaggepi eseva nayo. Evaṃ pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya yekeci saṅkhāre sammasitvā nibbattitamaggassa āsannapadese vuṭṭhitasamāpatti attano sadisabhāvaṃ karoti bhūmivaṇṇo viya godhāvaṇṇassa.

798. Herein, this is the progressive discourse: By the determination of insight, the path that arises for a dry-insight meditator, the path that arises for one who has attained absorption without making jhāna its basis, and the path produced by one who has made the first jhāna its basis and contemplated miscellaneous formations—all these are of the first jhāna. In all of them, there are seven enlightenment factors, eight path factors, and five jhāna factors. For them, the preliminary insight, though accompanied by joy or equanimity, having attained the state of equanimity towards formations, becomes accompanied by joy at the moment of emergence. In the fivefold method, in the paths produced by making the second, third, and fourth jhānas their basis, the jhāna is, respectively, four-factored, three-factored, and two-factored. In all of them, however, there are seven path factors. In the fourth, there are six enlightenment factors. This distinction arises due to the determination by the foundational jhāna and by insight. For them too, the preliminary insight is accompanied by joy or equanimity, but the insight leading to emergence is only accompanied by joy. In the path produced by making the fifth jhāna its basis, however, there are two jhāna factors by way of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, and six enlightenment factors and seven path factors. This distinction also arises due to both determinations. For in this method, the preliminary insight is accompanied by joy or equanimity, but the insight leading to emergence is only accompanied by equanimity. The same principle applies to the path produced by making the formless jhānas its basis. Thus, for one who has emerged from a foundational jhāna, the attainment from which one has emerged in the vicinity of the path produced by contemplating any formations makes that path similar to itself, just as the color of the earth makes the color of an iguana similar to it.

799. Dutiyattheravāde pana yato yato samāpattito vuṭṭhāya ye ye samāpattidhamme sammasitvā maggo nibbattito hoti, taṃtaṃsamāpattisadisova hoti. Tatrāpi ca vipassanāniyamo vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

799. However, in the view of the second elder, the path that is produced by emerging from whatever attainment and contemplating the phenomena of that attainment, is similar to that very attainment. Here too, the determination by insight should be understood in the way already stated.

800. Tatiyattheravāde attano attano ajjhāsayānurūpena yaṃ yaṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā ye ye jhānadhamme sammasitvā maggo nibbattito, taṃtaṃjhānasadisova hoti. Pādakajjhānaṃ pana sammasitajjhānaṃ vā vinā ajjhāsayamatteneva taṃ na ijjhati. Svāyamattho nandakovādasuttena (ma. ni. 3.398 ādayo) dīpetabbo. Etthāpi ca vipassanāniyamo vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Evaṃ tāva saṅkhārupekkhā bojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānaṅgāni niyametīti veditabbā.

800. In the view of the third elder, according to one’s own inclination, the path that is produced by making whichever jhāna the basis and contemplating the factors of that jhāna, is similar to that very jhāna. However, without either the foundational jhāna or the contemplated jhāna, it does not succeed merely through inclination. This meaning should be illustrated by the Nandakovāda Sutta. Here too, the determination by insight should be understood in the way already stated. Thus, it should be understood that equanimity towards formations determines the enlightenment factors, path factors, and jhāna factors.

801. Sace panāyaṃ ādito kilese vikkhambhayamānā dukkhena sappayogena sasaṅkhārena vikkhambhetuṃ asakkhi, dukkhāpaṭipadā nāma hoti. Vipariyāyena sukhāpaṭipadā. Kilese pana vikkhambhetvā vipassanāparivāsaṃ maggapātubhāvaṃ saṇikaṃ kurumānā dandhābhiññā nāma hoti. Vipariyāyena khippābhiññā. Iti ayaṃ saṅkhārupekkhā āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano attano maggassa nāmaṃ deti. Tena maggo cattāri nāmāni labhati.

801. Furthermore, if this equanimity, while suppressing defilements from the outset, was able to suppress them only with difficulty, with effort, and with exertion, it is called the painful practice. Conversely, it is the pleasant practice. Then, having suppressed the defilements, if it slowly brings about the manifestation of the path with a probation of insight, it is called slow direct knowledge. Conversely, it is quick direct knowledge. Thus, this equanimity towards formations, standing in the position of the source, gives a name to its respective path. Thereby, the path obtains four names.

Sā [M 2.0307][V 2.0305] panāyaṃ paṭipadā kassaci bhikkhuno nānā hoti, kassaci catūsupi maggesu ekāva. Buddhānaṃ pana cattāropi maggā sukhāpaṭipadā khippābhiññāva ahesuṃ. Tathā dhammasenāpatissa. Mahāmoggallānattherassa pana paṭhamamaggo sukhāpaṭipado khippābhiñño ahosi. Upari tayo dukkhāpaṭipadā dandhābhiññā. Yathā ca paṭipadā, evaṃ adhipatayopi kassaci bhikkhuno catūsu maggesu nānā honti. Kassaci catūsupi ekāva. Evaṃ saṅkhārupekkhā paṭipadāvisesaṃ niyameti. Yathā pana vimokkhavisesaṃ niyameti, taṃ pubbe vuttameva.

Now, for some bhikkhus this practice is different for each path, while for others it is the same in all four paths. For the Buddhas, however, all four paths were of pleasant practice and quick direct knowledge. So too for the General of the Dhamma. For the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, however, the first path was of pleasant practice and quick direct knowledge, while the three higher paths were of painful practice and quick direct knowledge. And just as the practice, so too the dominant factors are different for some bhikkhus in the four paths, while for others they are the same in all four. Thus, equanimity towards formations determines the specific practice. As for how it determines the specific liberation, that has already been stated.

802. Apica maggo nāma pañcahi kāraṇehi nāmaṃ labhati sarasena vā paccanīkena vā saguṇena vā ārammaṇena vā āgamanena vā. Sace hi saṅkhārupekkhā aniccato saṅkhāre sammasitvā vuṭṭhāti, animittavimokkhena vimuccati. Sace dukkhato sammasitvā vuṭṭhāti, appaṇihitavimokkhena vimuccati. Sace anattato sammasitvā vuṭṭhāti, suññatavimokkhena vimuccati. Idaṃ sarasato nāmaṃ nāma.

802. Furthermore, the path obtains its name for five reasons: by its own nature, by its opposite, by its own quality, by its object, or by its source. For if equanimity towards formations arises after contemplating formations as impermanent, one is liberated by the signless liberation. If it arises after contemplating them as suffering, one is liberated by the desireless liberation. If it arises after contemplating them as non-self, one is liberated by the emptiness liberation. This is called naming by its own nature.

Yasmā panesa aniccānupassanāya saṅkhārānaṃ ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā niccanimittadhuvanimittasassatanimittāni pajahanto āgato, tasmā animitto. Dukkhānupassanāya pana sukhasaññaṃ pahāya paṇidhiṃ patthanaṃ sukkhāpetvā āgatattā appaṇihito. Anattānupassanāya attasattapuggalasaññaṃ pahāya saṅkhārānaṃ suññato diṭṭhattā suññatoti idaṃ paccanīkato nāmaṃ nāma.

Because this path, through the contemplation of impermanence, has come having dismantled the compactness of formations and abandoning the signs of permanence, stability, and eternality, it is therefore called 'signless.' Because, through the contemplation of suffering, it has come having abandoned the perception of pleasure and having dried up longing and aspiration, it is called 'desireless.' Because, through the contemplation of non-self, it has abandoned the perceptions of a self, a being, and a person, and has seen formations as empty, it is called 'emptiness.' This is called naming by its opposite.

Rāgādīhi panesa suññattā suññato, rūpanimittādīnaṃ rāganimittādīnaññeva vā abhāvena animitto, rāgapaṇidhiādīnaṃ abhāvato appaṇihitoti idamassa saguṇato nāmaṃ.

Because this path is empty of lust and so on, it is 'emptiness.' Due to the absence of signs such as form, or of signs of lust and so on, it is 'signless.' Due to the absence of longing for lust and so on, it is 'desireless.' This is its naming by its own quality.

Svāyaṃ suññaṃ animittaṃ appaṇihitañca nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karotītipi suññato animitto appaṇihitoti vuccati. Idamassa ārammaṇato nāmaṃ.

This path is also called empty, signless, and desireless because it makes empty, signless, and desireless Nibbāna its object. This is its naming by its object.

803. Āgamanaṃ pana duvidhaṃ vipassanāgamanaṃ maggāgamanañca. Tattha magge vipassanāgamanaṃ labhati, phale maggāgamanaṃ. Anattānupassanā hi suññatā nāma, suññatavipassanāya maggo suññato, aniccānupassanā animittā nāma[M 2.0308], animittavipassanāya [V 2.0306] maggo animitto. Idaṃ pana nāmaṃ na abhidhammapariyāyena labbhati, suttantapariyāyena labbhati. Tatra hi gotrabhuñāṇaṃ animittaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā animittanāmakaṃ hutvā sayaṃ āgamanīyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā maggassa nāmaṃ detīti vadanti. Tena maggo animittoti vutto. Maggāgamanena pana phalaṃ animittanti yujjatiyeva. Dukkhānupassanā saṅkhāresu paṇidhiṃ sukkhāpetvā āgatattā appaṇihitā nāma, appaṇihitavipassanāya maggo appaṇihito, appaṇihitamaggassa phalaṃ appaṇihitaṃ. Evaṃ vipassanā attano nāmaṃ maggassa deti, maggo phalassāti idaṃ āgamanato nāmaṃ. Evamayaṃ saṅkhārupekkhā vimokkhavisesaṃ niyametīti.

803. Furthermore, the approach is twofold: the approach of insight and the approach of the path. Herein, in the path is obtained the approach of insight, and in the fruition is obtained the approach of the path. For contemplation of not-self is called emptiness; the path of insight into emptiness is the empty path. Contemplation of impermanence is called the signless; the path of insight into the signless is the signless path. This name, however, is not obtained by way of the Abhidhamma exposition, but by way of the Sutta exposition. For in the latter, they say that change-of-lineage knowledge, having taken signless Nibbāna as its object and thus being named 'the signless,' stands in the position of the source and gives its name to the path. Therefore, the path is called 'the signless.' And it is indeed fitting that by the approach of the path, the fruition is called 'the signless.' Contemplation of suffering is called the desireless because it proceeds by having dried up desire concerning formations; the path of insight that is desireless is the desireless path; of the desireless path, the fruition is desireless. Thus insight gives its name to the path, and the path gives its name to the fruition. This is the naming that comes from the approach. In this way, this equanimity towards formations determines the specific kind of liberation.

Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The knowledge of equanimity towards formations is concluded.

Anulomañāṇakathā

The Exposition of Conformity Knowledge

804. Tassa taṃ saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇaṃ āsevantassa bhāventassa bahulīkarontassa adhimokkhasaddhā balavatarā nibbattati, vīriyaṃ supaggahitaṃ hoti, sati sūpaṭṭhitā, cittaṃ susamāhitaṃ, tikkhatarā saṅkhārupekkhā uppajjati. Tassa “dāni maggo uppajjissatī”ti saṅkhārupekkhā saṅkhāre aniccāti vā dukkhāti vā anattāti vā sammasitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Bhavaṅgānantaraṃ saṅkhārupekkhāya katanayeneva saṅkhāre aniccāti vā dukkhāti vā anattāti vā ārammaṇaṃ kurumānaṃ uppajjati manodvārāvajjanaṃ. Tato bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭetvā uppannassa tassa kiriyacittassānantaraṃ avīcikaṃ cittasantatiṃ anuppabandhamānaṃ tatheva saṅkhāre ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjati paṭhamaṃ javanacittaṃ, yaṃ parikammanti vuccati. Tadanantaraṃ tatheva saṅkhāre ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjati dutiyaṃ javanacittaṃ, yaṃ upacāranti vuccati. Tadanantarampi tatheva saṅkhāre ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjati tatiyaṃ javanacittaṃ, yaṃ anulomanti vuccati. Idaṃ nesaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ nāmaṃ.

804. For one who frequents, develops, and cultivates that knowledge of equanimity towards formations, resolute faith becomes stronger, energy is well exerted, mindfulness is well established, the mind is well concentrated, and a sharper equanimity towards formations arises. For him, at the moment when it can be said, 'Now the path will arise,' equanimity towards formations, after contemplating formations as impermanent, or as suffering, or as not-self, descends into the life-continuum. Immediately after the life-continuum, mind-door adverting arises, taking as its object the formations as impermanent, or as suffering, or as not-self, in the very same way that equanimity towards formations did. Then, immediately after that functional consciousness which arose turning from the life-continuum, continuing the mental continuum without interruption, the first impulsion-consciousness arises, having taken formations as its object in the very same way; this is called 'preparation.' Immediately after that, the second impulsion-consciousness arises, having taken formations as its object in the very same way; this is called 'access.' Immediately after that, too, the third impulsion-consciousness arises, having taken formations as its object in the very same way; this is called 'conformity.' These are their respective names.

Avisesena pana tividhampetaṃ āsevanantipi parikammantipi upacārantipi anulomantipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Kissānulomaṃ? Purimabhāgapacchimabhāgānaṃ. Tañhi purimānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ [V 2.0307] vipassanāñāṇānaṃ tathakiccatāya ca anulometi, upari ca sattatiṃsāya bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ. Tañhi aniccalakkhaṇādivasena saṅkhāre ārabbha [M 2.0309] pavattattā, “udayabbayavantānaṃyeva vata dhammānaṃ udayabbayañāṇaṃ uppādavaye addasā”ti ca, “bhaṅgavantānaṃyeva vata bhaṅgānupassanaṃ bhaṅgaṃ addasā”ti ca, “sabhayaṃyeva vata bhayatupaṭṭhānassa bhayato upaṭṭhita”nti ca, “sādīnaveyeva vata ādīnavānupassanaṃ ādīnavaṃ addasā”ti ca, “nibbinditabbeyeva vata nibbidāñāṇaṃ nibbinna”nti ca, “muñcitabbamhiyeva vata muñcitukamyatāñāṇaṃ muñcitukāmaṃ jāta”nti ca, “paṭisaṅkhātabbaṃyeva vata paṭisaṅkhāñāṇena paṭisaṅkhāta”nti ca, “upekkhitabbaṃyeva vata saṅkhārupekkhāya upekkhita”nti ca atthato vadamānaṃ viya imesañca aṭṭhannaṃ ñāṇānaṃ tathakiccatāya anulometi, upari ca sattatiṃsāya bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ tāya paṭipattiyā pattabbattā.

Generally, however, it is fitting to call all three of these 'repetition,' 'preparation,' 'access,' and 'conformity.' To what does it conform? To the preceding and subsequent parts. For it conforms both to the proper function of the eight preceding insight knowledges and to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that are to come. For, since it proceeds with formations as its object by way of the characteristic of impermanence and so on, it is as if stating in effect: 'Indeed, the knowledge of rise and fall saw the rise and fall only of things that have a rise and fall'; 'Indeed, the contemplation of dissolution saw the dissolution only of things that are subject to dissolution'; 'Indeed, what is fearsome appeared as fearsome only to the knowledge of appearance as terror'; 'Indeed, the contemplation of danger saw danger only in what is fraught with danger'; 'Indeed, the knowledge of disenchantment was disenchanted only with what is to be regarded with disenchantment'; 'Indeed, the knowledge of desire for deliverance arose with a desire to be delivered only from what one should desire deliverance from'; 'Indeed, what was reflected upon by the knowledge of reflection was only what ought to be reflected upon'; 'Indeed, what was regarded with equanimity by equanimity towards formations was only what ought to be regarded with equanimity.' Thus it conforms to the proper function of these eight knowledges, and also to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that are to come, because they are to be attained by this very practice.

Yathā hi dhammiko rājā vinicchayaṭṭhāne nisinno vohārikamahāmattānaṃ vinicchayaṃ sutvā agatigamanaṃ pahāya majjhatto hutvā “evaṃ hotū”ti anumodamāno tesañca vinicchayassa anulometi, porāṇassa ca rājadhammassa, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Rājā viya hi anulomañāṇaṃ, aṭṭha vohārikamahāmattā viya aṭṭha ñāṇāni, porāṇo rājadhammo viya sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyā. Tattha yathā rājā “evaṃ hotū”ti vadamāno vohārikānañca vinicchayassa, rājadhammassa ca anulometi, evamidaṃ aniccādivasena saṅkhāre ārabbha uppajjamānaṃ aṭṭhannañca ñāṇānaṃ tathakiccatāya anulometi, upari ca sattatiṃsāya bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ. Teneva saccānulomikañāṇanti vuccatīti.

For it is as when a righteous king, seated in the hall of justice, having heard the verdict of his ministers of justice, abandons all bias, becomes impartial, and gives his approval, saying, 'Let it be so,' thereby conforming to their verdict and to the ancient royal law. This is how the matter should be understood. For conformity knowledge is like the king; the eight knowledges are like the eight ministers of justice; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are like the ancient royal law. Just as the king, in saying, 'Let it be so,' conforms both to the verdict of the ministers and to the royal law, so too this knowledge, arising with formations as its object by way of impermanence and so on, conforms both to the proper function of the eight knowledges and to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that are to come. For that reason it is called 'knowledge that conforms to the truths.'

Anulomañāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Conformity knowledge is concluded.

Vuṭṭhānagāminīvipassanākathā

The Exposition of Insight Leading to Emergence

805. Idañca pana anulomañāṇaṃ saṅkhārārammaṇāya vuṭṭhānagāminiyā vipassanāya pariyosānaṃ hoti. Sabbena sabbaṃ pana gotrabhuñāṇaṃ vuṭṭhānagāminiyā vipassanāya pariyosānaṃ. Idāni tassāyeva vuṭṭhānagāminiyā vipassanāya asammohatthaṃ ayaṃ suttasaṃsandanā veditabbā.

805. Now, this conformity knowledge is the culmination of the insight leading to emergence that has formations as its object. But it is change-of-lineage knowledge that is in every way the culmination of the insight leading to emergence. Now, for the sake of non-bewilderment regarding this same insight leading to emergence, this correlation with the Suttas should be understood.

Seyyathidaṃ [M 2.0310][V 2.0308] –

That is to say:

Ayañhi vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasutte “atammayataṃ, bhikkhave, nissāya atammayataṃ āgamma yāyaṃ upekkhā ekattā ekattasitā, taṃ pajahatha taṃ samatikkamathā”ti (ma. ni. 3.310) evaṃ atammayatāti vuttā.

For this insight leading to emergence is spoken of as 'non-identification' in the Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta, thus: 'Bhikkhus, relying on non-identification, being dependent on non-identification, that equanimity which is unified and based on unity—abandon that, transcend that.' In this way it is called 'non-identification.'

Alagaddasuttante “nibbindaṃ virajjati, virāgā vimuccatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.245) evaṃ nibbidāti vuttā.

In the Alagadda Sutta, it is said: “Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion one is liberated” (MN 1.245). Thus it is spoken of by the name of disenchantment.

Susimasuttante “pubbe kho, susima, dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ, pacchā nibbāne ñāṇa”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.70) evaṃ dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇanti vuttā.

In the Susima Sutta, it is said: “First, Susima, is the knowledge of the stability of things, and afterwards the knowledge in Nibbāna” (S II 124). Thus it is spoken of by the name of knowledge of the stability of things.

Poṭṭhapādasuttante “saññā kho, poṭṭhapāda, paṭhamaṃ uppajjati, pacchā ñāṇa”nti (dī. ni. 1.416) evaṃ saññagganti vuttā.

In the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, it is said: “Perception, Poṭṭhapāda, arises first, and afterwards knowledge” (D I 185). Thus it is spoken of by the name of the peak of perception.

Dasuttarasuttante “paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga”nti (dī. ni. 3.359) evaṃ pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅganti vuttā.

In the Dasuttara Sutta, it is said: “The purification of knowledge and vision of the way of practice is a principal factor for purity” (D III 288). Thus it is spoken of by the name of a principal factor for purity.

Paṭisambhidāmagge “yā ca muñcitukamyatā yā ca paṭisaṅkhānupassanā yā ca saṅkhārupekkhā, ime dhammā ekatthā byañjanameva nāna”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.227) evaṃ tīhi nāmehi vuttā.

In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is said: ‘The desire for deliverance, the contemplation of reflection, and equanimity towards formations—these states are one in meaning, only the letter is different’ (Ps I 93). Thus it is spoken of by three names.

Paṭṭhāne “anulomaṃ gotrabhussa, anulomaṃ vodānassā”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.417) evaṃ tīhi nāmehi vuttā.

In the Paṭṭhāna, it is said: “Conformity is a condition for change-of-lineage; conformity is a condition for purification” (Paṭṭh I 7). Thus it is spoken of by three names.

Rathavinītasuttante “kiṃ panāvuso, paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhatthaṃ bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.257) evaṃ paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhīti vuttā.

In the Rathavinīta Sutta, it is said: “But, friend, is it for the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision of the way of practice that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One?” (M I 147). Thus it is spoken of by the name of purification of knowledge and vision of the way of practice.

Itinekehi [M 2.0311][V 2.0309] nāmehi, kittitā yā mahesinā;

Vuṭṭhānagāminī santā, parisuddhā vipassanā.

Thus by many a name has been extolled by the Great Sage that insight leading to emergence which is peaceful and utterly pure.

Vuṭṭhātukāmo saṃsāra-dukkhapaṅkā mahabbhayā;

Kareyya satataṃ tattha, yogaṃ paṇḍitajātikoti.

A person of wise birth, desiring to rise from the great fear, from the mire of the suffering of saṃsāra, should constantly apply himself to that practice.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, made for the purpose of gladdening good people,

Paññābhāvanādhikāre

in the section on the development of wisdom,

Paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso nāma

the chapter named the Exposition of the Purification of Knowledge and Vision of the Way of Practice,

Ekavīsatimo paricchedo.

the Twenty-first Chapter.

22. Ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso

22. The Exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision

Paṭhamamaggañāṇakathā

Discourse on the Knowledge of the First Path

806. Ito [M 2.0312][V 2.0310] paraṃ gotrabhuñāṇaṃ hoti, taṃ maggassa āvajjanaṭṭhāniyattā neva paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiṃ na ñāṇadassanavisuddhiṃ bhajati, antarā abbohārikameva hoti. Vipassanāsote patitattā pana vipassanāti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Sotāpattimaggo sakadāgāmimaggo anāgāmimaggo arahattamaggoti imesu pana catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ ñāṇadassanavisuddhi nāma.

806. After this, change-of-lineage knowledge arises. Since it is in the position of adverting to the path, it partakes of neither the purification of knowledge and vision of the way of practice nor the purification by knowledge and vision; it is simply unclassifiable in between. But since it has fallen into the stream of insight, it is reckoned as insight. However, the knowledge in these four paths—the path of stream-entry, the path of once-return, the path of non-return, and the path of arahantship—is called the purification by knowledge and vision.

Tattha paṭhamamaggañāṇaṃ tāva sampādetukāmena aññaṃ kiñci kātabbaṃ nāma natthi. Yañhi anena kātabbaṃ siyā, taṃ anulomāvasānaṃ vipassanaṃ uppādentena katameva. Evaṃ uppannaanulomañāṇassa panassa tehi tīhipi anulomañāṇehi attano balānurūpena thūlathūle saccapaṭicchādake tamamhi antaradhāpite sabbasaṅkhāragatesu cittaṃ na pakkhandati, na santiṭṭhati, nādhimuccati, na sajjati, na laggati, na bajjhati. Padumapalāsato udakaṃ viya patilīyati patikuṭati pativattati. Sabbaṃ nimittārammaṇampi sabbaṃ pavattārammaṇampi palibodhato upaṭṭhāti. Athassa sabbasmiṃ nimittapavattārammaṇe palibodhato upaṭṭhite anulomañāṇassa āsevanante animittaṃ appavattaṃ visaṅkhāraṃ nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ kurumānaṃ puthujjanagottaṃ puthujjanasaṅkhaṃ puthujjanabhūmiṃ atikkamamānaṃ ariyagottaṃ ariyasaṅkhaṃ ariyabhūmiṃ okkamamānaṃ nibbānārammaṇe paṭhamāvaṭṭanapaṭhamābhogapaṭhamasamannāhārabhūtaṃ maggassa anantarasamanantarāsevanaupanissayanatthivigatavasena chahi ākārehi paccayabhāvaṃ sādhayamānaṃ sikhāppattaṃ vipassanāya muddhabhūtaṃ apunarāvaṭṭakaṃ uppajjati gotrabhuñāṇaṃ.

Herein, for one who wishes to accomplish the knowledge of the first path, there is nothing further to be done. For whatever needed to be done by him has been done by producing the insight that culminates in conformity. For one for whom conformity knowledge has thus arisen, when the grosser and grosser darkness that conceals the truths has been made to disappear by those three conformity knowledges according to their strength, his mind does not plunge into, settle upon, become resolved upon, cling to, adhere to, or become bound by any formations. Like water on a lotus leaf, it recoils, shrinks back, and turns away. All sign-objects and all objects of occurrence appear as an obstruction. Then, when all sign-objects and objects of occurrence appear to him as an obstruction, at the end of the repetition of conformity knowledge, there arises the change-of-lineage knowledge, which makes the signless, non-occurrence, the unconditioned, cessation, Nibbāna, its object; which transcends the lineage, designation, and plane of the ordinary person, and enters the lineage, designation, and plane of the noble ones; which is the first turning, first adverting, first attending to the object of Nibbāna; which establishes its conditionality for the path in six ways—by way of contiguity, immediate contiguity, repetition, decisive support, absence, and disappearance; which has reached the summit, is the crown of insight, and is non-reverting.

Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

In reference to which it was said:

“Kathaṃ [V 2.0311] bahiddhā vuṭṭhānavivaṭṭane paññā gotrabhuñāṇaṃ? Uppādaṃ abhibhuyyatīti gotrabhu. Pavattaṃ…pe… upāyāsaṃ abhibhuyyatīti gotrabhu. Bahiddhā saṅkhāranimittaṃ abhibhuyyatīti gotrabhu. Anuppādaṃ pakkhandatīti gotrabhu. Appavattaṃ…pe… anupāyāsaṃ nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ pakkhandatīti [M 2.0313] gotrabhu. Uppādaṃ abhibhuyyitvā anuppādaṃ pakkhandatīti gotrabhū”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.59) sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

“How is wisdom in the emergence and turning away from the external change-of-lineage knowledge? Because it overcomes arising, it is change-of-lineage. Because it overcomes occurrence… because it overcomes distress, it is change-of-lineage. Because it overcomes the external sign of formations, it is change-of-lineage. Because it enters into non-arising, it is change-of-lineage. Because it enters into non-occurrence… into non-distress, into cessation, Nibbāna, it is change-of-lineage. Because, having overcome arising, it enters into non-arising, it is change-of-lineage” (Ps I 60). All this should be elaborated.

807. Tatrāyaṃ ekāvajjanena ekavīthiyaṃ pavattamānānampi anulomagotrabhūnaṃ nānārammaṇe pavattanākāradīpikā upamā – yathā hi mahāmātikaṃ laṅghitvā paratīre patiṭṭhātukāmo puriso vegena dhāvitvā mātikāya orimatīre rukkhasākhāya bandhitvā olambitaṃ rajjuṃ vā yaṭṭhiṃ vā gahetvā ullaṅghitvā paratīraninnapoṇapabbhārakāyo hutvā paratīrassa uparibhāgaṃ patto taṃ muñcitvā vedhamāno paratīre patitvā saṇikaṃ patiṭṭhāti, evamevāyaṃ yogāvacaropi bhavayonigatiṭṭhitinivāsānaṃ paratīrabhūte nibbāne patiṭṭhātukāmo udayabbayānupassanādinā vegena dhāvitvā attabhāvarukkhasākhāya bandhitvā olambitaṃ rūparajjuṃ vā vedanādīsu aññataradaṇḍaṃ vā aniccanti vā dukkhanti vā anattāti vāti anulomāvajjanena gahetvā taṃ amuñcamānova paṭhamena anulomacittena ullaṅghitvā dutiyena paratīraninnapoṇapabbhārakāyo viya nibbānaninnapoṇapabbhāramānaso hutvā tatiyena paratīrassa uparibhāgaṃ patto viya idāni pattabbassa nibbānassa āsanno hutvā tassa cittassa nirodhena taṃ saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ muñcitvā gotrabhucittena visaṅkhāre paratīrabhūte nibbāne patati. Ekārammaṇe pana aladdhāsevanatāya vedhamāno so puriso viya na tāva suppatiṭṭhito hoti, tato maggañāṇena patiṭṭhātīti.

807. Herein, this is an illustration to clarify the mode of occurrence, with different objects, of conformity and change-of-lineage, even though they arise in a single cognitive series with a single adverting. Just as a man, wishing to establish himself on the far shore after leaping over a great channel, runs swiftly, grabs a rope or a stick tied to a tree branch on the near shore and hanging down, leaps over, and with his body inclined and sloping towards the far shore, reaches the upper part of the far shore, releases that, and, trembling, lands on the far shore and slowly establishes himself; so too, this meditator, wishing to establish himself in Nibbāna, which is the far shore to existences, births, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes, runs swiftly by means of the contemplation of rise and fall and so on. With the adverting for conformity, he grasps the rope of material form or the staff of one of the other aggregates such as feeling—which are like things tied to a branch of the tree of personal existence—as ‘impermanent,’ or ‘painful,’ or ‘not-self.’ Without releasing it, he leaps with the first conformity consciousness. With the second, his mind becomes inclined and sloping towards Nibbāna, like the man's body inclined towards the far shore. With the third, he becomes close to Nibbāna, which is now to be attained, like the man who has reached the upper part of the far shore. With the cessation of that consciousness, he releases that object of formations and, with the change-of-lineage consciousness, lands upon the unconditioned, the far shore which is Nibbāna. However, like that trembling man, he is not yet well established because the power of repetition with a single object has not been obtained. Then, he becomes established by means of path knowledge.

808. Tattha anulomaṃ saccapaṭicchādakaṃ kilesatamaṃ vinodetuṃ sakkoti, na nibbānamārammaṇaṃ kātuṃ. Gotrabhu nibbānameva ārammaṇaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, na saccapaṭicchādakaṃ tamaṃ vinodetuṃ. Tatrāyaṃ upamā – eko kira cakkhumā puriso “nakkhattayogaṃ jānissāmī”ti rattibhāge nikkhamitvā candaṃ passituṃ uddhaṃ ullokesi, tassa valāhakehi paṭicchannattā cando na paññāyittha. Atheko vāto uṭṭhahitvā thūlathūle valāhake viddhaṃseti. Aparo majjhime, aparo sukhumeti. Tato so puriso vigatavalāhake nabhe candaṃ disvā nakkhattayogaṃ aññāsi.

808. Herein, conformity knowledge can dispel the darkness of defilements that conceals the truth, but it cannot make Nibbāna its object. Change-of-lineage knowledge can make Nibbāna its object, but it cannot dispel the darkness of defilements that conceals the truth. Herein, this is a simile: It is said that a man with good eyesight went out at night, thinking, “I will learn the conjunction of the constellations.” Looking up to see the moon, he could not perceive it because it was covered by clouds. Then one wind arose and dispersed the thickest clouds. Another dispersed the medium ones, and another the subtle ones. Then that man, seeing the moon in the cloudless sky, came to know the conjunction of the constellations.

Tattha [M 2.0314][V 2.0312] tayo valāhakā viya saccapaṭicchādakathūlamajjhimasukhumaṃ kilesandhakāraṃ, tayo vātā viya tīṇi anulomacittāni, cakkhumā puriso viya gotrabhuñāṇaṃ, cando viya nibbānaṃ, ekekassa vātassa yathākkamena valāhakaviddhaṃsanaṃ viya ekekassa anulomacittassa saccapaṭicchādakatamavinodanaṃ, vigatavalāhake nabhe tassa purisassa visuddhacandadassanaṃ viya vigate saccapaṭicchādake tame gotrabhuñāṇassa visuddhanibbānadassanaṃ.

Herein, the thick, medium, and subtle darkness of defilements that conceals the truth should be understood as like the three clouds. The three conformity consciousnesses should be understood as like the three winds. The change-of-lineage knowledge should be understood as like the man with good eyesight. Nibbāna should be understood as like the moon. The dispelling of the darkness that conceals the truth by each conformity consciousness in turn should be understood as like the dispersal of the clouds by each wind in turn. The clear vision of the purified Nibbāna by the change-of-lineage knowledge when the darkness that conceals the truth has been dispelled should be understood as like that man’s seeing of the purified moon in the cloudless sky.

Yatheva hi tayo vātā candapaṭicchādake valāhakeyeva viddhaṃsetuṃ sakkonti, na candaṃ daṭṭhuṃ, evaṃ anulomāni saccapaṭicchādakaṃ tamaññeva vinodetuṃ sakkonti, na nibbānaṃ daṭṭhuṃ. Yathā so puriso candameva daṭṭhuṃ sakkoti, na valāhake viddhaṃsetuṃ, evaṃ gotrabhuñāṇaṃ nibbānameva daṭṭhuṃ sakkoti, na kilesatamaṃ vinodetuṃ. Teneva cetaṃ maggassa āvajjananti vuccati. Tañhi anāvajjanampi samānaṃ āvajjanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā “evaṃ nibbattāhī”ti maggassa saññaṃ datvā viya nirujjhati. Maggopi tena dinnasaññaṃ amuñcitvāva avīcisantativasena taṃ ñāṇaṃ anuppabandhamāno anibbiddhapubbaṃ apadālitapubbaṃ lobhakkhandhaṃ dosakkhandhaṃ mohakkhandhaṃ nibbijjhamānova padālayamānova nibbattati.

For just as the three winds can only disperse the clouds that conceal the moon, but cannot see the moon, so the conformity knowledges can only dispel the darkness that conceals the truth, but cannot see Nibbāna. Just as that man can only see the moon, but cannot disperse the clouds, so the change-of-lineage knowledge can only see Nibbāna, but cannot dispel the darkness of defilements. For that reason, it is called the ‘adverting of the path.’ For although it is not an adverting, it stands in the place of an adverting and ceases as if giving a signal to the path, saying, ‘Arise thus!’ The path, too, without relinquishing the signal given by it, arises in uninterrupted continuity, following upon that knowledge, piercing and splitting the masses of greed, hatred, and delusion, which have never before been pierced or split.

809. Tatrāyaṃ upamā – eko kira issāso aṭṭhausabhamatte padese phalakasataṃ ṭhapāpetvā vatthena mukhaṃ veṭhetvā saraṃ sannahitvā cakkayante aṭṭhāsi. Añño puriso cakkayantaṃ āvijjhitvā yadā issāsassa phalakaṃ abhimukhaṃ hoti, tadā tattha daṇḍakena saññaṃ deti. Issāso daṇḍakasaññaṃ amuñcitvāva saraṃ khipitvā phalakasataṃ nibbijjhati. Tattha daṇḍakasaññaṃ viya gotrabhuñāṇaṃ, issāso viya maggañāṇaṃ. Issāsassa daṇḍakasaññaṃ amuñcitvāva phalakasatanibbijjhanaṃ viya maggañāṇassa gotrabhuñāṇena dinnasaññaṃ amuñcitvāva nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā anibbiddhapubbānaṃ apadālitapubbānaṃ lobhadosamohakkhandhānaṃ nibbijjhanapadālanaṃ.

809. Herein, this is a simile: It is said that an archer, having had a hundred planks set up in a space of eight usabhas, stood on a revolving platform with his face wrapped in a cloth and his arrow nocked. Another man turned the revolving platform, and when a plank was in front of the archer, he gave a signal with a stick. The archer, without failing to heed the signal of the stick, shot the arrow and pierced the hundred planks. Here, the signal of the stick is like the change-of-lineage knowledge; the archer is like the path knowledge. The piercing of the hundred planks by the archer without failing to heed the signal of the stick is like the piercing and splitting of the masses of greed, hatred, and delusion—which have never before been pierced or split—by the path knowledge, which takes Nibbāna as its object without failing to heed the signal given by the change-of-lineage knowledge.

810. Na kevalañcesa maggo lobhakkhandhādīnaṃ nibbijjhanameva karoti, apica kho anamataggasaṃsāravaṭṭadukkhasamuddaṃ soseti, sabbaapāyadvārāni pidahati, sattannaṃ ariyadhanānaṃ sammukhībhāvaṃ karoti, aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ micchāmaggaṃ pajahati, sabbaverabhayāni vūpasameti, sammāsambuddhassa orasaputtabhāvaṃ upaneti[M 2.0315][V 2.0313], aññesañca anekasatānaṃ ānisaṃsānaṃ paṭilābhāya saṃvattatīti evaṃ anekānisaṃsadāyakena sotāpattimaggena sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ sotāpattimagge ñāṇanti.

810. Not only does this path accomplish the piercing of the masses of greed and so forth, but it also dries up the ocean of suffering in the beginningless round of rebirths, closes all doors to the planes of misery, brings the seven noble treasures to presence, abandons the eightfold wrong path, allays all enmities and fears, leads to the state of being a true-born son of the Perfectly Enlightened One, and conduces to the attainment of many hundreds of other benefits. Thus, the knowledge associated with the path of stream-entry, which bestows these many benefits, is called ‘knowledge in the path of stream-entry.’

Paṭhamamaggañāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The knowledge of the first path is concluded.

Sotāpannapuggalakathā

The Discourse on the Person of the Stream-Enterer

811. Imassa pana ñāṇassa anantaraṃ tasseva vipākabhūtāni dve tīṇi vā phalacittāni uppajjanti. Anantaravipākattāyeva hi lokuttarakusalānaṃ “samādhimānantarikaññamāhū”ti (khu. pā. 6.5) ca “dandhaṃ ānantarikaṃ pāpuṇāti āsavānaṃ khayāyā”ti (a. ni. 4.162) ca ādi vuttaṃ. Keci pana ekaṃ dve tīṇi cattāri vā phalacittānīti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

811. Furthermore, immediately after this knowledge, two or three fruition-consciousnesses arise, which are its very fruit. Indeed, it is because supramundane wholesome states yield immediate results that it is said: 'They call concentration that which has an immediate result,' and 'Slowly one attains the immediate path for the destruction of the cankers,' and so on. Some, however, say that one, two, three, or four fruition-consciousnesses arise, but that should not be accepted.

Anulomassa hi āsevanante gotrabhuñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Tasmā sabbantimena paricchedena dvīhi anulomacittehi bhavitabbaṃ. Na hi ekaṃ āsevanapaccayaṃ labhati, sattacittaparamā ca ekāvajjanavīthi. Tasmā yassa dve anulomāni, tassa tatiyaṃ gotrabhu catutthaṃ maggacittaṃ tīṇi phalacittāni honti. Yassa tīṇi anulomāni, tassa catutthaṃ gotrabhu pañcamaṃ maggacittaṃ dve phalacittāni honti. Tena vuttaṃ “dve tīṇi vā phalacittāni uppajjantī”ti.

For at the end of the repetition of conformity, the change-of-lineage knowledge arises. Therefore, at a minimum, there must be two conformity-consciousnesses. For a single one does not obtain the repetition condition, and a cognitive process with a single adverting has at most seven consciousness-moments. Thus, for one who has two conformity-consciousnesses, the third is change-of-lineage, the fourth is the path-consciousness, and there are three fruition-consciousnesses. For one who has three conformity-consciousnesses, the fourth is change-of-lineage, the fifth is the path-consciousness, and there are two fruition-consciousnesses. Therefore it was said, 'two or three fruition-consciousnesses arise.'

Keci pana yassa cattāri anulomāni, tassa pañcamaṃ gotrabhu chaṭṭhaṃ maggacittaṃ ekaṃ phalacittanti vadanti, taṃ pana yasmā catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ vā appeti, na tato paraṃ āsannabhavaṅgattāti paṭikkhittaṃ. Tasmā na sārato paccetabbaṃ.

Some, however, say that for one who has four conformity-consciousnesses, the fifth is change-of-lineage, the sixth is path-consciousness, and there is one fruition-consciousness. But this is rejected, since absorption is attained at the fourth or fifth moment, and not beyond that, due to the proximity of the life-continuum. Therefore, this should not be accepted as the essential teaching.

812. Ettāvatā ca panesa sotāpanno nāma dutiyo ariyapuggalo hoti. Bhusaṃ pamattopi hutvā sattakkhattuṃ devesu ca manussesu ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantassa karaṇasamattho hoti. Phalapariyosāne panassa cittaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ otarati, tato bhavaṅgaṃ upacchinditvā maggapaccavekkhaṇatthāya uppajjati manodvārāvajjanaṃ, tasmiṃ niruddhe paṭipāṭiyā satta maggapaccavekkhaṇajavanānīti. Puna bhavaṅgaṃ otaritvā teneva nayena [M 2.0316] phalādīnaṃ paccavekkhaṇatthāya āvajjanādīni [V 2.0314] uppajjanti. Yesaṃ uppattiyā esa maggaṃ paccavekkhati, phalaṃ paccavekkhati, pahīnakilese paccavekkhati, avasiṭṭhakilese paccavekkhati, nibbānaṃ paccavekkhati.

812. And with this, one becomes the one called a stream-enterer, the second noble person. Even if one were to be extremely heedless, after running and wandering on among devas and humans for at most seven times, one is capable of making an end of suffering. At the conclusion of the fruition, one's consciousness descends into the life-continuum. Then, having interrupted the life-continuum, mind-door-adverting arises for the purpose of reviewing the path. When that has ceased, in sequence seven path-reviewing impulsion-consciousnesses arise. Again, having descended into the life-continuum, adverting and so on arise in the same way for the purpose of reviewing the fruition and the rest. By the arising of these, this one reviews the path, reviews the fruition, reviews the abandoned defilements, reviews the remaining defilements, and reviews Nibbāna.

So hi “iminā vatāhaṃ maggena āgato”ti maggaṃ paccavekkhati, tato “ayaṃ me ānisaṃso laddho”ti phalaṃ paccavekkhati. Tato “ime nāma me kilesā pahīnā”ti pahīnakilese paccavekkhati. Tato “ime nāma me kilesā avasiṭṭhā”ti uparimaggattayavajjhe kilese paccavekkhati. Avasāne ca “ayaṃ me dhammo ārammaṇato paṭividdho”ti amataṃ nibbānaṃ paccavekkhati. Iti sotāpannassa ariyasāvakassa pañca paccavekkhaṇāni honti. Yathā ca sotāpannassa, evaṃ sakadāgāmianāgāmīnampi. Arahato pana avasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇaṃ nāma natthīti. Evaṃ sabbānipi ekūnavīsati paccavekkhaṇāni nāma.

For one reviews the path thus: 'Indeed, by this path have I come.' Then one reviews the fruition thus: 'This benefit has been gained by me.' Then one reviews the abandoned defilements thus: 'These defilements have been abandoned by me.' Then one reviews the remaining defilements—those to be abandoned by the three higher paths—thus: 'These defilements remain for me.' And finally, one reviews the deathless Nibbāna thus: 'This state has been penetrated by me as its object.' Thus, for the noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, there are five kinds of reviewing. And as for the stream-enterer, so too for the once-returner and the non-returner. For the Arahant, however, there is no reviewing of remaining defilements. Thus, all together, there are what are called the nineteen kinds of reviewing.

Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedoyeva ceso. Pahīnāvasiṭṭhakilesapaccavekkhaṇañhi sekkhānampi hoti vā na vā. Tassa hi paccavekkhaṇassa abhāveneva mahānāmo bhagavantaṃ pucchi “kosu nāma me dhammo ajjhattaṃ appahīno, yena me ekadā lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhantī”ti (ma. ni. 1.175) sabbaṃ vitthārato veditabbaṃ.

This, however, is only the maximum reckoning. For even for trainees, the reviewing of abandoned and remaining defilements may or may not occur. Indeed, it was precisely because of the absence of such reviewing that Mahānāma asked the Blessed One: 'What state, venerable sir, has not been abandoned within me, on account of which states of greed at times invade my mind and remain?' The entire matter should be understood in detail.

Dutiyamaggañāṇakathā

The Explanation of the Knowledge of the Second Path

813. Evaṃ paccavekkhitvā pana so sotāpanno ariyasāvako tasmiññeva vā āsane nisinno, aparena vā samayena kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ tanubhāvāya dutiyāya bhūmiyā pattiyā yogaṃ karoti. So indriyabalabojjhaṅgāni samodhānetvā tadeva rūpavedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇabhedaṃ saṅkhāragataṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti ñāṇena parimaddati, parivatteti, vipassanāvīthiṃ ogāhati. Tassevaṃ paṭipannassa vuttanayeneva saṅkhārupekkhāvasāne ekāvajjanena anulomagotrabhuñāṇesu uppannesu gotrabhuanantaraṃ sakadāgāmimaggo uppajjati. Tena sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ sakadāgāmimagge ñāṇanti.

813. Having reviewed thus, that noble disciple, the stream-enterer, either while seated on that very seat or at a later time, applies himself to the attenuation of sensual desire and ill will, and to the attainment of the second stage. Having brought the faculties, powers, and enlightenment factors into harmony, one crushes and turns over with knowledge that same conditioned reality—differentiated as form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—as impermanent, suffering, and not-self, and one enters upon the path of insight. For one so practicing, in the way already described, at the culmination of equanimity towards formations, with a single adverting, when the conformity and change-of-lineage knowledges have arisen, immediately after change-of-lineage the path of the once-returner arises. The knowledge associated with that is the knowledge in the once-returner's path.

Dutiyañāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Second Knowledge is concluded.

Tatiyamaggañāṇakathā

Exposition of the Knowledge of the Third Path

814. Imassāpi [M 2.0317][V 2.0315] ñāṇassa anantaraṃ vuttanayeneva phalacittāni veditabbāni. Ettāvatā cesa sakadāgāmī nāma catuttho ariyapuggalo hoti sakiṃdeva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā dukkhassantakaraṇasamattho. Tato paraṃ paccavekkhaṇaṃ vuttanayameva.

814. Immediately after this knowledge also, the fruition-consciousnesses are to be understood in the way already described.
