And with this, one becomes the one called a once-returner, the fourth noble person, who is capable of making an end of suffering after having come to this world only one more time. Thereafter, the reviewing is just as has been described.

Evaṃ paccavekkhitvā ca so sakadāgāmī ariyasāvako tasmiññeva vā āsane nisinno aparena vā samayena kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ anavasesappahānāya tatiyāya bhūmiyā pattiyā yogaṃ karoti, so indriyabalabojjhaṅgāni samodhānetvā tadeva saṅkhāragataṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti ñāṇena parimaddati, parivatteti, vipassanāvīthiṃ ogāhati. Tassevaṃ paṭipannassa vuttanayeneva saṅkhārupekkhāvasāne ekāvajjanena anulomagotrabhuñāṇesu uppannesu gotrabhuanantaraṃ anāgāmimaggo uppajjati, tena sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ anāgāmimagge ñāṇanti.

And having reviewed thus, that noble disciple, the once-returner, either while seated on that very seat or at a later time, applies himself to the abandoning without remainder of sensual desire and ill will, and to the attainment of the third stage. Having brought the faculties, powers, and enlightenment factors into harmony, one crushes and turns over with knowledge that same conditioned reality as impermanent, suffering, and not-self, and one enters upon the path of insight. For one so practicing, in the way already described, at the culmination of equanimity towards formations, with a single adverting, when the conformity and change-of-lineage knowledges have arisen, immediately after change-of-lineage the path of the non-returner arises. The knowledge associated with that is the knowledge in the non-returner's path.

Tatiyañāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Third Knowledge is concluded.

Catutthamaggañāṇakathā

Exposition of the Knowledge of the Fourth Path

815. Imassapi ñāṇassa anantaraṃ vuttanayeneva phalacittāni veditabbāni. Ettāvatā cesa anāgāmī nāma chaṭṭho ariyapuggalo hoti opapātiko tatthaparinibbāyī anāvattidhammo paṭisandhivasena imaṃ lokaṃ puna anāgantā. Tato paraṃ paccavekkhaṇaṃ vuttanayameva.

815. Immediately after this knowledge, the fruition consciousnesses are to be understood in the manner stated earlier. And by this much, this person is called a non-returner, the sixth noble person, who is spontaneously born and attains final Nibbāna there, whose nature is not to return, not coming again to this world by way of rebirth-linking. Thereafter, the reviewing is in the same manner as stated earlier.

Evaṃ paccavekkhitvā ca so anāgāmī ariyasāvako tasmiññeva vā āsane nisinno, aparena vā samayena rūpārūparāgamānauddhaccaavijjānaṃ anavasesappahānāya catutthāya bhūmiyā pattiyā yogaṃ karoti, so indriyabalabojjhaṅgāni samodhānetvā tadeva saṅkhāragataṃ aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti ñāṇena parimaddati, parivatteti, vipassanāvīthiṃ ogāhati. Tassevaṃ paṭipannassa vuttanayeneva saṅkhārupekkhāvasāne ekāvajjanena anulomagotrabhuñāṇesu [M 2.0318] uppannesu gotrabhuanantaraṃ arahattamaggo uppajjati, tena sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ arahattamagge ñāṇanti.

Having reviewed thus, that non-returner noble disciple, whether seated in that very seat or at another time, makes an effort for the attainment of the fourth stage, for the abandoning without remainder of lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. Having unified the faculties, powers, and factors of awakening, with wisdom he thoroughly scrutinizes and turns over that same conditioned phenomenon as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, and he enters the path of insight. For one practicing thus, in the manner stated earlier, at the culmination of equanimity towards formations, with a single advertence, upon the arising of the adaptation and change-of-lineage knowledges, immediately after the change-of-lineage, the path of Arahantship arises. The knowledge associated with it is called the knowledge in the path of Arahantship.

Catutthañāṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The fourth knowledge is concluded.

Arahantapuggalakathā

The Discourse on the Arahant

816. Imassapi [V 2.0316] ñāṇassa anantaraṃ vuttanayeneva phalacittāni veditabbāni. Ettāvatā cesa arahā nāma aṭṭhamo ariyapuggalo hoti mahākhīṇāsavo antimadehadhārī ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammādaññā vimutto sadevakassa lokassa aggadakkhiṇeyyoti.

816. Immediately after this knowledge, the fruition consciousnesses are to be understood in the manner stated earlier. And by this much, this person is called an Arahant, the eighth noble individual, a great one whose taints are destroyed, bearing his final body, with the burden laid down, having attained his own true goal, with the fetters of existence completely destroyed, rightly liberated through final knowledge, the supreme recipient of offerings in the world with its deities.

Iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ “sotāpattimaggo sakadāgāmimaggo anāgāmimaggo arahattamaggoti imesu pana catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ ñāṇadassanavisuddhi nāmā”ti, taṃ imāni iminā anukkamena pattabbāni cattāri ñāṇāni sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Thus, that which was stated: "The path of stream-entry, the path of once-returning, the path of non-returning, and the path of Arahantship—the knowledge in these four paths is called the purification by knowledge and vision." That was said with reference to these four knowledges, which are to be attained in this sequence.

Bodhipakkhiyakathā

The Discourse on the Factors of Awakening

817. Idāni imissāyeva catuñāṇāya ñāṇadassanavisuddhiyā ānubhāvavijānanatthaṃ –

817. Now, for the purpose of understanding the power of this very purification by knowledge and vision, which comprises four knowledges—

Paripuṇṇabodhipakkhiya, bhāvo vuṭṭhānabalasamāyogo;

Ye yena pahātabbā, dhammā tesaṃ pahānañca.

The state of having complete factors of awakening, the endowment with the strength of emergence; which states are to be abandoned by which means, and the abandoning of them;

Kiccāni pariññādīni, yāni vuttāni abhisamayakāle;

Tāni ca yathāsabhāvena, jānitabbāni sabbānīti.

and the functions, such as full understanding, which are spoken of in connection with the time of realization—all these are to be known according to their true nature.

818. Tattha paripuṇṇabodhipakkhiya, bhāvoti bodhipakkhiyānaṃ paripuṇṇabhāvo. Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, satta bojjhaṅgā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggoti hi ime sattatiṃsa dhammā bujjhanaṭṭhena bodhoti laddhanāmassa ariyamaggassa pakkhe bhavattā bodhipakkhiyā nāma. Pakkhe bhavattāti upakārabhāve ṭhitattā.

818. Therein, 'the state of having complete factors of awakening' means the completeness of the factors of awakening. The four establishments of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases of success, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the Noble Eightfold Path—these thirty-seven states are called 'factors of awakening' (bodhipakkhiyā) because they exist on the side (pakkhe) of the Noble Path, which has received the name 'awakening' (bodhi) in the sense of awakening. 'Existing on the side' means standing in a supportive role.

819. Tesu [M 2.0319] tesu ārammaṇesu okkhanditvā pakkhanditvā upaṭṭhānato paṭṭhānaṃ. Satiyeva paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Kāyavedanācittadhammesu panassā asubha-dukkha-anicca-anattākāragahaṇavasena [V 2.0317] subha-sukha-nicca-atta-saññāpahānakiccasādhanavasena ca pavattito catudhā bhedo hoti. Tasmā cattāro satipaṭṭhānāti vuccanti.

819. It is an 'establishment' (paṭṭhāna) because it is an establishing (upaṭṭhāna) that plunges into and rushes into those various objects. Mindfulness itself is an establishment; thus, it is the 'establishment of mindfulness' (satipaṭṭhāna). Moreover, in relation to the body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena, it is divided into four, since it proceeds by way of apprehending their aspects as unattractive, suffering, impermanent, and not-self, and by way of accomplishing the task of abandoning perceptions of attractiveness, pleasure, permanence, and self. Therefore, they are called the four establishments of mindfulness.

820. Padahanti etenāti padhānaṃ. Sobhanaṃ padhānaṃ sammappadhānaṃ. Sammā vā padahanti etenāti sammappadhānaṃ. Sobhanaṃ vā taṃ kilesavirūpattavirahato padhānañca hitasukhanipphādakattena seṭṭhabhāvāvahanato padhānabhāvakāraṇato cāti sammappadhānaṃ. Vīriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tayidaṃ uppannānuppannānaṃ akusalānaṃ pahānānuppattikiccaṃ anuppannuppannānañca kusalānaṃ uppattiṭṭhitikiccaṃ sādhayatīti catubbidhaṃ hoti, tasmā cattāro sammappadhānāti vuccanti.

820. One strives by this, thus it is 'striving' (padhāna). Excellent striving is 'right striving' (sammappadhāna). Or, one strives rightly by this, thus it is 'right striving.' Or, it is 'right' (sammā) because it is free from the ugliness of defilements, and it is 'striving' (padhāna) because it brings about welfare and happiness, leading to the highest state, and because it is the cause of the state of being primary—thus it is 'right striving.' This is a term for energy (vīriya). This is fourfold, as it accomplishes the task of abandoning arisen unwholesome states and preventing unarisen ones from arising, and the task of causing unarisen wholesome states to arise and maintaining arisen ones. Therefore, they are called the four right strivings.

821. Pubbe vuttena ijjhanaṭṭhena iddhi. Tassā sampayuttāya pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena phalabhūtāya pubbabhāgakāraṇaṭṭhena ca iddhiyā pādoti iddhipādo. So chandādivasena catubbidho hoti, tasmā cattāro iddhipādāti vuccanti. Yathāha – “cattāro iddhipādā chandiddhipādo cittiddhipādo vīriyiddhipādo vīmaṃsiddhipādo”ti (vibha. 457). Ime lokuttarāva. Lokiyā pana “chandañce bhikkhu adhipatiṃ karitvā labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassa ekaggataṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati chandasamādhī”tiādivacanato (vibha. 432) chandādiadhipativasena paṭiladdhadhammāpi honti.

821. As stated before, 'success' (iddhi) is so called in the sense of accomplishing. The 'basis of success' (iddhipāda) is the basis (pāda) for that success with which it is associated, in the sense of being its precursor; or it is the means (pāda) to that success which is its fruit, in the sense of being its preliminary cause. It is fourfold according to desire (chanda), etc.; therefore, they are called the four bases of success. As it is said: 'There are four bases of success: the basis of success consisting of desire, the basis of success consisting of consciousness, the basis of success consisting of energy, and the basis of success consisting of investigation.' These are exclusively supramundane. However, mundane states are also called this when they are attained through the predominance of desire, etc., as stated in the passage: 'If a monk, having made desire the predominant factor (adhipati), gains concentration, gains one-pointedness of mind, this is called concentration based on desire,' and so on.

822. Assaddhiyakosajjapamādavikkhepasammohānaṃ abhibhavanato abhibhavanasaṅkhātena adhipatiyaṭṭhena indriyaṃ. Assaddhiyādīhi ca anabhibhavanīyato akampiyaṭṭhena balaṃ. Tadubhayampi saddhādivasena pañcavidhaṃ hoti, tasmā pañcindriyāni pañca balānīti vuccanti.

822. It is a 'faculty' (indriya) in the sense of sovereignty, because it overcomes faithlessness, laziness, heedlessness, distraction, and delusion. It is a 'power' (bala) in the sense of being unshakable, because it cannot be overcome by faithlessness and the rest. Both of these are fivefold according to faith, etc. Therefore, they are called the five faculties and the five powers.

823. Bujjhanakasattassa pana aṅgabhāvena satiādayo satta bojjhaṅgā. Niyyānikaṭṭhena ca sammādiṭṭhiādayo aṭṭha maggaṅgā honti. Tena vuttaṃ “satta bojjhaṅgā ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti.

823. Furthermore, the seven qualities beginning with mindfulness are 'factors of awakening' (bojjhaṅgā) because they are factors (aṅga) for the person who is awakening (bujjhanaka). And the eight qualities beginning with right view are 'path factors' (maggaṅgā) because they have the characteristic of leading out (niyyānika). Hence it is said: 'The seven factors of awakening and the Noble Eightfold Path.'

824. Iti [M 2.0320] ime sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhammā pubbabhāge lokiyavipassanāya vattamānāya cuddasavidhena kāyaṃ pariggaṇhato ca kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ, navavidhena vedanaṃ pariggaṇhato ca vedanānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ, soḷasavidhena cittaṃ pariggaṇhato ca cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ, pañcavidhena dhamme pariggaṇhato ca dhammānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ. Imasmiṃ attabhāve [V 2.0318] anuppannapubbaṃ parassa uppannaṃ akusalaṃ disvā “yathā paṭipannassetaṃ uppannaṃ, na tathā paṭipajjissāmi evaṃ me etaṃ nuppajjissatī”ti, tassa anuppādāya vāyamanakāle paṭhamaṃ sammappadhānaṃ. Attano samudācārappattaṃ akusalaṃ disvā tassa pahānāya vāyamanakāle dutiyaṃ. Imasmiṃ attabhāve anuppannapubbaṃ jhānaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā uppādetuṃ vāyamantassa tatiyaṃ. Uppannaṃ yathā na parihāyati, evaṃ punappunaṃ uppādentassa catutthaṃ sammappadhānaṃ. Chandaṃ dhuraṃ katvā kusaluppādanakāle chandiddhipādo. Micchāvācāya viramaṇakāle sammāvācāti evaṃ nānācittesu labbhanti. Imesaṃ pana catunnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ uppattikāle ekacitte labbhanti. Phalakkhaṇe ṭhapetvā cattāro sammappadhāne avasesā tettiṃsa labbhanti.

824. Thus, these thirty-seven qualities conducive to enlightenment, during the preliminary stage when mundane insight is occurring, are obtained as follows: for one who comprehends the body in fourteen ways, the establishment of mindfulness in contemplating the body; for one who comprehends feelings in nine ways, the establishment of mindfulness in contemplating feelings; for one who comprehends the mind in sixteen ways, the establishment of mindfulness in contemplating the mind; and for one who comprehends phenomena in five ways, the establishment of mindfulness in contemplating phenomena. When, seeing an unwholesome quality arisen in another that has not previously arisen in oneself in this existence, one thinks, 'I will not practice in the way that one who has so practiced has caused this to arise; thus it will not arise in me,' at the time of striving for its non-arising, the first right exertion is obtained. When, seeing an unwholesome quality that has come into manifestation in oneself, one strives for its abandonment, the second is obtained. For one striving to arouse a jhāna or insight not previously arisen in this existence, the third is obtained. For one who repeatedly arouses what has arisen so that it does not decline, the fourth right exertion is obtained. When zeal is made the chief factor in arousing wholesome qualities, the basis of spiritual power of zeal is obtained. At the time of abstaining from wrong speech, right speech is obtained. Thus they are obtained in various consciousnesses. But at the time of the arising of these four knowledges, they are obtained in a single consciousness. At the moment of fruition, excepting the four right exertions, the remaining thirty-three are obtained.

825. Evaṃ ekacitte labbhamānesu cetesu ekāva nibbānārammaṇā sati kāyādīsu subhasaññādippahānakiccasādhanavasena cattāro satipaṭṭhānāti vuccati. Ekameva ca vīriyaṃ anuppannānaṃ anuppādādikiccasādhanavasena cattāro sammappadhānāti vuccati. Sesesu pana hāpanavaḍḍhanaṃ natthi.

825. Thus, when these are obtainable in a single consciousness, the single mindfulness with Nibbāna as its object is called the four establishments of mindfulness because it accomplishes the task of abandoning the perception of beauty and so on regarding the body and so forth. And the single energy is called the four right exertions because it accomplishes the task of the non-arising of the unarisen and so on. But in the remaining factors, there is no decrease or increase.

826. Apica tesu –

826. Furthermore, among them:

Nava ekavidhā eko, dvedhātha catu pañcadhā;

Aṭṭhadhā navadhā ceva, iti chaddhā bhavanti te.

Nine are of one kind, one is twofold; then one is fourfold, one fivefold; one is eightfold, and one ninefold—thus they are of six kinds.

Nava ekavidhāti chando, cittaṃ, pīti, passaddhi, upekkhā, saṅkappo, vācā, kammanto, ājīvoti ime nava chandiddhipādādivasena ekavidhāva honti, na aññaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ bhajanti. Eko dvedhāti saddhā indriya, balavasena dvedhā ṭhitā. Atha catu pañcadhāti athañño eko catudhā, añño pañcadhā ṭhitoti attho. Tattha samādhi eko indriya, bala, bojjhaṅga, maggaṅgavasena catudhā ṭhito. Paññā tesañca catunnaṃ iddhipādakoṭṭhāsassa ca [M 2.0321] vasena pañcadhā. Aṭṭhadhā navadhā cevāti aparo eko aṭṭhadhā, eko navadhā ṭhitoti attho. Catusatipaṭṭhāna, indriya, bala, bojjhaṅga, maggaṅgavasena sati aṭṭhadhā ṭhitā. Catusammappadhāna, iddhipāda, indriya, bala, bojjhaṅga, maggaṅgavasena vīriyaṃ navadhāti. Evaṃ –

'Nine are of one kind' means: aspiration, consciousness, joy, tranquility, equanimity, thought, speech, action, and livelihood—these nine are of one kind, being counted once as the basis of spiritual power of zeal, etc.; they do not belong to any other division. 'One is twofold' means: faith stands as twofold by way of faculty and power. 'Then one is fourfold, one fivefold' means: then another one stands as fourfold, and another as fivefold. Therein, concentration stands as fourfold by way of faculty, power, enlightenment factor, and path factor. Wisdom stands as fivefold by way of those four and the division of the bases of spiritual power. 'One is eightfold, and one ninefold' means: another one stands as eightfold, and another as ninefold. Mindfulness stands as eightfold by way of the four establishments of mindfulness, faculty, power, enlightenment factor, and path factor. Energy stands as ninefold by way of the four right exertions, the basis of spiritual power, faculty, power, enlightenment factor, and path factor.

Cuddaseva [V 2.0319] asambhinnā, hontete bodhipakkhiyā;

Koṭṭhāsato sattavidhā, sattatiṃsappabhedato.

Fourteen are unmixed indeed, these qualities conducive to enlightenment; sevenfold by category, thirty-seven by subdivision.

Sakiccanipphādanato, sarūpena ca vuttito;

Sabbeva ariyamaggassa, sambhave sambhavanti teti.

By the accomplishment of their respective functions, and by their being stated according to their intrinsic nature, they all arise together with the arising of the Noble Path.

Evaṃ tāvettha paripuṇṇabodhipakkhiyabhāvo jānitabbo.

Thus, the state of the complete qualities conducive to enlightenment should be understood here.

Vuṭṭhānabalasamāyogakathā

The Discourse on the Combination of Emergence and Strength

827. Vuṭṭhānabalasamāyogoti vuṭṭhānañceva balasamāyogo ca. Lokiyavipassanā hi nimittārammaṇattā ceva pavattikāraṇassa ca samudayassa asamucchindanato neva nimittā na pavattā vuṭṭhāti. Gotrabhuñāṇaṃ samudayassa asamucchindanato pavattā na vuṭṭhāti. Nibbānārammaṇato pana nimittā vuṭṭhātīti ekato vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tenāha “bahiddhāvuṭṭhānavivaṭṭane paññā gotrabhuñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. mātikā 1.10). Tathā “uppādā vivaṭṭitvā anuppādaṃ pakkhandatīti gotrabhu, pavattā vivaṭṭitvā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.59) sabbaṃ veditabbaṃ. Imāni pana cattāripi ñāṇāni animittārammaṇattā nimittato vuṭṭhahanti, samudayassa samucchindanato pavattā vuṭṭhahantīti dubhato vuṭṭhānāni honti.

827. The combination of emergence and strength means both emergence and a combination of strength. For mundane insight, since it has a sign as its object and because it does not cut off the origin which is the cause of the process, it emerges from neither the sign nor the process. Change-of-lineage knowledge does not emerge from the process because it does not cut off the origin; but since its object is Nibbāna, it emerges from the sign. Thus, it is an emergence from one side. Therefore, it is said: 'Wisdom in the emergence and turning away from the external is change-of-lineage knowledge.' Likewise, it should all be understood from: 'It is change-of-lineage because it turns away from arising and enters into non-arising; turns away from the process...' But these four knowledges emerge from the sign because their object is the signless, and they emerge from the process because they cut off the origin; thus, they are emergences from both sides.

Tena vuttaṃ –

Therefore it was said:

“Kathaṃ dubhato vuṭṭhānavivaṭṭane paññā magge ñāṇaṃ?

How is knowledge in the path the wisdom of emergence and turning away from both sides?

“Sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe dassanaṭṭhena sammādiṭṭhi micchādiṭṭhiyā vuṭṭhāti, tadanuvattakakilesehi ca khandhehi ca vuṭṭhāti, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittehi vuṭṭhāti. Tena vuccati dubhato vuṭṭhānavivaṭṭane paññā magge ñāṇaṃ. Abhiniropanaṭṭhena sammāsaṅkappo micchāsaṅkappā…pe… pariggahaṭṭhena sammāvācā micchāvācāya. Samuṭṭhānaṭṭhena sammākammanto. Vodānaṭṭhena sammāājīvo. Paggahaṭṭhena sammāvāyāmo[M 2.0322]. Upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena sammāsati. Avikkhepaṭṭhena sammāsamādhi micchāsamādhito vuṭṭhāti, tadanuvattakakilesehi ca [V 2.0320] khandhehi ca vuṭṭhāti, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittehi vuṭṭhāti. Tena vuccati ‘dubhato vuṭṭhānavivaṭṭane paññā magge ñāṇa’nti.

At the moment of the path of stream-entry, right view, in the sense of seeing, emerges from wrong view; it emerges from the defilements and aggregates that accord with it; and it emerges from all external signs. Therefore, it is said, 'wisdom is knowledge in the path in the emergence and turning away from both sides.' Right thought, in the sense of directing the mind, emerges from wrong thought... Right speech, in the sense of encompassing, from wrong speech... Right action, in the sense of initiating, from wrong action... Right livelihood, in the sense of cleansing, from wrong livelihood... Right effort, in the sense of endeavoring, from wrong effort... Right mindfulness, in the sense of establishing, from wrong mindfulness... Right concentration, in the sense of non-distraction, emerges from wrong concentration; it emerges from the defilements and aggregates that accord with it; and it emerges from all external signs. Therefore, it is said, 'wisdom is knowledge in the path in the emergence and turning away from both sides.'

“Sakadāgāmimaggakkhaṇe dassanaṭṭhena sammādiṭṭhi…pe… avikkhepaṭṭhena sammāsamādhi oḷārikā kāmarāgasaṃyojanā paṭighasaṃyojanā oḷārikā kāmarāgānusayā paṭighānusayā vuṭṭhāti…pe….

At the moment of the once-returner path, right view in the sense of seeing... right concentration in the sense of non-distraction emerges from the gross fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of ill-will, the gross underlying tendency of sensual desire, and the underlying tendency of ill-will...

“Anāgāmimaggakkhaṇe dassanaṭṭhena sammādiṭṭhi…pe… avikkhepaṭṭhena sammāsamādhi anusahagatā kāmarāgasaṃyojanā paṭighasaṃyojanā anusahagatā kāmarāgānusayā paṭighānusayā vuṭṭhāti…pe….

At the moment of the non-returner's path, right view in the sense of seeing... right concentration in the sense of non-distraction emerges from the subtle fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of aversion, the subtle underlying tendency of sensual desire, and the underlying tendency of aversion...

“Arahattamaggakkhaṇe dassanaṭṭhena sammādiṭṭhi…pe… avikkhepaṭṭhena sammāsamādhi rūparāgā arūparāgā mānā uddhaccā avijjāya mānānusayā bhavarāgānusayā avijjānusayā vuṭṭhāti, tadanuvattakakilesehi ca khandhehi ca vuṭṭhāti, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittehi vuṭṭhāti. Tena vuccati ‘dubhato vuṭṭhānavivaṭṭane paññā magge ñāṇa’”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.61).

At the moment of the path of Arahantship, right view in the sense of seeing... right concentration in the sense of non-distraction emerges from lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency of conceit, the underlying tendency of lust for existence, and the underlying tendency of ignorance; it emerges from the defilements and aggregates that follow upon them, and it emerges from all external signs. Therefore, it is said: 'Wisdom in the emergence and turning away from both is knowledge in the path' (Paṭis. 1.61).

828. Lokiyānañca aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ bhāvanākāle samathabalaṃ adhikaṃ hoti. Aniccānupassanādīnaṃ bhāvanākāle vipassanābalaṃ. Ariyamaggakkhaṇe pana yuganaddhā te dhammā pavattanti aññamaññaṃ anativattanaṭṭhena. Tasmā imesu catūsupi ñāṇesu ubhayabalasamāyogo hoti. Yathāha –

828. At the time of developing the eight mundane attainments, the strength of serenity is predominant. At the time of developing the contemplation of impermanence and so on, the strength of insight is predominant. However, at the moment of the noble path, these states proceed yoked together, in the sense of not exceeding one another. Therefore, in these four knowledges, there is a union of both strengths. As it is said:

“Uddhaccasahagatakilesehi ca khandhehi ca vuṭṭhahato cittassa ekaggatā avikkhepo samādhi nirodhagocaro, avijjāsahagatakilesehi ca khandhehi ca vuṭṭhahato anupassanaṭṭhena vipassanā nirodhagocarā. Iti vuṭṭhānaṭṭhena samathavipassanā ekarasā [M 2.0323] honti, yuganaddhā honti, aññamaññaṃ nātivattantīti. Tena vuccati vuṭṭhānaṭṭhena samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ bhāvetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.5).

For one who has emerged from defilements accompanied by restlessness and from the aggregates, concentration—the mind's one-pointedness and non-distraction—has cessation as its object. For one who has emerged from defilements accompanied by ignorance and from the aggregates, insight, in the sense of contemplation, has cessation as its object. Thus, in the sense of emergence, serenity and insight are of a single essence, are yoked together, and do not surpass one another. Therefore, it is said, 'One develops serenity and insight yoked together in the sense of emergence.'

Evamettha vuṭṭhānabalasamāyogo veditabbo.

Thus, the union of the strengths of emergence should be understood herein.

Pahātabbadhammapahānakathā

Discourse on the Abandoning of States to be Abandoned

829. Ye [V 2.0321] yena pahātabbā dhammā, tesaṃ pahānañcāti imesu pana catūsu ñāṇesu ye dhammā yena ñāṇena pahātabbā, tesaṃ pahānañca jānitabbaṃ. Etāni hi yathāyogaṃ saṃyojanakilesamicchattalokadhammamacchariyavipallāsaganthaagatiāsavaoghayoganīvaraṇaparāmāsaupādānaanusayamalaakusalakammapathacittuppādasaṅkhātānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānakarāni.

829. Regarding the states to be abandoned and their abandonment—among these four knowledges, it should be understood which states are to be abandoned by which knowledge, and their abandonment. For these knowledges, as is appropriate, bring about the abandonment of the states enumerated as: fetters, defilements, wrongness, worldly conditions, stinginess, distortions, bonds, wrong courses, taints, floods, yokes, hindrances, misapprehension, clinging, underlying tendencies, stains, unwholesome courses of action, and unwholesome thought-arisings.

Tattha saṃyojanānīti khandhehi khandhānaṃ phalena kammassa dukkhena vā sattānaṃ saṃyojakattā rūparāgādayo dasa dhammā vuccanti. Yāvañhi te, tāva etesaṃ anuparamoti. Tatrāpi rūparāgo arūparāgo māno uddhaccaṃ avijjāti ime pañca uddhaṃnibbattanakakhandhādisaṃyojakattā uddhaṃbhāgiyasaṃyojanāni nāma. Sakkāyadiṭṭhi vicikicchā sīlabbataparāmāso kāmarāgo paṭighoti ime pañca adhonibbattanakakhandhādisaṃyojakattā adhobhāgiyasaṃyojanāni nāma.

Therein, 'fetters' are the ten states beginning with lust for form, so called because they bind aggregates to aggregates, fruit to kamma, or beings to suffering. For as long as these fetters exist, there is no cessation of this round of existence. Among them, lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance—these five are called the 'higher fetters' because they bind one to rebirth in the higher realms. Identity view, doubt, adherence to rites and rituals, sensual lust, and ill will—these five are called the 'lower fetters' because they bind one to rebirth in the lower realms.

Kilesāti sayaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhattā sampayuttadhammānañca saṃkilesikattā lobho doso moho māno diṭṭhi vicikicchā thinaṃ uddhaccaṃ ahirikaṃ anottappanti ime dasa dhammā.

‘Defilements’ are these ten states: greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing—so called because they are themselves defiled and because they defile associated states.

Micchattāti micchāpavattanato micchādiṭṭhi micchāsaṅkappo micchāvācā micchākammanto micchāājīvo micchāvāyāmo micchāsati micchāsamādhīti ime aṭṭha dhammā. Micchāvimuttimicchāñāṇehi vā saddhiṃ dasa.

'Wrongness' refers to these eight states, so called because of their wrong mode of occurrence: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. Or, together with wrong liberation and wrong knowledge, they are ten.

Lokadhammāti lokappavattiyā sati anuparamadhammakattā lābho alābho yaso ayaso sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ nindā pasaṃsāti ime aṭṭha. Idha pana kāraṇopacārena lābhādivatthukassa anunayassa alābhādivatthukassa paṭighassa cetaṃ lokadhammaggahaṇena gahaṇaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ.

'Worldly conditions' are these eight: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, pleasure and pain—so called because they are states that do not cease as long as the world proceeds. Here, however, it should be understood that what is meant by 'worldly conditions' are the attraction based on gain and the like, and the aversion based on loss and the like, this being a figurative expression where the effect is named for the cause.

Macchariyānīti [M 2.0324] āvāsamacchariyaṃ kulamacchariyaṃ lābhamacchariyaṃ dhammamacchariyaṃ vaṇṇamacchariyanti imāsu āvāsādīsu aññesaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ asahanākārena pavattāni pañca macchariyāni.

'Stinginesses' are these five: stinginess regarding dwellings, families, gains, the Dhamma, and good qualities. These five kinds of stinginess occur in the manner of being unable to tolerate others sharing in these things, such as dwellings.

Vipallāsāti [V 2.0322] aniccadukkhaanattaasubhesuyeva vatthūsu “niccaṃ sukhaṃ attā subha”nti evaṃ pavatto saññāvipallāso cittavipallāso diṭṭhivipallāsoti ime tayo.

'Distortions' are these three: the distortion of perception, the distortion of thought, and the distortion of view. They occur with regard to things that are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul, taking them to be 'permanent, pleasant, self, and beautiful.'

Ganthāti nāmakāyassa ceva rūpakāyassa ca ganthanato abhijjhādayo cattāro. Tathā hi te abhijjhā kāyagantho, byāpādo kāyagantho, sīlabbataparāmāso kāyagantho, idaṃsaccābhiniveso kāyagantho icceva vuttā.

'Bonds' are the four beginning with covetousness, so called because they bind the mental body and the physical body. For they are spoken of thus: 'Covetousness is a bodily bond, ill will is a bodily bond, adherence to rites and rituals is a bodily bond, and dogmatic adherence that "this alone is true" is a bodily bond.'

Agatīti chandadosamohabhayehi akattabbakaraṇassa, kattabbākaraṇassa ca adhivacanaṃ. Tañhi ariyehi agantabbattā agatīti vuccati.

'Wrong courses' is a term for doing what should not be done and not doing what should be done, out of desire, hatred, delusion, or fear. It is called a 'wrong course' (agati) because it is a course not to be taken (a-gantabba) by the noble ones.

Āsavāti ārammaṇavasena āgotrabhuto, ābhavaggato ca savanā, asaṃvutehi vā dvārehi ghaṭachiddehi udakaṃ viya savanato niccapaggharaṇaṭṭhena saṃsāradukkhassa vā savanato kāmarāgabhavarāgamicchādiṭṭhiavijjānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

'Taints' is a designation for sensual lust, lust for existence, wrong view, and ignorance. They are so called because they flow (savanti) by way of their objects up to (ā) the change-of-lineage knowledge and up to (ā) the peak of existence; or because they flow out from unguarded doors like water from cracks in a pot, in the sense of constantly oozing; or because they cause the suffering of saṃsāra to flow on.

Bhavasāgare ākaḍḍhanaṭṭhena duruttaraṇaṭṭhena ca oghātipi, ārammaṇaviyogassa ceva dukkhaviyogassa ca appadānato yogātipi tesaññeva adhivacanaṃ.

These same things are also designated 'floods' because they drag one down into the ocean of existence and because they are difficult to cross. They are also designated 'yokes' because they do not grant separation from their objects or separation from suffering.

Nīvaraṇānīti cittassa āvaraṇanīvaraṇapaṭicchādanaṭṭhena kāmacchandādayo pañca.

'Hindrances' are the five states beginning with sensual desire, so called because they obstruct, hinder, and conceal the mind.

Parāmāsoti tassa tassa dhammassa sabhāvaṃ atikkamma parato abhūtaṃ sabhāvaṃ āmasanākārena pavattanato micchādiṭṭhiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

'Misapprehension' is a designation for wrong view, so called because it proceeds by way of grasping a false nature, having transgressed the true nature of each particular thing.

Upādānānīti sabbākārena paṭiccasamuppādaniddese vuttāni kāmupādānādīni cattāri.

'Clinging' refers to the four kinds, beginning with clinging to sensual pleasures, as explained in all their aspects in the exposition of dependent origination.

Anusayāti thāmagataṭṭhena kāmarāgānusayo, paṭigha, māna, diṭṭhi, vicikicchā, bhavarāga, avijjānusayoti evaṃ vuttā kāmarāgādayo satta[M 2.0325]. Te hi thāmagatattā punappunaṃ kāmarāgādīnaṃ uppattihetubhāvena anusentiyevāti anusayā.

Latent tendencies (anusayā), in the sense of having the potential to arise, are these seven states beginning with sensual lust, thus stated: the latent tendency of sensual lust, of ill will, of conceit, of wrong view, of doubt, of lust for existence, and of ignorance. For they, having the potential to arise, lie dormant (anusenti) as the cause for the repeated arising of sensual lust and so on; therefore, they are called 'latent tendencies'.

Malāti [V 2.0323] telañjanakalalaṃ viya sayañca asuddhattā, aññesañca asuddhabhāvakaraṇato lobhadosamohā tayo.

Stains (malā) are these three: greed, hatred, and delusion—because they are themselves impure and cause impurity in others, like oily mud.

Akusalakammapathāti akusalakammabhāvena ceva duggatīnañca pathabhāvena pāṇātipāto adinnādānaṃ kāmesumicchācāro musāvādo pisuṇavācā pharusavācā samphappalāpo abhijjhā byāpādo micchādiṭṭhīti ime dasa.

Unwholesome courses of action (akusalakammapathā) are these ten: taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. They are so called because they are unwholesome actions and because they are paths to bad destinations.

Akusalacittuppādāti lobhamūlā aṭṭha dosamūlā dve mohamūlā dveti ime dvādasa.

Unwholesome arisings of consciousness (akusalacittuppādā) are these twelve: eight rooted in greed, two in hatred, and two in delusion.

830. Iti etesaṃ saṃyojanādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ etāni yathāyogaṃ pahānakarāni. Kathaṃ? Saṃyojanesu tāva sakkāyadiṭṭhi vicikicchā sīlabbataparāmāso apāyagamanīyā ca kāmarāgapaṭighāti ete pañca dhammā paṭhamañāṇavajjhā, sesā kāmarāgapaṭighā oḷārikā dutiyañāṇavajjhā, sukhumā tatiyañāṇavajjhā, rūparāgādayo pañcapi catutthañāṇavajjhā eva. Paratopi ca yattha yattha evasaddena niyamaṃ na karissāma. Tattha tattha yaṃ yaṃ “upariñāṇavajjho”ti vakkhāma, so so purimañāṇehi hatāpāyagamanīyādibhāvova hutvā upariñāṇavajjho hotīti veditabbo.

830. Thus, for these states—fetters and so on—these knowledges are the means of their abandonment, each according to its suitability. How so? Among the fetters, identity view, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, and the sensual lust and ill will that lead to the lower realms—these five states are to be abandoned by the first knowledge. The remaining coarse sensual lust and ill will are to be abandoned by the second knowledge; the subtle ones, by the third knowledge. The five beginning with lust for form are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge only. Furthermore, wherever we do not make a restriction with the word 'only', and we state that something is 'to be abandoned by a higher knowledge', it should be understood that this state, having had its aspect of leading to the lower realms etc. destroyed by the preceding knowledges, is then to be abandoned by the higher knowledge.

Kilesesu diṭṭhivicikicchā paṭhamañāṇavajjhā, doso tatiyañāṇavajjho, lobhamohamānathinauddhaccaahirikaanottappāni catutthañāṇavajjhāni.

Among the defilements: wrong view and doubt are to be abandoned by the first knowledge; hatred is to be abandoned by the third knowledge; greed, delusion, conceit, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Micchattesu micchādiṭṭhi musāvādo micchākammanto micchāājīvoti ime paṭhamañāṇavajjhā, micchāsaṅkappo pisuṇavācā pharusavācāti ime tatiyañāṇavajjhā, cetanāyeva cettha vācāti veditabbā. Samphappalāpamicchāvāyāmasatisamādhivimuttiñāṇāni catutthañāṇavajjhāni.

Among the wrongnesses (micchattā): wrong view, false speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood are to be abandoned by the first knowledge. Wrong intention, divisive speech, and harsh speech are to be abandoned by the third knowledge—and here, volition itself should be understood as speech. Idle chatter, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong liberation, and wrong knowledge are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Lokadhammesu paṭigho tatiyañāṇavajjho, anunayo catutthañāṇavajjho, yase ca pasaṃsāya ca anunayo catutthañāṇavajjhoti eke. Macchariyāni paṭhamañāṇavajjhāneva.

Among the worldly conditions: ill will is to be abandoned by the third knowledge; attachment is to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge. Some say that attachment to fame and praise is also to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge. The forms of stinginess are to be abandoned by the first knowledge only.

Vipallāsesu [M 2.0326][V 2.0324] anicce niccaṃ, anattani attāti ca saññācittadiṭṭhivipallāsā, dukkhe sukhaṃ, asubhe subhanti diṭṭhivipallāso cāti ime paṭhamañāṇavajjhā, asubhe subhanti saññācittavipallāsā tatiyañāṇavajjhā, dukkhe sukhanti saññācittavipallāsā catutthañāṇavajjhā.

Among the distortions: the distortions of perception, consciousness, and view that perceive permanence in the impermanent and self in what is not-self; and the distortion of view that perceives pleasure in suffering and beauty in the foul—these are to be abandoned by the first knowledge. The distortions of perception and consciousness that perceive beauty in the foul are to be abandoned by the third knowledge. The distortions of perception and consciousness that perceive pleasure in suffering are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Ganthesu sīlabbataparāmasaidaṃsaccābhinivesakāyaganthā paṭhamañāṇavajjhā, byāpādakāyagantho tatiyañāṇavajjho, itaro catutthañāṇavajjho.

Among the bonds: the bodily bonds of adherence to rules and observances and of dogmatic insistence that 'this is the only truth' are to be abandoned by the first knowledge. The bodily bond of ill will is to be abandoned by the third knowledge. The remaining one (the bodily bond of covetousness) is to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Agati paṭhamañāṇavajjhāva.

The wrong courses of action are to be abandoned by the first knowledge only.

Āsavesu diṭṭhāsavo paṭhamañāṇavajjho, kāmāsavo tatiyañāṇavajjho, itare dve catutthañāṇavajjhā. Oghayogesupi eseva nayo.

Among the taints: the taint of views is to be abandoned by the first knowledge; the taint of sensual desire is to be abandoned by the third knowledge; the other two (the taint of existence and the taint of ignorance) are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge. This same method applies to the floods and yokes as well.

Nīvaraṇesu vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ paṭhamañāṇavajjhaṃ, kāmacchando byāpādo kukkuccanti tīṇi tatiyañāṇavajjhāni, thinamiddhauddhaccāni catutthañāṇavajjhāni.

Among the hindrances: the hindrance of doubt is to be abandoned by the first knowledge. Sensual desire, ill will, and remorse—these three are to be abandoned by the third knowledge. Sloth-and-torpor and restlessness are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Parāmāso paṭhamañāṇavajjhova.

Adherence is to be abandoned by the first knowledge only.

Upādānesu sabbesampi lokiyadhammānaṃ vatthukāmavasena kāmāti āgatattā rūpārūparāgopi kāmupādāne patati, tasmā taṃ catutthañāṇavajjhaṃ, sesāni paṭhamañāṇavajjhāni.

Among the forms of clinging: since all worldly states are designated as 'sensual pleasures' (kāma) in the sense of being objects of desire (vatthukāma), even lust for the form and formless realms falls under the clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna). Therefore, that is to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge, while the remaining three are to be abandoned by the first knowledge.

Anusayesu diṭṭhivicikicchānusayā paṭhamañāṇavajjhāva, kāmarāgapaṭighānusayā tatiyañāṇavajjhā, mānabhavarāgāvijjānusayā catutthañāṇavajjhā.

Among the latent tendencies: the latent tendencies of wrong view and doubt are to be abandoned by the first knowledge only. The latent tendencies of sensual lust and ill will are to be abandoned by the third knowledge. The latent tendencies of conceit, lust for existence, and ignorance are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Malesu dosamalaṃ tatiyañāṇavajjhaṃ, itarāni catutthañāṇavajjhāni.

Among the stains: the stain of hatred is to be abandoned by the third knowledge; the other two (the stains of greed and delusion) are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Akusalakammapathesu pāṇātipāto adinnādānaṃ micchācāro musāvādo micchādiṭṭhīti ime paṭhamañāṇavajjhā[V 2.0325], pisuṇavācā pharusavācā byāpādoti tayo tatiyañāṇavajjhā, samphappalāpābhijjhā catutthañāṇavajjhā.

Among the unwholesome courses of action: taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and wrong view—these five are to be abandoned by the first knowledge. Divisive speech, harsh speech, and ill will—these three are to be abandoned by the third knowledge. Idle chatter and covetousness are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Akusalacittuppādesu cattāro diṭṭhigatasampayuttā vicikicchāsampayutto cāti pañca paṭhamañāṇavajjhāva, dve paṭighasampayuttā tatiyañāṇavajjhā, sesā catutthañāṇavajjhāti.

Among the unwholesome arisings of consciousness: the four associated with wrong view and the one associated with doubt—these five are to be abandoned by the first knowledge only. The two associated with ill will are to be abandoned by the third knowledge. The remaining five are to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge.

Yañca yena vajjhaṃ, taṃ tena pahātabbaṃ nāma. Tena vuttaṃ “iti etesaṃ saṃyojanādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ etāni yathāyogaṃ pahānakarānī”ti.

And whatever is to be abandoned by a certain knowledge is called 'that which is to be abandoned' by it. Therefore it was said: 'Thus, for these states—fetters and so on—these knowledges are the means of their abandonment, each according to its suitability.'

831. Kiṃ [M 2.0327] panetāni ete dhamme atītānāgate pajahanti udāhu paccuppanneti. Kiṃ panettha yadi tāva atītānāgate, aphalo vāyāmo āpajjati. Kasmā? Pahātabbānaṃ natthitāya. Atha paccuppanne, tathāpi aphalo, vāyāmena saddhiṃ pahātabbānaṃ atthitāya, saṃkilesikā ca maggabhāvanā āpajjati, vippayuttatā vā kilesānaṃ, na ca paccuppannakileso cittavippayutto nāma atthīti. Nāyaṃ āveṇikā codanā. Pāḷiyaṃyeva hi “svāyaṃ kilese pajahati, atīte kilese pajahati, anāgate kilese pajahati, paccuppanne kilese pajahatī”ti vatvā, puna “hañci atīte kilese pajahati, tenahi khīṇaṃ khepeti, niruddhaṃ nirodheti, vigataṃ vigameti, atthaṅgataṃ atthaṅgameti. Atītaṃ yaṃ natthi, taṃ pajahatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.21) ca vatvā, “na atīte kilese pajahatī”ti paṭikkhittaṃ.

831. But do these knowledges abandon these states when they are past or future, or when they are present? What is the issue here? If they abandon past and future states, the effort becomes fruitless. Why? Because the states to be abandoned do not exist. If they abandon present states, the effort is still fruitless, because the states to be abandoned exist together with the effort. In that case, the cultivation of the path would become defiled, or the defilements would be dissociated from the mind—and there is no such thing as a present defilement that is dissociated from the mind. This is not an objection unique to this text. For in the Pāli Canon itself, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, having asked, 'Does one abandon defilements? Does one abandon past defilements, future defilements, or present defilements?', it then raises an objection: 'If one abandons past defilements, then one exhausts what is already exhausted, brings to cessation what has already ceased, removes what is already removed, makes disappear what has already disappeared. One would be abandoning the past, which does not exist.' And thus, the abandoning of past defilements is rejected with the words, 'One does not abandon past defilements.'

Tathā “hañci anāgate kilese pajahati, tenahi ajātaṃ pajahati, anibbattaṃ pajahati, anuppannaṃ pajahati, apātubhūtaṃ pajahati. Anāgataṃ yaṃ natthi, taṃ pajahatī”ti ca vatvā, “na anāgate kilese pajahatī”ti paṭikkhittaṃ.

Similarly, having stated, “If one abandons future defilements, then one abandons what is unborn, unproduced, unarisen, and unmanifest. One abandons that which, being future, does not exist,” it is refuted thus: “One does not abandon future defilements.”

Tathā “hañci paccuppanne kilese pajahati, tenahi ratto rāgaṃ pajahati. Duṭṭho dosaṃ, mūḷho mohaṃ, vinibaddho mānaṃ, parāmaṭṭho diṭṭhiṃ, vikkhepagato uddhaccaṃ, aniṭṭhaṅgato vicikicchaṃ, thāmagato anusayaṃ pajahati. Kaṇhasukkā dhammā yuganaddhāva vattanti. Saṃkilesikā maggabhāvanā hotī”ti ca vatvā, “na atīte kilese pajahati, na anāgate, na paccuppanne kilese pajahatī”ti sabbaṃ paṭikkhipitvā, “tenahi natthi maggabhāvanā, natthi phalasacchikiriyā[V 2.0326], natthi kilesappahānaṃ, natthi dhammābhisamayo”ti pañhāpariyosāne “na hi natthi maggabhāvanā…pe… natthi dhammābhisamayo”ti paṭijānitvā “yathā kathaṃ viyā”ti vutte idaṃ vuttaṃ –

Similarly, “If one abandons defilements in the present, then a lustful person abandons lust; a hateful person abandons hatred; a deluded person abandons delusion; a conceited person abandons conceit; one who misapprehends abandons wrong view; a distracted person abandons restlessness; an undecided person abandons doubt; and one in whom the potential is present abandons latent tendencies. Dark and bright qualities would proceed as if yoked together, and the development of the path would be accompanied by defilement.” And having said this, and having rejected everything by stating, “One does not abandon defilements in the past, nor in the future, nor in the present,” then at the conclusion of the question, “Therefore, is there no development of the path, no realization of the fruit, no abandoning of defilements, no comprehension of the Dhamma?”, it is conceded, “Indeed, there is development of the path... there is comprehension of the Dhamma.” When asked, “In what way?” this was said:

“Seyyathāpi taruṇo rukkho ajātaphalo, tamenaṃ puriso mūle chindeyya, ye tassa rukkhassa ajātaphalā, te ajātāyeva na jāyanti, anibbattāyeva na nibbattanti, anuppannāyeva na uppajjanti, apātubhūtāyeva na pātubhavanti, evameva [M 2.0328] uppādo hetu uppādo paccayo kilesānaṃ nibbattiyāti uppāde ādīnavaṃ disvā anuppāde cittaṃ pakkhandati, anuppāde cittassa pakkhandattā ye āyūhanapaccayā kilesā nibbatteyyuṃ, te ajātāyeva na jāyanti…pe… apātubhūtāyeva na pātubhavanti, evaṃ hetunirodhā dukkhanirodho. Pavattaṃ hetu…pe… nimittaṃ hetu…pe… āyūhanā hetu…pe… anāyūhane cittassa pakkhandattā ye āyūhanapaccayā kilesā nibbatteyyuṃ, te ajātāyeva…pe… apātubhūtāyeva na pātubhavanti, evaṃ hetunirodhā dukkhanirodho. Evaṃ atthi maggabhāvanā, atthi phalasacchikiriyā, atthi kilesappahānaṃ, atthi dhammābhisamayo”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.21).

“Just as with a young tree that has not yet borne fruit, if a person were to cut it at the root, its fruits that have not yet been born, being unborn, would not be born; being unproduced, would not be produced; being unarisen, would not arise; being unmanifested, would not become manifest. In the same way, ‘Origination is a cause, origination is a condition for the arising of defilements.’ Seeing the danger in origination, the mind inclines towards non-origination. Because the mind inclines towards non-origination, whatever defilements might arise conditioned by accumulation, being unborn, are not born... being unmanifested, they do not become manifest. Thus, with the cessation of the cause, there is the cessation of suffering. Continuance is a cause... a sign is a cause... accumulation is a cause... Because the mind inclines towards non-accumulation, whatever defilements might arise conditioned by accumulation, being unborn... being unmanifested, they do not become manifest. Thus, with the cessation of the cause, there is the cessation of suffering. In this way, there is the development of the path, there is the realization of the fruit, there is the abandoning of defilements, and there is the comprehension of the Dhamma.”

832. Etena kiṃ dīpitaṃ hoti? Bhūmiladdhānaṃ kilesānaṃ pahānaṃ dīpitaṃ hoti. Bhūmiladdhā pana kiṃ atītānāgatā udāhu paccuppannāti. Bhūmiladdhuppannā eva nāma te.

832. What is shown by this? The abandoning of defilements that have obtained their plane is shown. But are these defilements that have obtained their plane past, future, or present? They are named ‘arisen having obtained their plane.’

833. Uppannaṃ hi vattamānabhūtāpagatokāsakatabhūmiladdhavasena anekappabhedaṃ. Tattha sabbampi uppādajarābhaṅgasamaṅgisaṅkhātaṃ vattamānuppannaṃ nāma. Ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavitvā niruddhaṃ anubhūtāpagatasaṅkhātaṃ kusalākusalaṃ uppādādittayaṃ anuppatvā niruddhaṃ bhūtāpagatasaṅkhātaṃ sesasaṅkhatañca bhūtāpagatuppannaṃ nāma. “Yānissa tāni pubbekatāni kammānī”ti (ma. ni. 3.248) evamādinā nayena vuttaṃ kammaṃ atītampi samānaṃ aññaṃ vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassokāsaṃ katvā ṭhitattā tathā katokāsañca vipākaṃ anuppannampi samānaṃ evaṃ kate okāse ekantena uppajjanato okāsakatuppannaṃ nāma. Tāsu tāsu bhūmīsu asamūhataṃ akusalaṃ bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāma.

833. Indeed, the ‘arisen’ is of many kinds, by way of being present, passed away, opportunity-made, and plane-obtained. Therein, all that is possessed of the characteristics of arising, aging, and dissolution is called ‘presently arisen.’ The ‘passed-away arisen’ includes wholesome and unwholesome kamma which has ceased after experiencing the taste of an object, and the remaining conditioned things which have ceased after reaching the three moments beginning with arising. Kamma spoken of in the manner of, “Whatever deeds one has done previously,” although it is past, is called ‘opportunity-made arisen’ because, having obstructed the result of other kamma, it stands having made an opportunity for its own result, and because that result for which the opportunity has been made will inevitably arise, even though it has not yet arisen. The unwholesome which has not been eradicated in the various planes is called ‘plane-obtained arisen.’

834. Ettha [V 2.0327] ca bhūmiyā bhūmiladdhassa ca nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Bhūmīti hi vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtā tebhūmakā pañcakkhandhā. Bhūmiladdhaṃ nāma tesu khandhesu uppattirahaṃ kilesajātaṃ. Tenahi sā bhūmi laddhā nāma hotīti tasmā bhūmiladdhanti vuccati, sā ca kho na ārammaṇavasena. Ārammaṇavasena [M 2.0329] hi sabbepi atītānāgate pariññātepi ca khīṇāsavānaṃ khandhe ārabbha kilesā uppajjanti mahākaccānauppalavaṇṇādīnaṃ khandhe ārabbha soreyyaseṭṭhi nandamāṇavakādīnaṃ viya. Yadi ca taṃ bhūmiladdhaṃ nāma siyā, tassa appaheyyato na koci bhavamūlaṃ pajaheyya. Vatthuvasena pana bhūmiladdhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yattha yattha hi vipassanāya apariññātā khandhā uppajjanti, tattha tattha uppādato pabhuti tesu vaṭṭamūlaṃ kilesajātaṃ anuseti. Taṃ appahīnaṭṭhena bhūmiladdhanti veditabbaṃ.

834. Here, the distinction between the plane (bhūmi) and what has obtained the plane (bhūmiladdha) should be understood. The ‘plane’ refers to the five aggregates of the three realms, which serve as the object for insight meditation. ‘What has obtained the plane’ refers to the host of defilements that is fit to arise in relation to those aggregates. It is so called because that plane is obtained by it; but this is not in the sense of being an object. For, in the sense of an object, defilements arise in relation to all past and future aggregates, and even in relation to the aggregates of arahants, though they have been fully comprehended—just as defilements arose for Soreyya the merchant and the youth Nanda in relation to the aggregates of Mahākaccāna and Uppalavaṇṇā. If that were to be called ‘what has obtained the plane,’ then, because it could not be abandoned, no one could ever abandon the root of existence. Rather, ‘what has obtained the plane’ should be understood in the sense of its basis. For wherever aggregates not fully comprehended by insight arise, in those very places, from the moment of their arising, the host of defilements that is the root of the cycle of existence lies latent. This should be understood as ‘what has obtained the plane’ in the sense that it has not yet been abandoned.

835. Tattha ca yassa yesu khandhesu appahīnaṭṭhena anusayitā kilesā, tassa te eva khandhā tesaṃ kilesānaṃ vatthu, na aññesaṃ santakā khandhā. Atītakkhandhesu ca appahīnānusayitānaṃ kilesānaṃ atītakkhandhāva vatthu, na itare. Esa nayo anāgatādīsu. Tathā kāmāvacarakkhandhesu appahīnānusayitānaṃ kilesānaṃ kāmāvacarakkhandhāva vatthu, na itare. Esa nayo rūpārūpāvacaresu. Sotāpannādīsu pana yassa yassa ariyapuggalassa khandhesu taṃ taṃ vaṭṭamūlaṃ kilesajātaṃ tena tena maggena pahīnaṃ, tassa tassa te te khandhā pahīnānaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ vaṭṭamūlakilesānaṃ avatthuto bhūmīti saṅkhaṃ na labhanti. Puthujjanassa sabbasova vaṭṭamūlakilesānaṃ appahīnattā yaṃkiñci kariyamānaṃ kammaṃ kusalaṃ akusalaṃ vā hoti. Iccassa kammakilesapaccayā vaṭṭaṃ vaṭṭati. Tassetaṃ vaṭṭamūlaṃ rūpakkhandheyeva, na vedanākkhandhādīsu. Viññāṇakkhandheyeva vā, na rūpakkhandhādīsūti na vattabbaṃ. Kasmā? Avisesena pañcasupi khandhesu anusayitattā.

835. In this context, for one whose defilements lie latent in certain aggregates due to not having been abandoned, those very aggregates are the basis for those defilements, not the aggregates belonging to others. And for defilements that lie latent in past aggregates, the past aggregates themselves are the basis, not others. The same principle applies to future aggregates and so on. Similarly, for defilements that lie latent in the aggregates of the sense sphere, the sense-sphere aggregates themselves are the basis, not others. The same principle applies to the form and formless spheres. However, for noble individuals such as stream-enterers and so on, in whose aggregates that particular collection of defilements which is the root of the round has been abandoned by that particular path, those very aggregates, being a non-basis for those abandoned root-defilements, do not receive the designation 'ground'. For an ordinary person, since the root-defilements of the round are entirely unabandoned, any action being performed becomes either wholesome or unwholesome kamma. Thus, for such a one, the round revolves due to the conditions of kamma and defilements. It should not be said that this root of the round lies latent only in the form aggregate and not in the feeling aggregate and so on, or only in the consciousness aggregate and not in the form aggregate and so on. Why? Because it lies latent in all five aggregates without distinction.

836. Kathaṃ? Pathavīrasādi viya rukkhe. Yathā hi mahārukkhe pathavītalaṃ adhiṭṭhāya pathavīrasañca āporasañca nissāya tappaccayā mūlakhandhasākhapasākhapallavapalāsapupphaphalehi vaḍḍhitvā nabhaṃ pūretvā yāva kappāvasānā bījaparamparāya rukkhapaveṇiṃ santānayamāne ṭhite taṃ pathavīrasādi mūleyeva, na khandhādīsu…pe… phaleyeva vā, na mūlādīsūti na vattabbaṃ. Kasmā? Avisesena sabbesu mūlādīsu anugatattāti.

836. How? Like the earth-essence and so on in a tree. For just as a great tree, established on the earth's surface and depending on the essence of earth and the essence of water, grows with roots, trunk, branches, twigs, foliage, flowers, and fruits, filling the sky and continuing its lineage through a succession of seeds until the end of the aeon—it cannot be said that this earth-essence exists only in the roots, not in the trunk and so on, or only in the fruits, not in the roots and so on. Why? Because it pervades all parts—the roots and so on—without distinction.

Yathā [V 2.0328] pana tasseva rukkhassa pupphaphalādīsu nibbinno koci puriso catūsu disāsu maṇḍūkakaṇṭakaṃ nāma visakaṇṭakaṃ ākoṭeyya, atha so [M 2.0330] rukkho tena visasamphassena phuṭṭho pathavīrasaāporasānaṃ pariyādiṇṇattā appasavanadhammataṃ āgamma puna santānaṃ nibbattetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya, evameva khandhapavattiyaṃ nibbinno kulaputto tassa purisassa catūsu disāsu rukkhe visayojanaṃ viya attano santāne catumaggabhāvanaṃ ārabhati. Athassa so khandhasantāno tena catumaggavisasamphassena sabbaso vaṭṭamūlakakilesānaṃ pariyādiṇṇattā kiriyabhāvamattaupagatakāyakammādisabbakammappabhedo hutvā āyatiṃ punabbhavānabhinibbattanadhammataṃ āgamma bhavantarasantānaṃ nibbattetuṃ na sakkoti. Kevalaṃ carimaviññāṇanirodhena nirindhano viya jātavedo anupādāno parinibbāyati, evaṃ bhūmiyā bhūmiladdhassa ca nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Just as a certain person, weary of the flowers and fruits of that very tree, might drive a poisonous thorn called 'Frog's Thorn' into it from the four directions. Then that tree, being struck by the contact of that poison and its essence of earth and water being exhausted, would come to a state of infertility and be unable to produce a further continuum. In the same way, a clansman weary of the continuation of the aggregates, like that person applying poison to the tree from the four directions, undertakes the development of the four paths in his own continuum. Then, that continuum of aggregates, being struck by the contact of the poison of the four paths, and with the root-defilements of the round being entirely exhausted, has all its various kinds of kamma—bodily kamma and so on—reduced to a state of mere functionality. Having come to the nature of not generating a future rebirth, it is unable to produce a continuum in another state of being. With the cessation of the final consciousness, like a fire without fuel, it is finally extinguished without clinging. Thus, the distinction between the ground and that which is established on the ground should be understood.

837. Apica aparampi samudācāraārammaṇādhiggahitaavikkhambhitaasamūhatavasena catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ. Tattha vattamānuppannameva samudācāruppannaṃ. Cakkhādīnaṃ pana āpāthagate ārammaṇe pubbabhāge anuppajjamānampi kilesajātaṃ ārammaṇassa adhiggahitattā eva aparabhāge ekantena uppattito ārammaṇādhiggahituppannanti vuccati, kalyāṇigāme piṇḍāya carato mahātissattherassa visabhāgarūpadassanena uppannakilesajātaṃ viya. Samathavipassanānaṃ aññataravasena avikkhambhitaṃ kilesajātaṃ cittasantatimanārūḷhampi uppattinivārakassa hetuno abhāvā avikkhambhituppannaṃ nāma. Samathavipassanāvasena pana vikkhambhitampi ariyamaggena asamūhatattā uppattidhammataṃ anatītatāya asamūhatuppannanti vuccati, ākāsena gacchantassa aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino therassa kusumitarukkhe upavane pupphāni uccinantassa madhurena sarena gāyato mātugāmassa gītasavanena uppannakilesajātaṃ viya. Tividhampi cetaṃ ārammaṇādhiggahitāvikkhambhitaasamūhatuppannaṃ bhūmiladdheneva saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti veditabbaṃ.

837. Furthermore, there is another fourfold 'arisen' by way of manifestation, being grasped by an object, being unsuppressed, and being uneradicated. Herein, that which is arisen in the present is the 'arisen by manifestation'. However, a collection of defilements, even if it does not arise in the initial phase when an object comes into the range of the eye and so on, is called 'arisen by being grasped by an object' because, due to the object having been grasped, it will certainly arise in a later phase—like the collection of defilements that arose for the Elder Mahātissa, while walking for alms in Kalyāṇigāma, upon seeing an unsuitable form. A collection of defilements that is unsuppressed by way of either serenity or insight, even if it has not ascended into the mental continuum, is called 'arisen by being unsuppressed' due to the absence of a cause that would prevent its arising. Furthermore, a collection of defilements, even if suppressed by way of serenity or insight, is called 'arisen by being uneradicated' because, not having been eradicated by the noble path, it has not transcended its nature of arising—like the collection of defilements that arose for the elder who was an attainer of the eight attainments and was travelling through the air, upon hearing the song of a woman who was singing with a sweet voice while picking flowers in a grove near a park. And it should be understood that these three—the arisen by being grasped by an object, by being unsuppressed, and by being uneradicated—are included only under that which is established on the ground.

838. Iccetasmiṃ vuttappabhede uppanne yadetaṃ vattamānabhūtāpagatokāsakatasamudācārasaṅkhātaṃ catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ, taṃ amaggavajjhattā kenacipi ñāṇena pahātabbaṃ na hoti. Yaṃ panetaṃ bhūmiladdhārammaṇādhiggahitaavikkhambhitaasamūhatasaṅkhātaṃ uppannaṃ, tassa taṃ uppannabhāvaṃ vināsayamānaṃ yasmā taṃ taṃ lokiyalokuttarañāṇaṃ uppajjati, tasmā taṃ sabbampi pahātabbaṃ hotīti. Evamettha ye yena pahātabbā dhammā, tesaṃ pahānañca jānitabbaṃ.

838. Thus, among this classification of the 'arisen' that has been explained, that fourfold 'arisen' designated as present, past, opportunity-made, and manifest, is not to be abandoned by any knowledge because it is not something to be abandoned by the path. But as for that 'arisen' designated as established on the ground, grasped by an object, unsuppressed, and uneradicated—since the respective mundane and supramundane knowledge arises while destroying its 'arisen' state, therefore all of it is to be abandoned. Thus, in this context, which states are to be abandoned by which knowledge, and the abandoning of them, should be known.

Pariññādikiccakathā

Discourse on the Functions of Full Understanding, etc.

839.

839.

Kiccāni [M 2.0331][V 2.0329] pariññādīni, yāni vuttāni abhisamayakāle;

Tāni ca yathāsabhāvena, jānitabbāni sabbānīti.

The functions—full understanding and so on— Which were stated at the time of direct comprehension, And all these should be known According to their intrinsic nature.

Saccābhisamayakālaṃ hi etesu catūsu ñāṇesu ekekassa ekakkhaṇe pariññā pahānaṃ sacchikiriyā bhāvanāti etāni pariññādīni cattāri kiccāni vuttāni, tāni yathāsabhāvena jānitabbāni. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ porāṇehi –

For at the moment of direct comprehension of the truths, for each of these four knowledges, in a single moment, these four functions—full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development—are stated. They are to be known according to their intrinsic nature. For this has been said by the ancients:

“Yathā padīpo apubbaṃ acarimaṃ ekakkhaṇe cattāri kiccāni karoti, vaṭṭiṃ jhāpeti, andhakāraṃ vidhamati, ālokaṃ parividaṃseti, sinehaṃ pariyādiyati, evameva maggañāṇaṃ apubbaṃ acarimaṃ ekakkhaṇe cattāri saccāni abhisameti, dukkhaṃ pariññābhisamayena abhisameti, samudayaṃ pahānābhisamayena abhisameti, maggaṃ bhāvanābhisamayena abhisameti, nirodhaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayena abhisameti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Nirodhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karitvā cattāripi saccāni pāpuṇāti passati paṭivijjhatī”ti.

“Just as a lamp, not severally but simultaneously, performs four functions in a single moment—it burns the wick, dispels darkness, manifests light, and consumes the oil—so too, path-knowledge, not severally but simultaneously, directly comprehends the four truths in a single moment. It directly comprehends suffering by the direct comprehension of full understanding; it directly comprehends the origin by the direct comprehension of abandoning; it directly comprehends the path by the direct comprehension of development; and it directly comprehends cessation by the direct comprehension of realization. What is meant by this? Having made cessation its object, it attains, sees, and penetrates all four truths.”

Vuttampi cetaṃ “yo, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ passati, dukkhasamudayampi so passati, dukkhanirodhampi passati, dukkhanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadampi passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) sabbaṃ veditabbaṃ.

And this has also been said: “Bhikkhus, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering” (SN 5.437). The entire passage should be understood.

Aparampi vuttaṃ “maggasamaṅgissa ñāṇaṃ, dukkhepetaṃ ñāṇaṃ, dukkhasamudayepetaṃ ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhepetaṃ ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāyapetaṃ ñāṇa”nti (vibha. 794; paṭi. ma. 1.109).

Furthermore, it has been said: “The knowledge of one endowed with the path—this is knowledge in suffering, this is knowledge in the origin of suffering, this is knowledge in the cessation of suffering, and this is knowledge in the path leading to the cessation of suffering” (Vibh 228; Paṭis I 119).

Tattha yathā padīpo vaṭṭiṃ jhāpeti, evaṃ maggañāṇaṃ dukkhaṃ parijānāti. Yathā andhakāraṃ vidhamati, evaṃ samudayaṃ pajahati. Yathā ālokaṃ parividaṃseti, evaṃ sahajātādipaccayatāya sammāsaṅkappādidhammasaṅkhātaṃ maggaṃ bhāveti. Yathā sinehaṃ pariyādiyati, evaṃ kilesapariyādānaṃ nirodhaṃ sacchikarotīti evaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Therein, just as the lamp burns the wick, so path-knowledge fully understands suffering. Just as it dispels darkness, so it abandons the origin. Just as it manifests light, so it develops the path—described as right intention and other states—by way of co-nascent conditionality and so on. Just as it consumes the oil, so it realizes cessation, which is the exhaustion of defilements. Thus the application of the simile should be understood.

840. Aparo [V 2.0330] nayo – yathā sūriyo udayanto apubbaṃ acarimaṃ saha pātubhāvā cattāri kiccāni karoti, rūpagatāni obhāseti, andhakāraṃ [M 2.0332] vidhamati, ālokaṃ dasseti, sītaṃ paṭippassambheti, evameva maggañāṇaṃ…pe… nirodhaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayena abhisameti. Idhāpi yathā sūriyo rūpagatāni obhāseti, evaṃ maggañāṇaṃ dukkhaṃ parijānāti. Yathā andhakāraṃ vidhamati, evaṃ samudayaṃ pajahati. Yathā ālokaṃ dasseti, evaṃ sahajātādipaccayatāya maggaṃ bhāveti. Yathā sītaṃ paṭippassambheti, evaṃ kilesapaṭippassaddhiṃ nirodhaṃ sacchikarotīti evaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

840. Another method: Just as the rising sun, not severally but simultaneously with its appearance, performs four functions—it illuminates forms, dispels darkness, shows light, and allays the cold—so too path-knowledge… directly comprehends cessation by the direct comprehension of realization. Here also, just as the sun illuminates forms, so path-knowledge fully understands suffering. Just as it dispels darkness, so it abandons the origin. Just as it shows light, so it develops the path by way of co-nascent conditionality and so on. Just as it allays the cold, so it realizes cessation, which is the allaying of defilements. Thus the application of the simile should be understood.

841. Aparo nayo – yathā nāvā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ ekakkhaṇe cattāri kiccāni karoti, orimatīraṃ pajahati, sotaṃ chindati, bhaṇḍaṃ vahati, pārimatīraṃ appeti, evameva maggañāṇaṃ…pe… nirodhaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayena abhisameti. Etthāpi yathā nāvā orimatīraṃ pajahati, evaṃ maggañāṇaṃ dukkhaṃ parijānāti. Yathā sotaṃ chindati, evaṃ samudayaṃ pajahati. Yathā bhaṇḍaṃ vahati, evaṃ sahajātādipaccayatāya maggaṃ bhāveti. Yathā pārimatīraṃ appeti, evaṃ pārimatīrabhūtaṃ nirodhaṃ sacchikarotīti evaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

841. Another method: Just as a boat, not severally but simultaneously, performs four functions in a single moment—it abandons the near shore, cuts through the current, carries the cargo, and reaches the far shore—so too path-knowledge… directly comprehends cessation by the direct comprehension of realization. Here also, just as the boat abandons the near shore, so path-knowledge fully understands suffering. Just as it cuts through the current, so it abandons the origin. Just as it carries the cargo, so it develops the path by way of co-nascent conditionality and so on. Just as it reaches the far shore, so it realizes cessation, which is the far shore. Thus the application of the simile should be understood.

842. Evaṃ saccābhisamayakālasmiṃ ekakkhaṇe catunnaṃ kiccānaṃ vasena pavattañāṇassa panassa soḷasahākārehi tathaṭṭhena cattāri kiccāni ekapaṭivedhāni honti. Yathāha –

842. Thus, at the time of the direct comprehension of the truths, for this knowledge that proceeds by way of four functions in a single moment, its four functions are of a single penetration by way of their true nature in sixteen aspects. As it is said:

“Kathaṃ tathaṭṭhena cattāri kiccāni ekapaṭivedhāni? Soḷasahi ākārehi tathaṭṭhena cattāri kiccāni ekapaṭivedhāni. Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho, saṅkhataṭṭho, santāpaṭṭho, vipariṇāmaṭṭho, tathaṭṭho. Samudayassa āyūhanaṭṭho, nidānaṭṭho, saṃyogaṭṭho, palibodhaṭṭho, tathaṭṭho. Nirodhassa nissaraṇaṭṭho, vivekaṭṭho, asaṅkhataṭṭho, amataṭṭho, tathaṭṭho. Maggassa niyyānaṭṭho, hetuṭṭho, dassanaṭṭho, adhipateyyaṭṭho, tathaṭṭho. Imehi soḷasahi ākārehi tathaṭṭhena cattāri saccāni ekasaṅgahitāni. Yaṃ ekasaṅgahitaṃ, taṃ ekattaṃ. Yaṃ ekattaṃ, taṃ ekena ñāṇena paṭivijjhatīti cattāri saccāni ekapaṭivedhānī”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.11).

“How are the four truths of a single penetration by way of their true nature? The four truths are of a single penetration by way of their true nature in sixteen aspects. For suffering, the meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of torment, and the meaning of change is the true nature. For the origin, the meaning of accumulation, the meaning of source, the meaning of connection, and the meaning of impediment is the true nature. For cessation, the meaning of escape, the meaning of seclusion, the meaning of the unconditioned, and the meaning of the deathless is the true nature. For the path, the meaning of outlet, the meaning of cause, the meaning of vision, and the meaning of dominance is the true nature. By these sixteen aspects, the four truths are included as one in their true nature. What is included as one is a unity. What is a unity is penetrated by a single knowledge. Thus the four truths are of a single penetration” (Paṭis II 10).

843. Tattha [M 2.0333] siyā yadā dukkhādīnaṃ aññepi rogagaṇḍādayo atthā atthi, atha kasmā cattāroyeva vuttāti. Ettha vadāma, aññasaccadassanavasena āvibhāvato. “Tattha katamaṃ [V 2.0331] dukkhe ñāṇaṃ? Dukkhaṃ ārabbha yā uppajjati paññā pajānanā”tiādinā (vibha. 794; paṭi. ma. 1.109) hi nayena ekekasaccārammaṇavasenāpi saccañāṇaṃ vuttaṃ. “Yo, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ passati, samudayampi so passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) nayena ekaṃ saccaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā sesesupi kiccanipphattivasenāpi vuttaṃ.

843. Here, it might be asked: “Since there are other meanings of suffering and so on, such as disease and boils, why are only four mentioned?” To this we say: because they become manifest by way of seeing the other truths. For, knowledge of the truths is stated by way of taking each single truth as an object, according to the method beginning: “Therein, what is knowledge in suffering? The wisdom, the understanding that arises in regard to suffering…” (Vibh 228; Paṭis I 119). And it is also stated by way of the accomplishment of the functions in the remaining truths after having made one truth the object, according to the method beginning: “Bhikkhus, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin…” (SN 5.437).

Tattha yadā ekekaṃ saccaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, tadā samudayadassanena tāva sabhāvato pīḷanalakkhaṇassāpi dukkhassa, yasmā taṃ āyūhanalakkhaṇena samudayena āyūhitaṃ saṅkhataṃ rāsikataṃ, tasmāssa so saṅkhataṭṭho āvibhavati. Yasmā pana maggo kilesasantāpaharo susītalo, tasmāssa maggassa dassanena santāpaṭṭho āvibhavati āyasmato nandassa accharādassanena sundariyā anabhirūpabhāvo viya. Avipariṇāmadhammassa pana nirodhassa dassanenassa vipariṇāmaṭṭho āvibhavatīti vattabbamevettha natthi.

Therein, when one makes each single truth the object, then, by seeing the origin, the meaning of ‘conditioned’ becomes manifest for suffering—which has the characteristic of oppression by its own nature—because it is accumulated, conditioned, and amassed by the origin, which has the characteristic of accumulation. Thus, its meaning of being conditioned becomes manifest. Furthermore, since the path removes the burning of defilements and is perfectly cool, by seeing the path, the meaning of ‘torment’ becomes manifest, just as the unattractiveness of Sundarī became manifest to the Venerable Nanda upon seeing a celestial nymph. And it is not even necessary to state here that by seeing cessation, which is of an unchanging nature, the meaning of ‘change’ becomes manifest.

Tathā sabhāvato āyūhanalakkhaṇassāpi samudayassa, dukkhadassanena nidānaṭṭho āvibhavati asappāyabhojanato uppannabyādhidassanena bhojanassa byādhinidānabhāvo viya. Visaṃyogabhūtassa nirodhassa dassanena saṃyogaṭṭho. Niyyānabhūtassa ca maggassa dassanena palibodhaṭṭhoti.

Similarly, for the truth of origin, which has the characteristic of accumulation by its own nature, its aspect as a source becomes manifest when the truth of suffering is seen—just as seeing an illness that has arisen from unsuitable food reveals food as the source of the illness. By seeing the truth of cessation, which is disjunction, its aspect as conjunction becomes manifest. And by seeing the truth of the path, which is the escape, its aspect as an obstruction becomes manifest.

Tathā nissaraṇalakkhaṇassāpi nirodhassa, avivekabhūtassa samudayassa dassanena vivekaṭṭho āvibhavati. Maggadassanena asaṅkhataṭṭho, iminā hi anamataggasaṃsāre maggo nadiṭṭhapubbo, sopi ca sappaccayattā saṅkhatoyevāti appaccayadhammassa asaṅkhatabhāvo ativiya pākaṭo hoti. Dukkhadassanena panassa amataṭṭho āvibhavati, dukkhaṃ hi visaṃ, amataṃ nibbānanti.

Likewise, for the truth of cessation, which has the characteristic of escape, its aspect of seclusion becomes manifest when the truth of origin—which is non-seclusion—is seen. By seeing the truth of the path, its unconditioned aspect becomes manifest; for this path had not been seen before in beginningless saṃsāra, and it too, being dependent on conditions, is conditioned. Thus the unconditioned nature of the reality that is without conditions becomes exceedingly clear. Furthermore, by seeing the truth of suffering, its aspect as deathlessness becomes manifest, for suffering is poison, and Nibbāna is the deathless.

Tathā niyyānalakkhaṇassāpi maggassa, samudayadassanena “nāyaṃ hetu nibbānassa pattiyā, ayaṃ hetū”ti hetuṭṭho āvibhavati. Nirodhadassanena dassanaṭṭho, paramasukhumāni rūpāni passato “vippasannaṃ vata me [M 2.0334] cakkhū”nti cakkhussa vippasannabhāvo viya. Dukkhadassanena adhipateyyaṭṭho, anekarogāturakapaṇajanadassanena issarajanassa uḷārabhāvo viyāti evamettha salakkhaṇavasena ekekassa, aññasaccadassanavasena ca itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ āvibhāvato ekekassa cattāro cattāro atthā vuttā. Maggakkhaṇe pana sabbe cete atthā ekeneva dukkhādīsu [V 2.0332] catukiccena ñāṇena paṭivedhaṃ gacchantīti. Ye pana nānābhisamayaṃ icchanti, tesaṃ uttaraṃ abhidhamme kathāvatthusmiṃ vuttameva.

Similarly, for the path, which has the characteristic of leading out, its aspect as a cause becomes manifest by seeing the truth of origin, revealing, 'This is not the cause for attaining Nibbāna; this is the cause.' By seeing the truth of cessation, its aspect as seeing becomes manifest, just as for one who sees extremely subtle forms, the clarity of the eye becomes evident, as they think, 'Indeed, my eye is clear.' By seeing the truth of suffering, its aspect of sovereignty becomes manifest, just as seeing many sick, afflicted, and wretched people reveals the greatness of a powerful person. Thus, herein, for each of the truths, four aspects are stated: one becomes manifest through its own characteristic, and the other three become manifest through seeing the other truths. However, at the moment of the path, all these sixteen aspects are penetrated by a single knowledge with its four functions regarding suffering and so on. As for those who prefer separate penetrations, the refutation for them has already been stated in the Abhidhamma, in the Kathāvatthu.

Pariññādippabhedakathā

An Exposition on the Divisions of Full Understanding and so on

844. Idāni yāni tāni pariññādīni cattāri kiccāni vuttāni, tesu –

844. Now, regarding those four functions that were stated, beginning with full understanding, among them:

Tividhā hoti pariññā, tathā pahānampi sacchikiriyāpi;

Dve bhāvanā abhimatā, vinicchayo tattha ñātabbo.

Full understanding is threefold; likewise are abandonment and realization. Two kinds of development are accepted; the analysis thereof should be understood.

845. Tividhā hoti pariññāti ñātapariññā tīraṇapariññā pahānapariññāti evaṃ pariññā tividhā hoti. Tattha “abhiññāpaññā ñātaṭṭhena ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. mātikā 1.20) evaṃ uddisitvā “ye ye dhammā abhiññātā honti, te te dhammā ñātā hontī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.75) evaṃ saṅkhepato, “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññeyyaṃ. Kiñca, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ abhiññeyyaṃ? Cakkhuṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññeyya”ntiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.2) nayena vitthārato vuttā ñātapariññā nāma. Tassā sappaccayanāmarūpābhijānanā āveṇikā bhūmi.

845. ‘Full understanding is threefold’ means: full understanding as knowing (ñātapariññā), full understanding as investigating (tīraṇapariññā), and full understanding as abandoning (pahānapariññā). Thus, full understanding is threefold. Therein, having first set forth the text, ‘Wisdom of direct knowledge is knowledge in the sense of what is known’ (Paṭis. M., Mātikā 1.20), there is what is called ‘full understanding as knowing,’ which is stated in brief as, ‘Whatever things are directly known, those things are known’ (Paṭis. M. 1.75), and in detail by the method beginning, ‘Bhikkhus, all is to be directly known. And what, bhikkhus, is all to be directly known? The eye, bhikkhus, is to be directly known,’ and so on (Paṭis. M. 1.2). Its specific domain is the direct knowledge of name-and-form together with its conditions.

846. “Pariññāpaññā tīraṇaṭṭhena ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. mātikā 1.21) evaṃ uddisitvā pana “ye ye dhammā pariññātā honti, te te dhammā tīritā hontī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.75) evaṃ saṅkhepato, “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, pariññeyyaṃ. Kiñca, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ pariññeyyaṃ? Cakkhuṃ, bhikkhave, pariññeyya”ntiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.21) nayena vitthārato vuttā tīraṇapariññā nāma. Tassā kalāpasammasanato paṭṭhāya aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti tīraṇavasena pavattamānāya yāva anulomā āveṇikā bhūmi.

846. Furthermore, having first set forth the text, ‘Wisdom of full understanding is knowledge in the sense of investigation’ (Paṭis. M., Mātikā 1.21), there is what is called ‘full understanding as investigating,’ which is stated in brief as, ‘Whatever things are fully understood, those things are investigated’ (Paṭis. M. 1.75), and in detail by the method beginning, ‘Bhikkhus, all is to be fully understood. And what, bhikkhus, is all to be fully understood? The eye, bhikkhus, is to be fully understood,’ and so on (Paṭis. M. 1.21). Its specific domain, which proceeds by way of investigating things as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, extends from the comprehension of groups up to conformity knowledge.

847. “Pahānapaññā pariccāgaṭṭhena ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. mātikā 1.22) evaṃ pana uddisitvā “ye ye dhammā pahīnā honti, te te dhammā pariccattā hontī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.75) evaṃ vitthārato [M 2.0335] vuttā “aniccānupassanāya niccasaññaṃ pajahatī”tiādinayappavattā [V 2.0333] pahānapariññā. Tassā bhaṅgānupassanato paṭṭhāya yāva maggañāṇā bhūmi, ayaṃ idha adhippetā.

847. Furthermore, having first set forth the text, ‘Wisdom of abandoning is knowledge in the sense of relinquishment’ (Paṭis. M., Mātikā 1.22), there is the full understanding as abandoning, which is stated in detail as, ‘Whatever things are abandoned, those things are relinquished’ (Paṭis. M. 1.75), and which proceeds according to the method beginning, ‘Through the contemplation of impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence,’ and so on. Its domain extends from the contemplation of dissolution up to path knowledge. This is the one intended here.

Yasmā vā ñātatīraṇapariññāyopi tadatthāyeva, yasmā ca ye dhamme pajahati, te niyamato ñātā ceva tīritā ca honti, tasmā pariññāttayampi iminā pariyāyena maggañāṇassa kiccanti veditabbaṃ.
