Alternatively, since full understanding as knowing and as investigating are for the sake of that abandoning, and since whatever phenomena one abandons are necessarily both known and investigated, therefore it should be understood that in this way the threefold full understanding is also the function of path knowledge.

848. Tathā pahānampīti pahānampi hi vikkhambhanappahānaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ samucchedappahānanti pariññā viya tividhameva hoti. Tattha yaṃ sasevāle udake pakkhittena ghaṭena sevālassa viya tena tena lokiyasamādhinā nīvaraṇādīnaṃ paccanīkadhammānaṃ vikkhambhanaṃ, idaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ nāma. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “vikkhambhanappahānañca nīvaraṇānaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ bhāvayato”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.24) nīvaraṇānaññeva vikkhambhanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pākaṭattā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Nīvaraṇāni hi jhānassa pubbabhāgepi pacchābhāgepi na sahasā cittaṃ ajjhottharanti, vitakkādayo appitakkhaṇeyeva. Tasmā nīvaraṇānaṃ vikkhambhanaṃ pākaṭaṃ.

848. ‘Likewise abandonment too’ means that abandonment, like full understanding, is threefold: abandonment by suppression, abandonment by substitution of opposites, and abandonment by cutting off. Therein, the suppression of the hindrances and other opposing states by this or that mundane concentration—like the pushing aside of algae by a pot thrown into water containing algae—is called abandonment by suppression. In the Pāli text, however, it is said: ‘Abandonment by suppression of the hindrances occurs for one developing the first jhāna’ (Paṭis. M. 1.24). Here, the suppression of only the hindrances is mentioned. This, it should be understood, is said because it is so evident. For the hindrances do not suddenly overwhelm the mind either in the preliminary part or the posterior part of the jhāna, whereas initial thought and so on are absent only at the moment of absorption. Therefore, the suppression of the hindrances is evident.

849. Yaṃ pana rattibhāge samujjalitena padīpena andhakārassa viya tena tena vipassanāya avayavabhūtena ñāṇaṅgena paṭipakkhavaseneva tassa tassa pahātabbadhammassa pahānaṃ, idaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ nāma. Seyyathidaṃ – nāmarūpaparicchedena tāva sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā. Paccayapariggahena ahetuvisamahetudiṭṭhiyā ceva kaṅkhāmalassa ca. Kalāpasammasanena “ahaṃ mamā”ti samūhagāhassa. Maggāmaggavavatthānena amagge maggasaññāya. Udayadassanena ucchedadiṭṭhiyā. Vayadassanena sassatadiṭṭhiyā. Bhayatupaṭṭhānena sabhaye abhayasaññāya. Ādīnavadassanena assādasaññāya. Nibbidānupassanena abhiratisaññāya. Muñcitukamyatāya amuñcitukāmabhāvassa. Paṭisaṅkhānena appaṭisaṅkhānassa. Upekkhāya anupekkhanassa. Anulomena saccapaṭilomagāhassa pahānaṃ.

849. Furthermore, just as a lit lamp in the night dispels the darkness, so too is there the abandoning of each particular state to be abandoned by its respective opposing factor of knowledge, which is a component of insight. This is called abandonment for the moment (tadaṅgappahāna). For instance: by the discernment of mind and matter, the personality view is abandoned; by the comprehension of conditions, the views of causelessness and inappropriate cause, as well as the stain of doubt, are abandoned; by the comprehension of groups, the grasping of 'I' and 'mine' as a mass is abandoned; by the determination of path and not-path, the perception of the not-path as the path is abandoned; by the seeing of arising, the annihilation view is abandoned; by the seeing of passing away, the eternalist view is abandoned; by the appearance of what is fearful, the perception of safety in what is fearful is abandoned; by the seeing of danger, the perception of gratification is abandoned; by the contemplation of disenchantment, the perception of delight is abandoned; by the desire for deliverance, the state of not desiring deliverance is abandoned; by reflection, non-reflection is abandoned; by equanimity, non-equanimity is abandoned; by conformity, the grasping of what is contrary to the truth is abandoned.

Yaṃ vā pana aṭṭhārasasu mahāvipassanāsu aniccānupassanāya niccasaññāya. Dukkhānupassanāya sukhasaññāya. Anattānupassanāya attasaññāya. Nibbidānupassanāya nandiyā. Virāgānupassanāya rāgassa. Nirodhānupassanāya [M 2.0336] samudayassa. Paṭinissaggānupassanāya [V 2.0334] ādānassa. Khayānupassanāya ghanasaññāya. Vayānupassanāya āyūhanassa. Vipariṇāmānupassanāya dhuvasaññāya. Animittānupassanāya nimittassa. Appaṇihitānupassanāya paṇidhiyā. Suññatānupassanāya abhinivesassa. Adhipaññādhammavipassanāya sārādānābhinivesassa. Yathābhūtañāṇadassanena sammohābhinivesassa. Ādīnavānupassanāya ālayābhinivesassa. Paṭisaṅkhānupassanāya appaṭisaṅkhāya. Vivaṭṭānupassanāya saṃyogābhinivesassa pahānaṃ. Idampi tadaṅgappahānameva.

Alternatively, in the eighteen great insights, there is the abandoning: of the perception of permanence by the contemplation of impermanence; of the perception of pleasure by the contemplation of suffering; of the perception of self by the contemplation of non-self; of delight by the contemplation of disenchantment; of lust by the contemplation of dispassion; of arising by the contemplation of cessation; of grasping by the contemplation of relinquishment; of the perception of solidity by the contemplation of destruction; of exertion by the contemplation of passing away; of the perception of stability by the contemplation of change; of the sign by the contemplation of the signless; of aspiration by the contemplation of the undirected; of adherence by the contemplation of emptiness; of adherence to grasping an essence by the higher-wisdom insight into phenomena; of adherence due to delusion by the knowledge and vision of things as they are; of adherence to attachment by the contemplation of danger; of non-reflection by the contemplation of reflection; of adherence to the fetters by the contemplation of turning away. This too is indeed abandonment for the moment.

850. Tattha yathā aniccānupassanādīhi sattahi niccasaññādīnaṃ pahānaṃ hoti, taṃ bhaṅgānupassane vuttameva.

850. Therein, how the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so forth occurs by means of the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence, that has already been stated in the section on the contemplation of dissolution.

Khayānupassanāti pana ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhenāti evaṃ khayaṃ passato ñāṇaṃ. Tena ghanasaññāya pahānaṃ hoti.

Now, the contemplation of destruction is the knowledge of one who, having broken down solidity, sees destruction thus: 'It is impermanent in the sense of destruction.' By this, the perception of solidity is abandoned.

Vayānupassanāti –

The contemplation of passing away is—

Ārammaṇānvayena, ubho ekavavatthānā;

Nirodhe adhimuttatā, vayalakkhaṇavipassanāti. –

By following the sequence of the object, both are determined as one; inclination towards cessation is insight into the characteristic of passing away.

Evaṃ vuttā paccakkhato ceva anvayato ca saṅkhārānaṃ bhaṅgaṃ disvā tasmiññeva bhaṅgasaṅkhāte nirodhe adhimuttatā, tāya āyūhanassa pahānaṃ hoti. Yesaṃ hi atthāya āyūheyya, “te evaṃ vayadhammā”ti vipassato āyūhane cittaṃ na namati.

As has been said: seeing the dissolution of formations both directly and by inference, there is an inclination towards that very cessation, which is known as dissolution. By this, the abandoning of exertion occurs. For, when one sees, 'Those formations for the sake of which one would exert are of a nature to pass away,' the mind does not incline toward exertion.

Vipariṇāmānupassanāti rūpasattakādivasena taṃ taṃ paricchedaṃ atikkamma aññathāpavattidassanaṃ. Uppannassa vā jarāya ceva maraṇena ca dvīhākārehi vipariṇāmadassanaṃ, tāya dhuvasaññāya pahānaṃ hoti.

The contemplation of change is the seeing of alteration into another state after transgressing each respective limit, by way of the septad of matter and so on. Or, it is the seeing of the change of what has arisen in two ways: through aging and death. By this, the perception of stability is abandoned.

Animittānupassanāti aniccānupassanāva, tāya niccanimittassa pahānaṃ hoti.

The contemplation of the signless is simply the contemplation of impermanence; by this, the sign of permanence is abandoned.

Appaṇihitānupassanāti dukkhānupassanāva, tāya sukhapaṇidhisukhapatthanāpahānaṃ hoti.

The contemplation of the undirected is indeed the contemplation of suffering; by this, the abandoning of aspiration for happiness and longing for happiness occurs.

Suññatānupassanāti anattānupassanāva, tāya “atthi attā”ti abhinivesassa pahānaṃ hoti.

The contemplation of emptiness is indeed the contemplation of non-self; by this, the adherence to the notion 'there is a self' is abandoned.

Adhipaññādhammavipassanāti [M 2.0337][V 2.0335] –

The higher-wisdom insight into phenomena is—

“Ārammaṇañca paṭisaṅkhā, bhaṅgañca anupassati;

Suññato ca upaṭṭhānaṃ, adhipaññā vipassanā”ti. –

'Having reflected on the object, one contemplates dissolution; and there is the appearance as empty—this is higher-wisdom insight.'

Evaṃ vuttā rūpādiārammaṇaṃ jānitvā tassa ca ārammaṇassa tadārammaṇassa ca cittassa bhaṅgaṃ disvā “saṅkhārāva bhijjanti, saṅkhārānaṃ maraṇaṃ, na añño koci atthī”ti bhaṅgavasena suññataṃ gahetvā pavattā vipassanā. Sā adhipaññā ca dhammesu ca vipassanāti katvā adhipaññādhammavipassanāti vuccati, tāya niccasārābhāvassa ca attasārābhāvassa ca suṭṭhu diṭṭhattā sārādānābhinivesassa pahānaṃ hoti.

As has been said: it is the insight that proceeds by grasping emptiness through dissolution, after having known an object such as form, and having seen the dissolution of both that object and the mind that has that object, reflecting: 'Only formations break up; it is the death of formations; there is no other who dies or breaks up.' It is called 'higher-wisdom insight into phenomena' because it is both higher wisdom and insight into phenomena. By this, since the absence of a permanent essence and the absence of a self as essence are well seen, the adherence to grasping an essence is abandoned.

Yathābhūtañāṇadassananti sappaccayanāmarūpapariggaho, tena “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna”ntiādivasena ceva, “issarato loko sambhotī”tiādivasena ca pavattassa sammohābhinivesassa pahānaṃ hoti.

The knowledge and vision of things as they are is the comprehension of name-and-form together with its causes. By this, the abandoning of the adherence due to delusion occurs, which arises in such ways as, 'Did I exist in the past?' and so on, and, 'The world arises from a creator god,' and so on.

Ādīnavānupassanāti bhayatupaṭṭhānavasena uppannaṃ sabbabhavādīsu ādīnavadassanañāṇaṃ, tena “kiñci allīyitabbaṃ na dissatī”ti ālayābhinivesassa pahānaṃ hoti.

The contemplation of danger is the knowledge of seeing danger in all forms of existence and so on, which has arisen by way of the appearance of the fearful. By this, because 'nothing is seen to which one could cling,' the adherence to attachment is abandoned.

Paṭisaṅkhānupassanāti muñcanassa upāyakaraṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhāñāṇaṃ, tena appaṭisaṅkhāya pahānaṃ hoti.

The contemplation of reflection is the knowledge of reflection, which is the means for release. By this, the abandoning of non-reflection occurs.

Vivaṭṭānupassanāti saṅkhārupekkhā ceva anulomañca. Tadā hissa cittaṃ īsakapoṇe padumapalāse udakabindu viya sabbasmā saṅkhāragatā patilīyati, patikuṭati, pativattatīti vuttaṃ. Tasmā tāya saṃyogābhinivesassa pahānaṃ hoti, kāmasaṃyogādikassa kilesābhinivesassa kilesappavattiyā pahānaṃ hotīti attho. Evaṃ vitthārato tadaṅgappahānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “tadaṅgappahānañca diṭṭhigatānaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ samādhiṃ bhāvayato”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.24) saṅkhepeneva vuttaṃ.

The contemplation of turning away is equanimity toward formations and conformity. At that time, it is said, one's mind withdraws, recoils, and turns away from all that has come to be formed, like a drop of water on a slightly tilted lotus leaf. Therefore, by this, the adherence to the fetters is abandoned; the meaning is that the adherence to defilements, such as the fetter of sensual pleasure—that is, the occurrence of defilements—is abandoned. Thus, abandonment for the moment should be understood in detail. In the Pāḷi Canon, however, it is stated only briefly: 'Abandonment for the moment is the abandoning of views for one who develops the concentration that partakes of penetration' (Paṭis I 24).

851. Yaṃ [V 2.0336] pana asanivicakkābhihatassa rukkhassa viya ariyamaggañāṇena saṃyojanādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ yathā na puna pavatti, evaṃ pahānaṃ, idaṃ samucchedappahānaṃ nāma. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “samucchedappahānañca lokuttaraṃ khayagāmimaggaṃ bhāvayato”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.24)[M 2.0338]. Iti imesu tīsu pahānesu samucchedappahānameva idha adhippetaṃ. Yasmā pana tassa yogino pubbabhāge vikkhambhanatadaṅgappahānānipi tadatthāneva, tasmā pahānattayampi iminā pariyāyena maggañāṇassa kiccanti veditabbaṃ. Paṭirājānaṃ vadhitvā rajjaṃ pattena hi yampi tato pubbe kataṃ, sabbaṃ “idañcidañca raññā kata”ntiyeva vuccati.

851. Furthermore, that abandonment of states such as the fetters by the knowledge of the noble path, such that they do not arise again—just as a tree struck by a thunderbolt does not flourish again—is called abandonment by eradication. It is with reference to this that it was said: 'Abandonment by eradication for one who develops the supramundane path leading to destruction' (Paṭis I 24). Thus, among these three kinds of abandonment, only abandonment by eradication is intended here. However, since for that yogī, abandonment by suppression and abandonment for the moment in the preliminary stage also serve that very purpose, all three kinds of abandonment should be understood, in this way, as the function of path knowledge. Indeed, whatever was done by one who has attained sovereignty after slaying a rival king, even what was done beforehand, is all spoken of thus: 'This and that was done by the king.'

852. Sacchikiriyāpīti lokiyasacchikiriyā lokuttarasacchikiriyāti dvedhā bhinnāpi lokuttarāya dassanabhāvanāvasena bhedato tividhā hoti. Tattha “paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhīmhi, vasīmhi, paṭhamajjhānaṃ sacchikataṃ mayā”tiādinā (pārā. 203-204) nayena āgatā paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ phassanā lokiyasacchikiriyā nāma. Phassanāti adhigantvā “idaṃ mayā adhigata”nti paccakkhato ñāṇaphassena phusanā. Imameva hi atthaṃ sandhāya “sacchikiriyā paññā phassanaṭṭhe ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. mātikā 1.24) uddisitvā “ye ye dhammā sacchikatā honti, te te dhammā phassitā hontī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.75) sacchikiriyaniddeso vutto.

852. Realization (sacchikiriyā), though divided twofold as mundane realization and supramundane realization, becomes threefold because the supramundane kind is further divided by way of seeing and development. Herein, the contacting of the first jhāna and so on, which comes in the manner of such statements as, 'I am a gainer of the first jhāna, a master of it; the first jhāna has been realized by me' (cf. Vin I 9), is called mundane realization. 'Contacting' means, having attained it, to touch it with the touch of knowledge directly, thinking, 'This has been attained by me.' Indeed, it was with reference to this meaning that, after stating the summary, 'Realization is wisdom; it is knowledge in the sense of contacting' (Paṭis Mātikā I 24), the exposition on realization was given: 'Whatever states are realized, those states are contacted' (Paṭis I 75).

Apica attano santāne anuppādetvāpi ye dhammā kevalaṃ aparappaccayena ñāṇena ñātā, te sacchikatā honti. Teneva hi “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, sacchikātabbaṃ. Kiñca, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ sacchikātabbaṃ? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, sacchikātabba”ntiādi (paṭi. ma. 1.29) vuttaṃ.

Moreover, even without having produced them in one's own continuum, those states that are known solely by knowledge that is not dependent on another are realized. For that very reason it was said: 'Bhikkhus, all is to be realized. And what, bhikkhus, is the all that is to be realized? The eye, bhikkhus, is to be realized,' and so on (Paṭis I 29).

Aparampi vuttaṃ “rūpaṃ passanto sacchikaroti. Vedanaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ passanto sacchikaroti. Cakkhuṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ…pe… amatogadhaṃ nibbānaṃ passanto sacchikarotīti. Ye ye dhammā sacchikatā honti, te te dhammā phassitā hontī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.29).

Furthermore, it was said: 'Seeing form, one realizes it. Seeing feeling… seeing consciousness, one realizes it. Seeing the eye… seeing aging and death… seeing Nibbāna which culminates in the deathless, one realizes it. Whatever states are realized, those states are contacted' (Paṭis I 29).

Paṭhamamaggakkhaṇe pana nibbānadassanaṃ dassanasacchikiriyā. Sesamaggakkhaṇesu bhāvanāsacchikiriyāti. Sā duvidhāpi idha adhippetā. Tasmā dassanabhāvanāvasena nibbānassa sacchikiriyā imassa ñāṇassa kiccanti veditabbaṃ.

However, at the moment of the first path, the seeing of Nibbāna is realization by seeing. In the moments of the remaining paths, it is realization by development. Both these kinds of supramundane realization are intended here. Therefore, it should be understood that the realization of Nibbāna by way of seeing and development is the function of this knowledge.

853. Dve [M 2.0339][V 2.0337] bhāvanā abhimatāti bhāvanā pana lokiyabhāvanā lokuttarabhāvanāti dveyeva abhimatā. Tattha lokiyānaṃ sīlasamādhipaññānaṃ uppādanaṃ, tāhi ca santānavāsanaṃ lokiyabhāvanā. Lokuttarānaṃ uppādanaṃ, tāhi ca santānavāsanaṃ lokuttarabhāvanā. Tāsu idha lokuttarā adhippetā. Lokuttarāni hi sīlādīni catubbidhampetaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppādeti. Tesaṃ sahajātapaccayāditāya tehi ca santānaṃ vāsetīti lokuttarabhāvanāvassa kiccanti.

853. As to 'Two kinds of development are intended': only two kinds of development are intended, that is, mundane development and supramundane development. Herein, the generation of mundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and the imbuing of the mental continuum with them, is mundane development. The generation of their supramundane counterparts, and the imbuing of the mental continuum with them, is supramundane development. Of these, the supramundane is intended here. For this fourfold knowledge generates the supramundane qualities of virtue and so on, owing to their being co-nascent conditions, etc., and it also imbues the continuum with them. Therefore, supramundane development is its function.

Evaṃ –

Thus—

Kiccāni pariññādīni, yāni vuttāni abhisamayakāle;

Tāni ca yathāsabhāvena, jānitabbāni sabbānīti.

The functions, beginning with full understanding, which are spoken of for the time of breakthrough; all of them should be known in accordance with their true nature.

Ettāvatā ca –

And thus far—

“Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvaya”nti. –

“Established in virtue, a wise person should develop concentration and wisdom.”

Evaṃ sarūpeneva ābhatāya paññābhāvanāya vidhānadassanatthaṃ yaṃ vuttaṃ “mūlabhūtā dve visuddhiyo sampādetvā sarīrabhūtā pañca visuddhiyo sampādentena bhāvetabbā”ti, taṃ vitthāritaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ bhāvetabbāti ayañca pañho vissajjitoti.

Thus, what was said in order to show the method for the development of wisdom as presented in its own form—namely, 'It should be developed by one who, having accomplished the two root purifications, accomplishes the five purifications that are its body'—has now been explained in detail. And the question, 'How should it be developed?' has also been answered.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, composed for the delight of good people,

Paññābhāvanādhikāre

in the Section on the Development of Wisdom,

Ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso nāma

the Exposition on the Purification by Knowledge and Vision,

Bāvīsatimo paricchedo.

the Twenty-Second Chapter.

23. Paññābhāvanānisaṃsaniddeso

23. Exposition on the Benefits of Developing Wisdom

Ānisaṃsapakāsanā

The Declaration of the Benefits

854. Yaṃ [M 2.0340][V 2.0338] pana vuttaṃ “paññābhāvanāya ko ānisaṃso”ti, tattha vadāma. Ayañhi paññābhāvanā nāma anekasatānisaṃsā. Tassā dīghenāpi addhunā na sukaraṃ vitthārato ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsetuṃ. Saṅkhepato panassā nānākilesaviddhaṃsanaṃ, ariyaphalarasānubhavanaṃ, nirodhasamāpattisamāpajjanasamatthatā, āhuneyyabhāvādisiddhīti ayamānisaṃso veditabbo.

854. Now, as to what was asked, 'What is the benefit of developing wisdom?', we shall speak on that. This development of wisdom has many hundreds of benefits. It is not easy to declare its benefits in detail even over a long period of time. In brief, however, its benefit should be understood as this: the destruction of manifold defilements, the experiencing of the taste of the noble fruit, the capability to enter the attainment of cessation, and the accomplishment of states such as being worthy of offerings.

Nānākilesaviddhaṃsanakathā

The Discourse on the Destruction of Manifold Defilements

855. Tattha yaṃ nāmarūpaparicchedato paṭṭhāya sakkāyadiṭṭhādīnaṃ vasena nānākilesaviddhaṃsanaṃ vuttaṃ, ayaṃ lokikāya paññābhāvanāya ānisaṃso. Yaṃ ariyamaggakkhaṇe saṃyojanādīnaṃ vasena nānākilesaviddhaṃsanaṃ vuttaṃ, ayaṃ lokuttarāya paññābhāvanāya ānisaṃsoti veditabbo.

855. Herein, the destruction of manifold defilements by way of abandoning identity view and so on, beginning from the defining of mentality-materiality, has been spoken of; this is the benefit of the mundane development of wisdom. The destruction of manifold defilements by way of abandoning the fetters and so on at the moment of the noble path has been spoken of; this should be understood as the benefit of the supramundane development of wisdom.

Bhīmavegānupatitā, asanīva siluccaye;

Vāyuvegasamuṭṭhito, araññamiva pāvako.

Like a thunderbolt of dreadful velocity falling upon a mountain peak; like a forest fire stirred up by the force of the wind;

Andhakāraṃ viya ravi, satejujjalamaṇḍalo;

Dīgharattānupatitaṃ, sabbānatthavidhāyakaṃ.

like the sun with its blazing, brilliant orb dispelling the darkness; that which has persisted for a long night, the cause of all misfortune—

Kilesajālaṃ paññā hi, viddhaṃsayati bhāvitā;

Sandiṭṭhikamato jaññā, ānisaṃsamimaṃ idha.

the net of defilements—is shattered by wisdom when it is developed. Therefore, one should know this as the benefit visible here.

Phalasamāpattikathā

The Discourse on the Attainment of Fruition

856. Ariyaphalarasānubhavananti [V 2.0339] na kevalañca kilesaviddhaṃsanaññeva, ariyaphalarasānubhavanampi paññābhāvanāya ānisaṃso. Ariyaphalanti hi sotāpattiphalādi sāmaññaphalaṃ vuccati. Tassa dvīhākārehi rasānubhavanaṃ hoti. Maggavīthiyañca phalasamāpattivasena ca pavattiyaṃ. Tatrāssa maggavīthiyaṃ pavatti dassitāyeva.

856. And the experience of the taste of the noble fruits: it is not only the destruction of defilements, but the experience of the taste of the noble fruits is also a benefit of the development of wisdom. Indeed, the noble fruit refers to the fruit of recluseship, such as the fruit of stream-entry and so on. The experience of its taste occurs in two ways: in the path-process and by way of the attainment of fruition. Therein, its occurrence in the path-process has already been shown.

857. Apica [M 2.0341] ye “saṃyojanappahānamattameva phalaṃ nāma, na koci añño dhammo atthī”ti vadanti, tesaṃ anunayatthaṃ idaṃ suttampi dassetabbaṃ – “kathaṃ payogapaṭippassaddhipaññā phale ñāṇaṃ? Sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe dassanaṭṭhena sammādiṭṭhi micchādiṭṭhiyā vuṭṭhāti, tadanuvattakakilesehi ca khandhehi ca vuṭṭhāti, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittehi vuṭṭhāti. Tampayogapaṭippassaddhattā uppajjati sammādiṭṭhi, maggassetaṃ phala”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.63) vitthāretabbaṃ.

857. Furthermore, for those who say, 'The fruit is merely the abandoning of fetters, and there is no other phenomenon,' this discourse should be shown to them for their persuasion: 'How is wisdom in the calming of application knowledge in the fruit? At the moment of the stream-entry path, by means of seeing, right view emerges from wrong view; it emerges from the defilements and aggregates that follow it; and it emerges from all external signs. Due to the calming of that application, right view arises—this is the fruit of the path.' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.63) This should be elaborated.

“Cattāro maggā apariyāpannā, cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni, ime dhammā appamāṇārammaṇā” (dha. sa. 1422). “Mahaggato dhammo appamāṇassa dhammassa anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 2.12.62) evamādīnipi cettha sādhakāni.

'Four paths are not included, and four fruits of recluseship; these phenomena have an immeasurable object.' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1422) 'An exalted phenomenon is a condition for an immeasurable phenomenon by way of the contiguity condition,' (Paṭṭhāna 2.12.62) and so on—these are also proofs here.

858. Phalasamāpattiyaṃ pavattidassanatthaṃ panassa idaṃ pañhākammaṃ – kā phalasamāpatti, ke taṃ samāpajjanti, ke na samāpajjanti, kasmā samāpajjanti, kathañcassā samāpajjanaṃ hoti, kathaṃ ṭhānaṃ, kathaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ, kiṃ phalassa anantaraṃ, kassa ca phalaṃ anantaranti?

858. Now, to show its occurrence in the attainment of fruition, this is the set of questions: What is the attainment of fruition? Who attains it, and who does not? Why do they attain it? How does its attainment come about? How does one abide? How does one emerge? What is immediately after fruition? And of what is fruition the immediate successor?

859. Tattha kā phalasamāpattīti yā ariyaphalassa nirodhe appanā.

859. Herein, what is fruition attainment? It is the absorption of the noble fruit into cessation.

860. Ke taṃ samāpajjanti, ke na samāpajjantīti sabbepi puthujjanā na samāpajjanti. Kasmā? Anadhigatattā. Ariyā pana sabbepi samāpajjanti. Kasmā? Adhigatattā. Uparimā pana heṭṭhimaṃ na samāpajjanti, puggalantarabhāvupagamanena paṭippassaddhattā. Heṭṭhimā ca uparimaṃ, anadhigatattā. Attano attanoyeva pana phalaṃ samāpajjantīti idamettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ.

860. Who attains it, and who does not attain it? All ordinary people do not attain it. Why? Because they have not attained it. However, all noble ones attain it. Why? Because they have attained it. Furthermore, the higher ones do not attain the lower, because it has been superseded by the attainment of the state of another person. And the lower do not attain the higher, because they have not attained it. But they attain only their own fruition—this is the conclusion here.

Keci pana “sotāpannasakadāgāminopi na samāpajjanti. Uparimā dveyeva samāpajjantī”ti [V 2.0340] vadanti. Idañca tesaṃ kāraṇaṃ, ete hi samādhismiṃ paripūrakārinoti. Taṃ puthujjanassāpi attanā paṭiladdhalokiyasamādhisamāpajjanato akāraṇameva. Kiñcettha kāraṇākāraṇacintāya. Nanu pāḷiyaṃyeva vuttaṃ – “katame dasa gotrabhudhammā vipassanāvasena uppajjanti? Sotāpattimaggapaṭilābhatthāya uppādaṃ pavattaṃ…pe… upāyāsaṃ bahiddhā saṅkhāranimittaṃ abhibhuyyatīti gotrabhu. Sotāpattiphalasamāpattatthāya sakadāgāmimaggaṃ [M 2.0342] …pe… arahattaphalasamāpattatthāya… suññatavihārasamāpattatthāya… animittavihārasamāpattatthāya uppādaṃ…pe… bahiddhā saṅkhāranimittaṃ abhibhuyyatīti gotrabhū”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.60). Tasmā sabbepi ariyā attano attano phalaṃ samāpajjantīti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

Some, however, say, 'Even stream-enterers and once-returners do not attain it. Only the two higher ones attain it.' And this is their reason: 'For they are fulfillers in concentration.' But that is no reason, since even a worldling can attain a mundane concentration that they have obtained. What is the use here of pondering over reasons and non-reasons? Is it not said in the Pāḷi itself: 'What are the ten change-of-lineage states that arise by way of insight? For the sake of gaining the stream-entry path, the arising, the occurrence... vexation, overcomes the external sign of formations, thus it is change-of-lineage. For the sake of the attainment of stream-entry fruition... for the sake of the once-returner path... up to... for the sake of the attainment of arahant fruition... for the sake of the attainment of the abiding in emptiness... for the sake of the attainment of the abiding in signlessness, the arising... overcomes the external sign of formations, thus it is change-of-lineage' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.60). Therefore, it should be concluded here that all noble ones attain their own respective fruitions.

861. Kasmā samāpajjantīti diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthaṃ. Yathā hi rājā rajjasukhaṃ, devatā dibbasukhaṃ anubhavanti, evaṃ ariyā “ariyaṃ lokuttarasukhaṃ anubhavissāmā”ti addhānapparicchedaṃ katvā icchiticchitakkhaṇe phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjanti.

861. Why do they attain it? For the sake of a pleasant abiding in this very life. Just as a king experiences the happiness of kingship and a deity experiences divine happiness, so too the noble ones, having made a determination of time, attain the attainment of fruition at any moment they wish, thinking, 'We shall experience the noble, supramundane happiness.'

862. Kathañcassā samāpajjanaṃ hoti, kathaṃ ṭhānaṃ, kathaṃ vuṭṭhānanti dvīhi tāva ākārehi assā samāpajjanaṃ hoti – nibbānato aññassa ārammaṇassa amanasikārā nibbānassa ca manasikārā. Yathāha – “dve kho, āvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā sabbanimittānañca amanasikāro, animittāya ca dhātuyā manasikāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.458).

862. How does its attainment come about, how does one abide, and how does one emerge? Firstly, its attainment comes about in two ways: by not attending to any object other than Nibbāna, and by attending to Nibbāna. As it is said: 'There are, friend, two conditions for the attainment of the signless liberation of mind: non-attention to all signs and attention to the signless element' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.458).

863. Ayampanettha samāpajjanakkamo. Phalasamāpattatthikena hi ariyasāvakena rahogatena paṭisallīnena udayabbayādivasena saṅkhārā vipassitabbā. Tassa pavattānupubbavipassanassa saṅkhārārammaṇagotrabhuñāṇānantarā phalasamāpattivasena nirodhe cittaṃ appeti. Phalasamāpattininnatāya cettha sekkhassāpi phalameva uppajjati, na maggo.

863. And this here is the sequence of attainment. A noble disciple who desires the attainment of fruition, having gone to a solitary place and being in seclusion, should contemplate formations by way of their arising and passing away, and so on. For one whose insight has progressed in sequence, immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge which has formations as its object, the mind enters absorption in cessation by way of the attainment of fruition. Here, because of the inclination towards the attainment of fruition, for a trainee too, only fruition arises, not the path.

Ye pana vadanti “sotāpanno ‘phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjissāmī’ti vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā sakadāgāmī hoti. Sakadāgāmī ca anāgāmī”ti, te vattabbā “evaṃ sati anāgāmī arahā bhavissati, arahā paccekabuddho, paccekabuddho ca buddho. Tasmā na kiñci etaṃ, pāḷivaseneva ca paṭikkhitta”ntipi na gahetabbaṃ. Idameva pana gahetabbaṃ – sekkhassāpi phalameva [V 2.0341] uppajjati, na maggo. Phalañcassa sace anena paṭhamajjhāniko maggo adhigato hoti. Paṭhamajjhānikameva uppajjati. Sace dutiyādīsu aññatarajjhāniko, dutiyādīsu aññatarajjhānikamevāti. Evaṃ tāvassā samāpajjanaṃ hoti.

Those who say, 'A stream-enterer, having established insight thinking, 'I will attain the attainment of fruition,' becomes a once-returner, and a once-returner becomes a non-returner,' should be told: 'If that were so, then a non-returner would become an arahant, an arahant a paccekabuddha, and a paccekabuddha a Buddha.' Therefore, this view is baseless and has been refuted by the Pāḷi itself; it should not be accepted. Instead, this alone should be accepted: 'For a trainee, only fruition arises, not the path.' And their fruition arises according to the path they have attained. If they have attained the first-jhāna path, the first-jhāna fruition arises. If they have attained a path of one of the second jhānas or higher, the fruition of one of the second jhānas or higher arises. Thus, firstly, does its attainment come about.

864. “Tayo [M 2.0343] kho, āvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā ṭhitiyā sabbanimittānañca amanasikāro, animittāya ca dhātuyā manasikāro, pubbe ca abhisaṅkhāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.458) vacanato panassā tīhākārehi ṭhānaṃ hoti. Tattha pubbe ca abhisaṅkhāroti samāpattito pubbe kālaparicchedo. “Asukasmiṃ nāma kāle vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti paricchinnattā hissā yāva so kālo nāgacchati, tāva ṭhānaṃ hoti. Evamassā ṭhānaṃ hotīti.

864. 'Friend, there are three conditions for the stability of the signless liberation of mind: non-attention to all signs, attention to the signless element, and a prior determination.' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.458) According to this statement, its stability occurs in three ways. Here, 'a prior determination' refers to a determination of time made before the attainment. Because one determines, 'I will emerge at such and such a time,' its stability lasts until that time arrives. Thus its stability occurs.

865. “Dve kho, āvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā vuṭṭhānāya sabbanimittānañca manasikāro, animittāya ca dhātuyā amanasikāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.458) vacanato panassā dvīhākārehi vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tattha sabbanimittānanti rūpanimittavedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇanimittānaṃ. Kāmañca na sabbānevetāni ekato manasikaroti sabbasaṅgāhikavasena panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā yaṃ bhavaṅgassa ārammaṇaṃ hoti, taṃ manasikaroto phalasamāpattivuṭṭhānaṃ hotīti evamassā vuṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

865. 'Friend, there are two conditions for emerging from the signless liberation of mind: attention to all signs and non-attention to the signless element.' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.458) According to this statement, emergence from it occurs in two ways. Here, 'all signs' refers to the signs of form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. Although one does not attend to all of these at once, this is stated in a comprehensive sense. Therefore, when one attends to whatever is the object of the life-continuum, emergence from the attainment of fruition occurs. Thus, emergence from it should be understood.

866. Kiṃ phalassa anantaraṃ, kassa ca phalaṃ anantaranti phalassa tāva phalameva vā anantaraṃ hoti, bhavaṅgaṃ vā. Phalaṃ pana atthi maggānantaraṃ, atthi phalānantaraṃ, atthi gotrabhuanantaraṃ, atthi nevasaññānāsaññāyatanānantaraṃ. Tattha maggavīthiyaṃ maggānantaraṃ, purimassa purimassa pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ phalānantaraṃ. Phalasamāpattīsu purimaṃ purimaṃ gotrabhuanantaraṃ. Gotrabhūti cettha anulomaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭṭhāne – “arahato anulomaṃ phalasamāpattiyā anantarapaccayena paccayo. Sekkhānaṃ anulomaṃ phalasamāpattiyā anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.417). Yena phalena nirodhā vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, taṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanānantaranti. Tattha ṭhapetvā maggavīthiyaṃ uppannaṃ phalaṃ avasesaṃ sabbaṃ phalasamāpattivasena pavattaṃ nāma. Evametaṃ maggavīthiyaṃ phalasamāpattiyaṃ vā uppajjanavasena,

866. What follows immediately after fruition, and what does fruition follow immediately after? First, for fruition, either fruition itself or the life-continuum follows immediately. Fruition, however, can follow immediately after the path, after another fruition, after change-of-lineage, or after the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Here, in the path cognitive process, it follows immediately after the path; in a sequence of fruitions, each subsequent fruition follows the preceding one. In fruition attainments, the initial fruition follows immediately after change-of-lineage. Here, 'change-of-lineage' should be understood as conformity. As it is stated in the Paṭṭhāna: 'For an arahant, conformity is a condition for fruition attainment by way of the immediacy condition. For trainees, conformity is a condition for fruition attainment by way of the immediacy condition.' The fruition by which emergence from cessation occurs follows immediately after the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Here, apart from the fruition that arises in the path cognitive process, all remaining fruition is said to occur by way of fruition attainment. Thus, whether arising in the path cognitive process or in fruition attainment,

Paṭippassaddhadarathaṃ[V 2.0342], amatārammaṇaṃ subhaṃ;

Vantalokāmisaṃ santaṃ, sāmaññaphalamuttamaṃ.

The supreme fruit of recluseship, with anguish pacified, having the Deathless as its object, sublime; with worldly allurements relinquished, serene.

Ojavantena sucinā, sukhena abhisanditaṃ;

Yena sātātisātena, amatena madhuṃ viya.

Is suffused with a pure bliss, rich in essence, which is surpassingly sweet, like honey mixed with the deathless.

Taṃ [M 2.0344] sukhaṃ tassa ariyassa, rasabhūtamanuttaraṃ;

Phalassa paññaṃ bhāvetvā, yasmā vindati paṇḍito.

Because the wise one, having developed wisdom regarding the fruit, attains that supreme happiness of the noble one, which is the very essence of taste.

Tasmā ariyaphalassetaṃ, rasānubhavanaṃ idha;

Vipassanābhāvanāya, ānisaṃsoti vuccati.

Therefore, this experiencing of the taste of the noble fruit is, in this context, called a benefit of cultivating insight.

Nirodhasamāpattikathā

Discourse on the Attainment of Cessation

867. Nirodhasamāpattisamāpajjanasamatthatāti na kevalañca ariyaphalarasānubhavanaṃyeva, ayaṃ pana nirodhasamāpattiyā samāpajjanasamatthatāpi imissā paññābhāvanāya ānisaṃsoti veditabbo.

867. Not only the experience of the taste of the noble fruit, but also this ability to enter the attainment of cessation should be understood as a benefit of this development of wisdom.

Tatridaṃ nirodhasamāpattiyā vibhāvanatthaṃ pañhākammaṃ – kā nirodhasamāpatti, ke taṃ samāpajjanti, ke na samāpajjanti, kattha samāpajjanti, kasmā samāpajjanti, kathañcassā samāpajjanaṃ hoti, kathaṃ ṭhānaṃ, kathaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ, vuṭṭhitassa kiṃninnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, matassa ca samāpannassa ca ko viseso, nirodhasamāpatti kiṃ saṅkhatā asaṅkhatā lokiyā lokuttarā nipphannā anipphannāti?

Herein is a set of questions for the clarification of the attainment of cessation: What is the attainment of cessation? Who enters it? Who does not enter it? Where does one enter it? Why does one enter it? How does its entry come about? How does it remain? How does emergence from it occur? Upon emerging, to what is the mind inclined? What is the difference between one who is dead and one who has entered this attainment? Is the attainment of cessation conditioned or unconditioned, worldly or supramundane, produced or unproduced?

868. Tattha kā nirodhasamāpattīti yā anupubbanirodhavasena cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ appavatti. Ke taṃ samāpajjanti, ke na samāpajjantīti sabbepi puthujjanā, sotāpannā, sakadāgāmino, sukkhavipassakā ca anāgāmino, arahanto na samāpajjanti. Aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino pana anāgāmino, khīṇāsavā ca samāpajjanti. “Dvīhi balehi samannāgatattā[V 2.0343], tayo ca saṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā, soḷasahi ñāṇacariyāhi, navahi samādhicariyāhi vasībhāvatā paññā nirodhasamāpattiyā ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. mātikā 1.34) hi vuttaṃ. Ayañca sampadā ṭhapetvā aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino anāgāmikhīṇāsave aññesaṃ natthi. Tasmā teyeva samāpajjanti, na aññe.

868. Herein, what is the attainment of cessation? It is the non-occurrence of mental and mental concomitant states by way of their gradual cessation. Who enters it, and who does not enter it? All worldlings, stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners and arahants who are bare-insight practitioners do not enter it. But non-returners and arahants who have obtained the eight attainments do enter it. For it is said: 'Through being endowed with two powers, through the pacification of three formations, with sixteen courses of knowledge, with nine courses of concentration, by mastery, wisdom is the knowledge of the attainment of cessation' (Paṭis. Ma. Mātikā 1.34). And this accomplishment does not exist for others apart from those non-returners and arahants who have obtained the eight attainments. Therefore, only they enter it, not others.

869. Katamāni panettha dve balāni…pe… katamā vasībhāvatāti? Na ettha kiñci amhehi vattabbaṃ atthi. Sabbamidaṃ etassa uddesassa niddese vuttameva. Yathāha –

869. What, here, are the two powers… and what is mastery? There is nothing for us to say on this matter; all this has already been stated in the explanation of this summary. As it is said:

“Dvīhi [M 2.0345] balehīti dve balāni samathabalaṃ vipassanābalaṃ. Katamaṃ samathabalaṃ? Nekkhammavasena cittassa ekaggatā avikkhepo samathabalaṃ. Abyāpādavasena… ālokasaññāvasena… avikkhepavasena…pe… paṭinissaggānupassiassāsavasena… paṭinissaggānupassipassāsavasena cittassa ekaggatā avikkhepo samathabalanti. Kenaṭṭhena samathabalaṃ? Paṭhamajjhānena nīvaraṇe na kampatīti samathabalaṃ. Dutiyajjhānena vitakkavicāre…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyā ākiñcaññāyatanasaññāya na kampatīti samathabalaṃ. Uddhacce ca uddhaccasahagatakilese ca khandhe ca na kampati na calati na vedhatīti samathabalaṃ. Idaṃ samathabalaṃ.

'By two powers' means the two powers: the power of serenity and the power of insight. What is the power of serenity? Unification of mind and non-distraction by way of renunciation is the power of serenity. By way of non-ill will... by way of the perception of light... by way of non-distraction... by way of contemplating relinquishment with inhalation... by way of contemplating relinquishment with exhalation, unification of mind and non-distraction is the power of serenity. In what sense is it the power of serenity? Through the first jhāna, the mind does not waver on account of the hindrances—this is the power of serenity. Through the second jhāna, on account of thought and examination... up to... through the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it does not waver on account of the perception of the base of nothingness—this is the power of serenity. It does not waver, shake, or tremble on account of restlessness, or on account of the defilements and aggregates associated with restlessness—this is the power of serenity. This is the power of serenity.

“Katamaṃ vipassanābalaṃ? Aniccānupassanā vipassanābalaṃ. Dukkhānupassanā… anattānupassanā… nibbidānupassanā… virāgānupassanā… nirodhānupassanā… paṭinissaggānupassanā vipassanābalaṃ. Rūpe aniccānupassanā…pe… rūpe paṭinissaggānupassanā vipassanābalaṃ. Vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe… cakkhusmiṃ…pe… jarāmaraṇe aniccānupassanā. Jarāmaraṇe paṭinissaggānupassanā vipassanābalanti. Kenaṭṭhena vipassanābalaṃ? Aniccānupassanāya niccasaññāya na kampatīti vipassanābalaṃ. Dukkhānupassanāya sukhasaññāya na kampatīti… anattānupassanāya attasaññāya na kampatīti… nibbidānupassanāya nandiyā na kampatīti… virāgānupassanāya rāge na kampatīti… nirodhānupassanāya samudaye na kampatīti… paṭinissaggānupassanāya ādāne na kampatīti vipassanābalaṃ. Avijjāya [V 2.0344] ca avijjāsahagatakilese ca khandhe ca na kampati na calati na vedhatīti vipassanābalaṃ. Idaṃ vipassanābalaṃ.

What is the power of insight? The contemplation of impermanence is the power of insight. The contemplation of suffering... the contemplation of non-self... the contemplation of disenchantment... the contemplation of dispassion... the contemplation of cessation... the contemplation of relinquishment is the power of insight. The contemplation of impermanence in form... up to... the contemplation of relinquishment in form is the power of insight. In feeling... in perception... in formations... in consciousness... in the eye... up to... in aging-and-death, the contemplation of impermanence... the contemplation of relinquishment in aging-and-death is the power of insight. In what sense is it the power of insight? Through the contemplation of impermanence, one is not shaken by the perception of permanence; therefore, it is the power of insight. Through the contemplation of suffering, one is not shaken by the perception of pleasure... Through the contemplation of non-self, one is not shaken by the perception of self... Through the contemplation of disenchantment, one is not shaken by delight... Through the contemplation of dispassion, one is not shaken by lust... Through the contemplation of cessation, one is not shaken by arising... Through the contemplation of relinquishment, one is not shaken by grasping; therefore, it is the power of insight. One is not shaken, does not move, and does not tremble on account of ignorance, the defilements associated with ignorance, and the aggregates; therefore, it is the power of insight. This is the power of insight.

“Tayo ca saṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyāti katamesaṃ tiṇṇannaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā? Dutiyajjhānaṃ samāpannassa vitakkavicārā vacīsaṅkhārā paṭippassaddhā honti. Catutthaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa assāsapassāsā kāyasaṅkhārā paṭippassaddhā honti. Saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca cittasaṅkhārā paṭippassaddhā honti. Imesaṃ tiṇṇannaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā.

‘By the stilling of the three formations’: by the stilling of which three formations? For one who has attained the second jhāna, the verbal formations—initial and sustained thought—are stilled. For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, the bodily formations—in-breathing and out-breathing—are stilled. For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, the mental formations—perception and feeling—are stilled. This is by the stilling of these three formations.

“Soḷasahi [M 2.0346] ñāṇacariyāhīti katamāhi soḷasahi ñāṇacariyāhi? Aniccānupassanā ñāṇacariyā. Dukkhā… anattā… nibbidā… virāgā… nirodhā… paṭinissaggā… vivaṭṭānupassanā ñāṇacariyā. Sotāpattimaggo ñāṇacariyā. Sotāpattiphalasamāpatti ñāṇacariyā. Sakadāgāmimaggo…pe… arahattaphalasamāpatti ñāṇacariyā. Imāhi soḷasahi ñāṇacariyāhi.

‘By sixteen courses of knowledge’: by which sixteen courses of knowledge? The contemplation of impermanence is a course of knowledge. The contemplation of suffering... of non-self... of disenchantment... of dispassion... of cessation... of relinquishment... the contemplation of turning away is a course of knowledge. The path of stream-entry is a course of knowledge. The fruition attainment of stream-entry is a course of knowledge. The path of the once-returner... up to... the fruition attainment of arahantship is a course of knowledge. By these sixteen courses of knowledge.

“Navahi samādhicariyāhīti katamāhi navahi samādhicariyāhi? Paṭhamajjhānaṃ samādhicariyā. Dutiyajjhānaṃ…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpatti samādhicariyā. Paṭhamajjhānapaṭilābhatthāya vitakko ca vicāro ca pīti ca sukhañca cittekaggatā ca…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ paṭilābhatthāya vitakko ca vicāro ca pīti ca sukhañca cittekaggatā ca. Imāhi navahi samādhicariyāhi.

‘By nine courses of concentration’: by which nine courses of concentration? The first jhāna is a course of concentration. The second jhāna... up to... the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a course of concentration. The initial thought, sustained thought, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind for the purpose of attaining the first jhāna are a course of concentration. By these nine courses of concentration.

“Vasīti pañca vasiyo – āvajjanavasī, samāpajjanavasī, adhiṭṭhānavasī, vuṭṭhānavasī, paccavekkhaṇavasī. Paṭhamajjhānaṃ yatthicchakaṃ yadicchakaṃ yāvaticchakaṃ āvajjati, āvajjanāya dandhāyitattaṃ natthīti āvajjanavasī. Paṭhamajjhānaṃ yatthicchakaṃ yadicchakaṃ yāvaticchakaṃ samāpajjati, samāpajjanāya dandhāyitattaṃ natthīti samāpajjanavasī…pe… adhiṭṭhāti adhiṭṭhāne…pe… vuṭṭhāti vuṭṭhāne…pe… paccavekkhati paccavekkhaṇāya dandhāyitattaṃ natthīti paccavekkhaṇavasī. Dutiyaṃ…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ yatthicchakaṃ yadicchakaṃ yāvaticchakaṃ āvajjati [V 2.0345] …pe… paccavekkhati. Paccavekkhaṇāya dandhāyitattaṃ natthīti paccavekkhaṇavasī. Imā pañca vasiyo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.83).

‘Mastery’: there are five masteries—mastery in adverting, mastery in attaining, mastery in resolving, mastery in emerging, and mastery in reviewing. One adverts to the first jhāna wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes; there being no sluggishness in adverting, it is mastery in adverting. One attains the first jhāna wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes; there being no sluggishness in attaining, it is mastery in attaining. One resolves on the first jhāna...; there being no sluggishness in resolving, it is mastery in resolving. One emerges from the first jhāna...; there being no sluggishness in emerging, it is mastery in emerging. One reviews the first jhāna...; there being no sluggishness in reviewing, it is mastery in reviewing. For the second jhāna... up to... the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one adverts wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes... and one reviews; there being no sluggishness in reviewing, it is mastery in reviewing. These are the five masteries.

870. Ettha ca “soḷasahi ñāṇacariyāhī”ti ukkaṭṭhaniddeso esa. Anāgāmino pana cuddasahi ñāṇacariyāhi hoti. Yadi evaṃ sakadāgāmino dvādasahi sotāpannassa ca dasahi kiṃ na hotīti? Na hoti, samādhipāribandhikassa pañca kāmaguṇikarāgassa appahīnattā. Tesaṃ hi so appahīno. Tasmā samathabalaṃ na paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ aparipūre dvīhi balehi samāpajjitabbaṃ nirodhasamāpattiṃ balavekallena samāpajjituṃ na sakkonti. Anāgāmissa pana so pahīno, tasmā esa paripuṇṇabalo [M 2.0347] hoti. Paripuṇṇabalattā sakkoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakusalaṃ phalasamāpattiyā anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.417). Idañhi paṭṭhāne mahāpakaraṇe anāgāminova nirodhā vuṭṭhānaṃ sandhāya vuttanti.

870. Herein, the expression ‘by sixteen courses of knowledge’ is a designation of the highest instance. For a non-returner, however, it occurs with fourteen courses of knowledge. If so, why does it not occur with twelve for a once-returner and ten for a stream-enterer? It does not, because the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure, which is an obstruction to concentration, has not been abandoned. For them, it is indeed not abandoned. Therefore, their power of serenity is not complete. When that is incomplete, they are unable, due to insufficient strength, to attain the cessation attainment, which must be entered with two powers. For the non-returner, however, that has been abandoned; therefore, their power is complete. Because their power is complete, they are able. Therefore, the Blessed One said: ‘For one emerging from cessation, the wholesome state of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for the fruition attainment by way of proximity condition.’ This was said in the Great Treatise, the Paṭṭhāna, with reference to the emergence from cessation of a non-returner.

871. Kattha samāpajjantīti pañcavokārabhave. Kasmā? Anupubbasamāpattisabbhāvato. Catuvokārabhave pana paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ uppatti natthi. Tasmā na sakkā tattha samāpajjitunti. Keci pana “vatthussa abhāvā”ti vadanti.

871. ‘Where do they attain it?’ In the five-constituent existence. Why? Because of the presence of the sequential attainments. In the four-constituent existence, however, there is no arising of the first jhāna and so on. Therefore, it cannot be attained there. Some, however, say it is due to the absence of a physical basis.

872. Kasmā samāpajjantīti saṅkhārānaṃ pavattibhede ukkaṇṭhitvā diṭṭheva dhamme acittakā hutvā “nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ patvā sukhaṃ viharissāmā”ti samāpajjanti.

872. ‘Why do they attain it?’ Having become weary of the diverse continuity of formations, and having become mindless in this very life, they attain it, thinking: ‘Having reached cessation, Nibbāna, we shall dwell in peace.’

873. Kathañcassā samāpajjanaṃ hotīti samathavipassanāvasena ussakkitvā katapubbakiccassa nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ nirodhayato, evamassa samāpajjanaṃ hoti. Yo hi samathavaseneva ussakkati, so nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiṃ patvā tiṭṭhati. Yo pana vipassanāvaseneva ussakkati, so phalasamāpattiṃ patvā tiṭṭhati. Yo pana ubhayavaseneva ussakkitvā pubbakiccaṃ katvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ nirodheti, so taṃ samāpajjatīti ayamettha saṅkhepo.

873. And how does his attainment occur? For one who has striven by means of serenity and insight, and has performed the preliminary duties, while causing the cessation of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—thus does his attainment occur. One who strives only by means of serenity reaches the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and remains there. But one who strives only by means of insight reaches fruition-attainment and remains there. But one who strives by means of both, having performed the preliminary duties and causing the cessation of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—such a one attains it. This is the summary here.

874. Ayaṃ pana vitthāro – idha bhikkhu nirodhaṃ samāpajjitukāmo katabhattakicco sudhotahatthapādo [V 2.0346] vivitte okāse supaññattamhi āsane nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā, so paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya tattha saṅkhāre aniccato dukkhato anattato vipassati.

874. Now, here is the detailed explanation: Here, a bhikkhu who wishes to attain cessation, having finished his meal, with hands and feet well-washed, sits down in a secluded place on a well-prepared seat. He folds his legs crosswise, sets his body erect, establishes mindfulness before him, and first attains the first jhāna. Upon emerging from that, he contemplates the formations therein as impermanent, as suffering, and as not-self.

Vipassanā panesā tividhā hoti – saṅkhāraparigaṇhanakavipassanā, phalasamāpattivipassanā, nirodhasamāpattivipassanāti. Tattha saṅkhāraparigaṇhanakavipassanā mandā vā hotu tikkhā vā, maggassa padaṭṭhānaṃ hotiyeva. Phalasamāpattivipassanā [M 2.0348] tikkhāva vaṭṭati maggabhāvanāsadisā. Nirodhasamāpattivipassanā pana nātimandanātitikkhā vaṭṭati. Tasmā esa nātimandāya nātitikkhāya vipassanāya te saṅkhāre vipassati.

This insight is of three kinds: insight that comprehends formations, insight for fruition-attainment, and insight for cessation-attainment. Among these, the insight that comprehends formations, whether weak or sharp, serves as the basis for the path. The insight for fruition-attainment is suitable only when sharp, like the development of the path. The insight for cessation-attainment, however, is suitable when it is neither too weak nor too sharp. Therefore, he contemplates those formations with insight that is neither too weak nor too sharp.

Tato dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya tattha saṅkhāre tatheva vipassati. Tato tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ…pe… tato viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya tattha saṅkhāre tatheva vipassati. Tathā ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya catubbidhaṃ pubbakiccaṃ karoti – nānābaddhaavikopanaṃ, saṅghapaṭimānanaṃ, satthupakkosanaṃ, addhānaparicchedanti.

Then, he attains the second jhāna and, upon emerging, contemplates the formations therein just as before. Next, he attains the third jhāna... and so on... up to the base of infinite consciousness. Upon emerging, he contemplates the formations therein just as before. Similarly, after attaining the base of nothingness and emerging, he performs four preliminary duties: ensuring the non-disturbance of separate requisites, awaiting the Saṅgha, the Teacher’s summons, and determining the duration.

875. Tattha nānābaddhaavikopananti yaṃ iminā bhikkhunā saddhiṃ ekābaddhaṃ na hoti, nānābaddhaṃ hutvā ṭhitaṃ pattacīvaraṃ vā mañcapīṭhaṃ vā nivāsagehaṃ vā aññaṃ vā pana kiñci parikkhārajātaṃ, taṃ yathā na vikuppati, aggiudakavātacoraundūrādīnaṃ vasena na vinassati, evaṃ adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ.

875. Herein, “ensuring the non-disturbance of separate requisites” means that whatever is not attached to this bhikkhu, but stands apart—such as a bowl and robes, a bed and chair, a dwelling, or any other kind of requisite—should be resolved upon so that it is not disturbed, so that it is not destroyed by fire, water, wind, thieves, rats, and so on.

Tatridaṃ adhiṭṭhānavidhānaṃ “idañca idañca imasmiṃ sattāhabbhantare mā agginā jhāyatu, mā udakena vuyhatu, mā vātena viddhaṃsatu, mā corehi hariyatu, mā undūrādīhi khajjatū”ti. Evaṃ adhiṭṭhite taṃ sattāhaṃ tassa na koci parissayo hoti.

The method of resolution is as follows: “May this and that not be burned by fire, carried away by water, scattered by wind, stolen by thieves, or gnawed by rats and so on within these seven days.” When it is thus resolved, no danger will occur to it for those seven days.

Anadhiṭṭhahato pana aggiādīhi vinassati mahānāgattherassa viya. Thero kira mātuupāsikāya gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Upāsikā yāguṃ datvā āsanasālāya nisīdāpesi. Thero nirodhaṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdi. Tasmiṃ nisinne āsanasālāya agginā gahitāya sesabhikkhū attano attano nisinnāsanaṃ gahetvā palāyiṃsu. Gāmavāsikā sannipatitvā [V 2.0347] theraṃ disvā “alasasamaṇo”ti āhaṃsu. Aggi tiṇaveṇukaṭṭhāni jhāpetvā theraṃ parikkhipitvā aṭṭhāsi. Manussā ghaṭehi udakaṃ āharitvā nibbāpetvā chārikaṃ apanetvā paribhaṇḍaṃ katvā pupphāni vikiritvā namassamānā aṭṭhaṃsu. Thero paricchinnakālavasena vuṭṭhāya te disvā “pākaṭomhi jāto”ti vehāsaṃ uppatitvā piyaṅgudīpaṃ agamāsi. Idaṃ nānābaddhaavikopanaṃ nāma.

But for one who does not make such a resolution, they may be destroyed by fire and so on, as in the case of the Elder Mahānāga. It is said that the elder entered his mother-laywoman's village for alms. The laywoman offered him rice gruel and had him sit in the assembly hall. The elder attained cessation and sat there. While he was seated, the assembly hall caught fire, and the other bhikkhus grabbed their own sitting mats and fled. The villagers gathered and, seeing the elder, said, “A lazy monk!” The fire burned the grass, bamboo, and wood, but it encircled the elder and stopped. People brought water in pots, extinguished the fire, cleared away the ashes, prepared the ground, scattered flowers, and stood paying homage. The elder, emerging at the predetermined time, saw them and, thinking “I have become conspicuous,” rose into the air and went to Piyaṅgu Island. This is what is called “ensuring the non-disturbance of separate requisites.”

Yaṃ ekābaddhaṃ hoti nivāsanapāvuraṇaṃ vā nisinnāsanaṃ vā, tattha visuṃ adhiṭṭhānakiccaṃ natthi. Samāpattivaseneva naṃ rakkhati āyasmato sañjīvassa viya[M 2.0349]. Vuttampi cetaṃ “āyasmato sañjīvassa samādhivipphārā iddhi, āyasmato sāriputtassa samādhivipphārā iddhī”ti.

Whatever is attached to one, whether it be the lower or upper robe, or the sitting cloth, there is no need for a separate act of resolution regarding it. The attainment itself protects it by its power, as in the case of the Venerable Sañjīva. For it has been said: “The psychic power of the Venerable Sañjīva was by the diffusion of concentration; the psychic power of the Venerable Sāriputta was by the diffusion of concentration.”

876. Saṅghapaṭimānananti saṅghassa paṭimānanaṃ udikkhanaṃ. Yāva eso bhikkhu āgacchati, tāva saṅghakammassa akaraṇanti attho. Ettha ca na paṭimānanaṃ etassa pubbakiccaṃ, paṭimānanāvajjanaṃ pana pubbakiccaṃ. Tasmā evaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ “sace mayi sattāhaṃ nirodhaṃ samāpajjitvā nisinne saṅgho uttikammādīsu kiñcideva kammaṃ kattukāmo hoti, yāva maṃ koci bhikkhu āgantvā na pakkosati, tāvadeva vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti. Evaṃ katvā samāpanno hi tasmiṃ samaye vuṭṭhātiyeva.

876. “Awaiting the Saṅgha” means awaiting or looking out for the Saṅgha. The meaning is that no formal act of the Saṅgha should be performed until this bhikkhu arrives. Here, the awaiting itself is not his preliminary duty, but advertence to the awaiting is the preliminary duty. Therefore, one should advert thus: “If, while I am sitting for seven days having entered the attainment of cessation, the Saṅgha wishes to perform any formal act, such as one initiated by a motion, and so on, I will emerge even before a bhikkhu comes and summons me.” Having done so, one who has entered the attainment will indeed emerge at that time.

Yo pana evaṃ na karoti, saṅgho ca sannipatitvā taṃ apassanto “asuko bhikkhu kuhi”nti “nirodhasamāpanno”ti vutte saṅgho kañci bhikkhuṃ peseti “gaccha naṃ saṅghassa vacanena pakkosāhī”ti. Athassa tena bhikkhunā savanūpacāre ṭhatvā “saṅgho taṃ āvuso paṭimānetī”ti vuttamatteva vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Evaṃ garukā hi saṅghassa āṇā nāma. Tasmā taṃ āvajjitvā yathā sayameva vuṭṭhāti, evaṃ samāpajjitabbaṃ.

But for one who does not do so—when the Saṅgha has gathered and, not seeing him, asks, “Where is such-and-such a bhikkhu?” and is told, “He has entered the attainment of cessation”—the Saṅgha sends a certain bhikkhu, saying, “Go, summon him in the Saṅgha’s name.” Then, when that bhikkhu stands within earshot and says, “The Saṅgha is waiting for you, friend,” his emergence occurs as soon as these words are spoken. For the Saṅgha’s command is indeed weighty. Therefore, having adverted to this, one should enter the attainment in such a way that one emerges on one’s own.

877. Satthupakkosananti idhāpi satthupakkosanāvajjanameva imassa kiccaṃ. Tasmā tampi evaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ “sace mayi sattāhaṃ nirodhaṃ samāpajjitvā nisinne satthā otiṇṇavatthusmiṃ sikkhāpadaṃ vā paññapeti, tathārūpāya vā atthuppattiyā dhammaṃ deseti, yāva maṃ [V 2.0348] koci āgantvā na pakkosati, tāvadeva vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti. Evaṃ katvā nisinno hi tasmiṃ samaye vuṭṭhātiyeva.

877. “The Teacher’s summons”: Here too, his duty is simply advertence to the Teacher’s summons. Therefore, one should advert thus: “If, while I am sitting having entered into cessation for seven days, the Teacher lays down a training rule concerning a matter that has arisen or teaches the Dhamma because of such an occurrence, I shall arise even before someone comes and summons me.” For one who has done so and is sitting will indeed arise at that time.

Yo pana evaṃ na karoti, satthā ca saṅghe sannipatite taṃ apassanto “asuko bhikkhu kuhi”nti “nirodhasamāpanno”ti vutte kañci bhikkhuṃ peseti “gaccha naṃ mama vacanena pakkosā”ti. Athassa tena bhikkhunā savanūpacāre ṭhatvā “satthā āyasmantaṃ āmantetī”ti vuttamatteva vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Evaṃ garukaṃ hi satthupakkosanaṃ, tasmā taṃ āvajjitvā yathā sayameva vuṭṭhāti, evaṃ samāpajjitabbaṃ.

But as for one who does not do so—when the Teacher, with the Saṅgha assembled, does not see him and asks, “Where is that bhikkhu?” and is told, “He has attained cessation”—he sends a bhikkhu, saying, “Go, summon him in my name.” Then, when that bhikkhu stands within earshot and says, “The Teacher summons the venerable one,” his arising occurs upon those very words being spoken. For the Teacher’s summons is indeed weighty. Therefore, having adverted to this, one should enter the attainment in such a way that one emerges on one’s own.

878. Addhānaparicchedoti jīvitaddhānassa paricchedo. Iminā bhikkhunā addhānaparicchede sukusalena bhavitabbaṃ. Attano “āyusaṅkhārā sattāhaṃ [M 2.0350] pavattissanti na pavattissantī”ti āvajjitvāva samāpajjitabbaṃ. Sace hi sattāhabbhantare nirujjhanake āyusaṅkhāre anāvajjitvāva samāpajjati, nāssa nirodhasamāpatti maraṇaṃ paṭibāhituṃ sakkoti. Antonirodhe maraṇassa natthitāya antarāva samāpattito vuṭṭhāti. Tasmā etaṃ āvajjitvāva samāpajjitabbaṃ. Avasesaṃ hi anāvajjitumpi vaṭṭati. Idaṃ pana āvajjitabbamevāti vuttaṃ.

878. “Determining the duration” is the determination of the duration of life. This bhikkhu must be very skilled in determining the duration. He should enter the attainment only after adverting, “Will my life-formations continue for seven days, or will they not?” For if he enters the attainment without adverting to his life-formations that are liable to cease within seven days, his attainment of cessation will not be able to avert death. Since there is no death within cessation, he arises from the attainment in the interim. Therefore, one should enter the attainment only after adverting to this. For it is permissible not to advert to the rest, but this must indeed be adverted to—so it is said.

879. So evaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya imaṃ pubbakiccaṃ katvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjati. Athekaṃ vā dve vā cittavāre atikkamitvā acittako hoti, nirodhaṃ phusati. Kasmā panassa dvinnaṃ cittānaṃ uparicittāni na pavattantīti? Nirodhassa payogattā. Idañhi imassa bhikkhuno dve samathavipassanādhamme yuganaddhe katvā aṭṭha samāpattiārohanaṃ anupubbanirodhassa payogo, na nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyāti nirodhassa payogattā dvinnaṃ cittānaṃ upari na pavattanti.

879. Having attained the base of nothingness in this way, he emerges and performs this preliminary task, then attains the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. After one or two mind-moments pass, he becomes without mind and touches cessation. But why do no further minds arise for him after those two mind-moments? Because of the application for cessation. For this bhikkhu, having yoked together the two qualities of serenity and insight, this ascent through the eight attainments is an application for gradual cessation, not for the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Thus, because of the application for cessation, no further minds arise beyond those two mind-moments.

Yo pana bhikkhu ākiñcaññāyatanato vuṭṭhāya idaṃ pubbakiccaṃ akatvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjati, so parato acittako bhavituṃ na sakkoti, paṭinivattitvā puna ākiñcaññāyataneyeva patiṭṭhāti. Maggaṃ agatapubbapurisūpamā cettha vattabbā –

But if a bhikkhu, having emerged from the base of nothingness, attains the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception without performing this preliminary task, he cannot become without mind afterwards. Instead, he turns back and re-establishes himself in the base of nothingness. Here, the simile of a man who has never travelled that road before should be given.

Eko [V 2.0349] kira puriso ekaṃ maggaṃ agatapubbo antarā udakakandaraṃ vā gambhīraṃ udakacikkhallaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhapitaṃ caṇḍātapasantattapāsāṇaṃ vā āgamma taṃ nivāsanapāvuraṇaṃ asaṇṭhapetvāva kandaraṃ orūḷho parikkhāratemanabhayena punadeva tīre patiṭṭhāti. Pāsāṇaṃ akkamitvāpi santattapādo punadeva orabhāge patiṭṭhāti. Tattha yathā so puriso asaṇṭhapitanivāsanapāvuraṇattā kandaraṃ otiṇṇamattova, tattapāsāṇaṃ akkantamatto eva ca paṭinivattitvā oratova patiṭṭhāti, evaṃ yogāvacaropi pubbakiccassa akatattā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpannamattova paṭinivattitvā ākiñcaññāyatane patiṭṭhāti.

It is said that a man who had never traveled a certain path before came upon a water ravine or a deep, muddy mire. Without properly arranging his lower and upper garments, he descended into the ravine but, fearing his robes would get wet, returned to the bank. Or, having stepped onto a scorching hot stone, his foot was burned, and he retreated back to the near side. Just as that man, due to not having properly arranged his lower and upper garments, turned back and remained on the near side as soon as he descended into the ravine or stepped onto the hot stone, so too does the yogi, having failed to perform the preliminary task, revert and re-establish himself in the base of nothingness immediately upon attaining the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Yathā pana pubbepi taṃ maggaṃ gatapubbapuriso taṃ ṭhānaṃ āgamma ekaṃ sāṭakaṃ daḷhaṃ nivāsetvā aparaṃ hatthena gahetvā kandaraṃ uttaritvā tattapāsāṇaṃ [M 2.0351] vā akkantamattakameva karitvā parato gacchati, evamevaṃ katapubbakicco bhikkhu nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpajjitvāva parato acittako hutvā nirodhaṃ phusitvā viharati.

But just as a man who has traveled that path before, upon reaching that spot, firmly fastens one cloth, takes another in his hand, crosses the ravine, or merely takes a quick step onto the hot stone and then proceeds onward, so too does a bhikkhu who has performed the preliminary task. Immediately after attaining the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he becomes without mind, touches cessation, and dwells therein.

880. Kathaṃ ṭhānanti evaṃ samāpannāya panassā kālaparicchedavasena ceva antarāāyukkhayasaṅghapaṭimānanasatthupakkosanābhāvena ca ṭhānaṃ hoti.

880. How does it last? For this attainment, entered into thus, its duration is due to the determination of the time period and to the absence of the exhaustion of life in the interim, the Saṅgha's waiting, or the Teacher's summons.

881. Kathaṃ vuṭṭhānanti anāgāmissa anāgāmiphaluppattiyā, arahato arahattaphaluppattiyāti evaṃ dvedhā vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti.

881. How does emerging occur? For a non-returner, it is through the arising of the fruit of non-returning; for an arahant, it is through the arising of the fruit of arahantship. Thus, emerging occurs in these two ways.

882. Vuṭṭhitassa kiṃninnaṃ cittaṃ hotīti nibbānaninnaṃ. Vuttaṃ hetaṃ “saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhitassa kho, āvuso visākha, bhikkhuno vivekaninnaṃ cittaṃ hoti vivekapoṇaṃ vivekapabbhāra”nti (ma. ni. 1.464).

882. Toward what is the mind inclined after arising? It is inclined toward Nibbāna. For it was said: “Friend Visākha, when a bhikkhu arises from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, his mind inclines toward seclusion, leans toward seclusion, and slopes toward seclusion.”

883. Matassa ca samāpannassa ca ko visesoti ayampi attho sutte vuttoyeva. Yathāha – “yvāyaṃ, āvuso, mato kālaṅkato, tassa kāyasaṅkhārā niruddhā paṭippassaddhā, vacīsaṅkhārā… cittasaṅkhārā niruddhā paṭippassaddhā, āyu parikkhīṇo, usmā vūpasantā, indriyāni paribhinnāni. Yo cāyaṃ bhikkhu saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpanno, tassapi kāyasaṅkhārā [V 2.0350] niruddhā paṭippassaddhā, vacīsaṅkhārā… cittasaṅkhārā niruddhā paṭippassaddhā, āyu aparikkhīṇo, usmā avūpasantā, indriyāni aparibhinnānī”ti (ma. ni. 1.457).

883. What is the difference between one who is dead and one who has entered this attainment? This matter too is stated in the sutta. As it is said: “Friend, in the case of one who has died and passed away, their bodily formations have ceased and subsided, their verbal formations... their mental formations have ceased and subsided, their life is exhausted, their warmth has subsided, and their faculties are broken up. But in the case of a bhikkhu who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, their bodily formations have also ceased and subsided, their verbal formations... their mental formations have ceased and subsided, yet their life is not exhausted, their warmth has not subsided, and their faculties are not broken up.”

884. Nirodhasamāpatti saṅkhatātiādipucchāyaṃ pana saṅkhatātipi asaṅkhatātipi lokiyātipi lokuttarātipi na vattabbā. Kasmā? Sabhāvato natthitāya. Yasmā panassā samāpajjantassa vasena samāpannā nāma hoti, tasmā nipphannāti vattuṃ vaṭṭati, no anipphannā.

884. As for the question, 'Is the attainment of cessation conditioned?' and so on, it should be said neither that it is conditioned, nor unconditioned, nor mundane, nor supramundane. Why? Because of its non-existence in terms of its own nature. However, since by virtue of the one who attains it, it comes to be called 'attained,' it is therefore fitting to say it is accomplished, not unaccomplished.

Iti santaṃ samāpattiṃ, imaṃ ariyanisevitaṃ;

Diṭṭheva dhamme nibbānamitisaṅkhaṃ upāgataṃ;

Bhāvetvā ariyaṃ paññaṃ, samāpajjanti paṇḍitā.

Thus, this peaceful attainment, frequented by the Noble Ones, has come to be reckoned as Nibbāna in this very life. Having developed noble wisdom, the wise attain it.

Yasmā tasmā imissāpi, samāpattisamatthatā;

Ariyamaggesu paññāya, ānisaṃsoti vuccatīti.

Therefore, the very capability for this attainment is also said to be a benefit of the wisdom in the Noble Paths.

Āhuneyyabhāvādisiddhikathā

The Discussion on the Accomplishment of Being Worthy of Offerings and So Forth

885. Āhuneyyabhāvādisiddhīti [M 2.0352] na kevalañca nirodhasamāpattiyā samāpajjanasamatthatāva, ayaṃ pana āhuneyyabhāvādisiddhipi imissā lokuttarapaññābhāvanāya ānisaṃsoti veditabbo. Avisesena hi catubbidhāyapi etissā bhāvitattā bhāvitapañño puggalo sadevakassa lokassa āhuneyyo hoti pāhuneyyo dakkhiṇeyyo añjalīkaraṇīyo anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa.

885. The accomplishment of being worthy of offerings and so forth: not only is the ability to attain the attainment of cessation a benefit, but this accomplishment of being worthy of offerings and so forth should also be understood as a benefit of developing this supramundane wisdom. For, without distinction, a person who has developed this fourfold wisdom becomes worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world with its gods.

886. Visesato panettha paṭhamamaggapaññaṃ tāva bhāvetvā mandāya vipassanāya āgato mudindriyopi sattakkhattuparamo nāma hoti, sattasugatibhave saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti. Majjhimāya vipassanāya āgato majjhimindriyo kolaṃkolo nāma hoti, dve vā tīṇi vā kulāni [V 2.0351] sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti. Tikkhāya vipassanāya āgato tikkhindriyo ekabījī nāma hoti, ekaññeva mānusakaṃ bhavaṃ nibbattetvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti.

886. Specifically, in this regard, one who has developed the wisdom of the first path, having come by way of dull insight and possessing dull faculties, is called a 'seven-times-at-most' one; having wandered through seven happy existences, he makes an end of suffering. One who has come by way of middling insight and possessing middling faculties is called a 'family-to-family' one; having run on and wandered through two or three families, he makes an end of suffering. One who has come by way of sharp insight and possessing sharp faculties is called a 'one-seed' one; having brought about only one human existence, he makes an end of suffering.

887. Dutiyamaggapaññaṃ bhāvetvā sakadāgāmī nāma hoti, sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti.

887. Having developed the wisdom of the second path, he becomes one called a once-returner. Having come to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering.

888. Tatiyamaggapaññaṃ bhāvetvā anāgāmī nāma hoti. So indriyavemattatāvasena antarāparinibbāyī, upahaccaparinibbāyī, asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmīti pañcadhā. Idha vihāyaniṭṭho hoti. Tattha antarāparinibbāyīti yattha katthaci suddhāvāsabhave upapajjitvā āyuvemajjhaṃ appatvāva parinibbāyati. Upahaccaparinibbāyīti āyuvemajjhaṃ atikkamitvā parinibbāyati. Asaṅkhāraparinibbāyīti asaṅkhārena appayogena uparimaggaṃ nibbatteti. Sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyīti sasaṅkhārena sappayogena uparimaggaṃ nibbatteti. Uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmīti yatthupapanno, tato uddhaṃ yāva akaniṭṭhabhavā āruyha tattha parinibbāyati.

888. Having developed the wisdom of the third path, he becomes one called a non-returner. According to the diversity of faculties, he is of five kinds: one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī), one who attains final Nibbāna upon landing (upahaccaparinibbāyī), one who attains final Nibbāna without prompting (asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), one who attains final Nibbāna with prompting (sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī), and one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsoto akaniṭṭhagāmī). He is one who makes an end by abandoning this world. Therein, the 'one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval' is one who, having been reborn in some Pure Abode, attains final Nibbāna without reaching the midpoint of the lifespan. The 'one who attains final Nibbāna upon landing' is one who attains final Nibbāna after passing the midpoint of the lifespan. The 'one who attains final Nibbāna without prompting' is one who produces the higher path without prompting, without exertion. The 'one who attains final Nibbāna with prompting' is one who produces the higher path with prompting, with exertion. The 'one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm' is one who, from where he has been reborn, ascends up to the Akaniṭṭha existence and there attains final Nibbāna.

889. Catutthamaggapaññaṃ bhāvetvā koci saddhāvimutto hoti, koci paññāvimutto hoti, koci ubhatobhāgavimutto hoti, koci tevijjo, koci chaḷabhiñño, koci paṭisambhidappabhedappatto mahākhīṇāsavo. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “maggakkhaṇe panesa taṃ jaṭaṃ vijaṭeti nāma[M 2.0353]. Phalakkhaṇe vijaṭitajaṭo sadevakassa lokassa aggadakkhiṇeyyo hotī”ti.

889. Having developed the wisdom of the fourth path, someone becomes one liberated by faith, someone one liberated by wisdom, someone one liberated in both ways, someone a possessor of the three true knowledges, someone a possessor of the six direct knowledges, or someone a great one whose cankers are destroyed who has reached the diversity of the analytical knowledges. It is with reference to him that it was said: 'At the moment of the path, he is called one who disentangles this tangle. At the moment of fruition, he has disentangled the tangle and is the foremost one worthy of gifts in the world with its gods.'

Evaṃ anekānisaṃsā, ariyapaññāya bhāvanā;

Yasmā tasmā kareyyātha, ratiṃ tattha vicakkhaṇo.

Thus the development of noble wisdom has many benefits; therefore a discerning person should take delight in it.

890. Ettāvatā ca –

890. And thus far –

Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ;

Ātāpī nipako bhikkhu, so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭanti. –

“A wise man, established in virtue, developing mind and wisdom, an ardent, discerning bhikkhu, can disentangle this tangle.” –

Imissā [V 2.0352] gāthāya sīlasamādhipaññāmukhena desite visuddhimagge sānisaṃsā paññābhāvanā paridīpitā hotīti.

In the Path of Purification, which is taught by way of virtue, concentration, and wisdom as expressed in this verse, the development of wisdom with its benefits has thus been fully elucidated.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus, in the Path of Purification, made for the delight of good people,

Paññābhāvanādhikāre

In the Section on the Development of Wisdom,

Paññābhāvanānisaṃsaniddeso nāma

Is the chapter named the Exposition of the Benefits of the Development of Wisdom,

Tevīsatimo paricchedo.

The Twenty-Third Chapter.

Nigamanakathā

The Concluding Account

891. Ettāvatā [M 2.0354] ca –

891. And thus far –

“Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ;

Ātāpī nipako bhikkhu, so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭa”nti. –

“A wise man, established in virtue, developing mind and wisdom, an ardent, discerning bhikkhu, can disentangle this tangle.” –

Imaṃ gāthaṃ nikkhipitvā yadavocumha –

Having set down this verse, what we said was:

“Imissā dāni gāthāya, kathitāya mahesinā;

Vaṇṇayanto yathābhūtaṃ, atthaṃ sīlādibhedanaṃ.

“Now, explaining as it truly is the meaning of this verse spoken by the Great Seer, with its divisions of virtue and so on...

“Sudullabhaṃ labhitvāna, pabbajjaṃ jinasāsane;

Sīlādisaṅgahaṃ khemaṃ, ujuṃ maggaṃ visuddhiyā.

“Having gained the going-forth, so very hard to gain, in the Dispensation of the Conqueror; the secure, straight path to purity, comprised of virtue and so on...

“Yathābhūtaṃ ajānantā, suddhikāmāpi ye idha;

Visuddhiṃ nādhigacchanti, vāyamantāpi yogino.

“Those yogis here who, though desiring purity, do not know it as it really is, fail to attain purity even though they strive.

“Tesaṃ [V 2.0353] pāmojjakaraṇaṃ, suvisuddhavinicchayaṃ;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, desanānayanissitaṃ.

“Causing delight for them, with its completely pure decisions, relying on the teaching method of the dwellers in the Great Monastery...

“Visuddhimaggaṃ bhāsissaṃ, taṃ me sakkacca bhāsato;

Visuddhikāmā sabbepi, nisāmayatha sādhavo”ti.

“I shall speak the Path of Purification; so let all you good people who desire purity listen attentively to me as I speak.”

Svāyaṃ bhāsito hoti.

That very Path of Purification has now been spoken.

892. Tattha ca –

892. And therein:

Tesaṃ sīlādibhedānaṃ, atthānaṃ yo vinicchayo;

Pañcannampi nikāyānaṃ, vutto aṭṭhakathānaye.

The decision on the meaning of those divisions, such as virtue and so on, has been stated according to the method of the commentaries to the five Nikāyas.

Samāharitvā taṃ sabbaṃ, yebhuyyena sanicchayo;

Sabbasaṅkaradosehi, mutto yasmā pakāsito.

Since, having brought all that together, it has been for the most part explained with its decisions, freed from all faults of confusion,

Tasmā visuddhikāmehi, suddhapaññehi yogihi;

Visuddhimagge etasmiṃ, karaṇīyova ādaroti.

Therefore, by yogis of pure understanding who desire purification, respect should be shown for this Path of Purification.

893.

893.

Vibhajjavādiseṭṭhānaṃ[M 2.0355], theriyānaṃ yasassinaṃ;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, vaṃsajassa vibhāvino.

Of the discerning descendant of the dwellers in the Great Monastery, the best of the Analysts, the glorious Elders,

Bhadantasaṅghapālassa, sucisallekhavuttino;

Vinayācārayuttassa, yuttassa paṭipattiyaṃ.

Of the venerable Saṅghapāla, of pure and austere life, endowed with the discipline and good conduct, devoted to the practice;

Khantisoraccamettādi-guṇabhūsitacetaso;

Ajjhesanaṃ gahetvāna, karontena imaṃ mayā.

Having accepted the request of him whose mind is adorned with the virtues of patience, gentleness, loving-kindness, and so on, this was composed by me.

Saddhammaṭṭhitikāmena[V 2.0354], yo patto puññasañcayo;

Tassa tejena sabbepi, sukhamedhantu pāṇino.

By the store of merit I have acquired by doing this, out of a desire for the True Dhamma's long endurance, by the power of that merit, may all beings grow in happiness.

894.

894.

Visuddhimaggo eso ca, antarāyaṃ vinā idha;

Niṭṭhito aṭṭhapaññāsa-bhāṇavārāya pāḷiyā.

This Path of Purification, free from obstacles here, is completed in fifty-eight recitation portions of the Pāli.

Yathā tatheva lokassa, sabbe kalyāṇanissitā;

Anantarāyā ijjhantu, sīghaṃ sīghaṃ manorathāti.

Likewise, may all aspirations of the world, grounded in goodness, succeed without obstacle, swiftly, swiftly.

895. Parama visuddha saddhā buddhi vīriya paṭimaṇḍitena sīlācārajjava maddavādiguṇasamudayasamuditena sakasamaya samayantaragahanajjhogāhaṇasamatthena paññāveyyattiyasamannāgatena tipiṭakapariyattibhede sāṭṭhakathe satthusāsane appaṭihatañāṇappabhāvena mahāveyyākaraṇena karaṇasampattijanitasukhaviniggatamadhurodāravacanalāvaṇṇayuttena yuttamuttavādinā vādīvarena mahākavinā chaḷabhiññāpaṭisambhidādi bhedaguṇapaṭimaṇḍite uttarimanussadhamme appaṭihatabuddhīnaṃ theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ therānaṃ mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ vaṃsālaṅkārabhūtena vipulavisuddhabuddhinā buddhaghosoti garūhi gahitanāmadheyyena therena mudantakhedakavattabbena kato visuddhimaggo nāma.

895. The Path of Purification has been composed by the Elder whose name, Buddhaghosa, was given by his preceptors, a native of Morandakheṭaka; who is of vast and pure wisdom, an adornment to the lineage of the Elders dwelling in the Great Monastery—the lamps of the Elder's lineage, of unhindered intellect in states surpassing the human; adorned with the qualities of the sixfold higher knowledge, analytical knowledges, and so forth; a great poet, the foremost debater, speaking what is logical and excellent; endowed with the charm of sweet and noble speech issuing forth from the bliss born of the perfection of the vocal organ; a great grammarian with unhindered power of knowledge in the Teacher's Dispensation, which is divided into the Tipiṭaka and its commentaries; endowed with skill in wisdom; capable of penetrating the depths of his own school and other schools; endowed with the aggregate of virtues such as morality, good conduct, straightforwardness, gentleness, and so forth; and adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy.

896.

896.

Tāva tiṭṭhatu lokasmiṃ, lokanittharaṇesinaṃ;

Dassento kulaputtānaṃ, nayaṃ sīlādisuddhiyā.

May this treatise remain in the world for so long, showing the method for the purity of virtue and so forth to the sons of good family who seek liberation from the world.

Yāva [M 2.0356] buddhoti nāmampi, suddhacittassa tādino;

Lokamhi lokajeṭṭhassa, pavattati mahesinoti.

As long as even the name 'Buddha'—of the One with pure mind, the Such, the foremost in the world, the Great Seeker—persists and continues in the world.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya katā visuddhimaggakathā,

Thus, the discourse on the Path of Purification, made for the delight of good people,

Pāḷigaṇanāya pana sā aṭṭhapaññāsabhāṇavārā hotīti.

According to the Pāᄷi reckoning, it consists of fifty-eight recitation portions.

Visuddhimaggapakaraṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Treatise on the Path of Purification is finished.
